p3-50.y: In PI planning, which is part of SAFe, all teams plan the next program increment of several sprints together, agree objectives and map dependencies. Grooming, or refinement, is where we clarify stories, acceptance criteria and estimates. Each sprint then has planning, daily stand-ups, a demo and a retrospective. I take part in all of these in our engineering organisation of about 100 people.
p3-50.k: pi planning, safe, grooming, refinement, sprint demo, agile
x: We follow SAFe, the Scaled Agile Framework, because our engineering organisation is about 100 people across several teams, and the ceremonies work at two levels.

PI planning is the big-picture event. A program increment is several sprints, usually around ten weeks. All the teams plan it together: we look at the features coming up, agree each team's objectives, and map dependencies between teams, like one team needing an API from another before it can finish its feature. Risks are raised openly and someone owns each one. The output is a plan everyone has agreed, not one handed down.

Grooming, or backlog refinement, happens during the sprints. We take upcoming stories, clarify what they really mean with the product owner and BA, write clear acceptance criteria, split stories that are too big, and estimate them. In a GxP product, we also agree early what validation evidence each story needs.

Then each sprint has the usual ceremonies. Sprint planning, where we commit to stories based on our capacity. A daily stand-up to share progress and blockers. A sprint review or demo, where we show working software to the product owner and stakeholders and get feedback. And a retrospective, where we discuss what to improve in how we work.

I take part in all of these. Because I also coordinate release integration across [about 5] teams, PI planning is especially useful for me, as that's where I spot cross-team dependencies that could affect a release.

p3-51.q: I break stories into tasks and estimate relatively in story points, including testing, reviews, validation evidence and release work, not just coding; I call out unknowns and add spikes, and check commitments against past velocity.
i: Planning poker exposes different assumptions; discuss the high and low estimates.
Spikes timebox research to reduce uncertainty.

Re-estimate or split if a story grows.
f: Points vs hours?
Points measure relative complexity and avoid false precision; hours suit task-level tracking.
What if you're behind?
Say so early with options: cut scope, get help or move the date.
w: I give realistic estimates and flag risk early.
p3-51.y: I break the story into tasks and estimate in story points relative to similar past work. I include everything, not just coding: testing, reviews, validation evidence and release work, which matters a lot in GxP. If something is unclear, I call it out and suggest a short spike. Then I check the sprint commitment against our past velocity.
x: I estimate in story points, relative to similar work we've already done, because relative estimates are more reliable than guessing hours.

First, I make sure I understand the story and its acceptance criteria. Then I break it into tasks, which shows the real size and often reveals hidden work. The key is to estimate everything that "done" really needs, not just the coding: unit and integration tests, code review, database scripts, documentation, validation evidence, and release work. In a GxP product, testing and evidence can be as big as the coding itself, and leaving them out is the most common reason estimates are wrong.

Then I compare with similar stories from the past: is this bigger or smaller than that one? The team estimates together, for example with planning poker, and big differences are useful, because they usually mean someone knows something the others don't.

If there's real uncertainty, like a new library or an unclear integration, I say so openly and suggest a short time-boxed spike to investigate first, instead of pretending to know. For example, before adding the Rebex SFTP provider, a short spike against the vendor's test server made the actual estimate much more accurate.
Finally, we check the total sprint commitment against our past velocity, so we commit to what we can actually finish, rather than what we hope to finish.

p3-52.q: I clarify impact and deadlines with the product owner or lead, handle production and patient-safety issues first, then committed sprint goals, then improvements, communicate trade-offs openly and early, and automate repeated work so it stops being urgent.

p3-52.y: First I clarify the real impact and deadlines with the product owner or my lead. Production issues and anything that affects patient safety come first, then our committed sprint goals, then improvements. I explain the trade-offs openly and early, so nobody is surprised. And when the same urgent work keeps coming back, I automate it so it stops being urgent.
p3-52.k: prioritisation, urgent work, time management, hr
x: When everything seems urgent, my first step is to find out what's actually urgent, because often not everything is.

I clarify the real impact and the real deadlines with the product owner or my lead. Who is affected, how badly, and what happens if this waits a day? Then I prioritise in a clear order. Production issues, and anything that could affect patient safety or trial data, come first, because in a clinical system that's non-negotiable. Next come our committed sprint goals, because other teams and the release depend on them. Then improvements and nice-to-haves.

When something new and urgent comes in, I don't silently try to do everything. I explain the trade-off openly and early: "if I take this on, this other item will slip by two days. Which do you prefer?" That way the decision is made by the right person, with full information, and nobody gets surprised at the end of the sprint.

I also look at why things keep becoming urgent. If the same kind of urgent work keeps coming back, I automate it, so it stops being urgent. Our deployments are a good example. They used to take about 6 people and 6 hours every release, constantly pulling people off their work. By building the CIRT MCP server, they now take 1 person and about 2 hours, which removed a recurring fire drill for the whole team.

p3-53.q: I involve QA and validation early in refinement to agree testable acceptance criteria, provide test data, automated tests (Playwright, Cucumber) and clear release notes, fix defects quickly with root-cause explanations, and treat their sign-off as part of done, because in GxP it is.
i: Shared understanding: walk through features with QA before they test.

p3-53.y: I involve QA and validation early, in refinement, so we agree on testable acceptance criteria. I give them test data, automated tests and clear release notes, and I fix defects quickly with an explanation of the root cause. I treat their sign-off as part of done, because in a GxP product it really is.
x: I see QA and validation as partners, not as a gate at the end, and in a GxP product, their sign-off is genuinely part of being done.

I involve them early. In refinement, we agree on clear, testable acceptance criteria together, so there's no argument later about what the story was supposed to do. For bigger features, I walk them through the design, so they can plan tests in parallel with development instead of waiting for the code.

Then I make their work easier. I provide realistic test data, and I write automated tests where I can, unit and integration tests, plus Playwright and Cucumber end-to-end tests for key flows, which speed up regression. I write clear release notes saying exactly what changed, what to test, and any configuration or database changes.
When they find a defect, I fix it quickly and explain the root cause, not just the fix, so they can judge what else might be affected and what to retest. I never treat a bug report as criticism.

A good example is the CSV bulk import. I worked closely with QA from the start: we agreed the validation rules with the BA, QA built test files for every rule, and I wrote unit tests matching each one. When a time-zone bug of mine was found during formal verification, I owned it in stand-up and fixed it within a day. That kind of trust makes releases much smoother.

p3-54.q: Done means code reviewed and merged, unit and integration tests passing, SonarQube gate green, documentation and release notes updated, deployed and verified in the test environment with acceptance criteria met, and, in regulated work, validation evidence captured.
i: A shared DoD prevents "done but not really" work.
Includes non-functionals: logging, metrics, security checks.
Feature flags: done can mean deployed dark.
f: DoD vs acceptance criteria?
DoD applies to every story; acceptance criteria are specific to one story.
Who owns the DoD?
The team, agreed with the product owner and quality.
w: I care about finished, shippable work, not just coded work.
p3-54.y: For me, done means the code is reviewed and merged, unit and integration tests pass, the SonarQube gate is green, documentation and release notes are updated, and it is deployed and verified in the test environment against the acceptance criteria. In our regulated work, it also means the validation evidence is captured.
x: For me, a story is done only when it's genuinely ready to release, not just when the code works on my machine.

That means several things. The code is reviewed by at least one colleague and merged through a pull request. Unit tests and integration tests are written and passing, and the build pipeline is green, including the SonarQube quality gate, so coverage on new code, bugs and vulnerabilities all meet the standard. Any database changes have reviewed migration scripts, and any new configuration has been added for every environment. Documentation and release notes are updated, so QA, support and the release team know what changed. And the change is deployed to the test environment and verified against the acceptance criteria, ideally with the product owner seeing it in the sprint demo.

In our regulated work, there's one more important part: validation evidence. The test results and traceability to the requirement must be captured, because in a GxP product, if it isn't documented, it effectively didn't happen.

I'm strict about this because "almost done" work causes problems later, usually right before a release. I learned that from a release where a missing configuration setting caused errors in UAT. Since then, "configuration added for every environment" has been an explicit item in our definition of done and our release checklist.

The first is strong .NET backend and API engineering across the whole lifecycle. p4-5.k: technical decision, csv import, trade-off, story
x: A decision I'm proud of was the design of our CSV bulk import for clinical study data. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles.

The situation was that study teams wanted to upload large CSV files instead of entering data one record at a time. The key choice was: if some rows are bad, do we save the good rows, a partial import, or nothing at all?

I owned the design, so I weighed both options. Partial imports feel friendlier, but in a GxP system they leave a study half-configured, they make rollback and the audit trail messy, and users have to work out what got saved. All-or-nothing is safer, but frustrating if users only find errors at the end.

So I proposed a two-step design: first a validate-only preview that checks every row and shows all errors with row numbers, and then an all-or-nothing save in one transaction, but only once the file is clean. I walked the BA and the QA lead through the trade-off and we agreed on it.

The result: it's live in production, users fix every error before saving, and we've never had a half-imported study. I learned that the best decision often combines both options. I can go into the technical design too.

The situation was that all our vendor file transfers were tied to one SFTP library, ComponentPro. In [2024] a depot vendor hardened their server security, and our connection broke. Because the library calls were spread across the code, switching libraries was risky.
My task was to fix it, and to make sure a library change would never touch business code again.

I introduced a common ISftpClient interface for connect, upload, download and list, with a factory that picks the provider for each vendor from configuration. I added a base class for the shared parts like retries, timeouts and logging. Then I implemented three providers behind it, ComponentPro, SSH.NET and Rebex, and moved vendors over one at a time by configuration, verifying each one in UAT first.
The result was that Rebex went to production with [no failed transfers caused by the switch], no business code changed, and a future library change is now one class plus a config entry.
It's a nice real example of the open-closed principle and the strategy pattern.

p4-17.q: The four OOP principles are encapsulation (bundle data with behaviour and hide state), abstraction (expose what, hide how), inheritance (reuse via is-a) and polymorphism (one interface, many implementations). Together they let us hide details, define contracts and swap behaviour, as with ISftpClient and three providers.
i: Modern C# favours composition and interfaces over deep inheritance.
SOLID builds on these principles.
Example map: Shipment.MarkDelivered (encapsulation), ISftpClient (abstraction/polymorphism), SftpClientBase (inheritance).
Interview tip: give one example per principle from your own code, not textbook animals and shapes.
f: Which is most important?
Encapsulation, because it protects invariants.
Is C# purely OOP?
No, it's multi-paradigm with strong functional features (LINQ, records, pattern matching).
p4-17.y: The four main OOP principles are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism. Encapsulation hides data behind methods, abstraction shows only what is needed, inheritance reuses behaviour from a base class, and polymorphism lets one interface have many implementations. In my SFTP component, all libraries implement one interface, which uses abstraction and polymorphism together.
p4-17.k: oop, object oriented programming, four pillars, principles
x: The four main OOP principles are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.

Encapsulation means an object keeps its data private and changes it only through its own methods, so it protects its rules. Abstraction means exposing what something does and hiding how it does it, usually through an interface. Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend the behaviour of a base class. And polymorphism means one interface, many implementations, where the right method is chosen at runtime.

They work best together. In my SFTP integration component, business code depends on an ISftpClient interface, which is abstraction. Three providers, ComponentPro, SSH.NET and Rebex, implement it, which is polymorphism, since the caller just calls UploadAsync and configuration decides which one runs. They inherit shared retry and logging logic from a base class, which is inheritance. And each provider keeps its connection details private, which is encapsulation.
In practice I prefer composition over deep inheritance trees. I can go deeper into any of the four.

p4-18.q: Encapsulation bundles data with the methods that change it and hides internal state behind a controlled public surface, so invariants can't be broken. A Shipment exposes MarkDelivered() which checks the current status and sets the delivery time, instead of a public settable Status.
i: Private setters, readonly fields, and validation in methods.
Rich domain models vs anemic models (data bags with logic elsewhere).
Expose collections as IReadOnlyCollection.
f: Encapsulation vs abstraction?
Encapsulation hides state and protects it; abstraction hides complexity behind a simple contract.
Can EF Core map private setters?
Yes, it uses backing fields.
p4-18.y: Encapsulation means keeping an object's data private and allowing changes only through its methods, so the object protects its own rules. For example, a Shipment class doesn't let anyone set the status directly. It has methods like MarkDispatched that check the change is allowed. This keeps the data valid and makes the code safer to change.
p4-18.k: encapsulation, oop, private fields, data hiding
x: Encapsulation means bundling an object's data with the methods that change it, and hiding the internal state, so the object can protect its own rules.

In C# that means private fields, properties with private setters where needed, and public methods that enforce business rules. The outside world can only ask the object to do something; it can't put it into an invalid state directly. The benefit is that the rules live in one place, so the data stays valid and the code is safer to change later, because callers don't depend on the internals.

A real example is a shipment in our system. Instead of a public Status property anyone can set, the Shipment class has methods like MarkDispatched and MarkDelivered. MarkDelivered checks that the shipment was actually dispatched first, and records the time. If someone tries to deliver a cancelled shipment, it throws a clear domain exception. In a GxP system that's important, because every state change must be valid and auditable.
I can explain how this relates to rich versus anaemic domain models if that helps.

p4-19.q: Inheritance lets a class derive from a base class to reuse and extend its behaviour (is-a). SftpClientBase holds retry and logging, and each provider class inherits it and implements library-specific calls. I prefer composition when the relationship isn't truly is-a or behaviour varies independently.
i: C# supports single class inheritance and multiple interface implementation.
Template method pattern: base defines the algorithm, subclasses fill steps.
Fragile base class problem: base changes break subclasses.
Default interface methods (C# 8) add some shared behaviour to interfaces.
f: Why no multiple inheritance?
To avoid the diamond problem; interfaces give the flexibility instead.
Abstract class vs interface?
Abstract classes share code and state; interfaces define contracts and allow multiple implementation.
p4-19.y: Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend the behaviour of a base class, which is an "is-a" relationship. In C#, a class can inherit from only one class but implement many interfaces. I use it carefully, for real shared behaviour. For example, our SFTP providers inherit from a base class that has the common retry and logging logic.
p4-19.k: inheritance, oop, base class, derived class
x: Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend the behaviour of another class, called the base class. It models an "is-a" relationship; for example, a Rebex SFTP client is an SFTP client.

In C#, a class can inherit from only one base class, but it can implement many interfaces. The derived class gets the base members, can add its own, and can override virtual methods to change behaviour. It's powerful for sharing real code, but it creates tight coupling, because changes in the base class ripple into every child. Deep hierarchies also become hard to understand.

So I use it carefully. In our SFTP component, an abstract SftpClientBase class holds the common retry, timeout and logging logic, and each provider class inherits it and only implements the library-specific connect, upload and download. That removed a lot of duplication.
But when the relationship is really "has-a", or behaviour varies a lot, I prefer composition, injecting a collaborator instead of inheriting. I can talk about when I'd avoid inheritance if you like.

p4-20.q: Polymorphism means one interface, many implementations: the method that runs is chosen at runtime through virtual/override or interfaces, or at compile time through overloading and generics. Code calls ISftpClient.UploadAsync and the Rebex, SSH.NET or ComponentPro implementation runs.
i: Runtime dispatch uses virtual method tables; the JIT can devirtualize sealed or known types (and dynamic PGO helps).
Parametric polymorphism: generics.
Pattern matching offers an alternative for closed hierarchies.
Example: an INotifier interface with EmailNotifier and SmsNotifier; a loop over IEnumerable<INotifier> sends through all without knowing types.
f: Overloading vs overriding?
Overloading is compile-time by signature; overriding is runtime by actual type.
What is dynamic PGO?
Profile-guided optimisation at runtime, on by default since .NET 8, which can devirtualize hot calls.
p4-20.y: Polymorphism means one interface, many forms. The same method call behaves differently depending on the actual object. In C#, that's done with virtual and override, or with interfaces. For example, I call Upload on an ISftpClient, and depending on configuration it runs the Rebex, SSH.NET or ComponentPro version, without the calling code knowing which.
x: Polymorphism means "one interface, many forms". The same method call behaves differently depending on the actual object behind it.

In C# there are two kinds. Runtime polymorphism happens through virtual and override methods, or through interfaces: the method that runs is decided at runtime based on the real type of the object. Compile-time polymorphism is method overloading, where the compiler picks a method by its parameters. Runtime polymorphism is the important one for design, because it lets code depend on an abstraction and lets new behaviour plug in without changing the caller.

My real example is the SFTP integration. The business code calls UploadAsync on an ISftpClient. Depending on the vendor's configuration, the Rebex, SSH.NET or ComponentPro implementation runs, and the calling code has no idea which one. When we added Rebex, nothing in the callers changed.
It also makes testing easy, because in unit tests I just pass a mock that implements the same interface. I can explain how dependency injection uses this too.

p4-21.q: Abstraction exposes what something does and hides how; interfaces and abstract classes model the essential contract. Callers depend on ISftpClient without knowing any library details.
i: Good abstractions are small and stable; leaky abstractions expose implementation details (library exceptions).
We mapped provider exceptions to our own to avoid leaking.
Don't abstract too early; wait for a second implementation or a testing need.
Abstraction levels: repository hides SQL, ISftpClient hides libraries, the service layer hides workflow; each layer talks only to the one below.
f: What is a leaky abstraction?
One where callers must understand the hidden implementation to use it correctly.
Abstraction vs interface keyword?
Abstraction is the concept; interfaces are one way to express it.
p4-21.y: Abstraction means showing only what a user of a class needs and hiding the details. An interface like ISftpClient only exposes connect, upload and download, while each library deals with its own complex details inside. Callers work with the simple idea of a file transfer, which makes the code easier to use, test and change.
x: Abstraction means showing only what the user of a class needs to know, and hiding the complex details of how it works.

In C#, we usually express abstraction with interfaces and abstract classes. They describe the essential contract, the operations and their meaning, while the implementation details stay inside. It's slightly different from encapsulation: encapsulation is about protecting an object's data, while abstraction is about modelling a simple concept that hides complexity. Good abstractions make code easier to use, easier to test and easier to change.

For example, our ISftpClient interface only exposes a few things: connect, upload, download and list files. Behind it, each library deals with its own complexity, like different authentication APIs, key formats, timeouts and error types. Business code just thinks "send this file to the vendor", and doesn't care about any of that.

The trap is creating abstractions too early, or leaking details, like exposing library-specific exceptions through the interface. I mapped all provider errors to our own exception types to avoid that. I can show the interface design if useful.

p4-22.q: A class is the blueprint (type definition with fields, properties and methods); an object is an instance created from it at runtime with its own state on the heap. Many objects can come from one class.
i: Static members belong to the type, not instances.
Records and structs are also types; structs create values, not heap objects (unless boxed).
Object header holds sync block and method table pointer.
Records add value-based equality and with-expressions; structs are copied by value; classes are referenced.
f: Where are objects stored?
On the managed heap; references point to them.
What's a static class?
A class that can't be instantiated and holds only static members.
p4-22.y: A class is the blueprint, it defines the properties and methods. An object is an actual instance created from that class at runtime, with its own data in memory. For example, Shipment is the class, and each shipment loaded from the database is a separate object.
x: A class is the blueprint, and an object is an actual instance created from that blueprint.

The class defines the type: what data it holds through fields and properties, and what it can do through methods. It's written once in code. An object is created at runtime with new, it has its own copy of the data in memory, and you can create as many objects from one class as you need. Changing one object's data doesn't affect the others, unless they share static members, which belong to the class itself rather than to any one object.

For example, Shipment is a class in our code. It defines properties like ShipmentId, Status and Destination, and methods like MarkDispatched. When EF Core loads ten shipments from the database, it creates ten Shipment objects, each with its own id and status.
A simple analogy is the plan of a house versus actual houses built from that plan. I can also explain how classes differ from records and structs.

p4-23.q: Overloading is the same method name with different parameters in one class, resolved at compile time; overriding is a derived class replacing a virtual base method with the same signature, resolved at runtime by the actual object type.
i: Return type alone can't distinguish overloads.
Overload resolution picks the best match; optional parameters and params can create ambiguity.
Covariant return types (C# 9) let overrides return a more derived type.
Overload resolution happens at compile time on static types: passing an object-typed variable picks the object overload even if it holds a string.
f: Can you override a non-virtual method?
No; you can only hide it with new.
Can static methods be overridden?
No; static abstract interface members are a different feature for generic math.
p4-23.y: Overloading means the same method name with different parameters in the same class, and the compiler picks the right one at compile time. Overriding means a derived class provides its own version of a virtual method from the base class, and the right one is chosen at runtime based on the actual object. So overloading is compile-time, overriding is runtime polymorphism.
p4-23.k: overloading, overriding, polymorphism, compile time, runtime
x: Both let one method name have multiple versions, but they work at different times.

Overloading means having several methods with the same name but different parameters in the same class, for example a Log method that takes a string, and another that takes a string and an exception. The compiler picks the right one at compile time based on the arguments, so it's compile-time polymorphism. The return type alone isn't enough to overload.

Overriding means a derived class provides its own version of a virtual or abstract method from the base class, with the same signature. The decision is made at runtime, based on the actual object, even if you call it through a base-class reference. That's runtime polymorphism.

A real example: in our SFTP providers, the base class has a virtual method for building connection settings, and the Rebex provider overrides it to add its own key handling. Separately, we have overloaded upload methods, one taking a file path and one taking a stream.
I can also explain new versus override, which is a related trap.

p4-24.q: virtual in the base class marks a method as replaceable; override in the derived class supplies the new implementation, and a call through a base reference runs the override because dispatch uses the runtime type.
i: abstract methods are implicitly virtual and must be overridden.
base.Method() calls the base implementation from an override.
Calling virtual methods in constructors is risky: the derived override runs before the derived constructor finishes.
Virtual calls go through the method table (vtable); the JIT can devirtualize when the exact type is known, e.g. sealed classes.
f: Are methods virtual by default in C#?
No, unlike Java; you must mark them.
Why avoid virtual calls in constructors?
Derived fields may not be initialised yet.
p4-24.y: The virtual keyword on a base class method says derived classes are allowed to replace it. The override keyword in the derived class actually replaces it. Then even if I call the method through a base class reference, the derived version runs. Without virtual, the method can't be overridden.
x: The virtual keyword is used on a base-class method to say derived classes are allowed to replace it. The override keyword is used in the derived class to actually replace it.

When you call a virtual method, the runtime looks at the actual type of the object, not the type of the variable. So even if I hold the object through a base-class reference, the derived override runs. Without virtual, a method can't be overridden at all; C# methods are non-virtual by default, which is a deliberate design choice for performance and safety. An override can call the base version with base dot method name, and it can be marked sealed to stop further overriding.

In our SFTP component, the base class has a virtual method that builds connection options with sensible defaults. The Rebex provider overrides it, calls the base version first, and then adds its specific settings. That way the shared defaults live in one place.
Abstract methods are similar but have no body, so derived classes must override them. I can explain the difference between override and new as well.

p4-25.q: override replaces a virtual method so base-typed references call the derived version; new hides the base method (method hiding), so which runs depends on the declared reference type, a common source of bugs.
i: The compiler warns (CS0108) when hiding without new.
Hiding breaks polymorphism; use rarely, e.g. when a base library adds a conflicting member.
Real-world use: hiding happens accidentally when a base library adds a member with the same name; treat CS0108 as an error.
f: When is new useful?
To intentionally shadow a member you can't change, with a clear reason.
What does the CS0108 warning mean?
You're hiding an inherited member without saying new.
p4-25.y: Override replaces a virtual method, so the derived version runs even through a base reference. The new keyword hides the base method instead: if I call through a base reference, the base version runs, and through the derived reference, the new one runs. That's method hiding, and it is usually confusing, so I avoid it and treat that compiler warning as an error.
p4-25.k: new keyword, method hiding, override, inheritance
x: Override and new both put a method with the same name in a derived class, but they behave very differently.

Override replaces a virtual method. Whichever reference you use, base type or derived type, the derived version runs, because it's decided at runtime by the actual object. That's normal polymorphism. The new keyword hides the base method instead, which is called method hiding. Then the version that runs depends on the declared type of the variable: through a base-class reference the base version runs, and through a derived reference the new version runs. So the same object can behave differently depending on how you hold it.
That's confusing and a common source of bugs, so I avoid it. If you forget both keywords, the compiler warns you that you're hiding a member, and in our projects we treat warnings as errors in CI.
The only legitimate use I've seen is when a base class you don't control adds a member with the same name as yours. I can show a small code example if you like.

p4-26.q: A sealed class can't be inherited (string is sealed); a sealed override stops further overriding down the chain. I use it to express design intent and safety, and it lets the JIT devirtualize calls for a small performance gain.
i: Many analyzers (CA1852) suggest sealing internal types that aren't inherited.
Sealed records are common for DTOs and messages.
Sealing public library types is a compatibility decision.
Records can be sealed and their ToString can be sealed (C# 10) so derived records keep it.
f: Why is string sealed?
For immutability and security guarantees and performance.
Can you seal a method that isn't an override?
No, sealed applies to overrides only.
p4-26.y: A sealed class can't be inherited, which protects its design and can even let the runtime optimise calls. A sealed method is an override that stops further overriding in deeper classes. I seal classes by default when they aren't designed for inheritance, like most of our service classes.
x: A sealed class is a class that can't be inherited from. A sealed method is an override that can't be overridden again by classes further down the hierarchy.

Sealing communicates design intent: this class wasn't designed for extension, so nobody should depend on its internals by subclassing it. It also prevents subtle bugs where a subclass breaks the class's assumptions. There's a small performance benefit too, because the JIT can devirtualise calls on sealed types. The string class is a well-known example of a sealed class. A sealed method is useful when you've overridden something carefully and want to lock that behaviour down.

In our code, we seal classes by default when they aren't meant to be inherited, which is most service classes, handlers and DTOs, and some analyzers even suggest it. If later we really need extension, we usually add an interface rather than unsealing.
For example, our concrete SFTP providers are sealed, while the shared base class is abstract, so the hierarchy is exactly one level deep. I can explain how that keeps the design simple.

p4-27.q: The stack is per-thread LIFO memory for method frames, locals and value types, very fast and freed when the method returns; the heap is shared managed memory for objects (reference types), cleaned by the GC. Value types live where they're declared: inside a heap object's fields, they're on the heap.
i: Default stack size about 1 MB per thread (Windows main thread); deep recursion causes StackOverflowException, which can't be caught.
stackalloc and Span<T> allow stack buffers.
Large objects (85,000 bytes or more) go to the Large Object Heap.
Captured locals in lambdas or async methods move to heap objects.
f: Are structs always on the stack?
No; fields of a class, array elements, boxed values and captured variables live on the heap.
What is the LOH?
The Large Object Heap for objects of 85 KB or more, collected with Gen 2.
p4-27.y: The stack stores method calls and their local variables, it's very fast and is cleared automatically when the method returns. The heap stores objects created with new, which live until the garbage collector removes them. Reference types live on the heap, while value types live wherever they are declared, so a local int is on the stack but an int field of a class is on the heap.
p4-27.k: stack, heap, memory, value types, reference types
x: The stack and the heap are two areas of memory that .NET uses in different ways.

The stack is per thread. It stores method call frames: parameters, local variables and return addresses. It works last-in, first-out, so it's extremely fast, and the memory is freed automatically when a method returns. The heap is shared memory where objects created with new live, mostly reference types. Objects on the heap stay until the garbage collector finds nothing references them.

A common misconception is that value types always live on the stack. Actually, a value type lives where it's declared. A local int is on the stack, but an int field inside a class object is on the heap, as part of that object. And boxing moves a value type onto the heap.

In practice this matters for performance. Fewer heap allocations means less GC work. For example, when tuning CSV parsing, using Span of T to slice strings without allocating new ones reduced GC pressure noticeably. I can explain how the GC cleans up the heap if useful.

p4-28.q: Boxing wraps a value type in an object on the heap (int to object); unboxing casts it back to the exact type. Each box costs an allocation and GC work, so I avoid it with generics (List<int> instead of ArrayList) and by avoiding object parameters for value types.
i: Hidden boxing: string.Format with value types (older), interfaces on structs, non-generic collections, enums in some APIs.
Unboxing to the wrong type throws InvalidCastException.
Interpolated string handlers (C# 10) avoid boxing in many cases.
Generic constraints (where T : struct) and generic interfaces (IEquatable<T>) avoid boxing in comparisons.
f: How do you find boxing?
Allocation profilers or IL inspection (box instructions).
Does calling an interface method on a struct box?
Yes through an interface reference, but not with a constrained generic.
p4-28.y: Boxing is when a value type, like an int, is wrapped into an object on the heap, for example when you put it into an object variable or an old non-generic collection. Unboxing is getting the value back with a cast. It costs memory and time, so in hot code I avoid it by using generics, like List of int instead of ArrayList.
p4-28.k: boxing, unboxing, value types, performance, generics
x: Boxing is when a value type, like an int or a struct, is wrapped inside an object on the heap. Unboxing is extracting the value back out with an explicit cast.

Boxing happens implicitly, for example when you assign an int to an object variable, put it in an old non-generic collection like ArrayList, or call an interface method on a struct through the interface. Each box is a new heap allocation, and it creates extra work for the garbage collector. Unboxing needs a cast to the exact type, or you get an InvalidCastException.

In normal business code it rarely matters, but in hot paths, like processing thousands of CSV rows or logging in a tight loop, it adds up. The fix is generics: List of int instead of ArrayList, generic methods instead of object parameters, and structured logging templates, which avoid boxing in newer .NET versions.
So my rule is simply: use generic collections and APIs, and watch allocations in a profiler when performance matters. I can talk about how I measure allocations if helpful.

p4-29.q: IDisposable.Dispose releases unmanaged or expensive resources (connections, streams, SFTP sessions) deterministically. A using statement calls Dispose at the end of the block even on exceptions; a C# 8 using declaration disposes at the end of the enclosing scope; IAsyncDisposable with await using handles async cleanup.
i: Dispose pattern with a finalizer only when you directly own unmanaged handles; prefer SafeHandle.
Don't dispose objects you don't own (DI-injected services).
HttpClient: don't dispose per request; use IHttpClientFactory.
f: What happens if you forget Dispose?
Resources stay open until the GC finalizes them, if ever, causing leaks like connection pool exhaustion.
Dispose vs finalizer?
Dispose is deterministic and called by you; finalizers run non-deterministically on the GC thread.
p4-29.y: IDisposable is for objects that hold resources the garbage collector doesn't manage, like files, database connections or streams, and its Dispose method releases them. The using statement calls Dispose automatically at the end of the block, even if there's an exception. The newer using declaration does the same at the end of the current scope, with less nesting.
p4-29.k: idisposable, using statement, using declaration, dispose, resources
x: IDisposable is the interface for objects that hold resources the garbage collector doesn't manage, like file handles, database connections, network streams or SFTP sessions. Its Dispose method releases them deterministically, right away, instead of waiting for the GC.

The using statement is the safe way to call Dispose. You write using, create the object, and put the code in a block; Dispose is called automatically at the end of the block, even if an exception is thrown, because it compiles into try-finally. The newer using declaration, from C# 8, is just using var x equals something, without braces, and it disposes at the end of the current scope, which means less nesting. For async cleanup there's IAsyncDisposable with await using.

In our SFTP component, every connection is wrapped in a using, so sessions are always closed, even when a transfer fails halfway. With dependency injection, the container disposes scoped and transient services at the end of the request, so I don't dispose injected services myself.
I can explain the full dispose pattern with finalisers if needed.

p4-30.q: const is a compile-time constant, implicitly static and baked into calling assemblies; readonly is set at declaration or in the constructor, per instance; static readonly is set once per type at runtime, for values like objects or computed values that can't be const.
i: Changing a public const requires recompiling consumers; prefer static readonly for public values that might change.
readonly on a reference prevents reassignment, not mutation of the object.
readonly struct and readonly members prevent defensive copies.
Example: public const int MaxRows = 10000 in a library; changing it to 20000 doesn't affect already-compiled consumers until rebuilt.
f: Can const be a DateTime?
No, only primitive types, strings and enums (or null).
Is a readonly List immutable?
No, you can still add items; use ImmutableList or IReadOnlyList.
p4-30.y: A const is fixed at compile time and copied into any code that uses it, so it's only for values that never change, like pi. A readonly field is set once, in the declaration or constructor, and can differ per object. A static readonly is set once for the whole class at runtime. I use static readonly for things like configuration defaults, because changing a const needs every caller recompiled.
x: All three make a value unchangeable, but at different times and in different ways.

A const is a compile-time constant. It's implicitly static, and its value is copied into every assembly that uses it. So it must be a simple literal, like a number or string, and if you change it, every calling assembly needs recompiling, otherwise they keep the old value. A readonly field can be set only in its declaration or in the constructor, so each object can have a different value, decided at runtime. A static readonly field is set once for the whole type at runtime, and it can hold any object, like a TimeSpan, a Regex or a list.

My rule is: const only for values that are truly fixed forever, like a header name. Static readonly for shared defaults and objects, like a compiled Regex for validating study codes. Readonly for injected dependencies in constructors, which is the most common use in our services.
And for configuration that can change between environments, I use the Options pattern, not constants at all. Happy to explain that further.

p4-31.q: ref passes a variable by reference (must be initialised; callee may change it); out requires the callee to assign it (TryParse pattern); in passes by read-only reference, avoiding copies of large structs. C# 12 added ref readonly parameters.
i: Not allowed in async methods or iterators (ref locals limited; C# 13 relaxed some rules).
ref returns and ref locals for high-performance code.
Prefer returning tuples or records for multiple results in normal code.
ref struct types (like Span<T>) can only live on the stack, which is why they can't be used in async methods.
f: Why use in?
To avoid copying large structs without allowing changes.
out vs returning a tuple?
out fits the Try pattern; tuples are often clearer otherwise.
p4-31.y: These are ways to pass parameters by reference. ref means the variable must be set before the call and the method can change it. out means the method must set it, like in int.TryParse. in passes a read-only reference, which avoids copying large structs without letting the method change them.
p4-31.k: ref, out, in, parameters, by reference
x: ref, out and in are all ways to pass an argument by reference, instead of passing a copy.

With ref, the variable must be initialised before the call, and the method can read and change it, and the caller sees the change. With out, the method must assign a value before it returns, and the caller doesn't need to initialise it. The classic example is int.TryParse, which returns a bool for success and gives the parsed number through an out parameter. With in, you pass a read-only reference: the method can't change it, and the point is to avoid copying a large struct.

In everyday code I use out mostly for Try-pattern methods. For example, our CSV validator has a TryParseRow method that returns true or false and gives the parsed row as an out parameter, so we avoid exceptions for normal validation failures.
I use ref and in rarely, mostly in performance-sensitive code. Usually returning a result object or a tuple is clearer. I can show an example if useful.

p4-32.q: Nullable reference types (C# 8) make reference types non-nullable by default; string? marks a nullable one, and the compiler warns on possible null dereferences or assigning null. It catches NullReferenceExceptions at compile time; it's enabled by default in new projects.
i: It's compile-time analysis only; runtime can still have nulls (deserialization, reflection).
Attributes like [NotNullWhen(true)], [MaybeNull] help the analysis.
The null-forgiving operator ! silences warnings; use sparingly.
Turn warnings into errors (Nullable enable plus TreatWarningsAsErrors) for new code.
f: Does it change runtime behaviour?
No, only warnings and metadata.
How do you migrate a big codebase?
File by file with #nullable enable, starting with core models.
p4-32.y: Nullable reference types, turned on with a project setting, make the compiler warn me when a reference might be null and I use it without checking. I mark things that can be null with a question mark, like string question mark. It catches many NullReferenceException bugs at compile time. All our newer projects have it enabled.
p4-32.k: nullable reference types, null safety, null reference exception
x: Nullable reference types are a C# 8 feature that makes null-safety part of the type system.

Once you enable it in the project, a normal reference type like string means "should never be null", and you mark something that can be null with a question mark, like string question mark. The compiler then does flow analysis and warns you if you might dereference something that could be null without checking, or if you assign null to a non-nullable reference. It doesn't change runtime behaviour, but it moves a whole class of NullReferenceException bugs to compile time.

All our newer IRT projects have it enabled, and we treat the warnings seriously in code review. It also makes APIs self-documenting: if a method returns Shipment question mark, callers know they must handle the not-found case.
When enabling it on an older project, I do it file by file, so the team isn't hit with hundreds of warnings at once. I can talk about how we rolled it out.

p4-33.q: Pattern matching tests and deconstructs values concisely: type patterns with is, switch expressions, property patterns, relational and logical patterns (and, or, not) and list patterns (C# 11). It replaces long if/else chains with readable, compiler-checked logic.
i: Switch expressions warn on non-exhaustive matches.
is not null is the clearest null check.
Real use: switch expressions on ShipmentStatus to compute next allowed transitions, with the compiler warning on missing cases.
f: What is a discard?
_ matches anything without binding it.
Is pattern matching slower?
No, it compiles to efficient type checks and comparisons.
p4-33.y: Pattern matching lets me check the shape or type of a value and pull data out of it in one step, using is, switch expressions, property patterns and relational patterns. It makes branching code shorter and clearer. For example, I use a switch expression on shipment status to decide the next allowed status, and the compiler warns me if I miss a case.
p4-33.k: pattern matching, switch expression, is, c#
x: Pattern matching lets me test the shape or type of a value and extract data from it in a single, readable step.

In C# there are several forms. The is keyword with type patterns, like if x is Shipment s. Switch expressions, which return a value. Property patterns, which check properties, like a status equal to Dispatched. Relational patterns like greater than 10, logical patterns with and, or and not, and list patterns. It replaces long if-else chains and casting code, and the compiler can warn you if a switch doesn't cover every case.

In our code, for example, I use a switch expression on shipment status to decide the next allowed status, and a property pattern to calculate shipping priority, like express shipments first, then heavy ones, then the rest. It also helps when handling messages: a switch on the message type routes each event to the right handler.
It makes business rules much easier to read and review. I can write a small example if you like.

p4-34.q: Extension methods are static methods in a static class whose first parameter has this T, so they can be called as if they were instance methods; LINQ is built on them. We use them for things like service registration (services.AddSftpProviders()) and small helpers.
i: They can't access private members and lose to real instance methods with the same signature.
C# 14 adds extension members (extension blocks) including extension properties and static extensions.
Keep them discoverable and in clear namespaces.
f: Can you extend a sealed class?
Yes, extension methods work on any type.
What's new in C# 14?
Extension blocks that allow extension properties and static members.
p4-34.y: An extension method is a static method that looks like a method on an existing type, by using the this keyword on its first parameter. All of LINQ is built this way. I use them for small helpers, like a ToPagedResult method on IQueryable, and for clean service registration, like AddSftpClients on IServiceCollection.
x: An extension method is a static method that you can call as if it were an instance method on an existing type, without modifying that type.

You write it in a static class, and you put the this keyword before the first parameter, which is the type you're extending. Then it appears in IntelliSense on that type. It's resolved at compile time, so it can't access private members, and a real instance method with the same signature always wins. All of LINQ, like Where and Select, is built as extension methods on IEnumerable and IQueryable.

I use them for small, focused helpers. For example, a ToPagedResultAsync method on IQueryable, so every list API pages in the same way. And for clean dependency injection registration, like services.AddSftpProviders and app.UseCorrelationId, so Program.cs reads like a story instead of fifty lines of setup.
The rule I follow is not to overuse them for business logic, because it hides where behaviour lives. I can show how we organise registration extensions.

p4-35.q: An enum is a named set of integer constants such as enum ShipmentStatus { Created, Shipped, Delivered }, type-safe and readable. [Flags] enums combine values with bitwise operations (powers of two), and HasFlag or bitwise checks test them.
i: Default underlying type is int; any int can be cast, so validate input (Enum.IsDefined).
Serialize as strings for APIs with JsonStringEnumConverter to keep contracts stable.
Store as strings or ints in the database deliberately; adding values in the middle changes numbers.
f: Why assign explicit values?
So reordering doesn't change stored or serialized values.
Enum vs smart enum class?
Classes can carry behaviour and data; enums are simple constants.
p4-35.y: An enum is a set of named constants, backed by numbers, like ShipmentStatus with Created, Dispatched and Delivered. It makes code readable and type-safe compared with magic numbers. With the Flags attribute, values can be combined. I always validate enums coming from APIs, because any number can be cast into an enum.
x: An enum is a set of named constants backed by an integer type. For example, ShipmentStatus with Created, Dispatched, Delivered and Cancelled.

It makes code readable and type-safe compared with magic numbers or strings. The compiler stops you passing a random int where a ShipmentStatus is expected, and switch expressions can warn about missing cases. With the Flags attribute, values can be combined bitwise, like permissions. One thing to remember is that any integer can be cast to an enum, even if it isn't defined, so values coming from APIs or files must be validated, for example with Enum.IsDefined.

We also decide deliberately how to store them. EF Core stores enums as int by default, but for audit-friendly tables we sometimes store them as strings, so the data is readable, and so reordering the enum can't silently change meaning. In APIs we serialise them as strings with JsonStringEnumConverter.

And when an enum starts needing behaviour, like each status having its own rules about which next status is allowed, I replace it with a small class or a state machine, so the rules live in one place instead of being spread across switch statements.

p4-36.q: An async deadlock happens when code blocks on a Task (.Result, .Wait()) while a SynchronizationContext (WinForms, WPF, classic ASP.NET) needs that same blocked thread to run the continuation: each waits for the other forever. ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext, so it doesn't deadlock that way, but blocking still causes thread pool starvation.
i: Fix: async all the way; never block on async in request code.
Libraries use ConfigureAwait(false) to avoid capturing contexts.
If you must call async from sync (Main, legacy), GetAwaiter().GetResult() at the very top, knowing the risks.
Thread pool starvation symptoms: latency climbs, thread count grows slowly (about one thread per second injection beyond min).
f: Why does ASP.NET Core avoid the classic deadlock?
It has no request SynchronizationContext, so continuations run on any pool thread.
Is .Result ever fine?
After the task has completed (e.g. after WhenAll), it doesn't block.
p4-36.y: An async deadlock happens when code blocks on async work, like calling .Result or .Wait, in an environment with a synchronization context, such as old ASP.NET or a UI app. The blocked thread waits for the task, but the task needs that same thread to continue, so both wait forever. The fix is to use async all the way and never block on tasks.
p4-36.k: async deadlock, result, wait, synchronization context, async all the way
x: An async deadlock happens when code blocks on async work, for example by calling .Result or .Wait() on a task, in an environment that has a synchronization context.

In classic ASP.NET or desktop UI apps, the synchronization context means the continuation after an await must resume on the original thread. If that same thread is blocked waiting on .Result, the task can never finish, because it needs the thread that's waiting for it. So both wait forever. ASP.NET Core doesn't have that synchronization context, so you don't get this exact deadlock, but blocking still causes thread-pool starvation under load, where requests pile up and the API slows to a crawl.
The fix is async all the way: await instead of blocking, and make callers async too. In library code we use ConfigureAwait(false) so it's safe in any environment.
I've seen the starvation version in practice: an old helper that called .Result on an HTTP call caused timeouts under load, and making it async fixed it. I can explain how I spotted it.

p4-37.q: ConfigureAwait(false) tells await not to resume on the captured SynchronizationContext or TaskScheduler, so the continuation runs on a thread pool thread. It matters in libraries and UI apps to avoid deadlocks and context-switch overhead; in ASP.NET Core app code it makes little difference because there's no context.
i: Library authors should still use it because their code may run under UI contexts.
.NET 8 added ConfigureAwaitOptions (e.g. SuppressThrowing, ForceYielding) for Task.
After ConfigureAwait(false), don't touch UI elements or context-bound state.
Rule of thumb: in app code (ASP.NET Core) skip it; in reusable libraries use ConfigureAwait(false) on every await.
f: Does ConfigureAwait(false) make code faster in ASP.NET Core?
Negligibly; it's mainly about correctness in libraries.
What does ForceYielding do?
Forces the continuation to be queued asynchronously even if the task already completed.
p4-37.y: ConfigureAwait false tells an await that it doesn't need to continue on the original synchronization context, so it can continue on any thread pool thread. It avoids deadlocks and is slightly faster. ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, so in app code it doesn't matter, but in reusable libraries I still use ConfigureAwait false.
x: ConfigureAwait controls where the code after an await continues running. ConfigureAwait(false) says "I don't need to come back to the original synchronization context; any thread-pool thread is fine."

This matters in environments that have a synchronization context, like WinForms, WPF or classic ASP.NET. There, by default, the continuation is posted back to the original UI or request thread. That costs a context switch, and if someone blocks on the task with .Result, it can deadlock, because the thread the continuation needs is the one that's blocked. With ConfigureAwait(false), the continuation runs on the pool, so it's a bit faster and avoids that deadlock.

ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, so in application code like controllers and services it makes no practical difference, and we don't clutter our code with it. But in reusable libraries, which might be used from any kind of app, I still add ConfigureAwait(false) to every await. For example, our shared SFTP library does that.
The real fix for deadlocks is still async all the way. I can explain that in more detail if useful.

p4-38.q: LINQ (Language Integrated Query) gives one syntax to query collections, databases (EF Core) and XML using operators such as Where, Select, GroupBy, Join and OrderBy, in method or query syntax. Over IEnumerable it runs in memory with delegates; over IQueryable it builds expression trees that providers translate, e.g. to SQL.
i: Deferred execution: queries run when enumerated (foreach, ToList, Count).
Multiple enumeration re-executes the query; materialise once if reused.
.NET 9 added CountBy, AggregateBy and Index; .NET 6 added Chunk, MinBy, MaxBy, DistinctBy.
c:
var late = await db.Shipments
    .Where(s => s.Status == ShipmentStatus.InTransit && s.ExpectedAt < now)
    .OrderBy(s => s.ExpectedAt)
    .Select(s => new { s.Id, s.SiteId, s.ExpectedAt })
    .ToListAsync(ct);
f: Query vs method syntax?
Same result; query syntax compiles to method calls and can be clearer for joins.
What does CountBy do?
Groups by a key and returns counts without creating groups (.NET 9).
p4-38.y: LINQ is Language Integrated Query, a way to query collections and databases with C# methods like Where, Select, OrderBy and GroupBy. It works on in-memory collections and, through EF Core, gets translated into SQL. It makes data code short and readable. I use it every day, being careful about what runs in the database and what runs in memory.
p4-38.k: linq, query, where, select, ef core
x: LINQ stands for Language Integrated Query. It's a set of query operators built into C#, like Where, Select, OrderBy, GroupBy, Join, Any and Sum, that work the same way on many data sources.

Over in-memory collections, which are IEnumerable, LINQ runs as normal C# code using delegates. Over IQueryable, like an EF Core DbSet, it builds an expression tree that the provider translates into SQL, so the work happens in the database. You can write it with method syntax, which is most common, or query syntax that looks like SQL. Most operators use deferred execution, so the query only runs when you enumerate it or call ToList.

I use LINQ every day. The important skill is knowing where each part runs. For example, on our shipment search I make sure the filters and paging are translated to SQL, and I check the generated SQL in logs, so we don't accidentally pull thousands of rows into memory or trigger client-side evaluation.
LINQ makes data code short and readable. I can explain IEnumerable versus IQueryable in more detail.

p4-39.q: IEnumerable<T> gives forward-only iteration; ICollection<T> adds Count, Add, Remove and Contains; IList<T> adds index access and Insert. I accept the smallest interface a method needs and return read-only interfaces (IReadOnlyList, IReadOnlyCollection) to communicate intent.
i: IEnumerable may be lazy or infinite; Count() may enumerate everything.
IReadOnlyList<T> gives Count and indexing without mutation.
Arrays implement IList<T> but throw on Add.
Method parameters: accept IEnumerable<T> or IReadOnlyCollection<T>; return concrete or read-only interfaces based on what callers need.
f: Why return IReadOnlyList instead of List?
It prevents callers mutating internal state and documents intent.
Is IEnumerable always lazy?
No, it depends on the source; it's an abstraction, not a guarantee.
p4-39.y: IEnumerable only lets you loop over items. ICollection adds Count, Add and Remove. IList adds access by index, like item number five. So each one adds more abilities. For method parameters, I accept the simplest one I need, often IEnumerable or IReadOnlyCollection, which keeps the method flexible.
x: These three collection interfaces build on each other, each one adding more abilities.

IEnumerable is the simplest. It only lets you loop over items, forward only, and it supports deferred execution. ICollection adds Count, Add, Remove, Contains and Clear, so you know the size and can change the contents. IList adds access by index, like getting item number five, plus Insert and RemoveAt. There are also read-only versions, IReadOnlyCollection and IReadOnlyList, which give Count and indexing without allowing changes.

My rule for API design is: accept the smallest interface you need, and return the most useful read-only type. If a method only loops over items, it takes IEnumerable, so callers can pass a list, an array or a query. If it needs the count up front, it takes IReadOnlyCollection. And methods usually return IReadOnlyList, so callers can index but can't modify our internal list.
One caution: accepting IEnumerable and enumerating it twice can run an expensive query twice. I can explain that trap if useful.

p4-40.q: First returns the first match and throws if none; FirstOrDefault returns default (null) instead. Single requires exactly one match and throws if none or more than one; SingleOrDefault returns default if none but still throws if more than one.
i: Use Single when duplicates indicate a data bug; First when order matters (with OrderBy).
In SQL, First becomes TOP(1); Single becomes TOP(2) to detect duplicates.
.NET 6 added FirstOrDefault(defaultValue) overloads.
FindAsync by key checks the change tracker first.
f: Which is faster in EF Core?
First (TOP 1) reads less than Single (TOP 2), but pick by meaning.
FirstOrDefault on value types?
Returns default (0 for int), which may be ambiguous.
p4-40.y: First returns the first match and throws if there's none, while FirstOrDefault returns null or default instead. Single expects exactly one match and throws if there are none or more than one, and SingleOrDefault allows zero but still throws for more than one. I use Single when duplicates would be a bug, like finding by a unique code, and FirstOrDefault when nothing found is normal.
x: These four LINQ methods all return one element, but they behave differently when there are zero or multiple matches.

First returns the first matching element and throws if there's none. FirstOrDefault returns the first match, or the default value, which is null for reference types, if there's none. Single expects exactly one match: it throws if there are none, and also throws if there's more than one. SingleOrDefault allows zero, returning default, but still throws if there's more than one. In SQL terms, Single fetches up to two rows to check for duplicates, while First fetches one.

So the choice expresses intent. I use Single or SingleOrDefault when looking up by something that must be unique, like a study code or a kit number, because if duplicates exist, that's a data bug and I want to know about it immediately rather than silently picking one. I use FirstOrDefault when "not found" is normal, usually with an OrderBy so "first" is well-defined.
Using First without an order is a subtle bug, because the database can return rows in any order. I can give more examples if helpful.

p4-41.q: Any() stops at the first match and translates to EXISTS in SQL; Count() counts every matching row. Use Any() to check existence; on in-memory collections the Count property is already O(1), and LINQ Count() uses it when available.
i: Any() on IEnumerable without a predicate can use TryGetNonEnumeratedCount-like optimisations.
Count() > 0 is a common code smell (CA1827 analyzer).
In memory, LINQ Count() checks for ICollection<T> and uses .Count without enumerating.
For IQueryable, Count() becomes SELECT COUNT(*), which scans more rows than EXISTS.
f: What does EF Core generate for Any()?
SELECT CASE WHEN EXISTS (...) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END.
When use Count?
When you actually need the number.
p4-41.y: Any stops as soon as it finds one item, so it's the right way to check if something exists. Count goes through everything to count it, unless the collection already knows its count. In EF Core, Any becomes an EXISTS query, which is much cheaper than SELECT COUNT. So I use Any for existence checks.
x: Any and Count can both tell you whether there are items, but Any is the right tool for checking existence.

Any stops as soon as it finds one matching item, so it's cheap no matter how big the data is. Count has to go through every item to count them, unless the collection already knows its size. In EF Core, Any translates into an EXISTS query, which SQL Server can stop at the first row, while Count translates to SELECT COUNT, which has to count every matching row. On a big table that difference is huge.
Note that the Count property on a List or an array is different, it's already stored, so reading it is free. The issue is the Count method on queries and lazy sequences.

So in our code, a check like "does this study already have an active import" is written with AnyAsync, never CountAsync greater than zero. Code analyzers even flag that pattern now. I can explain how to verify the generated SQL if useful.

p4-42.q: A closure is a lambda that captures variables from its outer scope; the compiler moves them into a hidden class so they live as long as the lambda. Pitfalls include capturing a loop variable in older for loops, accidentally keeping large objects alive, and hidden allocations on hot paths.
i: foreach variables are per-iteration since C# 5; for loop variables are shared.
static lambdas (C# 9) prevent capture and allocations.
Captured variables are shared: changing them later changes what the lambda sees.
f: Do closures allocate?
Yes, a display class instance and a delegate, unless the lambda is static or captures nothing.
Why can closures cause memory leaks?
Long-lived delegates (event handlers) keep captured objects alive.
p4-42.y: A closure is a lambda or function that captures variables from the surrounding code and keeps using them later. C# does this by moving those variables into a hidden class. A classic bug is capturing a loop variable in old for loops and all lambdas seeing the last value. I also watch for closures accidentally keeping large objects alive.
x: A closure is a lambda or local function that captures variables from the code around it, and keeps using them even after that outer method has finished.

Under the hood, the C# compiler moves captured variables into a hidden class, and both the outer method and the lambda share that object. That's why the lambda sees the latest value of the variable, not a copy from when it was created. This is very useful, for example in LINQ filters that use a method parameter, or in callbacks.

There are two classic pitfalls. First, capturing a loop variable: in old C# a foreach loop shared one variable, so all the lambdas saw the last value. Modern C# fixed foreach, but a for loop index can still surprise you. Second, a closure can keep a large object alive longer than expected, for example an event handler lambda that captures a big service, which becomes a memory leak if it's never unsubscribed.
In performance-sensitive code, I also watch for closures allocating on every call, and use static lambdas where possible. I can show the loop-variable bug in code if you like.

p4-43.q: Liskov Substitution says subtypes must work anywhere the base type is expected without breaking correct behaviour. Every ISftpClient provider honours the same contract (same exceptions, same semantics for overwrite), so callers never special-case one; the classic violation is Square inheriting Rectangle and breaking width/height expectations.
i: Violations: throwing NotSupportedException in overrides, stronger preconditions, weaker postconditions.
ReadOnlyCollection implementing IList and throwing on Add is a known framework compromise.
Contract tests run the same test suite against every implementation.
Our provider contract tests ran the same suite (upload, list, overwrite, error mapping) against Rebex, SSH.NET and ComponentPro, enforcing LSP.
f: How do you test LSP?
Shared contract tests for all implementations of an interface.
What smell suggests an LSP break?
Callers checking concrete types with is or casts.
p4-43.y: Liskov says a derived class must work anywhere the base class is expected, without surprises. The classic violation is a Square inheriting from Rectangle, where setting width also changes height. In my SFTP component, every provider passes the same contract tests for upload, list, overwrite and errors, so any library can replace another safely.
x: The Liskov Substitution Principle says that objects of a derived type must work anywhere the base type is expected, without the caller getting surprises. A subtype can add behaviour, but it must keep the base type's promises.

The textbook violation is Square inheriting from Rectangle. If code sets the width of a rectangle and expects the height to stay the same, a Square breaks that expectation. A more realistic violation is a read-only repository that inherits a Save method and throws NotSupportedException. The fix there is to split the interface, not to throw.

In my SFTP component, Liskov was a real design goal. All three providers implement ISftpClient, and they must behave the same way for the caller: same behaviour when a file already exists, same timeout handling, and every failure surfaces as our own SftpTransferException, never a silent failure or a library-specific exception. I enforced that with a shared set of contract tests that every provider must pass.
That's why we could switch a vendor from ComponentPro to Rebex with only a configuration change. I can explain the contract tests if useful.

p4-44.q: Interface Segregation says clients shouldn't depend on methods they don't use. Instead of one large IShipmentRepository, we use IShipmentReader for queries and IShipmentWriter for commands, so a reporting service only gets read access and tests mock less.
i: Small, role-based interfaces; one class can implement several.
Fits CQRS read/write split.
Fat interfaces force empty implementations and change ripple.
Microsoft's own example: IReadOnlyList<T> separated from IList<T> for consumers that only read.
f: Doesn't this create too many interfaces?
Only split where clients really differ.
Link to security?
Read-only interfaces make accidental writes impossible in reporting code.
p4-44.y: Interface segregation says don't force classes to depend on methods they don't use, so prefer small, focused interfaces over one big one. For example, a report service that only reads shipments should depend on a reader interface, not a full repository with update and delete. Microsoft does the same with IReadOnlyList separate from IList.
x: The Interface Segregation Principle says clients shouldn't be forced to depend on methods they don't use. So it's better to have several small, focused interfaces than one big "fat" interface.

When an interface is too large, every implementer must implement methods it doesn't need, often by throwing, and every consumer gets access to more than it should. Changes to unrelated methods also force recompiles and test changes everywhere. Microsoft follows this principle with IReadOnlyList being separate from IList.

A practical example from our code: instead of one big IShipmentRepository with read, update and delete, we can split it into an IShipmentReader for queries and an IShipmentWriter for commands. A reporting service only takes the reader, so it physically can't modify shipments, which is nice in a GxP system, and its unit tests only need to mock two or three methods. Similarly, in the MCP server, tools are grouped by capability, so read-only tools don't get access to deployment operations.
The balance is not to go too far, with one-method interfaces everywhere. I can talk about how I find the right size.

p4-45.q: Dependency Inversion says high-level modules depend on abstractions, not concrete classes, and abstractions are owned by the high-level side. VendorExchangeService depends on ISftpClient injected through ASP.NET Core DI, not on Rebex directly, so libraries can change without touching business logic.
i: DIP is the principle; DI is the technique; IoC containers are tooling.
Clean Architecture: interfaces in the domain/application layer, implementations in infrastructure.
Without DIP: VendorExchangeService news up RebexClient directly, so changing libraries means editing business code.
With DIP: the service owns the ISftpClient abstraction and infrastructure implements it.
f: DIP vs DI?
DIP is the design principle; DI is how dependencies are supplied.
Where should the interface live?
With the code that uses it, not with the implementation.
p4-45.y: Dependency inversion means high-level business code depends on abstractions, not on concrete classes. Without it, our vendor exchange service would create the Rebex client directly, so changing libraries means editing business code. With it, the service depends on ISftpClient, and the infrastructure layer provides the implementation through dependency injection. Changing the library becomes a configuration change.
p4-45.k: dependency inversion principle, dip, solid, abstractions
x: The Dependency Inversion Principle says high-level business code should depend on abstractions, not on concrete low-level classes. Both sides depend on the interface, so the dependency direction is inverted.

Without it, a business service creates its infrastructure directly, like new-ing up a specific SFTP library. Then the business logic is tied to that library, changing it means editing business code, and you can't unit test the service without a real server.

In our vendor file exchange, the VendorExchangeService depends only on ISftpClient, which is defined alongside the business logic. The infrastructure layer contains the Rebex, SSH.NET and ComponentPro implementations, and Program.cs registers them in the ASP.NET Core DI container. So the business code never references Rebex at all. When a vendor needed a different library, it was a configuration change, and in unit tests I simply inject a mock ISftpClient with Moq.
Dependency injection is the mechanism, and dependency inversion is the design principle behind it. I can explain how this shapes our project structure, if useful.

p4-46.q: I chose an interface to decouple callers from three SFTP implementations, enable DI and unit tests with Moq, and add providers without changing callers (open/closed). It also lets me map library-specific behaviour to one consistent contract.
i: Interfaces for seams: external systems, I/O, time (TimeProvider), randomness.
Don't create interfaces for every class "just because"; one implementation and no test need is a smell.
Interfaces also let you add decorators (logging, retry, metrics) around an implementation without changing it.
Consider an abstract base class when implementations share most code; we used both.
f: Interface vs abstract class here?
Interface for the contract plus an abstract base class for shared retry/logging.
How did it help testing?
Callers are tested with mocked ISftpClient, no real server needed.
p4-46.y: I chose an interface because I needed several interchangeable implementations, Rebex, SSH.NET and ComponentPro, behind one contract, and I wanted to mock it in unit tests. Interfaces also let me add decorators like retry and logging without changing the implementations. Where they shared a lot of code, I used an abstract base class as well.
x: I chose an interface for our SFTP integration for three concrete reasons.

First, I needed several interchangeable implementations behind one contract. We had three libraries, Rebex, SSH.NET and ComponentPro, and different vendors needed different ones. An interface let business code depend on ISftpClient and stay completely unaware of which library ran. Second, testability. With an interface I can inject a mock with Moq in unit tests, so testing the file-exchange logic doesn't need a real SFTP server. Third, extensibility. Interfaces let me add decorators, like retry and logging wrappers, around any provider without touching the providers, and adding a new library is just a new class.

I also used an abstract base class, because the providers shared real code like retry policies, timeouts and logging. So the interface is the contract, and the base class is shared implementation. Callers only see the interface.
The result was that switching a vendor to Rebex was a configuration change with no business code edits. I can explain how the factory chooses the provider.
