p6-31.y: Non-secret settings go in pipeline variables or variable groups per environment. Secrets go in secret variables or linked from a vault, and they're masked in logs. Even better, the app reads secrets at runtime from Secrets Manager, so the pipeline doesn't need to handle them at all. Nothing sensitive is committed to Git.
p6-31.k: ci/cd secrets, pipeline variables, variable groups, secrets
x: In CI/CD, my rule is that non-secret settings live with the pipeline or the application configuration, and secrets live in a secrets manager, never in code, YAML or logs.
For normal settings, like environment names, URLs or feature flags, I use variable groups or stage variables in Azure DevOps, per environment, or the application's appsettings files per environment.

For secrets, there are two kinds. Secrets the pipeline itself needs, like credentials to reach AWS or a registry, are stored as secret variables or service connections in Azure DevOps. Secret variables are encrypted, masked in logs, and not passed to forked pull request builds. Even better is OIDC to AWS, so there's no long-lived key at all. Secrets the application needs at runtime, like database passwords, shouldn't go through the pipeline. They live in AWS Secrets Manager, and the ECS task reads them at startup through its IAM role. The pipeline only deploys a reference to the secret, not the value. Azure Key Vault can also be linked to a variable group when it's needed during the pipeline.

On top of that: least privilege for service connections, approvals on who can use production connections, rotation of secrets, and never echoing secrets in scripts. And we scan the repository for accidentally committed secrets.

p6-32.q: Azure DevOps environments or release stages with pre-deployment approvals and checks (named approvers, business hours, change request reference, required template, invoking a REST API), plus post-deployment verification; approvals are recorded for audit.
i: Exclusive lock check prevents concurrent deployments to one environment.
Approver can't approve their own run (configurable).
The CIRT MCP server respects these; it can't bypass approvals.
GitHub environments with required reviewers, or the approval gate in our MCP release tools with a recorded audit trail.
f: What is an exclusive lock check?
Ensures only one run deploys to an environment at a time.
How does it help GxP?
Provides recorded, attributable approvals for each deployment.
p6-32.y: In Azure DevOps, I set approvals and checks on environments or release stages, so production deployment waits until named approvers say yes. Approvals are recorded with who and when, which is important for our GxP audit. Our MCP release tools never bypass these: the agent can only check if an approval is pending.
p6-32.k: deployment approvals, azure devops, environments, gates
x: Deployment approvals make sure a human, with the right authority, checks a release before it goes into a controlled environment.

In Azure DevOps, there are two main ways. In classic release pipelines, which we use, each stage, like UAT or production, can have pre-deployment approvals: named people or groups who must approve before the stage runs, and post-deployment approvals to confirm it went well. You can require more than one approver, prevent the person who started the release from approving it, and set a timeout. In YAML pipelines, the same is done with environments: you add approvals and checks to an environment, like production, and any stage deploying to it waits. Checks can also include things like business hours, a required branch, or a query that there are no open critical bugs.
Every approval is recorded with who approved, when, and their comments, which gives an audit trail.

In our GxP environment, this is essential: releases to controlled environments need approvals from named approvers, linked to a change request. When I built the CIRT MCP server to automate deployments, I deliberately kept these approvals exactly as they were. The agent can show pending approvals, but it can't approve anything. So we cut deployments from 6 hours to 2, without weakening the approval process.

p6-33.q: Kafka is a distributed, durable, append-only event log. A broker is a Kafka server; a topic is a named stream of events; a partition is an ordered shard of a topic; an offset is a record's position in a partition; producers append records (choosing partitions by key); consumers read and track offsets, usually in consumer groups.
i: Since Kafka 4.0 (2025), KRaft replaces ZooKeeper entirely for metadata.
Records have key, value, headers and timestamp.
Consumers pull; brokers don't push.
Offsets are per partition per consumer group; committing after processing gives at-least-once.
f: Why pull instead of push?
Consumers control their pace and batching.
What replaced ZooKeeper?
KRaft, Kafka's built-in Raft-based metadata quorum.
p6-33.y: Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. A broker is a Kafka server. A topic is a named stream of events, split into partitions for parallelism. An offset is the position of a message in a partition. A producer writes events to topics, and a consumer reads them, keeping track of its offset so it can continue where it left off.
p6-33.k: kafka, broker, topic, partition, offset, producer, consumer
x: Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. It stores streams of events in an ordered, durable log, and lets many applications publish and read those events at high volume. Unlike a traditional queue, reading a message doesn't delete it; events are kept for a retention period, so several consumers can read the same data independently, and even replay it.

The main terms: a broker is a Kafka server, and several brokers form a cluster. A topic is a named stream of events, like shipment-status. Each topic is split into partitions, which are the unit of parallelism and scaling; each partition is an ordered, append-only log stored on brokers. An offset is the position of a message inside a partition, a number that only increases, and consumers track their offset to know where they've got to. A producer is an application that writes events to a topic; it chooses the partition, usually by hashing the message key, so all events with the same key, like the same shipment id, go to the same partition and stay in order. A consumer reads events, and consumers with the same group id form a consumer group, where each partition is read by only one consumer in the group, so the group shares the work.
In [the AWS-side services I've worked on], we use Kafka for events like shipment status updates, which several services consume, each in its own consumer group, and which we sometimes need to replay.

p6-34.q: Scalability comes from partitions spread across brokers, consumer groups sharing partitions, sequential disk writes, zero-copy and batching with compression. Fault tolerance comes from replicating each partition to several brokers with leader election from in-sync replicas, plus consumers resuming from committed offsets.
i: Producer batching (linger.ms, batch.size) and compression (lz4, zstd).
Page cache use makes reads fast.
Scale: partitions spread across brokers and consumers in a group.
Fault tolerance: replicas with ISR; min.insync.replicas=2 with acks=all prevents data loss on single broker failure.
f: What is zero-copy?
Sending data from page cache to the network socket without copying into user space.
What happens when a broker fails?
Leadership of its partitions moves to in-sync followers.
p6-34.y: Kafka scales by splitting topics into partitions spread across brokers, so many producers and consumers can work in parallel. For fault tolerance, each partition is copied to several brokers. If a broker fails, a copy takes over as leader. With acks set to all and min in-sync replicas, no acknowledged data is lost.
p6-34.k: kafka scalability, fault tolerance, partitions, replication
x: Kafka achieves scalability mainly through partitioning, and fault tolerance mainly through replication.

For scalability: each topic is split into partitions, and the partitions are spread across the brokers in the cluster. Producers write to different partitions in parallel, and in a consumer group, each partition is read by one consumer, so adding consumers, up to the number of partitions, increases processing in parallel. Adding brokers spreads the load further. Kafka is also very efficient by design: it writes sequentially to an append-only log, batches and compresses messages, and relies on the operating system's page cache, so it handles very high throughput.

For fault tolerance: each partition is replicated to several brokers, usually three, set by the replication factor. One replica is the leader, which handles reads and writes, and the others are followers, which copy from the leader. The replicas that are fully caught up are the in-sync replicas. If the leader's broker fails, one of the in-sync followers automatically becomes the new leader, and clients carry on. With producer acks set to all, and a minimum of two in-sync replicas, a write is only confirmed once it's safely on more than one broker, so a single failure doesn't lose data. Consumers also store their offsets in Kafka, so after a consumer crashes, another one continues from the last committed position.

p6-35.q: Replication factor is how many copies of each partition exist across brokers (typically 3); the leader handles reads and writes, followers copy it, and the in-sync replicas (ISR) are followers that are caught up. With acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2, a write is acknowledged only when at least two replicas have it.
i: unclean.leader.election.enable=false prevents data loss by not electing out-of-sync replicas.
Followers can serve reads (KIP-392, rack-aware fetching) to reduce cross-AZ traffic.
Leader handles reads and writes for a partition; followers replicate; a new leader is elected from the ISR on failure.
RF=3 is the production norm.
f: What if ISR drops below min.insync.replicas?
Producers with acks=all get errors instead of risking loss.
Why RF 3?
Survives one broker failure while still meeting min ISR 2.
p6-35.y: Replication factor is how many copies of each partition exist, usually three in production. One copy is the leader, which handles all reads and writes, and the others are followers that copy its data. If the leader's broker fails, one of the in-sync followers is elected as the new leader, so the partition stays available.
p6-35.k: replication factor, leader, follower, isr, kafka
x: The replication factor is how many copies of each partition Kafka keeps, on different brokers. A replication factor of three, which is the common choice for production, means every partition exists on three brokers, so the cluster can lose a broker without losing data.

Among those copies, one is the leader and the others are followers. The leader handles all the writes for that partition, and usually the reads too. The followers continuously copy new messages from the leader. Followers that are fully caught up are called in-sync replicas, the ISR. If a follower falls too far behind, it's removed from the ISR until it catches up.

If the leader's broker fails, the cluster controller chooses one of the in-sync followers as the new leader, and producers and consumers automatically switch to it. Because it was in sync, nothing confirmed is lost. Leaders are spread across brokers, so the load is balanced.

Two settings work together for durability. On the producer, acks set to all means a write is only acknowledged when all in-sync replicas have it. On the topic, min.insync.replicas set to two means a write is rejected if fewer than two replicas are in sync. So with a replication factor of three and a minimum of two in-sync replicas, the cluster tolerates one broker failure with no data loss and no downtime.

p6-36.q: Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, not across a topic. I use a key (such as ShipmentId) so all events for one entity go to the same partition in order, and enable the idempotent producer (default since Kafka 3.0) so retries don't reorder or duplicate.
i: Changing partition count changes key mapping for new records.
Consumer-side parallelism must preserve per-key order.
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection up to 5 is safe with idempotence.
Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition; use a key (e.g. ShipmentId) to keep related events ordered.
f: Global ordering?
Only with one partition, which limits throughput.
How can a consumer break ordering?
Processing messages of the same key in parallel threads.
p6-36.y: Kafka guarantees order only within a single partition, not across the whole topic. So to keep related events in order, I give them the same key, like the shipment id, and they all go to the same partition. That's how our shipment status events stay in the right order for each shipment.
p6-36.k: kafka ordering, partition key, message ordering
x: Kafka guarantees ordering within a partition, but not across a whole topic.

Each partition is an append-only log. Messages are written in order and each gets an increasing offset, and a consumer reads them in that same order. But a topic has several partitions, processed in parallel by different consumers, so there's no global order between messages in different partitions.

In practice, you usually don't need global ordering; you need ordering per entity, like all the events for one shipment or one order. You get that by using a message key. The producer hashes the key to choose the partition, so every event with the same key, like the shipment id, always goes to the same partition, and stays in order. So "shipment created", "shipped" and "delivered" for one shipment are always processed in sequence.

There are some things that can break ordering. Retries on the producer can reorder messages, which the idempotent producer, now the default, prevents. Increasing the number of partitions changes which partition a key maps to, so existing keys can move. And on the consumer side, if you process messages from one partition in parallel threads, you lose the order, unless you parallelise per key.

If you really need a total order across everything, you'd use a single partition, but that limits throughput to one consumer. In our shipment events, we key by shipment id, which gives the ordering that matters.

p6-37.q: Retention keeps records for a time or size limit (e.g. 7 days) whether consumed or not, allowing replay. Log compaction keeps at least the latest record per key and removes older ones, so a topic acts like a changelog of current state; a null value (tombstone) deletes a key.
i: cleanup.policy=delete, compact, or both.
Compacted topics suit state like "current shipment status per id" or KTable sources.
Tiered storage moves old segments to S3-like storage.
Compaction keeps the latest value per key, useful for state topics like "current shipment status".
f: What is a tombstone?
A record with a key and null value that marks the key for deletion in compaction.
Is compaction immediate?
No, it runs in the background on closed segments.
p6-37.y: Retention is how long Kafka keeps messages, by time or size, whether or not they've been read, which allows replay. Log compaction is a different mode where Kafka keeps at least the latest message for each key and removes older ones. It's useful for topics that hold the current state, like the latest status per shipment.
x: Retention and log compaction are the two ways Kafka decides when to remove old messages from a topic.

Retention removes messages based on time or size. By default, messages are kept for seven days, set by retention.ms, or until the partition reaches a size limit. After that, old segments of the log are deleted, whether or not anyone has read them. Consumers just need to read within the retention window. Because consumption doesn't delete data, many consumers can read independently, and you can replay events within that window, for example after fixing a bug in a consumer.

Log compaction works differently. Instead of deleting by age, Kafka keeps at least the latest message for each key, and removes older messages with the same key. So the topic becomes a snapshot of the current state of every key. For example, a topic of customer addresses keyed by customer id would keep the latest address for each customer forever. To delete a key completely, you send a message with that key and a null value, called a tombstone. Compacted topics are great for rebuilding a cache or state store, and Kafka uses one internally to store consumer offsets.
The choice depends on the use: for event history, like shipment status events, time-based retention; for "latest value per key" data, compaction. A topic can also combine both.

p6-38.q: Its group rebalances and its partitions move to the remaining consumers, which resume from the last committed offset. Messages processed but not committed are processed again, so handlers must be idempotent; commit after processing for at-least-once.
i: session.timeout.ms and heartbeat detect crashes; max.poll.interval.ms detects stuck processing.
Cooperative sticky assignor and the new consumer group protocol (KIP-848, Kafka 4.0) reduce rebalance pauses.
Static membership avoids rebalances on quick restarts.
Its partitions are rebalanced to other consumers in the group, which resume from the last committed offset.
f: Commit before or after processing?
After, for at-least-once; before risks loss.
What's max.poll.interval.ms?
Maximum time between polls before the consumer is considered failed.
p6-38.y: If a consumer crashes, the group coordinator notices and rebalances, giving its partitions to the other consumers in the group. They continue from the last committed offset. Because I commit offsets only after processing, a few messages might be processed again, so my consumers are idempotent.
p6-38.k: consumer crash, rebalance, committed offset, kafka
x: When a Kafka consumer crashes, the consumer group recovers automatically, and the key question is just whether messages get processed twice.

Each consumer in a group sends heartbeats. When one crashes, it stops sending them, and after the session timeout, the group coordinator considers it dead. Then a rebalance happens: its partitions are reassigned to the remaining consumers in the group. The new owner of each partition starts reading from the last committed offset for that partition.

Here's the important part. If the crashed consumer had processed some messages but hadn't committed their offsets yet, those messages will be processed again by the new consumer. That's at-least-once delivery. So consumers must be idempotent, meaning processing the same message twice has the same effect as once, for example by recording processed message ids, or using upserts with a unique key. The opposite mistake is committing the offset before processing; then a crash would skip messages, so I commit after processing.

To make crashes less disruptive: tune the session timeout, use the cooperative rebalancing strategy, so only the affected partitions move, and handle shutdown gracefully, committing offsets before leaving the group.
And while a consumer is down and before the rebalance, lag grows on its partitions, which is why we alert on consumer lag.

p6-39.q: Lag is the latest offset minus the committed offset: how far a consumer group is behind. I troubleshoot by checking which partitions lag (hot keys), slow processing or downstream dependencies, errors and retries, rebalances, and too few consumers; then fix the bottleneck, scale consumers up to the partition count, or batch work.
i: kafka-consumer-groups --describe shows lag per partition.
Monitor lag in time (seconds behind), not just messages.
Burrow, CloudWatch MSK metrics or Grafana.
f: Lag on one partition only?
Likely a hot key or a poison message blocking it.
Will adding consumers always help?
Only up to the number of partitions.
p6-39.y: Consumer lag is how far behind a consumer group is, the difference between the latest offset and the committed offset. Growing lag means consumers can't keep up. I check if processing got slower, for example a slow database, if a poison message is stuck, or if traffic spiked. Then I fix the slow step or add consumers, up to the partition count.
x: Consumer lag is the difference between the latest offset written to a partition and the offset the consumer group has committed. In simple words, it's how many messages are waiting to be processed. Some lag is normal, but lag that keeps growing means consumers can't keep up, and data is getting more and more delayed. And if lag grows beyond the retention period, messages are deleted before they're processed.
I monitor it per partition, with tools like Burrow, Kafka exporters for Grafana, or the cloud provider's metrics, and alert when it keeps growing.

To troubleshoot, I ask a few questions. Is the lag on all partitions or just one? If one, it might be a hot key, where one key gets most of the traffic, or a poison message that keeps failing. Did the incoming volume increase? Then I may need more consumers, up to the number of partitions. Did processing get slower? Then I check what each message does: often a slow database call, an external API, or processing one message at a time where batching would help. Are consumers rebalancing a lot? Frequent rebalances, often because processing takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, stop consumption repeatedly. And are the consumers healthy, with enough CPU and memory?
The fix follows the cause: scale out, add partitions, optimise processing, batch, tune poll settings, or move poison messages to a dead-letter topic.

p6-40.q: Add consumers to the group up to the partition count, increase partitions (key mapping changes for new data), or process in parallel inside a consumer while keeping per-key order. Consumers beyond the partition count sit idle as hot standbys.
i: Size partitions for future peak throughput.
Parallel processing libraries (Confluent parallel consumer pattern) key-ordered.
Add consumers up to the number of partitions; extra consumers sit idle.
To go beyond, add partitions (this changes key-to-partition mapping) or process in parallel inside a consumer.
f: Can you decrease partitions?
No; create a new topic and migrate.
Idle consumers useless?
They take over quickly if another consumer fails.
p6-40.y: I scale by adding consumers to the same group, and Kafka spreads the partitions between them. But each partition goes to only one consumer in a group, so if there are more consumers than partitions, the extra ones sit idle. To scale further, I add partitions, or process messages in parallel inside each consumer while keeping order per key.
p6-40.k: scaling consumers, consumer group, partitions, kafka
x: Kafka consumers scale through consumer groups. All consumers with the same group id share the work: each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group, and one consumer can handle several partitions. So with six partitions and two consumers, each gets three. Adding consumers spreads the partitions out, and the group rebalances automatically.

That means the number of partitions is the maximum parallelism for a consumer group. If you have more consumers than partitions, the extra consumers sit idle, with no partitions assigned. They do act as hot standbys, taking over if another consumer fails, but they don't add throughput.

So to scale beyond the number of partitions, you have a few options. Add partitions to the topic, keeping in mind that this changes which partition each key maps to, which can affect ordering for existing keys, so it's best to plan enough partitions from the start. Or increase parallelism inside each consumer, processing messages concurrently with a worker pool, while keeping order per key if it matters. Or make processing itself faster, with batching and efficient database writes.
Separate applications that need the same events use different consumer groups; each group gets every message independently.
For autoscaling, I'd scale consumers on consumer lag rather than CPU, for example with KEDA in Kubernetes, up to the partition count.

p6-41.q: One topic per event type or business stream (e.g. irt.shipments.status-changed.v1) with a clear naming convention and a versioned schema (Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema in a registry); partitions sized for throughput; keys chosen for ordering; retention and compaction set per use case; and ACLs per producer and consumer.
i: Compatibility rules (backward/forward) in the schema registry.
Events should be facts in past tense with ids and timestamps.
Avoid too many tiny topics or one giant topic for everything.
One topic per event type or aggregate, keys for ordering, enough partitions for future consumer parallelism.
f: Fat vs thin events?
Fat events carry full data (fewer callbacks); thin events carry ids (consumers fetch details).
How do you evolve a schema?
Add optional fields; never remove or change types without a new version.
p6-41.y: I usually create one topic per event type or business entity, with clear names, like shipment status changed. I choose a key that keeps related events in order, like shipment id, and enough partitions for future consumer parallelism. I define retention and use a schema for the event with versioning.
p6-41.k: kafka topic design, partitions, keys, schema
x: When I design Kafka topics, I think about what the events represent, who consumes them, how they need to be ordered, and how they'll change over time.

First, one topic per type of business event or entity, like shipment-status or order-events, named with a clear convention, for example domain, entity and version. Not one giant topic for everything, and not one topic per customer. Second, the key. I choose the message key based on ordering needs. If events for one shipment must be in order, the key is the shipment id. A good key also spreads load evenly, so one key doesn't overload a partition. Third, the number of partitions: enough for the consumer parallelism I need now and in the near future, because increasing it later changes key placement. Fourth, retention: time-based for event streams, or compaction for "latest value per key" topics. Fifth, the replication factor, three for production, with a minimum of two in-sync replicas.

Sixth, the schema. Events have a defined schema, with Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema, preferably in a schema registry, with backward-compatible changes. Events include an event id, a timestamp, a type, a version and a correlation id. And seventh, a plan for failures: a retry topic and a dead-letter topic.
Our shipment status topic follows this: keyed by shipment id, with versioned events and correlation ids.

p6-42.q: A poison message always fails and blocks the partition. I retry transient errors a few times with backoff (in-process or via retry topics), send permanently failing messages to a dead-letter topic with error headers, commit and move on, and alert and replay after a fix.
i: Distinguish transient (timeout) from permanent (deserialization, validation) errors.
Retry topics with delays preserve throughput but break strict ordering.
Store original topic, partition, offset and exception in headers.
Retry topics with delays, then a DLT carrying the error and original headers for reprocessing.
f: Why not retry forever?
It blocks all later messages in that partition.
How do you replay a DLT?
A tool consumes it and republishes to the original topic after the fix.
p6-42.y: A poison message is one that keeps failing. I retry temporary errors a few times, sometimes through retry topics with delays. If it still fails, I send it to a dead-letter topic with the error details, so the main flow continues. We alert on the dead-letter topic, fix the cause, and replay the messages.
p6-42.k: poison messages, retries, dead letter topic, dlq, kafka
x: A poison message is a message that a consumer can never process successfully, for example because it's malformed, has invalid data, or triggers a bug. Without handling, the consumer keeps retrying it forever. In Kafka, that's especially bad, because it blocks every message behind it in that partition.

My approach separates two kinds of failure. Transient failures, like a database timeout or an unavailable service, are worth retrying. Permanent failures, like a message that can't be deserialised or fails validation, will never succeed, so retrying is pointless.

For transient errors, I retry a few times in the consumer with exponential backoff. If it still fails, or for longer delays, I publish the message to a retry topic, sometimes several with increasing delays, like one minute, then ten, so the main partition isn't blocked while waiting. For permanent errors, or after the maximum attempts, the message goes to a dead-letter topic, with headers saying the original topic, partition, offset, the error, and the number of attempts. Then the consumer commits the offset and moves on.

The dead-letter topic is monitored, with an alert, and after investigating and fixing the cause, messages can be replayed to the main topic. Consumers are idempotent, so retries never cause duplicates.
We use exactly this pattern with RabbitMQ too: limited retries with backoff, then a dead-letter queue, with alerts.

p6-43.q: Secure Kafka with TLS in transit, SASL authentication (SCRAM or IAM on Amazon MSK), ACLs per topic and group, encryption at rest and private networking. Monitor broker health, under-replicated partitions, request latency, disk usage, producer errors and consumer lag, with alerts.
i: MSK IAM auth uses AWS credentials and IAM policies for topic access.
Key metrics: UnderReplicatedPartitions, OfflinePartitionsCount, ActiveControllerCount.
Security: TLS, SASL or IAM auth (MSK), ACLs per topic.
Monitor consumer lag, under-replicated partitions and request latency.
f: Most important broker alert?
Under-replicated or offline partitions.
How do clients authenticate on MSK?
IAM, SASL/SCRAM or mutual TLS.
p6-43.y: For security, I use TLS for encryption, authentication with SASL or IAM on Amazon MSK, and ACLs so each service can only read or write its own topics. For monitoring, the key things are consumer lag, under-replicated partitions, broker health, and request latency, with alerts on lag.
p6-43.k: kafka security, kafka monitoring, tls, acl, consumer lag
x: To secure Kafka, I cover four things: encryption, authentication, authorisation and network access.

Encryption in transit with TLS, between clients and brokers and between the brokers themselves, so messages can't be read on the network. Encryption at rest on the broker disks, which managed services like Amazon MSK provide. Authentication with SASL, for example SCRAM, or mutual TLS, or IAM authentication on MSK, so only known applications can connect. Authorisation with ACLs, applying least privilege: each service can only write to the topics it produces, and read from the topics it consumes, with its own consumer group. And network access: brokers in private subnets, reachable only from our services, never from the internet. Also, sensitive data in messages should be minimised or encrypted, and schemas validated.

For monitoring, the key metrics are: consumer lag per group and partition, which is usually the first sign of trouble; under-replicated partitions, which mean data is at risk; offline partitions and controller status; broker CPU, disk usage and network; and request latency, errors and throughput for producers and consumers. I'd collect these with Prometheus exporters or CloudWatch for MSK, show them in Grafana, and alert on growing lag, under-replicated partitions and disk space.
Consumers also log and trace with correlation ids from message headers, so one event can be followed across services.

p6-44.q: RabbitMQ is a message broker (AMQP 0-9-1, plus AMQP 1.0 native since 4.0) that routes messages from producers through exchanges to queues for consumers. A queue stores messages until consumers process them; a binding is a rule linking an exchange to a queue, with a routing key or pattern.
i: Producers publish to exchanges, never directly to queues (the default exchange routes by queue name).
Queue types: classic, quorum (replicated, Raft) and streams.
Classic mirrored queues were removed in 4.0; use quorum queues for HA.
Producers publish to exchanges; bindings route to queues by routing key (direct, topic, fanout, headers).
f: What is a vhost?
A logical namespace isolating exchanges, queues and permissions.
Quorum vs classic queues?
Quorum queues are replicated and safer; classic queues are single-node.
p6-44.y: RabbitMQ is a message broker. Producers send messages to an exchange, and the exchange routes them to queues based on bindings, which are rules linking an exchange to a queue with a routing key. Consumers read from queues. Once a message is acknowledged, it's removed. We use it for task-style work like notifications.
p6-44.k: rabbitmq, queues, bindings, exchange, message broker
x: RabbitMQ is a message broker. Applications send messages to it, and it routes them to queues, where consumers pick them up and process them. It decouples services: the sender doesn't wait for the receiver, and if the receiver is slow or down, messages wait safely in the queue.

The main concepts come from the AMQP protocol. Producers don't publish directly to queues. They publish to an exchange, with a routing key. A queue is where messages wait until a consumer receives and acknowledges them. A binding is the rule that connects an exchange to a queue, saying which messages should go there.

There are four main exchange types. Direct sends a message to queues whose binding key exactly matches the routing key, which is great for commands like "process this file". Fanout sends every message to all bound queues, like a broadcast. Topic matches routing keys with patterns, like shipment dot star, so different queues can subscribe to different groups of messages. And headers routes based on message headers.

Unlike Kafka, once a message is acknowledged, it's removed from the queue. So RabbitMQ is ideal for tasks and work queues, where each message should be processed once by one consumer, with retries and dead-lettering.
In our platform, we use RabbitMQ for work like processing vendor updates and sending notifications.

p6-45.q: A consumer ack tells RabbitMQ the consumer processed the message so it can be deleted; nack or no ack (on disconnect) requeues or dead-letters it. A publisher confirm is the broker telling the publisher it safely received the message. Consumer acks protect the consumer side; confirms protect the publisher side; both are needed.
i: Manual acks after processing; autoAck=true loses messages on failure (Part 3 Q26).
Consumer timeout (default 30 minutes) closes channels with long-unacked messages.
Publisher confirms: the broker acks once the message is routed and (for persistent messages on durable/quorum queues) written; nacks mean resend.
Consumer acks: manual ack after processing; nack/reject with requeue=false sends it to the DLX.
f: What happens to unacked messages if a consumer dies?
They're requeued and redelivered with the redelivered flag set.
Ack multiple?
multiple=true acks all up to a delivery tag, reducing overhead.
p6-45.y: Acknowledgements confirm a message was handled. Publisher confirms are from the broker to the producer: RabbitMQ confirms it has safely stored the message, so the producer knows it wasn't lost. Consumer acknowledgements are from the consumer to the broker, saying I've processed it, now remove it. I use manual consumer acks after the work is committed.
p6-45.k: acknowledgement, publisher confirms, consumer ack, rabbitmq
x: Acknowledgements are how RabbitMQ makes sure messages aren't lost, and there are two separate kinds, one on each side.

Publisher confirms are about the producer. When a publisher sends a message, it can't assume the broker received and stored it. With confirms enabled on the channel, the broker sends back an acknowledgement once it has taken responsibility for the message, for a persistent message, that means written to disk. If something goes wrong, it sends a negative acknowledgement, and the publisher can retry. Without confirms, a message can be lost silently, for example if the connection drops at the wrong moment.

Consumer acknowledgements are about the consumer. When RabbitMQ delivers a message, it waits for the consumer to acknowledge it before deleting it. With manual acknowledgement, the consumer acks only after it has finished processing. If the consumer crashes before acking, RabbitMQ redelivers the message to another consumer. A consumer can also reject a message, and send it to a dead-letter queue. With automatic acknowledgement, the message is deleted as soon as it's delivered, so if processing fails, it's gone.

I learned this the hard way in [mid-2024]. Our publisher had no confirms, and during a [40-minute] problem, [about 1,200] updates were lost silently. We recovered them by replaying the vendor files that evening, then added publisher confirms, at about [5 percent] throughput cost. There's been no silent loss in the [12 months] since.

p6-46.q: A durable queue or exchange survives a broker restart (its definition); a persistent message (delivery mode 2) is written to disk. You need both for messages to survive a restart, and publisher confirms to know they were actually stored. Quorum queues are always durable and persist messages.
i: Persistence costs throughput; transient messages suit non-critical data.
Lazy behaviour (messages on disk) is default for quorum queues and classic v2.
Durable queue survives restart; persistent messages (delivery mode 2) are written to disk; you need both.
Quorum queues (Raft-replicated) are the recommended durable type since RabbitMQ 3.8; classic mirrored queues were removed in 4.0.
f: Durable queue with non-persistent messages?
The queue survives, but messages are lost on restart.
Does persistence alone prevent loss?
No; without confirms, messages can be lost before reaching disk.
p6-46.y: For messages to survive a broker restart, I need both a durable queue and persistent messages. A durable queue's definition survives the restart, and a persistent message is written to disk. If either is missing, messages can be lost. Today, quorum queues are the recommended durable, replicated queue type.
p6-46.k: durability, persistent messages, durable queue, quorum queues, rabbitmq
x: Durability in RabbitMQ means messages survive a broker restart, and it needs several settings to work together.

First, the queue must be durable. A durable queue's definition survives a restart; a non-durable one disappears. Second, the message itself must be persistent, by setting the delivery mode to persistent when publishing. A persistent message in a durable queue is written to disk. If either part is missing, the message is lost on restart: a persistent message in a non-durable queue disappears with the queue. The exchange should also be durable, so the routing still exists after a restart.

But durability alone isn't enough. A message can still be lost before it's written, for example if the connection fails right after publishing. That's why publishers should use publisher confirms, which tell the publisher the broker has really stored the message. And consumers should use manual acknowledgements, so messages aren't removed until they're processed.

For surviving the loss of a whole node, not just a restart, you need replication. Modern RabbitMQ uses quorum queues, which replicate each queue across several nodes using the Raft consensus algorithm, and are the recommended choice for important data.

Persistence does cost some throughput, because of disk writes, but for business messages, it's worth it. After we lost [about 1,200] updates in [mid-2024] without confirms, we made sure all of these were in place.

p6-47.q: Publishers can't send: they should retry with backoff or write to an outbox table and publish later; consumers reconnect automatically when it returns (automatic recovery in the .NET client). Durable queues with persistent messages keep data; quorum queues across nodes keep the service available if one node fails.
i: Health checks and alerts on connection failures.
Circuit breaker on publishing to avoid thread pile-ups.
Publishers fail or block; with an outbox, events wait in the database and flush on recovery, as in our [mid-2024] [~40 min] outage with [~1,200] updates replayed.
Consumers reconnect (client automatic recovery) and continue from unacked messages.
f: Does the .NET client reconnect?
Yes, with AutomaticRecoveryEnabled (default true) and topology recovery.
How do you avoid losing events while it's down?
Outbox pattern.
p6-47.y: Publishers can't send, and consumers lose their connection. That's why we use the outbox pattern, so events wait in the database and are sent when RabbitMQ is back. Clients reconnect automatically, and unacknowledged messages are delivered again. During our [mid-2024] outage, we replayed about [1,200] missed updates safely.
x: If RabbitMQ goes down, what happens depends on how it's set up, and on how well producers and consumers handle it.

On the broker side: with a single node, everything stops until it's back. Durable queues with persistent messages are recovered from disk after a restart, but non-durable queues and transient messages are lost. In a cluster with quorum queues, losing one node isn't a problem: the queue's leader moves to another node, and clients reconnect, with no data loss.

On the producer side: while the broker is unavailable, publishing fails. Without publisher confirms, a producer might think a message was sent when it wasn't. So producers should use confirms, retry with backoff, and, for critical messages, use the outbox pattern, saving the message in the database with the business change, and publishing it later, when the broker is back. That way nothing is lost during an outage.

On the consumer side: consumers lose their connection. Unacknowledged messages go back to the queue and are redelivered when consumers reconnect, so consumers must be idempotent. Client libraries support automatic connection recovery, and our services also have health checks and alerts on connection failures.

In [mid-2024], we had a [40-minute] problem where our publisher had no confirms, and [about 1,200] updates were lost silently. We recovered them by replaying vendor files, and adding confirms has prevented silent loss since.

p6-48.q: For transient errors I retry in-process a few times, then nack to a retry queue with a TTL that dead-letters back to the main queue (delayed retry); after a maximum number of attempts (tracked via the x-death header or a count header), the message goes to a DLQ with an alert.
i: Quorum queues support delivery limits (x-delivery-limit, default 20 in 4.0) to stop poison loops.
Exponential backoff with several retry queues of increasing TTL.
Libraries like MassTransit provide retry and redelivery policies.
Delayed retries via a retry queue with TTL dead-lettering back to the main queue, with a retry-count header and a final parking queue.
f: Why not requeue immediately?
It creates hot loops hammering a failing dependency.
What is x-death?
A header RabbitMQ adds with dead-lettering history, including counts.
p6-48.y: For temporary errors, I don't requeue immediately, because that creates a tight loop. Instead, I send the message to a retry queue with a delay, using a message TTL that dead-letters it back to the main queue, and count the attempts in a header. After a few attempts, it goes to a parking or dead-letter queue for investigation.
p6-48.k: rabbitmq retries, retry queue, ttl, dead letter exchange
x: RabbitMQ doesn't have a single built-in retry feature, so I build retries from a few pieces, separating transient failures from permanent ones.
For quick transient failures, like a brief database timeout, the consumer retries in memory a few times with exponential backoff, for example using Polly, before giving up on the message.

For longer delays, I use a retry queue. When processing fails, the consumer rejects the message, or publishes it to a retry queue that has a message time-to-live, like 30 seconds, and a dead-letter exchange pointing back to the main queue. So the message waits in the retry queue, expires, and returns to the main queue to be processed again. Several retry queues with increasing delays give backoff. I track the number of attempts in a message header. Another option is the delayed message exchange plugin.

After the maximum attempts, or immediately for permanent errors like invalid data, the message goes to a final dead-letter queue, with the error details, and an alert, so someone can investigate and replay it after fixing the cause.
What I avoid is simply requeueing a failed message straight away, because it goes back to the front and can loop forever, blocking the queue.

A real case: some kit-assignment notifications vanished because the consumer used autoAck. I switched to manual acknowledgement, added [3] retries with exponential backoff, and then a dead-letter queue.

p6-49.q: Publisher confirms (our outage fix), durable queues, persistent messages, quorum queues, manual consumer acks after processing, dead-letter queues, the outbox pattern for publish-after-commit, and monitoring of queue depth, unroutable messages and memory alarms.
i: mandatory flag or alternate exchange for unroutable messages.
Idempotent consumers because redelivery happens.
Chain: outbox on the producer, publisher confirms, durable quorum queues with persistent messages, manual consumer acks, DLQ.
Confirms cost us about [~5 percent] throughput, an easy trade for no lost updates.
f: What's the most commonly missed piece?
Publisher confirms.
What are unroutable messages?
Messages with no matching binding, dropped silently unless handled.
p6-49.y: I protect every step. The producer saves events in an outbox and uses publisher confirms. The broker uses durable quorum queues with persistent messages. The consumer acknowledges manually only after committing its work, and failed messages go to a dead-letter queue. Confirms cost us about [5 percent] throughput, which is well worth it.
p6-49.k: message loss, reliability, publisher confirms, outbox, manual ack
x: To prevent message loss in RabbitMQ, I protect every step of the message's journey: publishing, storing, and consuming.

First, publishing. Use publisher confirms, so the publisher knows the broker actually stored each message, and retry when a confirm doesn't arrive. Use the mandatory flag, or an alternate exchange, so messages that can't be routed to any queue aren't silently dropped. For critical business messages, use the outbox pattern: save the message in the database in the same transaction as the business change, and a background process publishes it, so even a broker outage doesn't lose it.
Second, storing. Durable exchanges and queues, persistent messages, and quorum queues, which replicate across nodes, so a node failure doesn't lose data.

Third, consuming. Manual acknowledgements, only after processing has completed, for example after the database transaction commits. Never auto-ack for important messages. Failed messages are retried, and then go to a dead-letter queue, not discarded.
And finally, monitoring: alerts on dead-letter queues, unroutable messages and connection failures, plus idempotent consumers, because these measures can cause duplicates.

I learned this from a real incident in [mid-2024]: without publisher confirms, [about 1,200] updates were lost silently in [40 minutes]. We recovered them by replaying the vendor files, added confirms at about [5 percent] throughput cost, and there's been no silent loss since.

p6-50.q: Scale with more competing consumers per queue and tuned prefetch, clustering with quorum queues, splitting hot queues, and bigger nodes or Amazon MQ. Monitor queue depth, publish/deliver/ack rates, unacked counts, consumer counts, memory and disk alarms, connection churn and DLQ size via Prometheus and Grafana or CloudWatch.
i: One queue is bound to one node's leader; spread queues across nodes.
Avoid huge backlogs; queues work best near empty.
Watch for connection and channel leaks.
Scale with competing consumers and prefetch tuning; monitor queue depth, unacked counts, and consumer utilization via the management plugin or Prometheus.
f: Why do huge queues hurt?
Memory pressure, slow recovery and triggered alarms.
How do you choose prefetch?
Based on processing time and consumers; start small (10–50) and measure.
p6-50.y: I scale consumers by running more instances on the same queue, the competing consumers pattern, and tune the prefetch count. I monitor queue depth, unacknowledged messages, consumer count, memory and disk alarms, using the management UI or Prometheus with Grafana, and alert when queues keep growing.
p6-50.k: rabbitmq scaling, monitoring, prefetch, competing consumers
x: To scale RabbitMQ, I first scale the consumers, and only then think about the broker.

Scaling consumers: several consumers on the same queue share the work, with RabbitMQ distributing messages between them. The prefetch count controls how many unacknowledged messages each consumer gets at once; a sensible value, like 10 to 50, balances throughput and fairness. Consumers can be autoscaled on queue depth. Scaling the broker: run a cluster of three nodes, with quorum queues for important data, replicated for availability. A single queue is handled by one node, so for very high throughput, you can spread load across several queues, for example with the consistent hash exchange, or use RabbitMQ streams. Keep messages small and queues short, because RabbitMQ performs best when queues are near empty. Use long-lived connections with several channels, instead of opening a connection per message.

For monitoring, the key metrics are: queue depth and how it's changing, publish and acknowledge rates, unacknowledged messages, consumer count per queue, dead-letter queue size, connections and channels, memory and disk alarms, which block publishers, and node health. We use the management UI and Prometheus with Grafana dashboards, with alerts on growing queues, dead letters, zero consumers and resource alarms.
A queue with growing depth and no consumers is the classic warning sign I always alert on.

p6-51.q: I start from symptoms and scope, then follow the request: application errors and exceptions in logs; database waits, blocking, slow queries and connection pool usage; infrastructure metrics (CPU, memory, network, task restarts, load balancer target health); and recent changes. Traces show which hop spends the time.
i: If all services slow at once, suspect shared infrastructure (DB, network, DNS).
If one endpoint, suspect code or a query.
Compare with a healthy baseline period.
Correlate: app errors with a DB wait spike points to DB; all services degrading at once points to infra or a shared dependency.
f: Quick sign of a database issue?
Latency rising across endpoints with DB time dominant in traces.
Infrastructure sign?
Task restarts, node CPU saturation or network errors.
p6-51.y: I look at where the time and errors are. If database waits or slow queries spike at the same time, it points to the database. If only one service has errors, especially after a deploy, it's likely the application. If many unrelated services fail together, it points to infrastructure or a shared dependency, like the network or broker. Traces make this quick.
p6-51.k: troubleshooting, root cause, application vs database vs infrastructure
x: To work out whether an issue is in the application, the database or the infrastructure, I start with the scope and timing of the problem, then follow the evidence layer by layer.

First, scope. Is it every endpoint or one? Every user or some? One service instance or all of them? Did it start suddenly, and did it line up with a deployment, a configuration change or a traffic spike? A deployment at that time points to the application.

Then I check each layer's signals. Infrastructure: CPU, memory, disk, network, container restarts, and the health of hosts and load balancers. If one node is out of disk or memory, or tasks are being killed, it's infrastructure. Database: database CPU, active connections, blocking, deadlocks, and slow queries, using Query Store or the monitoring tools. If the database is slow and the app is just waiting, it's the database. Application: error logs and exceptions, response times broken down by dependency in traces, and thread pool or connection pool exhaustion.
Distributed tracing is the most useful tool here, because a trace shows exactly where the time goes: in our code, in a database call, or in a call to another service.

A real example: an API suddenly became slow, around [200 milliseconds to 3 seconds]. The application and servers looked healthy, but the trace showed one query taking all the time. It was parameter sniffing in SQL Server, a database issue, fixed with a better plan.

p6-52.q: A correlation or trace id is generated at the edge and passed in headers (W3C traceparent) through HTTP calls and message headers; every log line includes it, and a tracing system (OpenTelemetry to X-Ray, Jaeger or Grafana Tempo) shows the full path with timings.
i: ASP.NET Core and HttpClient propagate Activity context automatically.
Add the id to error responses so users can report it.
Our correlation-id middleware ([2024], [4] services) cut triage from [about an hour to minutes] (Part 10 Q4).
OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation propagates W3C traceparent through HttpClient and messaging headers.
f: How do you correlate across RabbitMQ?
Put the trace context in message headers and restore it in the consumer.
What is baggage?
Key-value context propagated with traces across services.
p6-52.y: Every request gets a correlation id at the edge, which our middleware adds to every log line and passes in headers and message metadata to the next service. With OpenTelemetry, we also get trace ids and spans. So I search one id in CloudWatch, or open the trace, and see the whole journey across services.
p6-52.k: request tracing, correlation id, distributed tracing, opentelemetry
x: To trace a request across microservices, I use two things together: a correlation id in every log, and distributed tracing.

Distributed tracing, with OpenTelemetry, is the standard approach. When a request enters the system, it gets a trace id. Every operation along the way, like the API handling it, a database query, an HTTP call to another service, or publishing a message, is recorded as a span, with its duration and its parent. The trace context is passed between services in the W3C traceparent header for HTTP calls, and in message headers for RabbitMQ or Kafka. The result is a timeline of the whole request, across every service, which shows exactly where time is spent and where it failed. ASP.NET Core and HttpClient support this with very little code.

Logs are the other half. Every log line includes the trace id, or a correlation id, using structured logging with Serilog. So when I find an error, I search for that id and see all the related logs from every service, in order. The id is also returned in error responses, so a user or support person can give it to us.

I implemented correlation id middleware in [2024] across [4] services. It reads the id from the incoming header or creates one, adds it to the logging scope, and passes it on to downstream calls. Triage time went from [about an hour] to [a few minutes].

p6-53.q: Application error logs for the affected service and time window (exceptions, 5xx) first, then load balancer or gateway logs (status codes, latency, target errors), then dependency logs (database, broker), then infrastructure events (deployments, task restarts, scaling).
i: Filter by correlation id from a user report.
Look at the first error, not the loudest.
First: the error logs for the failing correlation id around the incident start, then the deploy history.
Then dependency logs (DB, broker) and infrastructure events (ECS task restarts, OOM).
f: Why the first error?
Later errors are often consequences of the first.
Where are ALB logs?
Access logs in S3, queryable with Athena.
p6-53.y: First, the error logs of the failing service around the time the issue started, filtered by correlation id if I have one. Then I check the deployment history for recent changes. After that, the logs of its dependencies, like the database or message broker, and infrastructure events, like containers restarting or running out of memory.
x: Which logs I check first depends on the symptom, but I always start closest to where the problem is visible, and use a correlation id to follow it inward.

First, the application logs of the service that's failing, filtered by the time window and by errors and warnings. If the user or the error response gave me a correlation id or trace id, I search for that, which shows the whole path of that request across services. I look for the first error, not the loudest, because later errors are often just consequences.

Second, the edge: the load balancer or API gateway logs. They show whether requests reached our service at all, the status codes, and the response times. If the load balancer shows 502 or 503 errors, the service might be down or failing health checks.

Third, the platform: container or task events, like ECS stopped-task reasons or Kubernetes events, which show crashes, out-of-memory kills or failed health checks. Then deployment history, to see if something changed.
Fourth, dependencies: database logs and slow query data, message broker logs, and logs of downstream services.
Along with logs, I check the dashboards, like error rate, latency and resource usage, because they show the pattern and the start time quickly.
With our correlation id middleware, this usually takes [a few minutes], instead of [about an hour] of searching through separate logs.

p6-54.q: I keep asking why (5 whys) until I reach something that, if fixed, prevents the whole chain; I check the cause explains all symptoms and timing, and that removing it stops the problem. Symptoms are what you observe (timeouts); root causes are why they happen (missing index after data growth).
i: Separate trigger, root cause and contributing factors.
Validate with a reproduction or a controlled change.
Ask "why" repeatedly (5 whys): high CPU is a symptom; a missing index causing scans is the cause.
Validate the root cause by reproducing it or showing that the fix removes the symptom.
f: Example?
Symptom: shipment statuses stale; trigger: memory alarm; root cause: no publisher confirms.
Can there be multiple root causes?
Yes, often several contributing factors.
p6-54.y: A symptom is what we see, like high CPU or slow responses. The root cause is why it happens, like a missing index causing table scans. I keep asking why until fixing that one thing would stop the problem. Then I prove it, by reproducing it, or showing that the fix removes the symptom.
p6-54.k: symptoms vs root cause, root cause analysis, 5 whys
x: A symptom is what you see; the root cause is why it happened. Distinguishing them means not stopping at the first explanation that makes the alarm go away.

My main technique is to keep asking "why" until I reach something that, if fixed, would stop the problem from ever happening again. For example: the API is slow, that's the symptom. Why? The database CPU is high. Why? One query is doing a full scan. Why? It got a bad execution plan. Why? Parameter sniffing, where the plan was compiled for an unusual parameter value. That's the root cause. Restarting the server, or adding more CPU, would only treat the symptom.

A few other habits help. I look for the first error in the timeline, not the most frequent one, because later errors are often side effects. I check what changed around the time it started: a deployment, configuration, data volume or traffic. And I confirm the cause with evidence, ideally by reproducing it, and by checking that the fix actually removes it.
Often there are two fixes: an immediate mitigation to restore service, and the real fix for the root cause. Both are fine, as long as the second one happens.
For example, a service leaking about [150 MB a day] was being restarted every [3 days]. The restarts were the mitigation. The root cause was a cache with no expiry, so I added a [30-minute] expiry.

p6-55.q: Acknowledge, assess impact and severity, communicate early, mitigate first (rollback, scale, disable a feature), then find the root cause. Afterwards run a blameless post-mortem with a timeline, root cause and actions (tests, alerts, automation) tracked to completion; in GxP, document deviations and CAPA.
i: Roles: incident commander, communicator, investigators.
Status updates at regular intervals.
Action items with owners and dates.
Post-incident: blameless review, timeline, action items with owners, and alerts/tests that would have caught it.
f: What makes a post-mortem useful?
Specific, owned actions that are actually completed.
How do you communicate with stakeholders?
Short updates on impact, actions and next update time.
p6-55.y: First I reduce the impact, often by rolling back, and keep people updated. Then I find the root cause with logs, metrics and traces. Afterwards we do a blameless review with a timeline and actions with owners, like an alert, a test, or a design fix. For example, after our RabbitMQ outage, we added publisher confirms and memory alerts.
p6-55.k: incident management, post-mortem, prevention, production incident
x: I handle production incidents in two phases: restore service first, then understand and prevent it.

During the incident: first, assess the impact. Who's affected, how badly, and is it getting worse? I raise the incident through our process, so the right people know, and one person coordinates, while others investigate. Second, mitigate quickly. The fastest safe way to restore service often isn't the real fix. It might be rolling back a recent deployment, turning off a feature flag, scaling up, or failing over. Third, communicate regularly with stakeholders, even if the update is "still investigating". Fourth, keep a timeline of what happened and what we did.

After the incident: a blameless post-incident review. We look at what happened, the root cause, why we didn't detect it earlier, and what made recovery slower. The focus is on systems and processes, not on blaming people. Then concrete actions with owners and dates, like a fix, a test, an alert, a runbook, or a pipeline check, so the same class of problem can't happen again, or is caught early.

A real example: a release caused about [8 percent] 5xx errors in UAT. We rolled back within [15 minutes], which restored service. Then we found the cause, a missing configuration value, and added a startup check so the service fails fast and visibly when configuration is missing.

p6-56.q: In [2024] a security review flagged that external links in the IRT UI used target="_blank" without rel="noopener", letting the opened page change our tab via window.opener (phishing risk). I fixed [about 40] links across React and Angular with rel="noopener noreferrer", updated window.open calls to pass noopener, and enabled the ESLint rule react/jsx-no-target-blank so the build fails if it returns. It passed retest with no regressions.
i: Found links with a code search across both front ends.
Angular templates checked separately since the React lint rule doesn't cover them.
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header as extra defence.
Lesson: pair every fix with an automated guard.
f: Why noreferrer too?
It also hides the Referer header, avoiding leaking internal URLs.
Don't browsers fix this now?
Modern browsers default to noopener for _blank, but explicit attributes and window.open still matter.
w: I close security gaps completely and prevent regressions.
p6-56.y: In [2024], a security review found that external links in our UI used target blank without noopener. That lets the opened page change our original tab, for example to a fake login page. I fixed about [40] links across React and Angular by adding rel noopener noreferrer, and turned on an ESLint rule so the build fails if it comes back. It passed retest with no regressions.
p6-56.k: reverse tabnabbing, security fix, noopener, story
x: Situation: in [2024], a security review of our web applications found a reverse-tabnabbing issue. Many external links in our UI opened in a new tab using target blank, without rel noopener. When a link opens that way, the new page gets a reference back to our original tab, through window.opener. A malicious or compromised external site could use that to quietly redirect our tab to a fake login page, and users might enter their credentials there.
Task: I was asked to fix it across our applications and make sure it couldn't come back.

Action: first, I searched the React and Angular codebases for every link and window.open call that opened a new tab, and found [about 40] of them. I added rel noopener noreferrer to each link. Noopener removes the reference back to our page, and noreferrer also stops sending our URL to the external site. For window.open calls, I passed the noopener option as well. Then, to prevent it from coming back, I turned on an ESLint rule that fails the build if anyone adds a target blank link without noopener. And I created a small shared external-link component, so developers don't need to remember the attributes.

Result: the issue passed the security retest, with no regressions, and since then, the lint rule has caught a couple of new cases before they were merged. It was a small fix, but a good example of fixing a class of problem, not just individual instances.

p6-57.q: Mocking replaces a real dependency with a test double so you can test a unit in isolation. A stub returns canned answers; a mock also verifies interactions (was it called, with what); a fake is a working lightweight implementation (in-memory repository, FakeTimeProvider).
i: Moq, NSubstitute; Moq's 2023 SponsorLink controversy led some teams to NSubstitute.
Don't mock what you don't own; wrap third-party APIs.
Over-mocking couples tests to implementation.
Over-mocking couples tests to implementation; prefer fakes (in-memory repository, FakeTimeProvider) for behaviour tests.
f: Spy?
A double that records calls on a real or partial object for later assertions.
When prefer fakes?
When behaviour matters more than calls, like repositories in domain tests.
p6-57.y: Mocking means replacing a real dependency with a test double. A stub just returns fixed answers. A mock also checks that certain calls were made, like verifying an email was sent once. A fake is a simple working version, like an in-memory repository. I prefer fakes and stubs, and use mocks only when the call itself is what matters.
p6-57.k: mocking, mock, stub, fake, test doubles
x: Mocking means replacing a real dependency, like a database, an email service or an external API, with a controlled stand-in during a unit test. That way, I test only my own code, the test is fast and reliable, and I can easily simulate situations like errors or timeouts.
The general term for any stand-in is a test double, and there are a few kinds.
A stub provides fixed answers to calls. For example, a repository stub that always returns a specific customer. It's used to set up the situation for the test, and I don't check how it was called.

A mock is set up with expectations about how it should be used, and the test verifies those interactions. For example, verifying that the email service's Send method was called exactly once with the right address. It's used when the interaction itself is the behaviour I care about.

A fake is a working, lightweight implementation, but not suitable for production. For example, an in-memory repository that stores items in a list, or an in-memory message bus. It behaves realistically, which is useful for more complex scenarios.
In .NET, I use Moq or NSubstitute, and in practice the same object often acts as a stub and a mock.

One guideline I follow is not to over-mock. If a test checks every internal call, it breaks whenever the code is refactored. I prefer checking results and state, and only verify interactions that really matter, like sending an email or publishing a message.

p6-58.q: Depend on interfaces, inject them, and in unit tests pass Moq mocks or fakes (repository, clock, HTTP client) to cover business logic; then add integration tests with real dependencies (database, broker in containers) for the wiring.
i: HttpClient: mock HttpMessageHandler or use a fake handler.
Time: FakeTimeProvider.
Logging: FakeLogger to assert important logs.
Testcontainers runs real SQL Server or RabbitMQ in Docker for integration tests.
f: How do you test code using HttpClient?
Inject a fake HttpMessageHandler returning prepared responses.
Why both unit and integration?
Units prove logic; integration proves real configuration and queries.
p6-58.y: For unit tests, I inject fakes or mocks for the dependencies, so I test only the service's logic. For integration tests, I use real dependencies where possible, like SQL Server or RabbitMQ in Docker with Testcontainers, and replace only external systems, like vendor APIs, with fakes.
p6-58.k: testing dependencies, unit test, integration test, testcontainers
x: To test a service that has dependencies, I make sure the dependencies can be replaced, then I test at two levels.

First, the design. The service gets its dependencies through constructor injection, using interfaces, like a repository, a message publisher, or an HTTP client for another API. Time is also a dependency, so I inject TimeProvider instead of using DateTime.Now directly. That makes everything controllable in tests.

Second, unit tests. I create the service with test doubles, using Moq or NSubstitute: stubs that return the data I need for the scenario, and mocks where I need to verify an important interaction, like a message being published. Then I test the business logic, including the important edge cases and error paths, like the repository returning nothing, or the other service timing out. These tests are fast and don't need any infrastructure.

Third, integration tests, because mocks can hide real problems, like a wrong SQL query or a serialisation issue. For these, I use real dependencies in containers with Testcontainers, like a real SQL Server or RabbitMQ, and WebApplicationFactory to run the API in memory. External third-party APIs are replaced with a fake HTTP server, like WireMock.
For example, for our shipment service, unit tests cover the status rules, and integration tests check the real database queries and message publishing end to end.

p6-59.q: Keep controllers thin and test logic in services. For controllers, use WebApplicationFactory integration tests that send HTTP requests and assert status codes, bodies and headers, with test authentication and replaced external services via ConfigureTestServices.
i: Test auth handler to simulate users and roles.
Test model validation and ProblemDetails responses.
WebApplicationFactory tests the full pipeline (routing, model binding, filters, auth) rather than calling action methods.
f: Why not unit test controllers directly?
Routing, binding, filters and auth are skipped, which is where bugs hide.
How do you fake authentication?
A test AuthenticationHandler that creates a ClaimsPrincipal.
p6-59.y: I prefer testing controllers through HTTP, using WebApplicationFactory, which runs the real pipeline with routing, model binding, validation, filters and authentication. Then I check status codes and responses. Unit testing controller methods directly misses most of that. Business logic is tested separately in the services.
x: I test ASP.NET Core controllers in two ways, and I prefer the second for most cases.

The first is a unit test of the controller class. I create the controller directly, passing mocked dependencies, like the service it calls, then call the action method and check the result. For example, if the service returns null, the action should return NotFound; if it returns an order, the result should be Ok with that order. This is quick, but it doesn't test the important parts of the framework around the controller: routing, model binding, validation, filters, authentication, serialisation and status codes. And controllers should be thin anyway, with the logic in services, which have their own unit tests.

The second, which I prefer, is an integration test with WebApplicationFactory. It starts the whole API in memory, and I send real HTTP requests with its HttpClient. So I test the endpoint exactly as a client uses it: the URL, the JSON, the status code, the validation errors, and authorisation. I can replace dependencies, like the database with a Testcontainers SQL Server, or fake external services, by overriding service registrations. For authentication, I add a test authentication handler that creates a user with specific roles, so I can test both allowed and forbidden cases.
For example, I'd check that posting an invalid shipment returns 400 with a problem details response, and a user without the right role gets 403.

p6-60.q: Prefer a real database: SQL Server in Testcontainers or a test database, with migrations applied and data reset between tests (Respawn). SQLite in-memory is faster but differs from SQL Server; the EF Core InMemory provider isn't recommended for testing queries.
i: Test repositories and complex queries against the real provider.
Transactions rolled back per test, or Respawn to clean tables.
The EF Core InMemory provider doesn't enforce relational behaviour; Microsoft recommends a real database (Testcontainers) or SQLite with caveats.
f: Why not InMemory provider?
No relational behaviour: no transactions, constraints or real SQL translation.
What is Respawn?
A library that resets database tables quickly between tests.
p6-60.y: I test EF Core code against a real database, usually SQL Server in a Docker container with Testcontainers, because the in-memory provider doesn't behave like a real relational database, for example with constraints and transactions. Each test starts with known data. For pure business logic, I keep it outside the queries and unit test it.
p6-60.k: ef core testing, testcontainers, in-memory provider, database tests
x: For EF Core code, I choose the test approach based on what I'm actually testing.

If I'm testing business logic that just happens to use data, I keep it in a service that depends on a repository interface, or I keep queries simple, and unit test the logic with test doubles. That's fast and focused.

If I'm testing the data access itself, meaning the queries, mappings, relationships and constraints, I use a real database. The best option is Testcontainers, which starts a real SQL Server in a Docker container for the tests. I apply the migrations, seed test data, run the code, and check the results. This catches the things that matter: whether the LINQ query translates correctly to SQL, unique constraints, cascade deletes, transactions and concurrency tokens. To keep tests independent, I reset the data between tests, for example with Respawn, or run each test in a transaction that's rolled back.

What I avoid for this is the EF Core in-memory provider. It's not a relational database: it doesn't enforce constraints, it doesn't support transactions properly, and some queries that work in memory fail on SQL Server. Microsoft itself discourages it for testing. SQLite in-memory is closer, but still differs from SQL Server.
In our services, repository and query tests run against SQL Server in Testcontainers in the pipeline, which gives real confidence that the queries work in production.

p6-61.q: Playwright is a browser automation framework that drives Chromium, Firefox and WebKit for end-to-end tests, with auto-waiting, tracing and parallel runs. Cucumber is a BDD tool that runs Given/When/Then scenarios written in Gherkin; they combine well: Cucumber for readable scenarios, Playwright for the browser steps.
i: Playwright trace viewer helps debug CI failures.
Use role-based locators (getByRole) for resilient tests.
Gherkin scenarios double as living documentation for QA and validation.
c:
Scenario: Bulk import rejects duplicate sites
  Given I am a study manager on study "ST-42"
  When I upload "sites-with-duplicates.csv"
  Then I see 2 errors with reason "Duplicate site number"
f: Playwright vs Selenium?
Playwright is faster, auto-waits and has better tooling.
Why BDD in GxP?
Scenarios trace directly to requirements and are readable by validation teams.
p6-61.y: Playwright is a browser automation tool for end-to-end tests: it drives real browsers, clicks and checks pages, with auto-waiting. Cucumber is a BDD framework where tests are written in plain Given, When, Then language. They work together: Cucumber describes the scenario in business language, and Playwright does the actual steps in the browser.
x: Playwright and Cucumber solve different problems, so they're often used together rather than as alternatives.

Playwright is a browser automation and end-to-end testing tool from Microsoft. It drives real browsers, Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, to click, type, navigate and check what's on the page, just like a user. Its strengths are reliability and speed: it automatically waits for elements to be ready, which reduces flaky tests, it can run tests in parallel, it can intercept network calls, and it records traces with screenshots and videos for debugging failures. It works with TypeScript, .NET, Java and Python.

Cucumber is a behaviour-driven development framework. Tests are written as scenarios in plain language using Gherkin, with Given, When and Then steps. For example: Given a study with two sites, When I create a shipment, Then the shipment status is Pending. Each step is linked to code that performs it. The benefit is that business analysts, testers and developers can all read and agree on the scenarios, and they act as living documentation of the requirements.
So Cucumber describes what should happen in business language, and Playwright does the actual work in the browser. In .NET, Reqnroll, the successor to SpecFlow, plays the Cucumber role.
I'd use Playwright alone for technical UI tests, and add Cucumber when business stakeholders need to read and own the scenarios.

p6-62.q: A flaky test passes and fails without code changes, usually from timing, shared state, order dependence, real time or network calls. I reproduce it (repeat runs), quarantine it so it doesn't block others, fix the root cause (awaits, isolation, fake time, deterministic data), and track flakiness rates.
i: Never just add sleeps; wait for conditions.
Retries hide problems; use only temporarily with tracking.
Azure DevOps flaky test detection can mark them.
Common causes: shared state, time, ordering, and real network calls; fix the cause, quarantine only temporarily.
f: Common async flakiness cause?
Not awaiting tasks or asserting before background work finishes.
How do you find order dependence?
Run tests in random order or isolation.
p6-62.y: A flaky test sometimes passes and sometimes fails without any code change. Common causes are timing and fixed sleeps, shared data between tests, dependence on test order, real time and dates, or network calls. I find the cause and fix it, and only quarantine the test briefly, because flaky tests make people ignore real failures.
