p9-31.y: I'd choose Spring Boot if the organisation's platform, libraries and people are already Java. I'd choose .NET if the team and code base are .NET, for its performance, LINQ and EF Core productivity, and great tooling. Both are excellent, so team skills and existing systems should decide, not personal preference.
x: Spring Boot and .NET are both excellent, mature platforms for backend services, so I'd choose based on the organisation and the team, not on personal preference.

I'd choose Spring Boot when the organisation's platform is already Java: the existing services, shared libraries, deployment tooling, monitoring and, most importantly, the people's skills. Then adding .NET would mean extra maintenance, hiring and support costs. Spring Boot also has a huge ecosystem, with Spring Cloud for distributed systems, and very wide community support.

I'd choose .NET when the team and codebase are already .NET, or for a new team that values productivity and performance. ASP.NET Core is one of the fastest mainstream web frameworks. C# has features like LINQ, async and await, and records, which make code concise. EF Core is very productive. The platform is very consistent, with dependency injection, configuration, logging and health checks built in, and the tooling, like Visual Studio and Rider, is excellent. It's cross-platform and runs well in containers.
Technically, they're very close. Both run well on AWS, in containers, with the same architecture patterns.

So my answer is that team skills and existing systems should decide. In our case, .NET was the right choice, because our team and our core IRT services are .NET. If I joined a Java team, I'd happily work in Spring Boot, because the concepts are the same.

Task: I didn't want to just complain, or ignore his requests. I wanted to understand what he needed, and find a way that worked for both him and the team.

Action: I asked him for a short one-to-one conversation, and asked what the updates were for. It turned out he had to report to the client regularly, and he felt he didn't have enough visibility, so he kept asking. Once I understood that, I offered a solution. I'd send him a short written update every [morning], covering progress, risks and blockers, and we'd keep a shared board that he could check at any time. For priority changes, I suggested that new requests go through the product owner, who could decide what came out of the sprint, so the team wasn't pulled in different directions. I kept the tone positive and focused on helping him do his job.
Result: he agreed. The interruptions dropped significantly, the team could focus, and our relationship improved. He even said the morning updates made his client reporting easier.
What I learned is that difficult behaviour often comes from an unmet need. If you understand that need, you can usually find a solution that works for everyone.

x: Situation: in [2023], I was asked to estimate a new [shipment reporting API]. I estimated it at one sprint, based on the development work.
Task: I was responsible for delivering it within that sprint.

Action: about halfway through, I realised my estimate was wrong. I had focused on the code, and missed the validation documentation and FV preparation that every change needs in our GxP environment. That work was significant. Instead of hoping to catch up, or staying quiet until the last day, I told the product owner [mid-sprint], as soon as I saw the problem. I explained what I'd missed, and proposed a way forward. We split the work, so the main reporting endpoint, which the client needed first, was completed and validated on time, and the export feature moved to the next sprint.
Result: the client's plan wasn't affected, because the most important part arrived on time. But it was still my mistake, and I took responsibility for it.

What I learned changed how I work. Now, I always include validation, documentation and testing effort in my estimates, not just the coding, and I check estimates against similar past work. I also raise risks early, because a problem raised in the middle of a sprint has options, while a problem raised on the last day only has excuses.
In general, I deal with failure by owning it quickly, fixing the impact, and changing something so it doesn't happen again.

p9-41.y: Let me take our Shipment service as an example. It has a REST API to create, get and list shipments, and its own SQL Server database. It publishes shipment status events to Kafka through an outbox, and processes depot status files from the SFTP integration with idempotent handlers. It runs stateless on ECS with autoscaling, uses Redis for reference data, Polly for vendor calls, and full logs, metrics and traces.
p9-41.k: microservice design, shipment service, system design
x: Let me take [a shipment-tracking service from IQVIA's newer AWS services I've worked on] as a real example, because it shows the main design choices.

Its responsibility is clear: it owns shipments of trial medication, from creation to delivery. It exposes a REST API, built with ASP.NET Core, to create a shipment, get one, and list shipments with filters and paging. It owns its own SQL Server database, which no other service reads directly, with audit tables recording every change, because we're in a GxP environment.

For communication, when a shipment changes status, the service publishes a shipment status event to Kafka. It uses the outbox pattern: the status change and the event are saved in the same database transaction, and a background publisher sends the event, so events are never lost. Other services, like supply, notifications and reporting, consume those events independently. Status updates from depot vendors arrive through our SFTP integration, and are processed by idempotent handlers, so duplicate files never cause duplicate updates.

For scalability, it's stateless, packaged as a Docker image, and runs on ECS across two availability zones behind a load balancer, with autoscaling on CPU and request count. Redis caches reference data, like depots and countries.
For resilience, calls to vendors use Polly, with timeouts, retries and circuit breakers. And for observability, it has structured logs with correlation ids, metrics and traces, plus health checks.
That combination makes it independent, scalable and reliable.

p9-42.y: .NET 6, in 2021, brought minimal APIs and the simpler Program.cs hosting model. .NET 8, in 2023, brought big performance gains, Native AOT for more apps, TimeProvider, keyed services and C# 12 primary constructors. .NET 10, in November 2025, brings C# 14, more performance work and built-in validation for minimal APIs. All three are long-term support releases, and I upgraded our services to .NET 10 in [early 2026].
x: I've worked with .NET 6, 8 and 10, which are all long-term support releases, each supported for three years.

.NET 6, released in 2021, was the release that brought .NET Core and the old .NET Framework world together into one platform. It introduced minimal APIs, and the simpler hosting model, where all the startup code lives in one short Program.cs file. It also brought C# 10, with global usings and file-scoped namespaces, and hot reload.

.NET 8, released in 2023, brought large performance improvements, Native AOT for more types of apps, so they start fast with low memory, and the TimeProvider abstraction, which makes time-dependent code testable. It added keyed services in dependency injection, frozen collections, and built-in resilience with Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience. C# 12 added primary constructors for classes and collection expressions.

.NET 10, released in November 2025, brings C# 14, with features like extension members and the field keyword, plus more performance work in the runtime and JIT, built-in validation for minimal APIs, and improvements in ASP.NET Core and EF Core.

I led the upgrade of our services to .NET 10 in [early 2026]. We started with [3 of 6] services, over [about six weeks]. We saw about [10 to 15 percent] better p95 latency, and at the same time, we added [Trivy] image scanning to the pipeline. The key to a smooth upgrade was good test coverage and upgrading service by service.

p9-43.q: Each .NET service is a Docker image in ECR and an ECS service with a task definition (CPU, memory, environment, secrets from Secrets Manager, task role), running across two availability zones in private subnets behind an ALB with health checks; autoscaling on CPU and request count; logs to CloudWatch; and Azure DevOps deploys with rolling updates.
i: Deployment circuit breaker with rollback.
Service Connect or ALB rules for routing between services.
Deployment circuit breaker rolls back failed deployments automatically.
Task roles give each service least-privilege AWS access.
f: How do you roll back?

p9-43.y: Each .NET service is a Docker image in ECR, running as an ECS service. The task definition sets CPU, memory, environment, secrets from Secrets Manager and an IAM task role. Tasks run across two availability zones in private subnets behind an ALB with health checks, and autoscale on CPU and request count. Logs go to CloudWatch, and Azure DevOps deploys with rolling updates.
p9-43.k: ecs architecture, aws, fargate, alb, task definition
x: [Each of the newer .NET services I've worked on in AWS] runs on Amazon ECS, and the architecture is the same for all of them, which makes them easy to operate.

Each service is built as a Docker image in our Azure DevOps pipeline, scanned, and pushed to Amazon ECR with a version tag. In ECS, each service has a task definition, which describes how to run it: the image, CPU and memory, the port, environment variables, secrets injected from AWS Secrets Manager, the logging configuration, and an IAM task role, which gives the service only the AWS permissions it needs, like reading a specific S3 bucket or secret.

The ECS service keeps the desired number of tasks running, spread across two availability zones, in private subnets, so they're not reachable from the internet. An Application Load Balancer in the public subnets receives traffic and routes it to the healthy tasks, using health check endpoints in each service. Security groups only allow traffic from the load balancer to the service, and from the service to the database. Autoscaling adjusts the number of tasks based on CPU and request count.
Logs go to CloudWatch, with alarms, and we use Grafana dashboards. The services connect to RDS SQL Server, ElastiCache Redis, and our messaging systems.
Deployments are rolling updates triggered from Azure DevOps: a new task definition revision, new tasks start and pass health checks, then old ones stop. Rollback is redeploying the previous revision.

Depends on platform team skills; Terraform/OpenTofu if multi-provider matters, otherwise CDK/CloudFormation.

[Newer, smaller pieces and tooling used Terraform modules], for reuse and multi-provider support. I can read and change both, and for new work I'd standardise on one to avoid duplication.

[Our core platform stacks were already in CloudFormation, owned by the platform team.] Things like the main networking and shared infrastructure were built that way years ago. Rewriting them in Terraform would have been a big, risky project with no direct benefit, so when we needed changes there, we extended the existing CloudFormation templates, following the platform team's process.

[Newer, smaller pieces and tooling used Terraform modules.] For new components, the team chose Terraform, because of its reusable modules, its readable plan output before every change, and the fact that it can manage things beyond AWS, through other providers. So new service infrastructure, like queues, alarms and service-specific resources, was written in Terraform.

I can read and change both. The concepts are similar: infrastructure as code, reviewed in pull requests, previewed before applying, with change sets in CloudFormation and plan in Terraform, and applied through pipelines.

Honestly, if I were designing it from scratch, I'd standardise on one tool, to avoid duplication, two sets of skills, and confusion about where things are defined. And I'd make sure each resource is managed by only one tool, never both, because that leads to conflicts.

My production container experience is mainly ECS, and I say so honestly.

I used Kubernetes for [some internal workloads, like the Node.js build-log summariser and the FastAPI vendor file validator in a shared non-production cluster], writing Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps and probes. So my production container experience is mainly ECS, but the concepts transfer directly.
x: To be honest and precise: [the production services I've worked on in AWS] run on Amazon ECS, not Kubernetes, and the CIRT platform itself is hosted on IIS on-premise. My Kubernetes experience is with [some internal workloads, like the Node.js build-log summariser and the FastAPI vendor file validator, in a shared non-production cluster].

For those, I wrote the Kubernetes manifests myself: Deployments with the image, replicas, resource requests and limits, and environment variables; Services to give them stable internal addresses; ConfigMaps for configuration, and Secrets for sensitive values; and readiness, liveness and startup probes connected to each app's health endpoints. I deployed them through our pipeline and troubleshot them with kubectl: describe, logs and events.

One real problem taught me a lot. One of these services kept crash-looping, but its logs showed no errors. The events showed that the liveness probe was killing it, because it needed [about 40 seconds] to warm up, but liveness checks started after [10 seconds]. I added a startup probe allowing [60 seconds], made part of the warm-up lazy, and updated our template so every new service gets a startup probe by default.

So my production container experience is mainly ECS, and my Kubernetes experience is practical but smaller scale. The core concepts, like desired state, health checks, rolling updates, configuration and secrets, are the same on both, so I'm confident working with Kubernetes in production.

p9-46.q: Kafka: shipment status events consumed by several services (supply, notifications, reporting), needing ordering per shipment key and replay. RabbitMQ: task-style messages like sending notifications and generating reports, where per-message acks, routing and retries matter; that's where I root-caused the outage fixed with publisher confirms.
i: Kafka key = ShipmentId; RabbitMQ topic exchange with DLQs.
Kafka retention allowed replaying events to rebuild reports.
RabbitMQ DLQs handled failed notification messages.
Publisher confirms cost [~5 percent] throughput but stopped lost messages.
f: Why not one broker?
Different delivery semantics fit different workloads.
Hardest bug?
Silent message loss without publisher confirms.
p9-46.y: We use Kafka for shipment status events, which several services consume, like supply, notifications and reporting. They need order per shipment and the ability to replay. We use RabbitMQ for task-style messages, like sending notifications and generating reports, where per-message acknowledgement, routing and retries matter. That's also where I root-caused the outage we fixed with publisher confirms.
p9-46.k: kafka use case, rabbitmq use case, messaging
x: I've used both, because they're good at different things: RabbitMQ in our on-premise CIRT platform, and Kafka in [some of IQVIA's newer services on AWS].

Kafka is for events that several services need to know about. [In those AWS services,] the main use case is shipment status events. When a shipment changes status, like dispatched, in transit or delivered, the Shipment service publishes an event to a Kafka topic, keyed by shipment id. Several services consume it independently, in their own consumer groups: supply, which updates site inventory, notifications, which informs site staff, and reporting. Kafka fits because the events must stay in order for each shipment, which the key guarantees, several consumers read the same events, and we can replay events, for example to rebuild a report or recover a consumer after a bug, because Kafka keeps them for the retention period.

RabbitMQ is for tasks: work that one consumer should do once. In CIRT, our use cases are things like AlertWatchDog notifications, processing vendor status updates, and cache refreshes. RabbitMQ fits because of acknowledgements for each message, flexible routing to different queues, retries, and dead-letter queues for failures.

RabbitMQ is also where I learned an important lesson. In [mid-2024], our publisher had no publisher confirms, and during a [40-minute] problem, [about 1,200] updates were lost silently. We recovered them by replaying the vendor files that evening. I root-caused it and added publisher confirms, at about [5 percent] throughput cost, and there's been no silent loss in the [12 months] since.

p9-47.q: Release deployments: an AI agent in Cursor or Claude Code uses the CIRT MCP server's tools in a loop (queue build, create release, deploy to environment, poll node status, summarise failures, retry a node) with humans confirming and approving. Also an [AutoGen experiment] with coder and reviewer agents drafting unit tests.

Tool design matters most: clear names, descriptions and structured outputs help the agent choose correctly.
Humans approve controlled environments.
Results: 6 hours to 2, 6 people to 1.

Humans approve and confirm; the agent executes and reports.

p9-47.y: I orchestrated release deployments. An AI agent in Cursor or Claude Code uses our CIRT MCP server's tools in a loop: queue the build, create the release, deploy to the environment, poll each node, summarise failures and retry a node, with humans confirming and approving. I also ran an [AutoGen experiment] with coder and reviewer agents drafting unit tests.
x: What I orchestrated was release deployments, using an AI agent and my CIRT MCP server.

The agent runs in Cursor or Claude Code, and the CIRT MCP server gives it about 77 tools for our on-premise Azure DevOps Server and our deployment process. When an engineer asks something like "deploy release 4.2 to UAT and verify it", the agent works in a loop. It queues the build and polls its status. It creates the release from the build artifacts. It starts the deployment to the chosen environment. It polls each of the [4 to 6] nodes and shows a per-node status table. If a node fails, it summarises the failing step and the key log lines, and with the user's confirmation, retries just that node. Finally, it verifies that every node is running the right version.

Humans stay in control at the important points. Every write action needs the user's confirmation, the agent uses each engineer's own permissions, and production approvals stay in Azure DevOps with named approvers, which the agent can't bypass.
The result was that deployments went from about 6 hours with 6 people to about 2 hours with 1 person.

Separately, I ran an [AutoGen experiment] with two agents, a coder that drafted unit tests and a reviewer that checked them against our conventions, with me approving the final output. That taught me when multi-agent setups help, and when one agent with good tools is enough.

p9-48.q: [An internal assistant over release runbooks, deployment guides and past incident notes]: documents are chunked and embedded into a vector index; questions are embedded, top-k chunks retrieved and re-ranked, sent with the question to Azure OpenAI, and answers cite source documents; it was evaluated against [a set of 30] real team questions, and no patient data is included.
i: Chunk by headings with overlap.
Refreshed when documents change.
Answers include citations so engineers can verify them.
Access control matches document permissions.
f: Which vector store?
[Azure AI Search] with hybrid search.
How good was it?
[Most answers correct with citations]; gaps fixed by improving source docs.
p9-48.y: It's an [internal assistant over our release runbooks, deployment guides and past incident notes]. Documents are split into chunks and stored as embeddings in a vector index. A question is embedded, the most relevant chunks are retrieved and re-ranked, and sent with the question to Azure OpenAI, and the answer cites the source documents. We tested it with [30] real team questions, and no patient data is included.
p9-48.k: rag architecture, rag, embeddings, vector search, azure openai
x: My main RAG system, built in Python, gives GitHub Copilot and Cursor the context of our existing codebase and coding standards, through MCP tools like search_codebase and get_coding_standards, so their code fits the project and hallucinations drop. [Its first version was an assistant over our release runbooks and incident notes], and the same design serves both.

The architecture has two parts. First, ingestion. Code is chunked by structure with tree-sitter, one method or class per chunk, and documents by headings, so each chunk has enough context. Each chunk is turned into an embedding, a vector representing its meaning, and stored in PostgreSQL with pgvector, along with metadata like the document title, section and link.

Second, answering. When someone asks a question, the question is embedded the same way, and the best chunks are retrieved with hybrid vector and keyword search. Those are re-ranked to put the most relevant first. Then the top chunks are sent, together with the question, to Azure OpenAI, with instructions to answer only from the provided content, to cite the source documents, and to say "I don't know" if the answer isn't there. That reduces made-up answers.
For quality, I built a golden set of [about 60] real questions, and tuning chunking and retrieval lifted [recall at five from about 62 to about 88 percent].
For safety, it only contains internal code and engineering documents. No patient or study data is included, and it runs on our enterprise Azure OpenAI, where data isn't used for training.

p9-49.q: [A configurable data table component] used across IRT screens: typed columns, sorting, paging, filtering, loading and empty states, row actions with role checks, and accessible keyboard navigation, documented with examples and covered by tests.

Server-side paging with React Query.
Used across many screens, which reduced duplicate code and kept the UI consistent.

type Column<T> = { key: keyof T; header: string; sortable?: boolean; render?: (row: T) => ReactNode };
function DataTable<T>({ rows, columns, onSort }: { rows: T[]; columns: Column<T>[]; onSort?: (k: keyof T) => void }) { /* ... */ }

Accessibility?

p9-49.y: I built a [configurable data table component] used across our IRT screens. It has typed columns, sorting, paging and filtering, loading and empty states, row actions that respect user roles, and keyboard accessibility. It's generic over the row type, documented with examples and covered by tests, so every screen looks and behaves the same.
p9-49.k: react reusable component, data table, typescript, example
x: A good example is a [configurable data table component] that I built and that's used across many of our IRT screens.
Before it, different screens had their own tables, each built slightly differently. Sorting, paging and filtering behaved inconsistently, and every new screen meant writing the same code again.

So I built one reusable table component in React with TypeScript. It's generic over the row type, so it's fully typed: a screen passes its rows and a list of column definitions, and TypeScript checks that each column matches a real property of the row. Each column can define its header, how to display the value, and whether it's sortable or filterable. The component handles sorting, paging and filtering, either on the client, or on the server for large data, by calling back to the screen. It shows consistent loading, empty and error states. Row actions, like edit or cancel, are passed in, and they respect the user's roles, so actions a user isn't allowed to perform aren't shown. And it's accessible, with keyboard navigation and proper table semantics for screen readers.
I documented it with examples, and covered it with tests using React Testing Library.
The result is that every screen's tables now look and behave the same, new screens are much faster to build, and when we improve the component, every screen benefits.

p9-50.q: For the vendor file pre-validation service: Pydantic models give quick, readable schema validation, automatic OpenAPI docs, async support and high performance, and the integration team already knew Python.
i: 422 responses with field-level errors out of the box.
Type hints and Pydantic give validation and docs with little code.
Async support handles many concurrent requests.
The integration team could maintain it easily.

FastAPI has built-in validation, async and docs; Flask is simpler and older.
How is it deployed?
Docker image with uvicorn, same pipeline template.
p9-50.y: I used FastAPI for the [vendor file pre-validation service]. Pydantic models made schema validation quick and readable, and FastAPI gives automatic API docs, async support and good performance. It returns a 422 with exact field errors out of the box. And the integration team already knew Python, so they could maintain it easily.
x: I used FastAPI for the [vendor file pre-validation service], and it was the right fit for a few reasons.

The service checks vendor files before our .NET import runs, and returns exact errors, so problems are found early and are easy to explain to vendors. The heart of that is describing each file format precisely. FastAPI is built on Pydantic, where each format is a Python model with types and validation rules, like required fields, date formats and allowed values. Those models are very readable, so the integration team can easily understand and update them when a vendor changes its format.

FastAPI also gave us a lot for free. When a request doesn't match a model, it automatically returns a 422 response with the exact field and reason, which was exactly the kind of error report we wanted. It automatically generates OpenAPI documentation, with an interactive docs page, which made it easy for others to try the service. It supports async, so it handles I/O efficiently, and its performance is very good for a Python framework. Dependency injection, through Depends, kept it clean and testable.
And practically, the integration team already knew Python, so they could maintain it without depending on me.
It follows our standards, like logging, health checks, Docker and the pipeline, while our core business services stay in .NET.

p9-51.q: For I/O-bound glue such as the build-log summariser: fetch logs, parse text and return JSON. Node handles that well, and TypeScript MCP and HTTP libraries made it quick; core domain services stay in .NET.
i: Same logging, health and pipeline standards as .NET services.
Node fits I/O-bound text processing and quick tooling.
TypeScript gives type safety.
Core domain services stay in .NET for consistency.
f: Why not put it in the MCP server?
Separate service let other tools reuse it.
How does it summarise?
Finds failed steps and key error lines with patterns, returns a compact summary.
p9-51.y: I used Node.js for input-output heavy tools, like the [build-log summariser], which fetches logs, parses text and returns JSON. Node handles that very well, and the TypeScript MCP and HTTP libraries made it quick to build. It follows the same logging, health and pipeline standards, while our core business services stay in .NET.
x: I used Node.js for small, I/O-heavy tools, where it was a better fit than .NET, while our core business services stay in .NET.

The main example is a [build-log summariser]. Build and deployment logs can be huge, and when something fails, engineers used to scroll through thousands of lines to find the problem. The summariser fetches the logs for a failed build or deployment step from Azure DevOps, parses the text to find the errors and the most relevant lines around them, and returns a short JSON summary. It's also used by our MCP tooling, so the agent gets a concise summary instead of a huge log.

Node fitted well for a few reasons. The work is mostly I/O and text processing, which Node handles very efficiently with its asynchronous model. TypeScript gave us type safety, and the TypeScript libraries for MCP and HTTP made it quick to build. And it's small and fast to start, which suits a lightweight tool.

Even though it's a different language, it follows the same standards as our .NET services: structured logging, health checks, Docker, the same Azure DevOps pipeline with tests, and the same security practices.

My general view is that every new language adds maintenance cost, so there should be a clear reason for it. Here there was, but our core business logic stays in .NET, for consistency and long-term maintainability.

p9-52.q: Technically, GxP means audit trails on every data change (who, when, old and new values, reason), role-based access and e-signature rules (21 CFR Part 11), validated releases with traceability from requirement to test, change control, controlled deployments, data integrity (ALCOA+), and backups with tested restores.
i: Implemented via interceptors, database constraints, pipelines and approvals.
Audit trails for every change to GxP data (who, what, when, why).
Access control, electronic signatures where needed, validated releases, and change control.
Data integrity following ALCOA+ principles.
f: How is an e-signature implemented?
Re-authentication with meaning of signature recorded and linked to the record.
How does it affect code?
Audit fields, no hard deletes, strict validation and full tests.
p9-52.y: Technically, GxP means an audit trail for every data change, with who, when, old and new values, and why. It means role-based access and electronic signature rules from 21 CFR Part 11, validated releases with traceability from requirement to test, change control, controlled deployments, data integrity following ALCOA principles, and backups with tested restores.
p9-52.k: gxp technical, 21 cfr part 11, alcoa, audit trail
x: Technically, GxP means the system must be able to prove that it works correctly and that its data can be trusted. That turns into concrete technical features and practices.

First, audit trails. Every change to important data records who made it, when, the old and new values, and the reason. Users can't edit or delete audit records. Second, access control and electronic signatures. Role-based access ensures people only do what they're authorised to do, and electronic signatures follow 21 CFR Part 11 rules, like re-entering credentials to sign, linking the signature to the record, and recording its meaning. Third, validated releases. Requirements are traced to their tests and results. Every release goes through formal validation, FV, and UAT, with documented evidence. Fourth, change control. Every change has an approved change request with a risk assessment. Fifth, controlled deployments. The same validated artifact is promoted through environments, production deployments need named approvers, and production access is limited and logged. Sixth, data integrity, following the ALCOA plus principles: data is attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original and accurate, plus complete, consistent, enduring and available. That means constraints, transactions, validation, idempotent processing and reconciliation. And seventh, backups with tested restores, and disaster recovery.

In my day-to-day work, this shows up everywhere: in how we design data changes, write tests, document releases, and even in how I built the CIRT MCP server, which kept every approval and logged every action.

p11-1.q: Angular is a complete front-end framework from Google for building single-page applications, written in TypeScript. Unlike React, which is a UI library, Angular gives you everything in one box: components, dependency injection, a router, forms, an HTTP client, and RxJS for asynchronous work, plus a CLI that generates code and builds the app.
p11-1.k: angular, angular basics, angular architecture, spa
x: Angular is a complete front-end framework from Google for building single-page applications, written in TypeScript. Unlike React, which is a UI library, Angular gives you everything in one box: components, dependency injection, a router, forms, an HTTP client, and RxJS for asynchronous work, plus a CLI that generates code and builds the app.

An Angular app is a tree of components. Each component has a TypeScript class with the logic, an HTML template, and its own styles. Business logic and API calls live in services, which Angular injects into components through its dependency injection system. Routes map URLs to components, and features are usually loaded lazily, so the browser only downloads what the user needs. Older apps group things into NgModules; newer apps use standalone components, which declare their own imports.
The main building blocks, then, are components for the UI, services for logic and data, directives and pipes to extend templates, the router for navigation, and RxJS or signals for reactive data.

In our IRT product, Angular is used in the legacy portal's sub-applications and our newer internal study builder, while new site modules are built in React with TypeScript. Both are component-based: small reusable UI components that call our .NET backends. So I work in Angular when a feature touches those older screens, and in React for the new ones.

p11-2.q: A component is the basic building block of an Angular user interface. It controls one part of the screen, like a header, a data table, or a whole page.
x: A component is the basic building block of an Angular user interface. It controls one part of the screen, like a header, a data table, or a whole page.

A component has three parts. A TypeScript class, decorated with @Component, that holds the data and the logic, like properties and event handlers. An HTML template that describes what to show, using Angular's binding syntax to display data and react to events. And styles, which are scoped to that component by default, so they don't leak into the rest of the app. The decorator also defines a selector, like app-shipment-table, which is the custom HTML tag used to place the component inside other templates.

Components receive data from their parent through inputs, and send events back up through outputs, so they stay reusable and loosely coupled. They usually delegate API calls and business rules to injected services, which keeps the component focused on presentation. Angular also gives components lifecycle hooks, like ngOnInit for setup and ngOnDestroy for cleanup.

The idea is the same as in React: the UI is built from small, reusable pieces. In our IRT UI, for example, the older Angular screens use shared components like a site selector and a status badge across many pages, and the newer React modules follow the same component-based approach.

p11-3.q: NgModules were Angular's original way of organising an application. An NgModule is a class decorated with @NgModule that declares a set of components, directives and pipes, imports other modules it needs, provides services, and exports what other modules can use. A typical app had an AppModule, a SharedModule for common components, and feature modules for each area, often lazy-loaded.
p11-3.k: ngmodule, standalone, standalone components, declarations, angular modules
x: NgModules were Angular's original way of organising an application. An NgModule is a class decorated with @NgModule that declares a set of components, directives and pipes, imports other modules it needs, provides services, and exports what other modules can use. A typical app had an AppModule, a SharedModule for common components, and feature modules for each area, often lazy-loaded.

The problem was extra boilerplate and indirection. To use a component, you had to know which module declared it and import that module, and it was a common source of confusing errors, like "is not a known element".

Standalone components, introduced in Angular 14 and the default since Angular 17, remove that layer. A standalone component lists its own imports directly in its @Component decorator, like CommonModule, other components or pipes. The application starts with bootstrapApplication, and routes can lazy-load a standalone component or a set of routes directly. Services are usually provided with providedIn root, or in route providers.

Both still work, and they can be mixed, which matters for real projects. In an older codebase like the Angular part of our IRT UI, most screens use NgModules. New Angular work can use standalone components, and migration can happen gradually, one feature at a time, using Angular's schematics. For new code, I'd choose standalone, because it's simpler, easier to understand, and makes lazy loading more direct.

p11-4.q: Data binding is how Angular keeps the template and the component's data in sync, without manually changing the DOM. There are four kinds.
p11-4.k: data binding, interpolation, property binding, event binding, two-way binding, ngModel
x: Data binding is how Angular keeps the template and the component's data in sync, without manually changing the DOM. There are four kinds.

Interpolation, with double curly braces, displays a value as text, like the patient count or a study name. Property binding, with square brackets, sets a property of an element or a child component from the component's data, for example binding the disabled property of a button to whether the form is valid, or passing an input to a child component. Event binding, with round brackets, listens for an event, like a click or a keyup, and calls a method in the component. And two-way binding, with the banana-in-a-box syntax, square brackets around round brackets, combines both: it shows a value and updates it when the user changes it. The classic example is ngModel on a form input.
So data flows from the component to the view with interpolation and property binding, from the view to the component with event binding, and both ways with two-way binding.

In practice, I use one-way flows most of the time, because they're easier to reason about, and I use reactive forms instead of ngModel for anything non-trivial. It's a similar mindset to React, where data flows down through props and events flow up through callbacks.

p11-5.q: A directive is a class that adds behaviour to elements in an Angular template. There are three kinds.
p11-5.k: directives, ngIf, ngFor, structural directive, attribute directive, control flow, @if, @for
x: A directive is a class that adds behaviour to elements in an Angular template. There are three kinds.

Components are technically directives with their own template. Structural directives change the structure of the DOM by adding or removing elements. The classic ones are ngIf, which shows an element only when a condition is true, ngFor, which repeats an element for each item in a list, and ngSwitch. They're written with an asterisk, like star ngIf. Attribute directives change the appearance or behaviour of an existing element, without adding or removing it. Built-in examples are ngClass and ngStyle, and you can write your own, for example a highlight directive, or a directive that disables a button when the user lacks a permission.

Since Angular 17, there's also built-in control flow syntax: @if, @for and @switch blocks in the template. It's easier to read, it doesn't need imports, and @for requires a track expression, which is like a key in React, so Angular can update lists efficiently.

A custom attribute directive is a good example of reuse. In an IRT-style app, a directive that hides or disables actions based on the user's role keeps permission checks out of every template, though the real authorisation is always enforced by the .NET API.

p11-6.q: A pipe transforms a value for display in a template, without changing the underlying data. You use it with the vertical bar. Built-in examples are the date pipe for formatting dates, currency and decimal pipes for numbers, uppercase and lowercase, json for debugging, and the very important async pipe, which subscribes to an observable or promise and shows its latest value.
p11-6.k: pipes, pure pipe, impure pipe, async pipe, date pipe, custom pipe
x: A pipe transforms a value for display in a template, without changing the underlying data. You use it with the vertical bar. Built-in examples are the date pipe for formatting dates, currency and decimal pipes for numbers, uppercase and lowercase, json for debugging, and the very important async pipe, which subscribes to an observable or promise and shows its latest value.

You can write a custom pipe by creating a class with the @Pipe decorator and a transform method. For example, a pipe that turns a shipment status code into a friendly label, or masks part of an identifier.

Pipes are pure by default. A pure pipe only runs again when its input reference changes, so Angular can skip it during change detection. That makes it efficient. But it also means that if you change an array in place, like pushing an item, a pure pipe won't notice; you need to create a new array. An impure pipe, marked with pure false, runs on every change detection cycle. That's needed for things that change internally, like the async pipe, but it can be expensive, so custom impure pipes should be rare and very cheap.
A practical rule I follow is to use pipes instead of calling methods in templates, because a method in a template runs on every change detection cycle, while a pure pipe is cached.

p11-7.q: A service in Angular is a class that holds logic or data that doesn't belong to one component, like calling an API, sharing state between components, logging, or permission checks. It's marked with the @Injectable decorator.
p11-7.k: angular services, angular dependency injection, injectable, providedIn root, inject function, hierarchical injector
x: A service in Angular is a class that holds logic or data that doesn't belong to one component, like calling an API, sharing state between components, logging, or permission checks. It's marked with the @Injectable decorator.

Angular then provides it through dependency injection. Instead of creating the service with new, a component asks for it, either in its constructor or with the inject function, and Angular gives it an instance. That keeps components small, and makes testing easy, because a test can provide a fake service.

The scope depends on where it's provided. With providedIn root, there's one shared instance for the whole app, a singleton, and it's tree-shakable, so it's removed from the bundle if nobody uses it. You can also provide a service in a route, or in a component's providers, which creates a separate instance for that part of the tree. Angular's injectors are hierarchical: a component looks for a provider in its own injector, then its parents, then the root.

It's the same principle as dependency injection in ASP.NET Core, which I use every day: register once, ask for the abstraction, and let the container create it. [In our IRT Angular screens, for example, a study service wraps the HTTP calls for study data and caches reference lists], and components just inject it.

p11-8.q: RxJS is a library for reactive programming, and Angular uses it heavily. Its core type is the Observable: a stream of values over time that you can subscribe to. HttpClient calls, router events, and form value changes are all observables in Angular.
p11-8.k: rxjs, observable, promise, observable vs promise, subscribe, reactive programming
x: RxJS is a library for reactive programming, and Angular uses it heavily. Its core type is the Observable: a stream of values over time that you can subscribe to. HttpClient calls, router events, and form value changes are all observables in Angular.

The differences from a Promise are important. A Promise represents one future value; it's eager, meaning the work starts immediately when it's created, and it can't be cancelled. An Observable can emit zero, one or many values over time, it's lazy, so nothing happens until someone subscribes, and it can be cancelled by unsubscribing. For an HTTP call, unsubscribing actually cancels the request.

Observables also come with operators, like map, filter, debounceTime, switchMap and catchError, which you chain with pipe to transform streams. That makes complex asynchronous flows, like a search box that waits for the user to stop typing, cancels the previous request, and handles errors, very concise.

For a single API call, a Promise or an Observable both work, but in Angular I stay with observables to use the async pipe and operators. In our IRT Angular screens, a typical example is a site search box: valueChanges, then debounceTime, distinctUntilChanged, and switchMap to the API, so only the latest search result is shown.

p11-9.q: All four take each value from a source observable and map it to an inner observable, like an HTTP request. The difference is what happens when a new value arrives while an earlier inner observable is still running.
p11-9.k: switchmap, mergemap, concatmap, exhaustmap, higher-order observables, rxjs operators
x: All four take each value from a source observable and map it to an inner observable, like an HTTP request. The difference is what happens when a new value arrives while an earlier inner observable is still running.

switchMap cancels the previous inner observable and switches to the new one. It's perfect for search-as-you-type or loading details for the currently selected item, because only the latest result matters, and stale responses can't overwrite newer ones. mergeMap runs them all in parallel and merges the results as they arrive, in any order. It's good for independent work, like saving several items at once, but you lose ordering. concatMap queues them and runs one at a time, in order, waiting for each to finish. That's right when order matters, like a sequence of updates to the same record. exhaustMap ignores new values while the current one is still running. That's ideal for a submit button, so double clicks don't send two requests.
Choosing the wrong one causes real bugs. For example, using mergeMap for a search box can show results for an old query if its response arrives last.

In practice: switchMap for searches and selections, concatMap for ordered saves, exhaustMap for submits and logins, and mergeMap for parallel independent calls. [In our Angular screens, the save button on a form uses exhaustMap], so a double click can never create a duplicate record.

p11-10.q: A Subject is both an observable and an observer: you can subscribe to it, and you can push values into it with next. It's used to multicast values to many subscribers, often inside a service to share state or events between components.
p11-10.k: subject, behaviorsubject, replaysubject, asyncsubject, rxjs subjects
x: A Subject is both an observable and an observer: you can subscribe to it, and you can push values into it with next. It's used to multicast values to many subscribers, often inside a service to share state or events between components.

The difference between the types is what a new subscriber receives. A plain Subject has no memory: subscribers only get values emitted after they subscribe. That suits events, like "a file was uploaded". A BehaviorSubject requires an initial value and always holds the current value. A new subscriber immediately receives the latest value, and you can read it synchronously with getValue. That makes it ideal for state, like the currently selected study or the logged-in user. A ReplaySubject replays a number of previous values, or values within a time window, to new subscribers, which is useful for things like a recent activity log. There's also AsyncSubject, which only emits the last value when it completes.
A common pattern in Angular services is a private BehaviorSubject for state, exposed publicly as a read-only observable with asObservable, so components can read but only the service can change it.
In newer Angular, signals cover much of this state use case more simply, but BehaviorSubject is still everywhere in existing code, including our older IRT screens.

p11-11.q: A memory leak happens when a component subscribes to a long-lived observable, like a service's state, a timer or router events, and never unsubscribes. When the component is destroyed, the subscription keeps it alive, and its callback keeps running, which wastes memory and can cause strange behaviour, like duplicated API calls.
p11-11.k: unsubscribe, memory leak angular, async pipe, takeUntilDestroyed, takeUntil, subscriptions
x: A memory leak happens when a component subscribes to a long-lived observable, like a service's state, a timer or router events, and never unsubscribes. When the component is destroyed, the subscription keeps it alive, and its callback keeps running, which wastes memory and can cause strange behaviour, like duplicated API calls.

There are several ways to prevent it. The best is the async pipe in the template. It subscribes when the view is created and unsubscribes automatically when it's destroyed, and it also works nicely with OnPush change detection. The modern option in code is takeUntilDestroyed, from Angular's rxjs-interop package, which completes the subscription when the component is destroyed. The older pattern is takeUntil with a destroy Subject that's completed in ngOnDestroy. And for signals, converting with toSignal handles cleanup automatically.
It's also worth knowing that HttpClient observables complete after one response, so they don't leak in the usual sense, but unsubscribing still cancels the request if the user leaves the page.

My rule is: prefer the async pipe, and if I must subscribe in code, always pair it with takeUntilDestroyed. In code reviews of our Angular screens, a bare subscribe without cleanup is something I always flag.

p11-12.q: Change detection is how Angular keeps the screen in sync with the component's data. After something happens that might change data, like a click, an HTTP response or a timer, Angular checks the component tree from the top and updates any bindings whose values changed.
p11-12.k: change detection, onpush, zone.js, changedetectionstrategy, markforcheck, zoneless
x: Change detection is how Angular keeps the screen in sync with the component's data. After something happens that might change data, like a click, an HTTP response or a timer, Angular checks the component tree from the top and updates any bindings whose values changed.

Traditionally, Angular knows when to run this through zone.js, which patches browser async APIs, so after any async event, Angular runs change detection. With the default strategy, every component is checked on every cycle. That's simple, but in large screens with big tables, it can become slow.

OnPush is an optimisation. A component with ChangeDetectionStrategy OnPush is only checked when one of its inputs changes by reference, when an event happens inside it, when an async pipe in its template receives a value, or when you call markForCheck. That means you must treat input data as immutable: create a new array or object instead of changing it in place, otherwise the component won't update.
Newer Angular adds signals, which tell Angular exactly which component needs updating, and supports zoneless change detection, removing zone.js entirely.

In practice, I use OnPush for presentational components, especially lists and tables, with immutable data and the async pipe. [On a large grid screen in our Angular UI, switching row components to OnPush noticeably reduced lag when filtering.]

p11-13.q: Lifecycle hooks are methods Angular calls at specific moments in a component's life, so you can run code at the right time.
p11-13.k: lifecycle hooks, ngoninit, ngonchanges, ngondestroy, ngafterviewinit, angular lifecycle
x: Lifecycle hooks are methods Angular calls at specific moments in a component's life, so you can run code at the right time.

In order: ngOnChanges runs whenever an input property changes, and receives the previous and current values. ngOnInit runs once after the first inputs are set; it's the usual place for initial setup, like loading data. Constructors should only do simple dependency injection, not real work. ngDoCheck runs on every change detection cycle, for custom change checks, and should be used rarely. ngAfterContentInit and ngAfterContentChecked run after projected content, from ng-content, is initialised and checked. ngAfterViewInit and ngAfterViewChecked run after the component's own view and child components are ready; that's where you can safely access elements with ViewChild, for example to focus an input or initialise a chart. And ngOnDestroy runs just before the component is removed, which is where you clean up, like unsubscribing or stopping timers.
Newer Angular also offers the DestroyRef and takeUntilDestroyed for cleanup, and afterNextRender for DOM work, but the classic hooks are still used everywhere.

The React equivalent is useEffect: an effect with an empty dependency array is similar to ngOnInit, and its cleanup function is similar to ngOnDestroy. Since our IRT product uses both Angular and React, I often map between these two models.

p11-14.q: There are three main ways components share data in Angular.
p11-14.k: input, output, eventemitter, component communication, parent child, input signal
x: There are three main ways components share data in Angular.

From parent to child, with inputs. The child declares a property with @Input, or the newer input function that creates a signal, and the parent binds a value to it in the template with square brackets. For example, a parent page passes a list of sites to a site table component.

From child to parent, with outputs. The child declares an @Output, an EventEmitter, or the newer output function, and emits an event, for example when a row is selected. The parent listens with round brackets and handles it in a method. This keeps the child reusable, because it doesn't know what the parent will do.

Between components that aren't directly related, through a shared service. The service holds the state, for example in a BehaviorSubject or a signal, and components inject it, read the state, and call methods to change it. For larger apps, a state management library like NgRx or a signal store plays this role.

There's also ViewChild, to call a method on a child directly, and the router, for passing ids through the URL. The design rule I follow is the same as in React: data down, events up, and shared state in one well-defined place. That's how our Angular and React screens in IRT stay consistent, even though they're built with different frameworks.

p11-15.q: The Angular router maps URLs to components, so a single-page application can have different pages and deep links without full page reloads. You define a list of routes, each with a path and a component, or a lazily loaded component or set of child routes. A router-outlet in the template marks where the routed component appears, and routerLink creates navigation links. Route parameters, like a study id in the URL, are read through ActivatedRoute, or bound directly to component inputs in newer versions.
p11-15.k: angular router, route guards, canactivate, canmatch, resolver, route parameters
x: The Angular router maps URLs to components, so a single-page application can have different pages and deep links without full page reloads. You define a list of routes, each with a path and a component, or a lazily loaded component or set of child routes. A router-outlet in the template marks where the routed component appears, and routerLink creates navigation links. Route parameters, like a study id in the URL, are read through ActivatedRoute, or bound directly to component inputs in newer versions.

Guards decide whether navigation is allowed. canActivate runs before entering a route, typically to check that the user is logged in or has a role, and can redirect to login. canMatch decides whether a route definition should even match, which also prevents lazy code from loading for users who can't use it. canDeactivate runs before leaving, for example to warn about unsaved changes on a form. Resolvers can load data before the route activates. In modern Angular, guards are simple functions that use inject.
An important point is that guards are for user experience, not security. They hide screens, but the real protection is the .NET API checking the token and permissions on every request.
[In our IRT UI, for example, guards check that the user has a role on the selected study before showing an admin screen, and a canDeactivate guard protects forms with unsaved changes.]

p11-16.q: Lazy loading means the browser only downloads the code for a feature when the user actually navigates to it, instead of downloading the whole application at the start. It makes the first load much faster, especially for large enterprise apps with many modules that most users never open.
p11-16.k: lazy loading, loadchildren, loadcomponent, code splitting, preloading, defer
x: Lazy loading means the browser only downloads the code for a feature when the user actually navigates to it, instead of downloading the whole application at the start. It makes the first load much faster, especially for large enterprise apps with many modules that most users never open.

In Angular, you configure it in the routes. For a whole feature, loadChildren points to a function that imports that feature's routes or module. For a single standalone component, loadComponent imports just that component. The Angular CLI then automatically splits the code into separate bundles, called chunks, and the router downloads a chunk the first time its route is visited.

There are some useful extras. Preloading strategies can download lazy modules in the background after the app has loaded, so navigation is still instant. A canMatch guard prevents loading a module for users who aren't allowed to use it. And the newer defer block can lazy load parts of a template, like a heavy chart, only when they become visible.

In a product like our IRT UI, with separate areas for different modules and roles, lazy loading is essential. Site users never download the admin screens, for example. The same idea exists in React with React.lazy and route-based code splitting, which we use in the newer React modules.

p11-17.q: Angular has two ways to build forms.
p11-17.k: reactive forms, template-driven forms, formgroup, formcontrol, validators, ngmodel forms
x: Angular has two ways to build forms.

Template-driven forms define the form mostly in the HTML template, using ngModel and validation attributes like required. Angular builds the form model behind the scenes. They're quick and simple for small forms, like a login or a search box, but harder to test and to manage when the logic grows.

Reactive forms define the form model explicitly in the component's TypeScript code, with FormGroup, FormControl and FormArray, usually created with FormBuilder. The template just binds to that model. Validation is done with validator functions, including custom and cross-field validators, like "end date must be after start date", and asynchronous validators, like checking on the server that a code is unique. Value and status changes are observables, so you can react to them, and since Angular 14 the forms are strongly typed.
For anything non-trivial, I prefer reactive forms. They're explicit, predictable, easy to unit test without a browser, and handle dynamic forms well, like adding rows to a FormArray.

In our IRT Angular screens, data entry forms, like the ones for site or study settings, use reactive forms with custom validators, and the server validates everything again, returning field-level ProblemDetails errors that we map back onto the form.

p11-18.q: HttpClient is Angular's service for calling HTTP APIs. You inject it into a service and call methods like get and post, typed with the response model, and they return observables. In a well-structured app, components don't call HttpClient directly; they call a service, like a shipment API service, which keeps URLs and mapping in one place.

x: HttpClient is Angular's service for calling HTTP APIs. You inject it into a service and call methods like get and post, typed with the response model, and they return observables. In a well-structured app, components don't call HttpClient directly; they call a service, like a shipment API service, which keeps URLs and mapping in one place.

Interceptors sit in the middle of every request and response, like middleware in ASP.NET Core. They're perfect for cross-cutting concerns. An auth interceptor adds the access token to the Authorization header. A correlation interceptor adds a correlation id header, so a request can be traced through the backend logs. An error interceptor handles common errors in one place: on 401, it redirects to login or refreshes the token; on 403, it shows a permission message; and on validation errors, it passes the ProblemDetails through to the form. A loading interceptor can show a global spinner. Interceptors run in the order they're provided, and in modern Angular they're simple functions registered with provideHttpClient and withInterceptors.
For testing, HttpTestingController lets unit tests check the exact request and return a fake response.

In our IRT UI, the Angular interceptors and the React axios interceptors do the same jobs: the Keycloak token, correlation id and error mapping, so both parts of the UI behave identically against our .NET APIs.

p11-19.q: Signals are Angular's newer reactive primitive, stable since Angular 17. A signal is a wrapper around a value that tells Angular when it changes. You create one with signal and an initial value, read it by calling it like a function, and update it with set or update. computed creates a derived signal that recalculates only when the signals it depends on change, and it's cached. effect runs side effects, like logging or saving to local storage, whenever the signals it reads change.

x: Signals are Angular's newer reactive primitive, stable since Angular 17. A signal is a wrapper around a value that tells Angular when it changes. You create one with signal and an initial value, read it by calling it like a function, and update it with set or update. computed creates a derived signal that recalculates only when the signals it depends on change, and it's cached. effect runs side effects, like logging or saving to local storage, whenever the signals it reads change.

The big benefit is fine-grained change detection. Angular knows exactly which component uses which signal, so it can update just that component, and it enables zoneless applications without zone.js. Signals are also simpler to read and write than observables for plain state. Inputs and queries can now be signals too.

Signals don't replace RxJS. Signals are best for synchronous state: the current value of something, like the selected site or a filter. RxJS is still best for asynchronous streams and events: HTTP calls, debouncing, cancellation and combining streams. The interop functions toSignal and toObservable connect the two, for example turning an HTTP observable into a signal for the template.

For new Angular code, I'd use signals for component and service state, and keep RxJS for async flows. It's similar in spirit to useState and derived values in React, which helps when moving between our Angular and React screens.

p11-20.q: I choose the simplest option that fits how widely the state is shared and how complex it is.
p11-20.k: ngrx, state management angular, store, signal store, services state, redux angular, ngrx, ngrx store
x: I choose the simplest option that fits how widely the state is shared and how complex it is.

Local state stays in the component, as properties or signals, like whether a panel is open. Shared state for one feature lives in a service, using a BehaviorSubject or signals, exposed as read-only, with methods to change it. That covers most needs, like the currently selected study and site shared across a few screens. Server data, like lists from the API, can be cached in those services too, with care to refresh it.

For large applications with complex, widely shared state, NgRx is the standard library. It follows the Redux pattern: a single store, actions that describe events, reducers that produce new state, selectors to read it efficiently, and effects for side effects like API calls. It's very predictable and has great dev tools, but it adds a lot of boilerplate, so I only use it where it pays off. The newer NgRx Signal Store is lighter and based on signals.

Whatever the tool, the principles are the same: one source of truth, immutable updates, and keeping server state separate from UI state. That's the same thinking as the Redux Toolkit slices in the React part of our IRT UI, which makes it easier for the team to work in both frameworks.

p11-21.q: I start by measuring, with Angular DevTools' profiler and the browser's performance tools, so I fix real problems rather than guesses. Then the usual improvements fall into three groups.

Loading time. Lazy load feature routes, so users only download what they open. Use defer blocks for heavy parts of a page, like charts. Keep bundles small: check them with a bundle analyser, remove unused libraries, and rely on tree-shakable providedIn root services. Production builds with ahead-of-time compilation are the default.

Rendering. Use OnPush change detection with immutable data, or signals, so Angular checks only what changed. Always use track in @for, or trackBy in ngFor, so lists reuse DOM elements instead of recreating them. Avoid calling methods in templates; use pure pipes or computed signals instead. For very long lists, use virtual scrolling from the CDK, so only visible rows are rendered.

Data. Avoid duplicate HTTP calls by caching reference data in services, use switchMap to cancel stale requests, debounce search inputs, and ask the API for paged, filtered data instead of loading everything.
[A real example from our Angular UI: a large grid felt slow when filtering. Adding trackBy, OnPush on the row component, and server-side paging made it responsive again.]

p11-22.q: I test Angular at three levels.
p11-22.k: angular testing, testbed, jasmine, karma, jest angular, httptestingcontroller, component testing
x: I test Angular at three levels.

Unit tests for services, pipes and plain logic. These don't need the framework much: I create the service, provide fakes for its dependencies, and check the results. For services that use HttpClient, HttpTestingController lets me check that the right request was made, with the right URL and body, and return a fake response or an error.

Component tests with TestBed. TestBed configures a small testing module with the component, its imports, and fake versions of its services. I create the component, set inputs, trigger events like clicks, run change detection, and check what the template shows. Angular Testing Library makes these tests read more like what a user does, querying by role and label rather than CSS classes. The test runner has traditionally been Karma with Jasmine; many teams now use Jest, and newer Angular moves towards Vitest.
End-to-end tests with Playwright or Cypress, running the real app in a browser, for the key user flows. We use Playwright, with Cucumber scenarios for business-readable flows.

The principles are the same as for React: test behaviour, not implementation details, keep unit tests fast, and keep a small number of reliable end-to-end tests for the critical paths, like randomising a subject in a test study.

p11-23.q: Angular templates aren't plain HTML; they have to be compiled into JavaScript instructions that create and update the DOM. There are two ways to do that.
p11-23.k: aot, jit, ivy, angular compiler, ahead of time compilation
x: Angular templates aren't plain HTML; they have to be compiled into JavaScript instructions that create and update the DOM. There are two ways to do that.

Just-in-time, or JIT, compiles templates in the browser at runtime. It was used for development in older versions, but it means shipping the compiler to the browser and doing extra work at startup. Ahead-of-time, or AOT, compiles templates during the build. The browser receives ready-to-run code, so the app starts faster, the bundle is smaller because the compiler isn't shipped, and template errors, like binding to a property that doesn't exist, are caught at build time instead of by users. AOT has been the default for both development and production builds for several versions.

Ivy is Angular's rendering and compilation engine, the default since Angular 9, replacing the older View Engine. Ivy compiles each component independently into efficient instructions, which made bundles smaller through better tree-shaking, builds faster, debugging easier, and it made features like standalone components and signals possible.

In day-to-day work, you rarely think about Ivy directly, but understanding AOT helps explain build errors in templates, and why strict template type-checking is worth enabling. [We keep strictTemplates switched on in our Angular projects], so template mistakes fail the build.

For example, a card or dialog component provides the frame, title bar and buttons, and the parent decides what goes inside. With multi-slot projection, using select, a component can have several slots, like a header, a body and a footer. It's the Angular equivalent of passing children in React.

x: Content projection lets a parent pass a piece of markup into a child component, which places it inside its own template using ng-content. It's how you build flexible container components. For example, a card or dialog component provides the frame, title bar and buttons, and the parent decides what goes inside. With multi-slot projection, using select, a component can have several slots, like a header, a body and a footer. It's the Angular equivalent of passing children in React.

ViewChild and ContentChild are ways for a component to get a reference to something. ViewChild looks inside the component's own template, for elements, directives or child components it declares itself. For example, getting a reference to an input to focus it, or to a child component to call a method. ContentChild looks at the content that was projected into the component by its parent. For example, a tab group component finding the tab components placed inside it. The plural versions, ViewChildren and ContentChildren, return lists. They're available after the view or content is initialised, and newer Angular offers signal-based versions.

These features are what make good reusable component libraries possible. In our shared component set, dialogs and panels use content projection, so every screen gets consistent layout and behaviour, while each feature supplies its own content.

p11-25.q: I handle errors at three levels, so users see helpful messages and we still get the details we need to investigate.
p11-25.k: angular error handling, errorhandler, catcherror, global error handler, problemdetails angular
x: I handle errors at three levels, so users see helpful messages and we still get the details we need to investigate.

First, HTTP errors, in one place. An HTTP interceptor catches failed responses. A 401 sends the user to login or refreshes the token, a 403 shows a "no permission" message, a 404 shows a not-found message, and 5xx errors show a friendly "something went wrong" with the correlation id, so support can find the request in the backend logs. Validation errors, returned by our .NET APIs as ProblemDetails, are passed back to the form and shown next to the right fields.
Second, local handling where the screen needs it, using the catchError operator in RxJS to show an inline error state, fall back to empty data, or let the user retry. I don't swallow errors silently.

Third, a global ErrorHandler. Angular lets you replace its default ErrorHandler with your own class, which catches any unhandled error in the app, logs it, ideally to a monitoring service with the user's context, and shows a generic message instead of a broken screen.

It's the same structure as our backend: specific handling where it's needed, plus a global safety net. The React modules mirror it with error boundaries and a shared API client, so both parts of the IRT UI behave consistently.

For props, I define an interface or a type, like ShipmentTableProps, with each prop and its type, marking optional ones with a question mark, and I type the function's parameter with it. I usually don't use React.FC; a plain function with typed props is clearer. For children, I use React.ReactNode. For event handler props, I type the callback, like onSelect taking a site id and returning void. For variants, union types are great: a status prop typed as "active", "on hold" or "closed" means you can't pass anything else.

Custom hooks return typed objects. For reusable components, like a data table, generics let one component work for any row type while keeping full type safety.
For API data, I use types generated from the backend's OpenAPI definition, so the front end and the .NET API share one contract.
When our team moved new modules from Angular to React, strict TypeScript was non-negotiable, because Angular had already given us typed code, and we didn't want to lose that safety.

p12-2.q: A custom hook is a JavaScript function whose name starts with "use", and which calls other hooks, like useState, useEffect or useContext. It's React's way to reuse stateful logic between components, without copying code and without wrappers like higher-order components.
p12-2.k: custom hooks, usehook, reusable logic, hooks rules, use prefix
x: A custom hook is a JavaScript function whose name starts with "use", and which calls other hooks, like useState, useEffect or useContext. It's React's way to reuse stateful logic between components, without copying code and without wrappers like higher-order components.

The important point is that a custom hook shares logic, not state. Each component that calls it gets its own independent state. And the rules of hooks apply: call hooks only at the top level of a component or another hook, never inside conditions or loops, so React can match them up on every render.

Some examples I've used. A useDebounce hook that takes a value and a delay, and returns the value only after the user stops typing, used for search boxes. A usePermission hook that reads the current user's roles from context and returns whether they can perform an action, so components just ask "can I edit this site?". And a useStudyContext hook that returns the currently selected study and site, and throws a clear error if it's used outside the provider.
For data fetching, I now mostly use React Query's useQuery inside small custom hooks, like useShipments with a study id, so components don't know about URLs or caching at all.

Custom hooks make components short and readable, and the logic is easy to unit test on its own. They're the React equivalent of injectable services in Angular, which is a comparison I often make, since our IRT UI uses both frameworks.

p12-3.q: React Query, now called TanStack Query, is a library for managing server state in React: data that lives on the backend and that the UI fetches, caches and keeps up to date.
p12-3.k: react query, tanstack query, usequery, usemutation, server state, caching, data fetching
x: React Query, now called TanStack Query, is a library for managing server state in React: data that lives on the backend and that the UI fetches, caches and keeps up to date.

Without it, every component needs its own useEffect, loading flag, error flag and caching logic, which leads to duplicated requests and stale data. With React Query, you call useQuery with a query key, like shipments and a study id, and a function that calls the API. It returns the data, plus isLoading and error states. It caches the result by that key, so other components asking for the same data reuse it, deduplicates requests that happen at the same time, retries failures, and refetches in the background when data becomes stale or the window regains focus.

For changes, useMutation sends a POST or PUT, and on success I invalidate the related query keys, so lists refresh automatically. Optimistic updates are also possible, where the UI updates immediately and rolls back if the server fails.
My rule is to keep server state in React Query and only UI state, like open panels or selected filters, in useState, context or Redux Toolkit. That removes a lot of state management code.

In the newer React modules of our IRT UI, data fetching is wrapped in small typed hooks around shared axios instances, which add the Keycloak token, with Redux Toolkit slices for shared state, calling our newer .NET 9 and 10 APIs.

p12-4.q: An error boundary is a React component that catches JavaScript errors thrown while rendering its child components, logs them, and shows a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole application. Without one, an error in a single component unmounts the entire React tree, and the user sees a blank screen.

x: An error boundary is a React component that catches JavaScript errors thrown while rendering its child components, logs them, and shows a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole application. Without one, an error in a single component unmounts the entire React tree, and the user sees a blank screen.

Error boundaries are still class components, because they rely on two lifecycle methods: getDerivedStateFromError, to switch to the fallback UI, and componentDidCatch, to log the error and component stack, for example to a monitoring service. In practice, most teams use the small react-error-boundary library, which gives a ready component with a fallback and a reset button, so you can write everything else as function components.

There are limits to know. Error boundaries don't catch errors in event handlers, in asynchronous code like promises and timeouts, or in server-side rendering. Those are handled with try-catch, or with the error states of React Query.

Placement matters. I put one boundary at the top of the app as a final safety net, and others around each major area or widget, like a dashboard panel, so one failing part doesn't take down the page. The fallback shows a friendly message and the correlation id, which helps support trace the failure in the backend logs.
It's the React counterpart to Angular's global ErrorHandler, and in our IRT UI both are set up to behave the same way.

p12-5.q: I test React components the way a user uses them, with React Testing Library, running on Jest or Vitest.

The idea is to test behaviour, not implementation. I render the component, find elements the way a user would, by role, label or text, for example getByRole button with the name Save, interact with user-event, like typing and clicking, and assert what the user sees, like a validation message or a new row in the table.
