p17-2.q: So for me, boundaries come from the business, not from technical layers or tables. Like, I won't make a "database service" and a "validation service". I use domain-driven design thinking, basically finding bounded contexts, where a word like "shipment" or "subject" has one clear meaning and one team owns the rules around it.
p17-2.k: microservice boundaries, service boundaries, how to split microservices, decompose monolith, bounded context, how do you decide services
x: So for me, boundaries come from the business, not from technical layers or tables. Like, I won't make a "database service" and a "validation service". I use domain-driven design thinking, basically finding bounded contexts, where a word like "shipment" or "subject" has one clear meaning and one team owns the rules around it.

Then I check a few things. Who owns the data? Each service should own its own data, and nobody else should be writing into its tables. Then, what changes together? If two things always go out in the same release, honestly they probably belong in one service. Then I look at the communication. If two services need lots of chatty synchronous calls just to finish one request, the boundary is wrong somewhere. And team ownership, one team should be able to own and deploy the service on its own.
One thing I'm careful about is not going too small. Nano-services with one table each give you network calls, distributed transactions and ops cost, and no real benefit.

In our IRT, if you look at it, randomisation, supply and shipments, drug accountability and notifications are natural boundaries, because each one has its own rules, its own data and its own users. And when I'm not sure, I start with a well-structured modular monolith and split a module out only when there's a clear reason, like independent scaling or a separate team. That's usually my approach.

p17-3.q: Okay, so when A calls B and B calls C and things get slow, two things I do. One, prove where the time is actually going. Two, stop the slowness from spreading to A and B.

x: Okay, so when A calls B and B calls C and things get slow, two things I do. One, prove where the time is actually going. Two, stop the slowness from spreading to A and B.

For the first part, I go to distributed tracing with the correlation id. The trace shows every hop with its duration, so I can clearly see A is waiting on B and B is waiting on C. Then I open C's own metrics, latency percentiles, error rate, CPU, memory, thread pool, database time, and whatever C itself is calling. Mostly the cause is in C's dependency, like a slow query, some lock, a missing index or an external API. Or it's plain saturation after a traffic jump or a recent release.

While C is being fixed, I protect the callers. Every call should have a timeout, so B doesn't wait forever. Retries are limited, with backoff and jitter, otherwise we just hammer C harder. A circuit breaker on B's calls to C fails fast when C is unhealthy, and B gives a fallback or a clear error. And bulkheads, so C's slowness doesn't eat up all of B's threads or connections.
Then longer term I ask, does this chain even need to be synchronous? If B is only informing C about something, put a message on a queue and the dependency is gone. So yeah, that's how I'd handle it.

p17-4.q: See, a circuit breaker is basically: if a dependency is clearly failing, stop calling it for some time and fail fast, instead of piling up slow requests.
p17-4.k: circuit breaker, implement circuit breaker, polly circuit breaker, circuit breaker pattern dotnet, open closed half open, resilience pipeline
x: See, a circuit breaker is basically: if a dependency is clearly failing, stop calling it for some time and fail fast, instead of piling up slow requests.

It has three states. Closed is normal, calls go through and failures are counted. When failures cross a threshold, say more than half the calls fail within 30 seconds, with at least 20 calls, the breaker opens. While it's open, calls fail immediately, we don't even touch the dependency. After a break duration it goes half-open and lets a few trial calls through. If they work, it closes again. If not, back to open.

In .NET I use Polly, which is now built into Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience. On a typed HttpClient I add a resilience pipeline with a timeout, a retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and the circuit breaker, in that order, so retries happen inside the breaker's view. Then I tune failure ratio, sampling duration, minimum throughput and break duration.

When the circuit is open, the caller gets a BrokenCircuitException. I handle that with a fallback, like cached data, a default value, or a clear 503 to the client. And I log state changes and push metrics, so we get an alert when a breaker opens.
One thing I learned is to count only real failures, like timeouts and 5xx. If you count 404s or validation errors, the breaker opens for no reason. That's pretty much how I implement it.

p17-5.q: So I think about it in layers. But for authentication specifically, my answer is OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, with JWT access tokens from one central identity provider. Never a home-grown login inside each service.
p17-5.k: secure microservices, microservices security, authentication for microservices, which authentication microservices, oauth microservices, service to service auth
x: So I think about it in layers. But for authentication specifically, my answer is OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, with JWT access tokens from one central identity provider. Never a home-grown login inside each service.

For users, the front end signs in through the identity provider with authorization code flow plus PKCE. The provider gives a short-lived access token, a JWT, and every API validates it, I mean the signature against the provider's public keys, the issuer, the audience and the expiry. Then authorization happens inside each service with roles, scopes or policies, because only that service really knows its own rules.

For service-to-service calls we use client credentials flow. So each service has its own identity and only the scopes it needs. On top of that, mutual TLS or a service mesh can encrypt and authenticate traffic inside the network.
Then there's the rest around it. API gateway for rate limiting and one entry point, HTTPS everywhere, secrets in a vault, least privilege on the databases, input validation, audit logging.

In our IRT, Keycloak is the identity provider. The React app uses OIDC, our newer .NET APIs validate Keycloak JWTs with the bearer handler, and permissions come from role, module and action rules. So that's how we've set it up.

p17-6.q: Backend, always. It has to be enforced in the API, normally in the middleware. The front end only helps the user sign in and carries the token. Because, see, you can't trust the client. Anybody can change JavaScript in the browser or just call the API directly from Postman.
p17-6.k: which layer authentication, authentication frontend or backend, authentication middleware layer, where to implement authentication, authenticate in ui or api
x: Backend, always. It has to be enforced in the API, normally in the middleware. The front end only helps the user sign in and carries the token. Because, see, you can't trust the client. Anybody can change JavaScript in the browser or just call the API directly from Postman.

So how it works in practice. The front end redirects the user to the identity provider, gets the tokens back, stores them safely, and attaches the access token on every API call, like with an axios interceptor in React or an HTTP interceptor in Angular. It can hide menus the user can't access, but that's just user experience, it's not security.

In the backend, ASP.NET Core's authentication middleware validates the JWT on every request, before any controller even runs, and builds the user's identity. After that authorization kicks in, roles and policies on the endpoints, and sometimes resource-level checks in business logic, like "can this user actually see this site's data".
An API gateway can also validate tokens early and throw out bad traffic. But each service still validates the token itself, defence in depth basically.

In our IRT, the React app uses Keycloak with OIDC, and every new .NET API validates the JWT in middleware, with role and module checks done through policies. So the answer is middleware in the backend, with the front end just helping.

p17-7.q: Okay, so idempotent means if you do the operation ten times, the effect is the same as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition. POST is not, and honestly POST is where all the trouble comes, retries and double clicks creating duplicate orders or payments.
p17-7.k: idempotency rest api, idempotent api, idempotency key, prevent duplicate requests, retry safe api, double submit api
x: Okay, so idempotent means if you do the operation ten times, the effect is the same as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition. POST is not, and honestly POST is where all the trouble comes, retries and double clicks creating duplicate orders or payments.

The standard way is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique key, like a GUID, and sends it in a header, say Idempotency-Key. On the server, before doing any work, I check a store for that key. If it's new, I mark it in progress, do the work, and save the response against the key. If the same key comes again, I just return the saved response, I don't do the work again. If it's still in progress, I return 409. And keys expire after some time, maybe 24 hours.

The check has to be atomic, that's the part people miss. A unique constraint in the database, or Redis SET with NX, so two parallel requests can't both pass. Ideally the key gets saved in the same transaction as the business change.

I also keep database constraints as the last safety net. In our IRT I used exactly this for re-randomisation. Idempotency key from the UI, plus a unique constraint of one assignment per subject per stage. So even if there's a retry, the subject can never get randomised twice. That's how we handled it.

p17-8.q: That's what we call a captive dependency. See, a singleton lives for the whole application. So if it takes a scoped service in its constructor, that scoped instance gets captured and lives forever too, instead of living for one request.
p17-8.k: singleton depends on scoped, captive dependency, scoped inside singleton, singleton scoped problem, inject scoped into singleton, cannot consume scoped service from singleton
x: That's what we call a captive dependency. See, a singleton lives for the whole application. So if it takes a scoped service in its constructor, that scoped instance gets captured and lives forever too, instead of living for one request.

And the drawbacks are pretty serious. DbContext is scoped, right? So a captured DbContext gets shared across all requests and all threads. DbContext isn't thread-safe, so you start seeing random concurrency exceptions, stale cached entities, memory growing because of change tracking, and in the worst case one user's data leaking into another user's request. Anything request-specific, like the current user, would be wrong for everybody after the first request.

ASP.NET Core does protect you in development. Scope validation is on, and you get an error like "Cannot consume scoped service from singleton". But in production that check is off by default, so if you didn't test properly, it can slip through.

Fix depends on the case. If the consumer doesn't really need to be a singleton, just make it scoped. If it has to be a singleton, like a background service, inject IServiceScopeFactory, create a scope for each unit of work, resolve the scoped service inside it, and dispose the scope after. For DbContext specifically, IDbContextFactory is a clean option.
And in our projects I always turn on ValidateScopes and ValidateOnBuild, so these mistakes fail at startup itself.

For state in a big React app, the first thing is to stop treating all state the same. There are different kinds and they need different tools. Server state, meaning data from APIs, I put in a data-fetching library like React Query or RTK Query, because you get caching, loading states, refetching, invalidation for free. Global client state, like the logged-in user, the selected study, UI preferences, that goes into Redux Toolkit or a small store like Zustand. Local stuff, like whether a dialog is open, just stays in useState in the component. Forms go into something like React Hook Form. And filters and paging I keep in the URL query string, so links can be shared.
The mistakes I try to avoid are dumping everything into Redux, and putting fast-changing values into one big Context, because then every consumer re-renders.

In our React shell, we use Redux Toolkit for shared state, with a slice per feature module, and axios with interceptors for the API calls. That way each npm feature package stays independent. So that's how we manage it.

p17-10.q: They're actually for different things. useState stores state, a value that belongs to the component, and when you change it through the setter, React re-renders. useMemo doesn't store state at all. It just caches the result of some calculation between renders, and recalculates only when its dependencies change.
p17-10.k: usestate vs usememo, use state vs use memo, usememo usestate difference, react usememo, react usestate
x: They're actually for different things. useState stores state, a value that belongs to the component, and when you change it through the setter, React re-renders. useMemo doesn't store state at all. It just caches the result of some calculation between renders, and recalculates only when its dependencies change.

Let me take an example. With useState, I take count and setCount from useState with zero, and when I call setCount, the component re-renders with the new value. With useMemo, I'd write something like a total that reduces over items, with items in the dependency array, and React keeps giving me the old total until items actually changes.

Where do I use useMemo? Mainly two places. One is expensive calculations, like filtering or sorting a few thousand rows. The other is keeping the same object or array reference between renders, so a child wrapped in React.memo, or a useEffect dependency, doesn't think it got a new value every time.

The common mistake I see is people putting useMemo everywhere. It has its own cost and the code gets harder to read, so I add it only when the profiler shows a slow calculation or extra re-renders. Another mistake is storing derived values in useState and syncing them with useEffect. It's simpler to just calculate during render, with useMemo if it's heavy. That's the difference in short.

p17-11.q: First thing, I measure. React DevTools Profiler, and the highlight updates option, to see which components are re-rendering and why. Because optimising without measuring, honestly, mostly just adds complexity.
p17-11.k: prevent re renders react, unnecessary re-renders, react re render optimization, react performance, avoid re rendering, react memo usecallback
x: First thing, I measure. React DevTools Profiler, and the highlight updates option, to see which components are re-rendering and why. Because optimising without measuring, honestly, mostly just adds complexity.

Then I pick the right fix. Keep state close to where it's used, so typing in one input doesn't re-render the whole page. Wrap pure, expensive children in React.memo so they skip rendering when props haven't changed. But then the props need to be stable, so useCallback for functions and useMemo for objects and arrays going into those memoised children, because a new function on every render just breaks memo. If there's a big Context, I split it, or move fast-changing values into a store with selectors, like Redux Toolkit or Zustand, so components only subscribe to what they need. Stable keys in lists, never the array index if items can move. And for really long lists, virtualisation, so only the visible rows render.
One more small thing, don't define components inside other components. That remounts them every single time.

In our React shell, we had a drug accountability grid that was slow because every keystroke in a filter re-rendered all the rows. [Moving the filter state down, memoising the row component and virtualising the grid made typing smooth again.] So that's the kind of thing I do.

p17-12.q: So code splitting is breaking one big JavaScript bundle into smaller chunks. Lazy loading is downloading a chunk only when it's actually needed. Put together, the first page load becomes much faster.
p17-12.k: lazy loading code splitting, react lazy suspense, code splitting react, lazy load routes, dynamic import, angular lazy loading
x: So code splitting is breaking one big JavaScript bundle into smaller chunks. Lazy loading is downloading a chunk only when it's actually needed. Put together, the first page load becomes much faster.

In React I use React.lazy with a dynamic import, like a Reports component that's lazily imported from its own file, and wrap it in Suspense with a spinner as fallback. Where it helps most is route-level splitting. Each page is its own chunk, so the login page doesn't download the reporting module. I also lazy load heavy things that aren't visible at first, like charts, rich text editors, big dialogs. Vite and webpack create the chunks automatically from the dynamic imports. I put an error boundary around lazy parts, because a chunk download can fail right after a deployment. And sometimes I prefetch the likely next page on hover.
In Angular, it's built into the router. loadChildren for a feature module, loadComponent for a standalone component, and now the defer blocks in templates also.
After that I check the result with the bundle analyser and Lighthouse, just to confirm it actually got smaller.

In our React shell, each feature module is a separate npm package, and the shell lazy loads each one by route. So a site user who never opens drug accountability never downloads that code at all. That's how we did it.

First thing is evidence. Error monitoring, like Sentry or Datadog RUM, captures the JavaScript errors with stack traces mapped back to the TypeScript source, through source maps we upload in the pipeline. You also get the browser, the release version and what the user clicked before the error. In React, an error boundary catches render errors, shows a friendly message and reports it. p17-14.q: So GTmetrix is an online tool that tests how fast a web page loads, and more importantly tells you why it's slow. You give it a URL, it loads the page in a real browser from a test location and device you choose, and then you get a performance grade and a detailed report.
p17-14.k: gtmetrix, gt metrics, gt metrix, gtmetrics tool, page speed tool, website performance test
x: So GTmetrix is an online tool that tests how fast a web page loads, and more importantly tells you why it's slow. You give it a URL, it loads the page in a real browser from a test location and device you choose, and then you get a performance grade and a detailed report.

The report is built on Google Lighthouse underneath. It shows the Web Vitals, like Largest Contentful Paint, which is basically when the main content shows up, Total Blocking Time, and Cumulative Layout Shift, which is things jumping around on the page. The part I find most useful is the waterfall chart. It shows every request the page makes, in order, with size and timing, so you can spot that one huge image, a slow API call, render-blocking scripts, or just too many requests. It also gives specific suggestions, like compress images, enable caching, reduce unused JavaScript. And you can track a page over time and get alerts when it gets slower.

It's similar to PageSpeed Insights and WebPageTest. One limitation though, it tests public URLs from its own servers. So for an internal app behind a login, like ours, I'd rather use Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools or in the CI pipeline, plus real-user monitoring.
I mostly use these after a release, just to check bundle sizes and load times haven't gone worse.

p17-16.q: Honestly, I always start by measuring, because the slow part is almost never where you guess.
p17-16.k: python slow, optimize python, python performance, speed up python, profile python, python bottleneck

To find the bottleneck, I use cProfile, or py-spy, which is nice because it attaches to a running process without changing code and gives you a flame graph. If it's a web service, I look at traces and logs first, to see whether the time is going into the database, external calls, or the Python code itself.

Then the fix depends on what I find. If it's I/O, like DB or HTTP calls, I cut down the number of calls, batch them, add indexes, cache results, or use async with asyncio and httpx so calls run in parallel. If it's CPU, like pure Python loops, then better algorithms and data structures, sets and dicts for lookups instead of lists, vectorise with NumPy or pandas, use built-ins, or move the hot path to a compiled library. And because of the GIL, threads won't help CPU work, so there I go for multiprocessing or ProcessPoolExecutor. For memory, generators, so I stream large data instead of loading everything at once.
For web services I also check the server setup. Enough uvicorn or gunicorn workers, connection pooling, and no blocking calls inside async code, because that just freezes the event loop.
And then I measure again, to actually prove it got better. So yeah, measure, fix, measure.

p17-17.q: All three run your code on AWS. The difference is basically how much you manage yourself.
p17-17.k: ecs vs eks vs lambda, ecs eks lambda difference, aws container options, when to use eks, aws compute choices, eks vs ecs
x: All three run your code on AWS. The difference is basically how much you manage yourself.

ECS, Elastic Container Service, is AWS's own container orchestrator. You define a task definition with your Docker image, CPU, memory and environment, and an ECS service keeps the desired number of tasks running behind a load balancer. With Fargate you don't even manage servers. It's simple, and it's tightly integrated with IAM, CloudWatch and the load balancers.

EKS is managed Kubernetes. AWS runs the control plane, and you use normal Kubernetes objects, Deployments, Services, Ingress and so on. It's more powerful and portable across clouds, and the ecosystem is huge, Helm, service meshes, all that. But honestly you need more Kubernetes skill and more operational effort.

Lambda is serverless functions. You upload code, it runs in response to events, like an API Gateway request, an S3 upload, an SQS message. It scales automatically, even to zero, and you pay per invocation. The catches are the 15-minute limit, cold starts and less control.

So my rule of thumb is like this. Lambda for event-driven glue and spiky, short tasks. ECS for most containerised APIs and workers when you're on AWS. And EKS when the team already knows Kubernetes or you really need its ecosystem or portability. That's how I'd pick.

After that I fix the cause, load test the fix, and tune auto scaling and alarms, so next time we scale out before latency suffers. That's how I'd go about it.

p17-19.q: So when a task keeps starting and stopping, that's ECS replacing tasks that either exit or fail health checks. My job is to find why it stops.
p17-19.k: ecs task restarting, ecs task keeps stopping, ecs task crash loop, ecs stopped task reason, container keeps restarting ecs, task stops and starts
x: So when a task keeps starting and stopping, that's ECS replacing tasks that either exit or fail health checks. My job is to find why it stops.

First place I look is the stopped task's details. In the console or with describe-tasks, every stopped task has a stopped reason and an exit code. "Essential container exited" with exit code 1 usually means the app crashed at startup. Exit code 137 means it got killed, mostly out of memory, and you'll see OutOfMemoryError. "Task failed ELB health checks" means it started but the load balancer marked it unhealthy. And "CannotPullContainerError" is an image or permission problem.

Then the logs, in CloudWatch Logs for that task, just before it stopped. Startup crashes, honestly nine times out of ten, are a missing environment variable, a secret the task role can't read, a wrong connection string or a port mismatch.

Then health checks. If the app is slow to start, the grace period might be too short and ECS kills it before it's even ready. I check the health check path, the expected status code, the timeouts, and that the container is listening on the right port.
And resources, memory limit too low or CPU too small for startup.
The deployment circuit breaker can roll back automatically, which helps. Once it's fixed, I add a startup configuration check, so next time the failure is obvious in the logs.

p17-20.q: Yes, I have. In IQVIA's newer services on AWS, I've worked with RDS for SQL Server, for relational data where you need transactions and joins, and DynamoDB for simpler, high-volume lookups, like status and event data. Our main CIRT platform itself is on on-premise SQL Server, just to be clear.
p17-20.k: rds and dynamodb, partition key dynamodb, dynamo db partition key, dynamic db partition key, hash key dynamodb, what is partition key
x: Yes, I have. In IQVIA's newer services on AWS, I've worked with RDS for SQL Server, for relational data where you need transactions and joins, and DynamoDB for simpler, high-volume lookups, like status and event data. Our main CIRT platform itself is on on-premise SQL Server, just to be clear.

Now the partition key. In DynamoDB, it's the attribute DynamoDB uses to decide where an item physically lives. It hashes the partition key value and puts the item in one of many partitions. Every item must have it, and if the table has only a partition key, it has to be unique, like an order id.

You can also have a sort key. Then the primary key is the combination of both, and many items can share the same partition key, stored together and sorted by the sort key. Let me take an example, partition key is shipmentId and sort key is the event timestamp. Then I can query all events for one shipment in time order with one query.

The partition key matters a lot for performance. Each partition has throughput limits, so you want many distinct values with evenly spread traffic. If you pick something like "status" with only a few values, you get hot partitions and throttling. And queries need the partition key, without it you're doing a scan, which is slow and expensive. So that's the idea.

p17-21.q: So in DynamoDB you design keys from your access patterns, not from your entities. Because you can only query efficiently by key, that's the whole game.
p17-21.k: dynamodb key design, design partition keys large scale, dynamo db key design, single table design, hot partition dynamodb, dynamodb access patterns
x: So in DynamoDB you design keys from your access patterns, not from your entities. Because you can only query efficiently by key, that's the whole game.

What I do first is list every access pattern. Get shipment by id, list events for a shipment in time order, list shipments for a site by status, like that. Then I design the partition key and sort key to answer those.

The partition key needs high cardinality and even traffic, like a shipment id or customer id, so load spreads across partitions. Low-cardinality keys like status or date, I avoid, they create hot partitions. If one key is naturally very busy, I use write sharding, basically add a suffix like a random number from 1 to 10, and query all the shards in parallel.
The sort key gives you ordering and range queries. I often use composite values, like EVENT, a hash sign and then the timestamp, so begins_with and between work nicely.

For other access patterns I add global secondary indexes with their own partition and sort keys, keeping in mind they're eventually consistent. A lot of teams go with single-table design, where related entities sit in one table with generic keys like PK and SK, so one query fetches a whole aggregate.
And then TTL to expire old items, and on-demand capacity if the traffic is unpredictable. That's usually how I approach it.

p17-22.q: Honestly, it depends on what I'm caching, and usually there are a few layers.
p17-22.k: caching in aws, aws caching service, elasticache, which cache aws, redis aws, cloudfront caching
x: Honestly, it depends on what I'm caching, and usually there are a few layers.

For application data, like reference data, config, sessions or expensive query results, I use ElastiCache, normally with the Redis or Valkey engine, because you get rich data types, expiry, persistence and replication. The pattern is cache-aside. Service checks Redis first, on a miss it reads the database, stores the value with a TTL and returns it. On writes, I update the database and then delete the cache key, so the next read refreshes it. I add a bit of random jitter to TTLs so lots of keys don't expire together, and use a lock or single-flight on hot keys so we don't get a stampede.

For static content and cacheable API responses at the edge, CloudFront, which caches close to the users. API Gateway has its own response cache also. For DynamoDB there's DAX, which is a microsecond read cache. And inside each service, a small in-memory cache like IMemoryCache in .NET is the fastest layer, for data that hardly changes.
What I don't cache is equally important. Anything that has to be strongly consistent, or user-specific data without a proper key.
In our CIRT platform, which runs on-premise, Redis caches study configuration and it gets refreshed by RabbitMQ events. So that's how we use it.

p17-23.q: Yes, I do. It's part of AWS Systems Manager. Basically a managed, central place to keep configuration values for your apps, URLs, feature flags, timeouts, connection settings, outside the code and outside the container image.
p17-23.k: aws parameter store, ssm parameter store, systems manager parameter store, what is parameter store, param store aws
x: Yes, I do. It's part of AWS Systems Manager. Basically a managed, central place to keep configuration values for your apps, URLs, feature flags, timeouts, connection settings, outside the code and outside the container image.

Parameters are organised in a hierarchy, like slash myapp, slash prod, slash Database, slash Timeout. So I can load all settings for one service and environment in one call, by path. You get three types, String, StringList, and SecureString, which is encrypted with a KMS key, so you can keep sensitive values too. Access is through IAM, so each service's role reads only its own path. Every change is versioned, so you can see history and roll back, and changes can trigger events through EventBridge.
There's a standard tier which is free, values up to 4 KB, and an advanced tier with bigger values and parameter policies like expiry.

In .NET I use the Amazon.Extensions.Configuration.SystemsManager package. Then Parameter Store just becomes a normal configuration source, bound to the options pattern, with optional reload. In ECS you can also inject parameters as environment variables in the task definition.
In IQVIA's newer services on AWS that I've worked on, settings live in Parameter Store. It's kind of the same role that Azure DevOps variable groups play for our on-premise CIRT releases.

p17-24.q: Both keep values outside your code and both can encrypt with KMS. But they're built for different jobs.
p17-24.k: parameter store vs secrets manager, secrets manager vs parameter store, ssm vs secrets manager, where to store secrets aws, secret rotation aws
x: Both keep values outside your code and both can encrypt with KMS. But they're built for different jobs.

Parameter Store is mainly for configuration. Plain strings and SecureStrings in a hierarchy, with versioning and IAM access. Standard tier is free, so it's great when you have lots of settings, URLs, timeouts, feature flags. You can put secrets in it as SecureString, but there's no built-in rotation.

Secrets Manager is made for secrets, like database passwords, API keys, SFTP credentials. The big advantage is automatic rotation. For RDS and other databases, it can rotate the password on a schedule using a Lambda function, and it updates both the database and the secret, so nobody touches the password at all. It also has cross-region replication, resource policies for cross-account access, and random password generation. But it costs per secret per month, plus API calls.

So the way I decide is simple. Configuration goes in Parameter Store, real secrets go in Secrets Manager, especially anything that should rotate. Apps read both at runtime with their IAM role, and cache the values so we don't hit throttling or extra cost.
In our AWS services, database credentials sit in Secrets Manager with rotation, and normal settings sit in Parameter Store. That's how we've split it.

p17-25.q: Okay, 2 GB is way too big. It's slow to push, slow to pull, slow to start, and the attack surface is bigger. So I'd shrink it step by step.
p17-25.k: reduce docker image size, docker image 2gb, docker image too big, smaller docker image, optimize docker image, slim docker image
x: Okay, 2 GB is way too big. It's slow to push, slow to pull, slow to start, and the attack surface is bigger. So I'd shrink it step by step.

First I look at what's actually inside. docker history, and a tool called dive, which shows the size of each layer. Mostly the culprits are a full SDK base image, build tools, caches, and random files that shouldn't be there.

The biggest fix is a multi-stage build. You compile in a stage based on the SDK image, and then copy only the published output into a small runtime image. For .NET, that means build with the sdk image and run on the aspnet runtime image, or an Alpine or chiselled Ubuntu variant, which can be around 100 MB or even less. Then a dockerignore file, so bin, obj, node_modules, the git folder and test data never even enter the build context. If you install packages, combine them in one RUN with no-install-recommends and clean the cache in the same layer, because deleting files in a later layer doesn't reduce anything. And don't copy big data files or models into the image, mount them or download at runtime.
For .NET you can go further with trimming, a self-contained single file, or even Native AOT if the app suits it.
After that I scan the smaller image and make sure startup and tests still pass. Usually you end up at a fraction of the original size.

p17-26.q: So in blue-green you run two identical production environments. Blue is what's live right now, green is the new version. You deploy and test the new version on green while blue keeps serving users. Once green looks good, you switch all the traffic from blue to green in one go, usually at the load balancer or DNS. And if something goes wrong, you just switch back to blue, because it's still running there.
p17-26.k: blue green deployment, blue-green, blue green release, zero downtime deployment, blue and green environment, switch traffic deployment
x: So in blue-green you run two identical production environments. Blue is what's live right now, green is the new version. You deploy and test the new version on green while blue keeps serving users. Once green looks good, you switch all the traffic from blue to green in one go, usually at the load balancer or DNS. And if something goes wrong, you just switch back to blue, because it's still running there.
What you get is near-zero downtime, instant rollback, and you can test the real production setup before any user sees it.

What it costs you is double capacity during the switch. And honestly the database is the hard part. Both versions usually share one database, so schema changes have to be backward compatible. We do it the expand-and-contract way, add new columns first, deploy code that works with both, and drop old columns only in a later release.

On AWS, ECS supports blue-green through CodeDeploy. You have two target groups behind the load balancer, a test listener, and automatic rollback on CloudWatch alarms. In Kubernetes you can do it by switching a Service's selector between two deployments.

And just to compare, canary is different, there you shift traffic gradually, like 10 percent first. Rolling is where instances get replaced one by one. Blue-green is the all-at-once switch with a ready fallback.

p17-27.q: For automatic rollback you basically need two things. A reliable signal that the deployment is bad, and a fast, safe way to go back to the last good version.
p17-27.k: automatic rollback, auto rollback pipeline, rollback cicd, rollback production deployment, deployment rollback strategy, rollback on failure
x: For automatic rollback you basically need two things. A reliable signal that the deployment is bad, and a fast, safe way to go back to the last good version.

For the way back, we build once and keep every versioned artifact or image. So rollback means redeploying the previous version, never rebuilding anything. And database changes are kept backward compatible, so the old code still works with the new schema. Otherwise rollback is just on paper.

For the signal, I use a few checks together. Readiness and health checks fail the deployment if the new instances don't start. Smoke tests run right after deployment against the key endpoints. Then during a bake period, monitoring alarms watch error rate and latency against the baseline.

Then the tools do the actual work. In ECS, the deployment circuit breaker with rollback enabled goes back to the last stable task definition if tasks don't get healthy, and CodeDeploy blue-green can roll back on CloudWatch alarms. In Kubernetes, rollout undo, and tools like Argo Rollouts automate canary analysis. In Azure DevOps, a post-deployment gate can query monitoring, and a failure stage redeploys the previous release.

Feature flags help too, so a risky feature can be switched off without any deployment. In our releases we always keep the previous tagged release ready, and [once we rolled back a UAT release within 15 minutes] when a setting was missing. So that's how we handle it.

p17-28.q: So I follow the test pyramid, but adjusted a bit for microservices. Lots of fast unit tests, a solid layer of integration and contract tests, and only a few end-to-end tests.
p17-28.k: microservices testing strategy, testing microservices, unit tests microservices, test pyramid microservices, contract testing, integration tests microservices
x: So I follow the test pyramid, but adjusted a bit for microservices. Lots of fast unit tests, a solid layer of integration and contract tests, and only a few end-to-end tests.

Unit tests cover business logic on its own, validators, domain rules, handlers, using xUnit or NUnit, with Moq or fakes for dependencies. They run in seconds on every build. I focus on behaviour and edge cases, I'm not trying to mock every single line.

Integration tests check the service with its real dependencies. In .NET, WebApplicationFactory hosts the API in memory, and Testcontainers starts a real SQL Server, PostgreSQL or RabbitMQ in Docker. So I'm testing real queries, real migrations, real message handling, not mocks pretending.

Then contract tests for the boundaries between services. With Pact, the consumer writes down what it expects from an API, and the provider's pipeline verifies it. So a breaking change gets caught before deployment, without spinning up all the services together.
End-to-end tests with Playwright, only for a few critical user journeys in a deployed environment, because honestly they're slow and fragile.
Around all this, performance tests for the key endpoints, security scans, and SonarQube quality gates on coverage of new code.
In our IRT, since it's regulated, there's formal verification on top. Like for the CSV import feature, every rule has a unit test matching it. That's basically my strategy.

p17-29.q: I go in a fixed order. Scope it, find the slow step, get the service back, and then fix the root cause properly.
p17-29.k: api 200ms to 5 seconds, api suddenly slow, response time increased, api latency increased production, slow api production, api slow troubleshoot
x: I go in a fixed order. Scope it, find the slow step, get the service back, and then fix the root cause properly.

Scope first. Is it every endpoint or just one? All users or some? Since when exactly? And what changed around that time, a deployment, a config change, data growth, a traffic spike, or something in a dependency?

Then I find where those 5 seconds are going. Distributed traces break the request into spans, so I can see if it's the database, a downstream API, a queue, or our own code. If it's the database, I go to Query Store or the slow query log, find the query whose duration jumped, and look at its plan. Usually it's a plan change from parameter sniffing, a missing index after some new filter, lock blocking, or just a table that grew. If it's the application, I look for thread pool starvation from sync-over-async, connection pool exhaustion, GC pauses, or a new N+1 query. If it's a downstream call, I check its latency and whether our timeouts and retries are making it worse.
To get service back quickly, I roll back the bad release, scale out, or force the last good query plan.

And then the real fix. [In March 2025, our shipments API went from about 200 milliseconds to 3 seconds because of parameter sniffing. I forced the good plan first, then fixed the index.] So that's how I'd approach it.

p17-30.q: If there are 500s but nothing in our logs, my first thought is, the error is happening before or outside our code, or our logging is losing it. So I go from the outside in.
p17-30.k: 500 errors no logs, http 500 not in logs, errors not logged, 500 but logs empty, missing logs 500 error, server error no log
x: If there are 500s but nothing in our logs, my first thought is, the error is happening before or outside our code, or our logging is losing it. So I go from the outside in.

First I confirm where the 500 is actually coming from. I check the response headers and body, and the load balancer or gateway logs. An ALB giving 502 or 503, or an API Gateway integration error, is a different thing from a 500 our app generated. On IIS, a 500.30 or 502.5 means the ASP.NET Core app failed to start, and that sits in the Windows event log, not in our app logs.
Then I check the hops in between, reverse proxy, ingress, a WAF, or the gateway timing out. Their access logs show which upstream actually answered.

Then, is our logging even working? A crash at startup happens before logging is configured. Some exception middleware might return 500 without logging anything. Logs can get dropped because the sink is down, or buffered and lost when the container dies, or filtered out by a wrong log level. And a process killed for memory leaves no log at all.
I also check the container or host, restarts, exit codes, out-of-memory kills.
Once I find it, I fix the cause and the visibility both. Global exception logging, startup logging to console, and correlation ids returned to users, so next time it's not a mystery.

p17-31.q: When it only happens in production, I stop guessing and focus on what's different between production and my machine.
p17-31.k: cannot reproduce locally, issue not reproducible, works on my machine, production only bug, reproduce production issue, hard to reproduce bug
x: When it only happens in production, I stop guessing and focus on what's different between production and my machine.

Start with evidence from production itself. Logs and traces filtered by correlation id for the failing requests, the exact time, the user, the data involved, the deployed version, the environment. And patterns, does it happen for one site, one study, one browser, or only under load?

Then I compare the differences. Data is the big one, production has volumes and weird edge cases, special characters, nulls, very old records, that test data just doesn't have. Configuration, maybe some setting, feature flag or secret is different. Infrastructure, several instances instead of one, a load balancer, time zones, culture settings, Linux instead of Windows. Concurrency, race conditions only show up under real parallel load. And dependencies, real third-party systems don't behave like mocks.

To reproduce, I copy the exact request, use masked production data in a lower environment, match the config, and use load tests for concurrency issues. If it still won't reproduce, I add targeted logging or metrics around the suspected code, release that, and wait for the next occurrence. For memory or CPU issues, I take a dump from production.
[Once, a date filter bug showed up only for US sites, because I'd tested only in Indian time. I fixed it by storing everything in UTC.] That's the kind of thing you only learn the hard way.

p17-32.q: So centralised logging means every service sends its logs to one searchable place, so I can follow one request across all of them.
p17-32.k: centralized logging microservices, centralised logging, log aggregation microservices, central logging, logs across services, aggregate logs
x: So centralised logging means every service sends its logs to one searchable place, so I can follow one request across all of them.

There are basically four pieces. One is structured logs. Each service writes JSON with the same fields, timestamp, level, service name, environment, version, message, exception, and most importantly a correlation or trace id. In .NET, I use Serilog or the built-in logger with message templates.

Second is correlation. The first service generates a trace id, or reads it from the incoming request, and every outgoing HTTP call and every message carries it in a header. With OpenTelemetry and W3C trace context, this happens automatically, and the same id links logs and traces.

Then collection and shipping. Either services write to stdout and an agent picks it up, like Fluent Bit, the CloudWatch agent or the Datadog agent, or they ship directly through a sink. I prefer agents, because the app doesn't block if the log platform is slow.
And last, the central store and tools, Elasticsearch with Kibana, Splunk, Datadog, CloudWatch Logs or Azure Log Analytics, with search, dashboards, alerts and retention rules.

One more thing, we mask personal data and secrets before logging. In our CIRT platform, Serilog sends logs to Splunk, and the correlation id in each message lets support trace one request across services. That's how we've done it.

p17-33.q: See, with different stacks, I won't force one logging library on everybody. What I standardise is the format, the correlation and the pipeline.
p17-33.k: centralized logging different languages, polyglot logging, logging across java and dotnet, logging standard multiple teams, opentelemetry logging, common log format
x: See, with different stacks, I won't force one logging library on everybody. What I standardise is the format, the correlation and the pipeline.

Number one, a shared logging standard every team follows. JSON output, a common set of field names like timestamp, level, service.name, environment, version, trace_id, span_id and message, and agreed log levels. If you pick a known schema, like OpenTelemetry's semantic conventions or the Elastic Common Schema, nobody wastes time arguing about names.

Then OpenTelemetry as the common layer. It has SDKs for .NET, Java, Node, Python, Go. It uses W3C trace context headers, so a trace started in a .NET service just continues in the Java service, and every log line carries the same trace id. Each team keeps its own library, Serilog or ILogger in .NET, Logback or Log4j2 with a JSON encoder in Java, pino in Node.

Then collection happens outside the apps. Services write to stdout, and the OpenTelemetry Collector or Fluent Bit collects, enriches, masks and forwards everything to one backend, Elastic, Splunk, Datadog or CloudWatch. And if we change backend later, no service needs to change.

Last is a bit of governance. A shared starter package or template per stack, and a pipeline check or dashboard that flags services missing trace ids. That way five teams stay consistent without anyone being forced into one language.

p17-34.q: Both clouds have managed services for this, and honestly they map quite closely.
p17-34.k: managed logging services aws azure, cloudwatch logs vs log analytics, azure monitor logging, aws logging services, centralized logging cloud services, cloud logging options
x: Both clouds have managed services for this, and honestly they map quite closely.

On AWS, the core is CloudWatch Logs. ECS, Lambda and EKS send logs there, through the awslogs driver, the Lambda runtime, or Fluent Bit. Logs go into log groups, you search them with CloudWatch Logs Insights, and you can turn them into metrics and alarms. For tracing there's X-Ray, or the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry. If you need heavy search and dashboards, Amazon OpenSearch Service gives you a managed Elasticsearch-style stack, usually fed by subscription filters or Kinesis Data Firehose. S3 for cheap long-term archive, queried with Athena. And CloudTrail is the audit log of AWS API calls.

On Azure, it's Azure Monitor with a Log Analytics workspace. Application Insights collects application logs, requests, dependencies and traces, and it can use OpenTelemetry now. Everything is queried with KQL, the Kusto query language, with workbooks for dashboards and alert rules. Diagnostic settings push platform logs from things like App Service and AKS into the workspace, and Container Insights covers AKS.
A lot of teams also use third-party platforms that work across clouds, like Datadog, Splunk, Elastic Cloud or Grafana Loki.
In our on-premise CIRT platform we use Splunk, and our newest services use OpenTelemetry with Datadog. So we've actually got a bit of both.

p17-35.q: For me it depends on how many services we have, how much control we need, and honestly how strong the team is on operations.
p17-35.k: azure web app vs aks, app service vs kubernetes, web app or aks, when to use aks, azure app service vs aks, paas vs kubernetes
x: For me it depends on how many services we have, how much control we need, and honestly how strong the team is on operations.

Azure App Service, what people call Web App, is a fully managed platform for web apps and APIs. You deploy code or a container, and Azure handles servers, patching, scaling, TLS certificates, and deployment slots for zero-downtime swaps. It plugs into Azure AD, Key Vault and Application Insights very easily. It's ideal when you have a handful of web apps or APIs, a small team, or you want to go live fast without much ops work.

AKS is managed Kubernetes. You get a lot more control and flexibility. Many microservices with complex networking, sidecars and service meshes, custom scaling with KEDA based on queue length, background workers, stateful workloads, GPU nodes, portability across clouds. But you need Kubernetes skills to handle cluster upgrades, node pools, ingress, security policies, monitoring, all of that.
There's also a middle option, Azure Container Apps. It runs containers with Kubernetes-style features like KEDA scaling and Dapr, but you don't manage a cluster.

So my rule of thumb is, a few web apps or APIs, go with App Service. Lots of containerised services and you have a platform team, go AKS. Containers but no appetite for cluster management, look at Container Apps. That's how I'd decide.

p17-36.q: Both are ways to coordinate a business process that runs across several services. The difference is who's in charge.
p17-36.k: orchestration vs choreography, saga orchestration, saga choreography, event choreography, workflow orchestration microservices
x: Both are ways to coordinate a business process that runs across several services. The difference is who's in charge.

In orchestration, there's one central component, the orchestrator, telling each service what to do and in what order. Like an order orchestrator calls payment, then inventory, then shipping, and it handles failures. The nice part is you can see the whole flow in one place, change it in one place, monitor it in one place. The risk is the orchestrator becoming a bottleneck, or a sort of god service that knows too much.

In choreography, nobody's in charge. Each service listens for events and reacts. Payment publishes PaymentCompleted, inventory hears it, reserves stock, publishes StockReserved, and so on. Services stay loosely coupled, which is good. But honestly the overall flow is scattered across many services, so it's harder to understand, debug and change, and you can end up with hidden cyclic dependencies.

So the way I decide, choreography for simple flows with a few steps, where services just react to facts. Orchestration for long, complex processes with many steps, compensation and timeouts, usually with a workflow engine like Step Functions, Durable Functions or a saga orchestrator.

In our IRT, actually we have both. Notifications are choreography, services publish events to RabbitMQ and the notification consumers react. But the study transfer is a clearly orchestrated sequence of steps. So it depends on the flow.

p17-37.q: Okay, so a saga is how you keep data consistent across microservices without a distributed transaction. Each service has its own database, so you can't wrap everything in one ACID transaction. Instead it's a sequence of local transactions, and each step publishes an event or message that kicks off the next one.
p17-37.k: saga pattern, distributed transaction microservices, compensating transaction, saga failure, saga rollback, long running transaction
x: Okay, so a saga is how you keep data consistent across microservices without a distributed transaction. Each service has its own database, so you can't wrap everything in one ACID transaction. Instead it's a sequence of local transactions, and each step publishes an event or message that kicks off the next one.

The important part is what happens on failure. If a step fails in the middle, the saga runs compensating transactions for the steps that already went through, in reverse order. So in this case, the order got created, payment was taken, but stock reservation failed. The saga refunds the payment and cancels the order. And see, a compensation is a business undo, not a database rollback. You have to design it explicitly, and it has to be idempotent, because it might run more than once.

Sagas can be coordinated by choreography, where services react to events, or by an orchestrator that tracks state and decides the next step. For a money flow like this I'd lean towards an orchestrator, it's easier to reason about.

I also design for the in-between states, because users actually see them, like "payment pending". Steps get retries for temporary errors, timeouts for stuck steps, and an outbox so the local change and its event are always saved together. And every saga carries a correlation id, so I can trace it end to end when someone asks what happened to their order.

p17-38.q: So this is the classic dual-write problem. The service saves data to its database, then publishes an event to the broker. Those are two separate systems. If the save works but the publish fails, or the service crashes in between, other services just never hear about the change. And if you publish first and the save fails, you've announced something that never happened.
p17-38.k: outbox pattern, transactional outbox, dual write problem, reliable event publishing, outbox table, publish event after save
x: So this is the classic dual-write problem. The service saves data to its database, then publishes an event to the broker. Those are two separate systems. If the save works but the publish fails, or the service crashes in between, other services just never hear about the change. And if you publish first and the save fails, you've announced something that never happened.

The outbox fixes it like this. The service writes the business change and the event into an outbox table, in the same database transaction. So either both get saved or neither does. Then a separate background publisher, or a change-data-capture tool like Debezium, picks up unsent rows from the outbox, publishes them to the broker, and marks them sent.

What you get is at-least-once delivery. The publisher might send the same event twice, say it crashes after publishing but before marking it. So consumers have to be idempotent, usually by storing processed message ids.

In .NET, MassTransit and NServiceBus have a built-in outbox. Or honestly you can build a simple one with EF Core and a BackgroundService, it's not much code. I also turn on publisher confirms in RabbitMQ, so the publisher knows the broker really accepted the message before marking it as sent. That's the last gap closed.

p17-39.q: An API gateway is basically a single entry point in front of your microservices. Clients call the gateway, it routes each request to the right service, so clients don't need to know how many services there are or where they run.
p17-39.k: api gateway pattern, what does api gateway do, gateway microservices, ocelot yarp, edge service, single entry point
x: An API gateway is basically a single entry point in front of your microservices. Clients call the gateway, it routes each request to the right service, so clients don't need to know how many services there are or where they run.

What should go in? Cross-cutting stuff that you want in one place. Authentication, so tokens get validated before requests even reach services. Rate limiting and throttling, per client or per API key. TLS termination. Some request and response transformation. Caching common responses. CORS. And logging and metrics for all traffic, usually adding a correlation id there.
It can also do aggregation, where one client call fans out to a few services and the results get combined. That helps mobile apps that would otherwise make lots of chatty calls.

What shouldn't go in is business logic. That's the trap. Slowly people start adding rules in the gateway, and then it becomes a mini monolith. I keep it thin, routing and cross-cutting concerns only. And since it's a single point of failure, it has to be highly available and scaled properly.
Examples are AWS API Gateway, Azure API Management, Kong, and in .NET, YARP or Ocelot. Each service still validates tokens itself, for defence in depth.
In IQVIA's newer AWS services, partner-facing APIs go through API Gateway with per-partner keys and throttling. So that's where we use it.

p17-40.q: BFF is Backend for Frontend. Basically, instead of one general-purpose API for everybody, you build a separate thin backend for each type of client, like one for the web app and one for the mobile app.
p17-40.k: backend for frontend, bff pattern, bff, separate backend per client, mobile backend web backend, bff authentication
x: BFF is Backend for Frontend. Basically, instead of one general-purpose API for everybody, you build a separate thin backend for each type of client, like one for the web app and one for the mobile app.

Why? Because different clients want different things. A mobile screen wants a small, combined response in one call, the network is slow. The web dashboard wants richer data. One generic API either over-fetches for mobile or forces lots of calls. With a BFF, each frontend team owns a backend shaped exactly for its screens. It calls the downstream microservices, aggregates and trims the data, and returns just what the screen needs.

Now the security part, which is why it's recommended for SPAs these days. The BFF does the OpenID Connect login, keeps the tokens on the server side, and the browser only gets a secure, HttpOnly cookie. So no access token sits in browser JavaScript, which really cuts down the risk from cross-site scripting. If some script gets injected, there's no token for it to steal.
The downside is more services to maintain and some duplicated logic between BFFs. So I keep business rules in the core services, and the BFF only does composition and client-specific shaping.
In .NET, a BFF is often just an ASP.NET Core app with YARP for proxying, plus the Duende BFF library for the security part. That's the usual setup.

p17-41.q: So in microservices, instances keep starting, stopping and moving, especially with autoscaling and containers. You can't call another service on a fixed IP. Service discovery is just how a service finds the current healthy instances of another one.
p17-41.k: service discovery, client side discovery, server side discovery, consul eureka, dns service discovery, how services find each other
x: So in microservices, instances keep starting, stopping and moving, especially with autoscaling and containers. You can't call another service on a fixed IP. Service discovery is just how a service finds the current healthy instances of another one.

There are two styles. Client-side discovery, the caller asks a registry like Consul or Eureka for the healthy instances and does the load balancing itself. Server-side discovery, the caller just calls a stable name or a load balancer, and the platform routes it to a healthy instance.
The registry stays up to date through registration. Instances register when they start, and get removed when health checks fail.

Honestly, today most platforms make this pretty invisible. In Kubernetes, every Service gets a stable DNS name, like orders dot default dot svc dot cluster dot local, and kube-proxy routes to healthy pods. In ECS, Cloud Map and Service Connect give you DNS names, or you use an internal load balancer. In .NET, Aspire's service discovery lets HttpClient use logical names that get resolved from config or the platform.

Health checks are the part you can't skip, otherwise traffic goes to a dead instance. In our on-premise CIRT platform, it's simpler, services use stable DNS names behind internal load balancers, and health checks take unhealthy nodes out. So that's how it works for us.

p17-42.q: Eventual consistency means that after a change, different parts of the system might show different data for a short while, but if nothing else changes, they all catch up. It's just the normal result of microservices owning separate databases and talking through events.
p17-42.k: eventual consistency, strong vs eventual consistency, consistency microservices, read your own writes, stale data, cap theorem consistency
x: Eventual consistency means that after a change, different parts of the system might show different data for a short while, but if nothing else changes, they all catch up. It's just the normal result of microservices owning separate databases and talking through events.

Let me take an example. A shipment gets marked as dispatched. The shipment service updates its own database immediately and publishes an event. Inventory and reporting update maybe a few hundred milliseconds later, when they process that event. In between, a report might still show the old status.

So how do I make it okay for users? I show honest states in the UI, like "Requested" or "Processing", instead of pretending something finished instantly. Where it matters, I support read-your-own-writes, so the person who made the change sees it straight away, like returning the updated data from the command, or reading from the owning service. The delay has to stay small and monitored, so we alert on queue lag. And consumers are idempotent with replay, so nothing gets lost.
When I explain it to users, I keep it simple, "it's saved, the report will update in a few seconds".

But where strong consistency is really required, like assigning a unique randomisation slot, I keep it inside one service and one database transaction. In our IRT, the randomisation assignment and the kit allocation get written together in one transaction. No eventual consistency there.

p17-43.q: So the strangler fig pattern is about replacing a legacy system bit by bit, instead of a big-bang rewrite. The name comes from a fig tree that grows around an old tree until it can stand on its own.
p17-43.k: strangler fig, strangler pattern, migrate monolith to microservices, incremental migration, legacy modernization pattern, strangle the monolith
x: So the strangler fig pattern is about replacing a legacy system bit by bit, instead of a big-bang rewrite. The name comes from a fig tree that grows around an old tree until it can stand on its own.

How it works, you put a routing layer in front of the old system, could be a proxy, a gateway, or honestly just links in the UI. Then you build new functionality one piece at a time in the new system, and route only that piece to it. Over time more and more routes move across, and legacy parts get switched off once nothing uses them.
Why I like it, each step is small and can be rolled back, you keep delivering value, and there's no long feature freeze where the business waits a year for a rewrite.
The hard parts are running two systems side by side, keeping data in sync, and not duplicating business rules. I try to make sure each rule has exactly one owner at any time.

This is actually how our IRT is being modernised. It started as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, on a .NET Framework 4.8 core with an ASP.NET MVC and Angular portal. New .NET APIs wrap the legacy transaction engine through an API, and the UI is moving to a React shell one module at a time. Drug accountability is the one being migrated right now. So I've seen this pattern in real life.

p17-44.q: I prefer database per service. Each microservice owns its data, and nobody else reads or writes its tables directly. Others get data through its API or its events.
p17-44.k: database per service, shared database microservices, separate database per microservice, data ownership, shared db anti pattern
x: I prefer database per service. Each microservice owns its data, and nobody else reads or writes its tables directly. Others get data through its API or its events.

The reason is mainly independence. A service can change its schema without breaking other teams. It can pick the right database, like SQL Server for transactions and DynamoDB for simple high-volume lookups. It can scale on its own. And there's one clear owner for each piece of data and its rules.

A shared database looks easier in the beginning, honestly. But it couples everyone together. One team changes a column and another service breaks, deployments need coordination, and nobody really owns the data.
Database per service isn't free though. Queries across services need API composition or a read model built from events. Transactions across services need sagas. And there are more databases to run.
So it's a trade-off. During a migration, I'm okay with a shared database for a while, as long as each table has a clear owner, and then we separate it step by step.

Our IRT actually has an interesting variation, database per study, which is basically per tenant. Each clinical trial gets its own SQL Server database from a common model schema of [about 560] tables. That gives really strong isolation between sponsors' trials. So in a way we went even further than per service.

p17-45.q: See, since each service owns its own database, I can't just write a SQL join across services. So there are mainly two approaches.
p17-45.k: query across microservices, join data across services, api composition, cqrs read model, data aggregation microservices, reporting across microservices
x: See, since each service owns its own database, I can't just write a SQL join across services. So there are mainly two approaches.

One is API composition. Some composer, could be the API gateway, a BFF, or one of the services, calls each service's API, mostly in parallel, and combines the results in memory. It's simple and the data is fresh. But it's slower, it fails if one service is down, and it's really bad for large result sets or filtering and sorting across services.

The other is a read model, the CQRS way. A dedicated query service listens to events from all the relevant services and keeps its own denormalised view, shaped exactly for that query, like a table or a search index. Then queries are fast and simple. You pay with eventual consistency, because the view is a little behind, and with more infrastructure.
For reporting and analytics there's a third option, stream the data into a warehouse or a lake and run the reports there.
So my choice depends on the need. API composition for small on-screen lookups. Read model for frequent, complex queries or search. Warehouse for heavy reporting.
In IQVIA's newer AWS services, shipment status events feed a reporting view, so reports don't hit the shipment service live. That worked out nicely for us.

p17-46.q: CQRS is Command Query Responsibility Segregation. In simple words, you separate the model that changes data, the commands, from the model that reads data, the queries.
p17-46.k: cqrs, command query responsibility segregation, separate read and write, read model write model, cqrs mediatr, when to use cqrs
x: CQRS is Command Query Responsibility Segregation. In simple words, you separate the model that changes data, the commands, from the model that reads data, the queries.

At the simple level it's just how you organise code. Commands like CreateShipment go through handlers with validation and business rules. Queries like GetShipments use simple, optimised reads, mostly projecting straight to DTOs. In .NET, MediatR makes this clean, one handler per command and per query, and pipeline behaviours for validation and logging. Honestly this level is useful in most services.

Then there's the advanced level, where the read side has its own separate data store, updated from events published by the write side. Now you can scale reads independently and shape read models exactly for each screen or search, like a denormalised table or an Elasticsearch index. But you get eventual consistency, more infrastructure, more complexity.
So I use the simple form a lot, and the separate-store form only where reads and writes really have very different needs, like heavy reporting or search sitting on top of a transactional system.
People often pair it with event sourcing, but you don't need event sourcing to do CQRS.
Our newer IRT APIs follow clean architecture with MediatR commands and queries, and FluentValidation runs as a pipeline behaviour before every command. So that's the flavour we use.

p17-47.q: In event sourcing, instead of storing just the current state of something, you store every change as an immutable event. Like ShipmentCreated, ShipmentDispatched, ShipmentDelivered. The current state is rebuilt by replaying those events in order, usually with snapshots so you're not replaying thousands of events every time.
p17-47.k: event sourcing, event store, events as source of truth, event sourcing pros cons, replay events, audit with events
x: In event sourcing, instead of storing just the current state of something, you store every change as an immutable event. Like ShipmentCreated, ShipmentDispatched, ShipmentDelivered. The current state is rebuilt by replaying those events in order, usually with snapshots so you're not replaying thousands of events every time.

The pros are pretty strong. You get a complete audit trail built in, what happened and when, which is very attractive in regulated domains like ours. You can rebuild state at any point in time, which really helps debugging. You can create new read models later just by replaying history. And events naturally feed other services.

But the cons are real. It's a different way of thinking, and the learning curve is steep. To query current state you need separate read models, so it usually comes with CQRS and eventual consistency. Event schemas have to evolve carefully, because old events stay forever. And if an event is wrong, you can't just edit it, you fix it with new correcting events.
So I'd use it where history and audit are core to the business and the team is actually ready for it. Not as a default.

In our IRT, we get audit through history tables and an audit trail for every change, without going full event sourcing. That keeps the model simpler, and honestly it's been enough for the compliance needs.

p17-48.q: So gRPC is a high-performance remote procedure call framework from Google. You define your services and messages in a proto file using Protocol Buffers, and the tooling generates strongly typed client and server code for lots of languages, C# included.
p17-48.k: grpc vs rest, what is grpc, grpc dotnet, protobuf, when to use grpc, grpc streaming
x: So gRPC is a high-performance remote procedure call framework from Google. You define your services and messages in a proto file using Protocol Buffers, and the tooling generates strongly typed client and server code for lots of languages, C# included.

Compared to REST with JSON, it's faster and the payloads are smaller, because Protocol Buffers is a compact binary format, and it runs over HTTP/2 with multiplexing on one connection. The contract is strict, so if someone makes a breaking change, it's obvious. And it supports streaming both ways, which is really nice for real-time feeds.

But there are downsides. Browsers can't call gRPC directly without gRPC-Web. The messages are binary, so you can't just look at them, and debugging with curl or Postman is more painful. HTTP/2 can be tricky through some proxies and load balancers. And honestly, public APIs and partners mostly expect REST anyway.

So how I decide, gRPC for internal service-to-service calls where performance and strong contracts matter, like high-volume internal lookups or streaming. REST for public APIs, browser clients and partner integrations.

In ASP.NET Core it's built in. You call AddGrpc, map the service, and use the generated client through the HttpClient factory, so it gets the same resilience policies as everything else. You can even expose both from one service with JSON transcoding. So it's not really either-or.

p17-49.q: A distributed monolith is when you've split the system into many services, but they're still so tightly coupled that you get all the problems of a monolith plus all the problems of distributed systems. Kind of the worst of both worlds.
p17-49.k: distributed monolith, microservices anti pattern, tightly coupled microservices, avoid distributed monolith, microservices mistakes
x: A distributed monolith is when you've split the system into many services, but they're still so tightly coupled that you get all the problems of a monolith plus all the problems of distributed systems. Kind of the worst of both worlds.

How do you spot it? You can't deploy one service without deploying a few others. One change touches many repos. Services share a database. One user request needs a long chain of synchronous calls. Releases have to be coordinated across teams. There's a shared library with business logic that everybody depends on. And one service going down takes everything down with it.

To avoid it, I start with good boundaries around business capabilities, so most changes stay inside one service. Each service owns its own data, no shared database. For side effects, communication is mostly asynchronous, so services don't need each other to be up. APIs are versioned and backward compatible, with contract tests, so services can deploy on their own. Shared libraries carry only technical stuff, like logging or messaging helpers, never business rules. And each service gets its own pipeline.

And honestly, sometimes the right answer is a modular monolith, until there's a real reason to split, like independent scaling or separate teams. Splitting early just because microservices are fashionable is how most distributed monoliths get born.

p17-50.q: Basically, a modular monolith is one deployable application, but inside it's split into well-defined modules. Each module has its own domain logic, its own tables or schema, and a clear public interface. Modules don't reach into each other's internals, they talk through interfaces or in-process events.
p17-50.k: modular monolith, monolith vs microservices, when not to use microservices, modular architecture, monolith first
x: Basically, a modular monolith is one deployable application, but inside it's split into well-defined modules. Each module has its own domain logic, its own tables or schema, and a clear public interface. Modules don't reach into each other's internals, they talk through interfaces or in-process events.

What you get is a lot of the design benefits of microservices, clear boundaries, clear ownership, without the operational cost. One deployment, one process, in-process calls instead of network calls, real ACID transactions, simple debugging, way simpler infrastructure.

When is it better? When the team is small. When the domain is still being figured out and boundaries will probably move. When the load doesn't need independent scaling. Or when the organisation doesn't have strong DevOps and observability yet. Splitting too early, honestly, mostly gives you a distributed monolith.

The trick is enforcing the boundaries, otherwise it slowly becomes a big ball of mud. What I do is separate projects per module, internal classes so others can't touch them, architecture tests with something like NetArchTest to block forbidden references, and separate database schemas.

Then later, if a module needs independent scaling, a different technology or its own team, you can pull it out as a microservice with much less pain, because the boundary is already clean. That's why I like starting this way.

p17-51.q: So a dead-letter queue is where messages go when they can't be processed, so one bad message doesn't block the queue or get retried forever.
p17-51.k: dead letter queue, dlq strategy, poison message, failed messages queue, rabbitmq dead letter, sqs dlq
x: So a dead-letter queue is where messages go when they can't be processed, so one bad message doesn't block the queue or get retried forever.

First thing I do is separate the failure types. Transient failures, like a database timeout, get a few retries with backoff, ideally delayed redelivery so we're not hammering a dependency that's already struggling. Permanent failures, like a message with invalid data, what we call a poison message, go straight to the DLQ, because retrying won't help anyway.

In RabbitMQ, I set a dead-letter exchange on the queue, so rejected or expired messages get routed there. In SQS it's a redrive policy, the message moves to the DLQ after a max receive count, like five.

But see, a DLQ is useless if nobody looks at it. So I put an alarm when its depth goes above zero, and with each message I keep the original headers, the error reason and how many attempts happened. Then there's a clear process. Inspect, fix the bug or the data, and replay the messages back to the main queue with a tool or a script. Since our consumers are idempotent, replaying is safe.
In our CIRT platform, failed vendor messages land in a dead-letter queue with an alert, and the support team replays them once the fix is in. That's how we handle it day to day.

p17-52.q: Ordering across the whole system is really hard to guarantee, so first I ask, ordering of what? Honestly, mostly we only need ordering per entity, like all events for one shipment in order, not every event everywhere.
