p17-52.k: message ordering, ordered messages, kafka ordering partition key, fifo queue, out of order events, sequence number
x: Ordering across the whole system is really hard to guarantee, so first I ask, ordering of what? Honestly, mostly we only need ordering per entity, like all events for one shipment in order, not every event everywhere.

The standard way is partitioning by key. In Kafka, messages with the same key, say the shipment id, go to the same partition, and one consumer in the group reads that partition in order. In SQS FIFO, the message group id does the same job. In RabbitMQ, order holds within one queue with one consumer, but once you have multiple consumers or redeliveries, things can get reordered.

But ordering can still break, through retries, redeliveries, or producers sending from different instances. So I make consumers tolerant as well. Each event carries a version or sequence number for its entity, and the consumer just ignores anything older than what it already applied. Or the consumer re-reads the current state from the source instead of trusting the payload.
I also avoid designs that need ordering across different entities, because that kills parallelism.

In IQVIA's newer AWS services, shipment events on Kafka are keyed by shipment id, and consumers store the last version they applied. So a late, older event can't overwrite newer data. That one check saved us from some really confusing bugs.

p17-53.q: For an hour-long outage, retries and circuit breakers alone won't cut it. You need to decide how the system behaves while that dependency is gone.
p17-53.k: dependency down for an hour, downstream outage, service unavailable long time, graceful degradation, fallback when service down
x: For an hour-long outage, retries and circuit breakers alone won't cut it. You need to decide how the system behaves while that dependency is gone.
First thing, fail fast. The circuit breaker opens, so requests aren't sitting on timeouts and threads aren't piling up. Health checks and alerts tell the team quickly which dependency is down.

Then graceful degradation, and that depends on how important the dependency is. If it's just enrichment, like recommendations or some non-critical widget, I hide that part or return cached or default data, and the main feature keeps working. If the work can wait, I make it asynchronous. Accept the request, put it on a queue, show the user "accepted, processing", and process it when the dependency is back. The queue just absorbs the backlog.
If it's truly critical, like a payment or a safety check, I fail clearly with a helpful message. I won't do something unsafe or half-done just to look available.
When it comes back, I control the recovery. The backlog drains at a limited rate, so we don't flatten the service that's just recovering, and I check the DLQ and replay anything that failed.
In our IRT, if a depot's system is down, shipment requests queue up and site users see "pending", and we clear it when the depot recovers. So users aren't blocked, they just know it's in progress.

p17-54.q: So a sidecar is a helper container that runs next to your main application container, in the same pod, sharing its network and lifecycle. It adds capabilities without touching the app code, like a logging agent, a proxy, or something that fetches secrets.
p17-54.k: sidecar pattern, service mesh, istio linkerd, envoy sidecar, what is service mesh, mtls service mesh
x: So a sidecar is a helper container that runs next to your main application container, in the same pod, sharing its network and lifecycle. It adds capabilities without touching the app code, like a logging agent, a proxy, or something that fetches secrets.

A service mesh basically takes that idea everywhere. It puts sidecar proxies, usually Envoy, next to every service, plus a control plane, and manages all service-to-service traffic. Tools are Istio, Linkerd, and historically AWS App Mesh. Since every call goes through the proxies, the mesh can give you, in one consistent way, mutual TLS between services, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, traffic splitting for canary releases, and detailed metrics and tracing for every call. All configured centrally, no code in each service.

The upside is consistency across languages and teams, and strong zero-trust security with mTLS. The downside, honestly, is complexity. Extra latency and memory for every proxy, and a steep learning curve. Newer things like Istio's ambient mode reduce that per-pod sidecar overhead.

When would I go for it? When there are many services in different languages, and strict security or traffic-control needs. For a smaller set of .NET services, Polly, OpenTelemetry and a gateway usually give you enough, with a lot less to operate. I wouldn't add a mesh just because it's cool.

p17-55.q: I don't measure size in lines of code. For me a service is the right size when it maps to one business capability, one team can own it, and most of the time it can be changed and deployed on its own.
p17-55.k: how big should microservice be, microservice size, too small microservices, nano services, granularity microservices
x: I don't measure size in lines of code. For me a service is the right size when it maps to one business capability, one team can own it, and most of the time it can be changed and deployed on its own.
How do I know it's too big? Several teams keep changing the same service. Deployments feel risky because unrelated features ship together. Or parts of it have very different scaling needs.

Too small, the nano-service problem, looks different. Almost every feature needs changes in several services. Services call each other constantly in long chains. You need sagas for things that should've been simple. And the operational overhead, pipelines, monitoring, on-call, is more than the benefit.

So I start from the domain, domain-driven design and bounded contexts, and I keep together things that change together and need strong consistency. If data has to be updated in one transaction, that's a strong hint it belongs in one service.

And honestly, it's fine to start a bit bigger and split later when there's a real reason, like independent scaling, a different release cadence or a separate team. Merging services back is much harder than splitting a clean module.
In our IRT, for example, inventory and shipments stay together, because kit allocation and the shipment request have to be consistent. Splitting them would just create a saga for no good reason.

p17-56.q: An anti-corruption layer is basically a translation layer between your domain and some external or legacy system, so their model doesn't leak into your code.
p17-56.k: anti corruption layer, acl ddd, translate legacy model, adapter for legacy system, protect domain model
x: An anti-corruption layer is basically a translation layer between your domain and some external or legacy system, so their model doesn't leak into your code.

See, legacy systems and third-party APIs usually have confusing names, odd formats, magic codes, different concepts. If your new service uses all that directly, its model gets "corrupted" by it, and every change on their side ripples through your code.

So I put an adapter in between. My domain code only talks to an interface in my own language, like an IShipmentGateway with a CreateShipment method taking my own Shipment type. The implementation behind it calls the external system, maps my types to theirs and back, converts the codes, handles their error formats and retries. If the external system changes or gets replaced, only the adapter changes, nothing else.
It's really useful during a strangler migration, where new services have to live with an old system for a long time.

In our IRT modernisation, that's exactly what we did. The new .NET APIs talk to the legacy transaction engine through a translation layer. So the new code uses clean names and DTOs, and the old procedures and formats stay hidden behind it. And when parts of the legacy side get replaced, the new code doesn't change at all. That's the whole point.

p17-57.q: I'm quite careful here, because shared libraries can couple services just as badly as a shared database.
p17-57.k: shared library microservices, nuget package shared code, code sharing microservices, common library, shared contracts
x: I'm quite careful here, because shared libraries can couple services just as badly as a shared database.

What I'm happy to share is technical, cross-cutting code. Logging and OpenTelemetry setup, a messaging wrapper, standard health checks, auth setup, error-handling middleware, maybe a result type. I publish these as versioned NuGet packages on a private feed, like Azure Artifacts or GitHub Packages, with semantic versioning. So each service upgrades when it's ready, nobody's forced to move all at once.

What I don't share is business logic and domain models. If two services share a domain library, a change for one forces a change and redeploy of the other, and you're back to monolith coupling. Honestly, a little duplication is better than the wrong coupling.

For contracts, like message schemas or API clients, I prefer generating them from one source, an OpenAPI spec, a protobuf file, or a schema registry, rather than hand-sharing DTO classes. That keeps each side independent and catches breaking changes early.
And shared libraries should stay small, well tested, backward compatible, with very few dependencies of their own.

In our CIRT platform, common logging and messaging helpers ship as internal NuGet packages from Azure DevOps Artifacts, while domain models stay inside each service. That balance has worked well for us.

p17-58.q: Both are messages, but they mean different things, and that changes how I design them.
p17-58.k: command vs event, events vs commands messaging, integration event, domain event, message types
x: Both are messages, but they mean different things, and that changes how I design them.

A command is a request to do something. It goes to one specific receiver that owns that action. It's named like an instruction, CreateShipment, SendEmail. The sender expects it to be handled, and the receiver can accept it or reject it. Usually it goes to a queue with one consumer.

An event is a statement that something already happened. Past tense, like ShipmentCreated or SubjectRandomised. The publisher doesn't know or care who's listening, could be zero, one or many subscribers. And you can't reject it, it's a fact. Events go to a topic or an exchange.

Why it matters is coupling. With commands, the sender depends on the receiver. With events, the publisher is independent of its subscribers, so you can add new consumers later without touching the publisher.

There's one more split, domain events versus integration events. Domain events are raised inside a service, between parts of its own domain. Integration events go outside to other services, they're part of the public contract, so we version them and keep them stable.
In our IRT, SubjectRandomised is an integration event, and both the notification and the reporting consumers listen to it. The randomisation side doesn't even know they exist.

p17-59.q: Honestly, both styles are valid. It depends on the consumers.
p17-59.k: event payload design, fat event vs thin event, event carried state transfer, notification event, event schema design
x: Honestly, both styles are valid. It depends on the consumers.

A thin event, or notification event, has just the id and type, like "Shipment 123 changed". Consumers then call the owning service to get the current data. It's small and the data is always fresh. But every consumer calls back, which adds load and coupling, and if the owner is down, consumers are stuck.

A fat event, what's called event-carried state transfer, has the relevant data inside it, like the shipment's status, site, kit count, timestamps. Consumers have everything without calling back, so they're more independent and resilient, and the owner gets less load. The catch is bigger messages, more care when the schema changes, and the risk of putting sensitive data in there that not every consumer should see.

What I usually do is go somewhere in the middle. Include the data most consumers need, plus the id and a version number so they can ignore stale events. I don't include sensitive personal data unless every subscriber really needs it, especially in clinical systems where patient data has to be kept to a minimum.
And event schemas get versioned, with fields added in a backward-compatible way.
In IQVIA's newer AWS services, shipment events carry status, location and a version, so most consumers never need to call back. That's worked well for us.

p17-60.q: I don't keep the HTTP request open for minutes. It ties up resources, and you'll hit gateway and load balancer timeouts anyway, usually somewhere between 30 and 120 seconds.
p17-60.k: long running request api, async request reply, 202 accepted, background job api, polling status endpoint, long running task web api
x: I don't keep the HTTP request open for minutes. It ties up resources, and you'll hit gateway and load balancer timeouts anyway, usually somewhere between 30 and 120 seconds.

What I do instead is the asynchronous request-reply pattern. The client sends the request, the API validates it, saves a job record, puts the work on a queue, and straight away returns 202 Accepted with a Location header pointing to a status endpoint, like jobs slash 123. A background worker picks up the job and keeps updating status and progress. The client polls that status endpoint, and gets pending, running, completed with a link to the result, or failed with the error. If you don't want polling, you can push a notification with SignalR or a webhook when it's done.
The worker has to be idempotent and able to resume, because it might crash halfway. For really big jobs, I split the work into chunks and track progress per chunk.
And I put an idempotency key on the submit request, so a double click doesn't start two jobs. That one can bite people.

This is actually how our study data transfer works. A transfer gets submitted, a worker moves the data in steps, and the UI shows the progress. [It took a transfer from around 40 minutes of manual steps to under 10 minutes, with clear status for the user.] So users stopped calling us to ask if it was still running.

p17-61.q: Backpressure is basically the situation where a producer sends work faster than the consumer can handle it, and also what you do about it. If nothing controls it, queues grow without limit, memory runs out, latency goes crazy and the system can fall over.
p17-61.k: backpressure, consumer slower than producer, queue growing, flow control, load shedding, bounded queue
x: Backpressure is basically the situation where a producer sends work faster than the consumer can handle it, and also what you do about it. If nothing controls it, queues grow without limit, memory runs out, latency goes crazy and the system can fall over.

I handle it in a few ways, depends on the system honestly. Buffering, a durable queue absorbs the spikes, which is fine if the consumer catches up later. But you have to monitor that queue, alerts on depth and on the age of the oldest message. Scaling consumers, autoscale the workers on queue depth, like KEDA on Kubernetes or ECS scaling on SQS backlog. Slowing down the producer, with bounded queues or channels, rate limits, or the consumer signalling to slow down. Like a bounded System.Threading.Channels channel just makes the writer wait when it's full. And load shedding, when you're overloaded, reject low-priority work quickly with a 429 or 503 instead of making everything slow.
In RabbitMQ, I set a prefetch count, so each consumer only takes a limited number of unacknowledged messages. That spreads the load and stops one consumer from hoarding work.
The main thing is to decide on purpose what happens under overload, instead of finding out in production.
In our CIRT notification consumers, prefetch limits plus a separate queue for bulk jobs keep the urgent emails flowing even during large imports. Before that, a big import could delay everything.

p17-62.q: Vertical scaling, or scaling up, is giving one machine more resources, more CPU, more memory, faster disks. It's simple and you don't change any code. But there's a ceiling, it gets expensive fast, resizing often needs downtime, and it's still one machine, so still a single point of failure.
p17-62.k: horizontal vs vertical scaling, scale out vs scale up, stateless services scaling, autoscaling, scale microservices
x: Vertical scaling, or scaling up, is giving one machine more resources, more CPU, more memory, faster disks. It's simple and you don't change any code. But there's a ceiling, it gets expensive fast, resizing often needs downtime, and it's still one machine, so still a single point of failure.

Horizontal scaling, scaling out, means adding more instances of the service behind a load balancer. There's almost no ceiling, you get redundancy, and it fits cloud autoscaling nicely, add instances when load goes up, remove them when it drops, which saves money.

But see, horizontal scaling needs the service to be stateless. No in-memory session or cache that other instances depend on, no local files that need sharing, no assumption that one instance handles all requests for a user. State goes to a shared store like Redis or a database, files go to blob storage, and background jobs need a lock or a queue so they don't run twice.
Databases are the tricky part. Relational databases usually scale up first, then you add read replicas, caching, and sometimes sharding.

In our on-premise CIRT, we actually use both. The web tier scales out across load-balanced IIS servers, with Redis for the shared cache. And each study's SQL Server database scales up. So it depends on the layer.

p17-63.q: So when a service runs on several instances, each one runs the same scheduled jobs. A nightly job could easily run three times. Honestly there are different ways to stop that.
p17-63.k: distributed lock, run job once multiple instances, scheduled job multiple servers, leader election, quartz clustering, hangfire
x: So when a service runs on several instances, each one runs the same scheduled jobs. A nightly job could easily run three times. Honestly there are different ways to stop that.

One is a distributed lock. Before running, each instance tries to grab a lock in a shared store, like a Redis key with SET NX and an expiry, a SQL Server application lock, or a DynamoDB conditional write. Only whoever gets it runs the job. The expiry is important, otherwise a crashed instance holds the lock forever.
Another is a clustered scheduler. Quartz.NET in clustered mode, or Hangfire, keep the job state in a shared database and make sure each trigger fires on only one node.

Or a separate worker. Take the scheduled jobs out of the web service and put them in one dedicated worker with a single instance. Or use the platform's scheduler, like EventBridge Scheduler or a Kubernetes CronJob, to start exactly one task.

And on top of any of these, I make the job itself idempotent. So even if it somehow runs twice, it doesn't send duplicate emails or process the same data twice, like by recording what it already handled.
In our CIRT platform, AlertWatchDog runs on Quartz, and the jobs are designed to be safe if a run overlaps or repeats. Honestly, the idempotency part is what really saves you.

p17-64.q: When I call several services in parallel, like with Task.WhenAll, some will succeed and some might fail. So what I do is decide up front what partial success means for that feature.
p17-64.k: partial failure, parallel calls failure, task whenall error handling, fan out fan in, aggregate results partial
x: When I call several services in parallel, like with Task.WhenAll, some will succeed and some might fail. So what I do is decide up front what partial success means for that feature.

First I classify each dependency, is it required or optional? If a required call fails, the whole operation fails with a clear error. If an optional one fails, like recommendations or some secondary widget, I return the rest with that section empty, plus a flag or warning, so the UI can say "some information is unavailable".

On the technical side, each call gets its own timeout and resilience policy, so one slow service doesn't hold up the whole response. One gotcha with Task.WhenAll, if any task throws, awaiting it rethrows only the first exception. So I look at each task's result individually, or wrap each call in a method that returns a result object with success or error, instead of throwing.
I also set an overall deadline for the whole aggregate request, and cancel whatever's still running with a CancellationToken once it's hit.
For writes it's more serious, because partial failure leaves inconsistent data. There I'd rather use a saga or a queue than parallel calls.
On our IRT dashboard, if the shipment summary call fails, the page still loads subject and inventory data and just shows a small warning on that panel. Users can still do their work.

p17-65.q: So twelve-factor is a set of principles for building cloud-friendly services that are easy to deploy and scale. Let me go through the ones I actually use every day.
p17-65.k: twelve factor app, 12 factor app, cloud native principles, 12 factor, stateless processes config in environment
x: So twelve-factor is a set of principles for building cloud-friendly services that are easy to deploy and scale. Let me go through the ones I actually use every day.

One codebase per app, in version control, deployed to many environments. Dependencies declared explicitly, like NuGet or npm packages, never assumed to be on the server. Config lives in the environment, not in the code, so the same build runs everywhere. Backing services, databases, caches, brokers, are attached resources, you swap them by changing a connection setting. Build, release and run are separate, build once, combine with config to make a release, then run it. Processes are stateless, any state goes to a backing service. Port binding, the app is self-contained and exposes itself on a port, like Kestrel does. Concurrency by scaling out processes. Disposability, meaning fast startup and graceful shutdown, handling SIGTERM properly. Dev and prod parity, using containers to keep environments similar. Logs as event streams, just written to standard output and collected by the platform. And admin tasks, like migrations, run as one-off processes.
ASP.NET Core on containers fits all this pretty naturally.
Honestly, our older on-premise CIRT predates some of these, it has config transforms and IIS. But our newer services follow them. So I've seen both sides.

p17-66.q: Adding a new optional field to a response is normally safe, but only if the clients are tolerant readers, meaning they ignore fields they don't recognise. Most JSON clients do that by default. But some strict deserialisers or generated clients can fail on unknown properties, so I actually check how the important clients are built.
p17-66.k: backward compatibility api, tolerant reader, adding fields to api, breaking change detection, openapi diff
x: Adding a new optional field to a response is normally safe, but only if the clients are tolerant readers, meaning they ignore fields they don't recognise. Most JSON clients do that by default. But some strict deserialisers or generated clients can fail on unknown properties, so I actually check how the important clients are built.

On the request side, a new field has to be optional with a sensible default, so old clients that don't send it behave exactly as before. If you make a new field required, that's a breaking change, no way around it.

And there are things that look small but break clients. Renaming a field, changing its type like number to string, removing enum values, changing date formats, changing default sorting or pagination, or changing what an existing value means. Even adding a new enum value can break a client that has a strict switch statement, so I document that enums may grow.

To catch this automatically, I generate the OpenAPI spec during the build and compare it with the previous version using a diff tool like oasdiff, and the build fails on breaking changes. Contract tests with Pact add the consumer's point of view on top.
For events it's the same rules. I treat the event schema as a published contract, just like the API. That's my approach.

p17-67.q: A stateless service doesn't keep any client-specific data in its own memory between requests. Every request carries what it needs, like a token, and anything that has to last goes to a shared backing service, a database, Redis, blob storage. So any instance can handle any request, you can add or remove instances freely, and if one crashes nothing important is lost. That's what makes horizontal scaling, rolling deployments and autoscaling easy.
p17-67.k: stateful vs stateless, stateless service, sticky sessions, session state microservices, why stateless
x: A stateless service doesn't keep any client-specific data in its own memory between requests. Every request carries what it needs, like a token, and anything that has to last goes to a shared backing service, a database, Redis, blob storage. So any instance can handle any request, you can add or remove instances freely, and if one crashes nothing important is lost. That's what makes horizontal scaling, rolling deployments and autoscaling easy.

A stateful service keeps state locally. In-memory sessions, a local cache that has to stay consistent, uploaded files on local disk, WebSocket connections. Then a user has to keep hitting the same instance, so you need sticky sessions, and restarting or scaling an instance loses or moves that state. Load balancing also gets harder.

Some things are just naturally stateful, like databases, brokers, SignalR connections. Those need special handling, StatefulSets in Kubernetes, managed services, or a backplane, like Redis for SignalR, so messages reach users on whichever instance they're connected to.
So my rule is, keep application services stateless and push state into managed, purpose-built stores.
In our CIRT web tier, we moved session data and cache into Redis, so the load balancer can send any request to any IIS server without sticky sessions. That made deployments a lot calmer.

p17-68.q: Chaos engineering is deliberately breaking things in your system, in a controlled way, to find the weak spots before they cause a real outage. The thinking is, systems will fail anyway, so better we learn how they fail on our own schedule, not at 2 AM.
p17-68.k: chaos engineering, chaos monkey, fault injection, resilience testing, aws fault injection service, game day
x: Chaos engineering is deliberately breaking things in your system, in a controlled way, to find the weak spots before they cause a real outage. The thinking is, systems will fail anyway, so better we learn how they fail on our own schedule, not at 2 AM.

It works like a scientific experiment. You define the steady state, what normal looks like in metrics, like error rate and latency. Then a hypothesis, say "if one instance of the shipment service dies, users won't notice". Then you inject the failure, kill instances, add network latency, make a dependency return errors, fill a disk, take down an availability zone. And you watch whether the steady state holds. Start with a small blast radius, have a clear way to stop the experiment, and grow it gradually.

Tools, there's AWS Fault Injection Service, Azure Chaos Studio, Chaos Mesh for Kubernetes, and in .NET, Polly's chaos strategies, which can inject faults and latency into HttpClient calls in test environments.
Teams also run game days, where everyone practises an incident scenario together. That tests the people and the runbooks too, not only the system.
But honestly, it's only worth it once the basics are there, monitoring, alerts, resilience patterns. Otherwise you're just breaking things without learning much.

p17-69.q: So during a rolling or blue-green deployment, old and new versions of the service run at the same time against the same database. That means every schema change has to work with both. The way I do it is expand and contract, some people call it parallel change.
p17-69.k: zero downtime database migration, expand contract pattern, backward compatible schema change, rolling deployment database, parallel change
x: So during a rolling or blue-green deployment, old and new versions of the service run at the same time against the same database. That means every schema change has to work with both. The way I do it is expand and contract, some people call it parallel change.

Expand first. Add new things without removing old ones. New column as nullable, or a new table. Deploy code that writes to both old and new, but still reads from the old. Backfill existing data in batches, so we don't lock big tables.
Then migrate. Deploy code that reads from the new column, and verify everything's fine in production.
Then contract. Only when no running version uses the old column, stop writing to it, and drop it in a later release.
So a column rename turns into add, copy, switch, remove, across a few deployments, instead of one risky rename.

A few other rules I follow. Never make a column required in the same release that starts filling it. Create indexes online on large tables, where the edition supports it. Keep migrations small and reversible.

With EF Core, I generate SQL migration scripts, review them, and apply them in the pipeline before the new code goes out. In our CIRT platform, the SSDT database projects follow the same idea, since hundreds of study databases have to be updated. So we're quite strict about it.

p17-70.q: Multi-tenancy means one application serves many customers, tenants, while keeping each tenant's data separate and secure.
p17-70.k: multi tenancy, multi tenant architecture, tenant isolation, database per tenant, shared schema tenant id, row level security
x: Multi-tenancy means one application serves many customers, tenants, while keeping each tenant's data separate and secure.

There are three main ways to isolate the data. Database per tenant, each tenant gets its own database. Strongest isolation, easy per-tenant backup, restore and deletion, and you can tune performance per tenant. But it costs more, and schema changes have to roll out to many databases. Schema per tenant, one database with separate schemas, kind of a middle ground. And a shared database with a tenant id column on every table. Cheapest and simplest to run at scale, but every query has to filter by tenant, and one mistake leaks data.

If it's the shared model, I enforce isolation in the platform, I don't just trust every developer to remember. EF Core global query filters on tenant id, SQL Server row-level security as a second layer, and tests that actually try to read across tenants.
The tenant gets resolved from the token or the host name early in the request, and stored in a scoped tenant context that the data layer uses.
Noisy neighbours are the other worry, one big tenant shouldn't slow everyone else, so per-tenant rate limits and monitoring.
Our IRT uses database per study. In clinical trials, sponsor data separation and audit requirements make strong isolation worth the cost. So for us it was an easy decision.

p17-71.q: Time zones cause so many subtle bugs. So I keep one simple rule, store and transfer instants in UTC, and convert to local time only at the edges, for display, or for business rules that really depend on local time.
p17-71.k: time zones microservices, utc dates, datetimeoffset, date handling distributed systems, store dates in utc
x: Time zones cause so many subtle bugs. So I keep one simple rule, store and transfer instants in UTC, and convert to local time only at the edges, for display, or for business rules that really depend on local time.

In .NET, I use DateTimeOffset or UTC DateTime for timestamps, never DateTime.Now in server code. And I inject a TimeProvider, which came in .NET 8, so both code and tests can control the clock. APIs use ISO 8601 with an explicit offset, ending with Z for UTC, so there's no ambiguity at all.

But some values aren't instants, and people miss this. A date of birth or a visit date is a calendar date. So I use DateOnly, not midnight UTC, otherwise it can shift by a day when converted. A recurring local time, like "send at 9 AM site time", needs the IANA time zone id stored, like Asia/Kolkata, and conversion with daylight saving rules. And with daylight saving, some local times happen twice or not at all, so scheduling code has to handle that.
Servers and containers should run in UTC too.

In our IRT, sites in many countries see dates in their own time zone, while everything's stored in UTC. [A visit window bug at US sites came from a midnight conversion, and we fixed it by storing the date as a date.] That's one I won't forget.

p17-72.q: I'd do it step by step, so every step is small and I can roll it back.
p17-72.k: extract service from monolith, migrate feature without downtime, monolith decomposition steps, carve out microservice
x: I'd do it step by step, so every step is small and I can roll it back.

To begin with, inside the monolith itself, I clean up the feature's boundary. Its code should depend on the rest only through an interface, and only its own code should touch its tables. Honestly, this refactoring alone takes out a lot of risk.
Then I build the new service with the same behaviour, its own API, its own database. Initially it can read data that's replicated or synced from the monolith.

Then I run both in parallel. Usually shadow traffic or parallel runs, requests still go to the old code, the new service gets called in the background, and I compare results and log the differences. Users aren't affected at all, and you catch logic differences safely.

After that I switch traffic gradually, behind a feature flag or at the routing layer. Start with a small group of users or tenants, watch errors, latency, data consistency. Rollback is just flipping the flag back.
Then the data ownership moves. The new service becomes the source of truth, and the monolith reads from it, through its API or events.
And only at the end, I delete the old code and tables.
This is pretty much how we're moving modules from the old MVC and Angular portal to the React shell, one module at a time. Drug accountability is the one in progress right now.

p17-73.q: Both describe something that happened, but the scope and purpose are different.
p17-73.k: domain event vs integration event, domain events ddd, mediatr notifications, internal vs external events
x: Both describe something that happened, but the scope and purpose are different.

A domain event is raised inside a service, inside its domain model, so other parts of the same service can react. Let me take an example. A kit's status changes to damaged, the Kit aggregate raises KitDamaged, and a handler in the same service updates the inventory count or writes an audit entry. These are in-process, often dispatched with MediatR notifications, usually in the same transaction or right after saving. And they can use rich internal types, because nobody outside ever sees them.

An integration event goes outside the service, through a broker, so other services can react. So KitDamaged might also become an integration event that reporting or the notification service consumes. Since it's a public contract between services, it uses simple, stable, versioned DTOs, carries only the data others need, and it's published reliably, ideally through the outbox, so it doesn't get lost if the broker is down.
The common flow is like this. Domain event gets raised, a handler converts it to an integration event, writes it to the outbox in the same transaction, and a publisher sends it later.
Why keep them separate? Because then internal refactoring doesn't break other services. You can change your domain model freely, and the contract stays the same.

p17-74.q: I'd push updates to the browser, instead of making it poll every few seconds.
p17-74.k: real time dashboard design, live updates, signalr dashboard, websockets dashboard, push updates to browser
x: I'd push updates to the browser, instead of making it poll every few seconds.

The flow would be like this. When something changes, the owning service publishes an event. A dashboard service consumes these events, updates a small read model or some aggregate counters, like shipments by status, in Redis or a database, and pushes a change notification to the connected browsers.

For the push part, in .NET I'd use SignalR. It uses WebSockets and falls back to other transports automatically. Clients join groups, like a study or a site, so they only get relevant updates, and authorisation is checked when they join a group. With several server instances, you need a Redis backplane, or a managed service like Azure SignalR Service, so a message reaches clients on any instance. On AWS, API Gateway WebSocket APIs are an option.

On the client side, when the page loads, it gets the full current state through a normal API call, and then applies live updates on top. If the connection drops, it reconnects and reloads the state, so it never misses anything.
To avoid flooding the browser, I'd batch or throttle updates, maybe at most once a second per widget.
And honestly, if the dashboard is fine with a bit of delay, just polling every 30 seconds is simpler, and that's a perfectly valid choice too. I wouldn't over-engineer it.

p17-75.q: So access tokens are short-lived, like 5 to 15 minutes, so a stolen one isn't useful for long. A refresh token is a longer-lived credential the client uses to get a new access token from the identity provider, without making the user log in again.
p17-75.k: refresh token, refresh token rotation, where to store tokens, token storage spa, access token expiry, silent refresh
x: So access tokens are short-lived, like 5 to 15 minutes, so a stolen one isn't useful for long. A refresh token is a longer-lived credential the client uses to get a new access token from the identity provider, without making the user log in again.

Since refresh tokens are powerful, I protect them carefully. That's where rotation comes in. Every time a refresh token is used, the provider issues a new one and invalidates the old one. If an old one ever gets used again, that smells like theft, and the provider revokes the whole token family. They also have an absolute lifetime and an idle timeout, and get revoked on logout or password change.

Now storage, that's the tricky part for single-page apps. Local storage is readable by any JavaScript, so one XSS bug and your tokens are gone. The safer options, best first, a BFF that keeps tokens on the server and gives the browser an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie. Or keep tokens only in memory, with rotation, and silent re-authentication when the page reloads.
Mobile apps are different, they use the platform's secure storage, like Keychain or Keystore.

In our React shell, the Keycloak adapter keeps tokens in memory and refreshes them before expiry. And there's an idle timer that logs the user out after inactivity, which is actually a Part 11 requirement for us.

p17-76.q: Role checks answer "is this user a site user?". But they can't answer "can this user see this particular subject?", because that depends on the resource itself, like which site or study it belongs to.
p17-76.k: resource based authorization, object level authorization, idor, bola, check ownership, iauthorizationservice
x: Role checks answer "is this user a site user?". But they can't answer "can this user see this particular subject?", because that depends on the resource itself, like which site or study it belongs to.

If an API only checks roles, a user at site A can just change the id in the URL, from subject 101 to subject 202, and see site B's subject. That's IDOR, insecure direct object reference, or BOLA, broken object level authorization. It's actually number one in the OWASP API Security Top 10.

Resource-based authorization fixes that. After loading the resource, I check the relationship between the user and that resource. Does this subject's site belong to the user's assigned sites? In ASP.NET Core, I inject IAuthorizationService and call AuthorizeAsync with the user, the subject and a requirement, and a handler compares the subject's site with the user's sites. If it fails, 403, or 404 if I don't even want to reveal the resource exists.
Even better, I filter at the query level, so a site user's queries only ever return their own sites' data, using a global filter. Then you can't forget the check.
I also write tests that deliberately try to access another user's resources, because honestly this bug is very easy to miss in review.
In our IRT, site users only see their own site's subjects and kits, enforced in queries and in checks.

p17-77.q: CSRF, cross-site request forgery, is when some malicious website makes the user's browser send a request to our application, and the browser automatically attaches our cookies. So the request runs as the logged-in user. Like a hidden form on a bad site posting to our "change email" endpoint.
p17-77.k: csrf, cross site request forgery, xsrf, antiforgery token, samesite cookie, prevent csrf
x: CSRF, cross-site request forgery, is when some malicious website makes the user's browser send a request to our application, and the browser automatically attaches our cookies. So the request runs as the logged-in user. Like a hidden form on a bad site posting to our "change email" endpoint.

It's mainly a risk when authentication is cookie-based, because browsers send cookies automatically. APIs that use bearer tokens in the Authorization header aren't vulnerable the same way, because the attacker's page can't add that header.

For defences, SameSite cookies are the first layer. Lax or Strict means the browser won't send the cookie on most cross-site requests. Lax is the default in modern browsers now, and it's a strong first layer. Then anti-forgery tokens. The server issues a secret token, it's included in forms or a header, and the server validates it on every state-changing request. The attacker's site can't read it, so it can't fake it. In ASP.NET Core MVC and Razor Pages, this is built in, ValidateAntiForgeryToken and the form tag helper do the work. And a couple of basics, never change state with GET requests, and check the Origin header for sensitive actions.
In our case, the legacy MVC portal uses anti-forgery tokens on its forms, and the React shell calls APIs with bearer tokens. So we're covered on both sides.

p17-78.q: XSS, cross-site scripting, is when an attacker manages to get their JavaScript running in another user's browser, inside our site. Then it can steal tokens, read whatever's on the page, or do actions as that user. Mostly it comes from showing user-supplied data without escaping it, like a comment with a script tag in it.
p17-78.k: xss, cross site scripting, prevent xss, dangerouslysetinnerhtml, angular sanitization, content security policy
x: XSS, cross-site scripting, is when an attacker manages to get their JavaScript running in another user's browser, inside our site. Then it can steal tokens, read whatever's on the page, or do actions as that user. Mostly it comes from showing user-supplied data without escaping it, like a comment with a script tag in it.

Honestly, modern frameworks help a lot by default. React escapes all values in JSX, so text shows as text, not HTML. Angular sanitises values bound in the template, and strips dangerous stuff from innerHTML bindings.

The risk comes when you bypass those protections. dangerouslySetInnerHTML in React, bypassSecurityTrustHtml in Angular, direct DOM manipulation, building URLs from user input, like a javascript colon link, or third-party libraries that inject HTML. If I really have to render HTML, I sanitise it first with something like DOMPurify.

And then other layers on top. A Content Security Policy header that only allows scripts from our own origin and blocks inline scripts, so even if markup gets injected, it can't run. HttpOnly cookies, so scripts can't read session cookies. Output encoding on the server for any HTML it generates. And input validation.
In our React screens, we never use dangerouslySetInnerHTML for user data, and email templates are encoded on the server. So that's how we keep it under control.

p17-79.q: SQL injection happens when user input gets concatenated into a SQL string, so the attacker can change the query itself, like adding OR 1 equals 1, or even dropping tables.
p17-79.k: sql injection, prevent sql injection, parameterized queries, ef core sql injection, fromsqlraw injection, dapper parameters
x: SQL injection happens when user input gets concatenated into a SQL string, so the attacker can change the query itself, like adding OR 1 equals 1, or even dropping tables.
The main defence is parameterised queries, always. The SQL text stays fixed, and user values go separately as parameters, so the database treats them as data, never as code.

In EF Core, LINQ queries are parameterised automatically. For raw SQL, FromSql and ExecuteSql with interpolated strings are actually safe, because EF converts the interpolated values into parameters. The dangerous one is FromSqlRaw with string concatenation. So with FromSqlRaw I always pass parameters separately. In Dapper, I pass an anonymous object of parameters, never concatenated values. In plain ADO.NET, SqlParameter.

One catch, parameters can't be used for identifiers, like table names, column names, or sort direction. So for dynamic sorting, I map the user's choice to a whitelist of known column names. I never put it in directly.
Stored procedures are safe too, unless they build dynamic SQL inside with concatenation. Then they have to use sp_executesql with parameters.
And defence in depth, the app's database login has least privilege, and static analysis flags string-built SQL.
In our IRT, data access uses parameterised queries and stored procedures, and code review specifically looks for raw SQL. That's how we keep it out.

p17-80.q: Never plain text, never reversible encryption. And not fast hashes like MD5 or SHA-256 alone either, because attackers can try billions of guesses per second with GPUs.
p17-80.k: password hashing, store passwords, bcrypt argon2, pbkdf2, salt and hash, aspnet identity password hasher
x: Never plain text, never reversible encryption. And not fast hashes like MD5 or SHA-256 alone either, because attackers can try billions of guesses per second with GPUs.

The right way is a slow, salted, adaptive password hashing algorithm, Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt, or PBKDF2 with a high iteration count. The salt is a unique random value per password, stored with the hash, so the same password gives different hashes, and precomputed rainbow tables don't work. The work factor makes each guess expensive, and you can increase it over time as hardware gets faster.

In .NET, ASP.NET Core Identity's PasswordHasher uses PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA512 and a high iteration count, and it can upgrade hashes when the user logs in next time. For Argon2 and bcrypt there are libraries.

But honestly the better approach is not handling passwords at all. Delegate login to an identity provider, Keycloak, Azure AD, Cognito, and let it handle hashing, lockout, MFA and password policies properly.
Then the related controls, lockout or throttling after failed attempts, checking new passwords against known breached lists, and MFA.
In our IRT, Keycloak handles passwords, with password policy and lockout configured. Those are also Part 11 requirements for us, so we had to get them right anyway.

p17-81.q: So the OWASP Top 10 is the well-known list of the most critical web app security risks, updated every few years from real data. The 2025 edition is honestly very similar to 2021, but a couple of things moved. Let me go through the ones I keep in mind.
p17-81.k: owasp top 10, owasp, web security risks, broken access control, security misconfiguration, owasp api top 10
x: So the OWASP Top 10 is the well-known list of the most critical web app security risks, updated every few years from real data. The 2025 edition is honestly very similar to 2021, but a couple of things moved. Let me go through the ones I keep in mind.

Broken access control is still number one, users acting outside their permissions, like IDOR, where you change an id and see someone else's data. Security misconfiguration, default settings, verbose errors, open storage, missing headers. Software supply chain failures, that's newer, vulnerable or compromised dependencies, packages and build tools. Cryptographic failures, weak or missing encryption, like plain-text passwords or no TLS. Injection, SQL injection, command injection, XSS. Insecure design, missing security thinking in the architecture, like no rate limiting on password reset. Authentication failures, weak passwords, no MFA, bad session handling. Software or data integrity failures, unsigned updates or insecure deserialisation. Logging and alerting failures, attacks nobody notices. And mishandling of exceptional conditions, like failing open or leaking errors.
There's also a separate OWASP API Security Top 10, where broken object level authorization is number one.

How I turn it into habits, authorization checks per resource, parameterised queries, dependency scanning in pipelines, security headers, central logging with alerts, and some threat modelling for new features. That's what actually makes a difference day to day.

p17-82.q: Security headers basically tell the browser to apply extra protections. These are the ones I add.
p17-82.k: security headers, content security policy, hsts, x content type options, x frame options, secure headers asp.net core
x: Security headers basically tell the browser to apply extra protections. These are the ones I add.
HSTS, Strict-Transport-Security, tells browsers to always use HTTPS for the site, so nobody can downgrade the connection. In ASP.NET Core, UseHsts adds it outside development.

Content-Security-Policy controls where scripts, styles, images and frames can load from. Honestly it's the strongest defence against XSS, like a script-src of self blocks inline and third-party scripts. I start in report-only mode to see what breaks, and then enforce it.
X-Content-Type-Options set to nosniff, so the browser doesn't guess content types, because that can turn an uploaded file into a script.
Frame protection, frame-ancestors in the CSP, or X-Frame-Options DENY, to stop clickjacking.
Referrer-Policy, like strict-origin-when-cross-origin, so full URLs with ids don't leak to other sites.
Permissions-Policy, to switch off browser features we don't use, camera, geolocation and so on.
And I remove headers that reveal technology versions, like Server and X-Powered-By.
For APIs, I also set Cache-Control no-store on responses with sensitive data.

I add these with middleware, or a library like NetEscapades.AspNetCore.SecurityHeaders, or at the gateway or reverse proxy. Then a scanner checks them as part of testing, so they don't quietly disappear.

p17-83.q: MFA means you need two or more different kinds of proof. Something you know, like a password. Something you have, like a phone or a security key. Something you are, like a fingerprint. So even if the password is stolen, the attacker still can't log in without the second factor. It blocks the vast majority of account takeover attacks, honestly.
p17-83.k: mfa, multi factor authentication, two factor authentication, totp, add 2fa, webauthn passkeys
x: MFA means you need two or more different kinds of proof. Something you know, like a password. Something you have, like a phone or a security key. Something you are, like a fingerprint. So even if the password is stolen, the attacker still can't log in without the second factor. It blocks the vast majority of account takeover attacks, honestly.

Common second factors are TOTP authenticator apps, which generate a 6-digit code every 30 seconds from a shared secret. Push notifications to an app. SMS codes, better than nothing, but vulnerable to SIM swapping. And the strongest, FIDO2 security keys or passkeys using WebAuthn, which are phishing-resistant because they're tied to the real website's domain.

How would I add it? Through the identity provider, not custom code. Keycloak, Azure AD, Cognito, Okta, all of them support MFA, conditional policies and passkeys with configuration. If I'm using ASP.NET Core Identity directly, it has built-in TOTP support with recovery codes.

A few details matter. Recovery codes for lost devices. Rate limiting on code entry. Asking for MFA again for sensitive actions, which is step-up authentication. And remembering trusted devices only for a limited time.
For our users, all these policies are configured centrally in Keycloak. So no service has to implement any of it itself.

p17-84.q: Least privilege basically means every user, service and process gets only the permissions it needs for its job, nothing extra, and only for as long as it needs them. So if something gets compromised, the damage stays small.
p17-84.k: least privilege, principle of least privilege, minimum permissions, iam least privilege, database least privilege
x: Least privilege basically means every user, service and process gets only the permissions it needs for its job, nothing extra, and only for as long as it needs them. So if something gets compromised, the damage stays small.
I try to apply it at every layer, not just IAM.
For application users, role-based permissions that match real job functions, plus resource-level checks, so a site user only sees their own site.

For services, each one gets its own identity, like an IAM role or a managed identity, with a policy that allows only specific actions on specific resources. Like s3 GetObject on one bucket, not s3 star on everything. I avoid wildcards, and tools like IAM Access Analyzer help find permissions nobody uses.

For databases, the application logs in with an account that can read and write its own tables or run its procedures, but can't change schema or drop tables. Migrations run with a separate, more privileged identity from the pipeline.
For pipelines, deployment credentials are scoped to one environment, and production deployments need approval.
For developers, no standing production access. If someone needs it, it's temporary and audited.
On the network side, services can only reach what they need, through security groups and network policies.
And regular access reviews, removing permissions that aren't used anymore. In regulated work like ours, honestly, those reviews are an audit requirement anyway.

p17-85.q: People mix these up a lot, but they're for different things.
p17-85.k: encryption vs hashing vs encoding, hashing vs encryption, base64 is not encryption, symmetric vs asymmetric encryption
x: People mix these up a lot, but they're for different things.

Encoding just transforms data into another format for compatibility. Like Base64 for binary data inside JSON, or URL encoding. It's not security at all, anyone can decode it, no key needed. I've seen people think Base64 protects a secret, which it doesn't.

Hashing is one-way. It turns data into a fixed-size fingerprint, like SHA-256, and you can't reverse it. Same input always gives the same hash, and a tiny change gives a totally different one. We use it for integrity checks, like verifying a file wasn't changed, and with slow, salted algorithms, for storing passwords.

Encryption is two-way. Data gets scrambled with a key and you can decrypt it with the right key. That's what protects confidentiality. Symmetric encryption, like AES, uses one shared key and it's fast, so it's used for data at rest. Asymmetric, like RSA or elliptic curve, uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt, or a private key to sign and a public key to verify. That's actually how TLS and JWT signatures work.

In .NET, I stick to the built-in System.Security.Cryptography classes, never write my own algorithms. And for app-level protection of things like cookies, I use the Data Protection API. That covers most cases.

p17-86.q: See, logs get copied to many places and kept for a long time. So sensitive data in logs is a real breach risk. I basically treat logs as if lots of people can read them.
p17-86.k: pii in logs, mask sensitive data logs, phi logging, log redaction, gdpr logging, data masking serilog
x: See, logs get copied to many places and kept for a long time. So sensitive data in logs is a real breach risk. I basically treat logs as if lots of people can read them.

The first rule is, don't log it at all. I log ids and outcomes, not personal data. Like log the subject id and the action, not the subject's date of birth or initials. Request and response bodies aren't logged by default, especially on endpoints that handle personal data.

Then structured logging helps control it. With Serilog, you can use destructuring policies to mask or drop specific properties. And in .NET, Microsoft.Extensions.Compliance redaction lets you classify data as sensitive, and it gets redacted in logs automatically.
Then scrubbing in the pipeline. The log shipper or the logging platform can mask patterns like email addresses or card numbers, as a safety net in case something slips through.
And the logs themselves need protection. Access control, encryption, retention limits.
Couple of sneaky ones to watch. Exception messages, because sometimes they contain data values. And tokens in URLs or headers, those should never be logged.

In clinical systems this matters double, because of patient privacy rules and audit requirements. In our CIRT services, we log subject and kit identifiers, never names or contact details, and Splunk access is restricted. That's how we keep it safe.

p17-87.q: With session cookies, the server creates a session after login, keeps the session data on the server or in a shared store, and gives the browser a cookie with just a session id. The browser sends that cookie automatically on every request. It's simple and pretty secure for traditional web apps, especially with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite flags, and you can revoke a session instantly by deleting it. The downsides are you need shared session storage when you scale out, it's tied to one domain, and you need CSRF protection.
p17-87.k: cookies vs tokens, session vs jwt, cookie authentication vs jwt, stateful vs stateless auth, which is better cookie or token
x: With session cookies, the server creates a session after login, keeps the session data on the server or in a shared store, and gives the browser a cookie with just a session id. The browser sends that cookie automatically on every request. It's simple and pretty secure for traditional web apps, especially with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite flags, and you can revoke a session instantly by deleting it. The downsides are you need shared session storage when you scale out, it's tied to one domain, and you need CSRF protection.

With tokens, the client gets a signed token, usually a JWT, and sends it in the Authorization header. The server validates it without storing anything, so it scales easily and works across domains, for mobile apps and service-to-service calls too. But revocation is harder, and in browsers, storing the token safely is honestly tricky, because anything JavaScript can read is exposed to XSS.

What people do nowadays for browser apps is kind of combine them. A BFF does the OAuth login on the server, keeps the tokens server-side, and talks to the browser with a secure cookie. And APIs called by other services or mobile apps use bearer tokens.
So I wouldn't say one is always better. It really depends on what kind of client you have.

p17-88.q: File uploads are a very common attack route, so I put several checks in place.
p17-88.k: secure file upload, file upload security, validate uploaded files, malware scan upload, upload vulnerabilities
x: File uploads are a very common attack route, so I put several checks in place.
Size limits first. A max request size and max file size, so nobody can fill up the disk or memory. In ASP.NET Core that's RequestSizeLimit, plus Kestrel or form options.

Then type validation. Only allow the types the feature actually needs, with an allow-list. And don't trust the file extension or the Content-Type header, because the client sets both. I check the file's real signature, the magic bytes, and for documents, parse them safely.
File names, never use the user's file name for storage, because of path traversal tricks like dot-dot-slash. I generate a random name and keep the original only as metadata, sanitised.

Storage, keep it outside the web root, ideally in object storage like S3 or blob storage, in a private bucket. Then the web server can never execute an uploaded file. Downloads go through the API with authorization checks, or short-lived signed URLs, with Content-Disposition set to attachment.
Then malware scanning before the file is marked available.
Some content risks too. CSV files can carry formula injection, so exports escape leading equals signs. And images can carry metadata with personal data, so I strip that.
And every upload gets logged for audit. That's pretty much my checklist.

p17-89.q: JWTs can be signed two ways, and for microservices the choice really matters.
p17-89.k: hs256 vs rs256, symmetric vs asymmetric signing, jwt signing algorithm, rs256 jwks, which jwt algorithm
x: JWTs can be signed two ways, and for microservices the choice really matters.

Symmetric signing, like HS256, uses one shared secret for both signing and verifying. It's simple and fast. The problem is every service that verifies tokens needs that same secret, and anyone with the secret can also create valid tokens. So if any one service leaks it, an attacker can forge tokens for the whole system. It's only okay when the issuer and the verifier are the same application.

Asymmetric signing, like RS256 with RSA or ES256 with elliptic curves, uses a private key to sign and a public key to verify. Only the identity provider holds the private key. APIs just need the public key, which isn't secret, so even a compromised API can't create tokens. The public keys are published at the JWKS endpoint with a key id, and that makes rotation easy. The provider adds a new key, starts signing with it, and APIs pick it up automatically.
So for distributed systems, asymmetric is the right choice, no question.

One classic attack to know is algorithm confusion. The attacker changes the header's algorithm to "none", or to HS256 and uses the public key as the secret. So validation must only accept the expected algorithms. ASP.NET Core's JWT handler handles this properly when you configure it with the authority. That's how we have it set up.

p17-90.q: A threat model is just a structured way of thinking about what could go wrong with a feature's security before you build it. So security is designed in, not patched on later.
p17-90.k: threat modeling, stride, threat model feature, security design review, attack surface
x: A threat model is just a structured way of thinking about what could go wrong with a feature's security before you build it. So security is designed in, not patched on later.

I keep it lightweight, honestly mostly a one-hour session with the team. We start by drawing a simple data-flow diagram, users, services, data stores, external systems, and the trust boundaries between them, like the internet to our API, or our service to a vendor.

Then we go through each element using STRIDE as a checklist. Spoofing, can someone pretend to be another user or service? Tampering, can data be changed in transit or at rest? Repudiation, can someone deny doing something because there's no audit trail? Information disclosure, can data leak through APIs, logs or errors? Denial of service, can someone overload it? Elevation of privilege, can a user do more than they should?

For each real threat, we agree a mitigation, like resource-level authorization, signing a webhook, rate limiting, and track it as a work item with an owner. Anything we decide to accept gets written down.
And we revisit the model when the design changes.
[When we threat-modelled the drug accountability return screens, it showed the return quantity API needed a site ownership check, which we added before release.] So it does catch real things.

p17-91.q: Webhooks are just HTTP calls between systems, so both sides need to be able to trust each other.
p17-91.k: webhook security, verify webhook signature, hmac webhook, secure webhook endpoint, webhook replay attack
x: Webhooks are just HTTP calls between systems, so both sides need to be able to trust each other.

When we're receiving, the big risk is someone calling our endpoint pretending to be the provider. So I verify a signature. The provider signs the request body with a shared secret using HMAC-SHA256 and sends it in a header. I recompute the HMAC over the raw body and compare using a constant-time comparison. I also check a timestamp header and reject old requests, say older than five minutes, so nobody can replay them. And I store the event id to ignore duplicates, because providers do retry. The endpoint replies quickly with a 2xx and queues the work, so the provider doesn't time out and send it again.

When we're sending, it's the same thing in reverse. Sign each payload, include a timestamp and unique id, HTTPS only, retry with backoff on failure, and let customers rotate their secrets. And since customers give us the URLs, I protect against SSRF, block internal addresses like localhost, private IP ranges and metadata endpoints.
Payloads carry minimal data, often just an id, and the receiver fetches details through the authenticated API.
[Our vendor status callbacks in the newer data transfer API verify an HMAC signature and timestamp before queuing the message.] That's how we did it.

p17-92.q: SSRF, server-side request forgery, is when an attacker gets our server to send a request to a URL they choose. It's a risk anytime the server fetches a user-provided URL, like importing an image from a link, previewing a URL, or calling a webhook URL a customer gave us.
p17-92.k: ssrf, server side request forgery, prevent ssrf, metadata endpoint attack, url fetch vulnerability
x: SSRF, server-side request forgery, is when an attacker gets our server to send a request to a URL they choose. It's a risk anytime the server fetches a user-provided URL, like importing an image from a link, previewing a URL, or calling a webhook URL a customer gave us.

The danger is our server sits inside the network. So the attacker can reach stuff they normally can't, internal admin APIs, databases with HTTP interfaces, or the cloud metadata endpoint, like 169.254.169.254 on AWS, which can hand out temporary credentials. Honestly, some well-known cloud breaches happened exactly like this.

To prevent it, first I avoid fetching user-supplied URLs if I can. If I really need to, I validate against an allow-list of domains, resolve the host name, and block private, loopback, link-local and metadata IP ranges. I check again after redirects, or just disable redirects, because an allowed URL can redirect to an internal one. DNS rebinding is another trick, so I connect to the exact IP I validated.

At the infrastructure level on AWS, I require IMDSv2, which uses session tokens and blocks simple SSRF access to metadata. And outbound traffic gets restricted with security groups or an egress proxy.
Least-privilege roles then limit the damage if something still gets through. So it's layers, like always.

p17-93.q: First I assess it. Are we actually using the vulnerable package, and is the vulnerable code path even reachable? How severe is it, is there a known exploit? Which apps and environments use it? And transitive dependencies matter, because mostly the vulnerable package is pulled in by some other package.
p17-93.k: vulnerable dependency, nuget vulnerability, npm audit, dependency scanning, cve in package, dependabot
x: First I assess it. Are we actually using the vulnerable package, and is the vulnerable code path even reachable? How severe is it, is there a known exploit? Which apps and environments use it? And transitive dependencies matter, because mostly the vulnerable package is pulled in by some other package.

The tools help here. dotnet list package with the vulnerable flag, NuGet audit warnings during restore, npm audit, and scanners like Dependabot, Snyk or GitHub's dependency graph, which open pull requests with the fixed version.

Then the fix. Normally, upgrade to the patched version, run the full test suite, deploy through the normal pipeline, just faster for critical ones. If the direct package doesn't have a fix yet, I pin the transitive dependency to a fixed version, with a direct reference, or npm overrides. If there's no fix at all, I mitigate, disable the affected feature, add input validation or a WAF rule, and track it.
After that, if the risk was high, I check logs for any signs of exploitation, and document everything.
To avoid surprises next time, the pipeline runs dependency scanning on every build and fails on high or critical findings, and we keep dependencies reasonably current so upgrades stay small.
In a validated environment even a security patch goes through change control, but we fast-track the critical ones. That's how we handle it.

p17-94.q: The Data Protection API is ASP.NET Core's built-in system for encrypting and signing data that the app needs to read back later. The framework itself uses it for authentication cookies, anti-forgery tokens and TempData, and you can use it for things like protecting a token in a URL.
p17-94.k: data protection api, asp.net core data protection, key ring, data protection keys, protect unprotect, cookie encryption keys
x: The Data Protection API is ASP.NET Core's built-in system for encrypting and signing data that the app needs to read back later. The framework itself uses it for authentication cookies, anti-forgery tokens and TempData, and you can use it for things like protecting a token in a URL.

You get an IDataProtector from IDataProtectionProvider with a purpose string, and then call Protect and Unprotect. The purpose string keeps uses isolated, so something protected for "password reset" can't be unprotected as something else. And ToTimeLimitedDataProtector adds expiry.

Now the important production part is the key ring. Keys get generated and rotated automatically, every 90 days by default. By default they're stored locally, which is fine on one machine. But with several instances behind a load balancer, or containers that restart, each instance ends up with different keys. So a cookie issued by one instance can't be read by another, and users randomly get logged out or see anti-forgery errors.

So in production, I persist the keys to a shared location, Redis, a database, blob storage or S3, set the same application name on all instances, and protect the keys at rest with Azure Key Vault, a certificate, or AWS KMS.
Honestly, this is a classic one when you move an app from a single server to a load-balanced or containerised setup.

p17-95.q: So a Content Security Policy is a response header that tells the browser which sources are allowed for scripts, styles, images, fonts, frames and API calls. If an attacker injects a script, the browser refuses to run it because it doesn't match the policy. It's one of the strongest XSS defences.
p17-95.k: content security policy, csp, csp rollout, csp report only, nonce csp, csp angular react
x: So a Content Security Policy is a response header that tells the browser which sources are allowed for scripts, styles, images, fonts, frames and API calls. If an attacker injects a script, the browser refuses to run it because it doesn't match the policy. It's one of the strongest XSS defences.

A strict policy would be something like default-src self, script-src self, object-src none, frame-ancestors none, and connect-src for our API and identity provider. Inline scripts get blocked unless they have a nonce, a random value per response, or a hash.
The thing is, rolling it out on an existing site can break stuff. Inline scripts, inline event handlers, third-party analytics, fonts from CDNs, older libraries that use eval.

So I start with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only. It doesn't block anything, it just reports violations to an endpoint. I collect reports for a couple of weeks, fix or allow the legitimate sources, move inline code out where possible, and only then switch to enforcing. And I keep reporting on, to catch new issues later.

Modern React and Angular builds with Vite or the Angular CLI work nicely with a strict CSP, because scripts are external files anyway. Angular also supports nonces for its inline styles. So for newer apps it's honestly not that painful.

p17-96.q: Honestly, you can't hide a secret in a browser app. Whatever's in the JavaScript bundle, including environment variables injected at build time, like Vite's VITE prefixed variables or Angular's environment files, anyone can see by opening developer tools.
p17-96.k: api keys in frontend, hide api key react, environment variables frontend secret, secrets in spa, vite env secret
x: Honestly, you can't hide a secret in a browser app. Whatever's in the JavaScript bundle, including environment variables injected at build time, like Vite's VITE prefixed variables or Angular's environment files, anyone can see by opening developer tools.

So my rule is simple, no real secrets in front-end code, ever. Only public values go there. The API base URL, the identity provider's URL, a public client id, or a publishable key that's designed to be public and restricted, like a maps key locked to our domain.

When the front end needs to call some service that requires a secret key, the call goes through our own backend. The browser calls our API with the user's token, our API reads the secret from a vault, adds it, and calls the third-party service. That's also the place where rate limits and authorization get applied.
For our own APIs, the front end doesn't use API keys at all. Users log in with OpenID Connect, and the app just sends a short-lived access token.
I also run secret scanning on the repo and the build output, because developers sometimes drop a key in an env file and it ends up in the bundle without anybody noticing.
In our React shell, the Vite variables contain only URLs and the public Keycloak client id. Nothing sensitive at all.

p17-97.q: So a normal network firewall works at the network and transport layers. It allows or blocks traffic based on IP addresses, ports and protocols. Like "allow HTTPS on 443 from anywhere, block everything else", or "only the app servers can reach the database on 1433". In the cloud, security groups, network ACLs and Azure network security groups do that job.
p17-97.k: waf vs firewall, web application firewall, aws waf, network firewall, what is waf
x: So a normal network firewall works at the network and transport layers. It allows or blocks traffic based on IP addresses, ports and protocols. Like "allow HTTPS on 443 from anywhere, block everything else", or "only the app servers can reach the database on 1433". In the cloud, security groups, network ACLs and Azure network security groups do that job.

A WAF, web application firewall, works at layer 7, the application layer. It actually understands HTTP and looks inside the requests, URLs, headers, query strings, bodies. So it can block common attack patterns, SQL injection strings, cross-site scripting payloads, known bad bots, traffic from certain countries, or too many requests from one IP. Examples are AWS WAF on CloudFront, an ALB or API Gateway, Azure's WAF on Front Door or Application Gateway, and Cloudflare.
They work together. The firewall limits who can talk to what, and the WAF filters bad content inside the traffic that's allowed.

But I'd say a WAF is a safety net, not a replacement for secure code. People bypass it with clever encoding, and it gives false positives too. So I start new rules in count mode, review what would've been blocked, and then turn on blocking. And the application still has to validate input and use parameterised queries. The WAF doesn't let you skip that.

p17-98.q: The trick is having two valid credentials during an overlap period, so nothing breaks while you switch.
p17-98.k: secret rotation, rotate database password, certificate rotation, zero downtime rotation, key rotation
x: The trick is having two valid credentials during an overlap period, so nothing breaks while you switch.

For database passwords or API keys, it's dual credentials. You create the new secret while the old one still works, and update the secret store. Applications pick up the new value, either by reloading config periodically, or by fetching a fresh secret when authentication fails and retrying. Once every instance is on the new one, you revoke the old one. AWS Secrets Manager actually automates this with rotation Lambdas using alternating users, so one is always valid.

For signing keys, like JWT keys, the identity provider publishes both old and new public keys in its JWKS. It starts signing with the new key, and once old tokens have expired, the old key is removed.

For TLS certificates, I automate renewal well before expiry, with AWS Certificate Manager, Key Vault auto-renewal, or Let's Encrypt with cert-manager, and for anything manual, an alert at 30 days before expiry. Honestly, expired certificates cause a surprising number of outages.
Even better is not having secrets at all where possible. IAM roles and managed identities rotate credentials automatically.
And on the app side, don't cache secrets forever, and don't need a restart to pick up a new one. Otherwise rotation means downtime anyway.

p17-99.q: Sometimes the question isn't can the user see this record, it's which fields of it can they see. In clinical trials this is critical. Blinded users must never see which treatment a subject got, while unblinded roles, like pharmacists or the safety team, can.
p17-99.k: field level security, data level authorization, hide fields by role, blinded unblinded access, column level security, mask fields by permission
x: Sometimes the question isn't can the user see this record, it's which fields of it can they see. In clinical trials this is critical. Blinded users must never see which treatment a subject got, while unblinded roles, like pharmacists or the safety team, can.
And I enforce it on the server, never just by hiding fields in the UI. Because anyone can call the API directly, or just look at the network response in the browser.

The way we do it, the user's permissions from their role decide a data access level. The API builds different DTOs, different projections, for different access levels, so for blinded users the sensitive fields are simply never selected from the database. A blinded user's response doesn't have the treatment arm at all, not even as a null that hints something's there. Reports and exports follow the same rules, and so do logs and error messages.
For extra safety, the database can enforce it too, with views or column permissions, so a reporting tool can't sneak around the application.
