p17-147.q: See, in Chain of Responsibility, a request passes through a chain of handlers. Each handler decides, do I process it, pass it to the next one, or stop the chain here? And the sender doesn't know which handler ends up dealing with it.
p17-147.k: chain of responsibility, chain of responsibility pattern, pipeline pattern, middleware chain, handler chain c#
x: See, in Chain of Responsibility, a request passes through a chain of handlers. Each handler decides, do I process it, pass it to the next one, or stop the chain here? And the sender doesn't know which handler ends up dealing with it.

ASP.NET Core's middleware pipeline is the best-known example. Each middleware gets the HttpContext and a next delegate. It can do work before calling next, after it, or short-circuit, like the authentication middleware returning 401 without calling the rest. HttpClient's DelegatingHandlers and MediatR pipeline behaviours are the same idea.

I've used it for validation and rule checks. Like before a subject can be randomised, a series of checks has to pass. Is the site active, is consent recorded, is the subject eligible, is there drug stock? Each check is a small class implementing a common interface. The chain runs them in order and stops with a clear message at the first failure. Adding a new rule means adding a class and registering it, nothing else gets touched, and each rule gets its own unit test.

The risks, the order of handlers matters and has to be explicit, and it can get hard to see which handler did what. So I log the outcome of each step. That's saved me more than once when someone asked why a subject got blocked.

p17-148.q: The Specification pattern puts a business rule, or query criteria, into its own small, named, reusable object. So instead of repeating the same Where conditions all over the place, I create a class like ActiveSitesInCountrySpecification that wraps the condition, and use it wherever I need that filter.
p17-148.k: specification pattern, specification pattern ef core, reusable query filters, ardalis specification, business rule objects
x: The Specification pattern puts a business rule, or query criteria, into its own small, named, reusable object. So instead of repeating the same Where conditions all over the place, I create a class like ActiveSitesInCountrySpecification that wraps the condition, and use it wherever I need that filter.

A specification usually exposes an expression, so it works both with EF Core, which translates it to SQL, and in memory, to check a single object. And you can combine specifications with And, Or and Not, so complex rules get built from simple named ones.

With repositories, it keeps the repository small. Instead of a method for every combination, like GetActiveSitesByCountryWithDepots, the repository has one method that takes a specification. The Ardalis.Specification library also lets specifications include related data, ordering and paging.
What you get is business rules with names the business actually understands, the logic in one place, and each specification easy to unit test.

The downside is more classes and more abstraction. Honestly, with EF Core, a lot of teams just use extension methods on IQueryable, like query dot ActiveOnly dot InCountry, which gives most of the benefit with less ceremony. That's often what I do too. I go for full specifications only when the rules are complex and reused heavily.

p17-149.q: So Template Method basically defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class, a fixed sequence of steps, and lets subclasses override specific steps without changing the overall flow.
p17-149.k: template method pattern, template method design pattern, abstract base class steps, hook methods, skeleton algorithm
x: So Template Method basically defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class, a fixed sequence of steps, and lets subclasses override specific steps without changing the overall flow.

Let me take an example. Every file import follows the same process. Open the file, validate the header, read each row, validate the row, transform it, save in batches, write a summary. A base class, ImportJobBase, implements Run with that sequence, and declares abstract or virtual methods for the bits that differ, like ValidateRow and MapRow. A KitImportJob and a SiteImportJob only implement those bits. The common stuff, batching, error collection, logging, progress reporting, is written once, so every import behaves the same way.
Hook methods are optional steps with an empty default, like OnCompleted, and subclasses override them only if they need to.

The downside is it relies on inheritance. That's tight coupling between base and derived classes, and deep hierarchies get hard to follow. So honestly, in modern code I often prefer composition. One ImportRunner class that takes an IRowHandler strategy for the varying parts. Same consistent flow, but the parts are swappable and easier to test.
BackgroundService in .NET is a small template method example actually. StartAsync is fixed, and you just override ExecuteAsync.

p17-150.q: Okay, so clean architecture organises code in layers, with the business rules in the centre and the technical details on the outside. The core idea is the dependency rule, source code dependencies only point inward. Inner layers know nothing about the outer ones.
p17-150.k: clean architecture, onion architecture, dependency rule, domain application infrastructure layers, hexagonal architecture
x: Okay, so clean architecture organises code in layers, with the business rules in the centre and the technical details on the outside. The core idea is the dependency rule, source code dependencies only point inward. Inner layers know nothing about the outer ones.

In a typical .NET solution, you'd have four projects. Domain is at the centre, entities, value objects, domain events and business rules, with no dependency on frameworks or databases. Application has the use cases, commands and queries with their handlers, and it defines the interfaces it needs, like IShipmentRepository or IEmailSender. It depends only on Domain. Infrastructure implements those interfaces with real technology, EF Core, SQL Server, RabbitMQ, SMTP, external APIs. And the API layer, the presentation, has the controllers or minimal API endpoints and wires everything together with DI.

Since Application defines the interfaces and Infrastructure implements them, the business logic doesn't depend on the database or frameworks. That's dependency inversion. So business rules are easy to unit test, and you can change technical details with less impact.
The cost is more projects, more mapping, some ceremony. For a simple CRUD service, honestly, it's overkill.
Our newer IRT APIs follow this structure, with MediatR handlers in the Application layer and EF Core in Infrastructure. So I work with it daily.

p17-151.q: Vertical slice architecture organises code by feature instead of by technical layer. Each feature or use case, like CreateShipment or GetSiteInventory, gets its own folder or file with everything it needs, the request, validation, the handler with its data access, and the response. And slices are independent of each other.
p17-151.k: vertical slice architecture, feature folders, vertical slices vs layers, organize by feature, minimal api vertical slice
x: Vertical slice architecture organises code by feature instead of by technical layer. Each feature or use case, like CreateShipment or GetSiteInventory, gets its own folder or file with everything it needs, the request, validation, the handler with its data access, and the response. And slices are independent of each other.

See, in a layered structure, adding one feature means touching a controller, a service, a repository, DTOs and mappings across several projects. With vertical slices, a change usually stays in one place, so it's easier to find, understand, and even delete code. Each slice can also pick the simplest approach it needs. One might use EF Core with projections, another raw SQL with Dapper, without forcing every feature through the same layers.

Compared with clean architecture, which is about the direction of dependencies between layers, slices are about cohesion around features. They aren't really opposites. A lot of teams combine them, keep a shared domain model and infrastructure, but organise the application layer by feature, often with MediatR handlers.
The risk with slices is duplication between them, and shared logic leaking around randomly. So when I notice repetition, I pull shared domain rules into the domain model.
For CRUD-heavy services with lots of independent features, I like slices. For complex domains, I add a richer domain layer on top. That's how I'd balance it.

p17-152.q: DRY, Don't Repeat Yourself, means each piece of knowledge should have one authoritative place in the code, so a change doesn't need to happen in ten places. KISS, Keep It Simple, means picking the simplest solution that works, because simple code is easier to understand, test and change. YAGNI, You Aren't Gonna Need It, means don't build features or abstractions for some imagined future need.
p17-152.k: dry kiss yagni, dont repeat yourself, keep it simple, you aint gonna need it, wrong abstraction, design principles
x: DRY, Don't Repeat Yourself, means each piece of knowledge should have one authoritative place in the code, so a change doesn't need to happen in ten places. KISS, Keep It Simple, means picking the simplest solution that works, because simple code is easier to understand, test and change. YAGNI, You Aren't Gonna Need It, means don't build features or abstractions for some imagined future need.

Now DRY can go wrong, and I've seen it. It happens when you apply it to code that only looks similar but actually represents different business concepts. If I merge them into one shared method or base class, they're now coupled. When one changes for its own reasons, the shared code starts getting parameters and flags for each caller, and it becomes harder to understand than the duplication ever was. That's the wrong abstraction. A rule of thumb I like is the rule of three. Tolerate duplication twice, and abstract when the third case shows you the real pattern.
Across microservices, DRY is even riskier. Sharing business code between services couples their deployments, so a little duplication is often the better deal.

YAGNI and KISS go together. No generic plugin framework for one use case, no repository on top of a repository. I'd rather keep code simple and refactor when a real need shows up, with good tests backing me.

p17-153.q: Honestly, I just use BenchmarkDotNet, because doing accurate micro-benchmarks by hand with a Stopwatch is surprisingly hard. The JIT needs warm-up, tiered compilation changes the code over time, the GC can pause right in the middle, and the compiler can optimise away code whose result isn't used. BenchmarkDotNet takes care of all that. It runs warm-up iterations, lots of measured iterations, in separate processes, and gives you stats like mean, error and standard deviation.
p17-153.k: benchmarkdotnet, benchmark c#, micro benchmark, measure performance c#, memorydiagnoser
x: Honestly, I just use BenchmarkDotNet, because doing accurate micro-benchmarks by hand with a Stopwatch is surprisingly hard. The JIT needs warm-up, tiered compilation changes the code over time, the GC can pause right in the middle, and the compiler can optimise away code whose result isn't used. BenchmarkDotNet takes care of all that. It runs warm-up iterations, lots of measured iterations, in separate processes, and gives you stats like mean, error and standard deviation.

I write a class with methods marked Benchmark, say comparing two ways of parsing a file line, mark one as the Baseline, add MemoryDiagnoser to see allocations per operation, and use Params to try different input sizes. Then I run it in Release mode, never Debug, with BenchmarkRunner.
The results show time and allocated bytes per operation, and the ratio to the baseline. In a server app, honestly, allocations matter as much as time, because they drive GC pressure.

A few practices I follow. Use realistic data. Return or consume the results so the code doesn't get eliminated. And remember a micro-benchmark only tells you about that tiny piece. Before optimising anything, I profile the real application first, with dotnet-trace or a profiler, to find the actual hot spot, and then use benchmarks to compare fixes.
I also keep the important benchmarks in the repo, to catch regressions later.

p17-154.q: These are the .NET diagnostic command-line tools, and they work on Windows, Linux and inside containers.
p17-154.k: dotnet counters, dotnet trace, dotnet dump, dotnet gcdump, diagnose production dotnet, diagnostic tools
x: These are the .NET diagnostic command-line tools, and they work on Windows, Linux and inside containers.

dotnet-counters is always my first step. It shows live counters for a running process, CPU, working set, GC heap size, collections per generation, allocation rate, thread pool thread count and queue length, exception count, ASP.NET Core request rates. It quickly tells me what kind of problem I'm dealing with, a memory leak, GC pressure, or thread pool starvation, without stopping the app.

dotnet-trace collects a detailed trace, like CPU sampling, over a period. I open it in Visual Studio, PerfView or speedscope to see which methods eat the most CPU. That's for "the service is slow and CPU is high".

dotnet-dump captures a full memory dump, and you can analyse it with commands like dumpheap stat, to see which object types use the most memory, and gcroot, to see what's keeping an object alive. That's for memory leaks and hangs. And clrstack shows what every thread is doing, which helps a lot with deadlocks and blocked threads.
dotnet-gcdump is a lighter heap snapshot, good for comparing two snapshots to find what's growing.

In containers, I either include the tools in a debug image, or attach a sidecar sharing the diagnostics socket. And dumps contain real data, so we handle them securely. That's important in our domain.

p17-155.q: Actually in modern .NET, AssemblyLoadContext is the way to load plugin assemblies at runtime. It replaced AppDomains from .NET Framework.
p17-155.k: plugin architecture, assemblyloadcontext, load assembly dynamically, plugin loading .net, isolated plugin dependencies
x: Actually in modern .NET, AssemblyLoadContext is the way to load plugin assemblies at runtime. It replaced AppDomains from .NET Framework.

How it's structured, a shared contracts assembly defines the plugin interface, like IDataTransferJob, and both the host and the plugins reference it. Each plugin is built as a separate assembly with its own dependencies. At startup, the host scans a plugins folder, creates a custom AssemblyLoadContext per plugin, loads its main assembly, finds types implementing the interface, and creates them, usually with ActivatorUtilities so they get DI services.

The custom load context uses AssemblyDependencyResolver, which reads the plugin's deps.json, so each plugin can use its own versions of dependencies without clashing with the host or other plugins. But the shared contracts assembly has to be loaded from the host's context. Otherwise the types won't match and casting to the interface fails. Honestly, that's the most common plugin bug.
Load contexts can be collectible, so a plugin can be unloaded, but only if no references to it are left anywhere.
A simpler alternative, when plugins are known at build time, is just to reference them as packages and register them in DI, selected by configuration. Often that's enough.
Our newer data transfer APIs run integration jobs as plugins, so new vendor integrations can be added without changing the host. That's been really handy.

p17-156.q: Okay, so .NET Aspire is a set of tools and libraries for building and running distributed, cloud-ready apps, and honestly its biggest win is the local development experience.
p17-156.k: dotnet aspire, aspire app host, aspire dashboard, aspire service defaults, local orchestration .net
x: Okay, so .NET Aspire is a set of tools and libraries for building and running distributed, cloud-ready apps, and honestly its biggest win is the local development experience.

You have an App Host, which is a small C# project where you describe the parts of your application in code. The API projects, a front end, and resources like SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ or PostgreSQL. When you run it, Aspire starts everything, runs the infrastructure in containers, and wires up connection strings and service discovery for you. So a new developer can clone the repo and press F5, instead of following some long setup document that's always out of date.

Then there's the Aspire dashboard. It shows all services, their logs, traces and metrics in one place, using OpenTelemetry, so I can follow a request across services locally. That's really nice for debugging.
Service defaults is a shared project that adds OpenTelemetry, health checks, service discovery and HTTP resilience to every service with one call, so they're all consistent.
And integrations are NuGet packages for common services, like Redis or Azure Service Bus, that register clients with health checks and telemetry built in.
For deployment, Aspire can generate manifests and deploy to Azure Container Apps or Kubernetes, but a lot of teams keep their own pipelines.
So I'd say it's very useful for local dev and consistency, even if production still goes through Terraform or the existing pipelines.

p17-157.q: Knowing this actually helps me pick the right collection, so let me go through the common ones.
p17-157.k: big o collections, collection complexity, list vs dictionary vs linkedlist, sorteddictionary complexity, choose collection c#
x: Knowing this actually helps me pick the right collection, so let me go through the common ones.

List of T is a dynamic array. Index access is O(1). Adding at the end is O(1) on average, with the occasional resize. Inserting or removing in the middle is O(n), because elements shift. Contains or IndexOf is O(n), since it scans. Sort is O(n log n).
Dictionary and HashSet are hash tables, so O(1) average for add, remove and lookup by key, and no ordering.

SortedDictionary is a balanced tree, O(log n) for add, remove and lookup, and it keeps keys sorted. SortedList is an array-backed sorted collection, O(log n) lookup with binary search, but O(n) inserts. It uses less memory though.
LinkedList has O(1) insert and remove when you already have the node, but O(n) to find anything, and poor cache locality. So honestly it's rarely the best choice in practice.
Queue and Stack are O(1) for enqueue, dequeue, push and pop.
PriorityQueue, which came in .NET 6, is a heap. O(log n) to enqueue and to dequeue the smallest priority item, and O(1) to peek.

In real projects, the biggest win I've seen is replacing repeated List.Contains or First lookups inside loops with a Dictionary or HashSet built once. That turns O(n squared) into O(n), and it's usually a five-minute fix.

p17-158.q: See, an async method that awaits I/O, like a database query or an HTTP call, doesn't hold a thread while it waits. The thread goes back to the pool, and when the I/O finishes, some thread picks up the continuation. That's what makes servers scale.
p17-158.k: task.run vs async, when to use task.run, task.run in asp.net core, cpu bound vs io bound, offload work thread pool
x: See, an async method that awaits I/O, like a database query or an HTTP call, doesn't hold a thread while it waits. The thread goes back to the pool, and when the I/O finishes, some thread picks up the continuation. That's what makes servers scale.

Task.Run is different. It queues a delegate to run on a thread pool thread, so it's for CPU-bound work, it moves the work off the current thread. In a desktop app, that's useful to keep the UI thread responsive while doing some heavy calculation.

But in ASP.NET Core, the request is already running on a thread pool thread. So wrapping work in Task.Run and immediately awaiting it just swaps one pool thread for another. Extra overhead, zero benefit. And wrapping a synchronous I/O call in Task.Run, what people call fake async, still blocks a thread, it just hides it somewhere else. The real fix there is a truly async API.

Task.Run in ASP.NET Core makes sense only in specific cases. Running several CPU-bound pieces of work in parallel, or kicking off fire-and-forget background work. Even for that, honestly, I prefer a hosted service with a queue, because it handles errors, scopes and shutdown properly.
So my rule is simple. async and await for I/O, and Task.Run only for CPU-bound work that really benefits from running somewhere else.

p17-159.q: So tuples basically let you group a few values together without defining a class. Modern C# uses ValueTuple, which is a struct, with nice syntax. A method can return a tuple of int Count and decimal Total, and the caller just reads result.Count and result.Total. The element names are compile-time only, so you get readable code without creating a type.
p17-159.k: tuples c#, value tuple, deconstruction, return multiple values, named tuple, tuple vs class
x: So tuples basically let you group a few values together without defining a class. Modern C# uses ValueTuple, which is a struct, with nice syntax. A method can return a tuple of int Count and decimal Total, and the caller just reads result.Count and result.Total. The element names are compile-time only, so you get readable code without creating a type.

Deconstruction splits a tuple, or any type with a Deconstruct method, into separate variables. Like var, open bracket count comma total, equals GetSummary. Records support it automatically through their positional parameters, and you can use underscore as a discard for values you don't care about. It also gives you neat tricks, like swapping two variables in one line, a comma b equals b comma a.
Tuples work nicely in pattern matching too. Like switching on a tuple of status and isUrgent together, which is way clearer than nested ifs.

Where I use them, private and internal helper methods returning two or three related values, and local grouping in LINQ. I avoid them in public APIs, DTOs and anything serialised, because the element names don't survive serialisation, and they don't carry meaning or validation. If a tuple is getting passed around a lot, that's a sign it should be a record.
The older System.Tuple class, with Item1 and Item2, is a reference type, and I don't use it in new code.

p17-160.q: Okay, so a local function is just a method declared inside another method. It's only visible inside that method, so you keep helper logic close to where it's used without cluttering up the class.
p17-160.k: local functions, local function vs lambda, static local function, nested method c#
x: Okay, so a local function is just a method declared inside another method. It's only visible inside that method, so you keep helper logic close to where it's used without cluttering up the class.

How it's different from a lambda, a few things. Local functions can be declared after they're used, they're named, and recursion is easy. They support generics, ref and out parameters, params, and iterators with yield return. And there's performance. A lambda that captures variables allocates a closure object and a delegate on the heap. A local function that's only called directly can capture variables into a struct on the stack, so no allocation. In hot paths, that adds up.
If you mark a local function static, it can't capture any variables of the enclosing method. That makes dependencies explicit and avoids accidental captures.

Two places I use them a lot. One is argument validation for iterators and async methods. An iterator's body runs lazily, so I validate arguments in the outer method, which runs immediately, and put the yield return logic in a local function. Same for async methods, when I want validation exceptions thrown right away and not inside the task. The other is breaking a long method into readable steps that don't really make sense as class-level methods.
And I use lambdas when I need a delegate to pass somewhere, like into LINQ or an event.

p17-161.q: I always paginate list endpoints. Returning everything works fine in testing and then blows up in production when the table grows, I've seen that happen.
p17-161.k: api pagination design, paged response, page size limit, next page link, continuation token, cursor pagination api
x: I always paginate list endpoints. Returning everything works fine in testing and then blows up in production when the table grows, I've seen that happen.
The request takes either a page number and page size, or a cursor. Page size has a sensible default, like 25, and a hard max, like 100, enforced on the server, so nobody can ask for a million rows.

The response wraps the items with some metadata. For page-based paging, the page number, page size and total count. For cursor-based paging, a next cursor or continuation token, and whether there's more. Some APIs also return links to next and previous pages, or use the Link header, so clients don't build URLs themselves.

Which style depends on the data. Offset paging, skip and take, is simple and lets users jump to page 10, so it suits admin screens. But it gets slow on deep pages, because the database still reads all the skipped rows. And results shift if rows get added while someone's paging. Cursor or keyset paging uses the last item's sort key, like created after this date and id, which is fast at any depth and stable. So that's better for big tables, infinite scrolling, and API consumers syncing data.
One thing people forget, ordering must be deterministic, so I always add a unique tie-breaker like the id to the sort.
And total counts can be expensive on big tables, so I make them optional.

p17-162.q: So an ETag is a version identifier for a resource, sent back in a response header. It can be a hash of the content, or a version number like SQL Server's rowversion. Clients use it in conditional requests, and it helps with two things.
p17-162.k: etag, if none match, if match, conditional request, 304 not modified, 412 precondition failed, optimistic concurrency http
x: So an ETag is a version identifier for a resource, sent back in a response header. It can be a hash of the content, or a version number like SQL Server's rowversion. Clients use it in conditional requests, and it helps with two things.

One is caching. The client sends If-None-Match with the ETag it already has. If the resource hasn't changed, the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body. That saves bandwidth and processing, which really helps for large resources fetched often, like study configuration.

The other is concurrency control. When updating, the client sends If-Match with the ETag it got when it read the resource. The server compares it with the current version. If someone else changed it in the meantime, they don't match, and the server returns 412 Precondition Failed instead of silently overwriting the other person's change. That's the lost update problem. The client then reloads and the user can merge or retry. Some APIs even return 428 Precondition Required if If-Match is missing on updates, just to force clients to use it.

In ASP.NET Core, I wire this up myself. Map the entity's row version to the ETag header, read If-Match in the update endpoint, and pass that version into EF Core's concurrency token check, so the database actually enforces it.
It's basically optimistic concurrency, just the HTTP version of it.

p17-163.q: Actually HTTP caching headers tell browsers, CDNs and proxies whether they can reuse a response and for how long. Done right, it can massively cut load.
p17-163.k: cache control header, http caching api, no store, max age, private public cache, vary header
x: Actually HTTP caching headers tell browsers, CDNs and proxies whether they can reuse a response and for how long. Done right, it can massively cut load.

Cache-Control is the main one. max-age equals 300 means the response can be reused for 300 seconds. public allows shared caches like a CDN to store it, while private means only the user's own browser can cache it, which is what you want for user-specific data. no-cache, and this confuses people, means the client can store it but has to revalidate with the server before using it, usually with an ETag. no-store means don't store it anywhere, which I use for sensitive stuff like patient information or tokens.
Vary tells caches which request headers change the response, like Accept-Language or Authorization, so different versions get cached separately.

For APIs, my defaults are like this. Sensitive or user-specific data gets no-store, or private with no-cache. Truly public data that rarely changes, like a list of countries or static reference data, gets public with a max-age, maybe through a CDN. And responses with ETags support cheap revalidation.

In ASP.NET Core, I set headers directly, use the ResponseCache attribute, or use output caching middleware. That last one is different actually, it's the server reusing its own response, regardless of what clients do.
Getting caching wrong with user data can leak information between users. So honestly, I'm conservative here.

p17-164.q: So content negotiation is how the server picks the response format based on what the client asks for. The client sends an Accept header, like application/json or application/xml, and the server picks a matching output formatter. If more than one is acceptable, it follows the client's preference order.
p17-164.k: content negotiation, accept header, output formatters, return xml or json, produces attribute, 406 not acceptable
x: So content negotiation is how the server picks the response format based on what the client asks for. The client sends an Accept header, like application/json or application/xml, and the server picks a matching output formatter. If more than one is acceptable, it follows the client's preference order.

In ASP.NET Core controllers, JSON is the default formatter, using System.Text.Json. You can add others, like XML with AddXmlSerializerFormatters, or a custom formatter for CSV. By default, if the client asks for a format the server doesn't support, it just falls back to JSON. If you set ReturnHttpNotAcceptable to true, it returns 406 Not Acceptable instead, which is stricter.

The Produces attribute restricts or documents which content types an action returns, and Consumes does the same for request bodies. That's checked against the Content-Type header, and you get 415 Unsupported Media Type if it doesn't match.
Minimal APIs are simpler. They return JSON by default and don't do full negotiation, so for other formats I return a specific result, like Results.Text or a file.

Honestly, in practice most modern APIs are JSON only, and that's fine. Where I've actually used negotiation is exports, where the same report endpoint returns JSON for the UI and CSV for download, based on the Accept header or a format parameter.
Accept-Language for localisation is a related kind of negotiation too.

p17-165.q: HATEOAS stands for Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State. It's the top level of the Richardson maturity model for REST. The idea is that responses include links telling the client what it can do next. Like a shipment response containing "cancel" or "track" links, only when those actions are allowed. So the client discovers actions from the response, instead of hard-coding URLs and business rules.
p17-165.k: hateoas, hypermedia, rest maturity model, richardson maturity model, links in api response
x: HATEOAS stands for Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State. It's the top level of the Richardson maturity model for REST. The idea is that responses include links telling the client what it can do next. Like a shipment response containing "cancel" or "track" links, only when those actions are allowed. So the client discovers actions from the response, instead of hard-coding URLs and business rules.
In theory, clients are less coupled to URL structures, and the server controls which actions are available based on the current state and the user's permissions.

But honestly, I rarely see full HATEOAS in real projects, ours included. Most front ends are built together with the API, so they already know the URLs. Client developers find parsing links more work than calling documented endpoints. And tooling, like OpenAPI clients, is built around fixed endpoints anyway.

What I do use are the practical bits. Pagination links in list responses, next and previous. A Location header on 201 Created pointing to the new resource. And flags in responses saying which actions are allowed, like canCancel or canReturn, computed on the server from the state and the user's permissions. So the UI shows the right buttons without duplicating business rules in the front end. That gets you most of the benefit, with way less complexity, so that's where I've landed.

FluentValidation is a library where the rules live in a separate validator class, like a CreateShipmentValidator inheriting AbstractValidator, written as fluent code. RuleFor Quantity GreaterThan zero, RuleFor SiteId NotEmpty, that kind of thing.

That's actually how our newer IRT APIs work. FluentValidation sits in a MediatR behaviour, so every command gets validated before its handler runs.

When would I need one? Like binding a strongly typed id, say StudyId, from a route string. Or parsing a comma-separated list in the query string, ids equals 1,2,3, into a list. Or combining values from different places, like a header and a route value, into one object.

To write one, you implement IModelBinder, read the value through the ValueProvider, convert it, and either set the result as success or add a model state error. Then register it with a ModelBinder attribute on the type or parameter, or globally through an IModelBinderProvider.

But honestly, there's often a simpler option. For simple types, if the type has a static TryParse method, both controllers and minimal APIs bind it from route and query values automatically. Minimal APIs also support a static BindAsync method for custom binding from the whole HttpContext.
So I try TryParse or BindAsync first, and only write a full model binder for the complex cases in controllers. Most of the time I never get that far.

Mainly they're for disambiguating routes. Say I have shipments slash an int id, and also shipments slash a text reference for lookups by reference. The int constraint makes sure a numeric value goes to the first one, and anything else goes to the second. Without constraints, they'd just conflict.

Now one thing people get wrong, constraints aren't validation. If a constraint fails, the route simply doesn't match, so the client gets a 404 Not Found, not a 400 Bad Request telling them what's wrong. That's really confusing for an API consumer who just passed a bad value. So I use constraints for routing decisions only, and do input validation separately, returning proper 400s with clear messages.

And the datetime and decimal constraints use the invariant culture, which is good actually, because routes shouldn't depend on the server's culture.

p17-169.q: So endpoint filters are basically the minimal API version of MVC action filters. They run before and after the endpoint handler. They can inspect and change the arguments, short-circuit with a different result, or modify the result after the handler runs.
p17-169.k: endpoint filters, minimal api filters, iendpointfilter, addendpointfilter, validation filter minimal api
x: So endpoint filters are basically the minimal API version of MVC action filters. They run before and after the endpoint handler. They can inspect and change the arguments, short-circuit with a different result, or modify the result after the handler runs.

You add one with AddEndpointFilter on an endpoint or on a route group, either as a lambda or a class implementing IEndpointFilter. The filter gets an EndpointFilterInvocationContext, which gives you the HttpContext and the handler's arguments, plus a next delegate to call the rest of the pipeline.

Where I use them, validation mostly. A generic filter finds the argument of a certain type, runs its FluentValidation validator, and returns a 400 validation problem if it fails, so the handler only ever runs with valid input. Also logging or timing for specific endpoints, checking a tenant or a feature flag, and wrapping results consistently.
Filters on a route group apply to every endpoint in that group, which keeps cross-cutting logic in one place. And multiple filters run in the order you add them, like middleware.

The difference from middleware is, endpoint filters run after routing. So they know which endpoint is executing and can see its typed arguments. Middleware runs for every request and only sees the raw HttpContext. So middleware for global stuff, endpoint filters for endpoint-specific stuff. That's how I split it.

p17-170.q: MapGroup came in .NET 7. It creates a group of minimal API endpoints that share a common route prefix and common configuration. Like you create a shipments group with MapGroup on slash api slash shipments, and then call MapGet and MapPost on that group for the individual routes.

The real benefit is applying configuration once to every endpoint in the group. RequireAuthorization with a policy, endpoint filters like validation, rate limiting, tags for OpenAPI docs, CORS policies, versioning. And groups can be nested, so an api group requires authentication, and an admin group inside it adds an admin policy on top.

Honestly, it's also the key to organising minimal APIs in a bigger project. A common pattern is one static class per feature with an extension method, like MapShipmentEndpoints, which takes the route builder, creates the group and maps its endpoints. Then Program.cs just calls MapShipmentEndpoints and the same for each feature. So Program.cs stays small, each feature's endpoints live together, and it fits vertical slice architecture nicely. Some teams use libraries like Carter or FastEndpoints for even more structure.
The handlers themselves I keep small. They bind input, call a service or MediatR, and return a typed result. The business logic lives somewhere else, not in the endpoint.

p17-171.q: Okay, so in minimal APIs, a handler can return results from the Results class, like Results.Ok or Results.NotFound, which give you the IResult interface. Or from TypedResults, which return concrete types, like Ok of ShipmentDto, or NotFound.
p17-171.k: typedresults, results union type, minimal api return types, openapi minimal api responses, results vs typedresults
x: Okay, so in minimal APIs, a handler can return results from the Results class, like Results.Ok or Results.NotFound, which give you the IResult interface. Or from TypedResults, which return concrete types, like Ok of ShipmentDto, or NotFound.
TypedResults help you in two ways, really.

One is OpenAPI documentation. Since the return type is concrete, the framework knows exactly what the endpoint returns, and generates the response schema and status codes automatically. No Produces attributes or extra metadata calls.
The other is testing. In a unit test, I can call the handler directly, check the result is of type Ok of ShipmentDto, and look at its Value, without casting or spinning up an HTTP server.

When a handler can return different things, like Ok or NotFound or ValidationProblem, I declare the return type as a union. Results of Ok of ShipmentDto, NotFound, ValidationProblem. Then the compiler checks the handler only returns those types, and OpenAPI documents all three responses. That's much clearer than returning IResult, where literally anything can come back.
Performance-wise there's no big difference. It's mainly about correctness, docs and testability.
So in new minimal APIs, I go with TypedResults and union return types by default, and plain Results only for quick prototypes.

p17-172.q: Basically, response compression shrinks the responses sent to the client, using algorithms like Brotli or Gzip. For JSON and HTML, you can get something like 70 to 90 percent smaller, which cuts bandwidth and speeds things up on slower networks.
p17-172.k: response compression, gzip brotli, compress api responses, usresponsecompression, breach attack compression
x: Basically, response compression shrinks the responses sent to the client, using algorithms like Brotli or Gzip. For JSON and HTML, you can get something like 70 to 90 percent smaller, which cuts bandwidth and speeds things up on slower networks.
The client says what it supports in the Accept-Encoding header, and the server compresses the response and sets Content-Encoding.

In ASP.NET Core, you add AddResponseCompression and UseResponseCompression, configure the Brotli and Gzip providers, pick the compression level, and the MIME types to compress. For HTTPS you have to opt in with EnableForHttps, because of security concerns, I'll come to that.

But honestly, the first question is where compression should happen at all. If the app is behind IIS, NGINX, a load balancer or a CDN that already compresses, I let them do it. They're usually more efficient, and you don't want to compress twice. The middleware is useful when the app is exposed directly through Kestrel or the proxy can't compress.
Compression costs CPU, so the fastest level is often the better deal for dynamic responses. And it's pointless for already-compressed stuff like images or zip files, or for tiny responses.

The security thing is attacks like BREACH, which can extract secrets from compressed HTTPS responses that mix secrets with attacker-controlled input. So I avoid compressing responses that carry tokens alongside user input.

p17-173.q: Right, so since .NET 8, ASP.NET Core has request timeout middleware. You register it with AddRequestTimeouts, add UseRequestTimeouts to the pipeline, and set a default timeout, plus named policies for specific endpoints, with the RequestTimeout attribute or WithRequestTimeout on minimal API endpoints. Like a long export endpoint might get two minutes, while normal endpoints get ten seconds.
p17-173.k: request timeout middleware, addrequesttimeouts, request timeout .net 8, cancel slow requests, timeout policy endpoint
x: Right, so since .NET 8, ASP.NET Core has request timeout middleware. You register it with AddRequestTimeouts, add UseRequestTimeouts to the pipeline, and set a default timeout, plus named policies for specific endpoints, with the RequestTimeout attribute or WithRequestTimeout on minimal API endpoints. Like a long export endpoint might get two minutes, while normal endpoints get ten seconds.

The thing to really understand is how it works. When the timeout expires, it doesn't kill the request. It triggers HttpContext.RequestAborted, the request's cancellation token. So it only helps if your code passes that token all the way down, to EF Core queries, HttpClient calls, other async operations, so they actually stop. If the code ignores the token, the work just carries on.
When the timeout fires and the response hasn't started yet, the middleware returns 504 Gateway Timeout by default, and you can customise that.
Timeouts are also disabled while debugging, so they don't get in your way.

Why bother? Without timeouts, slow requests keep holding resources, database connections and threads, long after the client has given up, because usually the load balancer times out first. Under load, that slows everything down. So I set a server-side timeout slightly shorter than the load balancer's, which frees those resources and keeps the service healthy.

p17-174.q: ASP.NET Core apps on IIS use the ASP.NET Core Module, ANCM, which comes with the .NET Hosting Bundle. And there are two hosting models.
p17-174.k: iis hosting asp.net core, in process vs out of process, aspnetcore module, ancm, host asp.net core on iis, web.config asp.net core
x: ASP.NET Core apps on IIS use the ASP.NET Core Module, ANCM, which comes with the .NET Hosting Bundle. And there are two hosting models.

In-process hosting is the default since ASP.NET Core 3.0. It runs the app inside the IIS worker process, w3wp.exe, using the IIS HTTP server instead of Kestrel. No extra hop for requests, so it's faster, more throughput.

In out-of-process hosting, IIS acts as a reverse proxy. ANCM starts the app as a separate process running Kestrel and forwards requests to it over a local port. Bit slower, but the app process is separate from IIS, which can help in some isolation scenarios.
You set it with the hostingModel attribute in web.config, or AspNetCoreHostingModel in the project file.

A few practical things from experience. With in-process hosting, each app needs its own application pool, with No Managed Code selected. Startup errors usually show up as a 500.30, and turning on stdout logging in web.config temporarily helps you figure out why. The app_offline.htm file takes the app offline during deployment so files aren't locked. And IIS handles Windows authentication, TLS and process recycling for you.

Our CIRT platform runs on IIS on-premise, so I've dealt with these settings quite a bit. Especially app pools and those 500.30 startup errors during deployments, honestly those were the most common headaches.

p17-175.q: See, when an ASP.NET Core app runs behind a reverse proxy or load balancer, like NGINX, an AWS ALB or Azure Front Door, the app sees the proxy as the client. So RemoteIpAddress shows the proxy's IP, and Request.Scheme shows http if the proxy terminated TLS, even though the user actually came in on https.
p17-175.k: forwarded headers, x forwarded for, x forwarded proto, behind load balancer asp.net core, client ip behind proxy, useforwardedheaders
x: See, when an ASP.NET Core app runs behind a reverse proxy or load balancer, like NGINX, an AWS ALB or Azure Front Door, the app sees the proxy as the client. So RemoteIpAddress shows the proxy's IP, and Request.Scheme shows http if the proxy terminated TLS, even though the user actually came in on https.

And that breaks a bunch of things. Redirect URLs and generated links use http instead of https. The OpenID Connect redirect URI is wrong, so login fails. HTTPS redirection goes into a loop. Rate limiting by IP lumps everyone together. And logs show the wrong client IP.

The proxy adds headers with the original values. X-Forwarded-For for the client IP, X-Forwarded-Proto for the original scheme, and X-Forwarded-Host. The forwarded headers middleware, UseForwardedHeaders, reads them and updates the request, so the rest of the app sees the real values. It needs to run early in the pipeline.

Security matters here, because clients can send fake X-Forwarded-For headers. So I configure KnownProxies or KnownNetworks, so the middleware only trusts headers from our real proxies, and ForwardLimit for chains of proxies.

On IIS with in-process hosting, and in some container setups, it's handled automatically. But behind a cloud load balancer, I configure it explicitly. I've seen the login redirect issue bite people, so I don't leave it to chance.

p17-176.q: Localization is about showing text, dates and numbers in the user's language and format.
p17-176.k: localization asp.net core, globalization, resource files, request localization, accept language, multi language api
x: Localization is about showing text, dates and numbers in the user's language and format.

ASP.NET Core supports it out of the box. You call AddLocalization, keep translated strings in resource files per culture, like Messages.fr.resx, and inject IStringLocalizer of T to get the translated text by key. UseRequestLocalization decides the culture for each request, with providers that check, in order, a query string, a cookie, and the Accept-Language header, then fall back to a default. I list the supported cultures explicitly.
Once the culture is set, dates, numbers and currencies format accordingly, as long as you use culture-aware formatting.

For APIs though, I think carefully about what to localise. Data values, like dates and amounts in JSON, should stay culture-neutral, ISO 8601 and plain numbers, and the front end formats them for display. What the API might localise is user-facing messages, like validation errors, and generated documents, like emails and PDF reports.
On the front end, React and Angular have their own i18n libraries, like react-i18next or Angular's built-in i18n.

In our IRT, sites are spread across lots of countries. So emails come from templates per language, and dates are shown in each site's format, while the stored data stays in UTC and neutral formats. That separation has kept things sane for us.

p17-177.q: In our IRT, sometimes clients need to create or update lots of items at once, like 500 kit status changes. Calling a single-item endpoint 500 times is slow and chatty. So I build a bulk endpoint, but carefully.
p17-177.k: bulk api, batch endpoint, bulk create api, partial success response, 207 multi status, batch operations api
x: In our IRT, sometimes clients need to create or update lots of items at once, like 500 kit status changes. Calling a single-item endpoint 500 times is slow and chatty. So I build a bulk endpoint, but carefully.
The first thing I decide is limits. A max number of items per request, like 1,000, to protect the server. For bigger volumes, an asynchronous job with a file upload instead.

Then the transaction semantics, which have to be explicit. Either all-or-nothing, where if any item fails validation nothing is saved and the response lists all the errors. That's simpler for clients and right when items depend on each other. Or partial success, where valid items get saved and the response has a result per item, with its index or a client-provided reference, the status, and any error. For partial success I return 200 with a detailed body, or 207 Multi-Status. Never just a 201, which would hide the failures.
After that, idempotency. An idempotency key for the whole request, or a client reference per item, so a retry doesn't create duplicates.

And efficient processing. Validate everything first, load the data you need in a few queries, not one per item, and write in batches. For long-running bulk work, return 202 Accepted with a status URL.
I document clearly which mode the endpoint uses, because clients handle those two very differently.

p17-178.q: A good error response helps two audiences, honestly. The developer debugging the integration, and the program that needs to react automatically.
p17-178.k: api error design, error codes api, problem details errors, error response format, machine readable errors
x: A good error response helps two audiences, honestly. The developer debugging the integration, and the program that needs to react automatically.

I use the standard ProblemDetails format, RFC 9457, with type, title, status, detail and instance. Then I add extensions. A stable, machine-readable error code, like SITE_NOT_ACTIVE or KIT_ALREADY_DISPENSED, that clients can switch on, because messages change but codes don't. A trace id, so support can find the logs. And for validation errors, an errors dictionary with field names and messages, so the UI can show them next to each field.

The HTTP status has to be right. 400 for invalid input, 401 and 403 for auth, 404 for not found, 409 for conflicts like duplicates or concurrency errors, 422 for valid input that breaks a business rule, 429 for rate limits, and 5xx only for actual server-side problems. Clients often decide whether to retry based on the status, so getting it wrong causes real trouble.
What I never include is stack traces, SQL errors, internal server names, anything that reveals internals, especially in production. Those go to the logs, linked by the trace id.

I document the error codes in the OpenAPI spec, and keep them consistent across services with shared middleware. In our newer IRT APIs, a global exception handler returns ProblemDetails with a trace id for every error.

p17-179.q: Okay, normally searching or filtering is a read, so GET with query parameters is the REST-correct choice. It's cacheable, bookmarkable, idempotent, and easy to call and log. For simple filters, like status, date range, site and page, I always use GET.
p17-179.k: post vs get for search, complex search api, search endpoint design, query string length limit, get with body
x: Okay, normally searching or filtering is a read, so GET with query parameters is the REST-correct choice. It's cacheable, bookmarkable, idempotent, and easy to call and log. For simple filters, like status, date range, site and page, I always use GET.

But some searches just don't fit in a query string. Complex filters with nested conditions, like status in these five values and site in these 200 sites, or created before some date. Long lists of ids can blow past URL length limits, around 2,000 characters in some browsers and proxies, and servers have limits too. And sensitive values in a URL get logged by proxies, load balancers and browser history, which matters a lot for personal data.

In those cases, I use POST to a dedicated search resource, like POST to api slash subjects slash search, with the criteria as a JSON body. It's a common, accepted pattern. I just document that it's a safe, read-only operation, even though it's a POST. GET with a body isn't a good option, because many clients, proxies and frameworks ignore it or reject it.
Another option is a saved search. You POST the criteria, get back a search id, and then GET the results with that id, which also lets you share and page through them.
HTTP also has a draft QUERY method for exactly this case, but support isn't widespread yet, so I wouldn't rely on it today. So that's how I'd decide between them.

p17-180.q: Right, so basically ASP.NET Core supports several authentication schemes side by side. A scheme is just a named handler, like the JWT bearer handler, a cookie handler, or your own custom one.
p17-180.k: multiple authentication schemes, api key authentication, jwt and api key, authentication handler custom, policy scheme
x: Right, so basically ASP.NET Core supports several authentication schemes side by side. A scheme is just a named handler, like the JWT bearer handler, a cookie handler, or your own custom one.

For API keys, which partners or older systems might use, I write a custom authentication handler by inheriting AuthenticationHandler. It reads the key from a header, like X-API-Key, and looks it up. And I compare a hash of the key, not plain text, with a constant-time comparison. If it's valid, it creates a ClaimsPrincipal with claims like the client id and its permissions. If the header isn't there at all, it returns NoResult, so other schemes get a chance.
Then I register both. AddAuthentication with JWT as the default, AddJwtBearer, and AddScheme for the API key handler.

To pick the scheme per request, you can go two ways. On the endpoints, use Authorize with AuthenticationSchemes listing what's accepted, or a policy that specifies them. Or a policy scheme, with AddPolicyScheme and a ForwardDefaultSelector, which looks at the request, like does it have a bearer Authorization header or an API key header, and forwards to the right handler.
After that, authorization policies just work on claims, no matter how the caller authenticated.
And the API keys themselves are long random values, stored hashed, scoped, rotatable, rate-limited, and only ever sent over HTTPS. That's my checklist for them anyway.

p17-181.q: So basically IClaimsTransformation lets you modify or add claims on the user's ClaimsPrincipal after authentication, before authorization runs. You implement TransformAsync, register it in DI, and ASP.NET Core calls it during authentication.
p17-181.k: iclaimstransformation, claims transformation, add claims after authentication, enrich claims, permissions from database
x: So basically IClaimsTransformation lets you modify or add claims on the user's ClaimsPrincipal after authentication, before authorization runs. You implement TransformAsync, register it in DI, and ASP.NET Core calls it during authentication.

The typical use is enriching the identity with app-specific data that isn't in the token. Identity providers usually issue tokens with generic claims, user id, email, maybe a few roles. But my application's permissions, like which studies and sites a user can access and what actions they can do, live in the application database. So the transformation looks up the user's permissions and adds them as claims, and then authorization policies just check for those claims. Nice and simple.

Other uses, mapping claim names from different identity providers to one standard set, or flattening nested role claims. Like Keycloak puts realm roles inside a JSON structure, and you flatten them into standard role claims that the Authorize attribute understands.

A few gotchas though. It can get called more than once per request, so it has to be idempotent, check whether the claims are already there. It runs on every request, so database lookups must be cached, in memory or Redis with a short expiry, or every single request pays for extra queries. And I don't stuff too many claims in, especially if they end up in a cookie. I learned that one when a cookie got way too big.

p17-183.q: Okay, the key thing is never loading the whole file into memory. If I read a 2 GB file into a byte array and return it, the server needs 2 GB of memory per concurrent download, it lands on the Large Object Heap, and the server can run out of memory pretty quickly.
p17-183.k: stream file download, filestreamresult, large file download api, range requests, download without loading memory
x: Okay, the key thing is never loading the whole file into memory. If I read a 2 GB file into a byte array and return it, the server needs 2 GB of memory per concurrent download, it lands on the Large Object Heap, and the server can run out of memory pretty quickly.

So I stream it instead. In ASP.NET Core, you return a file result with a Stream, like Results.File, or File in a controller, with a FileStream opened with async and sequential-scan options, or a stream from blob storage. The framework copies it to the response in small chunks, so memory stays small no matter how big the file is.

Setting enableRangeProcessing to true supports HTTP range requests, so clients can resume interrupted downloads and video players can seek. I also set the content type, a Content-Disposition header with a safe file name, and ETag and Last-Modified headers for caching.

For generated content, like a big CSV export, I write straight to the response body as I go, or return an IAsyncEnumerable for JSON. So rows stream from the database to the client without being collected in memory first.

And when files are in cloud storage, often the best option is to not stream through the API at all. The API checks permissions and returns a short-lived pre-signed URL, and the client downloads directly from S3 or Blob Storage. Way less load on our servers.

Health check and metrics endpoints I exclude, otherwise they just flood the logs.

And for debugging production issues, distributed traces with OpenTelemetry usually give better insight than logging bodies, without the privacy risk. In our domain with patient data, that matters a lot.

You register it with AddHttpContextAccessor, inject it, and read HttpContext from it. A common use is a CurrentUser service that reads the user's claims, or grabbing the correlation id for logging.
Under the hood it uses AsyncLocal, so the context flows with the async execution of the request.

But there are pitfalls, and I've hit some. Outside a request, like in a background service, a hosted service or a message consumer, HttpContext is just null, so code depending on it breaks there. If code captures the HttpContext and uses it after the request has ended, say in fire-and-forget work, it might be reading a recycled or disposed context, and you get really strange bugs. HttpContext isn't thread-safe either, so don't touch it from parallel tasks. And it couples business logic to the web layer, which makes testing and reuse harder.

So my approach is, the business layer depends on a small abstraction, like ICurrentUser with UserId and Permissions. The web implementation reads from IHttpContextAccessor. A background job or message consumer gives its own implementation, using the user from the message. And tests just use a fake.
Also, I copy the values I need while the request is still active, never the HttpContext itself.

p17-186.q: For a large MVC application, I'd avoid a big-bang rewrite, honestly. I'd migrate incrementally.
p17-186.k: migrate asp.net mvc to core, .net framework to .net core migration, system.web adapters, yarp incremental migration, upgrade assistant
x: For a large MVC application, I'd avoid a big-bang rewrite, honestly. I'd migrate incrementally.

Microsoft's recommended approach is the strangler fig with YARP. You create a new ASP.NET Core app that sits in front of the old one as a reverse proxy. Requests for migrated routes are handled by the new app, and everything else gets forwarded to the legacy app. Then you move controllers and views one area at a time. The System.Web adapters help share code, and can share session and authentication between the two apps, so users don't even notice which app served the page.

Before moving any code, I'd prepare it. Move business logic into class libraries targeting .NET Standard 2.0, so both old and new apps can use them. Remove System.Web dependencies like HttpContext.Current from business code. Update packages to versions that support modern .NET. The .NET Upgrade Assistant helps analyse and convert projects too.

The main differences you have to deal with, Global.asax and web.config become Program.cs, middleware and appsettings.json. HTTP modules and handlers become middleware. Built-in DI replaces third-party containers. Authentication changes. And bundling, Razor and some HTML helpers are different.

What we're doing is similar in spirit actually. Rather than converting the legacy MVC portal, we're moving modules into the React shell with new .NET APIs, and shared Keycloak SSO keeps it smooth for users, they don't feel the switch.

p17-187.q: Okay, SignalR is ASP.NET Core's library for real-time communication between server and clients. It lets the server push messages to browsers instantly, notifications, live dashboards, progress updates, without the client polling.
p17-187.k: signalr, signalr scale out, redis backplane, azure signalr service, websockets asp.net core, real time asp.net core
x: Okay, SignalR is ASP.NET Core's library for real-time communication between server and clients. It lets the server push messages to browsers instantly, notifications, live dashboards, progress updates, without the client polling.

It uses WebSockets when available, and automatically falls back to Server-Sent Events or long polling. You define a Hub class on the server with methods clients can call, and the server can call methods on clients too. All clients, a specific user, or a group, like everyone viewing a particular study. The JavaScript and .NET clients handle the connection and automatic reconnection.
Authentication uses the same JWT or cookie. But for WebSockets in browsers, the token is passed as a query string parameter, so I make sure that's not getting logged.

Scaling out is the tricky part, honestly. Each connection lives on one server. So if server A wants to send a message to a user who's connected to server B, it can't, on its own. You fix that with a Redis backplane, where every server publishes messages through Redis pub-sub so all servers get them. Or a managed service like Azure SignalR Service, which holds all the connections itself, so your app servers don't. And sticky sessions are needed for the fallback transports, unless you go WebSockets-only.
On AWS, API Gateway WebSocket APIs are an alternative, especially if you're going serverless.

p17-188.q: So Server-Sent Events is a simple standard where the server pushes a stream of text events to the browser over a normal HTTP connection. The browser uses the EventSource API, which reconnects automatically and can resume from the last event id. The response has the text/event-stream content type, and the server just writes events as they happen.
p17-188.k: server sent events, sse, sse vs websockets, eventsource, streaming updates http, typedresults serversentevents
x: So Server-Sent Events is a simple standard where the server pushes a stream of text events to the browser over a normal HTTP connection. The browser uses the EventSource API, which reconnects automatically and can resume from the last event id. The response has the text/event-stream content type, and the server just writes events as they happen.

Compared with WebSockets, SSE is one-way, server to client only, while WebSockets go both ways. SSE runs over plain HTTP, so it works through most proxies, load balancers and firewalls without special setup, and it gets HTTP/2 multiplexing. It's text-only, and reconnection is built in.

So SSE fits when the client mostly just listens. Live notifications, progress of a long-running job, a dashboard feed, or streaming an AI model's response token by token. That's actually exactly how a lot of LLM APIs stream output. WebSockets are better for real two-way interaction, like chat or collaborative editing, or binary data.

In ASP.NET Core, you can write SSE by hand, set the content type and flush writes to the response. And .NET 10 adds TypedResults.ServerSentEvents, which takes an IAsyncEnumerable and streams it as events. SignalR can also use SSE as one of its transports.
One catch, the browser's EventSource can't set an Authorization header. So I use cookies, or a fetch-based client instead.

p17-189.q: Let me start with HTTP/1.1. It sends one request at a time per connection, so browsers open several connections, and requests queue up behind each other.
p17-189.k: http2, http3, quic, kestrel http2, multiplexing, head of line blocking
x: Let me start with HTTP/1.1. It sends one request at a time per connection, so browsers open several connections, and requests queue up behind each other.

HTTP/2 multiplexes lots of requests and responses over a single TCP connection at the same time, as independent streams. It also compresses headers with HPACK, which saves a lot for APIs with big headers like tokens, and supports stream prioritisation. Fewer connections means less TLS handshaking too. And gRPC needs HTTP/2.

But HTTP/2 still runs over TCP. So if one packet gets lost, all the streams on that connection wait for the retransmission. That's TCP head-of-line blocking, and it hurts on flaky networks, like mobile.

HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which is built on UDP. Each stream is independent, so a lost packet only delays its own stream. QUIC also sets up connections faster, by combining the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes, and has connection migration, so a phone switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data keeps its connection.

Kestrel supports both. HTTP/2 is on by default with TLS. HTTP/3 is supported since .NET 7, needs TLS and the platform's QUIC library, and you configure the endpoint with Http1AndHttp2AndHttp3. Clients discover it through the Alt-Svc header.
In practice though, the load balancer or CDN in front usually handles HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 with clients, and talks to the app over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2.

p17-190.q: Honestly, in ASP.NET Core session state is opt-in. You call AddSession with a distributed cache, and UseSession. The browser gets a cookie with a session id, and on the server, ISession stores small values, strings or byte arrays, keyed by that id. Unlike classic ASP.NET, it doesn't store objects directly, so I serialise them, usually as JSON.
p17-190.k: session state asp.net core, addsession, distributed session, session vs cookie, isession
x: Honestly, in ASP.NET Core session state is opt-in. You call AddSession with a distributed cache, and UseSession. The browser gets a cookie with a session id, and on the server, ISession stores small values, strings or byte arrays, keyed by that id. Unlike classic ASP.NET, it doesn't store objects directly, so I serialise them, usually as JSON.
Storage is an IDistributedCache. The in-memory one only works on a single server. With multiple instances, you need Redis or SQL Server, so any instance can read the session.

A few behaviours that catch people out. The session loads on first access, and since session access can be synchronous, I call LoadAsync first to avoid blocking. Session data isn't locked, so concurrent requests from the same user can overwrite each other's changes, which is different from old ASP.NET. Sessions expire after an idle timeout. And the session cookie has to be marked essential, or it won't be set when the user hasn't consented to non-essential cookies.

Should you use it? For APIs, no. APIs should be stateless, with state in the client or the database. For server-rendered web apps, it's fine for small temporary data, like a multi-step wizard, but not for authentication or anything important.
Our legacy MVC portal uses session state, and that's actually one reason Redis came in for the load-balanced IIS servers.

p17-191.q: So all three are ways to build web UIs with .NET, just with different styles.
p17-191.k: razor pages vs mvc, blazor vs mvc, blazor server vs webassembly, server side rendering .net, which ui framework .net
x: So all three are ways to build web UIs with .NET, just with different styles.

MVC uses controllers and views. Controllers handle requests and pick views, with models in between. It suits large applications with lots of related actions, and teams who know the pattern well. It's also the basis of Web API controllers.

Razor Pages is page-focused. Each page has a .cshtml file and a PageModel class with handlers like OnGet and OnPost. For page-based apps, forms and admin screens, it's simpler and more cohesive than MVC, because everything for a page sits in one place. Microsoft recommends it for new server-rendered page apps.

Blazor lets you build interactive UIs with C# components instead of JavaScript. Since .NET 8, Blazor Web Apps support different render modes per component. Static server rendering. Interactive server, where the UI runs on the server and updates the browser over a SignalR connection. Interactive WebAssembly, where .NET runs in the browser. And auto, which starts on the server and switches to WebAssembly once it's downloaded.

How I'd choose, for APIs consumed by React or Angular, which is our main setup, controllers or minimal APIs. For a simple internal tool built by .NET developers, Razor Pages or Blazor, so you avoid a separate JavaScript stack. And for rich public-facing apps with a big front-end team, React or Angular. That's roughly my thinking.

p17-192.q: Well, by default the request body is a forward-only stream. Once something reads it, like model binding or some middleware, it's consumed, and anything after that just sees an empty body. You hit this when a middleware wants to log the body, or verify a webhook signature, and the controller also needs to bind it.
p17-192.k: read request body twice, enablebuffering, request body stream, body already read, middleware read body
x: Well, by default the request body is a forward-only stream. Once something reads it, like model binding or some middleware, it's consumed, and anything after that just sees an empty body. You hit this when a middleware wants to log the body, or verify a webhook signature, and the controller also needs to bind it.

The fix is Request.EnableBuffering. It makes the body seekable by buffering it, in memory for small bodies and in a temp file for bigger ones. After reading, you reset the position to zero, Request.Body.Position equals 0, so the next reader starts from the beginning.

The typical middleware goes like this. Call EnableBuffering, read the body asynchronously with a StreamReader, with leaveOpen set to true, do whatever you need, like computing the HMAC signature, then reset the position and call the next middleware.

A few cautions though. Buffering big bodies costs memory or disk, so I only do it where it's needed, like specific webhook routes, and with a size limit. I always read async, because synchronous I/O is disabled by default in Kestrel anyway. And for really high throughput, the newer Pipelines-based Request.BodyReader is more efficient.

For webhook signature checks, another option is to bind the body as a raw string or byte array right in the endpoint, verify it, and then deserialise it yourself. Honestly, that's often simpler than the middleware route.

p17-193.q: So open generic registration basically means you register a generic interface with a generic implementation once, without the type argument. Like AddScoped with typeof IRepository of open T, and typeof EfRepository of open T. Then when something asks for IRepository of Shipment, the container creates EfRepository of Shipment automatically. One registration covers every entity type.
p17-193.k: open generics di, register generic repository, typeof irepository<>, generic service registration, decorate open generic
x: So open generic registration basically means you register a generic interface with a generic implementation once, without the type argument. Like AddScoped with typeof IRepository of open T, and typeof EfRepository of open T. Then when something asks for IRepository of Shipment, the container creates EfRepository of Shipment automatically. One registration covers every entity type.
The framework actually uses this itself. ILogger of T is registered as an open generic, which is why any class can ask for ILogger of its own type. IOptions of T works the same way.
Other places I see it, generic handlers or validators, like IValidator of T. MediatR pipeline behaviours, which are open generics applied to every request type. And generic caching decorators.
Constraints work too. If the implementation has generic constraints, like where T is an entity, the container only uses it for types that satisfy them. That's been there since around .NET 5.

The built-in container has some limits though. It can't do convention-based scanning, like register every class ending in Service. So I use the Scrutor library for assembly scanning and for decorating open generics. And when there are several registrations for the same closed type, the last one wins when you resolve one, while IEnumerable gives you all of them.
I use this for cross-cutting behaviours. But I don't create generic repositories over EF Core by default, that's mostly an extra layer for nothing.

I have a VendorApiOptions class with BaseUrl, timeout and credentials, and there are three vendors, each needing its own settings. Instead of three almost identical classes, I register one class three times with names. Configure of VendorApiOptions named DepotA bound to one config section, DepotB bound to another, and so on.
