x: Named options let you have several configured instances of the same options class, each with a name. Let me take an example. I have a VendorApiOptions class with BaseUrl, timeout and credentials, and there are three vendors, each needing its own settings. Instead of three almost identical classes, I register one class three times with names. Configure of VendorApiOptions named DepotA bound to one config section, DepotB bound to another, and so on.

To read them, you use IOptionsMonitor or IOptionsSnapshot and call Get with the name, like Get DepotA. IOptions of T doesn't support names, it only gives you the default unnamed instance. People get stuck on that one.

The framework uses named options a lot. Each authentication scheme has its own named options, which is how you can configure two JWT bearer schemes differently. HttpClient factory's named clients use named options under the hood too.
Validation works per name as well, with ValidateDataAnnotations or a custom IValidateOptions, which receives the name. So I can validate each vendor's settings at startup with ValidateOnStart.
PostConfigure and ConfigureAll let you apply common defaults to every named instance, like a default timeout, and then override per name.
I used this pattern for integration settings, where each partner has its own endpoint and credentials. Adding a new partner is then just a new configuration section, no code change.

p17-195.q: Okay, so the Generic Host is the .NET foundation for running any long-lived app. It gives you dependency injection, configuration, logging, and lifetime management for hosted services, with graceful startup and shutdown. It's used for console apps, worker services, and as the base of web apps. Earlier you created it with Host.CreateDefaultBuilder and a chain of callbacks, like ConfigureServices and ConfigureWebHostDefaults.
p17-195.k: generic host, webapplication builder, host createdefaultbuilder, hostapplicationbuilder, worker service host
x: Okay, so the Generic Host is the .NET foundation for running any long-lived app. It gives you dependency injection, configuration, logging, and lifetime management for hosted services, with graceful startup and shutdown. It's used for console apps, worker services, and as the base of web apps. Earlier you created it with Host.CreateDefaultBuilder and a chain of callbacks, like ConfigureServices and ConfigureWebHostDefaults.

WebApplication came in .NET 6 with minimal hosting. It's a simpler, more direct API built on top of the Generic Host, specifically for web apps. WebApplication.CreateBuilder gives you a builder with Services, Configuration, Logging and Environment as properties. You register services, call Build, then configure middleware and endpoints on the app, and Run. No Startup class, no nested callbacks. It still uses the Generic Host underneath, so hosted services and everything else just work.
For non-web apps, .NET 7 added Host.CreateApplicationBuilder, which gives the same simple linear style as WebApplication, just without the web server. The Worker Service template uses it.

So these days, WebApplication.CreateBuilder for APIs and web apps, Host.CreateApplicationBuilder for workers and consumers, and the older callback style only in existing code. The concepts, DI, configuration, hosted services, are identical across all of them, so moving between them isn't a big deal.

p17-196.q: A Worker Service is a .NET app on the Generic Host with one or more BackgroundService classes. To run it as an OS service, you basically add one line and the matching package.
p17-196.k: windows service .net, systemd service .net, usewindowsservice, addwindowsservice, worker service deployment, run background service on server
x: A Worker Service is a .NET app on the Generic Host with one or more BackgroundService classes. To run it as an OS service, you basically add one line and the matching package.

For Windows, it's the Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.WindowsServices package and AddWindowsService with a service name. That makes the host respond to the Windows Service Control Manager. Start, stop and shutdown signals map to the host's lifetime, so StopAsync runs when the service stops. Then you install it with sc.exe create, or PowerShell New-Service, pointing at the published exe, and set the recovery options, like restart on failure, and the account it runs under. Ideally a managed service account with least privilege.

For Linux, it's the Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.Systemd package and AddSystemd. It hooks into systemd's notifications and logging format. Then you create a unit file under etc systemd system with the ExecStart path, the user, Restart equals always, and environment variables, and enable it with systemctl.

A few things to watch. The working directory is different for services, like System32 on Windows, so I use AppContext.BaseDirectory for file paths. I learned that the hard way with a config file not being found. Logging should go to a central sink or the event log, not just the console. And configuration and secrets per environment.
In our CIRT environment, some RabbitMQ consumers run as Windows services on the application servers, so this is pretty familiar for me.

p17-197.q: Honestly, I follow a few simple conventions so the API is predictable for whoever calls it.
p17-197.k: rest naming conventions, api url design, plural nouns api, nested resources url, resource naming, api endpoint naming
x: Honestly, I follow a few simple conventions so the API is predictable for whoever calls it.
Use nouns for resources, not verbs, because the HTTP method is already the verb. So GET shipments, POST shipments, GET shipments slash id. Not getShipments or createShipment.
Plural nouns for collections, and consistently. Sites, kits, subjects.

Nesting for clear parent-child relationships, but only one level deep, like sites slash site id slash subjects. Deep nesting, like studies, sites, subjects, visits all chained together, gets fragile. Once a resource has its own id, you can just address it directly, like visits slash 4.
Lowercase with hyphens for multi-word names, like return-shipments, and camelCase for JSON property names.
Query parameters for filtering, sorting and paging. Like status equals pending, sort by createdAt descending, page 2.

Then there are actions that don't fit CRUD neatly, like cancel or dispatch. Two reasonable choices there. Model it as a state change and PATCH the status, or a sub-resource action, like POST shipments slash id slash cancel. I prefer the second when the action has its own rules and side effects, because it's clearer and easier to authorise.
If you use URL versioning, put the version at the start of the path, like api slash v1.
And above everything, be consistent across the whole API, and write it down in the team's API guidelines. That matters more than any single rule.

p17-198.q: Okay, so PATCH is for partial updates, changing just some fields of a resource. And there are two common formats.
p17-198.k: json patch, json merge patch, patch partial update, jsonpatchdocument, partial update api
x: Okay, so PATCH is for partial updates, changing just some fields of a resource. And there are two common formats.

JSON Merge Patch, RFC 7396, sends a JSON object with only the fields to change, like status Cancelled. Fields you don't include stay the same, and a field set to null gets removed or cleared. Simple and intuitive for clients. The limitation is you can't really tell "set to null" apart from other intentions, and you can't update individual array elements. Arrays get replaced entirely.

JSON Patch, RFC 6902, sends a list of operations, add, remove, replace, move, copy and test, each with a path. Like op replace, path slash status, value Cancelled. It's more powerful. It can change array items and include test operations that act like preconditions. But it's more complex for clients.

In ASP.NET Core, JsonPatchDocument of T supports JSON Patch. It used to need Newtonsoft.Json, and .NET 10 added a System.Text.Json-based version. What I do is apply the patch to a DTO, not directly to the EF entity, then validate the DTO, and map only the allowed fields onto the entity. That prevents over-posting through patch paths.
For merge patch, I deserialise into a DTO with nullable or optional wrapper properties, so I know which fields were actually sent.
Honestly though, for simple partial updates I often prefer specific endpoints, like PUT status, which are easier to validate and authorise.

p17-199.q: For data annotations, you can create your own attribute by inheriting ValidationAttribute and overriding IsValid. The method gets the value and a ValidationContext, and returns ValidationResult.Success, or a ValidationResult with an error message and the member name. Like a FutureDate attribute that checks a date is after today, or a ValidCountryCode attribute that checks against a list.

x: For data annotations, you can create your own attribute by inheriting ValidationAttribute and overriding IsValid. The method gets the value and a ValidationContext, and returns ValidationResult.Success, or a ValidationResult with an error message and the member name. Like a FutureDate attribute that checks a date is after today, or a ValidCountryCode attribute that checks against a list.
The ValidationContext gives you the whole object being validated, so you can compare with other properties, and the service provider too. But I avoid pulling heavy dependencies inside attributes.

For rules involving multiple properties, like end date must be after start date, you can go two ways. A class-level attribute, or implement IValidatableObject on the model, where Validate returns any number of results. ASP.NET Core runs that after the property-level attributes pass.

Once you've built it, the attribute works anywhere data annotations work. ApiController's automatic 400 responses, Validator.TryValidateObject, options validation with ValidateDataAnnotations, and Blazor forms.

That said, for complex rules, especially ones that need the database or services, I go with FluentValidation. Attributes can't easily do async work or use injected services cleanly, and they get hard to test once they need dependencies. So for me, custom attributes are for small, reusable, self-contained rules, and that's about it.

p17-200.q: Actually both let you share data between different parts of the pipeline during a single request. Like a tenant id resolved in middleware and then used in a controller and a repository.
p17-200.k: httpcontext items, share data per request, scoped service per request, request context data, per request state
x: Actually both let you share data between different parts of the pipeline during a single request. Like a tenant id resolved in middleware and then used in a controller and a repository.

HttpContext.Items is a dictionary on the HttpContext, object keys and object values, and it lives only for the current request. It's built in and quick to use. But it's untyped, so you're casting values, keys can clash between components unless you use private object keys, and it ties consumers to HttpContext, which isn't there in background work and is annoying to set up in unit tests.

A scoped service is a class registered with AddScoped, so DI creates one instance per request. A middleware gets it injected through InvokeAsync parameters and sets properties, like TenantContext.TenantId. Then controllers, handlers and repositories inject the same instance and read it. It's strongly typed, easy to discover, easy to fake in tests, and it doesn't depend on HTTP. So the same TenantContext can be filled by a message consumer for background processing.

So my rule is, a scoped service for anything important that business code depends on, current user, tenant, study context, correlation data. HttpContext.Items is fine for small, web-layer-only details, like passing something between two middlewares.
One reminder, scoped services must never be captured by singletons, or they'll leak across requests. That's a nasty bug to track down.

p17-201.q: See, there are basically two ways to do it.
p17-201.k: host spa with asp.net core, serve react from asp.net core, static files spa fallback, mapfallbacktofile, spa deployment
x: See, there are basically two ways to do it.

One is serving the SPA from the ASP.NET Core app itself. The front-end build output, the index.html and the bundled JavaScript and CSS, gets copied into wwwroot. The app uses UseStaticFiles to serve the files, and MapFallbackToFile with index.html, so deep links, like shipments slash 123, return index.html and the client-side router handles them, while api routes go to the controllers. It's one deployment, one origin, so no CORS, and cookies just work. For caching, the hashed bundle files get a long max-age, while index.html isn't cached, so users pick up new versions after a deployment.

The other is serving the SPA separately. The front end goes to static hosting, like S3 with CloudFront, Azure Static Web Apps or a CDN, and calls the API on its own domain. It's cheaper and faster to serve globally, front end and back end deploy independently, and the API stays focused on data. The cost is CORS configuration, or putting both behind one domain with path routing on the CDN.
During development, Vite or the Angular CLI dev server runs the front end with hot reload and proxies API calls to the ASP.NET Core app, so you avoid CORS locally.
In our IRT, the React shell is built with Vite and deployed separately, and the MVC portal links into it, sharing the Keycloak SSO session. So we went with the second approach.

p17-202.q: The environment name comes from the ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT or DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT variable. IWebHostEnvironment, or IHostEnvironment for workers, exposes it, along with paths like the content root and web root.
Configuration uses it automatically. appsettings.json loads first, then the environment-specific appsettings file overrides it, then environment variables and other sources override those.
In code, IsDevelopment is typically used to turn on the developer exception page, Swagger UI or detailed errors only in development.

To use it safely, a few rules I stick to. Defaulting to Production is actually a good thing. If someone forgets the variable, the app runs with the safest settings. I keep environment checks few and at the edges, mostly in Program.cs, and drive differences through configuration values, like a feature flag for Swagger, instead of scattering IsDevelopment checks through business code. Business logic should behave the same in every environment, otherwise testing in UAT doesn't prove anything about production. And no secrets in a committed appsettings.Development.json. Local secrets go in user secrets.

You can also add custom environments, like UAT, checked with IsEnvironment UAT, and a matching appsettings.UAT.json. That fits validated release flows like ours, with separate UAT and production settings.

p17-203.q: This one's really common, and I check things in a fixed order.
p17-203.k: null request body, model binding null, frombody null, 415 unsupported media type, json not binding asp.net core
x: This one's really common, and I check things in a fixed order.

The first thing I check is the Content-Type header. If the client doesn't send application/json, ASP.NET Core can't use the JSON input formatter. With ApiController, that usually gives a 415 Unsupported Media Type, but in some setups the parameter is just null.

Then the JSON shape versus the DTO. If the JSON doesn't match, like a wrapping object the DTO doesn't expect, a string where a number should be, or a bad date format, deserialisation fails. With ApiController, that returns a 400 with details in the problem details response, so I read that response body carefully. Without ApiController, the parameter comes in null and ModelState has the error.

After that, property naming and casing. ASP.NET Core uses camelCase and case-insensitive matching by default, but custom JsonSerializerOptions might have changed that. Properties also need public setters or a matching constructor, and fields aren't bound by default.

Then the binding source. A complex type in an ApiController is inferred as FromBody, but without ApiController, or for simple types, you may need FromBody explicitly. And only one parameter can come from the body.
And one more, maybe something read the body earlier, like a logging middleware without EnableBuffering.

To actually see what's going on, I log ModelState errors, test with a known-good request from an HTTP file or Postman, and turn on debug logging for model binding. Usually one of those shows it pretty quickly.

For controllers through AddJsonOptions, and for minimal APIs with ConfigureHttpJsonOptions. Then the JSON says Delivered, or delivered in lower case if you pass a camelCase naming policy. And incoming requests accept the string names too.

From .NET 8 there's also a generic JsonStringEnumConverter of TEnum, which works with source generation and Native AOT, and you can put JsonConverter attributes on specific enums. .NET 9 added JsonStringEnumMemberName to customise individual member names.

A few related habits. I still give enum members explicit numeric values, especially if they're stored in the database, so reordering doesn't corrupt data. I document in the API that new values may get added, so clients handle unknown values gracefully. And I check that OpenAPI shows the string values, which the built-in generator does once the converter is configured.
For EF Core, storing enums as strings is a separate decision, done with HasConversion of string.

p17-205.q: Honestly, Kestrel's defaults are sensible, but for production I do review a few limits. It depends on whether Kestrel faces the internet directly or sits behind a reverse proxy.
p17-205.k: kestrel limits, max request body size, kestrel configuration, connection limits, request header limits
x: Honestly, Kestrel's defaults are sensible, but for production I do review a few limits. It depends on whether Kestrel faces the internet directly or sits behind a reverse proxy.

MaxRequestBodySize defaults to about 30 MB. I lower it for normal APIs, so nobody can send huge bodies, and raise it only on specific upload endpoints with the RequestSizeLimit attribute, or DisableRequestSizeLimit for streaming uploads to storage. Form and multipart limits are separate, in FormOptions.

Request header limits, like MaxRequestHeadersTotalSize and MaxRequestLineSize, protect you against oversized headers. Sometimes I actually have to raise them, like when SSO cookies or large tokens make headers bigger. That's a known cause of random 400 or 431 errors.

Then timeouts. KeepAliveTimeout and RequestHeadersTimeout stop slow clients holding connections open, which helps against slowloris-style attacks. MinRequestBodyDataRate and MinResponseDataRate drop connections that send or read data too slowly.
Connection limits, MaxConcurrentConnections and MaxConcurrentUpgradedConnections for WebSockets, can cap resource use per instance. And there are HTTP/2 settings too, like max streams per connection.

I configure these in appsettings under the Kestrel section, or in code with ConfigureKestrel. And I keep them consistent with the limits on the proxy or load balancer in front. Otherwise whichever one rejects first gives you a confusing error, and you waste time figuring out who rejected it.

p17-206.q: So a covering index is basically a non-clustered index that has every column a query needs, so SQL Server can answer the query from the index alone, without going back to the table.
p17-206.k: covering index, include columns, index include, avoid key lookup, nonclustered index include
x: So a covering index is basically a non-clustered index that has every column a query needs, so SQL Server can answer the query from the index alone, without going back to the table.

Normally a non-clustered index stores the key columns plus a pointer to the row. If the query needs other columns, SQL Server does a key lookup for each matching row, jumping to the clustered index to fetch them. For a few rows that's fine. For thousands of rows, those lookups get really expensive, and the optimiser may just give up on the index and scan the whole table.

INCLUDE columns solve this. You create the index with key columns for filtering and sorting, and add the other columns with INCLUDE. Like an index on SiteId and Status, including ShipmentDate and KitCount. Included columns are stored only at the leaf level, not in the key, so they don't affect sorting and the key stays small, but the query is fully covered.

It's not free though. Every included column makes the index bigger and makes inserts and updates slower, because the index has to be maintained. So I don't include everything. I cover the important, frequent queries, and check the execution plan to confirm the key lookup is actually gone.
[Adding one covering index to the shipment search query removed a key lookup on about 40,000 rows and cut its time from several seconds to under 200 milliseconds.]

p17-207.q: Okay, so a key lookup shows up in a plan when SQL Server uses a non-clustered index to find the matching rows, but the index doesn't have all the columns the query needs. For each row found, it goes back to the clustered index, using the clustering key, to fetch the missing columns. On a heap, a table without a clustered index, the same thing is called a RID lookup.
p17-207.k: key lookup, rid lookup, bookmark lookup, execution plan key lookup, fix key lookup
x: Okay, so a key lookup shows up in a plan when SQL Server uses a non-clustered index to find the matching rows, but the index doesn't have all the columns the query needs. For each row found, it goes back to the clustered index, using the clustering key, to fetch the missing columns. On a heap, a table without a clustered index, the same thing is called a RID lookup.

In the plan, you see an Index Seek joined with Nested Loops to a Key Lookup. The cost is per row, one extra random read for every row. If the seek returns 10 rows, who cares. If it returns 50,000 rows, it can dominate the whole query.

To fix it, I look at the key lookup operator's Output List, which shows exactly which columns it fetched. Then a few options. Add those columns to the index as INCLUDE columns, making it covering. Or drop columns from the query that aren't really needed, like a SELECT star where the screen only uses four columns. In EF Core that means projecting to a DTO with Select instead of loading whole entities. Or, if the predicate also uses columns that aren't in the key, rethink the index key order.

I also watch for the opposite problem. When the estimate is wrong, SQL Server may choose a seek plus lookup for way more rows than it expected. That's usually a statistics or parameter sniffing issue, not an index issue.

p17-208.q: See, fragmentation happens as data gets inserted, updated and deleted. When a page is full and a new row has to go in the middle, SQL Server splits the page and moves half the rows to a new page somewhere else. Over time, the logical order of pages stops matching their physical order, that's external fragmentation. And pages get left partly empty, which is internal fragmentation, or low page density.
p17-208.k: index fragmentation, rebuild vs reorganize, index maintenance, fill factor, page splits
x: See, fragmentation happens as data gets inserted, updated and deleted. When a page is full and a new row has to go in the middle, SQL Server splits the page and moves half the rows to a new page somewhere else. Over time, the logical order of pages stops matching their physical order, that's external fragmentation. And pages get left partly empty, which is internal fragmentation, or low page density.

On spinning disks, logical order really mattered for range scans. On modern SSDs and SANs, external fragmentation matters much less. Low page density matters more, because more pages means more I/O and more memory used in the buffer pool.

You've got two maintenance options. Reorganize is lightweight and always online. It reorders the leaf pages and compacts them, good for moderate fragmentation. Rebuild drops and recreates the index, fully defragmenting it and updating its statistics with a full scan. It can be online in Enterprise edition and Azure SQL, but it's heavier.

The old rule of thumb was reorganize between 5 and 30 percent fragmentation, rebuild above 30. These days, honestly, a lot of experts say focus on updating statistics regularly, which often gives most of the benefit, and maintain indexes less often, based on measured impact. Ola Hallengren's maintenance scripts handle all this nicely.
And a suitable fill factor can reduce page splits on indexes with random inserts, like GUID keys.

p17-209.q: Okay, so by default SQL Server uses read committed with locking. Readers take shared locks, so a reader can get blocked by a writer holding an exclusive lock, and a writer can get blocked by readers. Under heavy mixed load, you get blocking and sometimes deadlocks.
p17-209.k: snapshot isolation, read committed snapshot, rcsi, row versioning, readers block writers, tempdb version store
x: Okay, so by default SQL Server uses read committed with locking. Readers take shared locks, so a reader can get blocked by a writer holding an exclusive lock, and a writer can get blocked by readers. Under heavy mixed load, you get blocking and sometimes deadlocks.

Row versioning is the alternative. When it's on, SQL Server keeps previous versions of modified rows in the version store, in tempdb, or in the database itself with Accelerated Database Recovery. Readers read the last committed version instead of waiting on locks.

Read committed snapshot isolation, RCSI, is a database setting that makes the default read committed level use versioning. Each statement sees data as it was when the statement started. Readers don't block writers, writers don't block readers. It's usually a big drop in blocking with zero code changes, and it's actually the default in Azure SQL Database.

Snapshot isolation is a separate level that a transaction has to ask for explicitly. The whole transaction sees a consistent snapshot as of its start. If it tries to update a row that another transaction changed after that snapshot, it gets an update conflict error, so the code has to handle it and retry.

What it costs you, more tempdb usage and a bit more overhead on updates. And code that relied on blocking behaviour, like a read-then-update pattern, may need explicit locking hints or a different approach. So I'd test that before switching it on.

p17-210.q: WITH NOLOCK is the same as the READ UNCOMMITTED isolation level. It tells SQL Server to read without taking shared locks and to ignore other transactions' locks. People add it to stop queries getting blocked, and yeah, the blocking goes away, but it can return wrong data.
p17-210.k: nolock, with nolock, read uncommitted, dirty reads, nolock problems, nolock hint
x: WITH NOLOCK is the same as the READ UNCOMMITTED isolation level. It tells SQL Server to read without taking shared locks and to ignore other transactions' locks. People add it to stop queries getting blocked, and yeah, the blocking goes away, but it can return wrong data.
The obvious problem is dirty reads. You read changes from a transaction that hasn't committed and might roll back, so you see data that never officially existed.

The less obvious problems are actually worse. Since the scan isn't protected while pages split and rows move around, a NOLOCK query can miss rows entirely, or read the same row twice. So a count or a sum can just be wrong, even for data that wasn't logically being changed. Queries can even fail with an error about data movement.
For approximate reports, like a dashboard estimate, maybe that's acceptable. But anywhere correctness matters, stock levels, financial data, clinical supply quantities, it's not acceptable at all.

The better fix for blocking is read committed snapshot isolation, which gives readers a consistent, committed version of the data without blocking. Plus good indexes and short transactions, so locks are held only briefly.
When I see NOLOCK sprinkled all over old stored procedures, I take it as a sign there was a blocking problem in the past, and I go looking for the real cause.

p17-211.q: Actually SQL Server normally takes fine-grained locks, row or page locks, so different transactions can work on different rows of the same table at once. But every lock uses memory. When a single statement grabs a lot of locks on one table, around 5,000, or when lock memory gets high, SQL Server converts them into a single table lock. That's lock escalation.
p17-211.k: lock escalation, row lock to table lock, escalation threshold, lock_escalation, large update blocking
x: Actually SQL Server normally takes fine-grained locks, row or page locks, so different transactions can work on different rows of the same table at once. But every lock uses memory. When a single statement grabs a lot of locks on one table, around 5,000, or when lock memory gets high, SQL Server converts them into a single table lock. That's lock escalation.

It saves memory, sure. But a table-level exclusive lock blocks everyone else on that table until the transaction ends. So a big update or delete, like updating 100,000 rows in one statement, can suddenly block every other user, even people working on completely unrelated rows.

What I do to avoid it is process large changes in batches. Like 2,000 to 4,000 rows per transaction in a loop, so each batch stays below the escalation threshold and locks get released frequently. That's my standard approach for purges, backfills and big data fixes. Good indexes help too, because without them a statement might scan and lock far more rows than it actually changes.

For partitioned tables, you can set the LOCK_ESCALATION table option to AUTO, so escalation goes to the partition level instead of the whole table. You can also disable it for a table, but that risks high lock memory, so I rarely do that.
Monitoring tools and extended events can show you when escalation is happening.

p17-212.q: When users say the system is hanging, blocking is one of the first things I check, honestly.
p17-212.k: find blocking sql server, sp_whoisactive, blocking chain, head blocker, sys.dm_exec_requests, blocked process report
x: When users say the system is hanging, blocking is one of the first things I check, honestly.

For a live problem, I query sys.dm_exec_requests. It shows each running request, its wait type, how long it's been waiting, and the blocking_session_id. Following those blocking session ids leads you to the head blocker, the session at the top of the chain, which is blocking others but isn't blocked itself. Then I look at what it's running with sys.dm_exec_sql_text, and at its open transactions.

The community procedure sp_WhoIsActive makes this much easier. It shows all active sessions with SQL text, waits, blocking info, and optionally plans and locks, in one result. Older stuff like sp_who2 works too, just with less detail.

What I usually find is one of a few things. A transaction left open by application code, like a transaction started and then an exception swallowed without a rollback, or a session that's sleeping with an open transaction. A long-running update or report without good indexes. Or a query waiting for user input inside a transaction.
For recurring or past blocking, I turn on the blocked process report with a threshold, like 10 seconds, and capture it with Extended Events, or use a monitoring tool.
Killing the head blocker is a last resort, because its transaction rolls back, and that can take a while. The real fix is shorter transactions, better indexes, or RCSI.

p17-213.q: So Query Store is a SQL Server feature, on by default for new databases since SQL Server 2022 and in Azure SQL. It records the history of queries, their execution plans, and runtime stats like duration, CPU, reads and executions, over time. Basically a flight recorder for query performance.
p17-213.k: query store, sql server query store, force plan, regressed queries, plan regression, query performance history
x: So Query Store is a SQL Server feature, on by default for new databases since SQL Server 2022 and in Azure SQL. It records the history of queries, their execution plans, and runtime stats like duration, CPU, reads and executions, over time. Basically a flight recorder for query performance.

It's really useful in a few situations. Plan regression is the big one. When a query suddenly gets slow, Query Store shows whether its plan changed, and you can compare the old good plan with the new bad one. Then you can force the good plan as an immediate fix while you work on the root cause. It also helps find top resource consumers, which queries eat the most CPU or I/O over a period. And comparing before and after a release or an index change. On SQL Server 2022, things like parameter-sensitive plan optimisation and query store hints build on it too.
To use it, I look at the Regressed Queries and Top Resource Consuming Queries reports in SSMS, or query the catalog views directly.

[That's how we diagnosed a query that went from 200 milliseconds to 5 seconds in March 2025: Query Store showed a new plan compiled for an unusual parameter value, a classic parameter sniffing case. Forcing the previous plan fixed it within minutes, and then we fixed the query properly.]

p17-214.q: Honestly, both store intermediate results in tempdb, but they behave quite differently.
p17-214.k: temp table vs table variable, #temp vs @table, table variable performance, temp table statistics, tempdb objects
x: Honestly, both store intermediate results in tempdb, but they behave quite differently.

A temporary table, with a hash prefix, like hash Kits, is a real table in tempdb. It has statistics, so the optimiser can estimate row counts properly. You can add indexes after creating it. It's visible to nested stored procedures called from the same session. It's affected by transactions and rollbacks. And it can trigger statement recompilations when its data changes a lot.

A table variable, like at Kits, is declared like a variable and scoped to the batch or procedure. Historically it had no statistics, and the optimiser assumed it held one row. That led to terrible plans when it actually held thousands. Since SQL Server 2019, deferred compilation helps by using the actual row count at first execution, but there are still no column statistics. Its data isn't rolled back by a transaction rollback, which is occasionally handy for logging. And it causes fewer recompilations.

My rule is, table variables for small sets, a few hundred rows or less, and for passing data around simply. Temp tables for bigger intermediate results, especially when they get joined or filtered further, because good statistics really matter there.
And table-valued parameters, which pass a set of rows from .NET into a procedure, are table variables too. So the same thinking applies to them.

p17-215.q: Okay, so a table-valued parameter lets you pass a whole set of rows from the app to a stored procedure or query in one parameter, instead of making lots of separate calls or building a long IN list.
p17-215.k: table valued parameters, tvp, pass list to stored procedure, sql where in list, user defined table type
x: Okay, so a table-valued parameter lets you pass a whole set of rows from the app to a stored procedure or query in one parameter, instead of making lots of separate calls or building a long IN list.

You start by creating a user-defined table type in SQL Server, like a KitIdList type with a KitId column, and a primary key if it helps. The procedure declares a parameter of that type, which has to be READONLY. Inside, you join to it like any table.

From .NET, with ADO.NET or Dapper, you build a DataTable, or a list of SqlDataRecord, or use Dapper's AsTableValuedParameter, and pass it as a SqlParameter with SqlDbType.Structured and the type name. EF Core can use it through raw SQL with a SqlParameter too.

And the gains are big. One round trip instead of thousands. Set-based processing in SQL, like inserting or updating many rows in one statement. Fully parameterised, so no SQL injection, and the plan gets reused. Dynamic IN lists of different lengths create a new plan for every different count, which is a hidden cost people miss.
For really large data, hundreds of thousands of rows, SqlBulkCopy into a staging table is faster.
Also, since EF Core 8, a list Contains in LINQ gets translated using OPENJSON with a single JSON parameter, which solves the varying plan problem for simple cases.

p17-216.q: So a scalar user-defined function returns a single value, and people often use it in a SELECT list or a WHERE clause, like a GetKitStatus function taking a KitId. It looks clean, but traditionally it's had serious performance problems.
p17-216.k: scalar udf performance, scalar function slow, inline table valued function, udf inlining, function in where clause
x: So a scalar user-defined function returns a single value, and people often use it in a SELECT list or a WHERE clause, like a GetKitStatus function taking a KitId. It looks clean, but traditionally it's had serious performance problems.

The function runs once per row, like a hidden loop, with its own overhead on every call. If the function itself queries tables, now you're running a query for every row, which is basically an N+1 problem inside the database. The optimiser couldn't see inside the function, so it estimated the cost badly. And queries using scalar functions couldn't go parallel at all, the whole query was forced into a serial plan.

SQL Server 2019 brought scalar UDF inlining, which automatically turns many simple scalar functions into inline expressions and removes a lot of that cost. But not every function qualifies, like ones with certain constructs or ones that depend on the time. So I don't rely on it blindly.

What I'd use instead, an inline table-valued function, which is a single SELECT statement returning a table. The optimiser expands it into the calling query like a view with parameters, so it's set-based and fully optimised, and you use it with CROSS APPLY. Or put the logic directly in the query with a join or a CASE expression. Or a computed column, persisted and indexed if needed.
Multi-statement table-valued functions have similar problems, so I keep them out of hot paths too.

p17-217.q: Okay, so a view is a stored SELECT query that acts like a virtual table. It doesn't store data itself. When you query it, SQL Server expands its definition into your query. Views help simplify complex joins, give consumers like a reporting tool a stable interface while the underlying tables change, and help with security, since you can give users access to a view with selected columns and rows instead of the base tables.
p17-217.k: sql views, indexed view, materialized view sql server, view vs table, schemabinding view
x: Okay, so a view is a stored SELECT query that acts like a virtual table. It doesn't store data itself. When you query it, SQL Server expands its definition into your query. Views help simplify complex joins, give consumers like a reporting tool a stable interface while the underlying tables change, and help with security, since you can give users access to a view with selected columns and rows instead of the base tables.

Performance-wise, a normal view is just a query. It's as fast as whatever it expands to. But views stacked on views get hard for the optimiser, and they can hide expensive joins, so I avoid deep nesting. I've seen a simple-looking view turn out to be six joins deep.

An indexed view, what other databases call a materialised view, has a unique clustered index, so its result is actually stored and kept up to date automatically when the base tables change. It's great for expensive aggregations that get read a lot, like totals of kits by site and status. The query reads pre-computed results instead of aggregating millions of rows.

But it comes with requirements and costs. The view has to be created WITH SCHEMABINDING, use two-part names, and follow a bunch of restrictions, like no outer joins or certain aggregates. And every insert, update and delete on the base tables also has to update the indexed view, so writes slow down and blocking can increase.
So I use indexed views for read-heavy aggregates on tables that aren't written to heavily.

p17-218.q: See, a trigger is code that runs automatically in the database when data changes, like AFTER INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on a table, or INSTEAD OF a change, which is often used on views. Inside it, the special inserted and deleted tables hold the new and old versions of the affected rows.
p17-218.k: triggers sql server, after trigger, instead of trigger, trigger pros cons, audit trigger, inserted deleted tables
x: See, a trigger is code that runs automatically in the database when data changes, like AFTER INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on a table, or INSTEAD OF a change, which is often used on views. Inside it, the special inserted and deleted tables hold the new and old versions of the affected rows.

The good part is, a trigger runs no matter how the data gets changed, by the application, a script, a data fix, or some other system. That makes triggers useful for audit trails and history tables, for enforcing complex integrity rules that constraints can't express, and for keeping denormalised data in sync.

The downsides are serious though. Triggers are hidden. Developers reading the application code don't see them, so behaviour feels magical and debugging is harder. They run inside the same transaction, so every write gets slower and locks are held longer. A really common bug is writing a trigger that assumes one row, when a statement can affect many rows at once. They have to be set-based. Triggers can call other triggers, creating chains nobody can follow. And business logic in triggers is hard to test and version.
So honestly, I use triggers sparingly. Mainly for audit or history capture, where guaranteed coverage matters, and I keep them simple and set-based. Business rules go in the application layer.
And for history, temporal tables are often a cleaner option now.

p17-219.q: So system-versioned temporal tables keep a full history of every change to a table, automatically. When you enable them, SQL Server adds two period columns, valid from and valid to, and creates a linked history table. Whenever a row is updated or deleted, the old version moves to the history table with the time range it was valid for. The application doesn't need any code for it.
p17-219.k: temporal tables, system versioned tables, history table, for system_time, point in time query, audit history sql
x: So system-versioned temporal tables keep a full history of every change to a table, automatically. When you enable them, SQL Server adds two period columns, valid from and valid to, and creates a linked history table. Whenever a row is updated or deleted, the old version moves to the history table with the time range it was valid for. The application doesn't need any code for it.

Then you can query data as it was at any point using FOR SYSTEM_TIME. AS OF a specific date and time, or BETWEEN two times, or ALL to see every version of a row. That's great for audits, for figuring out who changed this and what it was before, for recovering from accidental updates, and for reports that need data as of some past date.
EF Core supports them too. You configure IsTemporal in the model, and LINQ gets TemporalAsOf, TemporalAll and similar methods.

A few limitations though. Period times are in UTC, based on when the transaction started. It records what changed and when, but not who changed it or why. So for a regulated audit trail, you still need the user and the reason, usually stored in columns on the row itself. History tables can grow big, so you need a retention policy. And schema changes need some care.
For regulated systems like ours, I'd say temporal tables are a solid foundation for history, combined with application-level audit information.

p17-220.q: Okay, partitioning splits one large table into multiple partitions based on a column, usually a date, like one partition per month. To queries it's still one table. Underneath, each partition is stored separately and can sit on different filegroups.
p17-220.k: table partitioning, partition function, partition scheme, partition switching, partition elimination, large table management
x: Okay, partitioning splits one large table into multiple partitions based on a column, usually a date, like one partition per month. To queries it's still one table. Underneath, each partition is stored separately and can sit on different filegroups.

Now the thing is, it's mainly a data management feature, not a magic performance feature. The big wins are around managing data. Partition switching is the main one. You can move a whole partition in or out of the table almost instantly, as a metadata operation. So archiving or deleting a month of old data becomes switching that partition out to an archive table, instead of a huge, slow, log-heavy DELETE. Loading data can work the same way. You also get maintenance per partition, so index rebuilds and stats updates can target only the recent active partitions. And lock escalation can go to the partition level.

For queries, partition elimination helps when the query filters on the partition column, because SQL Server only reads the relevant partitions. But if queries don't filter on it, partitioning can actually make them slower, since every partition gets checked. Good indexes usually matter way more for query speed.

So I'd consider partitioning for really big tables, hundreds of millions of rows, with a natural time-based access pattern and data lifecycle needs, like logs, events or audit records. For normal-sized tables, it's just complexity with no benefit.

p17-221.q: Honestly, sharding is something I'd think hard about. It splits data across multiple separate databases, often on separate servers, where each shard holds a subset of the rows based on a shard key, like tenant id or customer id. It's horizontal scaling for the database, for when one server can't handle the data volume or the write load, even after scaling up, indexing, and adding read replicas.
p17-221.k: sharding, database sharding, shard key, horizontal partitioning across servers, resharding, tenant sharding
x: Honestly, sharding is something I'd think hard about. It splits data across multiple separate databases, often on separate servers, where each shard holds a subset of the rows based on a shard key, like tenant id or customer id. It's horizontal scaling for the database, for when one server can't handle the data volume or the write load, even after scaling up, indexing, and adding read replicas.

Picking the shard key is the most important decision. A good key spreads data and load evenly and keeps related data together, so most queries hit just one shard. Tenant id is a natural choice in multi-tenant systems. A bad key creates hotspots, where one shard takes most of the traffic.

And the challenges are real. Queries across shards, like global reports, have to fan out to every shard and combine results, which is slow and complex. You don't get transactions across shards, so you need sagas or careful design. Unique constraints and joins only work within a shard. Resharding, when a shard gets too big, means moving data while the system is live. And operations, backups, schema changes, monitoring, all multiply with the number of shards.
So for me sharding is a last resort. Before that, I'd try caching, read replicas, archiving old data, and splitting data by service.
Actually, database per tenant, like our database per study in IRT, is a simple form of sharding by tenant, where each study is fully isolated.

p17-222.q: Basically a read replica is a copy of the primary database, kept up to date through replication, that accepts read-only queries. Sending reporting and read-heavy queries to replicas takes load off the primary, which handles all the writes. In SQL Server that's Always On availability groups with readable secondaries, in AWS it's RDS and Aurora read replicas, and in Azure SQL it's read scale-out.
p17-222.k: read replicas, read scale out, always on availability groups readable secondary, replica lag, read write splitting
x: Basically a read replica is a copy of the primary database, kept up to date through replication, that accepts read-only queries. Sending reporting and read-heavy queries to replicas takes load off the primary, which handles all the writes. In SQL Server that's Always On availability groups with readable secondaries, in AWS it's RDS and Aurora read replicas, and in Azure SQL it's read scale-out.

In the app, I use separate connection strings. One for the primary, and one with ApplicationIntent set to ReadOnly for the replica, and route queries accordingly. Like a separate read-only DbContext for reports and search.

The main pitfall is replication lag. Asynchronous replicas can be seconds behind, or more under heavy load. So if a user saves something and the next screen reads from a replica, they might not see their own change, and that looks like a bug to them. For that, I read from the primary right after a write, or route that user's reads to the primary for a short window.

There are other gotchas too. Long-running queries on a replica can interfere with replication, depending on the database. Replicas need the same indexes, maybe extra ones for reporting. And failover changes which server is primary, so connect through the listener or cluster endpoint, never a server name.
So that's where replicas fit for me, reports, exports and search, where a little staleness is fine.

p17-223.q: So the recovery model controls how the transaction log is managed, and that decides which restore options you have.
p17-223.k: recovery model, full recovery model, simple recovery, transaction log backup, point in time restore, rpo rto database
x: So the recovery model controls how the transaction log is managed, and that decides which restore options you have.

In the simple recovery model, the log gets truncated automatically after checkpoints, so it doesn't grow much, but there are no log backups. You can only restore to the time of your last full or differential backup, and anything after that is gone. That's fine for dev databases or data you can easily rebuild.

In the full recovery model, every change stays in the log until a log backup is taken. With a chain of full, differential and regular log backups, say every 15 minutes, you can restore to any point in time. Like just before someone ran a bad update at 10:42. That's essential for production databases with important data. But the log has to be backed up regularly, otherwise it keeps growing until the disk fills up. Honestly, that's a classic production incident.
Bulk-logged is a variation that minimally logs bulk operations, used temporarily during large loads.
These choices tie into RPO, how much data we can afford to lose, which drives log backup frequency, and RTO, how fast we have to recover, which depends on database size and restore speed.

And backups are only real if restores are tested. I'd regularly restore to a test server to prove the backups work and to measure how long it takes. In managed services like RDS or Azure SQL, point-in-time restore is built in.

p17-224.q: Okay, an implicit conversion happens when SQL Server compares two values of different data types and silently converts one to match the other, following data type precedence rules.
p17-224.k: implicit conversion, convert_implicit, nvarchar vs varchar index, data type mismatch query, ef core varchar parameter
x: Okay, an implicit conversion happens when SQL Server compares two values of different data types and silently converts one to match the other, following data type precedence rules.

It becomes a problem when the conversion gets applied to the column instead of the parameter. Classic example, the column is varchar, but the app sends the parameter as nvarchar, which is .NET's default for strings. nvarchar has higher precedence, so SQL Server converts every value in the varchar column to nvarchar to compare. Depending on the collation, that can turn an index seek into a scan of the whole table, because the index is on the original varchar values. The query still returns the right result, just much slower, and CPU goes up. It's sneaky because nothing looks broken.
In the execution plan, you'll see CONVERT_IMPLICIT, and a warning icon on the SELECT operator saying the conversion may affect the cardinality estimate or seek plan.

The fix is making the types match. In EF Core, I configure the column as non-Unicode, IsUnicode false or column type varchar, so EF sends varchar parameters. In Dapper or ADO.NET, I specify DbType.AnsiString for varchar columns. In stored procedures, parameters should be declared with the same type and length as the columns.
Other common mismatches I've seen are numbers stored in string columns, and dates being compared to strings.

p17-225.q: GUIDs are attractive as keys, I get it. They're globally unique, the application can generate them before saving, they don't reveal record counts, and merging data from different databases is easy.
p17-225.k: guid primary key, uniqueidentifier clustered index, newsequentialid, guid fragmentation, uuid v7, int vs guid key
x: GUIDs are attractive as keys, I get it. They're globally unique, the application can generate them before saving, they don't reveal record counts, and merging data from different databases is easy.

The problem is using a random GUID, from NEWID or Guid.NewGuid, as the clustered index key in SQL Server. The clustered index orders the table by its key. Random values mean every new row goes to a random spot in the index, not at the end. So you get constant page splits, heavy fragmentation, lower page density, more I/O, and more memory needed to keep the active part of the index cached. It's also 16 bytes, four times an int, and the clustered key gets copied into every non-clustered index, so all your indexes get bigger.

What are the alternatives? Sequential GUIDs, either NEWSEQUENTIALID in SQL Server, or sequential generation in the app, like EF Core's default value generator for SQL Server, or the new UUID version 7 with Guid.CreateVersion7 in .NET 9, which is time-ordered. Then inserts go to the end, like an identity.
Or use an int or bigint identity as the clustered primary key, and add a GUID as a separate public identifier with a unique non-clustered index, so external APIs don't expose sequential ids.
For DynamoDB or other distributed stores though, random keys are actually good, because they spread load. So it really depends on the database, that's how I'd answer it.

p17-226.q: So an identity column basically generates incrementing values for one table when a row gets inserted. Simple, and the most common choice. The app only knows the new id after the insert, which EF Core reads back with OUTPUT. Identity values can have gaps, after rollbacks or server restarts, so don't use them where gaps matter, like invoice numbers that have to be continuous.
p17-226.k: identity vs sequence, sql sequence, hilo ef core, key generation, identity gaps, sequence cache
x: So an identity column basically generates incrementing values for one table when a row gets inserted. Simple, and the most common choice. The app only knows the new id after the insert, which EF Core reads back with OUTPUT. Identity values can have gaps, after rollbacks or server restarts, so don't use them where gaps matter, like invoice numbers that have to be continuous.

A sequence is an independent database object that hands out numbers on request with NEXT VALUE FOR. It's not tied to a table, so one sequence can provide ids for several tables, or a business number like a shipment reference. You can get a value before inserting, and control start, increment, cycling and caching. It also has gaps after restarts when caching is on.

HiLo is an EF Core strategy that uses a sequence efficiently. EF reserves a block of ids at once, say 10, with one round trip, and hands them out to new entities in memory. So the app knows ids before saving, which helps when building object graphs, and batched inserts get more efficient, because EF doesn't need to read back generated ids one by one. What you give up is bigger gaps, and ids that aren't strictly in insert order.

For business-facing numbers though, like a kit or shipment number with a format and no gaps allowed, I'd build a separate dedicated mechanism with proper locking. I wouldn't rely on identity values for that.

p17-227.q: Actually, soft delete just means marking a record as deleted, with an IsDeleted flag and usually DeletedAt and DeletedBy columns, instead of physically removing it. It's common when data has to be kept for audit, regulatory reasons or undo, and in clinical systems that's basically the norm.
p17-227.k: soft delete ef core, isdeleted flag, global query filter soft delete, hasqueryfilter, logical delete
x: Actually, soft delete just means marking a record as deleted, with an IsDeleted flag and usually DeletedAt and DeletedBy columns, instead of physically removing it. It's common when data has to be kept for audit, regulatory reasons or undo, and in clinical systems that's basically the norm.
In EF Core, I do it in two parts.

One part is intercepting deletes. In a SaveChanges interceptor, or a SaveChanges override, I look in the ChangeTracker for entities in the Deleted state that implement an ISoftDeletable interface, switch their state to Modified, and set IsDeleted, DeletedAt and DeletedBy. So the application code just calls Remove like normal.

The other part is hiding deleted rows. A global query filter, HasQueryFilter where not IsDeleted, gets added automatically to every query on that entity, Includes too. So deleted records disappear without every developer having to remember a Where clause. For admin or audit screens, IgnoreQueryFilters shows them. EF Core 10 adds named filters, so soft delete and tenant filters can be switched off separately.

A few gotchas I've run into. Unique constraints have to allow a deleted duplicate, so you use a filtered unique index where IsDeleted equals 0. Related entities aren't deleted automatically, so you decide how cascades work. Performance needs indexes that include IsDeleted. And soft-deleted personal data may still need real deletion for privacy laws. That's easy to forget.

p17-228.q: Okay, so when you load an entity with several collection navigations using Include, like a Shipment with its Kits and its StatusHistory, EF Core by default generates one SQL query with JOINs. The problem is that joining two independent collections multiplies the rows. A shipment with 100 kits and 20 history entries returns 100 times 20, so 2,000 rows, each one repeating all the shipment's columns. Add more collections or more parent rows and the data transferred just explodes. That's the cartesian explosion, and EF Core actually logs a warning about it.
p17-228.k: cartesian explosion, assplitquery, split query ef core, multiple include performance, single query vs split query
x: Okay, so when you load an entity with several collection navigations using Include, like a Shipment with its Kits and its StatusHistory, EF Core by default generates one SQL query with JOINs. The problem is that joining two independent collections multiplies the rows. A shipment with 100 kits and 20 history entries returns 100 times 20, so 2,000 rows, each one repeating all the shipment's columns. Add more collections or more parent rows and the data transferred just explodes. That's the cartesian explosion, and EF Core actually logs a warning about it.

AsSplitQuery tells EF Core to load each collection with a separate SQL query. One for the shipments, one for the kits, one for the history, and they get stitched together in memory. Total rows become 1 plus 100 plus 20, instead of 2,000. You can turn it on per query, or make it the default with UseQuerySplittingBehavior.

But split queries aren't free. More round trips to the database. And consistency, because the separate queries don't run as one snapshot. If data changes between them, results can be inconsistent, unless you use a transaction with snapshot or serialisable isolation. And ordering with Skip and Take needs a unique, stable sort.

So I use single queries for one collection or small data, split queries for multiple large collections. And honestly, often the best option is projecting with Select into exactly the DTO shape the screen needs.

p17-229.q: So interceptors basically let you hook into EF Core's operations and inspect, change or suppress them. You register them with AddInterceptors when configuring the DbContext, and they can use dependency injection.
p17-229.k: ef core interceptors, savechangesinterceptor, dbcommandinterceptor, audit with interceptor, connection interceptor
x: So interceptors basically let you hook into EF Core's operations and inspect, change or suppress them. You register them with AddInterceptors when configuring the DbContext, and they can use dependency injection.

You've got a few kinds. SaveChanges interceptors run before and after SaveChanges, with access to the ChangeTracker. Command interceptors wrap every SQL command, so they see the command text and parameters and can modify them or the results. Connection interceptors run when connections open and close, transaction interceptors around transactions, and materialisation interceptors when entities get created from query results.

In my project, what we used them for, audit fields first of all. A SaveChanges interceptor sets CreatedBy, CreatedAt, ModifiedBy and ModifiedAt on any entity implementing IAuditable, using the current user service, so no developer has to remember. Audit trail too, capturing old and new values of changed properties into audit records in the same SaveChanges. Soft delete, turning deletes into updates of an IsDeleted flag. Outbox, converting domain events raised by entities into outbox rows in the same transaction. Slow query logging, a command interceptor that logs commands above a threshold with their duration. And connection setup, like setting session context with the tenant id through sp_set_session_context, for row-level security.
The nice part is all these cross-cutting things live in one place, not scattered through business code.

p17-230.q: Okay, value converters transform a property's value when it's written to the database and when it's read back. You configure them with HasConversion in the model configuration.
p17-230.k: value converters, ef core hasconversion, store enum as string, strongly typed id ef core, encrypt column ef core
x: Okay, value converters transform a property's value when it's written to the database and when it's read back. You configure them with HasConversion in the model configuration.

Where I use them, enums as strings is the most common. HasConversion of string stores Delivered instead of 3, which is readable in the database and safe if enum members get reordered. Strongly typed ids, like a ShipmentId record struct wrapping a Guid or int, converted to the primitive for storage, so the domain model can't mix up a ShipmentId with a SiteId. Value objects, like a Money or EmailAddress type stored as a simple column. Collections or small objects stored as a delimited string or JSON, though JSON columns are better for that now. Date handling, like always storing DateTime as UTC and restoring the Kind on read. And encryption, encrypting a sensitive column on write and decrypting on read, though database features like Always Encrypted are usually stronger.
EF Core has lots of built-in converters, and since EF Core 6, pre-convention model configuration can apply a converter to every property of a type in one go.

The main catch is querying. EF translates queries using the stored values, so some operations on converted properties just can't be translated to SQL, like calling methods on a value object. Equality comparisons usually work fine, but anything fancier might fail or force client evaluation. So I always test the queries I actually need.

p17-231.q: Actually from EF Core 7, you can map an owned type, or a collection of owned types, to a single JSON column, using ToJson in the configuration. Like a Study entity storing its flexible settings, or a shipment its list of temperature readings, as JSON, while the rest of the entity stays in normal columns.
p17-231.k: json columns ef core, tojson, store json in sql server, openjson, json_value, owned types json
x: Actually from EF Core 7, you can map an owned type, or a collection of owned types, to a single JSON column, using ToJson in the configuration. Like a Study entity storing its flexible settings, or a shipment its list of temperature readings, as JSON, while the rest of the entity stays in normal columns.

The nice part is queries still work in LINQ. EF translates filters on JSON properties into SQL Server's JSON functions, like JSON_VALUE and OPENJSON. So you can write a Where on Settings.MaxKits greater than 10, and it becomes SQL. Updates can modify just part of the JSON. EF Core 8 added primitive collections, like a List of int stored as JSON. And SQL Server 2025 and Azure SQL now have a native json data type, which is more efficient than nvarchar.

When does it fit? Data that's naturally a document, owned by one entity and usually read together with it. Flexible attributes that vary by study or customer, configuration blobs, small nested lists. It saves you lots of tiny tables and joins.

When doesn't it fit? Data that needs relational integrity, foreign keys, frequent filtering and sorting, or joins with other tables. Filtering on JSON properties can't use normal indexes unless you add computed columns with indexes on the extracted values.
So I use it selectively. Honestly, it shouldn't become a way to avoid designing a schema.

p17-232.q: See, normally ASP.NET Core creates a new DbContext for each request and disposes it at the end. Creating one is fairly cheap, but in very high-throughput services, the setup work, initialising internal services and the change tracker, does add up.
p17-232.k: dbcontext pooling, adddbcontextpool, context pooling performance, pooled dbcontext factory
x: See, normally ASP.NET Core creates a new DbContext for each request and disposes it at the end. Creating one is fairly cheap, but in very high-throughput services, the setup work, initialising internal services and the change tracker, does add up.

With AddDbContextPool instead of AddDbContext, EF Core keeps a pool of DbContext instances. A request takes one from the pool, and at the end the context gets reset, tracked entities and state cleared, and goes back for the next request. That cuts allocation and setup overhead. AddPooledDbContextFactory does the same for code that creates contexts through a factory, like background services or Blazor.
Benchmarks show real gains only at very high request rates with simple queries, so for a lot of apps it's a minor optimisation. I'd turn it on when profiling shows context creation in the hot path.

Now the important limitation. Since instances are reused, the DbContext must not hold per-request state in its own fields, like a tenant id or current user injected through the constructor. A pooled instance could carry one request's state into another one, which is scary in a multi-tenant system. Constructor injection of scoped services into a pooled DbContext doesn't work the usual way. For multi-tenant cases, I set the per-request state after getting the context from the pool, with a factory or some custom approach that resets it.
And just to be clear, this is different from database connection pooling, which ADO.NET does anyway.

p17-233.q: Okay so ADO.NET keeps a pool of open database connections per connection string, 100 by default. When code opens a connection, it gets one from the pool, and closing or disposing it gives it back. If all connections are in use, the next request waits, and after the timeout it fails with that famous error, "Timeout expired, the timeout period elapsed prior to obtaining a connection from the pool", which says max pool size was reached.
p17-233.k: connection pool exhaustion, timeout expired max pool size, connection leak, sqlconnection pool, max pool size reached
x: Okay so ADO.NET keeps a pool of open database connections per connection string, 100 by default. When code opens a connection, it gets one from the pool, and closing or disposing it gives it back. If all connections are in use, the next request waits, and after the timeout it fails with that famous error, "Timeout expired, the timeout period elapsed prior to obtaining a connection from the pool", which says max pool size was reached.

What usually causes it? Connection leaks, number one. Code opening connections or data readers without disposing them, especially when an exception skips the close, so they never go back. Then long-running queries or transactions hogging connections. Sync-over-async or thread pool starvation, where connections are held while threads wait. A traffic spike with slow database responses, so more requests hold connections at once. And slightly different connection strings creating separate pools, which people don't expect.

To diagnose, I check how many connections the app's host has in sys.dm_exec_sessions, look at what those sessions are doing, and review the code for missing using statements or DbContexts that aren't disposed. EF Core with DI handles disposal correctly if contexts are scoped properly.
The fix is disposing connections with using, shorter transactions, faster queries, and async all the way. Bumping Max Pool Size just hides the problem, honestly, and it can overload the database.

p17-234.q: So Dapper is a micro-ORM. You write the SQL yourself, and Dapper maps results to objects and handles parameters. It's very fast, almost no overhead over raw ADO.NET, and you have full control over the SQL.
p17-234.k: dapper vs ef core, micro orm, dapper performance, use both dapper and ef, raw sql vs orm
x: So Dapper is a micro-ORM. You write the SQL yourself, and Dapper maps results to objects and handles parameters. It's very fast, almost no overhead over raw ADO.NET, and you have full control over the SQL.

EF Core is a full ORM. LINQ queries translated to SQL, change tracking, relationships, migrations, concurrency handling, interceptors, a lot more. Developers are productive, and the code is strongly typed and easy to refactor.
The performance gap has narrowed a lot in recent versions. EF Core with AsNoTracking and projections to DTOs is close to Dapper for most queries, so performance alone rarely decides it anymore.

I use EF Core for most application code, especially writes. Change tracking, relationship handling, concurrency tokens and transactions save a lot of code and a lot of mistakes. And for typical queries too.

I reach for Dapper, or EF Core's raw SQL features like SqlQuery, when I need hand-tuned SQL. Complex reporting queries with window functions or CTEs, calls to legacy stored procedures, bulk reads where every millisecond counts, or databases EF doesn't model well.
And using both in the same service is completely fine, they can even share the same connection and transaction.
In our CIRT platform, the newer APIs use EF Core, while the legacy parts lean heavily on stored procedures with ADO.NET-style data access. So I work with both every week.

p17-235.q: EnableRetryOnFailure turns on EF Core's retrying execution strategy for SQL Server. When a command fails with a transient error, like a brief network drop, a failover, or Azure SQL throttling, EF Core waits and retries automatically, with increasing delays, up to a max number of attempts. In cloud environments, where short blips are normal, that makes the app a lot more resilient.
p17-235.k: execution strategy ef core, enableretryonfailure, retry transient sql errors, user initiated transactions not supported, sql azure transient
x: EnableRetryOnFailure turns on EF Core's retrying execution strategy for SQL Server. When a command fails with a transient error, like a brief network drop, a failover, or Azure SQL throttling, EF Core waits and retries automatically, with increasing delays, up to a max number of attempts. In cloud environments, where short blips are normal, that makes the app a lot more resilient.

The catch is transactions. If I start a transaction myself with BeginTransaction, and a command fails halfway, EF can't just retry that one command, because the earlier work in the transaction was rolled back. So EF Core throws an error saying user-initiated transactions aren't supported with the retrying strategy. First time you see that it's confusing.

The fix is wrapping the whole unit of work in the strategy. You get it with Database.CreateExecutionStrategy and call ExecuteAsync with a delegate that begins the transaction, does all the work, saves and commits. If a transient failure happens, the strategy re-runs the whole delegate from the top, including starting a new transaction.

So the delegate has to be safe to repeat. It should reload any data it depends on instead of reusing state from the failed attempt, and avoid side effects outside the database, like sending an email, inside the retried block.

There's also a subtle case where the commit actually succeeded but the connection failed before confirming it. Making operations idempotent, or using verifySucceeded, protects you from applying it twice.

p17-236.q: char is fixed-length. char 10 always uses 10 bytes, padding shorter values with spaces. It's good for values that are always the same length, like a two-letter country code or a fixed-format code.
p17-236.k: char vs varchar, varchar vs nvarchar, unicode columns, utf8 collation, column data type choice, nvarchar max
x: char is fixed-length. char 10 always uses 10 bytes, padding shorter values with spaces. It's good for values that are always the same length, like a two-letter country code or a fixed-format code.
varchar is variable-length, it uses only the bytes needed plus two bytes overhead, so it's better for values of varying length, like names or descriptions.

nvarchar and nchar store Unicode, traditionally UTF-16, two bytes per character for most text. They can store any language, Japanese, Arabic, Hindi, accented names. varchar uses a code page, so characters outside it get lost or turn into question marks. Unless the column uses a UTF-8 collation, available since SQL Server 2019, which lets varchar store Unicode as UTF-8.

So for any text users type, names, addresses, comments, especially in a global system, I use nvarchar, or varchar with a UTF-8 collation. For internal codes and identifiers that are guaranteed ASCII, varchar saves space.

A couple more things I watch. Size columns realistically, not nvarchar max everywhere. Max types are stored differently, can't be index keys, and the declared size affects the memory grants the optimiser asks for. And match the parameter types from the app to the column types, because a mismatch, like nvarchar parameters against a varchar column, can cause implicit conversions and index scans. I've actually seen that one slow down a search screen badly.

p17-237.q: Honestly NULL trips people up a lot. NULL means unknown or missing. Not zero, not empty string. And it follows three-valued logic, so comparisons with NULL return unknown, not true or false.
p17-237.k: null in sql, count star vs count column, null comparison, is null, ansi nulls, coalesce isnull
x: Honestly NULL trips people up a lot. NULL means unknown or missing. Not zero, not empty string. And it follows three-valued logic, so comparisons with NULL return unknown, not true or false.

That gives you the classic surprises. WHERE Column equals NULL returns nothing, you have to use IS NULL. WHERE Status not equals Shipped excludes rows where Status is NULL, because NULL not equals Shipped is unknown. And NOT IN with a subquery that returns even one NULL returns no rows at all. That's a nasty one. NOT EXISTS doesn't have that problem, so I prefer it.

COUNT star counts all rows. COUNT of a column counts only rows where that column isn't NULL. COUNT DISTINCT ignores NULLs too. Aggregates like SUM and AVG ignore NULLs, so AVG of a column with NULLs isn't the same as SUM divided by COUNT star. And SUM of all NULLs gives NULL, not zero, so I wrap it in COALESCE.

For defaults, COALESCE is standard SQL and takes many arguments, while ISNULL is SQL Server-specific, takes two, and uses the first argument's data type, which can truncate values. That one's caught people out.
NULLs in unique constraints, SQL Server allows only one NULL in a unique column, unlike some databases, so you use a filtered unique index to allow many.
In design, I make columns NOT NULL unless a missing value genuinely means something.

p17-238.q: WHERE filters individual rows before they're grouped. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and aggregation. So conditions on raw columns go in WHERE, and conditions on aggregates, COUNT, SUM, AVG, go in HAVING.
p17-238.k: where vs having, having clause, filter aggregates, group by having, logical query processing order
x: WHERE filters individual rows before they're grouped. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and aggregation. So conditions on raw columns go in WHERE, and conditions on aggregates, COUNT, SUM, AVG, go in HAVING.

Let me take an example. Find sites with more than 50 dispensed kits this year. WHERE dispense date is this year and status is Dispensed limits the rows first, then GROUP BY SiteId, then HAVING COUNT star greater than 50 keeps only the groups with enough kits.

This follows the logical processing order of a query. FROM and JOINs, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, then ORDER BY, and last TOP or OFFSET. That order also explains why you can't use a SELECT alias in WHERE, because SELECT hasn't happened yet, but you can use it in ORDER BY.

For performance, I put row conditions in WHERE whenever possible, not HAVING, so fewer rows get grouped. The optimiser can often move simple HAVING conditions on grouping columns into WHERE, but writing it properly makes the intent clear and doesn't depend on that.

It sounds basic, but I've seen real bugs from it. Like a condition put in HAVING on a non-aggregated column. Or a filter on an outer-joined table sitting in WHERE, which quietly turned a LEFT JOIN into an inner join. That second one took a while to spot.

p17-239.q: Okay, so an upsert updates a row if it exists, or inserts it if it doesn't. Super common when syncing data from external systems, like vendor shipment statuses.
p17-239.k: upsert sql server, merge statement, insert or update, merge race condition, update then insert pattern
x: Okay, so an upsert updates a row if it exists, or inserts it if it doesn't. Super common when syncing data from external systems, like vendor shipment statuses.

SQL Server's MERGE can do it in one statement. MERGE into the target, USING the source, ON the key, WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE, WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT, and optionally WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE. It's powerful for syncing a whole set of rows from a staging table.
