But MERGE has a reputation, and honestly it's earned. It isn't safe under concurrency by default. Two sessions can both see a row doesn't exist and both try to insert, and you get primary key violations, unless you add a HOLDLOCK or SERIALIZABLE hint. It's had a bunch of bugs over the years, especially with filtered indexes, triggers and certain features. And it's easy to write it in a way that does something you didn't expect.

For single-row upserts, a lot of SQL Server developers, me included, prefer an explicit pattern inside a transaction. UPDATE with UPDLOCK and SERIALIZABLE hints, and if no rows were affected, INSERT. The lock hints prevent the race. For sets of rows, an UPDATE joined to the staging table, then an INSERT of the rows that don't exist yet, all in one transaction.
EF Core doesn't have a built-in upsert yet, so for high volumes I go to SQL directly or use a library.

p17-240.q: See, SQL Server is built for set-based operations. You describe the result you want for a whole set of rows in one statement, and let the optimiser figure out how to do it efficiently, with indexes, joins, parallelism and batching.
p17-240.k: cursor vs set based, sql cursor performance, row by row processing, rbar, while loop sql
x: See, SQL Server is built for set-based operations. You describe the result you want for a whole set of rows in one statement, and let the optimiser figure out how to do it efficiently, with indexes, joins, parallelism and batching.

A cursor processes rows one at a time, like a loop in procedural code. Each iteration fetches a row and runs separate statements for it. People call it RBAR, row by agonising row. On a big table, it's usually orders of magnitude slower than the equivalent set-based UPDATE or INSERT SELECT, because every row has its own overhead, locks are held longer, and the optimiser can't optimise the operation as a whole. WHILE loops that process one row at a time have exactly the same problem.
So when I see a cursor, I try to rewrite it as one or a few set-based statements. Joins, CASE expressions, window functions like ROW_NUMBER, running totals with SUM OVER, and CTEs.

There are legit uses though. Admin tasks that have to run something per database or per object, like maintenance across many study databases. Calling a stored procedure that only works one row at a time and that you can't change. And deliberately processing in batches, which is a loop over chunks of thousands of rows, not single rows, to control locking and log growth.
If I really must use a cursor, I declare it LOCAL FAST_FORWARD, so the overhead is lower. But that's rare for me.

p17-241.q: Okay, dynamic SQL means building a SQL statement as a string and executing it. Sometimes you really need it, like search screens with many optional filters, dynamic sorting, or admin scripts that work across tables or databases.
p17-241.k: dynamic sql, sp_executesql, exec vs sp_executesql, dynamic search query, quotename, dynamic sql injection
x: Okay, dynamic SQL means building a SQL statement as a string and executing it. Sometimes you really need it, like search screens with many optional filters, dynamic sorting, or admin scripts that work across tables or databases.

My rules for it. Use sp_executesql, not EXEC of a concatenated string. sp_executesql takes parameters separately, so user values never become part of the SQL text, and that's what prevents SQL injection. It also allows plan reuse, because the SQL text stays the same for different parameter values.

Never concatenate user input as values. Only the structure gets built dynamically, like adding "and SiteId equals the SiteId parameter" when that filter is present. The values always go in as parameters.

For identifiers, like table names, column names or sort direction, which can't be parameters, I validate them against a whitelist of allowed names and wrap them with QUOTENAME to handle special characters safely.

For catch-all search queries with optional filters, honestly, building the WHERE clause dynamically with only the filters actually used often gives much better plans than one static query full of "or parameter is null" conditions. Those tend to produce poor, generic plans. OPTION RECOMPILE is the other way out for those.
Dynamic SQL runs with the caller's permissions, and it's harder to read and review. So I keep it small, well commented, and print the generated SQL in debug mode.

p17-242.q: In stored procedures that change data, I use one standard pattern, so errors never leave a transaction half-done or hanging open.
p17-242.k: try catch sql server, xact_abort, t sql error handling, rollback in catch, throw vs raiserror, xact_state
x: In stored procedures that change data, I use one standard pattern, so errors never leave a transaction half-done or hanging open.

At the top, SET XACT_ABORT ON, and SET NOCOUNT ON. With XACT_ABORT on, most runtime errors automatically roll back the whole transaction and abort the batch. Without it, some errors only fail the current statement and the transaction carries on, which can leave partial changes. It also matters when the client times out. The transaction gets rolled back instead of staying open and holding locks.

Then BEGIN TRY, BEGIN TRANSACTION, the statements, COMMIT, END TRY. And in BEGIN CATCH, if there's an open transaction, which you check with TRANCOUNT greater than zero or XACT_STATE, ROLLBACK. Then log the error if needed, and rethrow with THROW, so the application knows it failed. THROW has been there since SQL Server 2012. It keeps the original error number and message, and it's simpler than RAISERROR.
One thing I learned the hard way, logging inside the CATCH has to happen after the rollback, otherwise your log row gets rolled back too.

Also, nested transactions in SQL Server aren't real nested transactions. An inner COMMIT only decrements the counter, and any ROLLBACK rolls back everything. So procedures called from other procedures need to be careful about starting their own transactions, or use save points.
And on the .NET side, I still handle SqlException and use transactions consistently.

p17-243.q: Okay, so whenever a SQL Server task can't proceed, it waits, and SQL Server records why and for how long. Wait statistics answer "what is this server spending its time waiting for?", and that points you to the kind of bottleneck before you start tuning anything.
p17-243.k: wait stats, sys.dm_os_wait_stats, pageiolatch, cxpacket, lck_m waits, sql server waits tuning
x: Okay, so whenever a SQL Server task can't proceed, it waits, and SQL Server records why and for how long. Wait statistics answer "what is this server spending its time waiting for?", and that points you to the kind of bottleneck before you start tuning anything.
I look at sys.dm_os_wait_stats for the whole server, filtering out the harmless background waits, and session wait stats or Query Store's wait categories for specific sessions or queries.

The common ones and what they tell me. PAGEIOLATCH is waiting to read data pages from disk, so not enough memory for the working set, or queries reading too much because of missing indexes. WRITELOG is waiting for log writes, so slow log storage or too many tiny commits. LCK_M waits mean blocking, waiting on locks held by others. CXPACKET and CXCONSUMER are parallelism, often normal, but lots of it may mean big scans or a cost threshold for parallelism that's too low. SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD is CPU pressure. RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE is queries waiting for memory grants, often from big sorts or hashes due to bad estimates. And ASYNC_NETWORK_IO means the client isn't consuming results fast enough, usually the app reading row by row or pulling huge result sets.
Wait stats are cumulative since the last restart. So I compare snapshots over a time window during the problem period, not just read the totals. The totals alone can really mislead you.

p17-244.q: Honestly tempdb is one of those things people ignore until it hurts. It's a shared system database that every database on the instance uses. Temp tables, table variables, sorts and hashes that spill out of memory, the row version store for snapshot isolation, and some internal work. Since everything shares it, it can easily become a bottleneck.
p17-244.k: tempdb contention, tempdb allocation contention, pagelatch tempdb, tempdb files, tempdb spills
x: Honestly tempdb is one of those things people ignore until it hurts. It's a shared system database that every database on the instance uses. Temp tables, table variables, sorts and hashes that spill out of memory, the row version store for snapshot isolation, and some internal work. Since everything shares it, it can easily become a bottleneck.

Allocation contention is the classic problem. When lots of sessions create and drop temp objects at a high rate, they all fight over the same allocation pages, and you see PAGELATCH waits on tempdb pages. To fix it, multiple tempdb data files of equal size, usually one per CPU core up to eight, which modern SQL Server setup does by default. Newer versions also reduced this contention a lot, and SQL Server 2019 added memory-optimised tempdb metadata.

Then there are other tempdb problems. Spills, where a sort or hash join doesn't get enough memory and writes to tempdb, which is slow and shows as a warning in the execution plan. Fixing estimates, indexes or the query usually sorts that out. Version store growth, where with RCSI or snapshot isolation a long-running transaction stops old row versions being cleaned up, so tempdb keeps growing. And running out of space, which can hit every database on the server.
So I monitor tempdb size and usage, keep it on fast storage, size it properly up front so it isn't constantly auto-growing, and look out for queries with spills or heavy temp object use.

p17-245.q: No, honestly, never blindly. SQL Server records missing index suggestions when the optimiser thinks an index would have helped a query. They show up in execution plans as a green hint, and in the missing index DMVs with an estimated improvement. They're a useful starting point, but that's all.
p17-245.k: missing index dmv, missing index suggestion, sys.dm_db_missing_index_details, index recommendations, database tuning advisor
x: No, honestly, never blindly. SQL Server records missing index suggestions when the optimiser thinks an index would have helped a query. They show up in execution plans as a green hint, and in the missing index DMVs with an estimated improvement. They're a useful starting point, but that's all.

Why not just create them? Suggestions are made per query, without looking at other indexes, so you often get several overlapping ones that should really be one index. They ignore the cost of maintaining the index on inserts and updates. The key column order isn't always ideal, equality columns come before inequality columns, but they're not ordered by selectivity. They often include tons of INCLUDE columns, sometimes almost the whole table. They ignore filtered indexes and columnstore options. And the DMVs reset when the server restarts.

What I do is look at the suggestion together with the actual query and its plan. Check the existing indexes on that table, maybe one can be extended instead of adding a new one. Think about the write load on that table. Design the index with the right key order and only the included columns that are needed. Test it on a copy with realistic data. And then deploy it through the normal database change process.
After deploying, I verify the query actually uses it, and check index usage stats later, removing indexes that never get used.

p17-246.q: So a query with LIKE percent term percent can't use a normal index, because of the leading wildcard. It scans the whole table, and it can't handle word forms, relevance ranking or multiple terms well.
p17-246.k: full text search sql server, contains freetext, like wildcard performance, elasticsearch vs sql, search engine
x: So a query with LIKE percent term percent can't use a normal index, because of the leading wildcard. It scans the whole table, and it can't handle word forms, relevance ranking or multiple terms well.

SQL Server full-text search builds a special full-text index of the words in text columns. You query with CONTAINS for precise word and phrase searches, including prefix searches like ship star, word forms through inflection, and proximity. And FREETEXT for meaning-based searching. CONTAINSTABLE and FREETEXTTABLE give relevance ranks. It handles stop words and language-specific word breaking, and the index updates automatically in the background as data changes. Azure SQL supports it too.
It's a good choice when search is part of a transactional app, the data is already in SQL Server, and the requirements are moderate. Like searching notes, descriptions or document text.

A dedicated search engine, like Elasticsearch, OpenSearch or Azure AI Search, is better when search is a core feature. Typo tolerance and fuzzy matching, faceted navigation, serious relevance tuning, autocomplete, searching across data from many services, very large volumes, or semantic and vector search. But that's another system to run and keep in sync, usually through events or change data capture, with eventual consistency.
So that's usually my approach. I start with what the database already gives me, and move to a search engine only when the requirements clearly need it.

p17-247.q: Okay, so SSDT, SQL Server Data Tools, is declarative, state-based. The database project holds the desired definition of every object, tables, views, procedures, indexes, as CREATE scripts in source control. Building the project validates all the references and produces a dacpac, which is a package describing the target schema.
p17-247.k: ssdt, dacpac, sql database project, sqlpackage, state based migrations, database ci cd
x: Okay, so SSDT, SQL Server Data Tools, is declarative, state-based. The database project holds the desired definition of every object, tables, views, procedures, indexes, as CREATE scripts in source control. Building the project validates all the references and produces a dacpac, which is a package describing the target schema.

At deployment, SqlPackage compares the dacpac with the actual database and generates a script to make the database match. Adding columns, altering procedures, creating indexes. Pre-deployment and post-deployment scripts handle data changes, like filling a new column or seeding reference data, and those have to be written so they're safe to re-run.

In the pipeline, the build creates the dacpac as an artifact. The release first generates the deployment script, or a deploy report, for review, which really matters in regulated environments. Then it publishes to each environment, with publish profiles setting options like BlockOnPossibleDataLoss, which stops the deployment if a change would drop data.

What you get is the full schema always visible in source control, drift gets detected, and the same package can go to many databases. The risk is that auto-generated scripts can do expensive things, like rebuilding a large table just to change column order. So reviewing the generated script is not optional.
Our CIRT platform uses SSDT database projects, and the same model schema gets deployed to every study database. So this is daily work for us.

p17-248.q: Actually a single DELETE of millions of rows is really risky. It runs as one huge transaction, so the transaction log grows enormously. It can escalate to a table lock and block everyone. It can take forever. And if you cancel it, the rollback takes just as long.
p17-248.k: delete millions of rows, purge old data, archive data sql, batch delete, data retention job
x: Actually a single DELETE of millions of rows is really risky. It runs as one huge transaction, so the transaction log grows enormously. It can escalate to a table lock and block everyone. It can take forever. And if you cancel it, the rollback takes just as long.

So I do it in batches. A loop deletes, say, 5,000 rows at a time, using DELETE TOP 5,000 with a condition on an indexed column like a date, and keeps going until no rows are affected. Each batch is its own short transaction, so locks get released quickly, under the escalation threshold, and log space can be reused between log backups. Sometimes I add a small delay between batches to reduce the impact on other users, and run it in quiet hours.

For archiving, each batch first copies rows to the archive table and then deletes them, in the same transaction. Often with DELETE plus an OUTPUT clause into the archive table, which does both in one statement. Pretty neat.
For tables partitioned by date, switching out an old partition is almost instant, which is much better for regular retention.

A few more things. Make sure the delete condition uses an index. Check foreign keys and cascades, which can multiply the work. And think about regulatory retention rules. In clinical systems, data often has to be kept for many years, so honestly we archive much more than we delete.

p17-249.q: So both are mature, powerful relational databases, and EF Core supports both well, with Npgsql as the PostgreSQL provider.
p17-249.k: sql server vs postgresql, postgres vs mssql, npgsql, postgresql for dotnet, switch to postgres
x: So both are mature, powerful relational databases, and EF Core supports both well, with Npgsql as the PostgreSQL provider.

Cost is the first big difference. PostgreSQL is open source and free, which makes it really attractive in the cloud, like RDS, Aurora PostgreSQL or Azure Database for PostgreSQL. SQL Server has licence costs, especially Enterprise edition.

Feature-wise, PostgreSQL has excellent JSON support with jsonb and GIN indexes, arrays as a column type, rich extensions like PostGIS and pgvector for vector search, and partial and expression indexes. SQL Server has strong tooling, SSMS, Query Store, SQL Server Agent for jobs, built-in columnstore, in-memory OLTP, and deep integration with Windows and Microsoft tools.

Then there are behaviour differences that bite you during a migration. PostgreSQL folds unquoted names to lowercase, so naming conventions matter. String comparison is case-sensitive by default in PostgreSQL. Concurrency internals differ, PostgreSQL uses MVCC by default, kind of like SQL Server's snapshot isolation, and needs VACUUM to clean up old row versions. The procedure language is different, T-SQL versus PL/pgSQL, so procedures have to be rewritten. And data types, like datetime2 versus timestamp with time zone, and identity versus serial or identity columns.
For us, the CIRT core runs on SQL Server, while the developer RAG index uses PostgreSQL with pgvector. So I've touched both.

p17-250.q: Okay, SELECT star returns every column of a table, and in application code, it causes a bunch of problems.
p17-250.k: select star, avoid select *, select all columns problem, select specific columns, projection performance
x: Okay, SELECT star returns every column of a table, and in application code, it causes a bunch of problems.

Performance first. It reads and sends more data than needed, over the network and into memory. Wide columns, like big text or binary columns, make it much worse. It also stops covering indexes from being used, since no non-clustered index includes every column, so SQL Server has to do key lookups or scan the clustered index.

Then it's fragile. If someone adds a column later, the query returns it automatically. Code that relies on column order breaks, views defined with SELECT star don't pick up changes properly until they're refreshed, and an INSERT SELECT star can fail or put data into the wrong columns.

There's a security angle too. New sensitive columns can leak into results, logs and APIs without anybody deciding they should. And for readability, you can't tell which columns the code actually uses.

In EF Core, loading entire entities is basically the same thing. For read-only screens, I project with Select into a DTO with only the needed columns, which EF turns into a SELECT of just those columns. That often makes a big difference.
SELECT star is fine for ad hoc queries while you're exploring data. And EXISTS with SELECT star in a subquery is fine too, because the columns aren't actually returned there.

p17-251.q: See, a transaction holds its locks until it commits or rolls back. So the longer it runs, the more damage it can do.
p17-251.k: long running transaction, open transaction problems, transaction log growth, blocking long transaction, keep transactions short
x: See, a transaction holds its locks until it commits or rolls back. So the longer it runs, the more damage it can do.
Blocking is the obvious one. Other sessions that need the locked rows, pages or tables just wait, so the app slows down for lots of users, and deadlocks get more likely.

Then transaction log growth. The log can't be truncated past the oldest active transaction, so a transaction left open for hours makes the log grow until the disk fills, even with regular log backups. People don't expect that.
Version store growth too. With snapshot isolation or RCSI, old row versions in tempdb can't be cleaned up while an old transaction might still need them, so tempdb grows.
And recovery and rollback time. If it fails or the server restarts, rolling it back takes ages, and the database may take longer to recover. Replication and availability group lag can go up as well.

What causes it in applications? Doing slow work inside a transaction, like calling an external API, sending an email or waiting for user input. Processing a huge batch in one transaction. Or a bug where an exception skips the commit and the connection stays open with the transaction.

So I keep transactions as short as possible. Prepare and validate data before starting, include only the writes that must be atomic, do external calls outside, process large changes in batches, and watch for old open transactions with DBCC OPENTRAN or the DMVs. That's how I keep it under control.

p17-252.q: Okay, so a normal rowstore index stores data row by row. A columnstore index stores it column by column, in compressed segments of around a million rows each.
p17-252.k: columnstore index, clustered columnstore, analytics sql server, batch mode, reporting performance, olap vs oltp
x: Okay, so a normal rowstore index stores data row by row. A columnstore index stores it column by column, in compressed segments of around a million rows each.

That's ideal for analytics, queries that scan lots of rows but only a few columns. Like summing quantities by site and month over millions of shipments. The query reads only the columns it needs, the data is heavily compressed, often 10 times smaller, and SQL Server processes it in batch mode, many rows per operation, so aggregations get dramatically faster. Segment elimination also skips segments that can't match the filter.

There are two main ways to use it. A clustered columnstore index makes the whole table columnar, which suits data warehouse fact tables and big history or log tables that are mostly appended and aggregated. A non-clustered columnstore index on a transactional table gives you real-time operational analytics. The OLTP workload keeps using the normal rowstore indexes, while reports use the columnstore, and you don't need a separate warehouse.
The downside is they're bad for single-row lookups and frequent small updates. Updates go through a delta store and deleted bitmaps, and they need maintenance to stay efficient.

So I'd consider a non-clustered columnstore for heavy reporting on a big transactional table, and clustered columnstore for warehouse or history tables. Aggregating supply and dispensing history for forecasting reports, for example, is a typical fit.

p17-253.q: See, both are SQL Server features for finding out what changed in tables, so other systems can sync or react, without adding timestamp columns or triggers everywhere.
p17-253.k: change data capture, cdc sql server, change tracking, debezium, stream database changes, sync data changes
x: See, both are SQL Server features for finding out what changed in tables, so other systems can sync or react, without adding timestamp columns or triggers everywhere.

Change Tracking is the lightweight one. It records that a row changed, the primary key and the type of change, plus a version number, but not the old or new values. A consumer asks "what changed since version X?", and then reads the current values from the table. It's synchronous with the transaction, low overhead, and great for syncing caches, mobile clients or search indexes, where only the latest state matters.

Change Data Capture is richer. It reads the transaction log asynchronously and records the full history of changes in change tables, inserts, deletes, and the before and after values of updates, in order. That suits auditing, data warehouse loading, and streaming changes to other systems. Tools like Debezium read CDC and publish each change as an event to Kafka, which is a common way to do the outbox pattern, or feed other services without touching application code.
CDC costs more storage, needs SQL Server Agent jobs for capture and cleanup on-premise, and adds some latency and ops work. Change Tracking is simpler but you lose the intermediate values.
So honestly the way I remember it, Change Tracking is "give me what's changed so I can sync", and CDC is "give me every change, with history".

p17-254.q: Honestly it depends on what kind of data it is, I've done it a few different ways.
p17-254.k: ef core seed data, hasdata, seeding reference data, useseeding, migration data seeding, lookup tables seed
x: Honestly it depends on what kind of data it is, I've done it a few different ways.

HasData, in the model configuration, defines seed rows for an entity with explicit primary key values. EF Core puts inserts, updates and deletes for that data into migrations, by comparing with the previous model. It works well for small, stable reference data, statuses, country codes, types, stuff that should be identical in every environment. But keys have to be hard-coded, it can't depend on data already in the database, and changing large seed sets creates noisy migrations.

EF Core 9 added UseSeeding and UseAsyncSeeding, configured on the DbContext options, which run custom seeding code when EnsureCreated or Migrate runs. That's more flexible. It can check whether the data's already there and use any logic you like.

Custom migration code with migrationBuilder.Sql, or a post-deployment script in a database project, is another option. Especially when the data change has to happen at a precise point in the schema's evolution.
For test data and local development, I keep it separate from reference data, in a seeding tool or test fixtures. Never in production migrations.

In regulated systems, reference data changes are part of the validated release, reviewed just like code. And configuration that differs per study or customer isn't seed data at all. That belongs in configuration tooling, like our Admin console.

p17-255.q: Okay, row-level security basically lets the database itself filter which rows a user can see or change, based on who's running the query, without changing the queries at all.
p17-255.k: row level security, rls sql server, security policy predicate, tenant isolation database, session_context
x: Okay, row-level security basically lets the database itself filter which rows a user can see or change, based on who's running the query, without changing the queries at all.

You create an inline table-valued function, the predicate, that returns a row when access is allowed. Like when the row's TenantId equals the tenant id stored in the session context. Then a security policy applies that function as a filter predicate on the table. So SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE silently see only allowed rows. Optionally you add a block predicate too, which stops anyone inserting or updating rows into another tenant.

For apps that connect with one shared database login, the user or tenant identity gets set per connection with sp_set_session_context. For example through an EF Core connection interceptor right after the connection opens. And the predicate reads it with SESSION_CONTEXT.
For multi-tenant databases it's a strong extra layer of defence. Even if a developer forgets a WHERE clause, or a reporting tool queries the table directly, other tenants' data isn't exposed.

A few cautions though. The predicate runs on every query, so it has to be simple and backed by indexes, or performance suffers. Session context must be reset properly on pooled connections, that one's easy to miss. Admin and maintenance processes need a safe way to bypass it. And it doesn't replace authorization in the application, which still decides what each user is allowed to do.

p17-256.q: So zone.js is a library that patches the browser's async APIs, setTimeout, promises, DOM events, XHR, so Angular knows whenever some async work finishes. After any of those, Angular runs change detection to update the view. That's why in classic Angular, changing a component property inside a click handler or an HTTP callback just works, without calling anything.
p17-256.k: zone.js, zoneless angular, ngzone, provideZonelessChangeDetection, run outside angular, change detection trigger
x: So zone.js is a library that patches the browser's async APIs, setTimeout, promises, DOM events, XHR, so Angular knows whenever some async work finishes. After any of those, Angular runs change detection to update the view. That's why in classic Angular, changing a component property inside a click handler or an HTTP callback just works, without calling anything.

But there are downsides. It's a fairly heavy library. It triggers change detection very often, even when nothing relevant changed. Async stack traces get harder to read. And native async await can't be patched, so Angular had to downgrade it during builds.
The NgZone service lets you control it a bit. Like runOutsideAngular for frequent events, mousemove or a polling timer, so they don't trigger change detection on every tick.

Zoneless Angular removes zone.js completely. Change detection is triggered explicitly by things Angular knows about, signals changing, the async pipe, event handlers bound in templates, and markForCheck. It was experimental in Angular 18, stable in 20, and it's the default for new apps since Angular 21. In older versions you configure it with provideZonelessChangeDetection.

You get smaller bundles, better performance and cleaner debugging. To migrate though, components need to work properly with OnPush and signals, because code that changes state outside those triggers just won't update the view anymore. That's where most of the migration effort goes.

p17-257.q: Since Angular 17, templates have built-in control flow blocks that replace the structural directives, ngIf, ngFor and ngSwitch.
p17-257.k: angular control flow, @if @for @switch, built in control flow, ngif vs @if, track in @for
x: Since Angular 17, templates have built-in control flow blocks that replace the structural directives, ngIf, ngFor and ngSwitch.

At-if with an expression shows a block, with else-if and else branches, and you can alias the result, like at-if user async as user. At-switch with case and default replaces ngSwitch. At-for loops over a collection, and it requires a track expression, like track item.id. That tells Angular how to identify each item so it can reuse DOM elements instead of recreating them when the list changes. There's also an empty block that shows when the collection is empty, and implicit variables like index, first, last and count.

Why it's better, it's built into the compiler, so no importing CommonModule or the directives. It's more readable, especially else branches, which used to need ng-template references. Type narrowing works better inside if blocks. And it's faster. The mandatory track also fixes a really common performance mistake, because lots of teams forgot trackBy with ngFor and got full re-rendering of lists.
The Angular CLI has a migration schematic for control-flow that converts existing templates automatically, so moving over isn't painful.
In our newer Angular 17 study builder, we use the new syntax, while the older Angular 8 and 12 sub-apps still use the directives. So I go back and forth between both, honestly.

p17-258.q: Okay so defer blocks came in Angular 17. A defer block lazily loads part of a template and its dependencies. Components, directives and pipes used only inside the defer block get split into a separate JavaScript chunk, which is downloaded and rendered only when some trigger condition happens.
p17-258.k: defer blocks, @defer angular, deferrable views, lazy load component template, on viewport, on idle
x: Okay so defer blocks came in Angular 17. A defer block lazily loads part of a template and its dependencies. Components, directives and pipes used only inside the defer block get split into a separate JavaScript chunk, which is downloaded and rendered only when some trigger condition happens.

The triggers are on idle, which is the default, when the browser's idle. On viewport, when the placeholder scrolls into view. On interaction, when the user clicks or types in the placeholder. On hover. On timer, after a delay. On immediate. And when, with a condition. There's also prefetch, so you can download the code earlier, like on idle, but render it later, on interaction.

Related blocks control what shows in the meantime. Placeholder before loading starts, with an optional minimum display time so it doesn't flicker. Loading while the chunk downloads. And error if loading fails.

It's useful for heavy parts of a page that aren't needed straight away. Charts below the fold, a rich text editor, a comments section, a big dialog. The initial bundle gets smaller and the first render is faster, which helps metrics like Largest Contentful Paint.

Before defer, lazy loading in Angular was mostly at the route level, or manual dynamic imports with ViewContainerRef. Now it's declarative and fine-grained. And with server-side rendering, Angular 19 added incremental hydration, where deferred blocks hydrate only when they're triggered.

p17-259.q: Actually since Angular 17.1, components can declare inputs with the input function instead of the Input decorator. Like name equals input of string, or input.required of string. The input is a read-only signal, so in the template you read it as name with brackets, and in code you can use it in computed signals, like fullName as a computed of first plus last. Angular updates the signal whenever the parent passes a new value. So this replaces ngOnChanges and setters for reacting to input changes. And with required inputs, the compiler errors if the parent doesn't provide them. Transforms like booleanAttribute still work.
p17-259.k: signal inputs, input function angular, model signal, output function, input required, two way binding signals
x: Actually since Angular 17.1, components can declare inputs with the input function instead of the Input decorator. Like name equals input of string, or input.required of string. The input is a read-only signal, so in the template you read it as name with brackets, and in code you can use it in computed signals, like fullName as a computed of first plus last. Angular updates the signal whenever the parent passes a new value. So this replaces ngOnChanges and setters for reacting to input changes. And with required inputs, the compiler errors if the parent doesn't provide them. Transforms like booleanAttribute still work.

The model function creates a writable input for two-way binding. A child declares value equals model of number, and can set it with value.set. The parent binds with the banana-in-a-box syntax, square brackets and parentheses, to a property or a signal, and changes flow both ways. Way simpler than the old pattern of an Input plus an Output with the Change suffix.

The output function replaces the Output decorator with EventEmitter. Like saved equals output of Shipment, and you call saved.emit. It's lighter, and outputFromObservable can turn an RxJS stream into an output.
There are also signal-based queries, viewChild, viewChildren, contentChild and contentChildren, which return signals instead of being set later.
Put together, they make components fully signal-based, which plays really well with OnPush and zoneless change detection.

p17-260.q: Okay, so a computed signal derives its value from other signals, like total as a computed of the items reduced to a sum. It's lazy and memoised. It only recalculates when one of the signals it read has changed, and only when someone actually reads it. It's read-only and should be a pure function. That's the right tool for derived state, filtered lists, totals, flags.
p17-260.k: computed signal, effect angular, signal effect pitfalls, untracked, derived state signals, allowsignalwrites
x: Okay, so a computed signal derives its value from other signals, like total as a computed of the items reduced to a sum. It's lazy and memoised. It only recalculates when one of the signals it read has changed, and only when someone actually reads it. It's read-only and should be a pure function. That's the right tool for derived state, filtered lists, totals, flags.

An effect runs a side-effect function whenever the signals it reads change. It tracks dependencies automatically, runs at least once, and gets cleaned up when its component is destroyed. Effects are meant for syncing with stuff outside Angular's signal world. Writing to local storage, logging, calling a third-party chart library, manual DOM work.

Now the pitfalls, and I've seen people fall into these. Using effects to derive state, like an effect that sets another signal whenever some signal changes. That's what computed is for. The effect version causes extra change detection cycles, timing issues, and maybe even loops. Angular originally blocked signal writes inside effects by default for exactly this reason. Then unintended dependencies. Every signal you read inside the effect becomes a dependency, so reading something incidental re-runs it. untracked lets you read a signal without tracking it. And async work inside effects can race, so use the cleanup function, onCleanup, to cancel the previous work.
For data loading driven by signals, the newer resource and httpResource APIs are usually a better fit than effects.

p17-261.q: These are newer signal APIs, from around Angular 19 and 20. They fill the gaps between computed and writable signals, and between signals and async data.
p17-261.k: linkedsignal, resource api angular, httpresource, rxresource, async data signals, loading state signals
x: These are newer signal APIs, from around Angular 19 and 20. They fill the gaps between computed and writable signals, and between signals and async data.

linkedSignal creates a writable signal whose value is derived from other signals, but the user can also set it. When the source changes, it resets to a new computed value. Classic example is a selected option. The list of options comes from an input, and the selected item should default to the first option, but the user can change it. When the options list changes, the selection resets. Before this, people did it with an effect writing to a signal, which was honestly messy.

resource connects signals to async data. You give it a params function that reads signals, like the selected site id, and a loader function that fetches data. Whenever the params change, it calls the loader again and cancels the previous request with an AbortSignal. It exposes signals for value, status, isLoading and error, so the template can show a spinner or an error easily. rxResource does the same with an Observable loader, and httpResource wraps HttpClient directly, so interceptors still apply.
They kill a lot of boilerplate for the common "reload data when a filter changes" pattern. And they avoid race conditions where a slower response arrives after a faster one and overwrites it.
They're still evolving though, so I check their stability status for whichever Angular version we're on.

p17-262.q: So basically they're the bridge between RxJS and signals, from the rxjs-interop package.
p17-262.k: tosignal, toobservable, rxjs signals interop, rxjs-interop, convert observable to signal
x: So basically they're the bridge between RxJS and signals, from the rxjs-interop package.

toSignal subscribes to an Observable and gives you back a signal with its latest value. I use it when a service exposes an Observable, like an HTTP call, route parameters or a store selector, but I want the value in a template or in computed signals. It subscribes immediately and unsubscribes automatically when the component or service is destroyed, so no manual subscription management. Since an Observable might not emit synchronously, the signal's initial value is undefined, unless you give an initialValue, or use requireSync for observables that emit right away, like a BehaviorSubject. Errors from the Observable are thrown when the signal is read, so I handle them in the stream first.

toObservable goes the other way. It turns a signal into an Observable that emits when the signal changes. Useful when you need RxJS operators on signal values, like debounceTime and switchMap on a search term signal, to call an API and cancel outdated requests. And then often I convert the result back with toSignal.
Both have to be called in an injection context, like a constructor or a field initialiser, or be given an Injector. People forget that and get an error.
My general approach is signals for synchronous state and templates, RxJS for complex async event streams, and these two functions right at the boundary between them.

p17-263.q: Right, so Angular has two ways to get dependencies. Constructor injection declares them as constructor parameters, like private http of type HttpClient in the constructor. The inject function, available since Angular 14, gets them from inside the class body or a function, like private http equals inject HttpClient.

p17-264.q: So Angular has a tree of injectors, and where you provide a service decides how many instances exist and who shares them.

At the top you've got the environment injector hierarchy. providedIn root in the Injectable decorator registers a singleton for the whole app, and it's tree-shakable, so if nothing injects it, it's removed from the bundle. Services provided in the application's providers, or in a lazy-loaded route's providers, live in environment injectors. A lazy route with its own providers gets its own child injector, so a service provided there is a separate instance just for that feature.

Then there's the element injector hierarchy, which follows the component tree. If a component lists a service in its providers array, each instance of that component gets its own instance of the service, shared with its children and destroyed with the component. That's handy for state that belongs to one part of the screen, like a form wizard's state service, or one editor instance per tab. viewProviders limits visibility to the component's own view, not projected content.

When a component injects something, Angular searches up the element injectors first, then the environment injectors, until it finds a provider. Modifiers change the search, Optional, Self, SkipSelf and Host, and those are options on the inject function.
A really common bug I've seen is accidentally providing a "global" service in a component's providers. You get separate instances, and shared state looks completely broken.

p17-267.q: In my project, the auth interceptor adds the access token to outgoing requests and deals with expired tokens without the user noticing.

x: In my project, the auth interceptor adds the access token to outgoing requests and deals with expired tokens without the user noticing.

How it flows, the interceptor attaches the bearer token to requests going to our API, and only to our API's URLs, never to third-party domains. If a response comes back 401, it tries to refresh the token, and if that works, retries the original request with the new token. If the refresh fails, it logs the user out and sends them to the login page.

The tricky part is concurrency. A screen often fires several requests at once, and they might all get 401 together. Without care, each one triggers its own refresh, and with refresh token rotation, the second refresh uses an already-used refresh token and fails, and the user gets logged out for no reason. So the interceptor keeps a single in-flight refresh, a flag plus a BehaviorSubject, or a shared Observable with shareReplay. The first 401 starts the refresh, and the other requests wait for it with filter and take one, then retry with the new token.

A few more details. Don't intercept the refresh call itself, or you get loops. Retry each request only once. And refresh proactively before expiry when you can, which avoids most 401s anyway. Libraries like angular-auth-oidc-client or keycloak-angular handle a lot of this.
In our apps, the Keycloak adapter refreshes tokens before expiry, and the interceptor just attaches the current token.

Like a kitStatus pipe that turns a status code into a friendly label, or a siteTime pipe that formats a UTC timestamp in the site's time zone. You'd use it as kit.status piped into kitStatus, or created piped into siteTime with the time zone as an argument.

Pipes are pure by default. A pure pipe only re-runs when its input value changes by reference, or its arguments change. That makes them very efficient, much better than calling a method in the template, which runs on every change detection cycle. So pure pipes should be pure functions, no side effects, same output for the same input.

An impure pipe, pure set to false, runs on every change detection cycle. You need it when the output depends on something other than the input reference, like a mutable array that changes internally, or some external state. The async pipe is the famous impure one. Impure pipes have to be really cheap, or they slow the whole page down.
Honestly, a better alternative to an impure pipe is often immutable data, or a computed signal.

Why it's recommended, a few reasons. Subscription management is automatic. It subscribes when the component renders and unsubscribes when the component is destroyed, so no memory leaks from forgotten subscriptions. It works nicely with OnPush, because it marks the component for check whenever a new value comes in, so the view updates even though no input changed. And it pushes you toward a declarative style. The component exposes streams, the template consumes them, no manual subscribe calls copying values into fields.

A few things to watch though. Each async pipe on the same Observable creates a separate subscription. So for an HTTP Observable used in three places, you'd make three HTTP calls. I've seen that in network tabs more than once. The fix is subscribing once with an if block, using the as syntax to alias the value, or sharing the stream with shareReplay. And errors in the stream need catchError in the component, otherwise the subscription just ends.

With signals, toSignal plays a similar role. It converts the Observable to a signal once, and the template reads it without a pipe. In newer code I often go that way, but the async pipe is still a perfectly good pattern, especially in existing RxJS-heavy apps like our older Angular sub-apps.

Better options are the child component's inputs, CSS custom properties, which pass through encapsulation, or the library's theming APIs.

In a big app, I keep component styles small, use a shared design system for consistency, and rely on CSS variables for theming. We keep the Angular sub-apps visually consistent with the React shell through shared design tokens.

p17-281.q: So NgRx is basically a Redux-style state management library for Angular, built on RxJS.
p17-281.k: ngrx, ngrx store, ngrx effects, ngrx selectors, redux in angular, ngrx actions reducers
x: So NgRx is basically a Redux-style state management library for Angular, built on RxJS.

The store holds the application state as one immutable object tree. Components never change it directly. Instead they dispatch actions, which are plain objects describing events, like "Shipments Page Opened" or "Shipment Cancelled", created with createAction or grouped with createActionGroup.

Reducers are pure functions. They take the current state and an action and return a new state, built with createReducer and on handlers. No side effects in there, so state changes are predictable and easy to test.

Selectors read and derive data from the store, created with createSelector. They're memoised, so derived values, like pending shipments for the selected site, only get recalculated when their inputs change. Components use store.select, or selectSignal to get a signal.

Effects handle side effects, like API calls. An effect listens for specific actions, calls a service, and dispatches a success or failure action with the result, usually with switchMap or exhaustMap and catchError. Then the reducers update state from those actions.
Redux DevTools shows every action and state change, with time-travel debugging, which honestly helps a lot when debugging.

The downside is boilerplate and indirection. For simple apps or local component state, it's overkill, and services with signals are enough. It pays off in big apps with lots of shared state and complex async flows, with several developers who need consistent patterns.

And withHooks runs logic on init and destroy. There are reusable features too, like withEntities for collections with ids, and community features for devtools and request status.
The store is an injectable service, so you can provide it at root for global state, or at component level for local, feature-specific state. I like that flexibility.

Compared with the classic NgRx store, there are no separate actions, reducers and effects files, so way less boilerplate. Components just call methods directly. It's signal-based, so it works naturally with OnPush, zoneless change detection and signal inputs. And it's more modular, stores per feature rather than one big global tree. What you lose is some of the strict event-driven traceability that actions give you, though NgRx has added an events plugin for people who want that back.
For new Angular apps, I'd start with SignalStore or simple signal-based services, and only use the classic store where the Redux pattern clearly adds value.

p17-283.q: In RxJS, when an Observable errors, the stream terminates. No more values come through. So in a long-lived stream, like a search box or a polling feed, one single error stops it working until the page is reloaded. That's honestly the most common RxJS bug I see.

x: In RxJS, when an Observable errors, the stream terminates. No more values come through. So in a long-lived stream, like a search box or a polling feed, one single error stops it working until the page is reloaded. That's honestly the most common RxJS bug I see.

catchError intercepts the error and returns a replacement Observable. A fallback value, like an empty array, with of. Or EMPTY to complete quietly. Or rethrow a friendlier error with throwError. The key trick for long-lived streams is putting catchError inside the inner Observable, inside switchMap, not at the end of the outer stream. Then only that one request fails, and the outer stream keeps listening for the next search term.

retry resubscribes to the source after an error, a number of times. Since RxJS 7, retry takes a config with count and a delay function, which allows exponential backoff, like retry with count 3 and a delay based on a timer and the retry count. I only retry for transient errors, network failures or 503, not 400 or 404.
finalize runs when the stream completes, errors or gets unsubscribed, which is useful for turning off a loading spinner.

In Angular, HTTP errors can also be handled centrally in an interceptor, for logging, notifications or redirects on 401, while components handle the errors specific to their screens. That split works well for us.

p17-284.q: So these all combine multiple Observables, but they emit at different times, and honestly that's the whole difference.
p17-284.k: combinelatest vs forkjoin, withlatestfrom, zip rxjs, combine observables, parallel http calls rxjs
x: So these all combine multiple Observables, but they emit at different times, and honestly that's the whole difference.

forkJoin waits until all the sources complete, then emits once with the last value from each. It's like Promise.all. The right choice for running several HTTP calls in parallel and using all the results together, like loading a site, its inventory and its users before showing a page. If any source errors, the whole thing errors. And if any source never completes, forkJoin never emits, so it's not for long-lived streams.

combineLatest emits whenever any source emits, once each source has emitted at least once, giving the latest value from each. It's for combining ongoing streams, like filters. When the status filter, the date range or the search term changes, recalculate with the latest of all three. A common surprise is nothing emits until every source has emitted once, so startWith helps there.

withLatestFrom is driven by one primary stream. When the primary emits, it combines that value with the latest of the others, but the others emitting doesn't trigger anything. Perfect for "when the user clicks save, take the current form value and the selected site".
zip pairs values by index, first with first, second with second, and so on. I rarely need it, mostly when values correspond one to one.
And with signals, computed covers a lot of combineLatest's use cases more simply.

p17-285.q: Let me walk through it. A typeahead calls an API as the user types, so it has to avoid flooding the server and deal with responses arriving out of order.

x: Let me walk through it. A typeahead calls an API as the user types, so it has to avoid flooding the server and deal with responses arriving out of order.
I start with a stream of the input's values, from a reactive form control's valueChanges, or a signal converted with toObservable. Then a pipeline of operators.
debounceTime of about 300 milliseconds waits till the user pauses typing, so we're not calling the API on every keystroke.
map to trim the text, and filter out terms that are too short, like under two characters, maybe returning an empty result for those.
distinctUntilChanged skips the call if the term is the same as last time, like when the user types a letter and deletes it.

switchMap calls the search API, and this is the key one. When a new term arrives, it unsubscribes from the previous request, and Angular's HttpClient cancels it. So a slow response for an old term can never overwrite the results for a newer term. That's the race condition people hit with mergeMap or plain promises.
Inside switchMap, catchError returns an empty result on failure, so one failed request doesn't kill the stream. And I can track loading state with a signal or startWith.
The template shows the results with the async pipe, or a signal from toSignal.
On the server side, the search endpoint should be fast, limited and indexed, because even with debouncing it gets hit a lot. So that's the full picture.

p17-286.q: Okay, a cold Observable starts producing values separately for each subscriber. Angular's HttpClient calls are cold, so each subscription sends a new HTTP request. If a template has two async pipes on the same HTTP Observable, or two components subscribe to the same service method's result, the request goes out twice.
p17-286.k: hot vs cold observable, shareReplay, share rxjs, multicast, duplicate http calls angular, cache http observable
x: Okay, a cold Observable starts producing values separately for each subscriber. Angular's HttpClient calls are cold, so each subscription sends a new HTTP request. If a template has two async pipes on the same HTTP Observable, or two components subscribe to the same service method's result, the request goes out twice.

A hot Observable produces values regardless of subscribers, and all subscribers share the same source. Like DOM events, a WebSocket stream, or a Subject. Late subscribers miss earlier values, unless the stream replays them.

share and shareReplay turn a cold Observable into a shared hot one. share multicasts to all current subscribers through one subscription to the source. shareReplay also replays the last N values to new subscribers. So shareReplay with bufferSize 1 is the common way to cache an HTTP result. The first subscriber triggers the request, and everyone after gets the cached value with no new call.

There are pitfalls though. With the old shareReplay of 1 signature, the source subscription stays alive even when all subscribers leave, which can leak for long-lived sources. Using the config with refCount true unsubscribes when nobody's left. A cached error or stale value stays cached, so you need a way to refresh, like a Subject that triggers reloading. And caching in a root service means the data sticks around for the whole session.
For simple shared state, honestly, a signal or BehaviorSubject in a service is often clearer.

p17-287.q: See, rendering thousands of rows with a simple loop creates thousands of DOM elements and component instances. Initial render gets slow, scrolling gets janky, and change detection gets expensive.
p17-287.k: virtual scroll angular, cdk virtual scroll, large list performance angular, render thousands of rows, infinite scroll angular

The main thing I'd reach for is virtual scrolling. The Angular CDK's virtual scroll viewport, with the cdkVirtualFor directive, only renders the rows visible in the viewport plus a small buffer, and recycles them as the user scrolls. The list can have 50,000 items, but only about 30 are in the DOM. It works best with a fixed row height, set with itemSize. Variable heights are harder. Data grids like AG Grid have virtualisation built in, even for columns.

Then server-side paging or infinite scrolling. Often the user doesn't need all items at once, so loading pages on demand, with filters and search on the server, beats sending everything to the browser.

After that, reduce the work per row. OnPush on row components, a proper track expression in the for block so rows get reused when data refreshes, pure pipes instead of method calls in templates, and no heavy components inside each row. Like rendering a dropdown only when a row is being edited.
You can also use defer for parts of each row that aren't needed immediately.
And I'd measure with Angular DevTools' profiler and the browser's performance panel, to see whether time goes to change detection or DOM rendering.
[Our material forecasting dashboard was the kind of screen where server-side paging and OnPush made the difference.]

The good thing about the built-in approach is performance. Translations are compiled in, so no runtime lookup cost. The bad part is a separate build and deployment per language, usually served under a path like slash fr, and switching language means loading a different version of the app, a full page reload.

Runtime libraries, like Transloco or the older ngx-translate, load translation files at runtime and translate with a pipe or directive. One build serves all languages, and users can switch instantly. You pay a small runtime overhead and lose some compile-time checking. Honestly, a lot of business apps choose this for the flexibility.

Either way, I keep dates and numbers in neutral formats in the data, format them in the UI with the user's locale, think about right-to-left layouts if needed, and avoid concatenating translated fragments. Word order differs between languages, so glued-together sentences come out wrong.

You can read them two ways. The snapshot, like route.snapshot.paramMap.get id, gives the value at the moment the component was created. Fine if the component always gets recreated when the parameter changes. But Angular reuses the component when you navigate from shipments 1 to shipments 2 within the same route, so the snapshot goes stale. I've seen that bug in code reviews. The Observables, paramMap and queryParamMap, emit every time the parameters change, so I combine them with switchMap to load the right data, which also cancels the previous request.

Route parameters, query parameters and resolver data get bound directly to component inputs with the same name. So the component just declares an id input, or a signal input, and reacts to changes. No ActivatedRoute dependency, easier to test and reuse, and it works nicely with computed signals and resource for loading data.
To update query parameters, like when the user changes a filter, I navigate with queryParams and queryParamsHandling set to merge. That keeps the URL shareable and the back button works.

p17-290.q: Right, so with lazy-loaded routes, each feature's code downloads only when the user navigates to it. That keeps the initial bundle small, but the first navigation to a feature waits for its chunk, which feels slow on bad networks.
p17-290.k: preloading strategy, preloadallmodules, custom preloading strategy, lazy loading preloading, quicklink angular
x: Right, so with lazy-loaded routes, each feature's code downloads only when the user navigates to it. That keeps the initial bundle small, but the first navigation to a feature waits for its chunk, which feels slow on bad networks.
Preloading downloads lazy-loaded route chunks in the background after the app has loaded and become interactive. So later navigation is instant, and the initial load stays fast.

Angular has built-in strategies. NoPreloading, the default, only loads on demand. PreloadAllModules preloads every lazy route once the app is stable. I'd say that's simple and fine for small to medium apps, but in big apps it downloads a lot of code that many users never touch, which wastes bandwidth.

A custom preloading strategy gives you more control. You implement PreloadingStrategy and decide per route. Like preloading only routes marked with data preload true, the ones most users visit. Or only routes the current user's role can access. Or skipping preloading on slow connections using the Network Information API. Libraries like ngx-quicklink preload routes whose links are currently visible on screen, which is a smart middle ground.
You configure it with withPreloading in provideRouter for standalone apps.
Defer blocks and canMatch guards complement this. canMatch stops users from even downloading features they're not allowed to use, which I like.

p17-291.q: Actually this error shows up in development mode when a value bound in a template changes after Angular has already checked it in the same change detection cycle. In dev mode, Angular runs an extra verification pass to make sure the view is stable. If a binding's value is different on the second pass, it throws, because the view would be showing inconsistent data.

If a binding's value is different on the second pass, it throws, because the view would be showing inconsistent data.

What usually causes it? A child component, or a lifecycle hook like ngAfterViewInit, changes a property on the parent that the parent's template already rendered. Like a child emitting an event in ngOnInit that sets the parent's title. Or a getter or method in the template that returns a new value every time, like new Date or a new object or array, so the second check sees something different. Or a service shared between parent and child that gets updated during rendering.

The fix is to correct the data flow, not hide the error. Move the logic earlier, into ngOnInit or the constructor, so the value's set before the view is checked. Don't update parent state from a child's lifecycle hooks. Let the parent compute it, or restructure into a shared service or signal that's set before rendering. And make template expressions stable, with computed signals or pure pipes instead of methods that create new objects.
Workarounds like setTimeout or calling detectChanges again do make the error go away. But honestly they hide a design problem and cause an extra render, so they're my last resort.

p17-292.q: Honestly, when an Angular screen feels sluggish, the first thing I want to know is whether the time goes to change detection, rendering, or our own code.
p17-292.k: angular devtools profiler, change detection profiling, slow angular app debug, too many change detection cycles, ng.profiler
x: Honestly, when an Angular screen feels sluggish, the first thing I want to know is whether the time goes to change detection, rendering, or our own code.

Angular DevTools, the browser extension, is my first tool. The component explorer shows the component tree with inputs, outputs and state. The profiler records change detection cycles while I click around. It shows how many cycles ran, what triggered them, and how long each component took. What I usually find is a mousemove or scroll listener, or a setInterval, triggering change detection constantly. Or one expensive component, often with a method call in the template doing heavy work. Or the whole tree getting checked because nothing uses OnPush. Recent versions also show signal graphs and injector trees.
The browser's Performance panel gives the full picture. Scripting versus rendering versus layout, long tasks, memory.

The fixes come from what you find. OnPush on components, so they're only checked when inputs change or events happen inside them. Signals, for more targeted updates. Running noisy events outside the Angular zone with runOutsideAngular, or going zoneless. Pure pipes or computed signals instead of template methods. Proper tracking in for loops. And defer or virtual scrolling for heavy parts.
And I always measure before and after. Guesses about performance are wrong surprisingly often, I've been wrong myself plenty of times.

For us, smaller bundles matter for users on slow hospital or clinic networks, which is a real thing for site users.

So they're useful in a few situations. Gradual migration, embedding new Angular components into a legacy app without converting the whole page. Sharing widgets across teams using different frameworks. And micro-frontends, where each team builds and deploys its own piece of the UI independently and a shell composes them.

The challenges are real though. Each element bundle includes Angular's runtime unless you share it carefully, so several separately built elements can mean duplicate framework code and bigger downloads. Global styles and Shadow DOM interactions need thought. Communication between elements should go through attributes, events, or a small shared event bus, not shared internal state. In our case, actually, the React shell uses npm feature packages instead of runtime micro-frontends.

p17-295.q: So both are methods on ChangeDetectorRef, and you use them when Angular doesn't automatically notice a change, usually with OnPush components.

x: So both are methods on ChangeDetectorRef, and you use them when Angular doesn't automatically notice a change, usually with OnPush components.

markForCheck marks the current component and all its ancestors up to the root as dirty, so they get checked in the next change detection cycle. It doesn't run change detection right away. It's the right tool when an OnPush component's state changed because of something Angular didn't see, like a value pushed from a service subscription, or a callback from a third-party library. The async pipe calls markForCheck internally, that's why it works with OnPush.

detectChanges runs change detection immediately and synchronously, but only for this component and its children. Useful when you need the view updated right now, like before measuring the DOM. Or for a component you've detached from the change detection tree with detach, and then update manually for performance, like something that redraws only on a timer. Calling it at the wrong moment, like during another change detection cycle, can cause errors.
There's also checkNoChanges, used in dev mode for verification.

In modern Angular with signals, you need these much less. When a signal read in a template changes, Angular marks the component for check automatically. Honestly, when I find myself calling them a lot, it usually means the state should be in signals, or Observables with the async pipe.

p17-296.q: I split components into two kinds, and it makes features much easier to test, reuse and change.
p17-296.k: smart vs dumb components, container presentational, angular component design, feature structure angular, reusable components angular
x: I split components into two kinds, and it makes features much easier to test, reuse and change.

Smart components, or containers, know about the application. They inject services or stores, load data, handle routing parameters, call APIs, and decide what happens on user actions. Usually they map to a page or a major section, like ShipmentListPage. Their templates mostly compose presentational components and pass data down.

Presentational components, the dumb ones, only know their inputs and outputs. They get data through inputs, render it, and emit events through outputs when the user does something. Like a ShipmentTable emitting a cancelClicked event with the shipment id. No services, no HTTP, no store. So they're easy to reuse in different places, easy to test with simple inputs, and perfect for OnPush, since they only change when inputs change.

A feature folder usually has the routes, the page-level smart components, the presentational components, the feature's data service or store, and its models. Shared generic UI components, buttons, dialogs, form fields, live in a shared library or the design system.

I don't follow it dogmatically though. A small component with one simple service call doesn't need splitting. But for anything substantial, keeping data logic separate from display pays off, especially when the same table or form shows up in several places. In my project, that's saved us a lot of duplicate code.

p17-297.q: See, by default when the user navigates away from a route, Angular destroys its component, and when they come back, it creates a new one. Any state in there, the scroll position, filters, an expanded row, data already loaded, is gone, and the data gets fetched again.

A RouteReuseStrategy lets you customise this. It's a class with methods the router calls during navigation. shouldDetach decides whether to keep a route's component when leaving. store saves the detached component tree. shouldAttach and retrieve decide whether to restore a stored component when coming back. And shouldReuseRoute decides whether to reuse the current component when navigating between two URLs that match the same route config.

A common use is a list-detail flow. The user filters a long list, opens a detail page, and comes back expecting the list exactly as they left it. By detaching and storing the list route, it reappears instantly with its state. Another is a tabbed interface where each tab is a route.

There are pitfalls. Stored components stay in memory with their subscriptions active, so you have to limit what's stored and clear it, like on logout. And lifecycle hooks like ngOnInit don't run again on reattach, so components may need to refresh data explicitly.
Honestly, a simpler solution is often keeping filter state in the URL's query parameters, or in a service or store, so a brand new component can just restore it.

Inside, you can inject ElementRef to get the host element, and Renderer2 to change it in a platform-safe way, which also works with server-side rendering.

HostListener subscribes to events on the host element, or globally on the window or document. Like a directive that listens for paste events on an input and strips spaces from pasted kit numbers. Or one that closes a dropdown on a document click outside it.
HostBinding binds a property of the host element to a directive property. Like adding a CSS class, class.overdue, when an input date is in the past, or setting attr.aria-label.

In modern Angular though, the recommended way is the host property in the Directive decorator. You map class.overdue to isOverdue, and click to onClick with the event, instead of using the decorators. That keeps all host bindings in one place and works well with signal inputs.
Directive composition, with hostDirectives, lets a component include existing directives on its own host, so behaviours like focus handling or tooltips can be reused.

Directives are a great way to package small behaviours once, autofocus, input masks, permission checks, click-outside detection, and use them everywhere. I've got a few of those I reuse all the time, that's how I like to package them.

p17-299.q: So this is a classic bug. A component fetches data in useEffect based on a prop, like the selected site id. The user switches from site A to site B quickly. Both requests are in flight, and if A's response comes back after B's, the component shows site A's data while site B is selected.

The fix is the effect's cleanup function. React runs the cleanup before running the effect again, and when the component unmounts. And you can use it two ways.

One is an ignore flag. Inside the effect, declare let ignore equals false, and in the cleanup, set ignore to true. When the response arrives, only update state if ignore is still false. The stale response just gets thrown away.

The other is AbortController, which I prefer. Create a controller in the effect, pass controller.signal to fetch, or to axios through its signal option, and call abort in the cleanup. Now the outdated request actually gets cancelled, which saves bandwidth, and the aborted promise rejects with an AbortError, which I ignore instead of showing as an error.
The cleanup also stops you setting state after unmount.

Honestly though, in real apps I avoid hand-written fetching in effects. Libraries like TanStack Query or RTK Query handle caching, deduplication, race conditions, retries and loading states for you, keyed by the query parameters. Effects are better kept for syncing with external systems.

The point is to surface bugs early. React is moving towards features, like keeping state when components are hidden and shown again, where components might be mounted and unmounted multiple times. If an effect doesn't clean up properly, like a subscription that isn't removed, a timer that isn't cleared, or an event listener added twice, the double run exposes it as duplicate behaviour. And double rendering exposes impure render functions with side effects.

So the right response isn't to disable StrictMode. Honestly, I've seen people do that. The right thing is making effects resilient. Every effect that sets something up should return a cleanup that tears it down, and the effect should work correctly when run twice. For data fetching, the abort or ignore pattern handles it, and the second request is the one that counts. For stuff that truly has to happen once per app, like initialising analytics, I do it outside components, at module level, or guard it with a ref.
The duplicate API call in development looks scary in the network tab, but it's expected, and libraries like TanStack Query deduplicate it anyway.
