It's basically the automatic rollback answer for Kubernetes. Health gets judged by real user signals, not by humans staring at dashboards.

p17-532.q: Okay, so trunk-based development means everyone integrates into one main branch at least daily, through short-lived branches that live a day or two, instead of long-running feature or develop branches that merge weeks later with painful conflicts.
p17-532.k: trunk based development, short lived branches, main branch always releasable, trunk based vs gitflow, continuous integration practice
x: Okay, so trunk-based development means everyone integrates into one main branch at least daily, through short-lived branches that live a day or two, instead of long-running feature or develop branches that merge weeks later with painful conflicts.
Making it work needs a few supporting habits.
Small changes. A big feature gets split into small, safe pull requests that each keep main working, like adding the database column first, then the API, then the UI.
Feature flags. Unfinished work merges behind a flag that's off in production, so code gets integrated before the feature is ready. Release becomes a flag switch, not a merge.
Fast, reliable CI. Every pull request runs build, unit tests and static checks in about ten minutes. Branch policies require a passing build and a review before merging.
Keep main releasable. If main breaks, fixing it is the team's top priority, and reverting is a normal, blame-free thing to do.
Release branches only when needed, cut from main for a release that needs stabilisation or hotfixes, and fixes go to main first, then get cherry-picked.

What you get is fewer merge conflicts, earlier feedback, and a codebase that's always close to shippable. In a regulated environment, the validated release is still a specific, tagged build from main, so traceability is kept. That was the main worry people had when I've seen teams move to it.

p17-533.q: So feature flags let you change behaviour at runtime without deploying, but they turn into technical debt if nobody manages them. I think about them by type.
p17-533.k: feature flags, feature toggles, release toggle, flag cleanup, feature management dotnet, kill switch
x: So feature flags let you change behaviour at runtime without deploying, but they turn into technical debt if nobody manages them. I think about them by type.

Release flags hide unfinished or new features until they're ready. They should be short-lived, removed within a few weeks of full rollout. Ops flags or kill switches let you turn off an expensive or risky path during an incident, like disabling a heavy export, and these can live longer. Experiment flags drive A/B tests. Permission flags turn on features for specific customers or plans, which is really configuration and belongs in the product's settings model.

In .NET, Microsoft.FeatureManagement gives you IFeatureManager and attributes for controllers, with filters for percentage rollout, user or group targeting, and time windows. Flags can come from configuration, Azure App Configuration, or a dedicated service like LaunchDarkly or Unleash, and OpenFeature gives a vendor-neutral API.

My rules for keeping it clean. Every flag has an owner and an expiry date, recorded when it's created. Check the flag in one place, near the edge, instead of scattering checks across the code. Test both states. Default to the safe value if the flag service is unreachable. And add a ticket to remove the flag and the dead code once rollout's done.
In a regulated product, a flag that changes validated behaviour is itself a configuration change, so its state per environment has to be controlled and recorded.

p17-534.q: See, semantic versioning is MAJOR dot MINOR dot PATCH. Bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new backward-compatible features, PATCH for backward-compatible fixes. Pre-release labels, like 2.1.0-beta.3, mark builds that aren't final. For libraries and packages it's essential, because consumers rely on it to know if an upgrade is safe.
p17-534.k: semantic versioning, semver, gitversion, conventional commits, automatic version number, build number strategy
x: See, semantic versioning is MAJOR dot MINOR dot PATCH. Bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new backward-compatible features, PATCH for backward-compatible fixes. Pre-release labels, like 2.1.0-beta.3, mark builds that aren't final. For libraries and packages it's essential, because consumers rely on it to know if an upgrade is safe.
Editing version numbers by hand doesn't scale, so I automate it.

GitVersion calculates the version from Git history, tags, branch names and commit messages. A tag v1.4.0 on main marks the release, builds after it become 1.4.1-something or 1.5.0 depending on configuration, and feature branches get pre-release labels.

Conventional commits put intent in commit messages, like feat colon for a feature, fix colon for a fix, and feat with an exclamation mark or BREAKING CHANGE for breaking changes. Tools like semantic-release or release-please read them, bump the version, create the tag and generate a changelog. That works really well for npm packages.

The build then stamps the version everywhere. Assembly versions in .NET through the Version property, package versions, container image tags, and the build name in the pipeline, so the running app can show its version on a health or about endpoint. That's saved us a lot of "which version is in prod" conversations.
For deployable services, I also add the commit SHA in the build metadata, like 1.4.2 plus abc1234, so any running instance traces back to its exact source.

p17-535.q: Honestly when lots of services have similar pipelines, copying YAML into each repo leads to drift and painful updates. Azure Pipelines templates fix that.
p17-535.k: azure pipelines templates, yaml templates, extends template, template parameters, reusable pipeline, pipeline standardization
x: Honestly when lots of services have similar pipelines, copying YAML into each repo leads to drift and painful updates. Azure Pipelines templates fix that.

You can template at a few levels. Step templates hold a sequence of steps, like restore, build, test and publish coverage for a .NET project. Job and stage templates hold whole jobs or stages, like a standard deploy stage with approvals and smoke tests. Variable templates hold shared variables. Templates take typed parameters, like the project path, .NET version or environment name, with defaults and allowed values, and can use template expressions with each loops and conditions, evaluated at compile time.

Templates usually live in a central repository, referenced with a resources repositories block and pinned to a tag or branch, so a change to the shared template is versioned and teams can adopt it deliberately.

Extends templates go further. The pipeline in each repo just extends a central template and passes parameters, and the template controls the overall structure. Combine that with a required template check on protected resources, like production environments or service connections, and you enforce that every pipeline deploying to production runs the mandatory security scans and approvals. That's a strong governance tool.

What I do is keep templates simple and well documented, avoid deep nesting, and test template changes on a sample pipeline before releasing a new version. Otherwise one bad change breaks every team at once.

p17-536.q: Okay, so an Azure Pipelines YAML pipeline has a pretty clear hierarchy.
p17-536.k: azure pipelines stages jobs steps, deployment job, environments azure devops, pipeline structure, run once rolling canary strategy
x: Okay, so an Azure Pipelines YAML pipeline has a pretty clear hierarchy.

Stages are the big phases, like Build, Deploy to Dev, Deploy to QA and Deploy to Production. They run sequentially by default, can depend on each other with dependsOn, and can have conditions, like only deploying from main. Approvals and checks are attached at the environment level, so a stage waits until they pass.
Jobs run inside stages. Each job runs on one agent, from a pool, and jobs in a stage can run in parallel. A job can be a normal job or a deployment job.
Steps are the individual tasks or scripts inside a job, like checking out code, running dotnet build, publishing artifacts, or running a PowerShell script.

Deployment jobs are special jobs for releases. They target an environment, which records deployment history, which build went to which environment and when. They support strategies, runOnce, rolling across virtual machines in the environment, and canary with increments. Each strategy has lifecycle hooks, like preDeploy, deploy, routeTraffic, postRouteTraffic, and on failure or success, so you can run smoke tests after routing traffic and roll back on failure.
Artifacts are published in the build stage and downloaded automatically in deployment jobs, so the exact same build output moves through every stage.
On our on-premise Azure DevOps Server, the older classic release pipelines are still used for some apps, but YAML pipelines with environments give us code review and history for pipeline changes.

p17-537.q: So build once, deploy many means the pipeline compiles and packages the app one time, and that exact artifact, the same zip, package or container image, gets deployed to dev, test, UAT and production. Only configuration differs per environment.
p17-537.k: build once deploy many, artifact promotion, immutable artifact, rebuild per environment problem, environment specific config
x: So build once, deploy many means the pipeline compiles and packages the app one time, and that exact artifact, the same zip, package or container image, gets deployed to dev, test, UAT and production. Only configuration differs per environment.

Why it matters. If you rebuild for each environment, you're not deploying what you tested. A different build agent, an updated base image, a newer dependency pulled in by a floating version, or a different commit can sneak in. Then a bug shows up in production that never existed in test, and you can't easily tell why.

With a single artifact, testing in each environment adds confidence to the same binary. It's faster, because the build happens once. And it's traceable, the artifact has a version and a hash, linked to a commit and a build, and each deployment records which artifact went where.

To make it work, configuration has to live outside the artifact. Environment variables, appsettings per environment loaded at runtime, a configuration service, or secrets managers, not build-time constants or per-environment build flags. Front ends need the same idea, loading a runtime config file instead of baking API URLs into the bundle.

In a validated GxP environment, this is close to mandatory, because the validated package has to be provably identical to what goes into production. In our team we keep the build artifact, its version and its approvals linked in Azure DevOps for exactly that reason.

p17-538.q: Actually both are mature CI/CD systems with YAML pipelines, hosted and self-hosted runners, and support for any language. The differences are mostly in ecosystem and enterprise features.
p17-538.k: github actions vs azure pipelines, github actions vs azure devops, ci cd tool comparison, workflows vs pipelines
x: Actually both are mature CI/CD systems with YAML pipelines, hosted and self-hosted runners, and support for any language. The differences are mostly in ecosystem and enterprise features.

GitHub Actions is built into GitHub. Workflows trigger on almost any repository event, pushes, pull requests, issues, releases, schedules or manual dispatch. Its marketplace has a huge number of actions. Reusable workflows and composite actions share logic. Environments have protection rules and secrets, and OIDC federation to AWS, Azure and GCP is straightforward. It ties in naturally with GitHub's security features, like Dependabot, code scanning and secret scanning. It's the default for open source and a lot of new projects.

Azure Pipelines is part of Azure DevOps, alongside Boards, Repos, Test Plans and Artifacts. It works with GitHub repos too. It's strong for enterprises with complex release processes. Multi-stage pipelines, environments with approvals, checks like business hours, required templates and exclusive locks, deep traceability from work items to commits to builds to deployments, classic release pipelines for older setups, and an on-premise version, Azure DevOps Server, which matters for organisations that can't use cloud services.

The choice usually follows where the code and work tracking live. In our case, the on-premise platform uses Azure DevOps Server, so Azure Pipelines is natural there, while newer cloud-based work can use either. The concepts, stages, jobs, runners, environments and secrets, transfer pretty easily between them.

p17-539.q: Okay, storing an AWS access key and secret as a pipeline secret is common but risky. The keys are long-lived, often over-privileged, hard to rotate, and if leaked, they work from anywhere. The better way is OpenID Connect federation.
p17-539.k: oidc github actions aws, assume role with web identity, pipeline aws credentials, no access keys ci, aws federation ci
x: Okay, storing an AWS access key and secret as a pipeline secret is common but risky. The keys are long-lived, often over-privileged, hard to rotate, and if leaked, they work from anywhere. The better way is OpenID Connect federation.

How it works with GitHub Actions. In the AWS account, I create an IAM OIDC identity provider for GitHub's token issuer, and an IAM role whose trust policy allows the STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity action from that provider, with conditions on the token's claims. The audience has to be sts.amazonaws.com, and the subject has to match a specific repository and branch or environment, like the shipments-api repo in our org with the production environment. In the workflow, I grant the id-token write permission and use the configure-aws-credentials action with the role ARN. Each run gets temporary credentials, valid for about an hour, and nothing's stored.
Azure Pipelines and GitLab support the same pattern, and so does Azure with federated credentials.

My rules here, separate roles per environment and per purpose, like a deploy role that can update ECS services and push to ECR, and a read-only plan role for Terraform pull requests. Least-privilege policies. Tight subject conditions, never a wildcard on the whole organisation. And CloudTrail monitoring of role usage.

For our on-premise Azure DevOps Server, federation depends on network and version support, so the same least-privilege idea applies with whatever mechanism is available, with credentials kept only in a protected library and rotated.

p17-540.q: So supply chain attacks go after the path from source code to production rather than the app itself. A compromised dependency, a tampered build agent, or a malicious package with the same name as an internal one. So I protect each step.
p17-540.k: software supply chain security, sbom, slsa, sign artifacts, pipeline security, dependency confusion
x: So supply chain attacks go after the path from source code to production rather than the app itself. A compromised dependency, a tampered build agent, or a malicious package with the same name as an internal one. So I protect each step.
Source. Branch protection with required reviews, signed commits where practical, and secret scanning to stop credentials getting committed.

Dependencies. Lock files and pinned versions, so builds are reproducible. Package source mapping in NuGet and scoped registries in npm, so internal package names can only come from the internal feed, which prevents dependency confusion. Vulnerability scanning with dotnet list package with the vulnerable flag, npm audit, Dependabot or a commercial scanner. And a review process for adding new dependencies.

Build. Pipelines defined as code and reviewed. Minimal permissions for the pipeline's token. Pinned versions of actions or tasks, ideally by commit SHA. Ephemeral, clean build agents. And no secrets available to builds from untrusted pull requests.

Artifacts. Generate a software bill of materials, an SBOM in CycloneDX or SPDX format, so we know exactly what's inside each release and can quickly answer "are we affected?" when a new vulnerability drops. Sign artifacts and images, with tools like Sigstore Cosign or Notation, and produce provenance attestations following SLSA. Verify signatures at deployment time.
Deployment. Only signed, scanned artifacts from the trusted pipeline can reach production. Honestly, the SBOM part is what pays off fastest when the next big CVE hits.

p17-541.q: Okay, outdated dependencies pile up security vulnerabilities and make future upgrades painful, because jumping several major versions at once is way harder than small, regular steps. Automating update pull requests keeps it manageable.
p17-541.k: dependabot, renovate, dependency updates, outdated packages, automated dependency pull requests, nuget updates
x: Okay, outdated dependencies pile up security vulnerabilities and make future upgrades painful, because jumping several major versions at once is way harder than small, regular steps. Automating update pull requests keeps it manageable.

Dependabot, built into GitHub, and Renovate, which works with GitHub, Azure DevOps, GitLab and others, scan manifests, like csproj files, Directory.Packages.props, package.json, Dockerfiles and pipeline files, and open pull requests to update versions. Security updates are raised as soon as a vulnerable version is known.
To make it workable and not just noise.
Group related updates, like all Microsoft.Extensions packages or all testing packages, into one pull request, and schedule non-security updates weekly.
Automerge low-risk updates, like patch versions of dev dependencies, when the pipeline passes. That depends on a good test suite, which is the real safety net.
Treat major versions separately, read the release notes and plan the changes, since they're often breaking.
Use central package management in .NET, so versions are defined in one place across a solution.
Keep base images current too, because OS packages in images are a big source of vulnerabilities.

The team also needs a habit, someone reviews update pull requests every week, so they don't turn into ignored noise. In a regulated product, dependency updates still go through the normal validated release process, but small regular updates make that process way lighter.

p17-542.q: See, the situation is production is on version 3.4, main already has weeks of changes for 3.5 that aren't ready, and a critical bug has to be fixed in production today.
p17-542.k: hotfix process, hotfix branch, cherry pick hotfix, emergency fix production, patch release, release branch hotfix
x: See, the situation is production is on version 3.4, main already has weeks of changes for 3.5 that aren't ready, and a critical bug has to be fixed in production today.
Here's what I'd do.
Branch from what's in production, not from main. That's the release branch or the tag for 3.4, like release slash 3.4. Create a hotfix branch from it.
Make the smallest possible fix, with a test that reproduces the bug first. Keep it focused, no refactoring or extra changes sneaking in.

Run it through the pipeline like any release. Build, automated tests, review and approvals. Even in an emergency, I don't skip the review or the regression tests that matter. In a regulated environment, there's often an expedited change process, but it still records the risk assessment, testing evidence and approvals.
Release it as 3.4.1, a new patch version, and deploy with the normal deployment pipeline, so the deployment itself is a known, tested process.

Bring the fix back to main. Merge or cherry-pick it into main, and into any other active release branches, so 3.5 doesn't bring the bug back. Ideally the fix is developed on main first and cherry-picked to the release branch, so it's never forgotten, but in urgent cases you can reverse the order.
Afterwards, a short review. Why did the bug escape, and what test or check would have caught it. That's the part people skip, and it's the part that actually prevents the next one.

p17-543.q: Actually a slow pipeline costs focus and pushes people to batch changes, which is the opposite of what we want. My target for pull request validation is around ten minutes. I start by measuring where the time goes, using the pipeline's step timings over several runs, then go after the biggest items.
p17-543.k: slow ci pipeline, speed up build, pipeline caching, parallel tests, ci performance, incremental build
x: Actually a slow pipeline costs focus and pushes people to batch changes, which is the opposite of what we want. My target for pull request validation is around ten minutes. I start by measuring where the time goes, using the pipeline's step timings over several runs, then go after the biggest items.

Caching. Restore NuGet and npm packages from a pipeline cache keyed on the lock file hash, instead of downloading everything every time. For Docker, reuse layer caches through BuildKit and a registry cache.
Parallelism. Split independent work into parallel jobs, like backend build and tests, front-end build and tests, and static analysis. Split large test suites across agents.

Do less work. Path filters, so front-end changes don't trigger the backend pipeline in a monorepo. Only build affected projects with tools like Nx for front ends. And move slow, broad tests, like full end-to-end suites or long performance tests, to a nightly or post-merge pipeline, keeping a fast smoke set on pull requests.

Faster tests. Find the slowest ones. Replace sleeps with proper waits. Share expensive fixtures like Testcontainers databases across a test class or collection. And run tests in parallel where they're isolated.
Better agents. More CPU, or self-hosted agents with warm caches, if the hosted agents are the bottleneck.
Then track pipeline duration as a metric, so it doesn't slowly creep back up. Trust me, it always creeps.

p17-544.q: Okay, both work. The choice just changes how builds, versioning and ownership get handled.
p17-544.k: monorepo vs polyrepo, monorepo ci, path filters pipeline, nx affected, repository strategy microservices
x: Okay, both work. The choice just changes how builds, versioning and ownership get handled.

In a monorepo, many services and packages live in one repository. The good side, atomic changes across services and shared libraries in a single pull request, one place to search, consistent tooling and standards, and easy refactoring. The CI/CD challenge is you don't want every commit to build and deploy everything, so pipelines need path filters or affected-project detection, like Nx affected for JavaScript, or a build graph tool. Ownership has to be explicit, with CODEOWNERS files per folder. Versioning is either one version for all, or independent versions per package with tooling. And the repo can get big, needing shallow clones and sparse checkouts.

With multiple repositories, each service or package has its own repo, pipeline and version. The good side, clear ownership and permissions, independent release cycles, smaller and faster pipelines. The challenges, changes across several repos need coordinated pull requests and releases, shared code becomes versioned packages, which brings dependency update work, and standards drift unless pipeline templates are shared.

What I've seen work is polyrepo for independently deployed services, with shared pipeline templates and packages published to an internal feed. Our React shell with npm feature packages is a good example. Each feature package is versioned and published to the Azure DevOps feed, and the shell consumes specific versions. A monorepo makes sense for tightly coupled front-end packages where changes usually span several of them.

p17-545.q: So protecting main is the simplest, highest-value control in the whole delivery process. Here's what I usually set up.
p17-545.k: branch policies, branch protection rules, required reviewers, pull request validation build, code owners, protect main branch
x: So protecting main is the simplest, highest-value control in the whole delivery process. Here's what I usually set up.
No direct pushes to main. All changes go through pull requests.

A required build validation. The pull request pipeline has to pass, compiling the code, running unit tests and static analysis, before merging. In Azure Repos that's a build validation policy, in GitHub it's a required status check. The build should run against the merged result, not just the branch.

Required reviewers. At least one or two approvals, with code owners automatically added for the areas they own, like the database schema or the security code. Approvals reset when new changes are pushed, so reviewers don't approve one version and then a different one gets merged.
Linked work items, so every change traces to a requirement or bug, which matters a lot in a regulated environment.
All comments resolved before merging.
A merge strategy. Squash merges for a clean history on main, or merge commits if detailed history matters.
Quality gates. A SonarQube or similar gate on new code, like no new critical issues and coverage on new code above a threshold, plus secret scanning and dependency checks.
Exceptions. Admins can bypass in emergencies, but bypasses are logged and reviewed.
These rules are only as good as the checks behind them, so I keep the pull request pipeline fast and reliable. Otherwise people honestly start looking for ways around it.

p17-546.q: See, DORA metrics come from the DevOps Research and Assessment program, and they measure software delivery performance with four key numbers.
p17-546.k: dora metrics, deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, mean time to restore, delivery performance
x: See, DORA metrics come from the DevOps Research and Assessment program, and they measure software delivery performance with four key numbers.

Deployment frequency, how often you deploy to production. Lead time for changes, how long from a commit to that commit running in production. Change failure rate, the percentage of deployments that cause a failure needing a fix, rollback or hotfix. And time to restore service, how long it takes to recover from a failure in production. DORA has since added deployment rework rate and refined the model, but these four are the core.

The research shows the first two, throughput, and the last two, stability, improve together in high-performing teams. Going faster with small changes doesn't have to mean more failures. Usually it means fewer, because each change is smaller and easier to understand.

How I'd use them. Measure from data the tools already have, like pipeline runs, deployment records and incident tickets, not manual reporting. Look at trends for a team over time, not comparisons between teams. Use them to find bottlenecks, like a long lead time caused by waiting days for a manual test environment, or a high failure rate pointing at weak tests.
What to avoid is turning them into targets for individuals, which leads to gaming, like splitting deployments artificially.
In a regulated release process, lead time includes validation and approval steps, so measuring it shows where automating evidence collection would help most.

p17-547.q: Okay, so in our front-end architecture, the React shell consumes feature packages, each built and versioned independently and published to a private npm feed on Azure DevOps. The pipeline for each package goes like this.
p17-547.k: publish npm package azure artifacts, private npm feed, versioning feature packages, npm package pipeline, shell app packages
x: Okay, so in our front-end architecture, the React shell consumes feature packages, each built and versioned independently and published to a private npm feed on Azure DevOps. The pipeline for each package goes like this.

On pull request, install with npm ci using the lock file, run lint, type checks with tsc, unit tests with coverage, and a build with Vite in library mode, producing ES module output and type declarations. The package.json lists React, MUI and Redux Toolkit as peer dependencies, so the shell provides a single copy of each, instead of every package bundling its own.

On merge to main, calculate the version, using conventional commits or a manual version bump reviewed in the pull request, then publish to the feed with an npmrc that authenticates through the pipeline's identity, never a personal token committed to the repo. Pre-release versions, like 2.3.0-beta.1, can be published from feature branches for testing in the shell without affecting stable consumers.
Feed views help promote versions. A package goes to the Prerelease view first, and once it's validated, gets promoted to Release, so consumers only see approved versions.

In the shell, versions are pinned exactly, and upgrading a feature package is a reviewed change with its own release notes. That gives us traceability, for any shell release we know exactly which version of each feature it had.
And changelogs per package make it clear what each version changes.

p17-548.q: So SSDT database projects keep the database schema as code. Tables, views, stored procedures and functions as .sql files in a project, compiled into a dacpac, which is a package describing the desired schema.
p17-548.k: ssdt dacpac deployment, sqlpackage publish, database project pipeline, schema drift sql server, dacpac pipeline
x: So SSDT database projects keep the database schema as code. Tables, views, stored procedures and functions as .sql files in a project, compiled into a dacpac, which is a package describing the desired schema.
In the build stage, the pipeline builds the database project, which validates references and syntax, and publishes the dacpac as an artifact, alongside the app artifacts, with the same version.

In the deployment stage, SqlPackage compares the dacpac with the target database and generates a change script to bring it to the desired state. What I do is generate the script first, with the Script action, publish it as an artifact and review it for production, especially in a regulated environment, instead of blindly applying it. Then apply with Publish, or by running the reviewed script.

Publish profiles control the dangerous behaviour. BlockOnPossibleDataLoss stays true, so a change that would drop a column with data fails instead of losing data. DropObjectsNotInSource is used carefully. Pre- and post-deployment scripts handle data changes, like seeding reference data, written to be idempotent.

Since our platform has a database per study plus a master database, the same dacpac gets applied to many databases. So the deployment loops over the target list, records each result, and stops or continues according to a clear rule when one database fails.
Drift reports catch changes made directly in production outside the process, which should then either be reverted or brought into source control.

p17-549.q: Actually for apps hosted on IIS, which is how our on-premise platform runs, deployments usually use Azure DevOps deployment groups or environments with VM resources, where an agent on each server runs the deployment steps.
p17-549.k: deploy to iis pipeline, web deploy, app_offline, iis deployment azure devops, zero downtime iis, deployment group iis
x: Actually for apps hosted on IIS, which is how our on-premise platform runs, deployments usually use Azure DevOps deployment groups or environments with VM resources, where an agent on each server runs the deployment steps.

The basic steps. Download the build artifact. Stop the site or drop app_offline.htm in place, which tells the ASP.NET Core Module or ASP.NET to stop the app and serve a maintenance page, releasing file locks. Copy the new files with Web Deploy, msdeploy, or a robocopy-style file copy. Apply configuration transforms or environment-specific settings. Start the app pool or remove app_offline. Then warm the site with a request and run smoke tests.

To get close to zero downtime with multiple servers behind a load balancer, I deploy one server or a batch at a time. Take it out of the load balancer pool, or let health checks drain it, deploy, warm up, verify, and put it back, then move to the next. The rolling strategy in deployment jobs supports this with a max number of targets in parallel.
For a single server, a blue-green style setup with two IIS sites or folders and a switch in the binding or reverse proxy, like ARR or URL Rewrite, lets you switch instantly and switch back.

Details that matter, the Application Initialization module to preload the app, consistent versions across all nodes, verified after deployment, and keeping the previous version's folder for quick rollback. That last one has saved us more than once.

p17-550.q: Okay, the goal is one build artifact and different configuration per environment, applied at deployment or runtime, never by rebuilding.
p17-550.k: web.config transformation, appsettings environment, configuration per environment, parameters.xml, environment variables dotnet config
x: Okay, the goal is one build artifact and different configuration per environment, applied at deployment or runtime, never by rebuilding.

For .NET Framework apps, configuration lives in web.config. Traditionally, build configurations had transforms, like Web.Release.config, applied at build time, which ties configuration to the build. Better options for build once, deploy many. Apply transforms at deployment time, which Azure DevOps IIS deployment tasks support with environment-named transform files. Use token replacement, where the web.config has placeholders, like DbServer wrapped in hash and curly brace markers, replaced from pipeline variables or variable groups during deployment. Or Web Deploy parameters.xml, which declares parameters that get values per environment. Since .NET Framework 4.7.1, configuration builders can also pull values from environment variables or a secrets store at runtime.

For modern .NET, configuration is layered at runtime. appsettings.json, then appsettings dot environment name dot json, then environment variables, then sources like Key Vault, App Configuration or Parameter Store, with later sources overriding earlier ones. The ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT or DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT variable picks the environment. Nested keys map to environment variables with double underscores, like ConnectionStrings double underscore Default.
Secrets never go in config files in the repo. They come from pipeline secret variables or secrets managers.

I also make the app validate its configuration at startup, with options validation, so a missing or wrong setting fails the deployment right away instead of failing later on the first request. I learned that one the hard way.

p17-551.q: So front-end frameworks push you towards build-time configuration. Vite injects import.meta.env values, Create React App had process.env, and Angular has environment files picked by build configuration. The values get baked into the JavaScript bundle. That means a separate build per environment, which breaks build once, deploy many, and in a regulated setting means the tested bundle isn't the one that goes to production.
p17-551.k: spa runtime configuration, react environment variables build time, angular environment per deployment, config.json spa, build once spa
x: So front-end frameworks push you towards build-time configuration. Vite injects import.meta.env values, Create React App had process.env, and Angular has environment files picked by build configuration. The values get baked into the JavaScript bundle. That means a separate build per environment, which breaks build once, deploy many, and in a regulated setting means the tested bundle isn't the one that goes to production.

The usual fix is runtime configuration. The app ships with a small config file, like a config.json at the site root or an env-config.js, that's not part of the bundle. At deployment, the pipeline writes the environment's values into that file, like the API base URL, the identity provider authority and client id, feature flags and the telemetry key. At startup, the app fetches the file before rendering, or index.html loads env-config.js, which sets a global object.

In Angular, an APP_INITIALIZER, or provideAppInitializer in newer versions, can load the config before the app bootstraps, and a config service exposes it. In React, the root component waits for the config before rendering the router.
For containers, the entrypoint can generate the file from environment variables at startup.

A few things matter. The config file must not be cached aggressively, or users get stale values after a change, so it gets no-cache headers. It must contain no secrets, since everything in a browser is public. And the app should fail clearly if the config is missing, not half-load. People miss that caching one a lot.

p17-552.q: Okay, so with a database per study, a schema change isn't one deployment, it's hundreds. Doing that reliably needs proper orchestration.
p17-552.k: deploy to many databases, multi tenant database migration, database per tenant deployment, schema rollout many databases, migration orchestration
x: Okay, so with a database per study, a schema change isn't one deployment, it's hundreds. Doing that reliably needs proper orchestration.

The change itself has to be backward compatible to begin with, because databases get updated over minutes or hours, and the app has to work with both old and new schemas during that time. Expand and contract again. Add new structures first, and remove old ones only in a later release once every database is updated.

Then the rollout process. Keep a registry of all target databases, from the master database, with each one's current schema version, recorded in a version table inside each database. Run the migration in waves. Internal test databases first, then a small canary group of production databases, then the rest in batches with limited parallelism, so the database server doesn't get overloaded. Each run is idempotent and records success or failure per database, with the script version and timestamps, which also gives you the audit evidence a regulated environment needs.

Failure handling. A failure in one database must not leave it half-migrated, so each database's change runs in a transaction where possible, or in carefully ordered idempotent steps. Failed databases get reported and retried after investigation, without blocking the others, unless the failure looks systemic, and then the whole rollout halts.
Long-running changes, like adding an index to a huge table, get scheduled for quiet periods per region, with online index operations where available.
And honestly, a dashboard showing the version of every database makes it obvious when something's behind.

p17-553.q: See, when a release causes problems, the decision is about restoring service fastest with the least risk. It's not about pride.
p17-553.k: rollback vs roll forward, fix forward, release went wrong decision, revert deployment, incident release decision
x: See, when a release causes problems, the decision is about restoring service fastest with the least risk. It's not about pride.

I lean towards rolling back when the previous version is known good and rollback is cheap and safe. Stateless services, the artifact still available, no irreversible database changes, and the impact is serious. Rolling back is usually a pipeline run or a traffic switch, and it gets you back to a known state while you investigate calmly. Feature flags are even faster, just switch off the new feature without redeploying.

I lean towards rolling forward, deploying a quick fix, when rollback isn't safe or possible. Like the release included database changes the old version can't handle, data's already been written in the new format, external partners have already integrated with a new API, or the fix is tiny, well understood and can go through the pipeline quickly. Rolling forward under pressure is risky though, so the fix still goes through tests and review.

Preparation makes all this easier. Backward-compatible database changes keep rollback possible. Every release has a documented rollback plan before it goes out. Deployments are automated, so rolling back isn't a manual scramble. And monitoring with clear signals, like error rate and key business events, tells you quickly if the action actually worked.
In a regulated environment, either action is a controlled change, so the decision, approvals and verification get recorded in the incident and change records.

p17-554.q: So in regulated companies, production changes often need approval from a change advisory board, a CAB. A heavyweight CAB meeting for every change slows delivery, pushes people towards big risky batches, and research shows external approval boards don't actually reduce failure rates. So the goal is to keep the control but make it lighter and smarter.
p17-554.k: change advisory board, cab approval, change management itil, standard change, regulated release approvals, change request
x: So in regulated companies, production changes often need approval from a change advisory board, a CAB. A heavyweight CAB meeting for every change slows delivery, pushes people towards big risky batches, and research shows external approval boards don't actually reduce failure rates. So the goal is to keep the control but make it lighter and smarter.
What's helped, in my experience.

Classify changes. Standard changes are pre-approved because they're low-risk and follow a proven, automated process, like a routine deployment through the validated pipeline. Normal changes get a review. Emergency changes have an expedited path with review afterwards. Getting our routine pipeline deployments classified as standard changes was a big win for us.

Bring evidence automatically. The pipeline produces what the CAB wants to see. Linked work items, test results, code review approvals, security scan results, the deployment plan and the rollback plan. The change record gets created and updated by the pipeline, not typed in by hand.
Shift approvals left. Peer review in pull requests and automated checks give most of the assurance, and the CAB focuses on genuinely risky stuff, like data migrations or infrastructure changes.
Make releases smaller and more frequent, so each change is easier to assess.
Show the data, like change failure rate, to build trust that the process works.
In our GxP context, validation evidence and approvals are mandatory, but automating their collection kept releases moving without cutting corners.

p17-555.q: Actually an ephemeral preview environment is a short-lived copy of the app created automatically for a pull request, with its own URL, and destroyed when the pull request is merged or closed. Reviewers, testers and product owners can try the change for real before it merges, instead of reading code or waiting for a shared test environment.
p17-555.k: preview environments, ephemeral environments, pull request environment, review apps, environment per branch
x: Actually an ephemeral preview environment is a short-lived copy of the app created automatically for a pull request, with its own URL, and destroyed when the pull request is merged or closed. Reviewers, testers and product owners can try the change for real before it merges, instead of reading code or waiting for a shared test environment.

How it's usually built. For front ends it's easy. Services like Azure Static Web Apps, Vercel or Netlify, or a pipeline that uploads to a bucket under a pull-request path, create a preview site per pull request automatically.

For back-end services on Kubernetes, the pipeline deploys the pull request's image into a new namespace named after the pull request, using the same Helm chart with a small values override, and a dynamic host name like pr-123.dev.example.com. Dependencies are either shared, like a common dev database with test data, or created per environment, like a small database container seeded with test data, depending on cost and isolation needs. A cleanup job deletes the namespace when the pull request closes, plus a nightly sweep for anything left behind.
On Azure Container Apps or AWS, infrastructure as code can create and destroy a small stack per pull request.

Watch-outs, cost, so environments are small and auto-expire. Secrets, which shouldn't be exposed to pull requests from forks. And data, which has to be synthetic, never copies of production data. That last one is non-negotiable in our domain.

p17-556.q: Okay, GitHub Actions gives you two main ways to reuse logic, at different levels.
p17-556.k: reusable workflows, composite actions, github actions reuse, workflow_call, github actions templates
x: Okay, GitHub Actions gives you two main ways to reuse logic, at different levels.

Composite actions bundle several steps into one action, defined in an action.yml with inputs and outputs. Like a setup-dotnet-build action that installs the SDK, restores with caching, builds and runs tests with coverage. Any job can use it as a single step. They're good for sharing step sequences, and they run inside the caller's job, on the caller's runner.

Reusable workflows are whole workflows triggered with workflow_call, with defined inputs, secrets and outputs. A caller job references them with a uses line pointing at the workflow file in the shared repo, pinned to a tag like v2. They can contain multiple jobs, use their own runners, environments and protection rules, and they're good for standardising entire processes, like build-and-push-image or deploy-to-environment with approvals.

What I do, keep shared workflows in a central repository, version them with tags, and have consumers pin a tag, or for third-party actions a full commit SHA, so an upstream change can't silently alter pipelines. Pass secrets explicitly instead of using secrets inherit everywhere. Set minimal permissions for the GITHUB_TOKEN at the workflow level. And document inputs clearly.
Organisation-level rulesets can require certain workflows to run on all repositories, like a security scan, which gives you similar governance to required templates in Azure Pipelines.
And changes to shared workflows get tested on a sample repository before a new version is tagged.

p17-557.q: So traceability means for any change running in production, I can answer which requirement or bug it came from, who wrote and reviewed it, which tests verified it, which build produced it, and when and by whom it was deployed and approved. In a GxP environment, auditors expect exactly this.
p17-557.k: traceability requirement to deployment, work item linking, audit trail release, gxp traceability, commit to production
x: So traceability means for any change running in production, I can answer which requirement or bug it came from, who wrote and reviewed it, which tests verified it, which build produced it, and when and by whom it was deployed and approved. In a GxP environment, auditors expect exactly this.
How the tooling gives it to you in Azure DevOps.
Work items. Every requirement, user story and bug is a work item. Branch policies require pull requests to link work items, and commits mention them too.
Pull requests record the reviewers, approvals, comments and the validation build.
Builds link to the commits and work items included since the last build, and publish test results and coverage, which attach to the build. The build number carries the version.

Releases and environments. The deployment records which build artifact went to which environment, with timestamps, approvals and who approved. Release notes can be generated from the linked work items.
Test management. Test cases link to requirements, and test runs, manual or automated, link to builds, so validation evidence connects requirement to verification.
Going the other way, from a requirement I can find all the code and every release that included it.

What actually makes it work is enforcement through policies, not just discipline. And keeping retention settings long enough, because pipeline runs and artifacts get deleted by default after a while, which would break the audit trail. In our setup we set retention to match our records requirements.

p17-558.q: See, Testcontainers is a library that starts real dependencies in Docker containers from inside the test code, and throws them away afterwards. There's a .NET version, with ready-made modules for SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Redis, RabbitMQ, Kafka, LocalStack for AWS, Azurite for Azure Storage, and lots more.
p17-558.k: testcontainers, testcontainers dotnet, real database in tests, docker integration tests, sql server container tests
x: See, Testcontainers is a library that starts real dependencies in Docker containers from inside the test code, and throws them away afterwards. There's a .NET version, with ready-made modules for SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Redis, RabbitMQ, Kafka, LocalStack for AWS, Azurite for Azure Storage, and lots more.

Why it beats the alternatives. In-memory fakes, like the EF Core in-memory provider or SQLite standing in for SQL Server, behave differently from the real database. No real transactions, different SQL translation, no stored procedures or constraints. Tests pass and production fails. A shared test database is slow to reset, and tests step on each other. Testcontainers gives each test run a real, clean instance of the same engine and version you use in production.

How I use it in .NET with xUnit. A fixture class implements IAsyncLifetime, creates an MsSqlBuilder and calls Build on it, starts the container in InitializeAsync, applies migrations, and exposes the connection string. WebApplicationFactory then overrides the app's connection string to point at the container, so the API runs end to end against the real database. The fixture is shared across a test collection, because starting a container takes a few seconds, and Respawn or transactions reset data between tests.

It runs the same on a developer laptop and in CI, as long as Docker is available on the agent, which is really the main setup requirement. Once teams try it, they honestly don't go back to in-memory fakes.

p17-559.q: Okay, integration tests that call secured endpoints need an authenticated user, but they shouldn't depend on a real identity provider like Keycloak. I've used two approaches for this.
p17-559.k: test authentication handler, fake jwt integration tests, webapplicationfactory auth, authorize in tests, test user claims
x: Okay, integration tests that call secured endpoints need an authenticated user, but they shouldn't depend on a real identity provider like Keycloak. I've used two approaches for this.

A test authentication handler. In WebApplicationFactory's ConfigureTestServices, I register a custom AuthenticationHandler under a test scheme and make it the default. Its HandleAuthenticateAsync builds a ClaimsPrincipal with the claims the test needs, user id, roles, site or study scopes, and returns success. Tests can control the claims per request, for example by reading a test header, so one test runs as a site user and another as an admin. Authorisation policies, role checks and resource-based handlers still run for real, which is exactly what I want to test.

Locally signed JWTs. Configure the JWT bearer options in tests to trust a signing key created in the test, then mint tokens with the claims you need. This exercises the real JWT bearer pipeline, including issuer, audience and expiry validation, which is good for testing token-related behaviour.

Whichever one, I always include negative tests. No token gives 401, a valid user without permission gives 403, and a user from one site can't read another site's data. Those are the tests that catch real security bugs.
What I avoid is disabling authorisation in tests altogether, with AllowAnonymous filters, because then the most important rules never get tested.

p17-560.q: So when a service calls an external HTTP API, like a partner's shipment API or an identity provider, tests shouldn't call the real thing. It's slow, flaky, might cost money, and you can't make it fail on demand.
p17-560.k: wiremock dotnet, stub http api, mock external service, fake http server tests, test third party api
x: So when a service calls an external HTTP API, like a partner's shipment API or an identity provider, tests shouldn't call the real thing. It's slow, flaky, might cost money, and you can't make it fail on demand.

WireMock.Net starts a real HTTP server inside the test process on a random port. I point the app's HttpClient base address at it, then set up stubs. When a GET comes in at slash shipments slash 123 with a certain header, return 200 with this JSON body. When a POST comes in, return 201. It records all requests, so tests can verify exactly what was sent, URL, headers and body.

Its real value is testing failure behaviour, which is hard with the real API. I can stub a 500, a 429 with a Retry-After header, a slow response that blows past the timeout, malformed JSON, or a connection reset. Then I check retries, circuit breakers and fallbacks behave as designed, like the Polly pipeline retrying twice and then the service returning a clear error.
Scenarios let stubs change state across calls, like failing on the first call and succeeding on the second.
Compared with mocking HttpMessageHandler in unit tests, WireMock exercises the real HTTP stack, serialisation and handler pipeline.

The stubs should match the real API's contract though. If the partner gives an OpenAPI spec or a sandbox, I check stubs against it, or use contract tests, so the fake doesn't drift from reality. That drift is where I've seen people get burned.

p17-561.q: Honestly in microservices, an API change can break a consumer without anyone noticing until integration or production. End-to-end tests catch it, but they're slow and fragile. Contract testing catches it earlier and cheaper.
p17-561.k: pact contract testing, consumer driven contracts, contract test microservices, pact broker, provider verification
x: Honestly in microservices, an API change can break a consumer without anyone noticing until integration or production. End-to-end tests catch it, but they're slow and fragile. Contract testing catches it earlier and cheaper.

With Pact, the consumer team writes tests describing the interactions they rely on. When I call GET slash shipments slash 123, I expect 200 with a body containing id, status and site. During the consumer's test run, Pact acts as a mock provider and records these expectations into a contract file, the pact. The pact gets published to a Pact Broker.

The provider then runs verification in its own pipeline. Pact replays each interaction from every consumer's pact against the real provider service, using provider states to set up data, like a shipment with id 123 exists, and checks the responses match. If the provider renamed a field a consumer uses, verification fails in the provider's pipeline, before release.
The broker tracks which versions of consumers and providers are compatible, and the can-i-deploy check answers whether a specific version can safely go to an environment.
What you get, each consumer only specifies what it actually uses, so providers can change everything else freely. Teams find breaking changes early. And you need fewer slow end-to-end tests.

It works for messages too, like event payloads on RabbitMQ or Kafka. The investment is mainly setting up the broker and provider states, so it pays off most with several teams and lots of service interactions.

p17-562.q: Okay, Mock Service Worker intercepts requests at the network level. In the browser it uses a service worker, and in Node, for Jest or Vitest, it hooks into the request layer. The app code keeps using fetch or axios normally. It has no idea requests are mocked.
p17-562.k: msw, mock service worker, mock api react tests, network level mocking, msw handlers, storybook msw
x: Okay, Mock Service Worker intercepts requests at the network level. In the browser it uses a service worker, and in Node, for Jest or Vitest, it hooks into the request layer. The app code keeps using fetch or axios normally. It has no idea requests are mocked.

I define handlers with the http helpers, like http.get for slash api slash shipments, returning a JSON response. Tests use the real data-fetching code, like RTK Query, TanStack Query or a service, so I'm testing what users actually experience. The component renders, fetches, shows a loading state, then shows data or an error.

Why it's better than mocking fetch or the API module. Module-level mocks tie tests to implementation details, so refactoring how data is fetched breaks tests even when behaviour hasn't changed. MSW tests survive refactors.
Per-test overrides make error cases easy. server.use with a handler returning 500 or a delayed response, then assert that the error message and retry button show up. After each test, handlers reset.
The same handlers get reused in Storybook, so components show realistic data in isolation, and in local development, so front-end work can carry on before the back-end endpoint even exists.
To keep mocks honest, I generate handlers or types from the OpenAPI spec where I can, so if the API changes, TypeScript flags the mismatch.
One config tip, fail tests on unhandled requests, so a missing handler gets caught instead of silently hitting nothing.

p17-563.q: So code coverage tells you which lines ran during tests, not whether the tests would notice if those lines were wrong. A test that calls a method and asserts nothing gives full coverage and catches nothing.
p17-563.k: mutation testing, stryker dotnet, stryker mutator, test quality, mutation score, coverage is not enough
x: So code coverage tells you which lines ran during tests, not whether the tests would notice if those lines were wrong. A test that calls a method and asserts nothing gives full coverage and catches nothing.

Mutation testing measures test quality directly. A tool makes small changes to the code, called mutants. Changing greater than to greater than or equal, flipping a boolean, swapping a plus for a minus, removing a method call, or returning a default value. Then it runs the tests against each mutant. If a test fails, the mutant is killed, which is good. If all tests still pass, the mutant survived, meaning nothing in the test suite would notice that bug. The mutation score is the percentage killed.

For .NET, Stryker.NET does this, and Stryker exists for JavaScript and TypeScript too. It produces an HTML report showing each surviving mutant in the code, which points straight to missing assertions or untested edge cases, like boundary conditions in a date or quantity check.

It's slow, because it runs the tests many times, so I don't run it on every build. I run it on critical modules, like calculation, validation or allocation logic, periodically or in a nightly pipeline, and use the since option to mutate only changed code in pull requests.
I don't chase 100 percent, some mutants are equivalent and can't be killed. The value is finding the important gaps that coverage hides. I think that's the best way to put it in an interview.

p17-564.q: Okay, so normal example-based tests check specific inputs. Given 10 kits and 3 requested, 7 remain. Property-based testing instead states a rule that has to hold for all valid inputs, and the framework generates hundreds of random inputs trying to break it.
p17-564.k: property based testing, fscheck, cscheck, hypothesis python, generative testing, invariants testing
x: Okay, so normal example-based tests check specific inputs. Given 10 kits and 3 requested, 7 remain. Property-based testing instead states a rule that has to hold for all valid inputs, and the framework generates hundreds of random inputs trying to break it.

Examples of properties. Serialising and then deserialising any object gives you back the same object. Sorting is idempotent and keeps all the items. For any sequence of reservations and releases, available stock never goes negative, and reserved plus available always equals the total. Or a parsing function never throws for any string, it either succeeds or returns a validation error.
When a property fails, the framework shrinks the input down to the smallest failing example, like an empty list or a value of exactly zero, which makes the bug really easy to understand.
Tools, FsCheck and CsCheck for .NET, which plug into xUnit. Hypothesis for Python. fast-check for TypeScript.

Where it pays off, algorithms with clear invariants, like allocation, scheduling, calculations, encoders and parsers. Code with lots of edge cases. And stateful systems, where the framework generates random sequences of operations and compares the system against a simple model.

It doesn't replace example tests, which document specific business cases clearly. And properties take some thought to write well. A property that just reimplements the code proves nothing. I use it for the most logic-heavy parts, and honestly it often finds bugs nobody thought of.

p17-565.q: See, snapshot or approval testing checks a complex output against a previously approved version stored in a file, instead of writing loads of individual assertions.
p17-565.k: snapshot testing, approval testing, verify dotnet, verify tests, snapshot test api response, received approved files
x: See, snapshot or approval testing checks a complex output against a previously approved version stored in a file, instead of writing loads of individual assertions.

With the Verify library in .NET, a test ends with await Verify on the result. The first time, Verify serialises the result, like an object graph, an API response, a generated document, or even the HTTP calls made, into a received file, and the test fails. A developer reviews it, and if it's correct, accepts it as the verified file, which gets committed to the repository. On later runs, the new output is compared with the verified file, and any difference fails the test and shows a diff.

It's great for API response shapes, so an accidental field rename or format change gets caught. Generated output like reports, emails, CSV or XML exports, PDFs and images. Complex mapping results. And characterising legacy code before refactoring, capturing its current behaviour.
Verify handles the noise. It scrubs values that change every run, like GUIDs and dates, replacing them with stable placeholders, and lets you ignore specific members.

The risk is if reviewers just accept every changed snapshot without reading it, the tests catch nothing. Snapshots should be small and focused enough to actually review. And for simple values, plain assertions are clearer.
Jest has the same idea for JavaScript, with toMatchSnapshot, usually for serialisable outputs rather than whole component trees.

p17-566.q: So load testing checks how a system behaves under realistic and peak traffic, before users find out the hard way.
p17-566.k: load testing, k6, nbomber, performance testing api, load test script, thresholds k6
x: So load testing checks how a system behaves under realistic and peak traffic, before users find out the hard way.

k6 is a popular open-source tool where tests are JavaScript scripts. A script defines what a virtual user does. Log in, list shipments, open one, create an allocation, with realistic think times and data. Scenarios define the load shape, like ramping to 200 virtual users over five minutes, or a constant arrival rate of 50 requests per second, which is better for APIs because it doesn't ease off when the system slows down. Thresholds define pass or fail, like p95 latency below 500 milliseconds and error rate below one percent. That makes load tests usable as pipeline gates. Results can stream to Grafana or other backends.
NBomber is a .NET alternative, scenarios in C#, which suits teams that want to reuse existing .NET clients and models, and it's handy for non-HTTP things too, like message consumers.

Getting meaningful results. Test in an environment sized like production, with production-like data volumes, because a query that's fast on 1,000 rows can crawl on 10 million. Generate load from outside the system under test, with enough load-generator capacity. Watch the server side during the test, CPU, memory, database waits, thread pool queue length, GC and dependency latency, so you know where the bottleneck is, not just that there is one. And run a baseline before changes, then compare.

p17-567.q: Actually different performance tests answer different questions, so I pick based on the risk.
p17-567.k: load test vs stress test, soak test, spike test, endurance test, capacity test, performance testing types
x: Actually different performance tests answer different questions, so I pick based on the risk.

A load test runs the expected normal and peak traffic, like the busiest hour of a typical day, for a while. It checks response times and error rates meet the targets under the load we actually expect.

A stress test pushes load past expectations until the system breaks, to find the breaking point and, more importantly, how it fails. Does it slow down gracefully, shed load with 429 or 503 responses, and recover when load drops? Or does it fall over and stay down?

A spike test applies a sudden jump, like ten times normal traffic within seconds, which tests autoscaling speed, connection pools, caches warming up, and queues absorbing bursts. Think of a study going live at lots of sites at once, or a batch import triggering a flood of events.

A soak or endurance test runs a moderate load for many hours or days. It finds problems that only show up over time. Memory leaks, connection leaks, growing queues, log disks filling up, slow degradation from fragmentation, and scheduled jobs interfering with traffic.
A capacity test finds how much load a given configuration can handle while meeting targets, which feeds sizing and cost decisions.
Breakpoint and scalability tests check whether adding instances actually increases throughput, or whether a shared resource, like the database, caps it.
All of them need clear targets defined up front, and server-side monitoring to explain the results. Without that, honestly, you just get numbers nobody can act on.

p17-568.q: Okay, tests get hard to read when the arrange section is 30 lines of object construction, and fragile when a new required property means updating hundreds of tests. Good test data tools fix both.
p17-568.k: test data builder, autofixture, bogus fake data, object mother, test data setup, arrange section too long
x: Okay, tests get hard to read when the arrange section is 30 lines of object construction, and fragile when a new required property means updating hundreds of tests. Good test data tools fix both.

The test data builder pattern. A ShipmentBuilder class with sensible defaults for every property and fluent methods to change only what matters for this test. Like a new ShipmentBuilder, then WithStatus Delivered, then ForSite with the site, then Build. The test shows only the relevant details, and when the model changes, only the builder changes. Builders can create valid object graphs that respect domain rules, which matters when constructors enforce invariants.

AutoFixture creates anonymous test data automatically, filling every property with generated values, and you can customise it for specific types. With xUnit's AutoData attributes, it removes boilerplate for tests where the values don't matter, and AutoMoq integration creates mocks for dependencies automatically.

Bogus generates realistic fake data. Names, addresses, dates, numbers in realistic ranges, with a seed for reproducibility. It's great for seeding dev databases, demo environments and load tests, and for UI work where realistic data shows layout problems.

My rule is, values that matter to the test's outcome should be visible in the test, not hidden in defaults. Generated data should be valid by default. Seeds make random data reproducible when a test fails. And never use real production or patient data in tests, which in a clinical domain is especially important.

p17-569.q: So code that calls DateTime.Now or DateTime.UtcNow directly is hard to test. A rule like "a kit expires after 30 days" or "send a reminder if a visit is overdue by two days" depends on the clock, and tests either get flaky or have to wait.
p17-569.k: testing datetime, timeprovider, faketimeprovider, mock datetime now, time dependent tests, clock abstraction
x: So code that calls DateTime.Now or DateTime.UtcNow directly is hard to test. A rule like "a kit expires after 30 days" or "send a reminder if a visit is overdue by two days" depends on the clock, and tests either get flaky or have to wait.

The fix is to inject the clock. Since .NET 8 there's a built-in abstraction, TimeProvider. Code depends on TimeProvider, registered as TimeProvider.System in production, and calls GetUtcNow, GetLocalNow, or the CreateTimer and Task.Delay overloads that accept a TimeProvider.

In tests, FakeTimeProvider, from Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing, lets me set the current time to an exact value and move it forward with Advance, passing TimeSpan.FromDays of 31. Timers and delays scheduled through the fake provider fire when time is advanced, so tests of timeouts, expiry, retries with delays, or periodic background work run instantly and deterministically.
Before .NET 8, teams wrote their own IClock or ISystemClock interface, which works the same way.

Things worth testing explicitly with a controllable clock. Boundaries, like exactly at the expiry moment versus one second before. Time zones, especially for sites in different countries and daylight saving transitions, where a visit window can be 23 or 25 hours. And month ends and leap years. Those daylight saving ones catch people all the time.
For front-end code, Jest and Vitest have fake timers and can set the system time, which does the same job.

p17-570.q: Honestly a BackgroundService is awkward to test directly. It runs a loop in ExecuteAsync, often reading from a queue or polling on a timer, so you've got the infinite loop, timing and cancellation all mixed in. So I separate concerns.
p17-570.k: test backgroundservice, test hosted service, test worker service, executeasync test, test queue consumer dotnet
x: Honestly a BackgroundService is awkward to test directly. It runs a loop in ExecuteAsync, often reading from a queue or polling on a timer, so you've got the infinite loop, timing and cancellation all mixed in. So I separate concerns.

Keep the loop thin. The hosted service only handles the mechanics. Wait for the next item or tick, create a DI scope, call a handler, and handle errors and cancellation. The real work lives in a separate class, like ProcessShipmentEventHandler, which is a normal class with injected dependencies and gets unit-tested like anything else. That's where most tests go.

Test the loop's mechanics separately, with a small number of focused tests. Start the service with a cancellation token, feed it an item through a fake queue or a Channel, wait until the handler is called, using a TaskCompletionSource instead of sleeps, then cancel and check it stops cleanly. Check an exception in one item doesn't kill the loop, and that a scope gets created per item. With TimeProvider and FakeTimeProvider, periodic services can be tested without real waiting.

Integration tests run the whole host with WebApplicationFactory or a test host, and a real broker through Testcontainers, publishing a message and asserting the expected database change shows up, with a timeout and polling.
I also test graceful shutdown. Stopping the host while an item is being processed should either finish it or leave it safely to be redelivered, never half-done.

p17-571.q: See, retry, timeout and circuit breaker logic is easy to get wrong and rarely exercised until an outage, so it deserves deliberate tests.
p17-571.k: test polly retry, test circuit breaker, test resilience pipeline, simulate transient failures, chaos testing httpclient
x: See, retry, timeout and circuit breaker logic is easy to get wrong and rarely exercised until an outage, so it deserves deliberate tests.

At the unit level, I test the policy configuration itself. With Polly v8, I can build the resilience pipeline and execute a delegate that fails a set number of times, like throwing HttpRequestException twice and then succeeding, and assert it was called three times. For circuit breakers, I fail enough calls to open the circuit, assert the next call fails fast with BrokenCircuitException, then advance a fake TimeProvider past the break duration and check a trial call is allowed. Injecting the TimeProvider means no real waiting on backoff delays.

At the integration level, I put a fake server, like WireMock.Net, behind the real typed HttpClient with its real resilience handler, configured from the real settings. Then stub sequences. 503 then 200, 429 with Retry-After, a delay longer than the attempt timeout. I assert what the caller experiences and how many requests actually reached the server.

The important cases, non-idempotent requests, like POSTs, shouldn't be retried unless they carry an idempotency key. The total timeout should cap the whole sequence. And no retries for 400-type errors.

Polly also has chaos strategies to inject faults, latency or fake results in a test environment, which validates the whole system's behaviour under failure. I've seen that surface stuff nobody expected.

p17-572.q: Okay, migrations change production data structures, often irreversibly, so they need testing beyond "it ran on my machine".
p17-572.k: test ef core migrations, migration testing, test schema changes, migration rollback test, migration ci check
x: Okay, migrations change production data structures, often irreversibly, so they need testing beyond "it ran on my machine".
The checks I put in the pipeline, pretty much always.

Model and migrations in sync. For EF Core, a test or a pipeline step fails if there are pending model changes without a migration, which .NET 8 and later can check with dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes.
Apply from scratch. Create an empty database in a container with Testcontainers and apply all migrations from the beginning. That catches broken or order-dependent migrations.

Apply to a realistic existing state. Restore a copy of the schema, or an anonymised dataset, at the current production version, then apply the new migrations. A lot of failures only happen with real data, like adding a NOT NULL column without a default, a unique index on a column that has duplicates, or a data conversion that fails on unexpected values.
Measure duration on production-sized data. A migration that takes two seconds on test data might lock a big table for 20 minutes. If it's slow, it needs redesigning as an online change or batched.
Compatibility. Run the previous app version's tests against the new schema, since during a rolling deployment the old version runs against the migrated database.
Rollback. If down migrations are supported, test them too, otherwise document the forward-fix plan.
For SSDT projects, same thing applies to the generated deployment script, reviewed and run against a production-like copy.

p17-573.q: So when important business logic lives in stored procedures, which is common in older systems like ours, it deserves tests just like C# code.
p17-573.k: test stored procedures, tsql unit testing, tsqlt, database unit tests, sql logic testing
x: So when important business logic lives in stored procedures, which is common in older systems like ours, it deserves tests just like C# code.

tSQLt is a unit testing framework that runs inside SQL Server. Tests are themselves stored procedures, grouped in test classes, and each test runs in a transaction that gets rolled back, so tests don't leave data behind. The key feature is faking. FakeTable replaces a table with an empty copy without constraints, so a test inserts only the rows it needs. SpyProcedure replaces a called procedure with a spy that records calls. And assertions like AssertEqualsTable compare expected and actual result sets. That isolates the logic of one procedure from the rest of the schema.

The alternative is testing procedures from .NET integration tests. Spin up a real SQL Server with Testcontainers, deploy the schema from the SSDT project or migrations, insert test data, call the procedure through Dapper or ADO.NET, and assert results. That tests the procedure and the calling code's mapping together, and fits the existing .NET test tooling and CI. In our kind of setup, I'd lean towards this one.

What I focus on, boundary conditions, null handling, transactions and error handling with THROW, concurrency-related logic, like whether two calls can allocate the same item, and performance with realistic data volumes, checking execution plans for scans.
Whatever the tool, the database schema should be in source control, so tests run in CI against the exact schema being released.

p17-574.q: Actually integration tests that share a database can really interfere. One test's data changes another test's results, tests pass alone but fail together, and order starts mattering. I've used a few strategies to keep them isolated.
p17-574.k: test database isolation, respawn, reset database between tests, transaction rollback tests, parallel integration tests
x: Actually integration tests that share a database can really interfere. One test's data changes another test's results, tests pass alone but fail together, and order starts mattering. I've used a few strategies to keep them isolated.

Reset between tests. Respawn is a .NET library that deletes data from all tables quickly, in the right order respecting foreign keys, while keeping reference tables you list. Calling it before each test gives you a clean database in milliseconds, much faster than recreating the database.

Wrap each test in a transaction and roll it back at the end. Fast and clean, but it doesn't work if the code under test manages its own transactions, uses multiple connections, or if you're testing through HTTP where the request runs on a different connection.

Unique data per test. Each test creates its own data with unique ids or names and only asserts on that data. That allows parallel tests on one database, but queries like "count all shipments" become unreliable.

Database per test class or collection. With Testcontainers, each test collection can get its own database inside a shared container, created from a template or snapshot, which allows parallel collections.

My typical setup, one container per test run, one database per test collection, Respawn before each test, and tests that create their own data. In xUnit, collections run in parallel and tests within a collection run sequentially, which fits this model nicely.

p17-575.q: Okay, concurrency bugs, like two requests reserving the same last kit, or a duplicate message being processed twice at the same time, rarely show up in normal tests, because tests run one call at a time.
p17-575.k: test concurrency, race condition test, concurrent requests test, double booking test, optimistic concurrency test
x: Okay, concurrency bugs, like two requests reserving the same last kit, or a duplicate message being processed twice at the same time, rarely show up in normal tests, because tests run one call at a time.
