So I test them deliberately.

Fire concurrent requests in integration tests. Start, say, 20 tasks that call the same endpoint at once, released together with a barrier or a SemaphoreSlim, against a real database. Then assert the invariant. Exactly one reservation succeeded, the others got a conflict, and the stock count is correct. Run it multiple times, because a race might not show up every run.

Test the concurrency control itself. For optimistic concurrency, load an entity in two DbContexts, save one, then assert the second save throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException, and that the app turns it into a 409 or a retry. For unique constraints, assert the database rejects duplicates and the code handles the error.
Test idempotency under concurrency. Deliver the same message twice in parallel to the consumer and assert the effect happened once.

Use deterministic tools where you can. For code using locks or channels, control the interleaving by pausing one operation at a specific point with hooks, so the test hits the dangerous window every time, not just by luck.
Load tests at higher concurrency also surface deadlocks and lock contention.
The mindset I go with is, figure out the invariant that has to hold, then try really hard to break it.

p17-576.q: So basically I don't treat security testing as one big activity at the end. It's layers, and most of it runs in the pipeline on its own.
p17-576.k: security testing, sast dast, owasp zap, penetration testing, dependency scanning, security tests pipeline
x: So basically I don't treat security testing as one big activity at the end. It's layers, and most of it runs in the pipeline on its own.

On every pull request we've got static analysis, so things like SonarQube security rules, Roslyn analyzers, Semgrep or CodeQL. They catch injection risks, unsafe deserialisation, weak crypto, hardcoded secrets, that kind of stuff. Then dependency scanning checks our NuGet and npm packages and the container images for known vulnerabilities, and the build fails if something critical shows up. Secret scanning sits on top so credentials never get committed in the first place.

Then on a deployed test environment we run OWASP ZAP. The baseline scan is quick, so it goes in the nightly pipeline, and the full scan runs less often. It finds missing security headers, cookie flags, reflected XSS, some injection issues.

Honestly though, the tests I value most are the ones teams usually skip, which is security tests on business logic. A user from site A shouldn't read site B's data, a role without permission should get a 403, IDs from another tenant get rejected, bad input gets rejected, and sensitive fields don't show up in responses or logs. Tools won't find those for you.

For infra, Checkov or something similar scans Terraform and Kubernetes manifests. And before big releases, specialists do a pen test, because they find logic flaws that automation misses. Whatever comes out of all this gets tracked like a normal bug, with fix deadlines based on severity.

p17-577.q: Okay, so accessibility is partly about users with disabilities and partly it's a legal or contract thing, usually WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 level AA. And the honest answer is tools only catch part of it, so you need some manual checking too.
p17-577.k: accessibility testing, axe core, wcag testing, a11y tests, screen reader testing, playwright accessibility
x: Okay, so accessibility is partly about users with disabilities and partly it's a legal or contract thing, usually WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 level AA. And the honest answer is tools only catch part of it, so you need some manual checking too.

On the automated side, axe-core is kind of the standard engine. We use it in unit tests with jest-axe or vitest-axe on rendered components, in end-to-end tests with the axe Playwright package so it scans full pages in a real browser, and in Storybook with the accessibility add-on, so designers and devs see the issues per component. It catches missing labels, poor colour contrast, missing alt text, wrong ARIA, duplicate ids. Lint rules, like eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y or Angular's accessibility lint rules, catch stuff while you're still coding. Lighthouse gives a score as well.
One thing I like is Testing Library queries. If my test can't find a button by its role and accessible name, a screen reader user probably can't find it either.

Then the manual part. I go through the whole flow with only the keyboard, checking the focus is visible and the tab order makes sense. I try key journeys with NVDA or VoiceOver. I zoom to 200 percent, try small screens, and check error messages are actually announced and make sense.
Using components like MUI or Angular Material gives you a big head start since they handle a lot of the ARIA and keyboard stuff. But custom components need the same checks.

p17-578.q: See, functional tests can tell you a button exists and works, but not that it's now hidden behind another element, or the layout broke on mobile, or a theme change made the text unreadable. Visual regression testing is for exactly that, catching changes in how the UI looks that nobody intended.
p17-578.k: visual regression testing, screenshot comparison tests, chromatic, playwright screenshot, ui visual tests, percy
x: See, functional tests can tell you a button exists and works, but not that it's now hidden behind another element, or the layout broke on mobile, or a theme change made the text unreadable. Visual regression testing is for exactly that, catching changes in how the UI looks that nobody intended.

How it works is pretty simple. You take screenshots of pages or components in a known state and store them as approved baselines. On later runs it takes new screenshots and compares them, pixel by pixel or perceptually. If the difference is over a threshold, the test fails and you get a diff image with the changes highlighted. Then the developer either approves it as an intended change or fixes it.

For tools, Playwright has screenshot assertions built in, toHaveScreenshot. Storybook with Chromatic captures every story on each pull request, which is really nice for a design system. Percy or Applitools give smarter comparison and review flows.

The hard part, honestly, is making it stable. Screenshots have to be deterministic, so fixed test data and dates, animations off, fonts loaded, same browser and OS, ideally the same container image in CI. Timestamps and other dynamic bits get masked, and a small threshold absorbs anti-aliasing noise.

I don't screenshot everything. I focus on shared components and a few key pages at the important screen sizes, so reviewing diffs stays quick. In our component-based front end, covering the shared library visually protects every feature package that uses it.

p17-579.q: Actually, with Redux Toolkit most of the logic is just plain functions, so it's one of the easier things to test.
p17-579.k: test redux slice, test selectors, renderhook, test custom hooks react, test rtk query, redux testing
x: Actually, with Redux Toolkit most of the logic is just plain functions, so it's one of the easier things to test.

Reducers are pure. So the test just calls the reducer with a previous state and an action from the slice's action creator, say allocation added with a kit, and checks the new state. No store, no rendering. I test the meaningful transitions and edge cases, I don't bother with every trivial setter.

Selectors are also pure functions of state. I build a state object and check what comes back, mainly for the memoised ones made with createSelector that calculate derived data, like kits expiring in the next 30 days or totals per site.

For thunks I create a real store with configureStore and the app's reducers, mock the API at the network level with MSW, dispatch the thunk and check the resulting state. Going through the store is closer to how the app actually uses it.

With RTK Query, I render the component that uses the generated hooks inside a test store provider, MSW handles the endpoints, and I check loading, success and error states. You do need to reset the API state between tests, otherwise cached data leaks across.

For custom hooks, renderHook from React Testing Library, with a wrapper that gives it the store, router or query client. I check the returned values, call the returned functions inside act, and check the updates.
But mostly I'd rather test components the way a user uses them, with a real store, and keep isolated reducer tests for the tricky logic.

p17-580.q: Honestly, yes, but selectively. I use it where it pays off, I'm not dogmatic about doing it everywhere.
p17-580.k: tdd, test driven development, red green refactor, do you write tests first, tdd benefits drawbacks
x: Honestly, yes, but selectively. I use it where it pays off, I'm not dogmatic about doing it everywhere.

The cycle is red, green, refactor. You write a small failing test for the next bit of behaviour, write the simplest code to make it pass, then clean up the code and tests while they stay green, and repeat in small steps.

Where it really works for me is business rules with clear inputs and outputs, like validation, calculations, allocation logic. Writing the test first forces me to pin down the behaviour and the edge cases before I get lost in the implementation. Bug fixes too. I always write a failing test that reproduces the bug first, so I know the fix actually works and the bug can't quietly come back. And it helps when I'm designing a class's API, because writing the test first shows you very quickly if the interface is awkward to use.

Where I'm more relaxed is exploratory work, where I don't know the shape of the solution yet. There I spike first, then write the tests and usually rewrite the code properly. Same for UI layout and thin glue code, where an integration test gives better value anyway.
What I've seen from it is cleaner, more decoupled code, because testable code tends to have clear dependencies, and a lot more confidence when refactoring.
Whether the test comes first or right after, my rule is the tests describe behaviour, not implementation, and no logic change goes in without one.

p17-581.q: So you can't stop everything and write tests for the whole legacy codebase, that never happens. What I follow is basically the approach from Working Effectively with Legacy Code, which is you add tests where you're about to make a change.
p17-581.k: testing legacy code, characterization tests, seams, working effectively with legacy code, refactor without tests
x: So you can't stop everything and write tests for the whole legacy codebase, that never happens. What I follow is basically the approach from Working Effectively with Legacy Code, which is you add tests where you're about to make a change.

I start with characterisation tests. Before touching a piece of code, I write tests that capture what it does today, not what it should do. Call it with realistic inputs and assert whatever comes back. Snapshot tools like Verify make that quick when the output is complex. Those tests protect the existing behaviour, including the weird bits other parts of the system might depend on.

Then you need seams. Legacy code usually creates its own dependencies directly, so new SqlConnection, static calls, DateTime dot Now, HttpContext dot Current. A seam is a place where you can swap behaviour for a test without changing the logic. So I extract an interface and inject it, or pull the hard call into a virtual method and override it in a test subclass, or wrap statics behind a small adapter, or just pass the value in as a parameter. All in small, safe refactoring steps, mostly tool-assisted.
For new functionality I use sprout and wrap. I write it as a new, tested class or method and call it from the old code, instead of adding more untested lines to a huge method.

And for really tangled code, integration tests around the edges, like the real API or stored procedure against a test database, give you protection fastest. That's how we change the risky areas in our .NET Framework core.

p17-582.q: Let me put it this way, randomisation decides which treatment arm a patient goes to, so if it's wrong, it hurts the scientific validity of the trial. So I test it two ways, normal tests and statistical checks.
p17-582.k: test randomization algorithm, randomisation testing, statistical testing allocation, test treatment allocation, irt randomization validation
x: Let me put it this way, randomisation decides which treatment arm a patient goes to, so if it's wrong, it hurts the scientific validity of the trial. So I test it two ways, normal tests and statistical checks.

For the normal tests, the algorithm has to take its random source as a dependency. Then tests can give it a seeded generator or a fixed sequence, and I can assert exact results. With block size four and a one to one ratio, each block has two of each arm. Stratification puts the patient in the right stratum based on their factors. When a site or stratum is capped, the right thing happens. And with a pre-generated randomisation list, patients get the next entry in their stratum in order, and no entry is ever used twice.

Then the edge cases, like the last slot in a block, the list running out, invalid strata, re-randomisation rules, and two sites randomising at the exact same moment. Those two must never get the same entry.

The statistical part is simulation. You run it thousands of times, [like 100,000 simulated patients], and check the allocation ratios match the design within tolerance, balance holds within strata and sites for dynamic methods like minimisation, and there's no predictable pattern. That runs as part of study configuration testing, not every build.

And since it's a regulated system, the tests, the simulation reports and the configuration they ran against are kept as validation evidence. The study config also goes through UAT before it goes live.

p17-583.q: Yeah, so the risk with flags is they double the paths through your code, and usually one state, the one that isn't switched on in test, never gets tested. Then someone flips it and it breaks.
p17-583.k: test feature flags, feature toggle testing, flag combinations testing, feature flag test strategy
x: Yeah, so the risk with flags is they double the paths through your code, and usually one state, the one that isn't switched on in test, never gets tested. Then someone flips it and it breaks.

What I do is, for every flag that changes logic, unit tests for both states. The flag check is injected, through IFeatureManager or a small interface, so the test just sets it on or off. Each flagged behaviour gets one test with it on and one with it off.

For integration and end-to-end tests, they run against the config production will actually have at release. If prod starts with the flag off, the main run uses off, and then there's a second run, or a subset of tests, with it on. I've seen test environments with every flag switched on, and then the off path, which is literally what production runs, isn't tested at all.
I don't test every combination though. With a few flags that explodes fast. Flags should be independent where possible, and I only test combinations for flags that actually interact.

For important flags I test the flip itself. Switching at runtime shouldn't break requests in flight or leave things inconsistent, like jobs started under the old behaviour. I also test the failure default, so if the flag service is down, the code falls back to the safe value.
And once a flag is fully rolled out and removed, the tests for the dead path go too. Keeps the suite honest about what the code really does.

p17-584.q: Honestly, the trick with serverless is keeping the handler thin, then testing is easy.
p17-584.k: test azure functions, test lambda function, unit test lambda dotnet, local testing serverless, lambda test tool
x: Honestly, the trick with serverless is keeping the handler thin, then testing is easy.

So the function method or Lambda handler just translates the trigger into a call. It parses the HTTP request, queue message or S3 event, calls a service class, and maps the result back. The business logic sits in that service class, injected through DI, which both the Azure Functions isolated worker and Lambda support. That way most of my tests are just plain unit tests on the service.

For the handler itself, I build the input object, like an SQSEvent with some sample records, an API Gateway HTTP request, or for Azure Functions a ServiceBusReceivedMessage or a fake HttpRequestData, plus a test context, like TestLambdaContext from the Lambda test utilities package, and then call the method. I check the response and that the service got called correctly. For SQS batch handlers I test that partial failures get reported properly. Sample events from the AWS docs, or captured from real environments, make good realistic inputs.
Locally, Azure Functions Core Tools runs the functions with Azurite emulating queues and blobs. For Lambda there's the Lambda Test Tool, SAM CLI local invoke, or LocalStack.

But emulators can't check everything. So we also deploy through the pipeline to a real cloud test environment and trigger it with a real message or HTTP call. That's what catches the classic serverless problems, like a missing IAM permission or a wrong queue binding, which no unit test is going to find.

p17-585.q: Okay, so OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics and logs. The nice part in .NET is the runtime already produces the raw signals, Activity for traces, System.Diagnostics.Metrics for metrics, and ILogger for logs. OpenTelemetry just collects and exports them.
p17-585.k: opentelemetry dotnet setup, otel dotnet, addopentelemetry, otlp exporter, instrument aspnet core opentelemetry
x: Okay, so OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics and logs. The nice part in .NET is the runtime already produces the raw signals, Activity for traces, System.Diagnostics.Metrics for metrics, and ILogger for logs. OpenTelemetry just collects and exports them.

In Program dot cs, you call AddOpenTelemetry on the services, then ConfigureResource to set the service name, version and environment, which every signal carries. WithTracing adds instrumentation for ASP.NET Core, HttpClient, SQL client or EF Core, plus any custom ActivitySource the app has. WithMetrics adds ASP.NET Core, HttpClient and runtime instrumentation, so you get request durations, GC, thread pool, exception counts, plus your own Meters. For logs you add OpenTelemetry to the logging builder, so log lines carry the trace and span ids. Then UseOtlpExporter sends everything over OTLP, usually to a local Collector, which forwards to Datadog, Grafana, Azure Monitor or CloudWatch. The endpoint and headers come from the standard environment variables, like OTEL exporter OTLP endpoint, so the same code works everywhere.

A few habits I stick to. Clear, stable names for custom spans and metrics. Useful attributes like tenant or study id, but never personal data. Record exceptions on spans. And filter out noise, like health check requests, otherwise they flood everything.

In our case the newest services use OpenTelemetry with Datadog, while older parts still log to Splunk with Serilog. The good thing about standardising on OpenTelemetry is if we change the backend later, it's config, not code.

p17-586.q: So the Collector is a separate process. It receives telemetry, processes it, and exports it to one or more backends. The apps just send to the collector over OTLP instead of talking to each vendor directly.
p17-586.k: opentelemetry collector, otel collector, collector pipeline receivers processors exporters, agent vs gateway collector
x: So the Collector is a separate process. It receives telemetry, processes it, and exports it to one or more backends. The apps just send to the collector over OTLP instead of talking to each vendor directly.

The config is pipelines for traces, metrics and logs, and each pipeline has receivers, processors and exporters. Receivers take data in, OTLP from apps, Prometheus scraping, host metrics, log files, Kafka and so on. Processors change it, so batching, memory limits, adding attributes like cluster and region, dropping noisy spans like health checks, redacting sensitive attributes, tail-based sampling. Exporters send it out to Datadog, Grafana, Jaeger, Prometheus, Azure Monitor, CloudWatch, or several of them at once.

Why bother? For me the big one is apps stay simple and vendor-neutral. Switching or adding a backend is a collector config change, not redeploying every service. Retries and buffering happen in the collector too, so if the backend has an outage, the app doesn't slow down. Redaction, sampling and enrichment rules are applied the same way for every service. And the backend credentials live in one place instead of in every app.
For deployment, you usually have an agent collector close to the apps, per host, as a sidecar or a DaemonSet, and optionally a gateway collector cluster for central stuff like tail sampling.
One catch, the collector is now part of your pipeline, so you have to monitor it and size it properly, otherwise it drops data right when load is highest.

p17-587.q: Picking the right type actually matters, because it decides what questions you can answer later.
p17-587.k: metric types, counter gauge histogram, updowncounter, percentile metrics, system diagnostics metrics
x: Picking the right type actually matters, because it decides what questions you can answer later.

A counter only goes up. Requests handled, orders created, errors, bytes sent. You never really look at the raw number, you look at the rate, like requests per second, or the increase over a window. And in Prometheus-style systems restarts are fine, because the rate functions handle resets.

Then a gauge or up-down counter is a current value that goes up and down. Up-down counter is for things you increment and decrement yourself, like active connections or items in an in-memory queue. A gauge is something you observe at a point in time, like memory used, queue depth read from the broker, or the temperature of a storage unit. For gauges you look at averages and max over time. Rates don't make sense there.

A histogram records the distribution, like request duration or payload size, into buckets. From that you get percentiles, p95, p99 latency, which matter way more than averages, because the average hides the slow requests users actually notice. Histograms also aggregate across instances correctly, which pre-computed percentiles can't do.

In .NET's System.Diagnostics.Metrics these are Counter, UpDownCounter, ObservableGauge and Histogram. So say an allocation service, I'd have a counter for allocations by outcome, a histogram for allocation duration, and an observable gauge for available kits per depot.
Just make sure the histogram buckets cover the expected range, or use exponential histograms so you don't have to pick them by hand.

p17-588.q: So technical metrics like CPU and latency tell you the system is up. Business metrics tell you if it's actually doing its job, like orders placed, patients randomised, shipments delivered, allocations failed because there's no stock. And quite often the business metric drops before any technical alarm fires. Say an integration is quietly sending nothing, CPU looks perfectly fine.
p17-588.k: custom metrics dotnet, meter dotnet, business metrics, system.diagnostics.metrics, imeterfactory, instrument business events
x: So technical metrics like CPU and latency tell you the system is up. Business metrics tell you if it's actually doing its job, like orders placed, patients randomised, shipments delivered, allocations failed because there's no stock. And quite often the business metric drops before any technical alarm fires. Say an integration is quietly sending nothing, CPU looks perfectly fine.

In .NET I use System.Diagnostics.Metrics. I get a Meter from IMeterFactory through dependency injection, which keeps it testable, and create the instruments once. A Counter for randomisations, a Histogram for end-to-end shipment processing time, an ObservableGauge for kits available per depot, calculated from a cached query. Then I record values right where the business event happens, with tags like outcome success or failure, or region.
On the OpenTelemetry side you just call AddMeter with the meter name and they get exported with the built-in metrics.

A few rules I follow. Tags have to be low cardinality, so outcome, region, study phase, maybe study id if the number of studies is bounded. Never patient ids, kit numbers or user ids, that creates millions of time series and a huge bill. Names are consistent, with units, following the OpenTelemetry conventions. And I record after the transaction commits, otherwise a failed transaction gets counted as a success.

Then the dashboard shows business flow at a glance, and you can alert on something like no randomisations in the last hour during business hours at an active study. That's exactly the kind of silent failure our AlertWatchDog jobs were built to catch.

p17-589.q: Okay, these come from site reliability engineering, and they basically give you a precise way to talk about reliability instead of just saying "it should be up".
p17-589.k: sli slo sla, error budget, service level objective, service level indicator, reliability targets
x: Okay, these come from site reliability engineering, and they basically give you a precise way to talk about reliability instead of just saying "it should be up".

An SLI, service level indicator, is a measurement of what users experience, usually good events divided by total events. Like the percentage of API calls that succeed, or the percentage served within 300 milliseconds, or the percentage of shipment events processed within five minutes.
An SLO is the target for that SLI over a window. So 99.9 percent of requests succeed over 28 days, or 95 percent finish within 300 milliseconds.
An SLA is the contract with the customer, with consequences like credits if you miss it. Your SLOs should be stricter than the SLA, so you get a warning before you breach the contract.

The error budget is what the SLO allows to fail. With 99.9 percent that's 0.1 percent, roughly 43 minutes of full downtime in 30 days. What I like is it turns reliability into a shared thing you can measure. If there's plenty of budget left, the team can ship faster and take more risk. If it's burning fast, you slow down releases and do reliability work.

For alerting you use burn rates. You alert when the budget's being used much faster than it should, say 14 times the normal rate over an hour. That catches real user-facing problems and ignores small blips.
And pick SLOs based on what users actually need. Not 100 percent, that's impossible and makes every change scary.

p17-590.q: See, they're two simple checklists for what to monitor, just from different angles.
p17-590.k: red method, use method, rate errors duration, utilization saturation errors, golden signals, what to monitor
x: See, they're two simple checklists for what to monitor, just from different angles.

RED is for services, from the user's point of view. For every service or endpoint you track Rate, requests per second, Errors, the count or percentage of failed requests, and Duration, the response times as percentiles. If you have those for every service, you can see very quickly which one is unhappy and how. It maps nicely to dashboards too, one row per service with three panels.

USE is for resources, from the infrastructure side. For every resource, CPU, memory, disk, network, connection pools, thread pools, queues, you track Utilisation, how busy it is, Saturation, how much work is waiting, like the run queue or the thread pool queue, and Errors, like disk errors or dropped packets. Saturation is the one people forget, and honestly it's often the most telling. 70 percent CPU might be totally fine, but a growing thread pool queue is a real problem.
Google's four golden signals are pretty similar, latency, traffic, errors and saturation.

How I use them together is RED tells me there's a problem, like the allocation API's p95 latency has tripled. Then USE on the resources behind it tells me why, like the database connection pool is saturated and requests are sitting there waiting for a connection. So one finds the symptom and the other one finds the cause.

p17-591.q: Actually it's simple once you know that every unique combination of metric name and label values is its own time series. A request counter with method, route and status code labels might give you a few hundred series, that's fine. Add a user id label and suddenly it's hundreds of thousands. That's high cardinality.
p17-591.k: high cardinality metrics, metric labels cardinality, time series explosion, metrics cost, label best practices
x: Actually it's simple once you know that every unique combination of metric name and label values is its own time series. A request counter with method, route and status code labels might give you a few hundred series, that's fine. Add a user id label and suddenly it's hundreds of thousands. That's high cardinality.

Why it hurts: the backend stores and indexes each series separately, so memory, storage and query time all grow with the series count. Prometheus can just run out of memory. Commercial tools like Datadog charge per custom metric series, so one careless label can create a huge bill overnight. And dashboards get slow.

The usual culprits are user ids, emails, request ids, raw URLs with ids in the path instead of the route template, timestamps, exception messages, kit or order numbers, and pod names in very dynamic setups.

What I do is keep labels to bounded values. Route templates like shipments slash id in braces, status code classes, region, outcome. The high-cardinality detail goes into traces and logs, which are built for per-request data and you can search them by id. New metrics get reviewed, and the pipeline or collector can drop or rewrite labels. I also watch the number of series per metric so growth gets caught early.
And if someone really needs per-entity analysis, like latency per customer, that's usually better answered from logs or traces, or an analytics store that's designed for high cardinality.

p17-592.q: Honestly, if levels aren't consistent, logs become noise and cost a lot. So here's roughly how I use them.
p17-592.k: log levels, when to log error vs warning, log level guidelines, information vs debug logging, too many logs
x: Honestly, if levels aren't consistent, logs become noise and cost a lot. So here's roughly how I use them.
Critical or Fatal is when the app or a key component can't continue. Like it fails to start because config is invalid, or the database is completely gone. Someone should get woken up.

Error is an operation failed and needs attention. An unhandled exception in a request, a message going to the dead-letter queue, an integration call that failed after all the retries. My rule is every error log should be actionable. If nobody needs to do anything, it's not an error.

Warning is something unexpected but handled. A retry worked after a transient failure, a fallback kicked in, a slow query crossed a threshold, a deprecated API got called. Warnings help you spot trends before they turn into errors.

Information is the important business and lifecycle events. Service started, shipment created, randomisation completed, a job processed 230 records. They tell the story of what happened without every little step.

Debug and Trace are detailed diagnostics for developers, intermediate values, which branch it took. Off in production by default, but you can switch them on per category at runtime, so we turn it on for one component during an investigation.

And a few other things. Log an exception once, where it's handled, not at every layer. Use structured properties, not string concatenation. Never log secrets or personal data. And set minimum levels per namespace to quiet the noisy libraries.

p17-593.q: So at high traffic, recording every single trace costs a lot in network, storage and money, and most successful traces look exactly the same anyway. Sampling keeps a representative subset.
p17-593.k: trace sampling, head based sampling, tail based sampling, sampling rate opentelemetry, keep error traces
x: So at high traffic, recording every single trace costs a lot in network, storage and money, and most successful traces look exactly the same anyway. Sampling keeps a representative subset.

Head-based sampling decides at the start of the trace, in the first service, usually as a percentage, like keep 10 percent. That decision travels in the trace context, so every downstream service keeps or drops the same trace and traces stay complete. It's simple and cheap and done in the SDK, with the ParentBased and TraceIdRatioBased samplers in OpenTelemetry. The problem is it decides before you know whether the request will fail or be slow, so you also throw away 90 percent of your interesting error traces.

Tail-based sampling decides after the trace is complete, usually in an OpenTelemetry Collector or in the backend, which buffers all the spans for a short time. Then rules decide. Keep every trace with an error, keep everything slower than a second, keep traces for important endpoints, and a small percentage of the rest. You get all the interesting ones and only a few boring ones. What you pay for it is the collector has to receive every span and hold them in memory, and all spans of one trace must land on the same collector instance, so you need load balancing by trace id.

What I'd go with usually is little or no head sampling in the SDK and tail sampling in a collector gateway. One thing, compute metrics before sampling, so your rates and error percentages stay accurate.

p17-594.q: Right, so distributed tracing only works if every hop passes the trace context along, that's how each service's spans join the same trace.
p17-594.k: trace context propagation, traceparent header, w3c trace context, propagate trace through rabbitmq, distributed tracing messages
x: Right, so distributed tracing only works if every hop passes the trace context along, that's how each service's spans join the same trace.

The standard is W3C Trace Context. The traceparent header carries the trace id, the parent span id and the sampling flag, and tracestate carries vendor-specific stuff. Then there's baggage, a separate header for app key-value pairs like tenant id that should travel with the request. You use that carefully because it goes everywhere.

For HTTP, .NET just does it for you. HttpClient instrumentation adds traceparent on outgoing calls and ASP.NET Core reads it on incoming ones and creates a child Activity. Most other languages' OpenTelemetry instrumentation does the same, which is why a mixed .NET and Java system can still be traced end to end.

Messaging is where it's more manual and, in my experience, more often broken. The producer has to inject the context into the message headers or properties, and the consumer has to extract it and start its processing span as a child or with a link. Some libraries handle it, like for Kafka, Azure Service Bus, MassTransit and NServiceBus. For the raw RabbitMQ client, I add small helpers using OpenTelemetry's propagator API to inject and extract. For batch consumers, span links connect one processing span to many producer spans.
And where context just gets lost, like a legacy system in the middle or a file transfer, I carry a correlation id in the payload and log it, so you can still join the pieces.

p17-595.q: Let me start with what usually goes wrong. Most bad dashboards have way too many panels and no story. A good one answers specific questions fast, especially at 3 AM during an incident.
p17-595.k: grafana dashboard design, dashboard best practices, service dashboard, too many panels, dashboard hierarchy
x: Let me start with what usually goes wrong. Most bad dashboards have way too many panels and no story. A good one answers specific questions fast, especially at 3 AM during an incident.
So I start from the questions. Is the service healthy for users? What changed? Which dependency is the problem? Each panel should help answer one of those.

Then a hierarchy. The top-level overview shows every service's health in one place with RED metrics, request rate, error percentage, latency percentiles, plus SLO status. You click through to a service dashboard with the detail, endpoints, dependencies, resource usage with USE metrics, queue depths. And deeper than that, component dashboards for things like the database or the message broker.
On a page, the top is the user-facing signals and SLOs, and below that the causes, dependencies, saturation, infrastructure.

I add deployments and incidents as annotations, so "latency went up right after release 3.4.2" is obvious just by looking. Same time ranges and units, percentiles instead of averages, same colours for the same meaning.
Template variables for environment, region and service, so one dashboard serves all of them instead of copies that drift apart.
Links out, from a latency spike to the traces for that time range through exemplars, and then to logs.

Dashboards live as code, JSON or Terraform or Grafana provisioning, reviewed in pull requests, so they don't rot. And I'd say delete the ones nobody uses. A few dashboards people trust beat a hundred abandoned ones.

p17-596.q: Yeah, alert fatigue is when people get so many alerts, mostly unimportant or false, that they start ignoring them, and then they miss the real one. So it's a reliability risk and honestly a morale problem as well.
p17-596.k: alert fatigue, too many alerts, noisy alerts, actionable alerts, on call burnout, alert tuning
x: Yeah, alert fatigue is when people get so many alerts, mostly unimportant or false, that they start ignoring them, and then they miss the real one. So it's a reliability risk and honestly a morale problem as well.

My first rule is every page has to be actionable and urgent. If the response is "let's wait and see" or "nothing to do", it shouldn't wake anyone up. That becomes a ticket, a dashboard item or a daily digest.

Alert on symptoms, not causes. Users care about errors, latency and business processes failing, so alerts are based on SLOs and burn rates. High CPU on one instance is a cause, and if users aren't affected, it's not a page.

Tune thresholds and durations. A one-minute spike shouldn't page anybody. The condition has to hold for a sensible period, you add hysteresis so it doesn't flap, and use dynamic thresholds where traffic changes a lot by time of day.
Deduplicate and group. One incident should be one notification, not fifty from every instance and every dependent service. A "database down" alert can suppress the downstream ones.
Route it to the owning team, and let severity decide paging versus just a message. Put context in the alert, a clear title, which service, the impact, a dashboard link and the runbook.
And review it. After every on-call week, look at what fired, what was useful, and fix or delete the noisy ones. We track alerts per week as a metric, which keeps the pressure on.

p17-597.q: Okay so synthetic monitoring is basically scripted checks that run against the system on a schedule, from outside, like a fake user. Every few minutes it calls the health endpoint, logs in, opens the dashboard, searches for a shipment, and checks the results look right.
p17-597.k: synthetic monitoring, synthetic checks, uptime checks, canary scripts, cloudwatch synthetics, availability tests
x: Okay so synthetic monitoring is basically scripted checks that run against the system on a schedule, from outside, like a fake user. Every few minutes it calls the health endpoint, logs in, opens the dashboard, searches for a shipment, and checks the results look right.

Why do you need it when you already have real-user monitoring and server metrics? Mainly because it finds problems when there's no traffic. At night, at weekends, or on a rarely used feature, real users won't show you the outage until Monday morning, the synthetic check will. It also tests from the user side, so it catches stuff server metrics can't see, DNS issues, expired certificates, CDN or load balancer misconfig, a broken login with the identity provider, a front-end bundle error. It gives a steady baseline for availability and latency from different regions, which helps for SLA reporting. And you can run it right after a deployment as an automated smoke test.

There are simple uptime checks on URLs with status code, content and certificate expiry, API checks with multi-step calls, and browser checks scripted with Playwright or Selenium that walk full journeys. Tools like CloudWatch Synthetics canaries, Application Insights availability tests, Datadog Synthetics, Grafana, or just a scheduled Playwright job.

The thing to be careful about is test data. Use dedicated test accounts so synthetic transactions never pollute production data or reports. In a clinical system that's critical, you never create real patient or shipment records. And keep the scripts maintained, or they turn into noisy false alarms.

p17-598.q: So real user monitoring collects performance and error data from actual users' browsers. A small script or SDK in the app reports page loads, route changes, API call timings, JavaScript errors and sessions. Synthetic tests run from a fast data centre, but this shows what people on real devices, networks and locations actually go through.
p17-598.k: real user monitoring, rum, core web vitals, lcp inp cls, front end monitoring, page performance real users
x: So real user monitoring collects performance and error data from actual users' browsers. A small script or SDK in the app reports page loads, route changes, API call timings, JavaScript errors and sessions. Synthetic tests run from a fast data centre, but this shows what people on real devices, networks and locations actually go through.

The main metrics are Google's Core Web Vitals. LCP, Largest Contentful Paint, is how fast the main content shows up, good is under 2.5 seconds. INP, Interaction to Next Paint, which replaced First Input Delay, is how quickly the page responds to clicks and key presses, good is under 200 milliseconds. CLS, Cumulative Layout Shift, is how much stuff jumps around while loading, good is under 0.1. Time to First Byte is useful too for server and network speed, and for single-page apps I look at route change duration and the key API calls.
Look at percentiles, the 75th is what Core Web Vitals use, and break it down by page, browser, country and device. Averages hide the people having a bad time.

RUM tools also capture JavaScript errors with stack traces mapped through source maps, and they can link the front-end session to the back-end trace with trace context headers, so a slow screen can be followed right into the API and the database.

Tools wise, Datadog RUM, Application Insights for JavaScript, CloudWatch RUM, Sentry, or the open-source web-vitals library reporting to your own backend. And privacy, you mask inputs and never capture personal or clinical data in session replays.

p17-599.q: Honestly this is one of my favourite features. Metrics are aggregated, so they're cheap and great for spotting problems, but you lose the detail. The latency histogram says p99 jumped to three seconds, but not which requests were slow or why. Traces have that detail, but finding the right trace in millions is painful. Exemplars connect the two.
p17-599.k: exemplars, metrics to traces, exemplar prometheus, link metric spike to trace, grafana exemplars
x: Honestly this is one of my favourite features. Metrics are aggregated, so they're cheap and great for spotting problems, but you lose the detail. The latency histogram says p99 jumped to three seconds, but not which requests were slow or why. Traces have that detail, but finding the right trace in millions is painful. Exemplars connect the two.

An exemplar is a sample data point attached to a metric value, and it carries the trace id of a real request that contributed to it. When the service records a request duration in a histogram, the OpenTelemetry SDK can attach the current trace id as an exemplar for that bucket. Backends like Prometheus or Grafana Mimir keep a few exemplars next to the metric.

In Grafana they show up as dots on the latency graph. So during an incident I see the spike, hover over a dot in the slow area, and click straight into the trace in Tempo or whatever tracing backend you have. The trace shows exactly where the time went, maybe a database call that took 2.8 seconds. From there I jump to logs filtered by the same trace id.
So the investigation becomes metric to trace to logs in a few clicks, instead of guessing time ranges and searching around.

To make it work, exemplars have to be enabled in the SDK, OpenTelemetry .NET supports that with an exemplar filter. The trace has to actually be sampled, otherwise the link goes nowhere. And the backend has to support storing them. Commercial APM tools give you similar navigation built in.

p17-600.q: Okay, so Prometheus is an open-source monitoring system and time-series database. It pulls metrics, it scrapes an HTTP endpoint, usually slash metrics, on each target every so often, like every 15 seconds. In Kubernetes it finds targets on its own through service discovery and annotations or ServiceMonitor resources. A .NET app exposes metrics with the OpenTelemetry Prometheus exporter, or pushes over OTLP to the newer Prometheus versions that accept it.
p17-600.k: prometheus, promql, prometheus scraping, rate function promql, histogram_quantile, prometheus basics
x: Okay, so Prometheus is an open-source monitoring system and time-series database. It pulls metrics, it scrapes an HTTP endpoint, usually slash metrics, on each target every so often, like every 15 seconds. In Kubernetes it finds targets on its own through service discovery and annotations or ServiceMonitor resources. A .NET app exposes metrics with the OpenTelemetry Prometheus exporter, or pushes over OTLP to the newer Prometheus versions that accept it.
The data is time series identified by a metric name plus labels, like the HTTP server request duration metric with method, route and status code.

The queries I write most. Request rate, that's sum by route of the rate of the request duration count over five minutes. Rate gives you the per-second increase of a counter over that window. Error percentage is the rate of requests with a 5xx status divided by the rate of all requests, times 100. For latency percentiles you use histogram quantile with 0.95, over the sum by le and route of the rate of the bucket series over five minutes. The le label is basically the bucket boundary. And saturation, like memory used versus the limit per pod, is just dividing one metric by another, matched on labels.
Alert rules use the same expressions with a "for" duration. Prometheus evaluates them and Alertmanager groups, silences and routes the notifications.
For long-term storage or many clusters, people usually add Thanos or Mimir, or use a managed one, like Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus or Azure Monitor managed Prometheus, with Grafana on top.

p17-601.q: See, observability bills can quietly get bigger than the compute they're monitoring, mostly from log volume and high-cardinality metrics. So I manage it on purpose.
p17-601.k: logging cost, observability cost, reduce log volume, log retention, datadog bill, log sampling
x: See, observability bills can quietly get bigger than the compute they're monitoring, mostly from log volume and high-cardinality metrics. So I manage it on purpose.

Logs first. Log less but better, information level for events that matter, not every step, debug off in production, and no full request and response bodies by default. Noise gets dropped at the source or in the collector, health check requests, chatty library logs. High-volume, low-value stuff like successful request logs can be sampled, while warnings and errors are always kept. Retention is tiered, hot searchable storage for 7 to 30 days, then archived to cheap object storage for compliance, and only rehydrated when you need it. And if people keep running the same log query, turn it into a metric, way cheaper to store and query.

For metrics, watch cardinality and remove labels like user or request ids. Drop unused metrics too, a lot of exporters spit out hundreds of series nobody looks at. For traces, tail-based sampling, keep errors and slow ones, sample the rest.

Then visibility. Show each team the cost of its own telemetry by service tags, so whoever's generating it sees it. Put quotas or alerts on daily ingestion, that catches a bad deployment logging in a loop.

But I never cut audit logs or anything compliance needs, in a regulated domain those have their own retention rules. And keep enough detail to investigate incidents. Saving money and then being blind during an outage is a false economy.

p17-602.q: Actually this one bit us early on. With async systems, a healthy API doesn't mean a healthy system. Messages can pile up silently and nothing shows as an error. So I treat queues as proper first-class components.
p17-602.k: monitor message queue, consumer lag, queue depth alert, age of oldest message, rabbitmq monitoring, kafka lag monitoring
x: Actually this one bit us early on. With async systems, a healthy API doesn't mean a healthy system. Messages can pile up silently and nothing shows as an error. So I treat queues as proper first-class components.

The main thing is queue depth or consumer lag, how many messages are waiting. For RabbitMQ that's ready and unacknowledged messages per queue, for Kafka it's consumer group lag per partition, for SQS the approximate number of visible messages.

Then the age of the oldest message, which is often more meaningful than depth. 10,000 messages that are draining fast might be fine, but 20 messages stuck for an hour means something's wrong. SQS gives you that directly. For others, the consumer can record the time between publish and processing as a histogram.
Throughput, publish rate versus consume rate. If consuming is always lower, the backlog just keeps growing.
The dead-letter queue. Anything landing there needs attention, so I alert on DLQ depth above zero, with which message types.
And consumer health, number of connected consumers, processing errors, redelivery counts, processing time.

The alerts depend on what the business expects though. Shipment events older than five minutes during business hours is a problem. A nightly batch queue with 50,000 messages at 2 AM might be totally normal.

In our platform the RabbitMQ queues and their retry and dead-letter exchanges are monitored like this, and the Grafana dashboards show depth and age per queue right next to the consumers' error rates.

p17-603.q: So Splunk is where our older platform's logs go, through Serilog, so it's usually my first tool in an investigation. The query language, SPL, is a pipeline, kind of like KQL.
p17-603.k: splunk search, spl query, splunk investigation, splunk stats timechart, search logs splunk, splunk transaction
x: So Splunk is where our older platform's logs go, through Serilog, so it's usually my first tool in an investigation. The query language, SPL, is a pipeline, kind of like KQL.
I start by narrowing the scope. Index, sourcetype or application, environment, and a tight time range around when the problem started. If you search everything over all time, it's slow and expensive.

Then find the errors and the trend. Filter on level Error and the service name, then timechart count by exception type with a five-minute span. That tells me when it started and whether it's one error type or a bunch of them.
Next I group to find patterns. Stats count by endpoint, study or site and error message, sorted descending. If all the failures come from one site or one integration, that's your lead.

Then I follow one request. I take the correlation id from an error and search it across all services, sorted by time, so I can see the whole path. Our correlation id middleware puts the same id on every log line for a request, including the calls into other services.
And compare with normal, same query for yesterday or last week, to see if the volume is actually unusual.
Commands I use a lot are rex to pull a field out of unstructured text, eval to compute values, transaction or stats by correlation id to group a request's events, and dedup to cut the noise.
Good searches become alerts or dashboard panels. And honestly structured logging makes a huge difference, with JSON fields your searches are precise instead of fragile text matching.

p17-604.q: In our setup the newest services send OpenTelemetry data to Datadog, so APM is where I start for anything performance related.
p17-604.k: datadog apm, datadog traces, flame graph, datadog service map, apm performance investigation
x: In our setup the newest services send OpenTelemetry data to Datadog, so APM is where I start for anything performance related.

The service page gives you RED metrics per endpoint, requests, errors and latency percentiles, with deployment markers. So I check which endpoints got slower and when, and whether that lines up with a deployment, a traffic increase or a change in some dependency.

The service map shows the dependencies with latency and errors on each edge. That quickly tells you whether the time is going in our service or in a downstream call, the database, another API, the broker.

Then I open traces for the slow endpoint, filtered to the slow ones, say above p95. The flame graph shows every span, the controller, the EF Core or SQL span with the query text, HTTP calls to other services, cache calls. What I usually find is one of a few things. A single slow query. Lots of repeated queries, the N plus one pattern. Sequential calls that could have run in parallel. A gap before the first span, which points to thread pool or connection pool starvation. Or retries hiding inside an HTTP span.
From the trace, the logs with the same trace id are one click away, and Database Monitoring shows the execution plan and wait events for that query.
If the continuous profiler is on, it shows which methods burn CPU and allocate memory, which helps when it's CPU-bound and traces can't explain it.
Then I fix it, deploy, and compare the same views before and after to make sure it actually helped.

p17-605.q: Yeah, this is a sneaky one. Normal alerting catches things that fail loudly, an error, an exception. A job that never starts produces no errors at all. Maybe the scheduler got stopped, a server was patched and not restarted, a trigger is misconfigured, or the job just hangs forever. Nothing alerts, and the business finds out days later that no reports or reconciliations happened.
p17-605.k: dead man switch, heartbeat monitoring, cron job monitoring, job did not run alert, missing job execution, watchdog job
x: Yeah, this is a sneaky one. Normal alerting catches things that fail loudly, an error, an exception. A job that never starts produces no errors at all. Maybe the scheduler got stopped, a server was patched and not restarted, a trigger is misconfigured, or the job just hangs forever. Nothing alerts, and the business finds out days later that no reports or reconciliations happened.
So the fix is to alert on the absence of a signal. People call it a heartbeat or a dead man's switch.

How it works is each job, when it completes successfully, sends a heartbeat. That can be a ping to a monitoring service, a metric like last success timestamp, or a row in a job history table. Then a separate monitor knows the expected schedule, like every hour, or daily at 2 AM plus some grace period, and alerts if no heartbeat turns up in time. Healthchecks.io, Cronitor, Datadog, or CloudWatch alarms with "treat missing data as breaching" all support this.

I'd also watch the duration, a job that normally takes five minutes and now takes three hours is a warning. Output sanity too, like records processed being zero when it's normally thousands. And overlap, a run starting before the last one finished.

This is a big part of what our AlertWatchDog does on the platform side. Quartz jobs that check the expected events actually happened, and raise an alert when they didn't. And the watchdog itself is monitored, because if it stops, nothing else is going to notice.

p17-606.q: For me on-call works when whoever gets paged can act fast without needing the one expert who wrote the code. Good runbooks and a sensible rotation are what make that possible.
p17-606.k: runbook, on call process, incident runbook, playbook operations, on call rotation, escalation policy
x: For me on-call works when whoever gets paged can act fast without needing the one expert who wrote the code. Good runbooks and a sensible rotation are what make that possible.

Every alert links to a runbook, and the runbook answers a few things. What the alert means and what the user impact is. How to confirm it's real, with direct links to the dashboard and log queries. Likely causes from past incidents. Step-by-step mitigations, like restarting a consumer, failing over, scaling out, replaying the dead-letter queue, switching off a feature flag. What not to do, like never purge a queue that has unprocessed clinical events. And when and how to escalate. Keep it short and specific, next to the code or in a wiki the team actually updates after incidents.
Over time the steps people repeat become automation, a button or script that does the safe mitigation and logs it. So humans decide and tools execute.

For the rotation, usually weekly, with a primary and a secondary, clear escalation to subject matter experts and managers, and a handover at the end of each shift covering open issues. And there's a limit on load. If someone's getting paged every night, the system needs fixing, not a tougher engineer. Severity routing makes sure only urgent, user-impacting stuff pages.

After incidents we do a blameless review, and the action items often improve the alerts and runbooks. And in a regulated environment, anything you do on production during on-call is a controlled change too, recorded with who did what and why.

p17-607.q: Honestly, the whole point is to turn an outage into improvements. Blameless means we assume everyone acted reasonably with what they knew at the time, and we look at how the system, process and tools let it happen, not who messed up. If people are scared of blame, they hide details and you learn nothing.
p17-607.k: postmortem, blameless postmortem, post incident review, root cause analysis, incident retrospective, five whys
x: Honestly, the whole point is to turn an outage into improvements. Blameless means we assume everyone acted reasonably with what they knew at the time, and we look at how the system, process and tools let it happen, not who messed up. If people are scared of blame, they hide details and you learn nothing.

How I run one. Facts first. I build a timeline from alerts, logs, chat messages and deployment records. When it started, when it was detected and by whom, what actions were taken, when it got resolved. Plus the impact, which users, how long, and whether any data was affected.

Then the contributing factors, not one single root cause. It's usually a few things together, a code change with an edge case, a missing test, an alert that didn't fire, an outdated runbook, a manual step done under pressure. Five whys helps, applied to each factor. And I ask what went well too, like a fast rollback.
I also look at detection and response, not just the trigger. Why did it take 40 minutes to notice? Why was diagnosis slow?

Then action items, each with an owner and a date, ordered by impact. A test, an alert, an automated safety check, maybe a design change. A few good actions that actually get done beat a long wish list.

The write-up gets shared widely, other teams learn from it, and we track the actions until they're closed. In our regulated context it also feeds the formal deviation or CAPA process when validated functionality was affected.

p17-608.q: So I treat observability as part of the feature's definition of done. Not something you bolt on after the first incident.
p17-608.k: observability driven development, instrument new feature, telemetry for new feature, release monitoring plan, measure feature health
x: So I treat observability as part of the feature's definition of done. Not something you bolt on after the first incident.
Before I write code I ask two questions. How will we know this works in production, and how will we know when it doesn't? That gives me a short list of signals.
Logs, information level for the key business events in the feature, with structured fields like study, site and outcome, and clear error logs with context when it fails. No personal data, obviously.
Metrics, a counter for the main operations by outcome, a histogram for duration, and a business metric if there is one, like the number of returns processed in the new DARM flow.
Traces, custom spans around the important internal steps, like calculating an allocation or calling an external system, with useful attributes, so a slow request shows you where the time went.
Then a panel or small dashboard for the feature, and alerts if the failure rate crosses a threshold or the expected events just stop.

For the release, if it's behind a flag, I compare the signals with flag on and flag off, and check them right after rollout to each environment and each batch of users. If the numbers look wrong, the flag goes off.

And I test the telemetry itself. In integration tests, or with FakeLogger and metric collectors, I check the important logs and metrics actually get emitted. I learned that the hard way, missing telemetry always gets discovered at the worst possible moment.

p17-609.q: Let me explain where it fits. Traces tell you which request and which span was slow, but not which line of code inside the service burned the CPU or allocated all that memory. Continuous profiling covers that.
p17-609.k: continuous profiling, production profiler, cpu profiling production, pyroscope, datadog profiler, flame graph cpu
x: Let me explain where it fits. Traces tell you which request and which span was slow, but not which line of code inside the service burned the CPU or allocated all that memory. Continuous profiling covers that.

A profiler runs inside the app in production, all the time, with low overhead, usually a few percent, by sampling stack traces many times a second. It records where CPU time goes, which methods allocate, where threads wait on locks, which exceptions get thrown. It's aggregated over time and shown as flame graphs you can filter by service, version, endpoint and host.

Tools would be Datadog Continuous Profiler, which supports .NET, Grafana Pyroscope, the Application Insights Profiler on Azure, Amazon CodeGuru Profiler for some runtimes, and the OpenTelemetry profiling signal, which is still maturing.

Where it helps most is when CPU is high but no endpoint looks especially slow. The profile shows the hot method, like JSON serialising a huge object, a regex getting compiled on every call, or a LINQ query re-evaluated inside a loop. Memory and GC pressure, the allocation profile tells you what's allocating, large strings or lists built per request. Comparing versions, you diff profiles before and after a deployment and see exactly what got more expensive. And cost, fixing the top hot spots can reduce instance counts.

Compared with a one-off dotnet-trace, the big thing is the data's already there from when the problem happened, which matters a lot for intermittent issues you can't reproduce. Profiles can have method names and types, but never actual data values.

p17-610.q: Okay, so two things in order. Protect the users, and grab the evidence before it disappears.
p17-610.k: iis high cpu, w3wp high cpu, app pool cpu 100, dotnet framework cpu spike, debugdiag, procdump cpu
x: Okay, so two things in order. Protect the users, and grab the evidence before it disappears.

Quick checks first. Is it one server or all of them? Did it start after a deployment, a traffic spike, a scheduled job? If it's one server behind the load balancer, I pull it out of rotation so users go to the healthy ones. But I don't recycle the app pool yet, because a recycle wipes out the evidence.

Then I capture. Two or three memory dumps of the w3wp process, about 10 to 20 seconds apart, using ProcDump with a CPU threshold trigger, or DebugDiag, or just Task Manager's create dump file. I also note which requests are executing, from the worker processes view in IIS Manager or the request monitoring logs, and check Performance Monitor counters like requests queued and percent time in GC.
Then I recycle to get the service back.

For analysis I open the dumps in DebugDiag's analysis or WinDbg with the SOS extension and look at what the busy threads are doing across the dumps. If the same threads are in the same code every time, that's your hot spot. What I've seen usually is an infinite or really long loop on some unexpected data, a regex with catastrophic backtracking, heavy GC from massive allocations, which shows up as high time in GC, or lock contention with threads spinning.
After that, fix the code, add a test with the data that triggered it, and add an alert on sustained CPU so next time we see it earlier.

p17-611.q: Actually a regular pattern is kind of good news. Regular means something scheduled or cyclic is causing it, so I go looking for things with the same period.
p17-611.k: periodic latency spikes, latency every few minutes, regular spikes, cache expiry spike, gc pause spike, cron job latency
x: Actually a regular pattern is kind of good news. Regular means something scheduled or cyclic is causing it, so I go looking for things with the same period.
I measure the period exactly from the latency graph. Every 5 minutes, every 15, on the hour? Then I line it up against the usual suspects.

Cache expiry is a common one. Lots of entries with the same absolute expiration, say five minutes, all expire together and a burst of requests hits the database at once. The fix is jittered expiration, refresh-ahead, or stampede protection like HybridCache.

Scheduled jobs. A Quartz job, cron, SQL Agent job, backup or index maintenance running on that schedule and fighting for the database or CPU. So I check job schedules and database activity at those exact times.

Garbage collection. Big gen 2 collections when memory builds up to a threshold, you see it in the GC metrics with pause times matching the spikes. Usually it's allocation-heavy code or large object heap usage.
Token or connection refresh. Credentials, certificates or config refreshed periodically and blocking requests while it happens, or connection pools recycling connections at a fixed lifetime.
And infrastructure, health check or autoscaling cycles, log shipping bursts, or noisy neighbours on shared hosts with their own schedules.

Once I've got a candidate, I correlate its metric with the spikes, change one thing, and watch if the pattern goes away. Traces of slow requests during a spike usually point you straight at whatever is waiting.

p17-612.q: So the timing basically makes the release suspect number one. I work from what changed, and try to keep the system usable while I do it.
p17-612.k: database cpu 100 after release, sql server cpu spike, bad query after deployment, regression query plan, db cpu high
x: So the timing basically makes the release suspect number one. I work from what changed, and try to keep the system usable while I do it.

I find the expensive queries right away. In SQL Server that's sys dot dm exec requests and the query stats DMV ordered by CPU, or Query Store's top resource-consuming queries for the last hour compared with the previous period. Usually it's one or two queries eating everything.

Then the question is, is it a new query from the release, or an old query that changed plan? New queries could be an EF Core change that now loads related data with a huge join, a missing filter, an N plus one pattern firing thousands of small queries, a LINQ expression that translates badly, or a new feature without the index it needs. A changed plan would be a schema or statistics change in the release giving a worse plan, or a new parameter pattern.

For mitigation I go quickest first. If a feature flag controls the new code, switch it off. If it's a plan regression, Query Store can force the old good plan. If an index is clearly missing, adding it online is often quick and low risk. If none of that works and the impact is serious, roll back the app release, as long as the database changes are backward compatible.

Then the real fix, rewrite or index the query and test it with production-sized data. And I'd add a check to the release process, like comparing query performance in a perf environment, because slow queries usually slip through when tests run on tiny data.

p17-613.q: Honestly, if the code didn't change, then the data changed or the plan changed. That's where I look.
p17-613.k: query suddenly slow, parameter sniffing, statistics out of date, plan regression, same query slow today
x: Honestly, if the code didn't change, then the data changed or the plan changed. That's where I look.

Plan change is my first guess. SQL Server compiles a plan using the parameter values from the first execution and caches it. If it got recompiled, after a restart, a stats update, memory pressure, with some unusual value, like a site with very few rows, you might get a nested loop plan that's terrible for the typical values with lots of rows. That's parameter sniffing. Query Store shows the query's plans over time, so I can see the plan change and the duration jump. Quick fix is to force the good plan in Query Store. Longer term, OPTION RECOMPILE for queries with wildly varying parameters, OPTIMIZE FOR, or restructuring the query. SQL Server 2022 also has parameter sensitive plan optimisation.
Statistics. After big data loads they can be stale, so the optimiser underestimates row counts. Updating stats fixes it more often than you'd think.
Data growth or skew. A table crossed some size where the plan or memory grant doesn't fit anymore, or one customer's data grew massively.
Blocking. The query's fine but it's waiting on locks from another process, like a new batch job. Wait stats and the requests DMV tell you if it's running or waiting.
And resource pressure, other workloads on the same server, tempdb contention, I/O problems.
I compare the actual execution plans from before and after and look at the waits. That usually tells you which of these it is pretty quickly.

p17-614.q: See, a stampede is when a popular cached item expires, or a restart empties the cache, and lots of concurrent requests all miss at the same time and run the same expensive query together. The database suddenly gets hundreds of identical queries, slows down, and that makes even more requests pile up. It's a classic outage right after a cache restart or a deployment.
p17-614.k: cache stampede, thundering herd, dog piling, cache expiry overload, hybridcache stampede protection, cache warmup
x: See, a stampede is when a popular cached item expires, or a restart empties the cache, and lots of concurrent requests all miss at the same time and run the same expensive query together. The database suddenly gets hundreds of identical queries, slows down, and that makes even more requests pile up. It's a classic outage right after a cache restart or a deployment.

How I prevent it. Request coalescing, so only one request recomputes a given key and the others wait for that result. In .NET 9, HybridCache does this automatically for concurrent callers in the same process. Otherwise a per-key SemaphoreSlim or a Lazy task does it, and across servers a short distributed lock in Redis.
Jittered expiration. Add a random bit to each item's TTL so they don't all expire at the same moment.

Refresh ahead. Popular items get refreshed in the background before they expire, so users never see a miss. Stale-while-revalidate is similar, you serve the slightly old value while one request refreshes it.
Warm up the known hot keys after deployments or cache restarts, before taking full traffic.
And protect the database anyway. Limit concurrency on expensive queries with a bulkhead and put a circuit breaker in, so even if the cache fails badly, the database survives and recovers.
I'd also monitor the cache hit ratio, so a sudden drop alerts us before the database falls over. That's usually the earliest sign something's off.

p17-615.q: It depends on how we use Redis and how the app handles it failing. That's why I'd rather design for it before it happens.
p17-615.k: redis down, cache unavailable, redis outage, redis failover, cache server down, graceful degradation cache
x: It depends on how we use Redis and how the app handles it failing. That's why I'd rather design for it before it happens.

If Redis is purely a cache, you want graceful degradation. Cache calls fail fast with a short timeout, get caught, logged and counted, and the app goes to the database. Users see slower responses but everything works. The risks are, every request might wait for a long Redis timeout before falling back, so timeouts must be short and a circuit breaker should skip Redis completely while it's down. And the database suddenly gets the full load, so it needs headroom, or we limit concurrency on expensive queries.

If Redis holds state, like sessions, distributed locks, rate-limit counters or data protection keys, it's a bigger deal. Users get logged out, locks aren't available, rate limiting fails open or closed. Each one needs a deliberate choice, like fail open for rate limits but fail safe for locks.

During the incident, I confirm with Redis metrics and connection errors. Check if a replica failed over, in Sentinel, cluster or a managed service, because clients might need to reconnect. Check memory, evictions and maxclients, since Redis going down is very often memory exhaustion. And tell people about the impact.
Afterwards, replicas with automatic failover, alerts on memory and connections, and stampede protection for when the cache comes back empty.
In our platform, Redis caches configuration and reference data, so the fallback is just the database, with short timeouts.

p17-616.q: Okay, a growing queue means messages are coming in faster than they're processed. So I figure out which side changed.
p17-616.k: rabbitmq queue growing, message backlog, queue depth increasing, consumers too slow, rabbitmq backlog, unacked messages growing
x: Okay, a growing queue means messages are coming in faster than they're processed. So I figure out which side changed.

What I do is check consumers first. In the management UI or metrics, how many consumers are connected and what's the consume rate? If it dropped to zero, they crashed, lost the connection, or a deployment stopped them. If they're connected but slow, I look at unacknowledged messages. High unacked with a low prefetch can mean consumers are stuck on slow work, like a slow database call or a dependency timing out. Consumer logs and traces show what each message is waiting on.

Then poison messages. A message that keeps failing and gets requeued goes back to the head and blocks progress. With a proper retry and dead-letter setup it moves aside after a few attempts. Without that it just loops forever.
Then the producer. Did the publish rate spike, like a batch import, a retry storm upstream, or a bug publishing duplicates?

Then act. Scale out consumers if the work can run in parallel and the downstream dependency, usually the database, can take more load. Fix the slow dependency. Move poison messages to the DLQ. Throttle the producer if you can. And with big backlogs, check the broker has enough memory and disk, because RabbitMQ blocks publishers when memory or disk alarms trigger, and then the problem spreads upstream.
Afterwards I'd add alerts on queue depth and age of the oldest message, and autoscale consumers on queue length so it handles itself next time.

p17-617.q: Yeah, a full disk breaks things in weird ways. Logging fails, databases stop writing, uploads fail, services won't start, sometimes the OS itself gets unstable. So I move quickly, but carefully.
p17-617.k: disk full production, no space left on device, disk space alert, log files filling disk, clean disk server
x: Yeah, a full disk breaks things in weird ways. Logging fails, databases stop writing, uploads fail, services won't start, sometimes the OS itself gets unstable. So I move quickly, but carefully.

First find what's using the space. On Windows, TreeSize or a PowerShell query for the biggest folders. On Linux, df to see which volume is full, then du or ncdu to find the big directories. The usual suspects are app logs with no rotation, IIS logs nobody ever cleans, crash dumps, temp files from uploads or exports, old deployment folders kept after every release, database transaction logs or backups, and Docker images and container logs.

Then free space safely. Delete or compress the clearly disposable stuff, old rotated logs, old dumps after copying anything needed, temp files, deployment folders beyond the last few. I never delete files I don't understand, and never touch database files or active transaction logs. Those need proper database actions, like a log backup.
One thing that catches people out, on Linux a deleted file that's still held open doesn't free space until the process closes it. So you might need to restart the logging process.
Then restore service and check everything actually recovered, because some components need a restart after write failures.

And prevent it. Log rotation and retention, cleanup jobs for temp files and old releases, logs shipped to central logging instead of sitting locally, and disk alerts at 80 and 90 percent with a time-to-full forecast.

p17-618.q: So an expired cert fails everything immediately. Browsers show warnings, API clients refuse to connect, service-to-service calls fail with trust errors. Recovery is all about speed.
p17-618.k: certificate expired, ssl certificate expired production, tls cert expiry outage, certificate monitoring, auto renew certificate
x: So an expired cert fails everything immediately. Browsers show warnings, API clients refuse to connect, service-to-service calls fail with trust errors. Recovery is all about speed.

First I identify exactly which certificate expired and where it's used. Sometimes it's not the website cert at all, it's an internal one, like a client certificate for a partner integration, a token signing cert, or one on an internal API. That makes it less obvious. The error logs will mention certificate validation or the remote certificate being invalid.

Then get it renewed from the CA or the internal PKI and install it everywhere it's used, load balancers, IIS bindings on every server, API gateways, Kubernetes secrets, and restart or rebind where needed. Then test from outside, the full chain, with openssl s_client or an SSL checker. A missing intermediate certificate is a really common second failure.

Prevention matters more, because an expired cert is almost always a process failure. Keep an inventory of every certificate with an owner and expiry date.
