Automate renewal where you can, ACME with Let's Encrypt or cert-manager in Kubernetes, AWS Certificate Manager, Key Vault auto-renewal. Monitor expiry from outside with synthetic checks alerting at 30, 14 and 7 days, including internal and client certs. And make sure the renewal reaches every location automatically, not just the first one somebody remembers. I've seen that happen, one server renewed and the other two forgotten.

p17-619.q: Right, errors like "No such host is known" or "Name or service not known" mean the app couldn't turn a hostname into an IP. The first thing I ask is, is it one host or all hosts, one server or all servers, constant or intermittent?
p17-619.k: dns resolution failure, name not resolved, no such host is known, dns errors production, dns troubleshooting
x: Right, errors like "No such host is known" or "Name or service not known" mean the app couldn't turn a hostname into an IP. The first thing I ask is, is it one host or all hosts, one server or all servers, constant or intermittent?

Then I test from the same place the app runs. nslookup or dig on the affected server or inside the container, and compare with a machine that works. Check which DNS server it's using, resolv.conf in Linux containers, adapter settings on Windows.
The usual causes. The record changed or got removed, a partner moved their API, someone deleted a record, a private endpoint changed. So check the authoritative DNS directly.
Private DNS. A service moved behind a private endpoint but the private DNS zone isn't linked to this network, so the name resolves to a public IP or nothing.

Resolver overload or limits. In Kubernetes, CoreDNS under heavy load, or the ndots setting making every lookup try several search domains first. On AWS there's a per-network-interface DNS query limit. Fixes are caching, NodeLocal DNSCache, and fully qualified names with a trailing dot.
Network, like firewall or security group changes blocking port 53, UDP and TCP, to the DNS servers.
And caching, stale entries after a change, in the OS, the runtime, or HttpClient's long-lived connections. Setting PooledConnectionLifetime helps there so it picks up DNS changes.
From what I've seen, intermittent failures usually mean overload or one bad DNS server in the list.

p17-620.q: Actually "off by one day" is almost always a time zone conversion happening where it shouldn't, or not happening where it should.
p17-620.k: date off by one day, time zone bug, utc conversion bug, date shifted timezone, datetime kind bug, visit date wrong timezone
x: Actually "off by one day" is almost always a time zone conversion happening where it shouldn't, or not happening where it should.

The most common one I've seen is a date-only value stored as a date-time at midnight. A visit date of 10 March gets stored as 10 March midnight local, converted to UTC, so for India it becomes 9 March 18:30 UTC, and then somewhere it's displayed as 9 March. Or the browser parses the string 2025-03-10 as UTC midnight with new Date, and users west of UTC see 9 March. The fix is to treat date-only values as dates. DateOnly in .NET, and plain date strings or a date library on the front end, with no time zone conversion at all.

Mixed DateTime kinds. A DateTime with Kind Unspecified gets treated as local on one server and UTC on another, especially when servers in different regions have different time zones. So store and send instants as UTC or DateTimeOffset, and convert to local only for display.
Wrong time zone for business rules. Something like "visit window ends at end of day" has to use the site's time zone, not the server's or the user's browser.
And daylight saving, where a day has 23 or 25 hours, breaks code that adds 24 hours instead of one calendar day.
So the fix includes tests across time zones, India, US, far-east sites, and around DST changes. I'd also run a test server in a non-UTC zone, that exposes hidden assumptions fast.

p17-621.q: Let me think about it this way, duplicates mean something ran twice. So I find what ran twice and why.
p17-621.k: duplicate emails, duplicate notifications, users get two emails, notification sent twice, idempotent notifications
x: Let me think about it this way, duplicates mean something ran twice. So I find what ran twice and why.

I start with facts. Which notifications, for which events, since when, and are the duplicates identical in content and timing? Exact duplicates seconds apart point to retries or concurrent processing. Hours apart, more like a scheduled job re-running or a replay.

Common causes. Message redelivery, the consumer sent the email, then failed or timed out before acking, so the broker delivered it again. With at-least-once delivery that will happen sometimes. Retries, the HTTP call to the email provider timed out but actually succeeded, and the retry sent it again. Multiple instances, a scheduled job like a daily reminder running on every server instead of one. That often shows up exactly when you scale out from one server to two. And duplicate events, the publisher emitted it twice, from two code paths or a DLQ replay.

The fixes. Make sending idempotent. Record each notification with a unique key, like event id plus recipient plus template, in a table with a unique constraint, and skip if it's already there, before sending or atomically with it. Use the provider's idempotency key if they support one. Make scheduled jobs run once with clustering or a distributed lock. And consumers dedupe by message id.
I'd also deal with the user side, explaining and apologising if needed, and add a metric for notifications per event, so duplicates actually show up somewhere.

p17-622.q: So if the code really is identical, the difference is in the environment. I compare things one by one instead of guessing.
p17-622.k: works on one server not another, config drift, environment difference, server inconsistency, same build different behavior
x: So if the code really is identical, the difference is in the environment. I compare things one by one instead of guessing.

Step one, verify it's actually the same version. File versions and hashes of the deployed binaries, the build number from a version endpoint, the deployment logs for that server. Partial deployments, where some files didn't copy because they were locked, are surprisingly common.

Then configuration. web.config or appsettings, environment variables, IIS settings like app pool identity, CLR version, 32-bit mode, pipeline mode, machine-level config. Export them and run a diff tool, that shows the differences fast.

Then runtime and OS. Installed .NET versions, Windows patches, TLS settings and cipher suites in the registry, installed certificates and their private key permissions, regional settings and time zone, which affect how dates and numbers get parsed.

Dependencies and network. Connection strings pointing to different databases, firewall rules, DNS, proxy settings, access to file shares. And permissions, what the app pool identity can access on folders, certs and databases.

Once I find it, I fix that difference. But honestly the real fix is stopping drift. Infrastructure and config defined as code, servers built from the same scripts, configuration applied by the pipeline and not by hand, and periodic drift detection that compares servers against what's expected.

p17-623.q: Honestly, it's nearly always caching plus code splitting.
p17-623.k: blank page after deployment, chunkloaderror, old version after release, spa cache issue, failed to fetch dynamically imported module
x: Honestly, it's nearly always caching plus code splitting.
A single-page app loads index dot html, which points to bundles with hashed names, like main dot some hash dot js, and lazy-loaded chunks. Two things go wrong after a release.

One is a stale index.html. If the browser, a proxy or the CDN cached it, users keep loading the old version, which might call APIs that changed. The fix is serving index.html with Cache-Control no-cache, so the browser revalidates every time, while the hashed assets get long cache times.

The other is missing old chunks. A user has the old app open, goes to a lazy route, and the old chunk it wants doesn't exist anymore because the deployment replaced all the files. The browser throws ChunkLoadError or "Failed to fetch dynamically imported module", and the route is just blank. So keep previous versions' assets around for a while after deploying instead of deleting them, and in the app, catch chunk load errors and reload the page once, which picks up the new index.html.
Service workers can also keep serving the old version until every tab closes. You need a proper update flow that detects a new version and asks the user to refresh.

Other blank-page causes are a JavaScript error early in startup on some browsers, missing runtime config, or a wrong base href on a sub-path. The browser console and front-end error tracking will tell you which, so I'd check those first.

p17-624.q: So in a single-page app with HTML5 routing, a URL like slash shipments slash 123 is handled by the router inside the browser. Moving around inside the app works fine because nothing goes to the server. But when you refresh, or open a bookmarked link, the browser actually asks IIS for slash shipments slash 123. IIS looks for that file, doesn't find it, and gives you a 404.
p17-624.k: spa refresh 404 iis, angular deep link 404, react router 404 refresh, url rewrite spa, history api fallback iis
x: So in a single-page app with HTML5 routing, a URL like slash shipments slash 123 is handled by the router inside the browser. Moving around inside the app works fine because nothing goes to the server. But when you refresh, or open a bookmarked link, the browser actually asks IIS for slash shipments slash 123. IIS looks for that file, doesn't find it, and gives you a 404.
The fix is a fallback rule. Any request that isn't a real file, a real folder or an API route should return index.html, and then the router shows the right screen.

On IIS I install the URL Rewrite module and add a rule in web.config. Match all URLs, with conditions that it's not a file, not a directory, and doesn't start with slash api, and then rewrite, not redirect, to slash index.html or the app's base path. If the app lives under a virtual directory, say slash study-admin, the base href in index.html and the rewrite target both need that path, otherwise the assets don't load.

Other hosts have the same idea. try_files in nginx, custom error responses or a function in CloudFront, navigationFallback in Azure Static Web Apps, and MapFallbackToFile in ASP.NET Core when it's serving the SPA.

One thing people miss, API calls to a route that doesn't exist should still get a real 404, not index.html. That's why the API exclusion matters. Otherwise the client gets HTML when it expects JSON and fails with a really confusing parse error.

p17-625.q: Okay, so CORS errors mean the browser's preflight or response check failed. I go to the network tab to find out why, not just the console message.
p17-625.k: cors error after deployment, no access-control-allow-origin, preflight failed, cors production issue, options request failing
x: Okay, so CORS errors mean the browser's preflight or response check failed. I go to the network tab to find out why, not just the console message.

I look at the actual request. Was it the OPTIONS preflight that failed or the real request? What status did it get? A CORS error often hides a different problem. If the API returned 500, 404 or 401 without CORS headers, the browser just calls it a CORS error. So a broken API, a wrong route after deployment, or an auth failure can all look like CORS.

Then what changed in the deployment. Allowed origins, maybe the new environment's front-end URL isn't in the list, or there's a trailing slash, http versus https, or a port difference. Origins have to match exactly.
Middleware order in ASP.NET Core. UseCors has to come after UseRouting and before UseAuthorization, and before anything that short-circuits, otherwise auth rejects the preflight.
Infrastructure. A new proxy, gateway or IIS setting stripping headers, or IIS handling OPTIONS itself through WebDAV or the OPTIONS verb handler before the app even sees it.
Credentials. If the front end sends cookies, you can't combine AllowAnyOrigin with AllowCredentials, the origin has to be listed explicitly.
Custom headers. If the front end started sending a new header, like a correlation id, it has to be in the allowed headers.
Longer term, I keep origin lists per environment in configuration, and add an automated smoke test that makes a cross-origin call after every deployment.

p17-626.q: See, when everything returns 401 at once, it's usually token validation failing for everybody, not someone's credentials. The JWT bearer handler logs the exact reason at information or debug level, and the WWW-Authenticate header often has it too, so that's where I start.
p17-626.k: all requests 401, jwt validation failed, signing key rotation 401, issuer mismatch, audience mismatch, 401 after keycloak change
x: See, when everything returns 401 at once, it's usually token validation failing for everybody, not someone's credentials. The JWT bearer handler logs the exact reason at information or debug level, and the WWW-Authenticate header often has it too, so that's where I start.

Most common is signing key rotation. The identity provider, like Keycloak, rotated its keys, and the API is still validating with the old ones, maybe because keys were configured statically instead of read from the JWKS endpoint, or there's a long cache. The error says the signature key wasn't found, with a kid. The fix is to always use the metadata and JWKS endpoints, which the handler refreshes automatically, and make sure the API can actually reach them through the firewall and proxy.

Issuer mismatch. The realm name, hostname or scheme changed, so the iss claim doesn't match the configured authority anymore. Behind proxies, the internal and external URLs can give different issuers.
Audience mismatch. The client config changed and tokens don't include the API's audience anymore.
Clock skew. A server clock drifted, so tokens look expired or not valid yet. Check NTP.
Network. The API can't download the metadata at all, so every validation fails.
And the front-end side. The client id or scopes changed, so it's getting tokens for something else, or the interceptor stopped attaching tokens.
What I usually do is decode a failing token in a safe local tool and compare its iss, aud, kid and expiry against the API's config. That shows the mismatch in about a minute.

p17-627.q: Actually it's usually because the role is baked into a token or session that hasn't been refreshed yet.
p17-627.k: role change not applied, stale claims, permissions not updated, token claims stale, user still has access after removal
x: Actually it's usually because the role is baked into a token or session that hasn't been refreshed yet.

Access tokens are self-contained. When the identity provider issues a JWT, the roles in it are fixed until it expires. So if an admin adds a role, the user's current token doesn't have it, and they keep getting 403 until they get a new token. And the worse case, when a role is removed, the user keeps access until the token expires. Cookie sessions that store claims behave the same way until the session refreshes.

There are other places it gets stuck too. The app caches permissions in memory or Redis. The front end caches the user's profile and shows or hides menus based on old data. Or the role was changed in the identity provider, but the app maps roles from its own database, which nobody updated.

How I handle it. Keep access tokens short-lived, five to fifteen minutes, so changes come through on the normal refresh. For removing access, which is the security-sensitive one, don't wait. Revoke the user's sessions and refresh tokens in the identity provider, and for really sensitive apps, check permissions server-side per request, or use a revocation list or a security stamp checked on each call. Clear permission caches on role changes through events. On the front end, refresh the profile after changes, and never rely on the front end to enforce anything.
And tell the support teams about the expected delay, so they don't raise bugs for what's normal behaviour.

p17-628.q: Honestly, the worst thing is hammering them with retries. A 429 means we're over the partner's rate limit, and retrying harder makes it worse and can get us blocked. So I handle it on our side.
p17-628.k: third party api 429, rate limited by partner, too many requests external api, throttled by vendor, retry-after handling
x: Honestly, the worst thing is hammering them with retries. A 429 means we're over the partner's rate limit, and retrying harder makes it worse and can get us blocked. So I handle it on our side.

Right away, respect Retry-After. If they say wait 30 seconds, we wait. Then check our retry policy isn't amplifying it, like three retries from each of ten instances turning one failure into thirty calls. And slow down, reduce concurrency for that client, pause non-urgent stuff like background syncs, and prioritise calls that matter to users.

Then understand why. Did our traffic grow? Did a new feature or a bug cause a burst, like an N plus one pattern calling the API once per item? Or did the partner lower the limit? I check our calls-per-minute metric for that API, and the partner's docs or dashboard for our quota.

Longer term, client-side rate limiting. A shared limiter across all instances, like a token bucket in Redis, or send all calls through one queue-based worker that goes at a controlled pace. Cache responses that don't change much. Use batch endpoints if they have them, instead of one call per item. Spread scheduled jobs out instead of everything at the top of the hour. And if our usage is legitimate, just ask the partner for a higher limit.
And monitor it, track the 429 rate and the remaining-quota headers if they send them, with an alert before we actually hit the limit.

p17-629.q: So my order is stop the damage, fix it, then protect against next time.
p17-629.k: partner api changed, breaking change external api, integration broke, deserialization error partner, vendor api contract change
x: So my order is stop the damage, fix it, then protect against next time.

To contain it, I find the failing integration from the errors, usually deserialisation failures or missing fields. If messages or files are failing, I make sure they're kept, in a dead-letter queue or an error folder, not lost, so we can reprocess them. If the integration is writing bad data instead of failing, which is actually worse, I pause it.

Then understand the change. Capture the real responses, compare with what we expect, and contact the partner, to confirm and to ask if it's intended or a mistake on their side. Sometimes they just roll it back.
The fix is updating our mapping for the new format, ideally accepting both old and new for a while. Then reprocess the stored failures and check the data.

For the future, a few things. A tolerant reader, so our deserialisation ignores unknown fields and doesn't break when optional fields are missing, it only fails on what we truly need. Validation at the boundary, so bad incoming data fails loudly with a clear error instead of writing nulls into the database. Contract tests or scheduled checks against the partner's sandbox, so we notice a change before production traffic does. An anti-corruption layer, so their format is translated in one place and not spread all over our code. Monitoring on integration health, success rates and records processed, with alerts.
And I'd agree with the partner on a change notification process and versioning in the contract, so it doesn't come as a surprise again.

p17-630.q: Let me think about what differs. If only some users are slow, the cause is something different about them, usually data size, permissions, config or location.
p17-630.k: slow for some users, slow for one customer, data skew performance, tenant specific slowness, site slow only
x: Let me think about what differs. If only some users are slow, the cause is something different about them, usually data size, permissions, config or location.

So I narrow it down. From traces or logs I group latency by user, site, tenant, region, browser. Is it one site, everyone with one role, one region? If I can, I reproduce it by calling the same endpoint with the same parameters, safely.

Data volume is the most common one. The slow site just has way more data, 50,000 kits versus 500. A query that scans or returns everything for a site is fine for small sites and awful for big ones. Paging, filters and indexes that suit the large case fix it.
Parameter sniffing. SQL Server built a plan that's good for small sites and slow for big ones, or the other way round. Query Store shows it.
Permission logic. An admin or multi-site user has access to loads of sites, so the permission filter builds a huge IN list or does a check per site, and it's only slow for them.
Configuration. Some feature or setting only that tenant has switched on, causing extra work.
Network. Users far away or behind a corporate proxy get high latency, or one CDN node is misbehaving. Real-user monitoring by geography shows that.
And client side, older devices or browsers struggling with a big page.
The fix depends on the cause. But I always add that dimension, like site, to the latency metrics afterwards, so next time this kind of thing shows up straight away.

p17-631.q: Yeah, test and production differ in a lot of ways, but nine times out of ten it's the data.
p17-631.k: slow in production fast in test, works in test slow in prod, production performance difference, test data too small
x: Yeah, test and production differ in a lot of ways, but nine times out of ten it's the data.

Test databases have thousands of rows, production has millions, with skew, like one huge customer. A query without the right index, or one that loads everything into memory, looks fast in test. Checking the actual execution plan in production, or in a perf environment with production-sized anonymised data, usually shows a scan or a bad join.
Concurrency. Test has one or two users, production has hundreds at once. Lock contention, connection pool limits, thread pool starvation, cache stampedes, those only show up under real load.
Config differences. Debug logging on, different cache settings, some feature flag on, smaller instances, or database settings like compatibility level or read committed snapshot being different.
Network and integrations. Production calls real external services with real latency, through proxies, firewalls and gateways, while test might use stubs sitting in the same network.
Background workload. In production, scheduled jobs, reports and integrations are running at the same time and competing for the database.
And the front end, users have more data on the page, older devices, slower networks, browser extensions.

My approach is measure in production first, with traces showing where the time actually goes, instead of guessing from test. Then reproduce that specific condition in a perf environment, fix it, and make that environment closer to production in data size so it catches the next one.

p17-632.q: Okay, the first question is whether it's legit. A study going live at loads of sites, a batch import, a partner resending data, that's legitimate. A bot, a client stuck in a retry loop, an attack, that's not. The response is different.
p17-632.k: sudden traffic spike, 10x traffic, traffic surge, handle load spike, scale under sudden load, load shedding
x: Okay, the first question is whether it's legit. A study going live at loads of sites, a batch import, a partner resending data, that's legitimate. A bot, a client stuck in a retry loop, an attack, that's not. The response is different.

If it's abusive or accidental, I find the source from logs, IP, API key, client id, user agent, and block or rate-limit it at the gateway or WAF. A client stuck in a retry loop can be throttled while we contact whoever owns it.

If it's real traffic, my approach is to go in order of what's fastest. Scale out the stateless tiers, bump instance counts or autoscaling limits. That only helps if the bottleneck isn't something shared though.
Then protect the shared bottleneck, which is usually the database. Serve more from cache, defer non-essential work like reports and exports, and switch off expensive optional features with flags.

Shed load gracefully. Rate limits per client, returning 429 with Retry-After, so most users still get served well instead of everyone failing. Queue-based workloads soak up bursts naturally, as long as the consumers don't swamp the database.
And communicate, tell stakeholders what's happening and what users might see.

Afterwards, load test for that level, add autoscaling on the right signals, and plan with the business for known events, like scaling up before a big study launch. The cheapest spike is the one you saw coming.

p17-633.q: So once a job overruns its window, it starts fighting users for the database, locks, slowness, all that. It needs attention before it turns into an outage.
p17-633.k: batch job running long, nightly job overrun, job takes too long, batch window exceeded, long running job business hours
x: So once a job overruns its window, it starts fighting users for the database, locks, slowness, all that. It needs attention before it turns into an outage.

Short term, if it's hurting users right now, I decide whether it's safe to pause or stop it. That depends on whether it's restartable and what happens if it doesn't finish. And I tell people about the impact.

Then figure out why it got slower. Data growth is the usual one. The job processes everything every night and the data has grown. Jobs that scale with total data instead of changed data break eventually. The fix is incremental processing, only records changed since the last run, using a watermark like a last-modified timestamp or change tracking.
Inefficient processing. Row-by-row work with a query per row, which can often become set-based SQL or batched operations. Or missing indexes for the job's queries.
Contention. Something new runs at the same time, a backup, index maintenance, another job, and they block each other. Job schedules and wait stats show that.
Or an external dependency, a slow partner API or file transfer.

Improvements I'd make, break it into chunks with a commit per batch, so it doesn't hold long locks and can resume after a failure. Parallelise independent parts, carefully. Run heavy reads on a readable replica if there is one. Spread the jobs across the night.
And record duration and records processed per run, with an alert when the duration trends up. Trust me, you want to see it long before it hits business hours.

p17-634.q: Right, jobs run twice for a few different reasons, and each one has its own fix.
p17-634.k: job ran twice, duplicate job execution, scheduled job multiple servers, distributed lock job, quartz clustering
x: Right, jobs run twice for a few different reasons, and each one has its own fix.

The most common is multiple instances. The app got scaled from one server to two, or deployed to several nodes, and every instance has the same scheduler, so each one runs the job. Fixes are a clustered scheduler, like Quartz with a shared database job store and clustering on, so only one node fires each trigger. Or a distributed lock at the start of the job, like a Redis lock or a SQL app lock with sp_getapplock. Or move scheduling to one external trigger, a Kubernetes CronJob, EventBridge Scheduler or an Azure Functions timer, which behaves like a singleton.

Overlapping runs, where the previous run hadn't finished when the next started. Quartz has the DisallowConcurrentExecution attribute, or use a lock, and Kubernetes CronJobs have concurrencyPolicy Forbid.
Misfire handling. After downtime, the scheduler fires the missed runs on startup. Configure the misfire instructions on purpose.
And manual reruns or retries after a partial failure.

But because some duplication is always possible, my rule is the job itself has to be idempotent. Track what's been processed with a run id or a per-record processed flag, put unique constraints on outputs like invoices or notifications, and design the steps so rerunning them doesn't double the effect.
Then clean up the data from the double run carefully, using the job's own records to work out what got duplicated.

p17-635.q: Actually let me explain what it is first. A poison message is one that can never succeed, malformed data, an unexpected null, a reference to something that doesn't exist. If the consumer crashes or rejects it with requeue, the broker delivers it again, it fails again, and the consumer's stuck in a loop blocking everything behind it.
p17-635.k: poison message, consumer crash loop, message causes exception, bad message queue, dead letter poison message
x: Actually let me explain what it is first. A poison message is one that can never succeed, malformed data, an unexpected null, a reference to something that doesn't exist. If the consumer crashes or rejects it with requeue, the broker delivers it again, it fails again, and the consumer's stuck in a loop blocking everything behind it.

The immediate fix is getting it out of the way without losing it. With a proper setup it goes to the dead-letter queue by itself after a few attempts. If not, I move it manually with the broker tooling to a parking queue so everything else starts flowing again. Never just purge the queue, especially with business events.
Then investigate. Look at the message, its headers and the consumer's error logs. Is it actually invalid, sent by a buggy producer, or is our consumer failing on a valid edge case?
Fix the cause, either the producer or the consumer, then replay the parked message, or correct it if it really is invalid.

For prevention, every consumer gets retry limits with backoff and a dead-letter queue, with retry counts tracked in headers. I separate error types, so transient ones like timeouts get retried, and permanent ones like validation failures go straight to the DLQ with no retries. Exceptions are caught per message, so one bad message never takes down the whole consumer process. Messages get validated at the start of processing. And we alert when anything lands in the DLQ, with tooling to inspect and replay.

p17-636.q: So a sudden jump in log volume is both a symptom and a problem. It might be telling you something's broken, and on its own it can fill disks, slow the app down and create a massive bill.
p17-636.k: log volume spike, logs increased suddenly, logging flood, log cost spike, disk filling with logs, noisy logs
x: So a sudden jump in log volume is both a symptom and a problem. It might be telling you something's broken, and on its own it can fill disks, slow the app down and create a massive bill.
First I find the source. In the logging tool I group counts by service, logger category, level and message template. Usually one or two messages make up most of the increase.

Then why. Most often it's an error loop. Something failing over and over, like a consumer retrying a poison message, a client in a retry loop, or a background job failing every second. The logs are just the symptom, so you fix the thing that's failing.

Or a config change, someone turned on debug or trace in production and forgot, or a library's log level got lowered. Or a code change, a new log line inside a hot loop, or logging full request bodies. Or just more real traffic, logs grew with it, and you might need sampling.

To mitigate quickly, I raise the log level for the noisy category through runtime config if that's supported, or filter it in the collector, no redeploy needed. If disks are at risk, I make sure rotation is actually working.

For prevention, alerts on log volume per service, rate-limited or deduplicated logging for repeating errors, like one summary per minute instead of every single occurrence, some attention in code review to logging inside loops, and budgets per team so they see the cost.
And one more thing, I check sensitive data didn't start showing up in the new logs, because that needs its own clean-up.

p17-637.q: See, if one instance fails and the others are fine, the code's probably fine. Something about that one instance is different.
p17-637.k: one instance errors, bad node, single server failing, one pod failing, instance specific errors
x: See, if one instance fails and the others are fine, the code's probably fine. Something about that one instance is different.

I contain it first. Take it out of the load balancer, or let health checks remove it, so users stop hitting it, but keep it running if I can so I can investigate. In Kubernetes you can change a label to pull the pod out of the service, it stays alive but out of rotation.

Then compare it with a healthy one. Version, did a deployment only partly succeed so it's running an old or mixed version? Configuration, some different setting, env variable or config file, maybe someone edited it by hand. Local state, a corrupted local cache, a full disk, a stuck background thread, exhausted connections or memory, or a leak that's built up because that instance started earlier. Uptime is a good clue actually, if the failing one has been up the longest, I'd bet on a leak.

Host problems too, the server or node underneath has hardware, network or noisy neighbour issues, or a different patch level. And the network path, maybe that instance can't reach a dependency because of a firewall rule, DNS or routing that only affects its subnet or availability zone.
I capture evidence, logs, metrics, a memory dump if it's relevant, and then replace or restart it to get capacity back.

To prevent it, health checks that test real dependencies so bad instances get removed automatically, immutable deployments instead of manual changes, and dashboards per instance so outliers stand out.

p17-638.q: Okay so these come from the load balancer or proxy, not the app directly, which is why the app logs might show nothing at all. A 502 means the proxy got a bad response or the connection failed. A 504 means it waited too long.
p17-638.k: intermittent 502, 504 gateway timeout, load balancer 502, bad gateway intermittent, alb 502 troubleshooting
x: Okay so these come from the load balancer or proxy, not the app directly, which is why the app logs might show nothing at all. A 502 means the proxy got a bad response or the connection failed. A 504 means it waited too long.

For 504s, some requests are taking longer than the proxy's timeout. I find which endpoints from the load balancer access logs, they record the target response time. Then fix the slow operations, or make long ones asynchronous. I only raise the timeout if the long duration is genuinely legitimate.

502s have a few usual causes. The one that catches people most is a keep-alive mismatch. The app server closes idle connections before the load balancer does, the load balancer reuses a connection the server just closed, and the request fails. So the rule is the app's keep-alive timeout must be longer than the load balancer's idle timeout. In Kestrel that's KeepAliveTimeout, in Node it's server keepAliveTimeout, in IIS the connection timeout settings.
Deployments, instances shutting down while still getting requests, with no connection draining or graceful shutdown. If the 502s cluster around deployment times, that's it.

App crashes or restarts, the process dies mid-request, out-of-memory kills or unhandled exceptions. Response problems, invalid or oversized headers, or the app resetting connections. And capacity, all targets briefly unhealthy, or the app hitting connection or thread limits so new connections get refused.
So it's mostly correlation. Load balancer logs with timestamps and target, against app logs, restarts and deployments. Whether it's random or clustered narrows it down really fast.

p17-639.q: Yeah, so if the app takes longer to get ready than the health check allows, the orchestrator kills or replaces it before it's ready. The deployment fails or loops, and old instances might get removed too early.
p17-639.k: slow startup health check failure, startup probe, warmup dotnet, deployment fails slow start, health check grace period
x: Yeah, so if the app takes longer to get ready than the health check allows, the orchestrator kills or replaces it before it's ready. The deployment fails or loops, and old instances might get removed too early.

First I find out why startup is slow. I measure the phases with logs or a trace. Usually it's loading config from remote stores, running database migrations at startup, warming caches by loading big reference data, connecting to lots of dependencies, JIT compiling a big app, or waiting on a slow dependency that's timing out.

Then I fix both sides. Make startup faster. Move migrations out of startup into a pipeline step. Load caches lazily or in the background, and serve from the database while the cache warms. Run independent initialisation in parallel. Use ReadyToRun compilation to cut JIT time in .NET. And put timeouts on dependencies so a missing one doesn't hang startup forever.

And make the health checks understand startup. In Kubernetes, a startup probe with enough time, separate from liveness, so a slow start isn't treated like a deadlock. In ECS, set the health check grace period. On IIS, Application Initialization warms the app before it takes traffic. Readiness should only go true once the app can really serve requests.
The rollout should also wait for new instances to be ready before removing old ones, so a slow start doesn't cut capacity.
I'd also keep a startup duration metric. That way, when some change quietly adds ten seconds to startup, you actually notice it.

p17-640.q: Honestly this one's urgent. Error 9002 means the transaction log is full, SQL Server can't write new transactions, so every write to that database fails.
p17-640.k: transaction log full, log file full sql server, error 9002, log_reuse_wait_desc, log backup, database log growth
x: Honestly this one's urgent. Error 9002 means the transaction log is full, SQL Server can't write new transactions, so every write to that database fails.
First I find out why the log can't be reused. I query sys dot databases for log reuse wait desc on that database, and the value tells me the cause.

If it's LOG_BACKUP, the database is in full recovery but log backups haven't been running, maybe the backup job failed. So I take a log backup right away, which lets the space be reused, then fix the job and alert on its failures.

If it's ACTIVE_TRANSACTION, some long-running or forgotten open transaction is holding the log. DBCC OPENTRAN or the active transactions DMV finds it, and I decide with the owner whether to wait or kill it. Remember killing it triggers a rollback, and that takes time too.

If it's REPLICATION or AVAILABILITY_REPLICA, a replica or replication isn't keeping up, so the log has to be kept for it. Or it's one huge operation, like an index rebuild or deleting millions of rows in a single transaction.

To get running quickly, if the disk has space, I can grow the log file or add another log file on a different drive. What I don't do is panic, switch to simple recovery and shrink everything. That breaks the backup chain and point-in-time recovery, which matters a lot with regulated data.
Prevention is working, monitored log backups, alerts on log usage percentage, and batching big data operations into smaller transactions.

p17-641.q: So tempdb is shared by everything on the server, which means when it fills up, queries in every database start failing. I figure out which kind of usage is growing.
p17-641.k: tempdb full, tempdb growth, tempdb contention, version store growth, sort spill tempdb, tempdb space usage
x: So tempdb is shared by everything on the server, which means when it fills up, queries in every database start failing. I figure out which kind of usage is growing.
The file space usage DMV for tempdb splits the space into user objects, internal objects and the version store.

User objects are temp tables and table variables created by queries or procedures. The session and task space usage DMVs show which sessions use the most, and that leads me to the query or job. Typical ones are a procedure loading millions of rows into a temp table, or temp tables never dropped on long-lived connections.

Internal objects are work tables and spills from sorts, hashes and spools, when a query's memory grant is too small, or it sorts or hashes a huge result. Execution plans with spill warnings show it. The fix is better indexes to avoid big sorts, fixing bad cardinality estimates, or rewriting the query.

Version store. With read committed snapshot or snapshot isolation on, row versions live in tempdb as long as the oldest open transaction needs them. One long-running transaction, even an idle open one, blocks cleanup, and the version store just keeps growing. So find the oldest active snapshot transaction and deal with it. I've seen this one catch people out more than the others.
For immediate relief, kill the offending session if that's okay after checking the impact, or add space. Restarting SQL Server resets tempdb, but that's a last resort, it's full downtime.
And prevent it, size tempdb properly with multiple equal data files, monitor usage, and alert on long-running transactions.

p17-642.q: Actually, when the identity provider is down, nobody can start a new session. So even if every app is healthy, it's a full outage for new logins.
p17-642.k: login down, keycloak down, identity provider outage, sso outage, users cannot login, auth server slow
x: Actually, when the identity provider is down, nobody can start a new session. So even if every app is healthy, it's a full outage for new logins.

I confirm the scope first. Is it failing for everyone, or only some apps or realms? Are people with existing sessions still okay? Access tokens that are already issued keep working until they expire, so existing sessions often survive for a bit, and refresh failures kick in later.

Then the identity provider itself. For Keycloak, the server health and logs, its database, which is a common bottleneck, memory and GC, and the cluster cache state if there are multiple nodes. Then what's in front of it, load balancer, certificates, DNS. And unusual load, like a credential-stuffing attack or a broken client hammering the token endpoint in a loop. That can take an identity provider down on its own.
To mitigate, scale or restart nodes, block abusive traffic at the WAF or gateway, fix the database problem. And communicate clearly, because support is going to get flooded.

On the app side, they shouldn't call the identity provider on every request. Local JWT validation with cached signing keys means APIs keep working with existing tokens. Front ends should show a clear message instead of looping on redirects.

Afterwards, run the identity provider highly available with health monitoring and synthetic login checks, rate-limit the token and login endpoints, and include it in capacity planning. I'd say it's the one dependency everything else has.

p17-643.q: Let me guess before even looking, it's a size limit or a timeout somewhere in the chain. Production just has more layers than local, and each one has its own limit.
p17-643.k: large file upload fails, 413 request entity too large, upload size limit, maxallowedcontentlength, request body too large, upload timeout
x: Let me guess before even looking, it's a size limit or a timeout somewhere in the chain. Production just has more layers than local, and each one has its own limit.

The status code tells you a lot. A 413 Request Entity Too Large is some component rejecting the size. A 404.13 on IIS is request filtering's max allowed content length. A 502 or 504 points to a timeout at a proxy. A connection reset means something closed the connection.

Then I go layer by layer. The CDN, WAF or API gateway, a lot of them have body limits, WAF inspection limits, or API Gateway's 10 MB payload limit. The load balancer or reverse proxy, nginx's client max body size defaults to 1 MB, which surprises people all the time with Kubernetes ingress. IIS, request limits max allowed content length is about 30 MB by default, plus max request length for classic ASP.NET. Kestrel and ASP.NET Core, MaxRequestBodySize is also around 30 MB by default, and the form options for multipart, which you can change per endpoint. And timeouts, slow uploads over corporate networks can go past proxy and server timeouts.

But the better design for big files is not sending them through the API at all. The client asks the API for a pre-signed upload URL, uploads straight to S3 or Blob Storage, maybe in chunks with multipart upload so it can resume, and the API processes the file asynchronously after an upload event. You avoid all those limits, the API stays light, and it copes with bad networks.

p17-644.q: So a synchronous export that builds the whole file inside one HTTP request works for small data and falls over for big data. It hits request timeouts, memory limits, or holds the database for ages.
p17-644.k: export timeout, large report timeout, csv export slow, excel export large data, async export, export job
x: So a synchronous export that builds the whole file inside one HTTP request works for small data and falls over for big data. It hits request timeouts, memory limits, or holds the database for ages.

If it's only slightly over the limits, there are quick wins. Stream the output straight to the response instead of building the file in memory, write rows as you read them with a forward-only reader, use AsNoTracking and select only the columns you need, and fix slow queries. Streaming a CSV handles really large data with very little memory.

But for truly big exports, what I do is change the design to asynchronous. The user requests an export, the API validates it, creates an export job and returns 202 Accepted with a job id. A background worker picks it up, queries the data in pages, writes the file to blob storage, records progress and marks it complete. The user sees progress in the UI and gets a notification, or the page polls, and then downloads through a short-lived signed URL. Files expire after a while.
What you get is no HTTP timeouts, retries if the worker fails, controlled concurrency so ten big exports at once don't kill the database, and you can run the heavy queries on a read replica.
I'd also ask if an export is really what they need. Sometimes users export everything just to filter it in Excel, and better filters or a report in the app serve them better.
And in a regulated context, exports of sensitive data are logged, who exported what.

p17-645.q: Okay, this is a classic one, heavy reporting and transactional work on the same database. Reports scan loads of data, eat CPU, memory and I/O, and can hold locks that block users' writes.
p17-645.k: reports slow down system, reporting load oltp, heavy queries blocking users, separate reporting database, read replica reporting
x: Okay, this is a classic one, heavy reporting and transactional work on the same database. Reports scan loads of data, eat CPU, memory and I/O, and can hold locks that block users' writes.

For short-term relief, I find the heaviest reports from Query Store or query stats and tune the worst queries with indexes or rewrites. Schedule the heavy ones outside peak hours. Limit how many run at once with a queue. And if read committed snapshot is on, readers don't block writers, which takes away a lot of the lock contention. What I avoid is sprinkling NOLOCK everywhere, because it gives you wrong results.

The structural fix is separating the workloads. Read replicas, so Always On readable secondaries in SQL Server, or read replicas in managed databases. Reports run there with slightly delayed data, which is fine for most reports.

Or a reporting database or data warehouse. Data gets copied through change tracking, change data capture or ETL into a schema built for reporting, denormalised tables and columnstore indexes, which make aggregations over millions of rows dramatically faster. Power BI or SSRS read from there.
And pre-aggregation, for dashboards showing the same summary again and again, compute it on a schedule or incrementally and serve it from a summary table or cache.
In our case, with a database per study, a central reporting store that aggregates across studies is also what makes cross-study reporting possible, instead of querying hundreds of databases live.

p17-646.q: Right, stay calm, stop the damage, then recover precisely. In that order.
p17-646.k: accidental delete production, restore deleted data, recover deleted rows, point in time restore, data loss incident
x: Right, stay calm, stop the damage, then recover precisely. In that order.
To stop the damage, I find out what was deleted, when, and by what, a person, a script, a bug, a job, and make sure it can't keep going. Disable the job or the feature if needed.
Then assess. Which tables, which rows, how many, and what's happened since? New writes after the deletion make it harder, because I can't just roll the whole database back without losing them.

For recovery, my approach is to pick the least disruptive option. If the system uses soft delete, you just flip the flag back. Audit or history tables, like temporal tables or audit logs, can give you the old values. Otherwise, point-in-time restore. Restore a copy of the database, never over production, to a moment just before the deletion, using full and log backups or the cloud's point-in-time restore. Then copy only the missing rows back into production with a careful, reviewed script that handles keys, foreign key order and identity values.
Then verify with the business that the data's right, and check dependent systems that may have reacted to the deletion, notifications already sent, partners already synced.
Document everything. In a regulated system the incident, the correction script, the approvals and the verification are all part of the record.

For prevention, restricted production access, reviewed scripts with the WHERE clause checked and run in a transaction with a row count check, soft deletes for important entities, tested backups, and least privilege so apps can't delete what they shouldn't.

p17-647.q: So the key point is, once a secret's pushed, assume it's compromised. Removing it from the code isn't enough. It's in the history, in everyone's clones, maybe in CI logs, and if the repo's public, bots scan for secrets within minutes.
p17-647.k: secret committed to git, leaked credentials, password in repo, api key leaked github, rotate leaked secret
x: So the key point is, once a secret's pushed, assume it's compromised. Removing it from the code isn't enough. It's in the history, in everyone's clones, maybe in CI logs, and if the repo's public, bots scan for secrets within minutes.

The first thing I do is revoke or rotate it. Create a new credential, update the apps using it through the proper secrets store, disable the old one. That's the most important step and it happens before any history cleanup.
Then check for misuse. Look at the access logs of whatever the secret protected, cloud audit logs, database logins, API usage, for activity from strange locations or times since the commit.
Remove it from the code and load it from a secrets manager or the environment instead.

Clean the history if needed, with git filter-repo or BFG, and force-push. That needs coordination because everyone has to re-clone. On hosted platforms you might need support to purge cached views. Honestly it matters less once the secret's rotated, but it reduces exposure and noise.
Report it through the security incident process. Depending on what was exposed, that might mean telling the security team or others.

And prevent it. Pre-commit hooks with a scanner like gitleaks, push protection on the platform, secret scanning in CI, a gitignore for local settings files, and making the right way easy, user secrets for local development and a secrets manager everywhere else.

p17-648.q: Okay, a spike of failed logins from lots of IPs is usually credential stuffing. Attackers are trying username and password pairs leaked from other sites, hoping people reused them. That's a security incident, so I pull the security team in early.
p17-648.k: credential stuffing, brute force login attack, failed logins spike, login attack, account takeover attempt, bot login attack
x: Okay, a spike of failed logins from lots of IPs is usually credential stuffing. Attackers are trying username and password pairs leaked from other sites, hoping people reused them. That's a security incident, so I pull the security team in early.

For immediate defence, what I do is rate limit and block at the edge. WAF rules limiting login attempts per IP and per account, bot detection, and blocking clearly malicious sources or regions if the business is okay with that.

Then protect accounts. Temporary lockout or progressive delays after repeated failures per account, but carefully, you don't want attackers locking out every real user. And step up verification, MFA or a CAPTCHA, when the risk signals are high.
Then the important bit, check for successful logins from the same sources, because those accounts may already be compromised. Force password resets, revoke their sessions, and notify those users.

To investigate, I go through identity provider and WAF logs, look at patterns in the targeted accounts, and check whether they're enumerating usernames. The login page shouldn't give that away with different error messages.

Longer term, MFA for everyone, especially privileged users, that kills most credential stuffing. Checking passwords against known breached lists at registration and password change. Same error message whatever went wrong. Alerts on failed login rates. And identity provider features like brute force detection, which Keycloak has built in.
Afterwards there's a review of what was accessed, and any notifications the company policy requires.

p17-649.q: So browser-specific bugs come from something that behaves differently between engines. Chrome and Edge are Blink, Safari is WebKit, Firefox is Gecko.
p17-649.k: works in chrome not safari, browser compatibility bug, safari bug, cross browser issue, ios safari issue
x: So browser-specific bugs come from something that behaves differently between engines. Chrome and Edge are Blink, Safari is WebKit, Firefox is Gecko.

I reproduce it in the real browser. Safari on a Mac, or an actual iPhone, because every iOS browser is WebKit underneath. Cloud device services help if I don't have the device. Then Safari's Web Inspector, connected to the phone if needed, and check the console for errors and the network tab for failed requests.

The culprits I've seen most. Date parsing is a big one. new Date with a non-standard string, like a date and time separated by a space, works in Chrome and gives Invalid Date in Safari. Use ISO formats or a date library.

Newer JavaScript or CSS that the user's Safari version doesn't support, some regex features, newer array methods, CSS properties. Build settings or polyfills should cover that, and checking browserslist and caniuse helps.

Third-party cookies and storage. Safari's tracking prevention blocks third-party cookies and limits storage, which breaks silent token renewal through hidden iframes, or embedded apps. The fix is same-site deployments, or the authorisation code flow with refresh token rotation.
Then smaller stuff, autoplay, file input and date input differences, iOS viewport and keyboard behaviour, and caching differences like a more aggressive back-forward cache.
After the fix, I add that browser to the test matrix, like running the Playwright tests in WebKit in CI, so it doesn't come back.

p17-650.q: See, if an app gets slower over hours, something's piling up. Usually memory, listeners or DOM nodes, so every interaction does a bit more work than before.
p17-650.k: angular app slow over time, spa memory leak, browser tab memory grows, angular subscription leak, detached dom nodes
x: See, if an app gets slower over hours, something's piling up. Usually memory, listeners or DOM nodes, so every interaction does a bit more work than before.

I confirm it with the browser tools. Chrome DevTools' Performance monitor shows JS heap size, DOM node count and event listeners over time. I do a repeated action, like opening and closing a dialog or going between two screens 20 times, and watch if the numbers keep climbing. Then heap snapshots before and after, and compare which objects are growing. Detached DOM trees are a strong clue.

In Angular the most common cause by far is subscriptions that never get unsubscribed. A component subscribes to a long-lived observable, a store selector, a router event, an interval, and never unsubscribes, so destroyed components stay in memory and keep reacting. The fix is the async pipe, takeUntilDestroyed, or toSignal.

Other ones, event listeners added manually to window or document and never removed in ngOnDestroy. Third-party libraries like charts or grids not being destroyed properly. Service caches that grow forever, like storing every record ever loaded. Timers and intervals still running after navigation. And growing change detection work, big lists without trackBy, or lots of components on default change detection.

The fix depends on what the heap comparison shows. Then I add a check to our testing, a scripted navigation loop that verifies memory goes back to a baseline. That catches regressions in shared components, which is where it hurts most in our component-based setup.

p17-651.q: Honestly I treat a cost spike like an incident. Find what changed, stop the bleeding, stop it happening again.
p17-651.k: aws bill spike, unexpected aws cost, cost anomaly, cloud cost increase, find aws cost driver
x: Honestly I treat a cost spike like an incident. Find what changed, stop the bleeding, stop it happening again.

To find the driver, I go to Cost Explorer, group by service, then usage type, region, account and tags, and compare daily costs before and after. It usually points at one or two line items. Cost Anomaly Detection might have flagged it already.

The usual causes. Data transfer, especially NAT gateway processing charges, when services in private subnets pull huge amounts through NAT instead of VPC endpoints, like container images from ECR or data from S3. Or cross-AZ and cross-region traffic.
Runaway compute. Autoscaling that went up and never came down, a Lambda in a loop, like an S3-triggered function writing back into the same bucket, or a retry storm.
Logging and monitoring, a debug level left on and CloudWatch Logs ingestion multiplied, or high-cardinality custom metrics.

Forgotten stuff, test environments, big instances, unattached EBS volumes, old snapshots, idle load balancers. Storage with a missing lifecycle rule, so logs or backups pile up in expensive tiers. Or the database, DynamoDB on-demand soaking up a huge traffic spike, or provisioned IOPS that got bumped.
Then stop it, fix the loop, scale down, delete what's unused, add the endpoints.
And prevent it with budgets and anomaly alerts per account and team, required cost tags, regular cost reviews, and guardrails like Lambda concurrency limits and max autoscaling sizes.

p17-652.q: Actually this is a nasty pattern. When tasks only go unhealthy under load, the health endpoint is usually suffering from the same resource exhaustion as the rest of the app. And killing tasks under load makes it worse, because the remaining ones get even more traffic. It turns into a death spiral.
p17-652.k: ecs health check fails under load, tasks killed under load, health check timeout load, unhealthy targets during peak
x: Actually this is a nasty pattern. When tasks only go unhealthy under load, the health endpoint is usually suffering from the same resource exhaustion as the rest of the app. And killing tasks under load makes it worse, because the remaining ones get even more traffic. It turns into a death spiral.

The first thing I check is whether the health endpoint is cheap. If it checks the database and every dependency deeply, under load those checks time out and every task looks unhealthy at the same time, even though the real problem is one shared dependency. A liveness-style check should only confirm the process can respond. Dependency checks belong in readiness logic or monitoring, not in a check that triggers replacement.

Then, is it getting starved? With thread pool starvation or a saturated request queue, the health request waits behind user requests and times out, and ALB health check timeouts are short by default. Thread pool metrics, request queue length and CPU show that.
Is the container CPU or memory limit too tight, causing throttling or out-of-memory kills? ECS stopped task reasons and Container Insights tell you.
And are the thresholds too aggressive? A couple of slow responses shouldn't remove a task, so raise the unhealthy threshold and timeout sensibly.
Then fix the actual bottleneck, scale out earlier with autoscaling on request count rather than CPU, and load test with health checks switched on, so we see this before production does.

p17-653.q: So growing lag means consumers are slower than producers. I find which side changed and where the time is going.
p17-653.k: kafka consumer lag growing, kafka lag, consumer cannot keep up, kafka backlog, slow kafka consumer
x: So growing lag means consumers are slower than producers. I find which side changed and where the time is going.

I look at lag per partition, not just the total. If it's high on all partitions, consumers are generally too slow or producers sped up. If it's on one or two partitions, it's a hot partition, where a popular key sends most messages to one place, or one consumer instance is stuck.

Then consumer health. Are all consumers in the group active, or did some crash so there are fewer consumers than partitions? Are there frequent rebalances in the logs? Each one pauses consumption. Rebalance storms happen when processing takes longer than max poll interval, so the broker thinks the consumer died.
Then processing time. What does each message wait on? Usually a database write or an external API call, and traces and per-message timing show it.

The fixes. Scale out consumers, but only up to the number of partitions. Beyond that the extra ones just sit idle, so you might need more partitions for future growth. Speed up processing, batch database writes, process concurrently within a partition where per-key ordering allows, cache lookups. Fix hot keys with a better partition key. Tune polling, smaller batches or a longer max poll interval when processing is slow, so rebalances stop, and cooperative rebalancing to reduce the pauses.
And then alert on lag and how fast it's growing. I'd say lag is basically how stale your downstream data is, so people care about it.

p17-654.q: Yeah, a batch import writes way faster than normal traffic, so it hits the table's capacity or a hot partition, and then normal user traffic gets throttled too.
p17-654.k: dynamodb batch import throttling, bulk load dynamodb, batchwriteitem throttled, dynamodb import s3, unprocessed items
x: Yeah, a batch import writes way faster than normal traffic, so it hits the table's capacity or a hot partition, and then normal user traffic gets throttled too.

The immediate fix is slowing the import down. Throttle the writer to a rate the table can handle, with retries and exponential backoff with jitter. And one thing people miss, BatchWriteItem returns UnprocessedItems when it's throttled. Your code has to retry those, otherwise data is silently lost. That's a classic bug.
Then key distribution. If the import file is sorted by partition key, like all items for one customer together, the writes hit one partition at a time. Just shuffling the order spreads the load.

Capacity. For a one-off import into a provisioned table, temporarily raise write capacity, or switch to on-demand for the import and switch back. On-demand still has a ramp-up behaviour for brand new peaks though.

For really big loads there are better approaches. DynamoDB's import from S3 loads CSV, JSON or Ion files into a new table without using write capacity at all, perfect for initial loads. For ongoing large imports, put the data on a queue and let consumers write at a controlled rate, which also protects user traffic.
Also check the secondary indexes. Every write to the table also writes to its GSIs, and if a GSI is under-provisioned, it throttles the base table writes too.
Afterwards I'd monitor throttled requests and consumed capacity per table and per index.

p17-655.q: Let me start with the fact that S3 access is decided by several policies at once, so I go layer by layer, guided by whatever changed.
p17-655.k: s3 access denied, s3 403 forbidden, bucket policy denied, kms access denied s3, iam permission s3 error
x: Let me start with the fact that S3 access is decided by several policies at once, so I go layer by layer, guided by whatever changed.

I start by getting the details, the exact action, like s3 GetObject or PutObject, the resource ARN, and the identity making the call. CloudTrail shows the failing call, and the newer error messages often tell you which kind of policy denied it.

Then the layers. Identity policy, does the role the app uses, like the ECS task role, allow that action on that bucket and prefix? A common mistake is allowing the bucket ARN but not bucket slash star, or the other way round. ListBucket needs the bucket ARN, GetObject needs the object path.

Bucket policy. An explicit deny beats everything. Policies that require encryption headers, specific VPC endpoints, TLS, or a specific organisation will deny calls that don't meet the conditions. After a network change, requests might not come through the expected VPC endpoint anymore.
KMS. If objects use a customer managed key, the role also needs kms Decrypt or GenerateDataKey, and the key policy has to allow it. In my experience this is one of the most common causes.

Object ownership, objects uploaded by another account might not be accessible unless bucket owner enforced is set. Organisation guardrails, a new SCP or Resource Control Policy can deny it. And Block Public Access, if the app expected public reads.
The IAM policy simulator and Access Analyzer help confirm the fix, and I make the fix through infrastructure as code, not by clicking around.

p17-656.q: Right, first thing, stop and don't apply. Destroying and recreating a production database means data loss and an outage, so I find out why Terraform thinks it needs replacing.
p17-656.k: terraform plan destroy database, forces replacement, terraform recreate resource, prevent destroy terraform, terraform replace production
x: Right, first thing, stop and don't apply. Destroying and recreating a production database means data loss and an outage, so I find out why Terraform thinks it needs replacing.
The plan marks the attribute causing it with "forces replacement". The common reasons are these.

A changed immutable attribute. Some properties can't be updated in place, like the database identifier, engine type, availability zone, encryption settings or some subnet group changes. Someone may have changed one on purpose without realising what it does.

A renamed or moved resource. The resource address changed, from a rename or moving it into a module, so Terraform sees an old resource to delete and a new one to create. A moved block fixes that, it updates state without touching the resource.
Provider or module upgrades that changed defaults or how an attribute is represented.
Drift, someone changed the resource outside Terraform and the config doesn't match reality anymore.

So the fix depends. Add a moved block, revert the attribute change, align the config with reality, use lifecycle ignore_changes for attributes managed somewhere else. Or if the change is really needed, plan a proper migration, snapshot, create new, migrate, switch over, instead of letting Terraform just do it.

For prevention, my rule is lifecycle prevent_destroy on critical resources, deletion protection on the database itself, plan review in pull requests with automated checks that fail on destroys of protected resource types, and applies only from the pipeline.

p17-657.q: Okay so this is exactly why we run smoke tests, it got caught early. Now the decision has to be quick, fix forward or roll back.
p17-657.k: smoke test failed production, release failed production, passed uat failed prod, post deployment failure, release night issue
x: Okay so this is exactly why we run smoke tests, it got caught early. Now the decision has to be quick, fix forward or roll back.

I assess impact first. Are real users affected or only the tested path? How bad is it? If a critical flow is broken and the cause isn't obvious within minutes, I'd rather roll back, if that's safe with the database changes, and investigate calmly. In a release window there's usually a defined time limit for that call anyway.
Then I look for what's different between UAT and production, because the code is the same build.
Configuration is the most common. A missing or different setting, connection string, feature flag or secret in production.
Infrastructure. Firewall rules, certificates, DNS, permissions of the production service account, or a dependency endpoint that exists in UAT but not in prod.
Data. Production has cases UAT doesn't, old records, bigger volumes, study configurations UAT never had.
Integrations, real partner endpoints behave differently from test ones.
Deployment issues, a step failed silently on one server, a migration didn't run, a cache didn't get cleared.
The logs and the exact smoke test failure usually point to one of these pretty quickly.

After it's resolved, a short review, and we add the missing check to the pre-production checklist or the pipeline. Like validating configuration at startup, or a connectivity check against production dependencies before switching traffic over.

p17-658.q: So "I saved it but the screen still shows the old value" usually means a cache wasn't invalidated, or you're reading from somewhere that hasn't caught up yet.
p17-658.k: stale data after update, cache invalidation bug, users see old data, cache not updated, read after write inconsistency
x: So "I saved it but the screen still shows the old value" usually means a cache wasn't invalidated, or you're reading from somewhere that hasn't caught up yet.

My approach is to find which layer is stale. Check the database first, is the new value there? If yes, I move outward. The API's in-memory or Redis cache, an HTTP or CDN cache, the front end's client cache like RTK Query or TanStack Query, or a read replica with replication lag.

The common causes. Cache-aside without invalidation, the update writes to the database but doesn't remove the cached entry, so readers see the old value until the TTL runs out. The fix is invalidating or updating the cache entry in the same code path as the write, after the commit.

Multiple instances with local in-memory caches. One instance clears its own cache, the others still have the old value. Use a distributed cache, or broadcast invalidation messages to all instances with something like Redis pub-sub, or short TTLs on local caches. HybridCache in .NET 9 helps with tags and a shared second level.
HTTP caching, responses with Cache-Control headers that allow caching data that changes. API responses for user data should usually be no-store or use ETags.
Front-end caches, after a mutation the client has to invalidate the related queries, with RTK Query tags or TanStack Query's invalidateQueries.
And read replicas, reading right after writing from a lagging replica. The fix is read-your-writes, reading from the primary for that user for a short time after a write.

p17-659.q: Honestly this is one of the most serious ones, a security and privacy incident. It goes to top priority and I bring in security and management straight away, following the incident process.
p17-659.k: user sees another users data, data leak between users, cross tenant data leak, wrong user data shown, singleton state bug
x: Honestly this is one of the most serious ones, a security and privacy incident. It goes to top priority and I bring in security and management straight away, following the incident process.
Contain first. If it's reproducible or still happening, disable the feature or take the endpoint offline. Preserve logs and evidence.

Then find the cause. The usual suspects in a web app. Shared state in a singleton, a service registered as singleton holding per-request data, like the current user or tenant in a field, so concurrent requests overwrite each other. Static fields for request data do the same thing.

Caching with wrong keys, a cached response or object keyed without the user or tenant, so the first user's data gets served to everyone. That includes a CDN or proxy caching personalised responses because Cache-Control private or no-store was missing.
Authorisation gaps, an endpoint that takes an id and never checks the record belongs to that user. Insecure direct object reference.

Async context mistakes, like AsyncLocal or thread-static values leaking between requests. And front-end issues, state kept in local storage and not cleared on logout, so the next person on the same device sees it.
Then assess impact. Which users and data were exposed and for how long, from access logs. You need that for notifications, which might be legally required for personal or clinical data.
Fix it, test with concurrent users, add isolation tests, and then do a thorough review. In my experience these bugs often have siblings.

p17-660.q: So email problems basically split into two, "we never sent it" and "we sent it but it didn't arrive".
p17-660.k: emails not delivered, email going to spam, smtp failure, spf dkim dmarc, notification email missing
x: So email problems basically split into two, "we never sent it" and "we sent it but it didn't arrive".

Did we send it? I check the app logs for the send attempt and the response from the SMTP server or the email API. Errors like authentication failure, relay denied, connection timeouts or rate limits mean it never left. Then any queue or outbox between the app and the sender, and whether a background worker is actually processing it.

Did the provider accept and deliver it? SES, SendGrid or the corporate mail relay all keep delivery logs, delivered, bounced, deferred, dropped. Bounces explain themselves, invalid address, mailbox full. Suppression lists are sneaky though, they silently drop mail to addresses that bounced or complained before.

Did it land in spam or quarantine? Corporate recipients often have strict filters. So check our domain's authentication. SPF has to authorise the sending servers, DKIM has to sign the messages, and DMARC has to align them. Adding a new sending service without updating SPF and DKIM is a classic cause. Content can trigger filters too, like links to unusual domains. The recipient's IT team can check their quarantine.

For important emails I also design for failure. Track send status per message, retry transient failures, show the important information in the app and not only by email, and monitor bounce and complaint rates.
In clinical systems, sites may depend on these emails for important notifications. So a delivery problem gets treated as a functional failure, not a cosmetic one.

p17-661.q: Okay, duplicate files can make a partner process orders or shipments twice, so I take it seriously and coordinate with them.
p17-661.k: file sent twice, duplicate file transfer, integration duplicate, sftp duplicate file, idempotent file transfer
x: Okay, duplicate files can make a partner process orders or shipments twice, so I take it seriously and coordinate with them.
To contain it, if more duplicates are coming, I pause the job or flow, and tell the partner which file is the duplicate so they skip it, or reverse it if they already processed it.

Then why it was sent twice. I've seen it happen a few ways. Retries after an uncertain failure, the upload worked but the connection dropped before confirmation, so the job retried and uploaded again. The job ran twice, on two servers without clustering, overlapping runs, or someone reran it manually. Or the selection logic picked the same data again, because the "already sent" marker never got saved, maybe the job crashed after sending but before updating the status.

The fix is making sending idempotent. Use deterministic file names, with a batch id and date in them, so a resend overwrites or gets detected instead of creating a second file, and agree with the partner that they dedupe by file name or batch id. Record each transfer in a table with a unique constraint on the batch and states like prepared, sent and confirmed, and before sending, check if that batch already went. When the outcome is uncertain, check the remote side, like listing the target folder, before retrying. And make sure the job runs once, with clustering or a lock.
I'd also add a dashboard of files per partner per day with alerts on unexpected counts. That catches duplicates or missing files quickly.

p17-662.q: See, JWTs have time-based claims, issued at, not before, and expiry. If a server's clock is ahead or behind the identity provider's, it might think a fresh token is expired or not valid yet. When it only happens on some servers, clock drift on those machines is my first suspect.
p17-662.k: clock skew jwt, token not yet valid, server time wrong, ntp time sync, intermittent token expired
x: See, JWTs have time-based claims, issued at, not before, and expiry. If a server's clock is ahead or behind the identity provider's, it might think a fresh token is expired or not valid yet. When it only happens on some servers, clock drift on those machines is my first suspect.

To confirm, the errors say lifetime validation failed, with the token's times and the server's current time. I compare the clock on the affected servers against a reliable time source. A few minutes off is enough to break it.

The fix is proper time sync. Windows servers should sync with the domain time hierarchy or an NTP source through w32time, Linux uses chrony or systemd-timesyncd. VMs sometimes drift after being suspended or migrated, or when the host's time sync and the guest's NTP fight each other. Containers use the host clock, so the fix is on the node.

The JWT handler in .NET has a ClockSkew setting, five minutes by default, which tolerates small differences. Some teams set it to zero to be strict, and then any drift shows up. I'd say something like 30 seconds to two minutes is a reasonable balance. Cranking it up a lot to hide a broken clock is the wrong fix.

And time affects way more than tokens. TOTP codes, certificate validity, correlating logs across servers, scheduled jobs, audit trail timestamps, which in a regulated system have to be accurate. So I add monitoring of clock offset on every server, with alerts.

p17-663.q: Actually users feel this one directly. Every recycle drops in-memory state, sessions and caches, and the first requests after it are slow.
