p17-663.k: iis app pool recycling, app pool restart frequent, w3wp restart, rapid fail protection, iis recycle causes
x: Actually users feel this one directly. Every recycle drops in-memory state, sessions and caches, and the first requests after it are slow.
So first I find out why each recycle happened. If recycle event logging is turned on in the app pool's advanced settings, the System log in Event Viewer records the reason from the WAS events.
The usual reasons. Memory limits, the private or virtual memory limit on the app pool got exceeded, so IIS recycled it. That points to high memory or a leak in the app, which needs memory dumps.

Config changes. Any change to web.config or files in the bin folder triggers a recycle. So something writing there, like the app writing logs or temp files into its own folder, or antivirus touching files, can cause it.
Periodic recycling. The default regular interval is 1,740 minutes, which means it recycles at a different time every day, sometimes right in peak hours. Better to set a specific off-peak time.

Crashes. An unhandled exception on a background thread, a stack overflow or an access violation kills the worker process, and after several crashes rapid-fail protection can stop the app pool completely. The Application event log shows the .NET runtime errors and Windows Error Reporting entries.
Idle timeout is a bit different, the pool shuts down after inactivity, and the symptom is a slow first request.
For crashes, what I do is set up ProcDump or DebugDiag to capture a crash dump, analyse it for the exception and stack, fix the bug, and check the recycle events stop.

p17-664.q: Honestly, when a process dies without logging anything, it's usually something the app just couldn't catch. A stack overflow, an out-of-memory kill from outside, a native crash, or an unhandled exception on a background thread before the logs got flushed.
p17-664.k: process crash no logs, stackoverflow crash dotnet, unhandled exception crash, app dies silently, crash dump analysis
x: Honestly, when a process dies without logging anything, it's usually something the app just couldn't catch. A stack overflow, an out-of-memory kill from outside, a native crash, or an unhandled exception on a background thread before the logs got flushed.

So I look for evidence outside the app first. On Windows, the Application event log usually has a .NET Runtime error with the exception type and stack, or an Application Error entry with the faulting module. On Linux or containers, the exit code tells you a lot. 137 means killed by SIGKILL, often out of memory, 139 is a segfault, 134 is an abort. The orchestrator shows the reason, like OOMKilled, and the kernel log has the OOM killer messages.

Then capture a crash dump for next time. On Windows, ProcDump with the e flag, or Windows Error Reporting local dumps. For .NET on Linux, the DOTNET DbgEnableMiniDump environment variables write a dump on crash. Then analyse it with dotnet-dump analyze, WinDbg or Visual Studio, looking at the exception and the thread stacks.

What I usually find is a stack overflow from infinite recursion, often a property calling itself, or a deep recursive algorithm on unexpected data. That can't be caught in .NET, it kills the process instantly. Or unhandled exceptions in async void methods or background threads. Or a native library crashing through interop.

Sometimes the logs were just lost because they were buffered. So configure sinks to flush on shutdown, log to stdout in containers, and add an AppDomain UnhandledException handler that logs synchronously as a last resort.

p17-665.q: So high latency with low CPU means threads are waiting, not working. In older ASP.NET apps on .NET Framework, I've seen two causes again and again.
p17-665.k: aspnet hangs low cpu, sync over async deadlock, result wait deadlock, requests stuck legacy aspnet, thread pool blocked
x: So high latency with low CPU means threads are waiting, not working. In older ASP.NET apps on .NET Framework, I've seen two causes again and again.

The first is sync over async. Code calls dot Result or dot Wait on a Task, say to call an async HttpClient method from a synchronous controller. Classic ASP.NET has a synchronisation context that allows one thread at a time per request. The async method tries to continue on that context, but the request thread is blocked waiting for it, so it deadlocks and the request hangs forever. And under load, even without full deadlocks, blocking threads drains the thread pool and new requests queue up.

The other is plain thread pool starvation. Lots of requests block threads on slow I/O, synchronous database calls or HTTP calls, and the thread pool only grows slowly, adding threads gradually, so requests sit waiting in queues.

To confirm, I take a memory dump during the hang and look at thread stacks with DebugDiag or WinDbg. Loads of threads waiting in Task Wait, Result, Monitor Enter, or in synchronous network calls, that's the pattern. Performance counters show requests queued going up while CPU stays low.

The fix is making the call chain async all the way, from the controller down, instead of blocking. If that's not possible right now, ConfigureAwait false in library code avoids the context deadlock, but it still blocks threads. Add timeouts to every outbound call. Raising the minimum threads is only temporary relief.

p17-666.q: Yeah, errors like "Only one usage of each socket address is normally permitted", or connection failures under load with thousands of connections in TIME_WAIT, almost always mean the app creates a new HttpClient for every request.
p17-666.k: socket exhaustion, httpclient per request, too many sockets time_wait, only one usage of each socket address, httpclientfactory fix
x: Yeah, errors like "Only one usage of each socket address is normally permitted", or connection failures under load with thousands of connections in TIME_WAIT, almost always mean the app creates a new HttpClient for every request.

Why it happens. Each HttpClient has its own connection pool. Disposing it closes the connections, but the OS keeps each closed socket in TIME_WAIT for a while, up to minutes. Under load you open new sockets faster than old ones get released, and you run out of ephemeral ports. The funny part is the using statement around HttpClient looks like good practice, but that's exactly the cause here.
To confirm, netstat shows tons of connections in TIME_WAIT to the same destination, and the code creates an HttpClient per call.

The fix is reusing connections. In ASP.NET Core, use IHttpClientFactory with typed or named clients, which pools and recycles the underlying handlers properly. Or one long-lived HttpClient, static or singleton, with SocketsHttpHandler and PooledConnectionLifetime set, say two minutes, so connections recycle periodically and DNS changes get picked up. A plain static client would miss those.
On .NET Framework, a shared static HttpClient plus ServicePointManager settings like ConnectionLeaseTimeout gives you similar behaviour.
I'd also check the connection limits per server, and that responses are disposed or fully read. Unread response bodies can keep connections busy, and that one can catch people out.

p17-667.q: Let me start with the pattern, because that tells you most of it. Disconnects usually come from something between client and server closing idle or long-lived connections, or from scaling.
p17-667.k: signalr disconnects, websocket disconnect, signalr reconnecting, websocket proxy timeout, real time connection drops
x: Let me start with the pattern, because that tells you most of it. Disconnects usually come from something between client and server closing idle or long-lived connections, or from scaling.

So, do they happen after a fixed idle time, like 60 seconds? That's a proxy or load balancer idle timeout. Do they happen when servers are deployed or scaled? Only for users behind certain corporate networks?

Proxy and load balancer timeouts are the most common. Idle timeouts on the load balancer, IIS, nginx or a corporate proxy. SignalR's keep-alive pings, every 15 seconds by default, should keep things alive, as long as that interval is shorter than every timeout along the path. Some proxies don't handle WebSockets properly, so SignalR falls back to Server-Sent Events or long polling, which behave differently.
WebSockets not enabled. On IIS the WebSocket Protocol feature has to be installed, and load balancers have to allow the upgrade.

Multiple servers without sticky sessions. SignalR's negotiate and connect requests have to hit the same server, unless you use Azure SignalR Service, or WebSockets only with skip negotiation. Without that, connections fail randomly as soon as there are two instances. You also need a backplane like Redis so messages reach users connected to other servers.

Deployments and restarts drop connections, so clients need withAutomaticReconnect, and the app should resync state after reconnecting. And on the client side, browsers throttle background tabs and mobile networks switch.
Logging on both sides, with the transport and close reasons, shows you which case it is pretty fast.

p17-668.q: Right, so rate limiting by IP assumes one IP is one user. Big organisations, like a hospital or a sponsor's office, often route everyone through a few NAT or proxy IPs, so hundreds of real users look like one really busy client and they all get 429s.
p17-668.k: rate limiter blocking users, rate limit by ip problem, corporate nat rate limit, false positive rate limiting, 429 legitimate users
x: Right, so rate limiting by IP assumes one IP is one user. Big organisations, like a hospital or a sponsor's office, often route everyone through a few NAT or proxy IPs, so hundreds of real users look like one really busy client and they all get 429s.

For immediate relief, I find the affected IP ranges from the logs and raise their limits or temporarily allowlist them. But I look at the rest of that traffic first so we're not opening a hole for attackers.

The better fix is rate limiting by a more meaningful key. For authenticated endpoints, partition by user id or client id from the token, so each user gets their own budget. ASP.NET Core's rate limiting middleware supports partitioned limiters with a custom key. For API clients, partition by API key or client application. Keep IP-based limits only for unauthenticated endpoints like login, set them higher, and combine them with per-account limits, that's where brute-force protection really matters.

Also check the app actually sees the real client IP. Behind a load balancer, without forwarded headers configured, every request looks like it came from the load balancer's IP, so literally everyone shares one bucket. ForwardedHeaders middleware with known proxies fixes that. I've seen that one be the whole problem.

Then tune with real data. Look at the distribution of request rates per user, set limits well above legitimate peaks, send Retry-After headers, and monitor 429 counts per client so false positives show up quickly.

p17-669.q: Okay, if the client says slow and our server says fast, the time's going somewhere our server metrics don't measure. So I get specifics first, which endpoints, what times, request ids or timestamps, and what latency they're seeing.
p17-669.k: partner says api slow, client reports slowness, server metrics fine client slow, latency discrepancy, network latency partner
x: Okay, if the client says slow and our server says fast, the time's going somewhere our server metrics don't measure. So I get specifics first, which endpoints, what times, request ids or timestamps, and what latency they're seeing.

Then I compare what we measure with what they experience. Our server metrics usually measure from when the request reaches the app to when the response leaves. They miss everything before that, TLS handshakes, load balancers, WAF inspection, API gateway processing, and queueing in the web server before the app even sees the request, like IIS queues or Kestrel connection limits. Load balancer and gateway logs record total time, so they help here.
Network. The partner might be far away, behind a slow proxy, or have packet loss. Big response bodies make it worse, so compression and smaller payloads help.

Connection handling. If their client opens a new connection for every request, each call pays for DNS, TCP and TLS setup, which can add hundreds of milliseconds across continents. Keep-alive and connection reuse on their side fixes that.
Their own processing. Their number might include their own retries, serialisation or queueing.
And averages hide tails. Our average could be fine while p99 is bad, and they might be hitting exactly those slow cases. So I check percentiles for their specific client id.
A joint test with timestamps on both sides, or a synthetic check from their region, usually settles where the time actually goes.

p17-670.q: So when dashboards say healthy and users say broken, the monitoring is checking the wrong things. I help the users first, then fix the blind spot.
p17-670.k: health checks green users errors, monitoring blind spot, false healthy, health check misleading, users report errors dashboards green
x: So when dashboards say healthy and users say broken, the monitoring is checking the wrong things. I help the users first, then fix the blind spot.
I go after the user problem directly. Get specific examples, the screen, the action, the time, the user, and trace those requests in the logs. Often it's one specific flow, one browser or one tenant.

The typical blind spots. Health checks that only test the process responds, not that it can do real work. The app returns 200 on slash health while the database, a queue or some external dependency is failing for real requests.

Errors that aren't errors to the server. The API returns 200 with an error message in the body, or business failures like "no kits available" get logged as information. And front-end failures, JavaScript errors, failed chunk loads, CORS problems, never reach server metrics at all.
Averages hiding things. Overall error rate is 0.5 percent and looks fine, but it's 100 percent for one feature or one site.
Async failures. The API accepted the request, but the background processing failed later.

The fixes, synthetic monitoring of real user journeys, real-user monitoring and front-end error tracking, SLIs per important flow and not just one overall number, business metrics like successful randomisations per hour, using correct HTTP status codes consistently, and alerts on dead-letter queues and async processing failures. My rule is every incident like this should add the signal that was missing.

p17-671.q: Honestly, when lots of alerts fire together, they usually share one root cause. The job is finding it fast, not chasing each alert.
p17-671.k: alert storm, many alerts at once, incident triage, on call triage, alert flood, where to start incident
x: Honestly, when lots of alerts fire together, they usually share one root cause. The job is finding it fast, not chasing each alert.

First I check user impact. Are key user journeys failing? I look at the top-level SLO or service overview dashboard and the synthetic checks. That sets the urgency, and whether to declare an incident and pull in others.

Then I look for the common factor. Group the alerts by time, which fired first? The earliest one is often closest to the cause, and the rest are downstream effects. Group by dependency, if every service is alerting on database latency or timeouts to the same component, that component's the suspect. And check recent changes, deployments, config changes, infra maintenance, certificate expiry, or a scheduled job that kicked off at 2 AM.
Shared infrastructure too, database, message broker, identity provider, DNS, network, storage, and the cloud provider's status page.
Then act on the likely cause, roll back the change, fail over, restart the stuck component, and watch whether the alerts clear.
Communicate early and keep updating, even if it's just "we're investigating", to stakeholders and support.

Afterwards, fix the alerting itself. Dependency-aware alerting, so a database outage gives one alert and not fifty, grouping in the alert manager, and runbooks linking symptoms to likely causes. An alert storm basically tells you your alerts describe symptoms everywhere instead of the problem once.

p17-672.q: So as incident commander, my job is coordination, not debugging. I make sure the right people are on the right things, decisions actually get made, and everyone knows what's going on.
p17-672.k: incident commander, major incident management, run an incident, incident roles, incident communication, severity 1 outage
x: So as incident commander, my job is coordination, not debugging. I make sure the right people are on the right things, decisions actually get made, and everyone knows what's going on.

To set up, I declare the incident with a severity, open a dedicated channel or bridge, and assign roles. A technical or ops lead who drives the investigation, a comms lead for stakeholders and customers, and a scribe recording the timeline. In a small team one person might hold two roles, but the commander shouldn't also be deep in the logs. Trust me, you lose the big picture the moment you start debugging.

Then I run it in short cycles. What do we know, what are we trying now, who's doing it, when do we check back, every 15 to 30 minutes. The focus is restoring service first, rollback, failover, disabling a feature, not finding the root cause. Decisions are made explicitly, even with imperfect information, and recorded with the time.

Managing people matters too. Bring in specialists when needed, stop too many people changing things at once, and keep side discussions out of the main channel. On long incidents, rotate people so nobody's exhausted.

Communication, regular updates to stakeholders with the impact, current status and the next update time, even if there's no news. For customer-facing systems, consistent messaging through support and status pages.

To close, confirm recovery with monitoring and users, stand down, and schedule a blameless review. In a regulated environment the incident record also captures data impact and any deviations for quality follow-up.

p17-673.q: Okay, so fix the problem, then fix the process, and treat the person with respect the whole way through.
p17-673.k: colleague broke production, config change outage, teammate mistake production, blameless incident, human error production
x: Okay, so fix the problem, then fix the process, and treat the person with respect the whole way through.

To restore service, I revert the config change, which is usually faster and safer than a forward fix, and verify it recovered. If the teammate's around I involve them, because they know exactly what they changed and why, and it makes them part of the fix instead of the one being blamed.

Then I talk to them privately, and supportively. Everyone makes mistakes. If the reaction is blame, people stop admitting mistakes, and the next incident takes longer to resolve because nobody says what they touched.
After that the focus is the system. Why could one config change break production without anyone catching it?

The questions I'd ask in the review. Was the change reviewed? Config deserves the same review as code. Was it tried in a lower environment first? Did the app validate the config at startup, or did it only fail on certain requests? Was it applied by hand on a server, outside the pipeline? Could we see the change quickly, with change logs and alerts linked to deployments? Could we roll it back in one step?

Usual improvements are config in source control and deployed through the pipeline, validation at startup with clear failures, staged rollout of config changes just like code, and audit logging of changes.
Honestly the best outcome I've seen is when the teammate presents the review themselves and leads one of the improvements.

p17-674.q: See, when a background job updates loads of rows in one big transaction, it holds locks for the whole duration. Users trying to read or update those rows wait, time out, or deadlock.
p17-674.k: background job blocking users, long running batch locks, batch update blocking, job causes timeouts, chunked batch processing
x: See, when a background job updates loads of rows in one big transaction, it holds locks for the whole duration. Users trying to read or update those rows wait, time out, or deadlock.
To confirm, during the problem the requests DMV and blocking queries show the job's session as the head blocker, holding tons of locks, maybe escalated to a table lock.

The main fix is processing in small batches. Update or delete maybe 1,000 to 5,000 rows per transaction, commit, carry on. Each transaction is short, so locks get released quickly, and you avoid lock escalation, which kicks in around 5,000 locks. The job also becomes restartable with progress tracking, and uses less transaction log.
Make sure the batch queries use indexes, so each batch touches only its own rows and doesn't scan the table, which takes way more locks.
Read committed snapshot isolation helps a lot, readers aren't blocked by the job's writes, so most of the user-facing blocking on read-heavy screens just goes away.
Schedule it away from peak hours, and throttle between batches with a short delay if you need to.
Avoid unnecessary work. Only update rows whose values actually change, and do the calculations before the transaction, not inside it.
For really big changes, I'd consider building the new data in a separate table and switching over, instead of updating in place.
And then monitor blocking and job duration, so if it creeps back we see it before users do.

p17-675.q: Actually index maintenance is supposed to help performance, but if it's done carelessly it takes locks, fills the transaction log and saturates I/O.
p17-675.k: index rebuild outage, index maintenance blocking, rebuild index locks, online index rebuild, maintenance window issue
x: Actually index maintenance is supposed to help performance, but if it's done carelessly it takes locks, fills the transaction log and saturates I/O.

What usually goes wrong. Offline rebuilds, on editions or settings without online operations, ALTER INDEX REBUILD takes a schema modification lock and blocks all access to the table for the whole time. On a big table that's minutes or hours of outage.
Log growth. Rebuilding a big index generates a lot of log, which can fill the log disk, especially if log backups don't run during the job. In availability groups it can overwhelm the replicas too.
Wrong timing, overlapping with business hours in another region, or with batch jobs and backups. And doing too much, rebuilding every index every night whether it needs it or not.
The fixes. Online rebuilds, with WAIT_AT_LOW_PRIORITY so the rebuild gives way to user queries, and resumable index operations that can be paused and resumed.

Be selective. Rebuild only the fragmented indexes that matter, reorganise the moderately fragmented ones, or skip them. On modern SSD storage fragmentation matters less than statistics, and updating stats is often the more valuable part.
Use a proven maintenance solution, like Ola Hallengren's scripts, with thresholds and time limits.

Schedule it in a window that's quiet for every region, make sure log backups run frequently during maintenance, and watch blocking and log usage while it runs. I'd say most of these outages come from a job someone set up years ago and nobody looked at since.

p17-676.q: Honestly, major .NET upgrades have breaking changes and behaviour changes that compile fine and then act differently at runtime.
p17-676.k: dotnet upgrade broke, behaviour change after upgrade, breaking change dotnet version, migration issue net 8, upgrade regression
x: Honestly, major .NET upgrades have breaking changes and behaviour changes that compile fine and then act differently at runtime.
If it's serious, I roll back to the previous build, which still targets the old version, and investigate from there.

Then the breaking changes docs. Microsoft publishes a list for every version, by area, ASP.NET Core, serialisation, globalisation, networking, containers. Matching the symptom to an area usually finds it.
Some examples I've seen or watch out for. Container images, since .NET 8 the default port moved from 80 to 8080 and images run as non-root, which breaks services and health checks expecting port 80.
Globalisation. ICU on Linux versus NLS on Windows behave differently, which changes string comparisons, culture formatting or sorting.
Serialisation. System.Text.Json differences, stricter handling, case sensitivity, new defaults, when moving from Newtonsoft or between versions.
EF Core. Query translation changes between major versions, like how collections or Contains get translated, which affects results or performance.
And security defaults, TLS versions, cipher suites, cookie settings getting stricter.
Fix it, then add a test that captures that behaviour so it's pinned down.

For prevention, upgrade non-production first, run full regression and performance tests, read the breaking changes list before you upgrade, not after, and upgrade regularly, version by version, instead of jumping several versions at once.

p17-677.q: So changing or upgrading a JSON serialiser can quietly change the shape of your API responses, and the front end depends on exact property names and formats, so it breaks.
p17-677.k: json serialization change, camelcase pascalcase json, newtonsoft to system text json, enum serialization changed, date format json changed
x: So changing or upgrading a JSON serialiser can quietly change the shape of your API responses, and the front end depends on exact property names and formats, so it breaks.

The typical differences, especially going from Newtonsoft to System.Text.Json. Property naming, camelCase versus PascalCase depending on configuration. If the front end expects shipmentId and now gets ShipmentId with a capital S, everything's undefined.
Enums get serialised as numbers by default unless you configure a JsonStringEnumConverter. The front end expected "Delivered" and now gets 3.
Dates, formats and time zone handling differ, DateTime with Kind Unspecified, offsets included or not.

Nulls, whether null properties are included or left out. Reference loops and polymorphism, Newtonsoft handled some cases with settings that System.Text.Json handles differently or needs attributes for.
And case-insensitive deserialisation. Newtonsoft was case-insensitive by default, System.Text.Json is case-sensitive unless configured, although ASP.NET Core's web defaults are case-insensitive.
The fix is configuring the serialiser explicitly to match the old contract, naming policy, enum converter, date handling, instead of trusting defaults. Then verify with the front end.

What I do to prevent it is treat the API's JSON as a contract. Snapshot tests of responses with Verify catch accidental shape changes. Contract tests with consumers, or OpenAPI checks in CI comparing the schema with the previous version, flag breaking changes before release.

p17-678.q: Yeah, off-by-a-cent is almost always floating point types for money, or inconsistent rounding.
p17-678.k: rounding error money, floating point currency, decimal vs double money, off by one cent, rounding mode, precision loss json
x: Yeah, off-by-a-cent is almost always floating point types for money, or inconsistent rounding.

Floating point first. double and float in C#, and number in JavaScript, are binary floating point, and they can't represent a lot of decimal fractions exactly. 0.1 plus 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3. Sum enough values and the tiny errors add up until you see a cent difference. So use decimal in C#, and DECIMAL or NUMERIC with fixed scale in SQL. Never FLOAT or REAL for money.

Rounding rules. .NET's Math Round uses banker's rounding by default, so 2.5 rounds to 2, while business users and other systems usually expect away from zero, 2.5 to 3. Pass MidpointRounding explicitly, and agree the rule with the business.

When to round. Rounding each line then summing gives a different total than summing then rounding. The business rules have to say which one, like per line item for invoices, and the code has to do it the same way everywhere, including reports and exports. That's where it usually goes wrong, one report does it differently.

Front end. JavaScript numbers can lose precision on very large values, and browser calculations can disagree with the server. Do the authoritative calculation on the server, send money as strings or with a known scale if precision matters, and only format on the client.
Currency, different currencies have different decimal places, so the scale comes from the currency.
Then I add tests with known tricky values and compare totals across the system.

p17-679.q: Let me be careful here, because a half-finished migration leaves data in a mixed state. The first job is understanding exactly what state it's in, before touching anything.
p17-679.k: data migration failed halfway, partial migration recovery, resume migration, batch migration failure, migration rollback data
x: Let me be careful here, because a half-finished migration leaves data in a mixed state. The first job is understanding exactly what state it's in, before touching anything.

So stop and assess. Make sure it's not still running or retrying. Find out which batches or rows got migrated and which didn't, and whether any batch was half applied. A good migration makes that easy because it logs progress per batch.

Then decide, resume or roll back. If it was designed to be resumable and idempotent, I fix the cause, bad data in one batch, a timeout, a constraint violation, and resume from the last completed batch. If it isn't resumable, or the data looks suspect, I restore the affected tables from the backup taken just before, or reverse the migrated batches with a tested script.
Then validate. Row counts, checksums, and business-level checks between source and target, like totals per study or site, plus samples reviewed with business users.

How I design migrations so this isn't painful. Batches with a progress table recording each completed batch, so it can resume. Idempotent operations, running a batch twice gives the same result, like upserts with stable keys. Keep the source data unchanged until it's verified, write to new tables or columns, then switch over. Dry runs on a production copy to measure duration and catch data surprises. And validation queries ready in advance.
In a regulated system, the migration plan, results and verification are documented and approved as part of the change.

p17-680.q: Okay, this is the case where availability directly affects patients and trials, so it's planned for in advance, not improvised on the day.
p17-680.k: irt down randomization, system outage clinical site, business continuity irt, randomization during outage, irt downtime procedure
x: Okay, this is the case where availability directly affects patients and trials, so it's planned for in advance, not improvised on the day.
On the system side, it's handled as top severity. The focus is getting service back as fast as possible, and clear communication to the support teams who talk to the sites.

On the business side, IRT providers have business continuity procedures agreed with the sponsor for each study. Usually the site calls the support helpdesk, which is available around the clock, and the procedure says what can be done manually and who can authorise it. [For example, the protocol may allow a short delay of the randomisation visit, or a documented manual process.] Any manual action has to be recorded with full details, so when the system's back, the transactions get entered or reconciled, the audit trail is complete, and the randomisation list and drug supply records stay consistent. Because blinding and allocation integrity matter so much, manual steps are tightly controlled.

What we do in engineering is make it rare and short. High availability infrastructure, tested failover and backups, careful releases with rollback plans, and monitoring that spots problems before the sites do.
After recovery, we check no transactions were lost or duplicated, especially the ones in flight when the outage started, and support any reconciliation.
For me the point to get across in an interview is that we design with this patient-facing impact in mind from the start.

p17-681.q: So this one's urgent, because a patient visit might be blocked. I look for why the system won't allocate kits it seems to have.
p17-681.k: site no kits available, inventory mismatch, stock discrepancy, kits not allocatable, drug supply discrepancy
x: So this one's urgent, because a patient visit might be blocked. I look for why the system won't allocate kits it seems to have.

First I clarify the symptom. What exactly did the site see, a "no kits available" message during dispensing, or a physical shipment that never showed up? Which patient, visit, treatment arm and kit type?

Then I go through the reasons a kit can exist but not be dispensable. Status, the kits might be in a status that excludes them, quarantined after a temperature excursion, damaged, lost, expired, or not received at the site yet.
Expiry and use-by rules. The kits are in stock but too close to expiry to cover the dosing period, based on the study's configured buffer days.
Treatment arm and blinding. The site has kits, just not the type this patient's arm needs. The site view is blinded, so it may only show total stock, and it looks like there's plenty.
Configuration, a recent study config change, like a new kit type or dosing rule, that the existing stock doesn't match.
Data issues, a shipment receipt not recorded properly, or a stuck transaction.
The immediate action is working with support and the supply team on an emergency shipment, or a documented manual process if the protocol allows it.

For root cause, if it's a supply shortfall, the resupply settings, trigger and resupply levels per site, might need tuning. If it's a defect, it gets fixed and assessed for other sites. The investigation, data checks and any correction all go through the controlled process.

p17-682.q: Right, a day before go-live the real question is how serious the bug is, and whether it can be fixed safely in time without compromising validation.
p17-682.k: study go live bug, config issue before go live, last minute defect, release decision go live, study launch issue
x: Right, a day before go-live the real question is how serious the bug is, and whether it can be fixed safely in time without compromising validation.

I assess impact quickly with the study team. Which functionality, which visits or sites, and what's the patient and data risk if we go live with it? Is it day-one stuff like screening and randomisation, or something used weeks later, like a later visit or a resupply rule?

Then there are basically three ways it can go. Fix and retest, if it's a small config change, apply it in the study build, rerun the affected test scripts and the relevant parts of UAT, and get approvals. Config changes still need validation evidence.
Go live with a workaround. If the affected bit isn't needed straight away, go live on schedule with a documented plan to fix it before it's needed, agreed and signed off by the sponsor and quality.

Or delay. If day-one functionality that affects patients or randomisation is wrong and can't be fixed and tested safely, a short delay is the right call. Going live with a randomisation or dosing error is far worse than a few days' delay.
Whatever we decide, it's made with the sponsor, study team and quality, documented, and communicated to everyone involved, including sites.
Afterwards we look at why it wasn't caught earlier, like a missing test scenario in the spec review or simulation, and improve the config checks and test templates.

p17-683.q: Honestly this is a serious data integrity finding in a GxP system, so the response has to be thorough and documented.
p17-683.k: audit trail gaps, missing audit records, audit finding, part 11 audit trail, data integrity finding
x: Honestly this is a serious data integrity finding in a GxP system, so the response has to be thorough and documented.

I start by understanding the scope precisely. Which records, which fields, what time period, which actions are missing audit entries? Is it every change of a certain type, changes through one particular path, like a back-end process, a data correction script or an integration, or is it intermittent?

Then the cause. A code path that bypasses the audit layer is the common one, like a bulk operation or a direct SQL update that doesn't go through the normal service, or a new feature that never got wired into audit logging. Audit writes failing silently, if audit entries are written separately from the main change and errors get swallowed, a failure leaves a change with no audit record. Data corrections done outside the controlled process. Or retention and archiving processes removing records too early.

For the response, assess impact with quality, figure out whether the missing information can be rebuilt from other sources, database logs, app logs, backups, and document what can and can't be recovered.

The fix I prefer is making the audit record part of the same transaction as the change, so neither can exist without the other. Or database-level mechanisms like triggers or temporal tables for completeness. Then tests that verify every write path creates audit records, and monitoring for audit write failures.
And the formal CAPA process tracks the corrective and preventive actions to closure.

p17-684.q: So with a database per study, every database has the same schema and the same code. That means the difference has to come from data, configuration, or the database's own state.
p17-684.k: one database slow, study database slow, tenant database performance, per tenant db slow, database per tenant performance
x: So with a database per study, every database has the same schema and the same code. That means the difference has to come from data, configuration, or the database's own state.

I compare the slow one with a typical one. Data volume first. A big, long-running study might have way more subjects, kits, visits and audit records, so queries that are fine elsewhere hit huge tables here. Sometimes specific tables have grown unusually, like audit or log tables with no archiving.

Statistics and plans. Stats might be stale after big data changes, so plans are poor. Query Store on that database shows the top queries and any plan changes. Parameter sniffing can hit one database differently, just because its data distribution is different.

Index health. Missing or fragmented indexes, or one that's in the standard schema but missing here because a deployment failed for this particular database. Schema drift between study databases is honestly worth checking against the expected version.
Study configuration. Features only this study uses, complex randomisation, more strata, particular integrations, which drive heavier queries.
Placement. The database might be on a busier server, sharing with other heavy databases, or its files sit on slower storage.
And maintenance, did index and stats maintenance actually run successfully for this one?

The fix follows the cause, update stats, add indexes, archive old data, tune specific queries, or move the database to a quieter server. Then I check whether other large studies are heading for the same problem, because usually they are.

p17-685.q: Okay, gradual slowdown with growth is predictable, so I treat it as capacity planning, not a surprise.
p17-685.k: database growing slow, data growth performance, archiving old data, partitioning large tables, long term database performance
x: Okay, gradual slowdown with growth is predictable, so I treat it as capacity planning, not a surprise.
What I do first is measure. Table sizes, row counts, query durations and resource usage over time, so I know which tables and queries are growing, how fast, and roughly when they'll start hurting.

Then the fixes, roughly from least effort to most. Indexes and queries, stuff written when tables were small often scans, and with millions of rows you need proper indexes, filters on indexed columns, only the data you need, and paging.

Archiving. Move old, rarely used data, closed records, old audit entries, historical logs, to archive tables or a separate archive database, but keep it accessible for reporting and regulatory needs. Retention requirements decide what can move and what has to stay.

Partitioning. For really big tables like audit or transaction history, partitioning by date makes maintenance and archiving efficient, and partition switching moves old data almost instantly. It only helps queries that filter on the partition key though.

Columnstore indexes for reporting over large historical data. Separating workloads, so reporting and analytics move to a replica or warehouse. And hardware and config, more memory to keep the working set cached, faster storage, database settings.
In a regulated system, archiving has to keep data complete, retrievable and auditable for the whole retention period. So I'd design it with quality and compliance in the room, not on my own.

p17-686.q: See, in a database-per-study design, the master database usually holds the shared stuff, users, permissions, the study registry, global config. Every request across every study might touch it. So as studies and users grow, it turns into a hotspot.
p17-686.k: master database bottleneck, shared database bottleneck, central database contention, multi tenant shared db hot, scaling shared database
x: See, in a database-per-study design, the master database usually holds the shared stuff, users, permissions, the study registry, global config. Every request across every study might touch it. So as studies and users grow, it turns into a hotspot.

First I find out what load it's actually carrying. Top queries by frequency and cost from Query Store, and which apps and features issue them. Often it's a few lookups that run on every single request.

The biggest win is usually caching. Study configuration, user permissions and reference data change rarely but get read constantly. Cache them in memory or Redis, with invalidation when they change, and most of the load just disappears.
Then query efficiency. Fix the expensive queries with indexes and better access patterns, and get rid of chatty patterns, like one query per study in a loop.
Read scaling, route read-only queries to a readable replica.
Reduce coupling. Move data that's really study-specific out of master into the study databases, and avoid cross-database queries from study databases to master in hot paths.
Split responsibilities. The master often plays several roles, identity, configuration, job scheduling. Separating those into their own stores or services lets them scale independently.
And connection management, make sure apps use pooled connections and don't hold them open.
I'd also check the master's availability setup. If everything depends on it, its outage is everyone's outage, so it deserves the strongest HA you've got.

p17-687.q: Actually the first thing is making sure they're even counting the same thing. Say our system and a partner's warehouse show different shipment or stock counts. The goal is finding which records differ and why, then fixing the data and the cause.
p17-687.k: data mismatch between systems, reconciliation, inconsistent data two systems, data sync issue, integration discrepancy
x: Actually the first thing is making sure they're even counting the same thing. Say our system and a partner's warehouse show different shipment or stock counts. The goal is finding which records differ and why, then fixing the data and the cause.

So define the comparison precisely, same entity, same time cut-off, same definition. A lot of "mismatches" are just different definitions, like counting shipped versus received, or different time zones for the cut-off.

Then compare at record level, not just totals. Export the keys and key attributes from both sides for the period and match them. You get records only in A, records only in B, and records in both but with different values. Each of those points to a different cause.
Only in one system usually means messages or files that failed, were never sent, got dead-lettered, or were rejected by the other side's validation. So check integration logs and DLQs.
Different values means updates that didn't propagate, out-of-order processing where an older update overwrote a newer one, or mapping differences like units or status codes.
Fix the data through the controlled process, reprocess failed messages, resend corrected records, or apply documented corrections.
Fix the cause, idempotent, ordered processing with version checks, and better error handling and alerts for integration failures.
And what I'd always add is an automated daily reconciliation job that compares counts or checksums and alerts on differences. Then you find mismatches in a day, not at month end.

p17-688.q: Honestly urgency changes the speed, not the safety rules. A config change in a validated study can affect patients, so it still follows the controlled process, just expedited.
p17-688.k: urgent configuration change, study amendment urgent, emergency config change, change production configuration safely, protocol amendment change
x: Honestly urgency changes the speed, not the safety rules. A config change in a validated study can affect patients, so it still follows the controlled process, just expedited.

I start by clarifying the need. What exactly has to change, why it's urgent, a protocol amendment taking effect, a safety issue, a supply problem, and what happens if we wait. That tells us how fast we really need to go.

Then impact. Which parts of the study it touches, visit schedules, dosing, randomisation, supply settings, eligibility, and what happens to subjects already enrolled. Amendments can apply differently to existing and new subjects, and that's easy to miss in a rush.

The change goes in the study build environment, never straight into production. Configure, then test with focused scripts on the affected areas plus a regression check on core flows like randomisation and dispensing, ideally with simulation.
Approvals through the expedited path, sponsor sign-off on the change, quality review of the test evidence. The documentation can be lighter in format, but it can't be missing.
Deploy through the standard study promotion process, UAT to production, so it's the same mechanism we trust, and verify in production afterwards.
Tell sites and support teams what changed and when.
Afterwards, look at why it became urgent, maybe late notice of an amendment, and whether this type of change could go faster next time, like pre-approved test templates for common config changes.

p17-689.q: So after a partner upgrades their SFTP server, failures are usually about security algorithms, keys or network changes. I go through the connection log details carefully.
p17-689.k: sftp connection refused after upgrade, ssh key algorithm not supported, sftp negotiation failed, host key changed, cipher mismatch sftp
x: So after a partner upgrades their SFTP server, failures are usually about security algorithms, keys or network changes. I go through the connection log details carefully.
I turn on verbose logging in the SFTP client. The handshake log shows exactly where it fails, key exchange, host key verification, authentication, or opening the channel.

Algorithm mismatch is the most common one in my experience. Newer servers disable old algorithms, ssh-rsa with SHA-1 signatures, older key exchange methods, CBC ciphers. If our client library or config only offers those, negotiation fails with "no matching algorithm". The fix is updating the client library and enabling modern ones, rsa-sha2-256 or ed25519 keys and curve25519 key exchange.

Host key changed. The upgrade generated a new host key, so our client, which pins the old fingerprint, refuses to connect. And it's right to refuse, it could be a man-in-the-middle. So get the new fingerprint from the partner through a trusted channel, verify it, and update our config.

Authentication, our public key didn't get migrated, or they now need a different key type, or password auth got disabled. Network, new IP or port, their firewall only allows our old IP, or our egress IP changed. Permissions, folders or paths changed.

One thing that helps us, our SFTP component supports multiple client libraries behind one interface. So if one library can't do the new algorithms, switching provider through config is an option, tested first of course.
And afterwards, agree with partners on advance notice of upgrades and a test endpoint.

p17-690.q: Okay, an actively exploited vulnerability flips the usual balance. Not patching is now riskier than the change. But a careless rollout can still cause an outage, so I move fast but with structure.
p17-690.k: emergency patch, urgent security patching, zero day patch servers, patch rollout plan, critical vulnerability servers
x: Okay, an actively exploited vulnerability flips the usual balance. Not patching is now riskier than the change. But a careless rollout can still cause an outage, so I move fast but with structure.

I assess exposure first. Which servers and components are affected, which ones are internet-facing or hold sensitive data. Those go first. And I check for temporary mitigations, a WAF rule, disabling a feature, blocking a port, that cut the risk right now while patching goes on.
Approval through the emergency change process, with the risk assessment written down. In a regulated environment that's required anyway.
Test quickly. Patch a non-production environment, run smoke and key regression tests, focusing on whatever the patch touches.

Roll out in waves. One production server or a small group first, out of the load balancer, patch, reboot, check health and functionality, put it back, then the next group. That keeps capacity up and lets us stop if something breaks. For clusters, drain nodes one at a time.
Have a rollback plan, snapshots or the ability to uninstall the patch.
Then verify it's installed everywhere with an inventory or scanning tool, and that nothing got missed. I've seen forgotten or rarely used machines get skipped more than once.
Keep everyone updated throughout, then close the change with evidence. Afterwards, look at how long patching took and how to make the routine process faster next time.

p17-691.q: Right, a weekly pattern means something builds up over the weekend, or load peaks at that exact time.
p17-691.k: slow monday morning, slow after weekend, cold start monday, cache cold after weekend, weekly peak performance
x: Right, a weekly pattern means something builds up over the weekend, or load peaks at that exact time.

I'd say the load pattern is the obvious one. Monday morning is often the busiest, everyone logs in, catches up on weekend work, processes backlogs. Add another time zone's Monday overlapping and peak load might just exceed capacity. Comparing Monday's metrics with other days confirms it. The fix is scheduled scaling ahead of the known peak, and fixing the queries that are most expensive at peak.

Cold caches and idle shutdown. If app pools idle out, containers scale to zero, or caches expire over a quiet weekend, the first users on Monday pay for warming everything, JIT, loading config, filling caches. Always On or Application Initialization, warm-up jobs before business hours, and minimum instance counts fix that.

Weekend jobs. Index rebuilds, stats updates, big batch imports running over the weekend and still going Monday morning, or leaving stats stale. So check schedules and durations, and make sure they finish well before business hours.
Backlogs. Messages or files that piled up over the weekend get processed Monday morning and compete with users. Process them continuously, or throttle background processing in peak hours.
Authentication too, lots of tokens and sessions expired over the weekend, so the identity provider gets a login surge all at once.
What I'd do is look at Monday's metrics hour by hour and see which of these lines up.

p17-692.q: Let me say the main thing first, I fix the tooling, I don't bypass it. Bypassing the pipeline undermines everything the release process guarantees, especially in a regulated environment.
p17-692.k: build agent offline, pipeline broken before release, cannot deploy release, self hosted agent down, release blocked pipeline
x: Let me say the main thing first, I fix the tooling, I don't bypass it. Bypassing the pipeline undermines everything the release process guarantees, especially in a regulated environment.

So I diagnose the agent. Is the agent service stopped, the machine down, out of disk, lost network access to the Azure DevOps Server, or has its access token expired? The agent pool page shows its status and last contact, and the diagnostic logs on the machine show errors. Disk full with old build folders and caches is super common. Cleaning the work folder often brings it straight back.

Alternatives, if another agent in the pool has the same capabilities, the job can run there. If the machine is really broken, a new agent can be set up quickly, as long as agents are built from a documented script or image, which is exactly why we keep that script.
I tell the release coordinator the expected delay, so stakeholders can decide whether to keep the window or move it.

What I don't do is build on my laptop and copy files to servers by hand. That artifact isn't traceable, tested or approved through the normal flow. If the release truly can't wait, it goes through the emergency change process with a documented justification.
Afterwards, monitor agent health and disk space, keep more than one agent capable of every critical job, and automate agent provisioning, so one machine isn't a single point of failure for releases.

p17-693.q: So if a request takes minutes, generating a big report, running a simulation, importing a large file, keeping the HTTP request open causes timeouts at proxies and browsers, holds server resources, and fails badly when the connection drops.
p17-693.k: long running request, request takes minutes, move to background processing, async request reply, 202 accepted pattern
x: So if a request takes minutes, generating a big report, running a simulation, importing a large file, keeping the HTTP request open causes timeouts at proxies and browsers, holds server resources, and fails badly when the connection drops.

The redesign is the asynchronous request-reply pattern. The API validates the request quickly, creates a job record with a status like Pending, puts a message on a queue, and returns 202 Accepted with a job id and a status URL.

A background worker, a hosted service, a separate worker or a function, picks up the message and does the work, updating progress and status, and stores the result somewhere like blob storage or a results table.
The client polls the status URL, or gets a push notification through SignalR or email when it's done, and then fetches the result.

What you get is no request timeouts, work that survives server restarts because it's queued, retries on failure, controlled concurrency so ten big jobs don't flatten the database, and a UI that can show progress while users keep working.

The details I'd get right are idempotency, so a retried submission doesn't create duplicate jobs, using an idempotency key. Authorisation on the status and result endpoints, so users only see their own jobs. Cancellation support, cleanup of old results, and clear error states.
For stuff under a minute, just optimising the work might be enough. Anything longer, I'd go with this pattern, it's the reliable answer.

p17-694.q: Yeah, a mystery value in production config is risky both ways. Change it and something might break, leave it and it might be hiding a problem. So I investigate before touching it.
p17-694.k: unknown config value, mystery configuration, undocumented setting, config archaeology, configuration ownership
x: Yeah, a mystery value in production config is risky both ways. Change it and something might break, leave it and it might be hiding a problem. So I investigate before touching it.

I look for its history first. Source control history for config files and pipeline variables, deployment logs, change tickets, the config store's audit history. Often a commit message or ticket explains it, like a timeout bumped during an incident years ago.
Then its usage. Search the code for the key, including libraries and scripts, to see what reads it and what it does. Sometimes nothing reads it anymore and it's just a leftover.
Ask people, the team, previous owners, operations, and the vendor docs if it's a framework setting.
Test the effect in a lower environment. Change it there and watch, ideally with load or integration tests that exercise the related path.
Then decide. Keep it and document why, change it through a normal change with monitoring, or remove it if it's unused, again through a normal change, not quietly.

To stop future mysteries, all config in source control with meaningful commit messages, non-obvious settings documented next to the value or in a config reference, strongly typed options classes with validation and comments, and regularly removing unused settings.
In a regulated system, config values that affect validated behaviour have to be controlled anyway, so this kind of documentation is part of the evidence people expect.

p17-695.q: Honestly I can't always fix the legacy system, but I can stop its slowness from becoming my users' problem.
p17-695.k: slow legacy dependency, protect from slow dependency, legacy system bottleneck, wrap slow service, cache legacy data
x: Honestly I can't always fix the legacy system, but I can stop its slowness from becoming my users' problem.
I measure first. Which calls are slow, how slow, and how often my service calls it per user action. Sometimes the biggest issue is actually my side calling it too often.

Then the protections. Timeouts on every call, so a slow response fails fast instead of holding threads and connections. Paired with a circuit breaker, so when the legacy system is struggling, we stop hammering it and fail fast or degrade.
Caching, if the data rarely changes, reference data, configuration, cache it with a sensible TTL so most requests never touch the legacy system at all.
Async integration. For writes or long operations, queue the requests and process them in the background at a pace the legacy system can handle, and give the user an immediate acknowledgement.

A replicated read model. For data that's read a lot, keep a local copy synced through change data capture, events or a scheduled sync, and serve reads from it. Users get fast responses and accept a small delay in freshness.
Bulkheads, isolate calls to the legacy system in their own limited pool, so its slowness can't eat all my service's resources.
Graceful degradation, show what's available and clearly mark what couldn't load, instead of failing the whole page.
And longer term, these protections often end up being the first step of a strangler fig migration, replacing the legacy system piece by piece.

p17-696.q: So if errors spike every time we deploy, something in the release process is either interrupting in-flight work or sending traffic to instances that aren't ready yet. I go through it phase by phase.
p17-696.k: errors during deployment, downtime during release, zero downtime deployment, deploy causes errors, graceful shutdown deploy
x: So if errors spike every time we deploy, something in the release process is either interrupting in-flight work or sending traffic to instances that aren't ready yet. I go through it phase by phase.

Instances starting. Are new ones getting traffic before they're ready, before caches warm, JIT finishes, connections are set up? The fix is readiness checks that only pass when the app can really serve, warm-up requests, and Application Initialization on IIS.

Instances stopping. Are old ones getting killed while handling requests? Take them out of the load balancer first, let connections drain with a deregistration delay, and implement graceful shutdown, so on SIGTERM the app stops taking new requests, finishes the in-flight ones and closes consumers cleanly within the timeout.
Capacity during rollout. If half the instances get replaced at once, the rest can get overloaded. Rolling updates with extra surge capacity mean capacity never drops.

Version incompatibility. During a rolling update, old and new run side by side and clients or other services hit both. So API changes have to be backward compatible, schema changes use expand and contract, and message formats need to be readable by both versions. This one can catch people out.

Sessions and state, in-memory sessions vanish when an instance stops, so keep services stateless with external session storage. And background workers, messages in progress at shutdown should be completed or returned to the queue, not lost.
I'd also track errors per deployment as a metric, so you can see things improving and catch regressions.

p17-697.q: Okay, a full region or data centre outage is exactly what disaster recovery plans exist for. So the response follows the plan, not improvisation.
p17-697.k: region outage, data centre outage, cloud outage response, failover to dr, disaster recovery activation
x: Okay, a full region or data centre outage is exactly what disaster recovery plans exist for. So the response follows the plan, not improvisation.

I confirm and assess first. Check the provider's status page and our own monitoring from outside the affected region. Work out which systems are hit and how long it might last, if the provider has an estimate.

Then decide whether to fail over. Failing over has its own risks and costs, especially with asynchronous replication, where you might lose some recent data, up to the recovery point objective. If the provider expects recovery soon, waiting might be better. Who decides and on what criteria is defined in the DR plan ahead of time, usually based on expected outage duration versus our recovery time objective.

If we fail over, promote the replicated databases in the secondary region, switch DNS or global load balancing over, start or scale up compute there from infrastructure as code, and verify the critical journeys. Keep users and stakeholders informed.
During the outage, track which data might be lost or in an uncertain state, like transactions that were in flight.
Fail back once the primary is healthy, resync data and switch back in a planned window. Honestly that's often harder than the failover itself.

Afterwards, review against the plan, measure the actual recovery time and data loss, and fix the gaps. The biggest thing is regular DR testing, because an untested DR plan usually fails right when you need it.

p17-698.q: See, full-text search, faceting and fuzzy matching are way better in a search engine like Elasticsearch, OpenSearch or Azure AI Search than in SQL. But then the same data lives in two places, and keeping the index reliably in sync is the actual challenge.
p17-698.k: elasticsearch sync sql, opensearch sync, search index synchronization, change data capture search, reindex search
x: See, full-text search, faceting and fuzzy matching are way better in a search engine like Elasticsearch, OpenSearch or Azure AI Search than in SQL. But then the same data lives in two places, and keeping the index reliably in sync is the actual challenge.

The simplest option is dual writes from the app. After saving to SQL, also update the index. Easy, but if the index call fails after the database commit, they drift apart and you have no easy way of knowing. I wouldn't use that as the only mechanism.

Better is events through an outbox. The service writes the change and an outbox record in the same transaction, a relay publishes the event, and an indexer consumer updates the search index. Reliable, with retries, and the index catches up even after failures.

Change data capture is another way. Read the database's change stream, SQL Server CDC or Debezium on the transaction log, and feed changes to the indexer. No app changes, and it captures everything, including changes made by scripts or other apps.
Or a periodic sync, an incremental job with a last-modified watermark. Simpler but more delay.

Whichever one, I design for drift. Index documents carry a version or timestamp so older updates can't overwrite newer ones. There's a full reindex capability, building a new index alongside and switching an alias atomically, for mapping changes or recovery. And a reconciliation check comparing counts or checksums.
One thing people forget is security trimming. Index the fields needed for permission filtering, like site or tenant, and always filter by them.

p17-699.q: Actually the core problem is concurrency. Two requests both see one item left, and both take it. So the design has to make the check and the update atomic.
p17-699.k: inventory reservation design, prevent overselling, stock reservation, concurrent allocation, kit allocation design, reserve and confirm
x: Actually the core problem is concurrency. Two requests both see one item left, and both take it. So the design has to make the check and the update atomic.

For the data model, either stock per location and item type with available and reserved quantities, or individual items, like kits with unique ids and statuses. That second one is how clinical supply works.

For atomic reservation you've got a few choices. A conditional update in the database, update stock set available to available minus one, where the id matches and available is at least one, and then check the affected row count. If it's zero, there was no stock. One statement, no race.

For individual items, select and lock one available item with UPDLOCK and READPAST hints, so concurrent requests skip each other's locked rows, then mark it reserved in the same transaction. Or optimistic concurrency with a row version, retrying on conflict.

Then reserve, then confirm. A reservation has an expiry. If the process completes, like a dispensing gets confirmed, it becomes final. If it's abandoned, a background job releases expired reservations so stock isn't locked forever.
Idempotency, every request carries an idempotency key so retries don't reserve twice.
The selection applies the business rules, expiry dates, first expiry first out, blinding constraints, the right item type for the patient's arm.

For scale, partition by location, so contention is only between requests for the same site's stock, and keep transactions short. And I'd add reconciliation jobs comparing reservations with confirmed transactions, flagging anything stuck.

p17-700.q: Honestly the requirement sounds simple. Send reminders at the right time, like three days before a patient's visit window opens, reliably, exactly once, and adapt when schedules change. The details are where it gets interesting.
p17-700.k: design reminder service, scheduled notifications design, visit reminder system, delayed jobs design, scheduler service design
x: Honestly the requirement sounds simple. Send reminders at the right time, like three days before a patient's visit window opens, reliably, exactly once, and adapt when schedules change. The details are where it gets interesting.

For the data model, a scheduled notifications table with the target, like subject and visit, the type, the due time in UTC, status and a version. Reminders get created or updated whenever the visit schedule changes, like after randomisation or when a visit is recorded.

For triggering, a scheduler process polls for due items in small batches, using an index on due time and status. Each item is claimed atomically, an update setting status to Processing where it's still Pending, or a select with UPDLOCK and READPAST, so multiple scheduler instances can run without double sending. You could use delayed messages instead, Service Bus scheduled messages, SQS delay up to 15 minutes plus a store, or EventBridge Scheduler. But a table gives you easy querying, cancellation and auditing.
Sending, the claimed item becomes a message to the notification service, which renders the template and sends email or SMS, with retries and idempotency by notification id.
Changes and cancellations. If the visit gets rescheduled, update the due time. If the subject withdraws, cancel pending reminders. A version check stops a stale reminder going out.
Time zones, due times are computed in the site's time zone, handling daylight saving.
And monitoring, overdue pending items trigger an alert, so a stuck scheduler gets noticed fast. That's the same kind of check our AlertWatchDog jobs do.

p17-701.q: So reports and documents, PDFs, Excel files, regulatory exports, are usually slow, heavy on resources, and fail now and then. That's why I'd put them in a separate asynchronous service.
p17-701.k: report generation service design, pdf generation service, document generation microservice, async report design, template rendering service
x: So reports and documents, PDFs, Excel files, regulatory exports, are usually slow, heavy on resources, and fail now and then. That's why I'd put them in a separate asynchronous service.

The flow. The client requests a report with parameters. The API validates input and permissions, stores a job record and returns 202 with a job id. A worker takes the job off a queue, gathers data through APIs or a read replica, renders it with a template engine, like a Razor or HTML template converted to PDF, or a library for Excel, stores the file in blob storage and marks the job complete. The client gets notified or polls, then downloads through a short-lived signed URL.
For me, a few design points matter here. Templates are versioned separately from code, so layouts can change through a controlled process. That matters a lot for regulated documents.
Determinism. Same inputs and same template version should give the same document. I record the template version, parameters and data timestamp in the job, for traceability.
Scaling. Rendering is CPU and memory heavy, so workers scale on their own based on queue depth, with limits per user or tenant so one huge request doesn't starve everybody else.
Resilience, retries with idempotency, timeouts for very large reports, clear error messages.
Security, authorisation checked again at download time, files encrypted at rest, old files expired and deleted, and an audit record of who generated and downloaded what.
And caching, identical requests within a short window can just reuse the previous result.

p17-702.q: Okay, outgoing webhooks push events to subscribers' URLs, and the hard parts are unreliable receivers, retries, ordering and security.
p17-702.k: webhook delivery design, outgoing webhooks, webhook retries, webhook dispatcher, deliver events to customers
x: Okay, outgoing webhooks push events to subscribers' URLs, and the hard parts are unreliable receivers, retries, ordering and security.
When an event happens, the service records it through an outbox. A dispatcher finds subscriptions for that event type, creates a delivery record per subscriber, and queues the deliveries.

Delivery workers send an HTTP POST with the payload, an event id, a timestamp and an HMAC signature header, so receivers can verify it's really us and reject replays. Short timeouts, like ten seconds, so slow receivers don't tie up workers.

Retries, on failure or a non-2xx response, retry with exponential backoff and jitter over hours or days, like 1 minute, 5, 30, 2 hours and so on. After the last attempt, mark it failed and tell the subscriber. Receivers have to dedupe by event id, because retries mean at-least-once delivery.

Isolation is the one I've seen people underestimate. One subscriber being down mustn't delay everyone else, so queues or concurrency limits are per subscriber. A circuit breaker per endpoint pauses deliveries to a dead endpoint, and subscriptions that fail consistently get disabled.
Ordering, if it matters, deliver sequentially per subscriber and entity, or include a sequence number so receivers can order or ignore stale events.
Visibility, a delivery log per subscriber with request, response code and timing, a replay function, and a test endpoint feature.
Security, validate subscriber URLs against SSRF, require HTTPS, and support secret rotation with two valid signatures during the switch.

p17-703.q: Let me go through them, because the id choice affects database performance, security, and how distributed systems create records.
p17-703.k: guid vs int id, sequential guid, snowflake id, distributed id generation, uuid v7, primary key choice
x: Let me go through them, because the id choice affects database performance, security, and how distributed systems create records.

Auto-increment integers are small, fast, naturally ordered, great for clustered indexes. But the database generates them, so you only know the id after the insert, merging data from several databases causes collisions, and putting them in URLs reveals counts and makes guessing other records easy.

Random GUIDs, version 4, can be generated anywhere without coordination, they're globally unique and unguessable. But they're 16 bytes, and the randomness fragments clustered indexes in SQL Server, because inserts land all over the index, page splits, slower writes.

Sequential GUIDs, NEWSEQUENTIALID in SQL Server, or UUID version 7, which .NET 9 supports with Guid dot CreateVersion7. They put a timestamp at the start, so values are roughly ordered and inserts go at the end of the index like integers, but they're still globally unique and generated in the app. I'd say that's a good default for distributed systems now.
Snowflake-style ids are 64-bit integers combining a timestamp, a machine id and a sequence. Ordered, compact, no coordination, but you need to hand out machine ids uniquely.

My approach, internal clustered keys can be integers or UUID v7. Public identifiers in URLs shouldn't be guessable, so UUIDs or a separate public id. And authorisation never relies on ids being secret.
Business identifiers like kit numbers or subject numbers follow their own business formats, separate from the technical keys.

p17-704.q: Right, two-phase commit is a protocol for making one transaction atomic across several resources, like two databases, or a database and a message broker. A coordinator first asks every participant to prepare, basically promise they can commit. If everyone says yes, it tells them all to commit. If anyone says no, everyone rolls back. In the .NET Framework world, MSDTC did this, often transparently with TransactionScope across connections.
p17-704.k: two phase commit, 2pc, distributed transaction, xa transaction, msdtc, why not distributed transactions
x: Right, two-phase commit is a protocol for making one transaction atomic across several resources, like two databases, or a database and a message broker. A coordinator first asks every participant to prepare, basically promise they can commit. If everyone says yes, it tells them all to commit. If anyone says no, everyone rolls back. In the .NET Framework world, MSDTC did this, often transparently with TransactionScope across connections.

Why microservices stay away from it. Availability, every participant has to be up and responsive for it to complete. If one service or database is slow or down, the whole thing waits or fails. Locks are held during prepare, so a stuck coordinator can leave stuff locked.

Coupling, services would have to share transaction infrastructure, which kills independent deployment and technology choice. And a lot of modern components, HTTP APIs, Kafka, cloud services, don't support it at all.
Scalability, the coordination round trips and held locks limit throughput.

So microservices accept eventual consistency, with patterns that give reliability without global locks. The outbox pattern, so a local database change and an event are recorded atomically. Idempotent consumers. And sagas, a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions if a later step fails.

Where you truly need strong consistency, the better answer is often to keep that data in one service and one database, and then a normal local transaction does the job. I think people sometimes split services too early and then fight this problem.

p17-705.q: So both solve coordination problems when you've got several instances of a service running at once.
p17-705.k: leader election, consistent hashing, distributed coordination, single leader pattern, partition assignment, hash ring
x: So both solve coordination problems when you've got several instances of a service running at once.

Leader election is for when exactly one instance has to do something, run a scheduler, process a singleton queue, coordinate the others. Instances compete for a leadership lease, one wins and does the work, renewing the lease periodically. If it dies or stops renewing, another takes over after the lease expires. You can do it with a Kubernetes Lease object, a distributed lock with expiry in Redis, a database row with an expiry timestamp, sp_getapplock in SQL Server, or coordination services like ZooKeeper and etcd. One thing to watch, a paused leader, say during a long GC pause, might think it's still leader after the lease expired. So work should carry a fencing token, an increasing number that downstream systems check to reject stale leaders.

Consistent hashing spreads keys across a changing set of nodes. Nodes sit on a hash ring, and each key goes to the next node clockwise. When a node is added or removed, only the keys near it move, instead of nearly all of them like with simple hash modulo N. Virtual nodes smooth out the distribution. You see it in distributed caches, Redis Cluster's slot model is a related idea, partitioned databases like Cassandra and DynamoDB, and load balancers with session affinity.
In application design I mostly use these through infrastructure rather than building them, but understanding them helps a lot when you reason about failover and rebalancing.

p17-706.q: Yeah, the thing with events is they outlive code. Consumers get deployed at different times, and stored events might be replayed months later. So schemas need careful evolution.
p17-706.k: event schema evolution, event versioning, schema registry, backward compatible events, breaking event change
x: Yeah, the thing with events is they outlive code. Consumers get deployed at different times, and stored events might be replayed months later. So schemas need careful evolution.
Adding optional fields is safe, as long as consumers ignore unknown fields. I make that a standard, tolerant readers.

Removing or renaming fields, changing types or meanings, that's breaking. Instead you add the new field next to the old one, fill both for a transition period, move consumers over, and only remove the old one once nobody uses it.
And never quietly change what an existing field means, like changing an amount from units to cents. That's the worst kind of break because nothing fails, the numbers are just wrong.
