Versioning, put an event type and version in the envelope, like ShipmentDelivered v2. For a truly breaking change, publish the new version as a new event type, maybe both in parallel for a while, and let consumers migrate at their own pace.

With Kafka, a schema registry using Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema enforces compatibility rules at publish time, backward or full compatibility, so an incompatible schema gets rejected before it reaches anyone.
Consumer-driven contract tests for messages catch breaking changes in the producer's pipeline.
For event-sourced systems, upcasting converts old event versions to the current shape when they're read, so the business logic only deals with the latest version.
And documenting events in a catalogue, like AsyncAPI, makes ownership and versions visible to everyone.

p17-707.q: Okay so hexagonal architecture, or ports and adapters, puts the core business logic in the middle with no dependency on technology, and connects everything else through ports and adapters.
p17-707.k: hexagonal architecture, ports and adapters, onion architecture, clean architecture vs hexagonal, domain isolation
x: Okay so hexagonal architecture, or ports and adapters, puts the core business logic in the middle with no dependency on technology, and connects everything else through ports and adapters.

Ports are interfaces the core defines. Incoming ports describe what the application can do, like an IAllocateKit use case. Outgoing ports describe what it needs from outside, like IKitRepository, IClock or INotificationSender.

Adapters implement those ports for specific technologies. Driving adapters call into the application, an ASP.NET Core controller, a message consumer, a CLI command. Driven adapters get called by it, an EF Core repository, a RabbitMQ publisher, an SMTP sender.
The dependency rule is adapters depend on the core, never the other way round. The core doesn't know HTTP, SQL or message brokers exist.

What you get is business logic you can test with simple in-memory fakes for the outgoing ports. Technology can change, like swapping the message broker, just by writing a new adapter. And the same use case can be triggered from an API, a queue or a scheduled job without duplicating anything.
Onion and clean architecture are close relatives with the same core idea, they mostly differ in how they name the layers.

The risk is over-engineering, tons of interfaces and mapping for simple CRUD services. I use it where there's real business logic and keep simple services simple. In our case the newer APIs follow clean architecture, which is pretty much this idea in practice.

p17-708.q: So basically, when a legacy system writes straight to a database and you can't modify it to publish events, change data capture lets other services react to its changes anyway.
p17-708.k: change data capture events, debezium, cdc to kafka, publish events from database, legacy database events
x: So basically, when a legacy system writes straight to a database and you can't modify it to publish events, change data capture lets other services react to its changes anyway.

How it works, CDC reads the database's transaction log, which records every committed insert, update and delete, and turns each change into an event. SQL Server has built-in CDC that writes changes into change tables. Debezium is the popular open-source option, it reads the logs from SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL and others and publishes change events to Kafka, usually through Kafka Connect. The cloud providers have similar services.

What I like is you don't touch the legacy app at all. Every change gets captured, including ones from scripts and other apps, ordering per row is preserved, and nothing's lost because it reads committed data from the log.

But there are challenges. Raw change events reflect table structure, not business meaning. An update on some table isn't a "ShipmentDelivered" event. So you need a translation step, people call it an event transformer, that turns low-level changes into proper domain events. Otherwise every consumer ends up coupled to the legacy schema, which is exactly what you were trying to escape.

Schema changes in the legacy database ripple into the event stream. The initial snapshot of existing data, and catching up after outages, need care. And there's operational overhead, running Kafka Connect, monitoring lag, and the impact on the database's log retention.
Still, it's a great tool for strangler fig migrations, syncing data into new services while the legacy system stays the source of truth.

p17-709.q: Honestly the database is usually the hardest part of breaking up a monolith. Lots of modules read and write the same tables, with joins, triggers and stored procedures crossing every boundary.
p17-709.k: split shared database, database decomposition, extract data from monolith database, shared tables migration, data ownership migration
x: Honestly the database is usually the hardest part of breaking up a monolith. Lots of modules read and write the same tables, with joins, triggers and stored procedures crossing every boundary.

So I'd do it gradually. Start by mapping data ownership. For each table, which module writes it and which ones read it. The goal is one owner per table, and everyone else gets the data through the owner's API or events.

Then separate inside the same database first. Move the new service's tables into their own schema, give the service its own database user that can only touch that schema, and replace cross-boundary joins and foreign keys with API calls or local copies. This flushes out hidden dependencies cheaply while the data's still in one place.
Shared reads, other modules that need the data get it through an API, or keep a read-only copy updated by events or CDC.
Shared writes, all writes for that data go through the owning service. Where the monolith still writes directly, sync temporarily with CDC while the code gets moved over.
Then move to a separate database once the service doesn't depend on cross-schema access anymore, with a data migration and a cutover, maybe dual writes with verification for a while.
Throughout the whole thing, reconciliation checks between old and new, feature flags to switch paths, and the ability to roll back each step.
It's slow, I won't pretend otherwise. But every step reduces coupling and the system keeps working the whole time.

p17-710.q: Okay, batch handles data in big chunks at intervals, like a nightly job processing all of yesterday's transactions. Streaming handles each event continuously as it arrives, within seconds.
p17-710.k: batch vs stream processing, real time vs batch, etl vs streaming, kappa lambda architecture, when to use streaming
x: Okay, batch handles data in big chunks at intervals, like a nightly job processing all of yesterday's transactions. Streaming handles each event continuously as it arrives, within seconds.

Batch fits reports and analytics where hourly or daily freshness is fine. Heavy computations over complete datasets, month-end reconciliation, billing, recalculating forecasts. Loading warehouses. And honestly simplicity, batch jobs are easier to reason about, rerun and test, and they can use cheap resources during quiet hours.

Streaming fits things that need fast reactions, alerts, fraud or anomaly detection, notifications, live dashboards. Keeping derived data fresh, like search indexes or caches. And spreading load evenly instead of one big nightly spike.

But streaming is more complex. Ordering, late-arriving events, exactly-once concerns, state for aggregations over windows, and more infrastructure, Kafka, Kinesis, or processors like Flink or Kafka Streams.

A lot of systems combine them. A stream handles the real-time needs, and batch jobs do periodic full recomputation and reconciliation to correct drift. Modern tools blur the line too, micro-batching gives near-real-time with batch simplicity.

My rule is start from the business's freshness requirement. If daily is genuinely fine, batch is simpler and cheaper. If people act on the data within minutes, it needs streaming, or at least frequent incremental processing.
In supply management, for example, resupply checks can be frequent incremental jobs, but temperature excursion alerts need near-real-time handling.

p17-711.q: See, contract-first means you design the API contract, usually an OpenAPI document, before writing the implementation, and that document is the source of truth.
p17-711.k: contract first api, api first design, openapi design first, swagger contract, generate client from openapi
x: See, contract-first means you design the API contract, usually an OpenAPI document, before writing the implementation, and that document is the source of truth.

The process is the team writes the OpenAPI spec, paths, operations, request and response schemas, error formats, examples. It gets reviewed in a pull request with the consumers, front-end developers, partner teams, other services, and they comment on naming, shapes and error handling before any code exists. Mock servers generated from the spec, with tools like Prism, let consumers start building against realistic responses straight away, in parallel with the backend.

Then code generation keeps everyone aligned. Server stubs or interfaces from the spec, and typed clients for consumers, like TypeScript clients for the React front end or C# clients for other services, with NSwag, Kiota or openapi-typescript. In CI, the implementation gets validated against the spec, and a diff against the previous version flags breaking changes.
What you get is better API design from early review, consistency across teams with shared style guides and Spectral linting, parallel development, and far fewer integration surprises.
The other way is code-first, where the spec is generated from code. That's convenient for internal APIs with one consumer, and .NET 9's built-in OpenAPI support makes it easy.
For public or partner APIs though, I'd go contract-first every time, because there the contract basically is the product.

p17-712.q: Actually it's a pretty simple idea. A golden path, or paved road, is the recommended, well-supported way to build and run a service in an organisation. Instead of every team figuring out logging, health checks, pipelines, containers and monitoring on their own, a platform team provides a ready-made path that already does it right.
p17-712.k: golden path, service template, platform engineering, internal developer platform, backstage, paved road
x: Actually it's a pretty simple idea. A golden path, or paved road, is the recommended, well-supported way to build and run a service in an organisation. Instead of every team figuring out logging, health checks, pipelines, containers and monitoring on their own, a platform team provides a ready-made path that already does it right.

What's usually in it. A service template, like a dotnet new template or a repo template, with the project structure, OpenTelemetry, structured logging, health checks, config and secrets handling, authentication, error handling, a Dockerfile and a test project already wired up. Pipeline templates for build, test, security scanning and deployment. Infrastructure modules for standard resources like a database, queue or cache, with secure defaults. Dashboards and alerts generated per service. And docs.

An internal developer portal like Backstage often hosts it. A software catalogue listing every service with owners and docs, and scaffolding where a developer fills in a form and gets a new repository, pipeline and environment in minutes.

The win is new services start production-ready, standards stay consistent, security and compliance are built in, and engineers spend their time on business logic. In regulated environments it's even more valuable, because consistency makes validation and audits much simpler.
The key thing for me is it's a path, not a cage. Teams can deviate when they've got good reasons, but the easy way should be the right way.

p17-713.q: So when personal data has to be deleted, say under GDPR's right to erasure, the problem with microservices is the data is spread everywhere. Lots of services and databases, caches, search indexes, logs, backups, event streams.
p17-713.k: right to erasure microservices, gdpr delete across services, delete personal data distributed, data retention vs deletion, crypto shredding
x: So when personal data has to be deleted, say under GDPR's right to erasure, the problem with microservices is the data is spread everywhere. Lots of services and databases, caches, search indexes, logs, backups, event streams.
First you need to know where personal data lives. A data inventory listing which services store which personal data, kept up to date as part of service design.

Then orchestrate the deletion. A deletion request kicks off a workflow, often a saga, that publishes a "delete data for this person" command or event. Each service that owns personal data handles it, deletes or anonymises the records, and confirms back. The workflow tracks confirmations and retries, and produces an audit record that the deletion completed, without keeping the deleted data itself, obviously.
Derived stores too, search indexes and caches get cleared, analytics data gets anonymised.

Event streams and backups are the tricky part, because immutable logs and backups make physical deletion hard. Crypto-shredding helps. You encrypt each person's data with a personal key and delete the key, so the data's unreadable everywhere. Backups that can't be edited are kept for limited periods, and deleted data never gets restored into live systems.

And in our world there are conflicting obligations. In clinical trials, regulations require keeping trial data for many years, which can override deletion requests, and clinical data is usually pseudonymised, with identities held by the sites, not in the IRT. Legal and privacy teams define what gets deleted versus retained, and the system implements their rules.

p17-714.q: Right, in active-active both regions accept writes and data replicates asynchronously. If the same record changes in both regions before replication catches up, you've got a conflict, and the system has to decide the final value.
p17-714.k: active active conflicts, multi region writes, last writer wins, conflict resolution, crdt, multi master replication
x: Right, in active-active both regions accept writes and data replicates asynchronously. If the same record changes in both regions before replication catches up, you've got a conflict, and the system has to decide the final value.

The approach I like most is avoiding conflicts by design. Route all writes for an entity to one home region, by tenant or customer, so each record has a single writer at a time, while reads can happen anywhere. You get most of the availability benefit with very few conflicts, and it's usually the most practical choice.

Last writer wins, the update with the latest timestamp wins. Simple, and it's the default in DynamoDB global tables and Cosmos DB, but it silently loses the other update and depends on clocks being accurate. Fine for data where losing a concurrent change doesn't matter, like user preferences.
Merge logic, application-specific resolution, like merging non-overlapping field changes, or a custom resolver in Cosmos DB.
CRDTs, conflict-free replicated data types. Counters, sets and maps designed so concurrent changes always merge to a consistent result. Used for collaborative editing or distributed counters.
Record and escalate, keep both versions and flag it for a human. That fits important business data.

But for critical operations with strict rules, like allocating a limited item, active-active writes are risky. I'd say one primary region for those writes, with fast failover, is usually the safer call.

p17-715.q: Let me put it simply, load shedding means deliberately rejecting some requests when you're overloaded, so you can keep serving the rest properly. Without it, an overloaded service tries to do everything, queues grow, every request gets slow, timeouts make clients retry, and it collapses for everyone.
p17-715.k: load shedding, admission control, shed load under overload, priority requests, graceful degradation overload
x: Let me put it simply, load shedding means deliberately rejecting some requests when you're overloaded, so you can keep serving the rest properly. Without it, an overloaded service tries to do everything, queues grow, every request gets slow, timeouts make clients retry, and it collapses for everyone.

How I'd implement it. Concurrency limits, cap how many requests are processed at once with a short queue, and beyond that return 503 or 429 right away with Retry-After. ASP.NET Core's rate limiting middleware has a concurrency limiter for this, and Kestrel and IIS have connection and queue limits.
Queue time limits. If a request has waited too long to even start, drop it, the client's probably given up already. Processing it just wastes capacity.

Prioritisation, because not all requests are equal. Keep capacity for critical operations like a patient randomisation or dispensing, and shed lower-priority stuff first, reports, exports, bulk syncs, background refreshes. You can do that with separate limiters per endpoint class, or separate deployments for critical and non-critical traffic.
Adaptive limits, adjust the concurrency limit based on observed latency, grow it when things are healthy, shrink it when latency climbs.
Client cooperation, clients back off on 429 and 503 with exponential backoff and jitter instead of retrying immediately.
And degradation, serve cached or simplified responses instead of the full thing.
Then load tests should show the system shedding load gracefully, not falling over. That's how you know it actually works.

p17-716.q: Yeah so in distributed systems a request often fans out to several backends, and the slowest one decides the total latency. Even if each backend is usually fast, the occasional slow response, from GC pauses, noisy neighbours, network hiccups, makes p99 way worse than the median. That's tail latency.
p17-716.k: hedged requests, tail latency, p99 latency reduction, speculative retry, backup requests
x: Yeah so in distributed systems a request often fans out to several backends, and the slowest one decides the total latency. Even if each backend is usually fast, the occasional slow response, from GC pauses, noisy neighbours, network hiccups, makes p99 way worse than the median. That's tail latency.

A hedged request sends the same request to a second replica if the first hasn't answered within a short delay, like that call's p95 latency, and uses whichever response comes back first, cancelling the other. Because the delay sits at a high percentile, only a few percent of requests get hedged, so the extra load is small, but you cut off the slow outliers.
Polly v8 has a hedging strategy, and the .NET resilience packages give you AddStandardHedgingHandler for HttpClient, which can also send the hedged request to a different endpoint.

When it's appropriate, reads, or idempotent operations, because the request might run twice. Never for non-idempotent writes without idempotency keys. And only when the backend has multiple independent replicas, so the second try is likely to land somewhere healthier.
The risk is under overload, hedging adds load exactly when the system's struggling. So what I do is limit the number of hedged attempts and combine it with circuit breakers.
Other tail latency tricks are timeouts with fast fallbacks, reducing fan-out, caching, and just fixing whatever causes the slow outliers, like the GC pauses.

p17-717.q: So at a visit, the system has to assign the right kit to the patient. Correct treatment, available at the site, not expiring before the next visit, keeping the blind, and never assigning the same kit twice.
p17-717.k: design allocation service, kit allocation design, drug dispensing design, clinical supply allocation, assign kit to patient design
x: So at a visit, the system has to assign the right kit to the patient. Correct treatment, available at the site, not expiring before the next visit, keeping the blind, and never assigning the same kit twice.
The inputs are the subject, their treatment arm from randomisation, the visit and its dosing requirements from the study config, and the site's inventory.

Selection logic, filter the site's kits to the kit type the arm needs, in an available status, not quarantined or damaged, with an expiry beyond the next visit plus a configured buffer. Then pick by a rule, usually first expiry first out to cut waste. Some visits need several kits.

I'd say concurrency is the critical bit. Two dispensing requests at the same site must never pick the same kit. Selection and status update happen atomically in one transaction, with row-level locking using UPDLOCK and READPAST, or a conditional update checking the status hasn't changed. And an idempotency key per dispensing request stops double allocation on retries.
Blinding, the site only sees the kit number, never the treatment, and the kit numbering itself mustn't reveal the treatment.

Low stock, if there's no suitable kit, return a clear error to the site and alert supply management. Separately, allocations feed the resupply calculations, which trigger shipments when inventory drops below thresholds.
Audit, every allocation recorded with who, when, which kit and why, including manual overrides with reasons and approvals.
And testing is simulation with lots of concurrent visits and edge cases around expiry, as part of validation.

p17-718.q: Okay, a hand-written saga stores state in a table, reacts to messages, handles timeouts with scheduled jobs, and implements compensations. For a few simple flows that's totally fine. But once workflows get longer, with timers, human approvals, retries and branches, that custom state machine code gets complex and fragile.
p17-718.k: workflow engine, temporal io, durable execution, orchestration engine vs custom saga, durable functions vs saga
x: Okay, a hand-written saga stores state in a table, reacts to messages, handles timeouts with scheduled jobs, and implements compensations. For a few simple flows that's totally fine. But once workflows get longer, with timers, human approvals, retries and branches, that custom state machine code gets complex and fragile.

Durable execution engines, Temporal, Azure Durable Functions, AWS Step Functions, or some newer .NET options, take over the hard parts. You write the workflow as normal code, or a definition for Step Functions. Call activity A, wait up to three days for an approval signal, then call B, and on failure run the compensation. The engine persists every step's result, so if the process crashes, the workflow picks up exactly where it was. Retries with backoff, timeouts, timers lasting days or months, and visibility into each running workflow come built in.

When it's worth it, long-running business processes spanning hours to weeks, workflows with lots of steps, waits and human interaction, complex compensation logic, and when seeing each instance's state really helps support and audit.

What you pay for it is a new platform to run or pay for, a learning curve, constraints like deterministic workflow code that can't call random or the current time directly, and versioning workflows that are already running when the code changes.
So for a two-step flow, I'd say just use a simple outbox and consumer. For something like a multi-day approval and transfer process, an engine saves you a lot of code and a lot of bugs.

p17-719.q: Honestly this comes up whenever one API needs to call another as the user. Say a user calls API A, and A has to call API B as that user, so B can apply the user's own permissions. Just forwarding the user's token is a problem. Its audience is API A, so B should reject it, and passing broad tokens everywhere makes the damage worse if one service gets compromised.
p17-719.k: on behalf of flow, token exchange, obo flow, downstream api user context, delegated token microservices
x: Honestly this comes up whenever one API needs to call another as the user. Say a user calls API A, and A has to call API B as that user, so B can apply the user's own permissions. Just forwarding the user's token is a problem. Its audience is API A, so B should reject it, and passing broad tokens everywhere makes the damage worse if one service gets compromised.

The on-behalf-of flow in Entra ID, and the standard OAuth 2.0 token exchange, RFC 8693, which Keycloak and others support, solve it. API A sends the incoming user token to the identity provider's token endpoint, authenticating as itself, and asks for a new token for API B. The identity provider checks A is allowed to call B on behalf of users, and issues a token with audience B, carrying the user's identity and often A's identity as the actor. A calls B with that, and B validates it like any other token.

What you get is every token scoped to exactly one audience, so it can't be replayed against other services. Downstream services see the real user and enforce their own authorisation. And the identity provider controls which services can delegate to which.

The alternative, if B doesn't need the user's identity for authorisation, A calls B with its own client credentials token and passes the user id as context. Simpler, but B is trusting A to have checked permissions.
So I'd use token exchange when downstream authorisation depends on the user, and client credentials otherwise.

p17-720.q: So in normal TLS only the server shows a certificate, so the client knows it's talking to the real server. In mutual TLS the client also presents a certificate, so the server knows exactly which client is connecting, right at the transport level, before any HTTP request is even processed.
p17-720.k: mutual tls, mtls, client certificate authentication, certificate based auth api, two way ssl
x: So in normal TLS only the server shows a certificate, so the client knows it's talking to the real server. In mutual TLS the client also presents a certificate, so the server knows exactly which client is connecting, right at the transport level, before any HTTP request is even processed.

How it works, the server is set up to request client certificates and trusts a specific certificate authority. During the handshake, the client proves it holds the private key for its certificate. The server validates the chain, expiry and revocation status, then maps the certificate, by thumbprint or subject, to a client identity. In ASP.NET Core that's Kestrel's ClientCertificateMode plus the certificate authentication handler. If a load balancer or gateway terminates TLS, the gateway validates the cert and forwards the details in a header, and the app must only trust that header from the gateway.

Where I'd use it. Service-to-service calls in a zero trust network, often automated through a service mesh that issues and rotates the certificates. Partner and B2B integrations, where a partner system connects to our API, certificates are much harder to steal and replay than API keys, and some industries require them. And device authentication, IoT devices or machines.
OAuth can also bind tokens to the client certificate, so a stolen token is useless without the private key.
The cost is certificate management. Issuing, distributing, rotating before expiry, revoking. Honestly, without automation it becomes painful very quickly.

p17-721.q: Okay, both authenticate a system, not a user, but they're really different in security terms.
p17-721.k: api keys vs oauth, partner api authentication, client credentials flow, api key security, machine to machine auth
x: Okay, both authenticate a system, not a user, but they're really different in security terms.

API keys are simple static secrets sent with every request, usually in a header. Partners find them easy, which is why they're popular. But they're long-lived and sent on every call, so any leak, in logs, proxies, code, gives access until someone notices and rotates. They have no scopes or expiry on their own unless the server builds that. And rotation needs coordination with the partner.

OAuth 2.0 client credentials, the partner authenticates to the token endpoint with its client id and a secret, or better, a private key JWT or a certificate, and gets a short-lived access token with specific scopes, which it sends to the API. The long-lived credential only ever goes to the identity provider, not to every API. Access tokens expire in minutes, scopes limit what the partner can do, and the identity provider handles management, rotation and revocation centrally.

I'd say for anything sensitive, clinical or personal data, or write operations, OAuth client credentials, ideally with private key JWT or mTLS for the client authentication. API keys are fine for low-risk, read-only or public-ish APIs, or as an extra identifier for rate limiting and analytics alongside OAuth.
And if we do use API keys, I store only hashes, support multiple active keys so rotation is smooth, scope them, log usage per key, and make revocation fast.

p17-722.q: See, an open redirect is when the app takes a URL from user input, like a return URL parameter after login, and redirects to it without checking. Attackers send phishing links that use our trusted domain, something like our site slash login with a return URL pointing at some evil site. The user sees our domain, logs in, and lands on a fake page that asks them to "log in again" and steals their credentials. In OAuth flows it can even leak authorisation codes or tokens.
p17-722.k: open redirect, returnurl validation, unvalidated redirect, redirect after login security, localredirect aspnet core
x: See, an open redirect is when the app takes a URL from user input, like a return URL parameter after login, and redirects to it without checking. Attackers send phishing links that use our trusted domain, something like our site slash login with a return URL pointing at some evil site. The user sees our domain, logs in, and lands on a fake page that asks them to "log in again" and steals their credentials. In OAuth flows it can even leak authorisation codes or tokens.

The main fix is only allowing local redirects. In ASP.NET Core, Url dot IsLocalUrl checks the URL is relative to our site, and LocalRedirect throws if it isn't. That's what the default login templates use. Be careful with tricky inputs like double slash evil dot com, or slash backslash evil dot com, which some naive checks treat as local. The built-in helpers handle those.
If you genuinely need redirects to other domains, like between our own apps, compare against an explicit allowlist of hosts, not a substring match.
Or use indirect references. Instead of passing a URL, pass an identifier, like a page key, that the server maps to a URL.
For OAuth and OpenID Connect, register exact redirect URIs in the identity provider, no wildcards, so codes can only ever go to our own apps.
And front-end code too. SPAs that read a redirect parameter from the URL and set window location need the same validation. It's a small fix, I'd say, with a big phishing protection payoff.

p17-723.q: Actually it's when the app turns untrusted data into objects with a serialiser that lets the data decide which types to create. Attackers craft payloads that instantiate dangerous types, called gadgets, whose constructors or setters run code, and you end up with remote code execution.
p17-723.k: insecure deserialization, binaryformatter, typenamehandling, deserialization attack, json deserialization security
x: Actually it's when the app turns untrusted data into objects with a serialiser that lets the data decide which types to create. Attackers craft payloads that instantiate dangerous types, called gadgets, whose constructors or setters run code, and you end up with remote code execution.

In .NET the classic danger is BinaryFormatter. It's fundamentally unsafe with untrusted data, and Microsoft removed it in .NET 9. Same story for NetDataContractSerializer, SoapFormatter, LosFormatter and ObjectStateFormatter used without protection. Legacy .NET Framework apps might still use them, in caches, session state, or ViewState with MAC validation turned off.

Then Newtonsoft with TypeNameHandling set to Auto, Objects or All. The JSON carries a dollar type property and the serialiser creates whatever type it names. That's exploitable. Keep TypeNameHandling at None, or if you really need polymorphism, use a strict SerializationBinder that only allows specific known types.

How I avoid it. Use System.Text.Json, which doesn't instantiate arbitrary types, and for polymorphic JSON use its explicit JsonDerivedType attributes, which only allow declared types. Deserialise into specific DTOs, never object or dynamic. Treat anything from outside as untrusted, including cookies, message queues and caches shared with other systems. And sign or encrypt serialised data that round-trips through clients, using Data Protection.
Scanners and analyzers flag dangerous serialiser use, which really helps when you're hunting for it in a big legacy codebase like ours.

p17-724.q: Honestly this one's simple but people still get it wrong. Path traversal is when user input builds a file path and the attacker sneaks in dot dot slash to escape the intended folder. A download endpoint that takes name equals report dot pdf gets called with dot dot slash dot dot slash web dot config, and the server hands back its own configuration, connection strings and all. On uploads, attackers might write files into executable locations.
p17-724.k: path traversal, directory traversal, dot dot slash attack, file download vulnerability, safe file paths
x: Honestly this one's simple but people still get it wrong. Path traversal is when user input builds a file path and the attacker sneaks in dot dot slash to escape the intended folder. A download endpoint that takes name equals report dot pdf gets called with dot dot slash dot dot slash web dot config, and the server hands back its own configuration, connection strings and all. On uploads, attackers might write files into executable locations.

Best is not using user input as a path at all. Store files with server-generated names, like a GUID, and keep the original name only as metadata in the database. The user asks for a file by id, the server checks authorisation and looks up the stored path.

If you have to use names, validate strictly. Take only the file name part with Path dot GetFileName, reject anything with path separators, dot dot, drive letters or invalid characters, and allowlist characters and extensions.

Then canonicalise and check containment. Combine the base folder with the name, get the full path with Path dot GetFullPath, and verify it still starts with the base folder's full path, with a trailing separator, before touching the file. That catches encoded tricks and different separator styles.
Least privilege, the app's identity should only access the folders it needs, read-only where possible.

Even better, put files in object storage like S3 or Blob Storage with server-generated keys, and the file system's out of the picture. And archives need care too. Extracting zip entries named dot dot slash something, Zip Slip, is the exact same bug.

p17-725.q: So command injection is when user input ends up in an operating system command, and the input contains shell syntax, like a semicolon followed by rm dash rf, or double ampersand net user, which the shell happily runs. In .NET it usually shows up when code builds a command string for Process Start with cmd.exe or bash, say to run a conversion tool or a script with a file name from the user.
p17-725.k: command injection, os command injection, process start security, shell injection, run external process safely
x: So command injection is when user input ends up in an operating system command, and the input contains shell syntax, like a semicolon followed by rm dash rf, or double ampersand net user, which the shell happily runs. In .NET it usually shows up when code builds a command string for Process Start with cmd.exe or bash, say to run a conversion tool or a script with a file name from the user.
My preference order. First choice, don't shell out at all. Use a library to do the job in-process, like an image library instead of a command-line tool.

If you do need an external program, don't go through a shell. Start the executable directly with ProcessStartInfo, UseShellExecute false, and pass arguments through the ArgumentList collection, which passes each argument separately and handles quoting, so input can't break out into new commands. Never concatenate input into one command string for cmd slash c or bash dash c.
Validate input strictly with an allowlist. If a parameter should be a file id or a known option, check it matches exactly, and map user choices to fixed values instead of passing raw input.
Watch for argument injection. Even without a shell, input starting with a dash can be read as an option by the target program. Use double dash to end options where it's supported, or validate.
Run the process with least privilege, a restricted account, a timeout, and in a sandbox or container where you can.
And the same thinking applies to PowerShell scripts in pipelines or automation. Parameters, not string-built commands. I've seen that one in build scripts more than in app code.

p17-726.q: Okay, XML External Entity attacks go after XML parsers that process DTDs, document type definitions. The attacker sends XML with an entity pointing to an external resource, like a file URL for win.ini on the C drive, or an internal URL. If the parser resolves it, the file's content lands in the parsed document and may get returned to the attacker, or the server makes requests into internal systems, which is SSRF. There's a related one, billion laughs or the XML bomb, where nested entities expand a tiny document into gigabytes and exhaust memory.
p17-726.k: xxe, xml external entity, xml parsing security, dtd processing, xmlreader secure settings, xml bomb
x: Okay, XML External Entity attacks go after XML parsers that process DTDs, document type definitions. The attacker sends XML with an entity pointing to an external resource, like a file URL for win.ini on the C drive, or an internal URL. If the parser resolves it, the file's content lands in the parsed document and may get returned to the attacker, or the server makes requests into internal systems, which is SSRF. There's a related one, billion laughs or the XML bomb, where nested entities expand a tiny document into gigabytes and exhaust memory.

Is .NET vulnerable? Modern .NET, and .NET Framework 4.5.2 onwards, have safe defaults for most XML APIs. XmlReader prohibits DTD processing by default, and XmlDocument doesn't resolve external resources by default in newer framework versions. But older code and explicit settings can bring the risk back. Setting DtdProcessing to Parse, using an XmlUrlResolver, or old XmlTextReader usage on framework versions before 4.5.2.

What I do is parse untrusted XML with XmlReader Create, with DtdProcessing set to Prohibit and the XmlResolver set to null, which also stops entity expansion. Set limits like MaxCharactersFromEntities and MaxCharactersInDocument. And validate against an expected schema where it makes sense.

This really matters in integrations that receive XML from partners, like older clinical data exchanges or SOAP services, which you see a lot in legacy systems. Scanners and analyzers flag unsafe XML settings, so I fix any findings in the legacy code.

p17-727.q: Right, SQL Server has a few encryption options and each protects against a different threat.
p17-727.k: tde vs always encrypted, sql server encryption at rest, column level encryption, always encrypted, encrypt pii database
x: Right, SQL Server has a few encryption options and each protects against a different threat.

TDE, Transparent Data Encryption, encrypts the database files, logs and backups at rest. Apps don't notice it, and it protects against someone stealing disks or backup files. But anyone who can query the database, DBAs, the app, sees plain data. It's a baseline, and usually on by default in cloud databases.

Always Encrypted encrypts specific columns in the client driver. Data's encrypted before it leaves the application and stays encrypted in the database, in server memory and in backups. The keys sit with the client, in Key Vault or a certificate store, not in SQL Server. So DBAs and anyone with database access can't read those columns. The catch is the server can't do much with encrypted data. Deterministic encryption allows equality lookups, randomised allows nothing. Secure enclaves extend that to some range comparisons and pattern matching. It needs driver support and careful key management.
Cell-level encryption with ENCRYPTBYKEY uses keys inside SQL Server. You get control, but the server and its admins can decrypt.
Application-level encryption, the app encrypts fields itself with envelope encryption through a key management service. Flexible and database-independent.

I'd say the right mix is TDE everywhere plus TLS in transit, and then Always Encrypted or app-level encryption for the few really sensitive columns, like personal identifiers, where even administrators shouldn't be able to read them.

p17-728.q: Let me start with the point that prevention isn't enough, you also need to notice attacks and misuse. And that starts with the app logging the right security events.
p17-728.k: security monitoring, siem, security logging, detect attacks application, security events logging, audit security events
x: Let me start with the point that prevention isn't enough, you also need to notice attacks and misuse. And that starts with the app logging the right security events.

What I log, structured, with user, source IP, time and correlation id. Authentication successes and failures, MFA events, password and permission changes, access denied, like 401s and 403s, especially repeated ones, validation failures that look like attacks, admin actions, exports of sensitive data, config changes, and use of emergency or privileged functions. Never passwords, tokens or sensitive data in the logs themselves.

They go to a central log platform, and for security analysis, a SIEM like Microsoft Sentinel, Splunk Enterprise Security or Elastic Security, which also pulls in identity provider logs, WAF logs, cloud audit logs, endpoint and network data.

Then detection rules. Lots of failed logins for one account or from one IP, logins from unusual countries or impossible travel, a user suddenly accessing loads of records or exporting a lot, privilege escalation, admin functions used outside normal hours, SQL injection patterns in WAF logs. Alerts go to the security operations team, with runbooks.
Integrity matters too. Security logs have to be protected from tampering, shipped off the server quickly, with restricted access, and kept according to policy.
And test it. During pen tests or simulated attacks, check the expected alerts actually fired. In my experience detection that's never tested often just doesn't work.

p17-729.q: Yeah, automated tools catch the common patterns, but a lot of real vulnerabilities are logic flaws only a human spots. So in a security-focused review I run through a mental checklist.
p17-729.k: security code review, secure code review checklist, review for vulnerabilities, security review pull request
x: Yeah, automated tools catch the common patterns, but a lot of real vulnerabilities are logic flaws only a human spots. So in a security-focused review I run through a mental checklist.

Authorisation first. Does every new endpoint have the right authorisation attribute or policy? Does it check the user can access this specific record, not just that they're logged in? Are tenant or site filters applied consistently?
Input handling. Is external input validated for type, length and allowed values? Any SQL built by string concatenation, raw HTML rendering, file paths, redirects or commands built from input?
Data exposure. Do responses return only what's needed, or whole entities with internal fields? Are sensitive values kept out of logs and error messages?
Secrets and config. Any hardcoded credentials, keys or connection strings? Are new settings secure by default?
Authentication and sessions, token handling, expiry, cookie flags, changes to the auth pipeline. Cryptography, standard libraries, no home-made crypto, no weak algorithms, secure random generators.
Error handling, no stack traces to users, and failures fail closed, denying access instead of allowing it.
Dependencies, any new packages, are they trustworthy, which versions.
And concurrency and business logic. Can actions be repeated, raced or done out of order to gain something, like double-submitting or skipping a step?
For high-risk changes, authentication or payment-like flows, my approach is to ask for a second reviewer with security experience and threat-model the feature.

p17-730.q: So a pen test report usually has findings rated critical, high, medium, low and informational. Handling them well comes down to triage, fixing the root cause and proving the fix.
p17-730.k: penetration test findings, pen test remediation, vulnerability remediation process, security findings triage, pentest report
x: So a pen test report usually has findings rated critical, high, medium, low and informational. Handling them well comes down to triage, fixing the root cause and proving the fix.

Triage first. For each finding, confirm it's valid in our context, understand the real risk, exploitability, data exposure, existing controls, and agree the severity with the security team. Sometimes the tester's rating gets adjusted, with justification, but I'm careful not to downplay findings just to avoid work.

Then plan. Each finding becomes a tracked work item with an owner and a deadline based on severity, critical within days, high within a few weeks, whatever the security policy says. Critical ones might need an immediate mitigation, like a WAF rule or switching off a feature, before the code fix lands.

Fix the root cause, not just the one instance. If they found an IDOR on one endpoint, review every endpoint for the same pattern. Missing output encoding in one place, find all the similar places. Often a central fix, a shared authorisation filter or a security header middleware, kills a whole class of issues.
Add tests, an automated test reproducing each finding so it can't come back.
Verify, ask the testers to retest, or verify internally with evidence, and record the closure.

And learn from it. Look at patterns across findings and feed them into coding guidelines, review checklists, training and automated scans. Any accepted risks get documented and approved by the right people, with review dates. That's pretty much how we close the loop.

p17-731.q: Honestly the core idea is no implicit trust based on network location. The old model assumed everything inside the corporate network or VPN was trusted, so once an attacker got in, they could wander freely. Zero trust says verify explicitly every time, use least privilege, and assume you're already breached.
p17-731.k: zero trust, zero trust architecture, never trust always verify, zero trust network, beyondcorp
x: Honestly the core idea is no implicit trust based on network location. The old model assumed everything inside the corporate network or VPN was trusted, so once an attacker got in, they could wander freely. Zero trust says verify explicitly every time, use least privilege, and assume you're already breached.

For applications, what that means in practice. Every request is authenticated and authorised, including internal service-to-service calls. Services verify tokens or mutual TLS identities, instead of trusting a call because it came from the internal network.
Strong identity for users and workloads. MFA and conditional access for users, managed or workload identities for services, and short-lived credentials everywhere.
Least privilege and just-in-time access. Services get only the permissions they need, and admins get elevated access temporarily, with approval.

Micro-segmentation. Network policies and security groups restrict which services can talk to which, so a compromised service can't reach everything, even though the network isn't the main defence anymore.

Encryption in transit everywhere, internal traffic included. Device and context awareness, so access decisions consider device health, location and risk. And continuous monitoring, logging and analysing access and spotting anomalies.

For legacy systems that rely on network trust, like intranet apps with Windows authentication, you apply it gradually. Put them behind an identity-aware proxy, add MFA, tighten the network paths. In our on-prem world that's realistically how it would happen, step by step.

p17-732.q: So admin tools are really high-value targets. They can change configuration, data and permissions for everyone. And yet they're often less protected, just because they're "internal". I actually treat them as the most sensitive apps we have.
p17-732.k: secure admin tools, internal tools security, back office app security, admin panel security, privileged application
x: So admin tools are really high-value targets. They can change configuration, data and permissions for everyone. And yet they're often less protected, just because they're "internal". I actually treat them as the most sensitive apps we have.

Access first. Strong authentication through the company identity provider with MFA, and conditional access, like requiring a managed device. No local accounts, no shared logins. Access by role with least privilege, reviewed periodically. Privileged functions can need just-in-time elevation with approval.
Network, not exposed to the internet, or only through an identity-aware proxy or VPN with IP restrictions. But never relying on the network alone.

Authorisation in depth. Every action is checked on the server, with fine-grained permissions for the dangerous stuff, bulk changes, deleting data, maybe needing a second person's approval, the four-eyes principle.
Safety. Confirmation steps that show the impact before applying a change, like "this will affect 3 studies and 120 sites", dry-run modes, and the ability to undo.
Audit, every action logged with who, what, when, old and new values, and a reason where it makes sense, stored somewhere admins can't alter it.
And secure development, the same code review, scanning and testing as customer-facing apps. Internal tools often get built quickly and skip all that.
Our admin console, which we use to configure studies, follows this thinking. Role-based access, controlled promotion from build to UAT to production, and full audit of configuration changes.

p17-733.q: Okay, a break-glass account is an emergency account you only use when the normal ways in fail. Like the identity provider's down, MFA is broken, conditional access policies have locked everyone out, or the usual admins aren't reachable during a critical incident.
p17-733.k: break glass account, emergency access account, emergency admin access, break glass procedure, privileged emergency access
x: Okay, a break-glass account is an emergency account you only use when the normal ways in fail. Like the identity provider's down, MFA is broken, conditional access policies have locked everyone out, or the usual admins aren't reachable during a critical incident.
Because it's powerful and skips some normal controls, it needs really strict management.

Setup, at least two emergency accounts, cloud-only so they don't depend on on-premise directory sync, excluded from conditional access policies that could lock them out, but protected with strong authentication. FIDO2 security keys stored securely, or very long passwords split between people and kept in a safe.
Storage and access, credentials sealed in a physical safe or a secure vault, with access needing more than one person, and documented rules for when use is allowed.

Monitoring, any sign-in with a break-glass account fires an immediate high-priority alert to the security team, because legitimate use is so rare. Every use gets a review afterwards, why it was used, what was done, and then the credentials get rotated.
Testing, check periodically that the accounts still work, say every few months, as a controlled exercise. Otherwise you find out they're broken right in the middle of the emergency.

And the same principle applies to apps and databases. A documented, audited emergency access path for production data fixes during incidents, with approval and full logging, instead of developers keeping permanent production access "just in case". I'd say that's the part teams most often get wrong.

p17-734.q: See, ReDoS is a denial of service caused by a regular expression that takes exponential time on certain inputs. Patterns with nested quantifiers or overlapping alternatives, like a group of "a plus" that's itself repeated with a plus, or word characters with an optional space, repeated with a star, can make the regex engine backtrack through a massive number of combinations when the input almost matches but fails right at the end. A short nasty string, a few dozen characters, can keep a CPU core busy for seconds or minutes. A handful of those requests can take down an API.
p17-734.k: redos, regex denial of service, catastrophic backtracking, regex timeout dotnet, nonbacktracking regex
x: See, ReDoS is a denial of service caused by a regular expression that takes exponential time on certain inputs. Patterns with nested quantifiers or overlapping alternatives, like a group of "a plus" that's itself repeated with a plus, or word characters with an optional space, repeated with a star, can make the regex engine backtrack through a massive number of combinations when the input almost matches but fails right at the end. A short nasty string, a few dozen characters, can keep a CPU core busy for seconds or minutes. A handful of those requests can take down an API.
Where it shows up, validating emails, URLs or names with home-made patterns, parsing log lines, and search features that accept user patterns.

How I prevent it in .NET. Set timeouts. Pass a TimeSpan to the Regex constructor, or set a default with the REGEX DEFAULT MATCH TIMEOUT AppContext setting, so a pathological match throws a timeout exception instead of running forever.
Use the NonBacktracking option, available since .NET 7. It's an automata-based engine with linear-time guarantees, for patterns that don't need lookarounds or backreferences.
Write safer patterns, avoid nested quantifiers on overlapping groups, anchor the patterns, and limit input length before matching. And never run user-supplied patterns without these protections.
Source-generated regexes with GeneratedRegex are good for performance, combined with all the above.
Analyzers can flag risky patterns, and fuzz tests with long near-matching inputs catch them in testing. Honestly, most teams don't think about this until it bites them.

p17-735.q: Actually files usually hold the most sensitive data, reports, exports, documents. And a common mistake is protecting the page that lists them but not the files themselves.
p17-735.k: secure file download, download authorization, signed url download, direct object reference files, protect documents access
x: Actually files usually hold the most sensitive data, reports, exports, documents. And a common mistake is protecting the page that lists them but not the files themselves.

What I look for. Files in a public web folder or public bucket, reachable by anyone who knows or guesses the URL. Predictable names, like report underscore 1001 dot pdf, so changing the number shows other people's files. And download endpoints that take an id without checking ownership.
The secure design. Store files privately, outside the web root, or in object storage with no public access.

Serve through an authorised endpoint. GET slash documents slash the id checks the current user may access that document, based on owner, site, study or tenant, and then streams the file. Resource-based authorisation keeps that check consistent.

Or issue short-lived signed URLs after the authorisation check. S3 pre-signed URLs or Azure SAS tokens valid for a few minutes, for one specific file, read-only. That takes the transfer off the API while keeping control.
Use unguessable ids like GUIDs as an extra layer, but never as the only protection.
Set the right headers, Content-Disposition attachment for downloads so active content doesn't render in the browser, the correct Content-Type, and X-Content-Type-Options nosniff.

Audit downloads of sensitive documents, who got what and when. And expire and clean up temporary files like generated exports after a while. In a clinical system, I'd say that audit part isn't optional.

p17-736.q: Honestly password reset is a favourite attack path, because it skips the password completely. So it needs care.
p17-736.k: password reset security, forgot password flow, reset token security, account recovery, password reset best practices
x: Honestly password reset is a favourite attack path, because it skips the password completely. So it needs care.

The request step, the user enters their email, and the response is always the same, like "if an account exists, we've sent a link", whether or not it exists. That way attackers can't use it to find registered emails. Rate-limit per account and per IP.

The token, long, random, single-use, from a cryptographically secure generator. Store only its hash, linked to the user, with a short expiry, 15 to 60 minutes. ASP.NET Core Identity's token providers do this, and tokens become invalid if the user's security stamp changes.

The link goes only to the registered email address, never to an address someone typed into the request. HTTPS, and don't leak the token through referrer headers, so no third-party resources on the reset page.

The reset itself, verify the token, require a strong new password checked against breached password lists, then invalidate the token, kill all existing sessions and refresh tokens, and email the user that their password changed.
MFA, if the account has it, the reset shouldn't quietly bypass it. Require the second factor during or after the reset.
Log reset requests and completions, and alert on unusual volumes.
And in enterprise setups with SSO, Keycloak or Entra ID, the identity provider owns this flow and the app just links to it. For me that's better than building our own, every time.

p17-737.q: So account enumeration means an attacker can figure out which usernames or emails are registered just by watching how the app responds. With a list of valid accounts, credential stuffing and targeted phishing work much better.
p17-737.k: username enumeration, account enumeration, user enumeration login, login error messages security, registration enumeration
x: So account enumeration means an attacker can figure out which usernames or emails are registered just by watching how the app responds. With a list of valid accounts, credential stuffing and targeted phishing work much better.
Where it leaks. Login, "user not found" versus "wrong password". Use one generic message, invalid username or password.
Password reset, "no account with that email" versus "email sent". Always respond the same way.
Registration, "this email is already registered". That's harder. One option is sending an email to the address saying "you already have an account", while the screen shows a neutral confirmation.

Timing. Even with identical messages, the response can be faster for unknown users because no password hash gets computed. So do equivalent work, like hashing against a dummy hash, so timing looks the same. People forget this one.
Other signals, different HTTP status codes, different response sizes, or lockout messages that only show for real accounts.
APIs, endpoints like users slash an email slash exists, or profile lookups, that confirm existence to unauthenticated callers.

Then the complementary defences, rate limiting and bot detection on these endpoints, CAPTCHA after repeated attempts, and monitoring for enumeration patterns, like lots of different usernames from one source.
There is a usability cost. For internal enterprise apps on SSO, the identity provider handles most of this anyway. For public-facing apps, I follow all of it.

p17-738.q: Okay, so Keycloak puts roles into access tokens in its own nested structure. Realm roles are under realm access dot roles, and client roles are under resource access, keyed by the client id, then roles. ASP.NET Core's role checks, the Authorize attribute with Roles, or User IsInRole, look for role claims with a specific claim type. So out of the box they just don't see Keycloak's nested roles.
p17-738.k: keycloak roles aspnet core, realm roles client roles, map keycloak claims, keycloak jwt roles, resource_access roles
x: Okay, so Keycloak puts roles into access tokens in its own nested structure. Realm roles are under realm access dot roles, and client roles are under resource access, keyed by the client id, then roles. ASP.NET Core's role checks, the Authorize attribute with Roles, or User IsInRole, look for role claims with a specific claim type. So out of the box they just don't see Keycloak's nested roles.

How I connect them. One way is a claims transformation. Implement IClaimsTransformation, which runs after authentication, read the realm access and resource access JSON from the token, pull out the roles for our client, and add them as role claims on the ClaimsPrincipal. Then normal role checks and policies just work.

The other way is a protocol mapper in Keycloak that puts roles in a flat claim, like "roles", and set RoleClaimType in the JWT bearer options to that name. That moves the mapping into Keycloak config and keeps app code simple.

On top of that, policies. Rather than checking raw role names everywhere, define policies like CanManageShipments that map to one or more roles, and use those in controllers. Then roles can change in Keycloak with no code change.

Fine-grained data permissions, like which sites or studies a user can see, usually come from the app's own database, not the token, because they change often and can be big. A claims transformation or authorisation handler loads them, with caching.
And I test the mapping with test tokens that have Keycloak's structure, so a config change can't silently remove someone's access.

p17-739.q: Right, Windows authentication lets users on domain-joined machines sign in to intranet apps automatically with their Windows login, no password prompt. IIS supports it, and so does ASP.NET Core with the Negotiate handler.
p17-739.k: windows authentication, kerberos vs ntlm, intranet authentication iis, negotiate authentication, integrated windows auth
x: Right, Windows authentication lets users on domain-joined machines sign in to intranet apps automatically with their Windows login, no password prompt. IIS supports it, and so does ASP.NET Core with the Negotiate handler.

It uses two protocols. Kerberos is the preferred one. The browser gets a service ticket from the domain controller for the web app's service principal name and presents it to the server, which validates it without calling the domain controller every time. It supports delegation, so the app can call another service, like SQL Server, as the user, if constrained delegation is set up. You need the correct SPNs registered for the service account, and the client has to reach the domain controller.
NTLM is the fallback when Kerberos isn't possible, like accessing by IP address or when SPNs are missing. It's challenge-response, weaker, no delegation, and Microsoft is deprecating it.

The limits. It only really works for domain-joined devices inside the corporate network. External users, mobile devices and other platforms struggle. It doesn't fit cloud and SaaS scenarios, it ties the app to Active Directory, and it's hard to combine with modern MFA and conditional access. Proxies and load balancers can also break NTLM, because it's connection-based. I've seen that cause some very confusing login loops.

For modern apps I'd use OpenID Connect against an identity provider like Entra ID or Keycloak. That can still use Kerberos so people sign in without a prompt on the corporate network, while supporting MFA, external access and token-based APIs.

p17-740.q: Let me explain it with where it's used. Reflection lets code inspect and use types at runtime. List a type's properties, methods and attributes, read or set properties by name, call methods dynamically, create instances with Activator CreateInstance. A lot of framework magic runs on it. ASP.NET Core model binding and controller discovery, DI containers, serialisers, ORMs like EF Core and Dapper mapping columns to properties, test frameworks finding test methods.
p17-740.k: reflection c#, system reflection, gettype getproperties, reflection performance, activator createinstance
x: Let me explain it with where it's used. Reflection lets code inspect and use types at runtime. List a type's properties, methods and attributes, read or set properties by name, call methods dynamically, create instances with Activator CreateInstance. A lot of framework magic runs on it. ASP.NET Core model binding and controller discovery, DI containers, serialisers, ORMs like EF Core and Dapper mapping columns to properties, test frameworks finding test methods.

The costs. Performance, reflective calls are much slower than direct ones, because of lookups, security checks, boxing arguments and no inlining. Calling GetProperties and GetValue in a hot loop, for every row or request, can be a real bottleneck.
Type safety, errors the compiler would normally catch, like a renamed property, only show up at runtime.
Trimming and Native AOT, the trimmer can't see what reflection will use, so it might remove code you need, and AOT doesn't support some dynamic features at all.

How I reduce the cost. Cache reflection results, like the PropertyInfo arrays per type, in a static dictionary. Compile expression trees or create delegates once with Delegate CreateDelegate, then call those fast delegates. And best of all, source generators that produce the code at compile time, which is what System.Text.Json, the logging generator and the regex generator do.

In our projects I'd use reflection for startup-time work, like scanning assemblies to register handlers or plugins, and keep it out of per-request paths, where a generated or cached approach is way faster.

p17-741.q: Yeah, they all run things in parallel, but they suit different kinds of work.
p17-741.k: parallel foreach, parallel foreachasync, plinq, asparallel, cpu bound vs io bound parallelism
x: Yeah, they all run things in parallel, but they suit different kinds of work.

Parallel For and Parallel ForEach are for CPU-bound work on in-memory data, like crunching thousands of records with calculations. They split the work across thread pool threads and block the calling thread until it's done. MaxDegreeOfParallelism controls how many run at once, usually around the number of cores.

PLINQ, with AsParallel, does the same thing for LINQ queries. Filtering, projecting and aggregating big in-memory collections across cores. Order isn't kept unless you add AsOrdered. Good for data-parallel queries, but the overhead makes it slower for small collections or cheap operations.

Task WhenAll is for I/O-bound async work, calling several APIs or databases at once. You start the tasks and await them together, and no threads are blocked while waiting. But starting thousands of tasks at once can flatten the downstream service or exhaust connections.

Parallel ForEachAsync, since .NET 6, sort of combines both. It runs an async delegate per item with a concurrency limit, like 500 files with at most 8 uploads at a time. That's my default for lots of I/O operations with throttling, instead of hand-writing SemaphoreSlim logic.

My rule of thumb is pretty simple. CPU-bound, Parallel or PLINQ. I/O-bound, async with WhenAll or ForEachAsync. Never use Parallel ForEach with async lambdas, because it treats them as async void and doesn't wait for them. And in ASP.NET Core request handling, avoid heavy CPU parallelism, because requests already share the thread pool.

p17-742.q: So the Mediator pattern cuts direct dependencies between objects by having them talk through a mediator. In .NET APIs it's usually done with a library like MediatR. A controller doesn't call a service directly. It sends a request object, like CreateShipmentCommand, and the mediator finds the one handler for that request type and calls it.
p17-742.k: mediator pattern, mediatr, pipeline behavior, ipipelinebehavior, request handler pattern
x: So the Mediator pattern cuts direct dependencies between objects by having them talk through a mediator. In .NET APIs it's usually done with a library like MediatR. A controller doesn't call a service directly. It sends a request object, like CreateShipmentCommand, and the mediator finds the one handler for that request type and calls it.
What you get is thin controllers, and each use case is its own handler class with its own dependencies. That fits vertical slices and CQRS nicely, and handlers are easy to test.

Pipeline behaviours are honestly the most useful part. They wrap every request, kind of like middleware for use cases. A behaviour gets the request and a next delegate, can run code before and after, and can short-circuit. Typical ones are validation, running FluentValidation validators and returning errors before the handler even runs. Logging and timing each request. Transactions, wrapping commands in a database transaction. Caching for queries. Authorisation checks. Retry or idempotency for commands. You register them once and they apply to all handlers, or to specific request types through generic constraints.

The downsides, it's an extra layer of indirection, so navigating is harder, you can't just jump from controller to service. A little overhead. And for small apps it can be over-engineering. Also, recent MediatR versions moved to a commercial licence, so some teams use alternatives or a small hand-written dispatcher.
I like it for medium to large APIs with lots of use cases and cross-cutting concerns, and I keep it simple. One request, one handler, behaviours for the cross-cutting stuff.

p17-743.q: Okay, C# lets a type define how operators like plus, minus, double equals and less than work on it, through static operator methods. Say a Money type defines plus to add two amounts and checks they're the same currency, or a Vector type defines arithmetic. If you overload double equals, you have to overload not-equals too, and override Equals and GetHashCode consistently. Comparison operators come in pairs as well.
p17-743.k: operator overloading c#, implicit operator, explicit operator, user defined conversion, value object operators
x: Okay, C# lets a type define how operators like plus, minus, double equals and less than work on it, through static operator methods. Say a Money type defines plus to add two amounts and checks they're the same currency, or a Vector type defines arithmetic. If you overload double equals, you have to overload not-equals too, and override Equals and GetHashCode consistently. Comparison operators come in pairs as well.

Conversion operators define how a type converts to or from another type. An implicit conversion happens automatically, like assigning a ShipmentId to a Guid variable, and should only be used when it can never fail and loses nothing. An explicit conversion needs a cast, like casting a Fahrenheit value to Celsius, and that's for conversions that might fail, lose precision or surprise the reader.

Where I find them useful is value objects and strongly typed ids. Like ShipmentId wrapping a Guid, where an explicit conversion from Guid stops you accidentally mixing up different ids, and an implicit conversion to Guid makes it easy to pass into data access code. Also maths or measurement types.

A few cautions. Don't overload operators with surprising meanings, like using plus for something that isn't addition. Avoid implicit conversions that hide expensive work or possible exceptions. And remember operators are static and resolved at compile time, so they don't behave polymorphically through base types or interfaces, except with static abstract interface members and generic math in newer C#.
And records give you value equality with double equals and not-equals automatically, which I think is the easiest win of the lot.

p17-744.q: So I try to use the newer features where they make code clearer, not just because they're new. The ones I actually use a lot are these.
p17-744.k: new c# features, c# 12 features, collection expressions, raw string literals, list patterns, c# 11 features
x: So I try to use the newer features where they make code clearer, not just because they're new. The ones I actually use a lot are these.

Collection expressions from C# 12. Square-bracket syntax to create arrays and lists with values, an empty list with just empty brackets, and the spread operator, two dots, to combine collections. One syntax for arrays, lists, spans and immutable collections, and the compiler picks an efficient implementation.

Raw string literals from C# 11. Triple quotes let me write JSON, SQL or XML snippets in tests and templates without escaping quotes, and you use a double dollar for interpolation when the content has braces in it.

Pattern matching. Switch expressions, property patterns, like checking an order's status is Shipped and its total is greater than 1000, relational and logical patterns like "greater or equal zero and less than 100", and list patterns from C# 11, which match on the first and last elements or a single-element list. Handy for parsing arguments or messages.
Records and with-expressions for DTOs and immutable values, required members and init setters for safe construction, and primary constructors from C# 12 for simple classes and DI.
File-scoped namespaces and global usings cut the noise, and nullable reference types are on for every new project.
Smaller ones too, target-typed new, the null-coalescing assignment, and the field keyword in C# 14 for properties with simple backing logic.

Honestly though, our legacy projects are on .NET Framework 4.8 with older C# versions, so I mostly use these in the newer .NET 8 services. That's actually one of the small productivity wins we point to when we make the case for migration.

p17-745.q: Okay, so .NET has a garbage collector, but leaks still happen whenever objects stay reachable when they shouldn't. The GC can't collect anything that's still referenced.
p17-745.k: memory leak dotnet, managed memory leak, event handler leak, find memory leak, dotnet-gcdump
x: Okay, so .NET has a garbage collector, but leaks still happen whenever objects stay reachable when they shouldn't. The GC can't collect anything that's still referenced.

The most common cause I've seen is event handlers. A short-lived object subscribes to a long-lived object's event, like a static event or a singleton service, and never unsubscribes. The publisher holds a reference to the subscriber forever.
Static collections and caches without limits. A static dictionary that only grows, or an in-memory cache with no size limit or expiry.
Captive dependencies, a singleton holding scoped or transient objects, which then live forever too.

Timers and background tasks holding on to objects they never release. Unmanaged resources not disposed, streams, connections, native handles, which leak memory outside the managed heap as well. Closures and lambdas accidentally capturing big objects and being held by long-lived delegates. And HttpClient created per request, which leaks sockets more than memory.

To find them, watch the trend. dotnet-counters or metrics showing the GC heap growing after each full GC instead of levelling off. Then take two memory snapshots some time apart, with dotnet-gcdump or a full dump with dotnet-dump, and compare them in Visual Studio, PerfView or another profiler. Which types grew in count, and what's the retention path, the chain of references keeping them alive. That path usually points straight at the event subscription or static collection to blame.
Then the fix follows the cause. Unsubscribe or use weak events, bound the caches, fix lifetimes, dispose properly.

p17-746.q: See, most code only needs List, Dictionary and HashSet, but knowing the others helps you pick the right tool.
p17-746.k: priorityqueue c#, sorteddictionary, sortedset, linkedlist c#, queue and stack c#, specialised collections
x: See, most code only needs List, Dictionary and HashSet, but knowing the others helps you pick the right tool.
Queue and Stack. First in first out and last in first out, with constant-time enqueue and dequeue, or push and pop. Queues for processing work in order, stacks for undo or depth-first traversal.

PriorityQueue, since .NET 6, is a min-heap where Dequeue always gives you the item with the lowest priority value, in log n time. Useful for scheduling, like processing the most urgent jobs first, merging sorted streams, or algorithms like Dijkstra's shortest path. It's not thread-safe and you can't update priorities directly.

SortedDictionary keeps keys sorted with a red-black tree, log n operations. Good when you insert and remove a lot and need ordered iteration. SortedList is similar but array-based, less memory and faster lookups, slower inserts. SortedSet gives a sorted unique set with range queries, like GetViewBetween.

LinkedList is a doubly linked list with constant-time insert and remove when you already have the node. I've used it for an LRU cache together with a dictionary. In general it's slower than List because of poor memory locality, so I rarely use it otherwise.

For multi-threading, the concurrent collections, ConcurrentQueue, ConcurrentBag, BlockingCollection, and Channels for async producer-consumer. And immutable and frozen collections for shared read-only data.
Picking correctly turns order n scans into log n or constant-time operations, which really matters at scale.

p17-747.q: Actually attributes are just metadata on code, classes, methods, properties, parameters. They don't do anything on their own. Some other code reads them and acts. Frameworks use them everywhere, Authorize, HttpGet, Required, JsonPropertyName, test attributes like Fact.
p17-747.k: custom attributes c#, create attribute, read attributes reflection, attribute usage, metadata attributes
x: Actually attributes are just metadata on code, classes, methods, properties, parameters. They don't do anything on their own. Some other code reads them and acts. Frameworks use them everywhere, Authorize, HttpGet, Required, JsonPropertyName, test attributes like Fact.

To create one, you write a class that inherits from Attribute, named with the Attribute suffix by convention, like AuditedAttribute, and put an AttributeUsage attribute on it saying where it can go, methods or classes, whether it can appear multiple times, and whether it's inherited. Constructor parameters and public properties become its arguments, and they have to be compile-time constants, strings, numbers, enums or types.
