To read it, reflection, GetCustomAttribute of AuditedAttribute on a type, method or property. In ASP.NET Core, endpoint metadata makes it easy. A middleware or filter gets the current endpoint, asks its metadata for the Audited attribute, and acts on it. For example, writing an audit record only for endpoints marked Audited, or applying a specific rate-limit policy.

Examples I've used, marking endpoints that need audit logging, marking properties that hold sensitive data so logging and serialisation can mask them, and marking handler classes for automatic registration.

A couple of considerations. Reading attributes through reflection costs something, so cache the results. For performance-critical or AOT scenarios, source generators can read attributes at compile time and generate code instead. And I don't hide important business logic in attributes, because it makes behaviour less obvious to whoever's reading the code.

p17-748.q: Honestly I like immutability a lot. An immutable object can't change after it's created, any "change" gives you a new object. That makes code easier to reason about, since nothing can modify an object behind your back, it's naturally thread-safe, and it's safe as a dictionary key or in shared caches.
p17-748.k: immutable types c#, immutability c#, immutable class, readonly properties, record with expression
x: Honestly I like immutability a lot. An immutable object can't change after it's created, any "change" gives you a new object. That makes code easier to reason about, since nothing can modify an object behind your back, it's naturally thread-safe, and it's safe as a dictionary key or in shared caches.

Records are the simplest way. A positional record, like an Address record with Street and City, gives you init-only properties, value equality, and with-expressions to make modified copies, like taking an address and creating a copy with the City set to Pune.

For classes, properties with get only or init, set through the constructor or object initialisers, and required members to make sure they're set. Fields marked readonly. No methods that modify state. Methods return new instances instead, like Money Add returning a new Money.

One thing to watch is shallow immutability. A record with a List of string property isn't truly immutable, because the list itself can still change. Use IReadOnlyList with a copy, ImmutableArray or ImmutableList, or FrozenSet for collection properties, and copy incoming collections in the constructor.
readonly struct for small value types guarantees all fields are read-only.

Where I use it, value objects in the domain, like Money, DateRange or strongly typed ids. DTOs and messages, which shouldn't change after creation. Config snapshots. And front-end state, like Redux, same idea.
The cost is more allocations when objects change a lot. That's rarely an issue in business code, but it matters in tight loops.

p17-749.q: Yeah, .NET has several timers and it does confuse people.
p17-749.k: periodictimer, system threading timer, system timers timer, timers in dotnet, run code every n seconds
x: Yeah, .NET has several timers and it does confuse people.

System.Threading.Timer is the lightweight one that calls a callback on a thread pool thread at intervals. Callbacks can overlap if one takes longer than the interval, exceptions in callbacks are unhandled and can crash the process, and you have to keep a reference to it so it isn't garbage collected.

System.Timers.Timer is a wrapper with an Elapsed event and an AutoReset property. It swallows exceptions from handlers, which hides errors, and it also allows overlapping callbacks. Mostly legacy now.
UI timers, the Windows Forms and WPF dispatcher timers, run on the UI thread, desktop only.

PeriodicTimer, since .NET 6, is built for async code. You write a loop, while awaiting the timer's WaitForNextTickAsync with the stopping token, do the work. Ticks never overlap, because the next wait only starts once the work finishes. Exceptions are handled like normal async code, and cancellation is built in. That's my default inside a BackgroundService for periodic jobs, polling an outbox table or refreshing a cache.
For testability, TimeProvider in .NET 8 can create timers, so tests control time.

And for schedules more complex than fixed intervals, like every weekday at 2 AM, or jobs that must survive restarts and run once across multiple instances, I'd go with a scheduler like Quartz.NET or Hangfire instead of a raw timer. That's how our alert watchdog runs its scheduled checks.

p17-750.q: Let me start with the problem. Compilers, the JIT and CPUs are allowed to reorder memory reads and writes, and cache values in registers, as long as single-threaded behaviour doesn't change. In multi-threaded code, that means one thread might not see another thread's writes when you expect, or sees them in a different order.
p17-750.k: volatile keyword c#, memory model dotnet, memory barrier, instruction reordering, volatile read write
x: Let me start with the problem. Compilers, the JIT and CPUs are allowed to reorder memory reads and writes, and cache values in registers, as long as single-threaded behaviour doesn't change. In multi-threaded code, that means one thread might not see another thread's writes when you expect, or sees them in a different order.

The .NET memory model defines what's guaranteed. volatile on a field gives reads acquire semantics and writes release semantics. A volatile read always reads the current value from memory, and operations after it can't move before it. A volatile write makes all earlier writes visible before it. The classic use is a stop flag. A private volatile bool stop-requested field, one thread sets it, a worker loop checks it, and the JIT can't hoist the read out of the loop and spin forever.

What volatile doesn't do is make compound operations atomic. count plus plus on a volatile field is still a read-modify-write race, you need Interlocked Increment for that. It also doesn't give full ordering between a write followed by a read.

In practice I rarely use volatile directly. Higher-level tools are clearer and safer. lock, which includes full memory barriers. Interlocked for atomic updates. Volatile Read and Volatile Write methods for explicit cases. CancellationToken for stop signals instead of a volatile bool. And concurrent collections, Lazy and Channels for coordination.
For me, knowing the memory model mostly helps me spot subtle bugs in lock-free code, and avoid writing lock-free code unless it's really necessary.

p17-751.q: So TaskCompletionSource lets you create a Task that you complete yourself. You hand its Task property to callers, they await it, and later your code calls SetResult, SetException or SetCanceled, or the Try versions, to finish it.
p17-751.k: taskcompletionsource, tcs c#, convert callback to task, manual task completion, wrap event in task
x: So TaskCompletionSource lets you create a Task that you complete yourself. You hand its Task property to callers, they await it, and later your code calls SetResult, SetException or SetCanceled, or the Try versions, to finish it.

Where I find it useful. Wrapping callback or event-based APIs into async ones. An older library raises a Completed event, you subscribe, and in the handler you set the result on the completion source. The method returns its Task, so callers just await it.

Request-response over messaging. When you send a request over a queue or WebSocket and wait for a reply with a matching correlation id, you store a TaskCompletionSource in a dictionary keyed by that id. When the response arrives, find it and complete it. Combine it with a timeout and cancellation, and remove the entry afterwards.
Signals between components, one part waits until another reaches some state, like "service is ready". And testing, controlling exactly when a fake async dependency completes.

The important detail people miss is creating it with the RunContinuationsAsynchronously option. Otherwise, when you call SetResult, the awaiting code's continuation can run synchronously on your thread, inside your lock or event handler, and that can cause deadlocks or weird re-entrancy. I learned that one the hard way.
Also make sure every path completes it, including errors and cancellation, by registering a cancellation callback that calls TrySetCanceled. Otherwise the awaiting code just waits forever.

p17-752.q: Okay, the .NET garbage collector has modes tuned for different kinds of apps.
p17-752.k: server gc vs workstation gc, gc modes dotnet, concurrent gc, background gc, dotnet gc settings
x: Okay, the .NET garbage collector has modes tuned for different kinds of apps.
Workstation GC is meant for desktop and client apps. Single heap, collects on the thread that triggered the collection, lower memory usage, so it's friendly to machines running lots of processes.

Server GC is meant for high-throughput server apps. It creates a separate heap and a dedicated GC thread per CPU core, so allocations scale across cores and collections run in parallel and finish faster. It uses more memory, since each heap has its own budget. ASP.NET Core apps use Server GC by default.
Both can run with concurrent or background GC, which is the default, so full gen 2 collections mostly run in the background while app threads keep going, reducing pauses.

Why it matters in practice. Containers, with Server GC on a machine with lots of cores but a small memory limit, heap counts and memory usage can surprise you. .NET respects container CPU and memory limits, and you can tune with GCHeapCount, GCHeapHardLimit, or the newer DATAS mode, dynamic adaptation to application sizes. That's on by default in .NET 9 for Server GC, and it adjusts heap count to the load and cuts memory for small apps.

Lots of small services on one host, Workstation GC or DATAS might be better to save memory. Latency-sensitive work, GC latency modes like SustainedLowLatency can reduce blocking collections during critical periods.
But my rule is, I don't change GC settings on a guess. I measure with dotnet-counters, GC pause time, heap size, allocation rate, and then adjust.

p17-753.q: Right, normal logging calls, like LogInformation with a "Processed Count items for StudyId" template and the values, are convenient but have hidden costs. Value-type arguments get boxed into an object array, the template gets parsed, and all that happens even when the level is disabled, unless you check IsEnabled first. In hot paths, like per-message processing in a busy consumer, that adds allocations and CPU.
p17-753.k: loggermessage, high performance logging, logger message source generator, logging allocations, logmethod attribute
x: Right, normal logging calls, like LogInformation with a "Processed Count items for StudyId" template and the values, are convenient but have hidden costs. Value-type arguments get boxed into an object array, the template gets parsed, and all that happens even when the level is disabled, unless you check IsEnabled first. In hot paths, like per-message processing in a busy consumer, that adds allocations and CPU.

LoggerMessage fixes it. The modern way is the source generator. You declare a static partial method, like LogProcessed taking a logger, a count and a study id, with the LoggerMessage attribute giving an event id, a level like Information, and the message template. The generator writes an optimised implementation at compile time. It checks the level is enabled before doing any work, avoids boxing with strongly typed parameters, and pre-parses the template.

Beyond speed, strongly typed log methods give consistent event ids and messages across the codebase, which makes searching and alerting in Splunk or Grafana easier. Parameter names get checked at compile time. And log calls in business code read cleanly, like logger dot LogProcessed with count and study id, when you write them as extension methods.
What I do is use it in libraries, and high-volume paths like message handlers, middleware and data processing loops. For rare log lines, like startup messages, regular calls are fine.
And I avoid string interpolation in log calls, because it builds the string even when the level is off, and you lose the structured properties.

p17-754.q: Actually the differences here matter more than people think.
p17-754.k: icomparable, icomparer, sort custom objects c#, orderby thenby, stable sort c#
x: Actually the differences here matter more than people think.

IComparable defines a type's natural order. The type implements CompareTo and returns negative, zero or positive. Think of a Version or a Money type that has an obvious order. Then List Sort and SortedSet use it automatically.

IComparer defines an order outside the type, so you can have several, by name, by date, by priority. You pass it to Sort, OrderBy or sorted collections. Comparer Create with a lambda builds one quickly, and StringComparer OrdinalIgnoreCase is a built-in one for strings.

LINQ OrderBy and ThenBy are the most readable for most business code, like ordering shipments by priority, then by created date descending. It returns a new sequence, and it's a stable sort, so items with equal keys keep their original order.

List Sort and Array Sort sort in place, faster with less allocation, but they're unstable, equal items can get reordered. If stability matters, like sorting a table by one column while keeping a previous order, use OrderBy or add a tie-breaker key like an id.

Common mistakes I've seen. Inconsistent comparers that break the rules, random results or not handling nulls, which can cause exceptions or wrong results. Subtracting integers in CompareTo, which can overflow, instead of calling CompareTo on the values. And culture-sensitive string sorting when ordinal was intended.
For data from a database, I sort in the SQL query, with a deterministic tie-breaker, especially for pagination.

p17-755.q: So var and dynamic look similar but they're completely different. var is static typing, the compiler infers the type at compile time and you get full type checking and IntelliSense. object is also static, you need casts to use its members.
p17-755.k: dynamic keyword c#, dynamic vs var vs object, dlr, dynamic language runtime, expandoobject
x: So var and dynamic look similar but they're completely different. var is static typing, the compiler infers the type at compile time and you get full type checking and IntelliSense. object is also static, you need casts to use its members.

dynamic switches off compile-time checking for that variable. Member access, method calls and operators get resolved at runtime by the Dynamic Language Runtime. If the member doesn't exist, you get a RuntimeBinderException at runtime instead of a compile error.

Where it's appropriate. COM interop, like automating Office, where the APIs are loosely typed. dynamic made that a lot simpler. Interop with dynamic languages like IronPython. Truly dynamic data structures, like ExpandoObject, or dynamic JSON in some cases, though System.Text.Json's JsonNode or JsonDocument are usually the better choice. And some reflection-heavy cases where dynamic is shorter, like calling a generic method with a runtime type, where dynamic dispatch picks the right overload.

Why I avoid it in normal code. No compile-time safety, so typos and refactoring mistakes turn into runtime errors. Slower than static calls, though the DLR caches call sites. No IntelliSense. And it doesn't work with trimming and Native AOT.

For me, in business apps and APIs, strong types, DTOs and generics win. If I see dynamic in a code review outside interop, I'd usually ask whether a proper type or JsonNode would be clearer. Most of the time it is.

p17-756.q: Okay, access modifiers control which code can use a type or member.
p17-756.k: access modifiers c#, protected internal, private protected, internal vs public, file access modifier
x: Okay, access modifiers control which code can use a type or member.

public, accessible from anywhere. private, only inside the same class or struct, and it's the default for members. protected, the class and derived classes, even in other assemblies. internal, anywhere in the same assembly but not from outside, and that's the default for top-level types.

Then the two that confuse people. protected internal means accessible from the same assembly, or from derived classes in any assembly. So it's protected OR internal. private protected, since C# 7.2, means only derived classes that are also in the same assembly. So protected AND internal. That OR versus AND is how I remember them, and interviewers love asking it.
And file, since C# 11, a type visible only inside the same source file, mostly useful for source generators and helper types.

How I use them in practice. Default to the most restrictive access and open up only when needed. In a library or shared NuGet package, anything that isn't meant to be public API is internal, so we can change implementations without breaking consumers.
InternalsVisibleTo lets a test project see internal types, so I don't make things public just for tests, though honestly I prefer testing through public behaviour anyway.
In clean architecture solutions, keeping the infrastructure implementations internal and exposing only interfaces and a registration extension method enforces the boundaries nicely.
And sealed, alongside the access modifiers, stops unintended inheritance.

p17-757.q: So a shallow copy creates a new object, but reference-type fields just copy the reference, so the copy and the original share nested objects. Change a nested list in the copy and it changes in the original too. A deep copy duplicates the nested objects as well, so the two are fully independent.
p17-757.k: deep copy c#, shallow copy c#, clone object c#, memberwiseclone, record with shallow copy
x: So a shallow copy creates a new object, but reference-type fields just copy the reference, so the copy and the original share nested objects. Change a nested list in the copy and it changes in the original too. A deep copy duplicates the nested objects as well, so the two are fully independent.

The ways to copy. MemberwiseClone, a protected method on object that makes a shallow copy, you can call it from a Clone method in your class. Records with with-expressions, also shallow. Copying an order with a new status copies the top-level values, but a List property is shared. ICloneable, an old interface that doesn't say shallow or deep, so it's not recommended for public APIs.

For actual deep copies. Manual copy methods or copy constructors are the most explicit and the fastest. Each class copies its own nested objects, like a new Order built from another one creating new item objects. Safe, but you have to maintain it when properties get added.

Serialisation round-trip, serialise to JSON with System.Text.Json and deserialise into a new object. Simple and generic, but slower, and it only copies serialisable data, so you lose private state, references and cycles unless configured.
Mapping libraries or source-generated mappers can produce copies too.

But often the best answer, I think, is to not need deep copies at all. Make objects immutable so they can be shared safely, and use immutable collections. Then "changing" means creating a new version and there's no risk of accidental shared mutation.
And I'd never use BinaryFormatter for cloning like older articles suggest. It's insecure and it's been removed.

p17-758.q: See, the Proxy pattern puts a stand-in object in front of a real one, implementing the same interface, to control access to it. The caller doesn't know it's talking to a proxy. The proxy can add behaviour before or after forwarding the call.
p17-758.k: proxy pattern, dynamic proxy, dispatchproxy, castle dynamicproxy, interceptor pattern c#
x: See, the Proxy pattern puts a stand-in object in front of a real one, implementing the same interface, to control access to it. The caller doesn't know it's talking to a proxy. The proxy can add behaviour before or after forwarding the call.

The common kinds. A virtual proxy delays creating an expensive object until it's needed, like lazy loading. A protection proxy checks permissions before calling through. A remote proxy represents an object in another process, like a generated gRPC or WCF client. And caching or logging proxies add those concerns.
It looks a lot like the Decorator pattern. The difference is intent. Decorators add behaviour and often get stacked, proxies control access. In code they can look identical.

Dynamic proxies generate the proxy classes at runtime, so you don't write one per interface. In .NET there's DispatchProxy, built in, which creates a proxy for any interface and handles every call in one Invoke method. And Castle DynamicProxy, a popular library supporting interfaces and virtual class members. Moq and NSubstitute use it to create mocks, and some frameworks use it for interceptors, adding logging, timing or retries to every method of a service.

Where it shows up in our stack, EF Core lazy-loading proxies, which override navigation properties to load data on access. Mocking libraries in unit tests. And HTTP client libraries like Refit, which generate implementations of an interface that make the API calls.
Because runtime proxies use reflection, people are increasingly using source generators to produce the same thing at compile time.

p17-759.q: Actually in .NET the go-to GraphQL server library is Hot Chocolate. You define the schema from C# types, a Query class with resolver methods like GetShipments, object types for Shipment and Site, and mutations for changes. Clients send one query describing exactly the fields they want, including nested data, like shipments with their site name and items, and they get back exactly that shape.
p17-759.k: graphql dotnet, hot chocolate, graphql n+1, dataloader, graphql asp.net core
x: Actually in .NET the go-to GraphQL server library is Hot Chocolate. You define the schema from C# types, a Query class with resolver methods like GetShipments, object types for Shipment and Site, and mutations for changes. Clients send one query describing exactly the fields they want, including nested data, like shipments with their site name and items, and they get back exactly that shape.

The N plus one problem is GraphQL's classic trap. If a query asks for 50 shipments and each one's site, a naive site resolver runs one database query per shipment. One query for shipments plus 50 for sites.

DataLoader solves it. Instead of loading the site right away, each resolver asks a DataLoader for a site id. The DataLoader collects all the ids requested in that execution step, makes one batched call, basically a where id is in this list query, and hands each resolver its result. It also caches within the request, so the same site isn't loaded twice. Hot Chocolate has DataLoader built in, and it integrates with EF Core projections so only the requested columns are queried.

Other things I'd set up. Query depth and complexity limits, so a client can't send some huge nested query that kills the server. Persisted or allow-listed queries for public APIs. Authorisation on fields and types, not just the endpoint. And cursor-based pagination.

When would I choose GraphQL? When lots of different front ends need different shapes of related data. For simple CRUD or service-to-service calls, I'd say REST or gRPC is simpler to run, cache and monitor.

p17-760.q: Honestly these are some of the most valuable tests we have. WebApplicationFactory, from the Mvc Testing package, starts the whole ASP.NET Core app in memory, with the real Program dot cs, middleware, routing, DI, filters and serialisation, on an in-memory TestServer. Tests get an HttpClient from it and make real HTTP calls, no network, no deployment.

WebApplicationFactory, from the Mvc Testing package, starts the whole ASP.NET Core app in memory, with the real Program dot cs, middleware, routing, DI, filters and serialisation, on an in-memory TestServer. Tests get an HttpClient from it and make real HTTP calls, no network, no deployment.

How I set it up. A custom factory class that inherits WebApplicationFactory of Program and overrides ConfigureWebHost. In ConfigureTestServices I swap out external dependencies. The DbContext points at a test database, often a real SQL Server in a container with Testcontainers. HTTP clients for third-party APIs get fakes or a stub server like WireMock.NET. The message bus gets an in-memory version or a test double. And I add a test authentication handler so tests can act as different users with specific roles.
A test then arranges data in the database, posts a request as JSON to slash api slash shipments, and asserts the status code, the response body, and the resulting database state or published message.

What these catch that unit tests miss is routing and attribute mistakes, model binding and validation behaviour, authorisation policies, serialisation settings, middleware order, and EF Core mappings against a real database.
Practically, share the factory across tests in a class fixture for speed, reset data between tests, with Respawn for example, keep tests independent, and run them in CI on every pull request.
One small thing, with top-level statements in .NET 6 and later, you add a public partial Program class declaration, or InternalsVisibleTo, so the test project can reference Program.

p17-761.q: So mapping between entities and DTOs is repetitive, which is why libraries exist. Each one has its pros and cons.
p17-761.k: automapper vs manual mapping, mapster, mapperly, object mapping dotnet, dto mapping
x: So mapping between entities and DTOs is repetitive, which is why libraries exist. Each one has its pros and cons.

AutoMapper uses conventions and reflection-based configuration. Properties with matching names map automatically, and profiles define the exceptions. It saves typing, and ProjectTo can turn mappings into EF Core query projections. But mistakes show up at runtime, not compile time. The mapping logic is hidden, so debugging and find-references get harder. Complex configurations turn into a puzzle. And recent versions moved to a commercial licence.
Mapster is similar in style, but faster, with optional code generation.

Mapperly is a source generator. You declare a partial mapper class with method signatures, and it generates plain mapping code at compile time. You get compile-time warnings for unmapped properties, no reflection, good performance, and generated code you can actually read and debug.

Manual mapping, writing the assignments yourself, often as extension methods like ToDto, or constructors. Explicit, fast, easy to debug, refactor-safe. It costs some typing, but with modern IDEs and AI assistants that's really small now.

My preference is manual mapping or Mapperly for most code, because mappings often contain little business decisions, formatting, combining fields, hiding data, and those are clearer in code. For EF Core queries I write Select projections directly, so only the needed columns come back. In an existing codebase that uses AutoMapper consistently I'd keep it, but always with configuration validation tests, AssertConfigurationIsValid, to catch mistakes early.

p17-762.q: Right, so in ASP.NET Core each request runs on a thread pool thread. If an action calls a database or another API synchronously, that thread just sits there blocked, doing nothing, until the response comes back. Under load, all the threads can end up blocked waiting on I/O. The thread pool grows slowly, requests queue up, latency spikes, while the CPU's mostly idle. That's thread pool starvation.
p17-762.k: async controller actions, async await scalability, why async in web api, thread pool web requests, async io scalability
x: Right, so in ASP.NET Core each request runs on a thread pool thread. If an action calls a database or another API synchronously, that thread just sits there blocked, doing nothing, until the response comes back. Under load, all the threads can end up blocked waiting on I/O. The thread pool grows slowly, requests queue up, latency spikes, while the CPU's mostly idle. That's thread pool starvation.

With async actions, when the code awaits an I/O operation, like awaiting ToListAsync on a DbSet, or an HttpClient GetAsync, the thread goes back to the pool while the OS waits for the I/O. When the result comes in, a pool thread continues the method. So a small number of threads can serve lots of concurrent requests that are mostly waiting.
A few important points. Async improves scalability and throughput under concurrency, not the speed of one request. A single request might even be a tiny bit slower because of the overhead.
It only helps I/O-bound work. CPU-bound work still needs a thread, and wrapping it in Task Run inside a request just moves it to another pool thread and adds overhead.
It has to be async all the way. Calling dot Result or dot Wait on async methods blocks a thread again and can bring the starvation right back.
And pass the request's CancellationToken into async calls, so work stops when the client disconnects.
In our legacy ASP.NET MVC applications, moving data access to async was one of the changes that helped handle peak usage better without adding servers.

p17-763.q: Yeah, in ASP.NET Core controllers you've basically got three return styles.
p17-763.k: iactionresult vs actionresult, actionresult t, return types web api, controller return type, typed results controllers
x: Yeah, in ASP.NET Core controllers you've basically got three return styles.

Returning the DTO directly, like a Get method that returns a ShipmentDto. Simple, and the framework serialises it with a 200. But you can't return other status codes like 404 without throwing exceptions or some workaround.

IActionResult. You can return anything, Ok with the DTO, NotFound, BadRequest with a problem, CreatedAtAction. Flexible, but the return type says nothing about the body, so OpenAPI generators can't infer the schema. You need ProducesResponseType attributes with the DTO type and status code.

ActionResult of T combines both. You can return a ShipmentDto directly, and it's implicitly converted to a 200 result, or return NotFound or anything else. The T tells OpenAPI and readers what the success body looks like. That's my default for controllers, an async Get returning a Task of ActionResult of ShipmentDto. I still add ProducesResponseType for the error codes so the docs are complete.
For minimal APIs, the equivalent is TypedResults with a Results type listing Ok of ShipmentDto or NotFound, which gives compile-time checked status codes and automatic OpenAPI metadata.
One caveat, ActionResult of T doesn't work with an interface as T, because implicit conversions from interfaces aren't allowed. So I return concrete DTO types, which I'd do anyway.
And consistency matters more than which one you pick. The team agrees on one style for new code, along with ProblemDetails for errors.

p17-764.q: Let me be honest, I've seen both in real systems. Some teams wrap every response in an envelope with success, data, errors and message. Others return the resource directly and use HTTP status codes and ProblemDetails for errors.
p17-764.k: api response wrapper, response envelope, standard api response format, wrap response data success, apiresponse class
x: Let me be honest, I've seen both in real systems. Some teams wrap every response in an envelope with success, data, errors and message. Others return the resource directly and use HTTP status codes and ProblemDetails for errors.

For an envelope, you get one consistent shape for the front end to handle, a place for metadata like pagination, warnings or request ids, and it was common practice in older systems where clients couldn't easily read status codes.

Against it, it duplicates what HTTP already gives you. Success false with a 200 status confuses monitoring, caches, gateways and retry logic, which all rely on status codes. It adds nesting to every client call. And standard tools, OpenAPI generators, HTTP clients, API gateways, work more naturally with plain resources and standard errors.

My preference is return resources directly with correct status codes. Use ProblemDetails, RFC 9457, for all errors, with extensions like an error code and validation errors. Put pagination in a consistent wrapper only for list endpoints, with items, a next cursor and a total count. And use headers for cross-cutting metadata like correlation ids.

If an existing API already uses an envelope, I keep it consistent rather than mixing styles, but I make sure the HTTP status still reflects the outcome, so failures aren't hidden behind 200s. In our legacy APIs that the Angular sub-apps consume, consistency for the front end was the priority, so new endpoints there follow the same contract.

p17-765.q: So a really common production failure is a missing or wrong config value, an empty connection string, a negative timeout, and nobody notices until the code using it runs, maybe hours after deployment, right in the middle of some business process. I want the app to fail fast at startup instead.
p17-765.k: validate options startup, validateonstart, validatedataannotations, options validation dotnet, fail fast configuration
x: So a really common production failure is a missing or wrong config value, an empty connection string, a negative timeout, and nobody notices until the code using it runs, maybe hours after deployment, right in the middle of some business process. I want the app to fail fast at startup instead.

The options pattern supports validation. With data annotations, you put Required, Range and Url attributes on the options class, and register it with AddOptions, Bind to the RabbitMq section, then ValidateDataAnnotations.

For custom rules, chain a Validate call with a lambda, say retry count must be less than or equal to max retries, with a message. Or a class implementing IValidateOptions for complex logic, like checking combinations of settings, or using FluentValidation.

The key one is ValidateOnStart. Without it, validation only runs the first time the options are accessed. With it, validation runs when the host starts, so bad config stops the app immediately with a clear error, and the deployment fails before it takes any traffic. In .NET 8 there's a source generator, the OptionsValidator attribute, that generates the validation code for AOT and performance.
Combine that with health checks and readiness probes, and a misconfigured instance never becomes healthy, so rolling deployments stop and the old instances keep serving.
I also check secrets exist without logging their values, and log the non-sensitive effective config at startup, which helps troubleshooting across environments.
This caught real issues for us, like a missing setting in one environment after a new feature, which otherwise would only have shown up when a scheduled job ran.

p17-766.q: Okay, versioning lets you bring in a new version, but retiring the old one needs a proper process, otherwise you end up maintaining old versions forever.
p17-766.k: api deprecation, sunset header, retire api version, deprecate endpoint, api lifecycle
x: Okay, versioning lets you bring in a new version, but retiring the old one needs a proper process, otherwise you end up maintaining old versions forever.
I announce early. A deprecation notice with the reason, the replacement, a migration guide and a sunset date, giving consumers enough time, often months for external partners.

Then signal it in the API itself. Add the Deprecation header and the Sunset header, RFC 8594, with the retirement date on responses from the old version, plus a Link header pointing to docs. Mark the operations deprecated in the OpenAPI document so generated clients show warnings. Asp.Versioning can report deprecated versions in the api-deprecated-versions header.
Measure usage. Log and dashboard calls to deprecated endpoints by client id. That tells us exactly who still needs to migrate, so we can contact them directly instead of guessing.
Help them migrate, examples, a side-by-side comparison of the old and new contracts, and a test environment where both work.
Brownouts before removal. Temporarily switch off the old version for short planned windows, returning a clear error, so the remaining consumers notice before the final shutdown.
Then retire it. After the sunset date, return 410 Gone with a helpful message for a while, then remove the code.

Internally, for APIs only our own front ends use, it's shorter since we can coordinate releases. But I still check usage logs before removing anything. Trust me, there's often some forgotten report or integration still calling it.

p17-767.q: So ASP.NET Core uses System.Text.Json by default, and its options decide how every request and response gets serialised. I configure them deliberately and consistently.
p17-767.k: json serializer options, camelcase json, ignore null json, reference loop handling, jsonoptions asp.net core
x: So ASP.NET Core uses System.Text.Json by default, and its options decide how every request and response gets serialised. I configure them deliberately and consistently.

Where you set them, for controllers it's AddControllers followed by AddJsonOptions with a lambda. For minimal APIs it's ConfigureHttpJsonOptions. HttpClient calls like GetFromJsonAsync use their own defaults, so shared settings matter there too.
The common settings. Property naming, the web defaults already use camelCase. If a legacy client expects PascalCase, you can set the naming policy to null.
Enums as strings, add JsonStringEnumConverter, so APIs return "Shipped" instead of 2.
Nulls, DefaultIgnoreCondition WhenWritingNull leaves null properties out and shrinks payloads, but some clients prefer explicit nulls, so agree on it.
Cycles, ReferenceHandler IgnoreCycles if entity graphs with back-references get serialised, although the better fix is returning DTOs without cycles.
Numbers, AllowReadingFromString for clients that send numbers as strings.
Unknown properties, .NET 8 added UnmappedMemberHandling to reject unexpected fields, which catches client mistakes.
Custom converters for special types, like DateOnly in older versions, or strongly typed ids. And source generation with JsonSerializerContext for performance and trimming.

The main thing I learned is changing these settings, or switching from Newtonsoft, changes the API contract. Casing, date formats, null handling. So I add contract tests that compare serialised output, to catch unintended changes before the front ends break.

p17-768.q: Okay so, with the ApiController attribute, ASP.NET Core automatically sends back a 400 Bad Request when model binding or validation fails, before your action even runs. The default body is a ValidationProblemDetails object, with a title, a status, a trace id and an errors dictionary mapping each field name to its messages.
p17-768.k: invalidmodelstateresponsefactory, customize validation response, apicontroller automatic 400, validation problem details, model state errors format
x: Okay so, with the ApiController attribute, ASP.NET Core automatically sends back a 400 Bad Request when model binding or validation fails, before your action even runs. The default body is a ValidationProblemDetails object, with a title, a status, a trace id and an errors dictionary mapping each field name to its messages.

Most of the time that default's fine. But teams sometimes need to customise it, to add an application error code, include a correlation id, match an error format the front ends already handle, or log validation failures.

How you customise it. The main hook is InvalidModelStateResponseFactory. You configure ApiBehaviorOptions and set a factory that gets the ActionContext with the ModelState, and returns your own result, like a BadRequestObjectResult wrapping a custom ProblemDetails.
AddProblemDetails with CustomizeProblemDetails lets you add extensions, like the trace id or an error code, to every ProblemDetails response, validation ones included, in one place.

Or you switch the automatic behaviour off with SuppressModelStateInvalidFilter and validate manually or through a filter. That's useful if you run FluentValidation in a MediatR pipeline and want one consistent validation path.
For minimal APIs, .NET 10 adds built-in validation with AddValidation, and before that you'd use endpoint filters that return a validation problem result.

What I aim for is one error format for all errors, validation, business rule or server error, using ProblemDetails, with field-level details the front end can show next to inputs, and stable error codes instead of relying on message text. Front-end folks really appreciate that, in my experience, because they can map codes to messages and stop parsing English sentences.

p17-769.q: YARP, Yet Another Reverse Proxy, is a Microsoft library for building reverse proxies on ASP.NET Core. You configure routes and clusters, usually in appsettings. Routes match incoming requests by path, host, headers or method, and clusters define the destination servers, with load balancing, health checks and session affinity. And because it's just an ASP.NET Core app, you can add any middleware you like, authentication, rate limiting, logging, request and response transforms.
p17-769.k: yarp, yet another reverse proxy, reverse proxy dotnet, yarp gateway, strangler proxy
x: YARP, Yet Another Reverse Proxy, is a Microsoft library for building reverse proxies on ASP.NET Core. You configure routes and clusters, usually in appsettings. Routes match incoming requests by path, host, headers or method, and clusters define the destination servers, with load balancing, health checks and session affinity. And because it's just an ASP.NET Core app, you can add any middleware you like, authentication, rate limiting, logging, request and response transforms.

Where I'd use it. Strangler fig migrations, honestly that's the big one. You put YARP in front of a legacy application and route specific paths, like slash api slash shipments, to a new .NET 8 service, while everything else still goes to the old system. As features move over, you change routes, and clients never notice. That fits moving from ASP.NET MVC 4.8 to ASP.NET Core gradually.

A lightweight API gateway or BFF, central authentication, token handling for SPAs, header transforms and routing to internal services, when a full gateway product is too heavy or just not available on-premise.
Internal routing in containers, or as an edge component, with custom logic off-the-shelf proxies can't easily do.

Compared to Nginx, Envoy or cloud gateways, those are excellent for standard proxying and might be faster or better tied into platform features. YARP shines when a .NET team needs custom C# logic in the proxy and wants familiar tools.
One thing to watch is it becomes critical infrastructure. So it needs high availability, monitoring, timeouts, and careful forwarding of headers like X-Forwarded-For and correlation ids.

p17-770.q: Okay, OData is a standard protocol for queryable REST APIs. Clients add query options to the URL. Dollar filter to filter, like status equals Shipped, dollar select to choose fields, dollar expand to pull in related entities, dollar orderby, dollar top and dollar skip for paging, and dollar count. In ASP.NET Core, the OData package turns those into LINQ on an IQueryable, so with EF Core they become SQL queries.
p17-770.k: odata, odata asp.net core, odata query options, filter select expand, queryable api
x: Okay, OData is a standard protocol for queryable REST APIs. Clients add query options to the URL. Dollar filter to filter, like status equals Shipped, dollar select to choose fields, dollar expand to pull in related entities, dollar orderby, dollar top and dollar skip for paging, and dollar count. In ASP.NET Core, the OData package turns those into LINQ on an IQueryable, so with EF Core they become SQL queries.

The good side, very flexible querying with little code, standard conventions with metadata describing the model, and good support in tools like Excel and Power BI, which can read OData feeds directly. So it's attractive for reporting and data-exploration endpoints.

The risks. Clients can build expensive queries, filtering on non-indexed columns or deep expands, and that hurts the database. Exposing the data model that directly couples clients to it, so changes get harder. Security needs care, so users can't expand or filter into data they shouldn't see. And honestly, the URL syntax is unfamiliar to a lot of front-end developers.

If I use it, I lock it down. Allow only specific properties for filtering and sorting, cap page size with MaxTop and page size settings, limit expand depth, apply authorisation filters before OData's query, and expose DTO projections instead of raw entities.

My view is for internal reporting or admin grids with lots of filter combinations, OData can save a lot of work. For public or core business APIs, I prefer purpose-built endpoints with explicit filters, which are easier to optimise, secure and evolve.

p17-771.q: Model binding decides where each action parameter comes from, and these attributes basically make that explicit.
p17-771.k: frombody fromquery fromroute, binding source attributes, fromservices, fromheader, model binding sources
x: Model binding decides where each action parameter comes from, and these attributes basically make that explicit.
FromRoute is from the URL path template, like the id in shipments slash id.
FromQuery is from the query string, like status equals Shipped and page equals 2. Complex types can bind from several query parameters, which is handy for filter objects.
FromBody is from the request body, deserialised by the input formatter, usually JSON. Only one parameter can bind from the body, because the body stream's read once.
FromForm is form fields and multipart data, IFormFile for uploads included.
FromHeader reads a request header, like X-Correlation-Id, using its Name property.
FromServices injects a service from DI into just that action, useful when only one action needs a dependency.

With ApiController, inference rules kick in. Complex types are assumed to be from the body, simple types matching route parameters come from the route, other simple types from the query, and registered services get inferred as FromServices in newer versions. Minimal APIs have similar inference, plus AsParameters to group parameters into one object.

Common problems I've hit. A complex filter type on a GET wrongly inferred as body, so it needs FromQuery. Content type mismatches, like sending form data to a FromBody parameter, which gives a 415 Unsupported Media Type. And JSON property names that don't match.
So I'm explicit with attributes whenever there's any ambiguity. It documents the API and avoids surprises.

p17-772.q: To test secured endpoints from Swagger UI, the OpenAPI document needs a security scheme, and the UI needs a way to get or enter a token.
p17-772.k: swagger jwt authorization, swagger bearer token, swagger authorize button, swagger in production, openapi security scheme
x: To test secured endpoints from Swagger UI, the OpenAPI document needs a security scheme, and the UI needs a way to get or enter a token.

The simple way is a bearer token. In Swashbuckle you add a security definition called Bearer, with type Http, scheme bearer and format JWT, and a security requirement so operations use it. The UI then shows an Authorize button where you paste a token, and it sends the Authorization Bearer header on each call. With the built-in OpenAPI support in .NET 9, a document transformer adds the security scheme.

The nicer way, for teams using an identity provider like Keycloak or Entra ID, is an OAuth flow. Define an OAuth2 scheme with the authorisation code flow and PKCE, configure Swagger UI with a client id, and users log in through the identity provider straight from the Authorize button. No copying tokens around, and real user roles get used.
An operation filter can mark only endpoints with the Authorize attribute as needing security, and show which scopes or policies they need.

Production? For internal APIs, a lot of teams enable the UI only in lower environments, Development and Test, with an environment check, and keep the OpenAPI JSON available in production behind authentication for client generation. For public partner APIs, a proper developer portal is better than Swagger UI on the live service. If it really has to be in production, protect it with authentication and keep internal or admin endpoints out of the document.
And never put real secrets, like client secrets, into the Swagger config in front-end code. I've seen that happen, and it's an easy leak.

p17-773.q: Writing HTTP client code by hand for every endpoint is repetitive, and it drifts from the real API. Generating clients from the OpenAPI document keeps them in sync with the contract.
p17-773.k: generate api client openapi, nswag, kiota, openapi typescript, typed http client generation
x: Writing HTTP client code by hand for every endpoint is repetitive, and it drifts from the real API. Generating clients from the OpenAPI document keeps them in sync with the contract.

Tools I'd look at. For .NET, NSwag generates C# client classes with a method per operation plus DTO classes. Kiota, from Microsoft, generates clients for lots of languages with a fluent, path-based style. Refit's different, you write an interface with attributes and it generates the implementation.

For TypeScript, openapi-typescript generates types only, which pair nicely with a small fetch wrapper like openapi-fetch. orval and openapi-generator can generate full clients, even React Query or Angular service code.

How I set it up. The API produces its OpenAPI document at build time, for example with the build-time document generation in .NET 9. The client gets generated in CI or as a build step, never edited by hand. And the generated code is versioned, either committed or published as a package, like an internal npm package on our Azure DevOps feed, so front ends depend on a specific API version.
What you get is compile-time errors when the contract changes, no typos in URLs or property names, and way less boilerplate.

Watch-outs. The OpenAPI document has to be accurate, correct nullability, enums and response types, otherwise the generated code is just wrong. Generated clients can be big. And breaking API changes show up as compile errors, which is good, but they still need coordinating.
Put that together with contract tests and you catch integration mistakes really early.

p17-774.q: Right, sometimes an app isn't at the root of a domain, it's under a path like company dot com slash portal, either as an IIS sub-application or behind a reverse proxy that routes slash portal to the app.
p17-774.k: usepathbase, iis sub application, virtual directory aspnet core, app under sub path, path base reverse proxy
x: Right, sometimes an app isn't at the root of a domain, it's under a path like company dot com slash portal, either as an IIS sub-application or behind a reverse proxy that routes slash portal to the app.
The challenge is the app has to generate correct links, redirects, cookie paths and static file URLs with slash portal in them, while routing ignores that prefix.
On IIS with the ASP.NET Core Module, sub-applications are handled for you. IIS passes the path base, Request PathBase gets set, and the URL helpers and redirects include it.

Behind a reverse proxy that forwards the full path, you call UsePathBase with slash portal early in the pipeline. It moves slash portal from Path into PathBase, so routes like slash api slash shipments still match. If the proxy strips the prefix, it should send it in an X-Forwarded-Prefix header, and the forwarded headers middleware can apply it to PathBase.

One thing I always check is cookie paths, so auth cookies are scoped correctly, especially when several apps share a domain. Then OpenID Connect redirect URIs, registered with the full path. Swagger and OpenAPI server URLs. SPA front ends, where the base href in Angular or the base option in Vite for React has to match, otherwise scripts and assets load from the wrong place. And any absolute URLs hardcoded in code or config.

This is a really common setup with on-premise IIS, where several applications share one site, like our MVC host with Angular sub-apps and APIs under different paths. Getting path base right avoids broken links and those annoying login loops.

p17-775.q: These register different sets of MVC services, and picking the right one keeps the app lean.
p17-775.k: addcontrollers vs addmvc, addcontrollerswithviews, addrazorpages, mvc service registration
x: These register different sets of MVC services, and picking the right one keeps the app lean.

AddControllers registers what API controllers need, controller discovery, model binding, validation, formatters, filters, authorisation and CORS integration. No views, no Razor, no tag helpers. That's the right one for Web APIs.

AddControllersWithViews adds view support on top. The Razor view engine, tag helpers, view components, antiforgery for forms, and temp data. You use it for traditional MVC apps that return HTML views.
AddRazorPages registers Razor Pages, the page-based model, and you can combine it with the others.
AddMvc registers everything, controllers, views and Razor Pages. It's mainly there for compatibility with older apps migrated from ASP.NET Core 2, where it was the standard call.

You also need the matching endpoint mapping. MapControllers for attribute-routed API controllers, MapDefaultControllerRoute or MapControllerRoute for conventional MVC routes, and MapRazorPages for pages.

Why does it matter? Registering services you don't need adds a bit of startup time and memory, and switches on features you don't want, like view-related behaviour in a pure API. Also AddControllers doesn't include antiforgery validation for views, so if a migrated app uses forms, you need the views version. That one can catch people out during migrations.
In a migration from ASP.NET MVC 4.8, a hybrid app with both views and APIs would use AddControllersWithViews and map both route styles, while new pure API services use AddControllers or minimal APIs.

p17-776.q: Sometimes clients only need a few fields of a big resource, like a mobile app that wants the shipment id, status and date, not the whole object with items and addresses. Sending everything wastes bandwidth and database work.
p17-776.k: sparse fieldsets, field selection api, partial response, fields query parameter, select fields rest
x: Sometimes clients only need a few fields of a big resource, like a mobile app that wants the shipment id, status and date, not the whole object with items and addresses. Sending everything wastes bandwidth and database work.

You've got a few choices. A fields query parameter, like get shipments with fields equals id, status, shipped-at. The API returns only those. To implement it, validate the requested fields against an allowlist, then either build a dynamic projection, a Select expression built from the field list, so the database only fetches those columns, or fetch a normal DTO and shape the output by serialising just the selected properties into a dictionary or JsonObject. JSON:API standardises this with a fields parameter per resource type.

Predefined views. Instead of arbitrary fields, offer a few named shapes, view equals summary or view equals detail, or separate endpoints like shipments slash summary. Easier to optimise, cache and document, and usually enough.
Expansion the other way round, return a lean resource by default and let clients ask for related data with expand equals items and site.
And GraphQL, if lots of clients need lots of different shapes. It's built for exactly this.

What you pay for arbitrary field selection is harder caching, since every combination's a different response, messier OpenAPI docs, and careful security so clients can't select fields they shouldn't see.

What I do usually is predefined summary and detail shapes, because they cover most needs and performance stays predictable. I'd add field selection only with a clear, measured need, like big payloads hurting a mobile or partner client.

p17-777.q: ASP.NET Core uses output formatters to serialise action results based on content negotiation. JSON's the default, but you can add formatters for other media types, like CSV, so a client sending an Accept header of text slash csv gets CSV from the same endpoint.
p17-777.k: custom output formatter, csv output formatter, textoutputformatter, return csv from api, custom media type
x: ASP.NET Core uses output formatters to serialise action results based on content negotiation. JSON's the default, but you can add formatters for other media types, like CSV, so a client sending an Accept header of text slash csv gets CSV from the same endpoint.

To write one, you create a class inheriting TextOutputFormatter. In the constructor, add the supported media types, text slash csv, and encodings, UTF-8. Override CanWriteType to say which types it handles, say an IEnumerable of some DTO. Override WriteResponseBodyAsync to write the data, a header row and then each item's values, escaping commas, quotes and newlines properly, writing to the response body asynchronously. Then register it in AddControllers by adding a new CSV output formatter to the output formatters list. Optionally add a format mapping so a format equals csv query, or a dot csv extension, works through the FormatFilter.
Things to watch. Use a proper CSV library like CsvHelper for escaping and culture-safe numbers and dates, not string concatenation. I learned that the hard way with decimal commas.
Large data, stream rows instead of building everything in memory, ideally from an IAsyncEnumerable, so big exports don't eat memory.
Security, CSV injection, where values starting with equals, plus, minus or at are treated as formulas when someone opens the file in Excel. Prefix or escape them for user-provided data.
Set Content-Disposition with a file name so browsers download it.
And for really large or slow exports, I'd generate the file in a background job and return a download link, instead of formatting it inside the request.

p17-778.q: Every HTTP request has a Host header saying which host name the client wants. Apps often use it to build absolute URLs, links in password reset emails, redirect URLs, callback URLs. If the app trusts any Host header, an attacker can send a request with the host set to evil dot com, and the app might generate links pointing to the attacker's site. Think of a password reset email whose link sends the token to the attacker, or caches poisoned with wrong URLs.
p17-778.k: allowedhosts, host filtering middleware, host header attack, host header injection, allowed hosts configuration
x: Every HTTP request has a Host header saying which host name the client wants. Apps often use it to build absolute URLs, links in password reset emails, redirect URLs, callback URLs. If the app trusts any Host header, an attacker can send a request with the host set to evil dot com, and the app might generate links pointing to the attacker's site. Think of a password reset email whose link sends the token to the attacker, or caches poisoned with wrong URLs.

ASP.NET Core's host filtering middleware checks the Host header against the AllowedHosts setting. The default template sets AllowedHosts to star, which allows anything. Convenient for development, not great in production. Set it to specific names, like app dot example dot com and api dot example dot com separated by a semicolon, and the app rejects other hosts with a 400 Bad Request.

When the app's behind a reverse proxy or load balancer, the forwarded headers middleware might replace the host with X-Forwarded-Host. So configure KnownProxies, KnownNetworks and AllowedHosts on the forwarded headers options too, so spoofed forwarded headers aren't trusted.
Even better, don't build security-sensitive URLs from the incoming request at all. Use a configured public base URL for emails and callbacks. That's my preferred fix, honestly.
Kestrel doesn't validate host headers by itself, and IIS bindings only partly protect you if a site binding accepts all hosts.
It's a small config change that closes a real class of attacks, so I include it in production readiness checks.

The JIT compiles code on first use, DI builds services, EF Core builds its model and compiles queries, connection pools are empty, caches are cold, and HttpClient connections and TLS handshakes are all new. Whoever hits the app first sees seconds of delay.
