That's the easiest fix for sync code, and a lot of people don't realise it.
For CPU-heavy work, threads don't help much because of the GIL, so use a ProcessPoolExecutor, or better, a background task queue like Celery, so the API stays responsive.

Detecting it, turn on asyncio debug mode, which logs callbacks that take longer than a threshold, watch for latency rising across all endpoints whenever one slow operation runs, and profile with py-spy.

The rule I follow, async def endpoints only call async I/O, and anything sync goes through to_thread or a sync endpoint. Mixing them carelessly is the most common cause of mysterious slowness in FastAPI services.

p17-875.q: To run several async operations at once, like calling three APIs in parallel, Python gives you a few tools.
p17-875.k: asyncio gather, taskgroup python, asyncio concurrency, asyncio timeout, structured concurrency python
x: To run several async operations at once, like calling three APIs in parallel, Python gives you a few tools.

asyncio gather, with a, b and c, runs the coroutines concurrently and returns their results in order. By default, if one raises, gather raises it, but the other tasks keep running in the background, which can leave work orphaned. With return_exceptions set to true, exceptions come back as results instead, so you can check each one.

TaskGroup, from Python 3.11, is structured concurrency. You write async with asyncio TaskGroup as tg, and inside it create tasks with tg create_task for a and for b. When the block exits, all the tasks are finished. If any task fails, the others get cancelled and the errors are raised together as an ExceptionGroup, which you handle with except-star. No orphaned tasks, so that's my default for new code. It's a lot like Task WhenAll in C#, but with automatic cancellation.
Timeouts, asyncio timeout of five seconds as an async context manager since 3.11, or wait_for for a single awaitable. Every external call should have one.

Limiting concurrency, when you're processing hundreds of items, don't start them all at once. Use an asyncio Semaphore inside each task, or process in batches, to protect downstream services and connection pools.
as_completed processes results as they finish, which is useful for showing progress.

Common mistakes I've seen, calling a coroutine without awaiting it, which means it never runs, creating tasks with create_task and not keeping a reference, so they can get garbage collected, and mixing blocking calls into async code, which serialises everything.

p17-876.q: So both are DataFrame libraries for tabular data, used for analysis, ETL, reports and preparing data for things like RAG ingestion or exports.
p17-876.k: pandas vs polars, polars python, dataframe performance, python etl, pandas performance tips
x: So both are DataFrame libraries for tabular data, used for analysis, ETL, reports and preparing data for things like RAG ingestion or exports.

pandas is the long-established standard. Huge ecosystem, integrations everywhere, and most data people know it. But it's mostly single-threaded and eager, it can eat a lot of memory, and some of its APIs are a bit inconsistent.

Polars is newer, written in Rust, and built for performance. It uses all the CPU cores, has a lazy API that builds a query plan and optimises it, pushing filters down and reading only the columns it needs, and it uses Apache Arrow memory, which is efficient. It's often much faster than pandas with lower memory, and the expression API is consistent.

How I choose, for new pipelines, especially with big files, Polars is a strong choice. For existing code, or when a library expects pandas, stay with pandas. Converting between them through Arrow is easy anyway.

Some performance tips apply to both. Vectorise, use column operations instead of Python loops or apply with a lambda row by row, which is really slow. I've seen jobs go from minutes to seconds just by fixing that.
Read only what you need. Select columns and filter early, use efficient formats like Parquet instead of CSV for intermediate data, and specify data types, like categories for repeated strings.
Process in chunks, or with lazy streaming, when the data's bigger than memory.
Push heavy filtering and aggregation down to the database with SQL when the data lives there, instead of loading everything into a DataFrame.
And for very large or distributed workloads, tools like DuckDB, which runs SQL directly on files, or Spark come into the picture.

p17-877.q: For RabbitMQ in Python the main libraries are pika, which is synchronous, and aio-pika, which is asyncio-based and fits FastAPI or other async services. For Kafka, confluent-kafka, which wraps the fast librdkafka C library, or aiokafka for asyncio.
p17-877.k: python rabbitmq consumer, aio-pika, pika, confluent kafka python, python message consumer
x: For RabbitMQ in Python the main libraries are pika, which is synchronous, and aio-pika, which is asyncio-based and fits FastAPI or other async services. For Kafka, confluent-kafka, which wraps the fast librdkafka C library, or aiokafka for asyncio.
Honestly the reliability rules are the same as in .NET and Node.

Manual acknowledgement after processing. With aio-pika you use the message process context manager, which acks on success and rejects on an exception, or you ack explicitly. In Kafka, turn off auto-commit and commit offsets after processing.
Prefetch, set_qos with a prefetch count to limit in-flight messages per consumer.
Retries and dead-lettering. Reject without requeue to send failures to a dead-letter exchange, use retry queues with TTLs for delayed retries, and track a max attempt count in the headers.
Idempotency, store processed message ids, because redelivery does happen.
Validation, parse message bodies with Pydantic models and dead-letter invalid ones straight away.
Connection resilience, aio-pika's connect_robust reconnects and restores channels automatically after network blips.
Concurrency, in asyncio you process messages concurrently up to the prefetch limit. For CPU-heavy processing, use separate processes, since the GIL limits threads.
Graceful shutdown, handle SIGTERM, stop consuming, finish in-flight messages, then close the connection.
Observability, structured logs with message and correlation ids, OpenTelemetry context propagated through message headers, and metrics for processing time and failures.
Celery's another option for task-style work over RabbitMQ or Redis, but for consuming domain events from other services, I'd go with a plain consumer because it gives more control.

p17-878.q: Python's standard library saves you a lot of code if you know it well. The ones I reach for most.
p17-878.k: python standard library, itertools, collections module, functools, pathlib python
x: Python's standard library saves you a lot of code if you know it well. The ones I reach for most.

collections. defaultdict for grouping without checking keys, like grouping shipments by site. Counter for counting and most_common. deque for queues and sliding windows. And namedtuple for lightweight records, though I mostly use dataclasses now.

itertools. chain to loop over several sequences as one, islice to take part of an iterator, groupby for consecutive grouping, after sorting, product and combinations, and batched, from 3.12, to split an iterable into chunks. That one's really handy for batching database inserts or API calls.

functools. lru_cache and cache to memoise pure functions, partial to pre-fill arguments, wraps for decorators that keep the wrapped function's name and docstring, reduce now and then, and cached_property.
pathlib, object-oriented paths, like Path of data slash file dot csv, reading and writing text, globbing. Cleaner and safer than string paths with os path.
datetime and zoneinfo for timezone-aware dates, with zoneinfo giving IANA time zones since 3.9.
json, csv and logging for everyday I/O and logs. dataclasses and enum for clear data and constants.
contextlib, contextmanager to write context managers with a generator, and suppress to ignore specific exceptions.
concurrent futures for thread and process pools, and subprocess for running commands safely with argument lists.
secrets for secure random tokens, and hashlib for hashing.
Knowing these, I mean, avoids extra dependencies, which also cuts supply chain risk.

p17-879.q: Python has caching at a few different levels.
p17-879.k: python caching, lru_cache, functools cache, redis python cache, cachetools ttl
x: Python has caching at a few different levels.

In-process with functools. Put lru_cache with a max size of, say, 1024 on a function and it memoises results based on the arguments, evicting the least recently used entries. cache is the unbounded version. Good for pure functions with hashable arguments, parsing config, expensive calculations, loading reference data that never changes. The limits, no expiry, arguments have to be hashable, it's per process so each worker has its own copy, and on methods it can keep instances alive. It also doesn't work on async functions directly, because it'd cache the coroutine object. That one catches people out. Libraries like async-lru handle it.
With expiry, cachetools gives you TTLCache and LRUCache classes with time-based expiry, for data that changes now and then.

Shared cache with Redis. When several processes or instances need the same cache, or the data should survive restarts, use Redis with redis-py, which has an asyncio interface too. The usual cache-aside pattern, try Redis, on a miss load from the source, then set it with an expiry. Serialise with JSON or orjson. Pydantic models can be dumped to JSON and validated on the way back.

Good practices, versions and identifiers in keys, jitter on expiries, stampede protection with a short lock or request coalescing, Redis timeouts with a fallback to the source if Redis is down, and measuring hit ratios.
In our RAG service, caching embeddings for repeated queries and caching document metadata are typical places where this saves time and model cost.

p17-880.q: Okay, when several Python services share code, like logging setup, auth helpers or API clients, an internal package stops you copying code between repos.
p17-880.k: private python package, internal pypi, azure artifacts python, publish python package, pyproject build twine
x: Okay, when several Python services share code, like logging setup, auth helpers or API clients, an internal package stops you copying code between repos.

Packaging. Define the package in pyproject dot toml with a name, version, dependencies and a build backend like hatchling or setuptools. Use a src layout, so tests run against the installed package and not local files by accident. Build with python dash m build or uv build, which gives you a wheel and a source distribution.
Versioning, semantic versioning, with the version coming from Git tags in CI through something like hatch-vcs or setuptools-scm, so nobody edits versions by hand.

Publishing to a private feed. Azure Artifacts supports Python feeds, so do AWS CodeArtifact, GitHub Packages and JFrog. In the pipeline, authenticate with the platform's mechanism, like the Twine authenticate task in Azure Pipelines or a short-lived CodeArtifact token, and upload with twine or uv publish. No personal credentials in scripts.

Consuming, configure pip or uv with the feed as an index URL, using a keyring or environment-based credentials in CI and on developer machines. Be careful mixing public and private indexes, because of dependency confusion attacks. Use a feed that proxies PyPI as an upstream source, and give internal packages a unique name prefix, so a public package with the same name can't get installed by mistake.
Quality, the package has its own tests, type hints with a py typed marker so consumers get type checking, a changelog, and dependency ranges that aren't too strict.
Honestly it's the same discipline we use for npm feature packages and NuGet packages on our Azure DevOps feed.

p17-881.q: Recent Python releases have been really focused on performance and developer experience.
p17-881.k: python 3.13 features, python 3.12 features, free threading python, no gil python, python jit
x: Recent Python releases have been really focused on performance and developer experience.
Faster CPython. Since 3.11 the interpreter's become a lot faster, often 10 to 60 percent over 3.10, through specialising adaptive interpretation. Just upgrading gives you a noticeable speed-up.

Free-threaded Python. 3.13 brought an experimental build without the GIL, and 3.14 made it officially supported, though still optional. Threads can run Python code truly in parallel across cores, which helps CPU-bound multi-threaded work. The catch is single-threaded code can be a bit slower, and C extensions have to be updated to be thread-safe, so ecosystem support is still maturing.
An experimental JIT compiler, a copy-and-patch JIT added in 3.13, off by default, laying groundwork for future speed-ups.
Better error messages, clearer suggestions like "did you mean", and precise locations in tracebacks. Honestly that one makes day-to-day debugging nicer.

Language features, exception groups and except-star in 3.11, the type statement and new generic syntax in 3.12, where a function can declare its type parameter T right after its name, f-string improvements in 3.12, template strings in 3.14, and deferred evaluation of annotations.
Standard library, tomllib for reading TOML in 3.11, asyncio TaskGroup and timeout, itertools batched in 3.12, and a much better interactive shell in 3.13.

My practical approach is run services on a recent supported version, upgrade yearly once dependencies support it, and test performance-sensitive services on the new version, since the speed gains often come for free.

p17-882.q: Python's a natural fit for Lambda, quick cold starts and a simple handler model. You write a handler function that takes the event and the context and returns a response.
p17-882.k: python lambda, aws lambda python, lambda powertools python, package python lambda dependencies, lambda layers python
x: Python's a natural fit for Lambda, quick cold starts and a simple handler model. You write a handler function that takes the event and the context and returns a response.

Structure, initialise clients like boto3 clients and config at module level, so they're reused across warm invocations. Keep the handler thin. Parse the event, call business logic in separate functions or modules, return the result. That way the logic's testable without Lambda.

Packaging dependencies. For pure-Python packages, a zip file with the dependencies installed into the package folder is enough. For packages with compiled parts, like pydantic-core, cryptography or numpy, they have to be built for Amazon Linux and the right architecture, x86 or arm64. So build in a matching container, or use the right platform flags with pip. This can bite people badly, it works locally and fails in Lambda. Big dependencies can go in layers shared across functions, or use a container image, up to 10 GB, for heavy data or ML libraries.

Tools, AWS SAM or CDK to define and deploy functions, with sam build handling dependency packaging. And Powertools for AWS Lambda for structured logging, metrics, tracing, event parsing with Pydantic, idempotency, and batch helpers for partial SQS failures.
Performance, more memory gets you more CPU, arm64 Graviton gives better price-performance, avoid importing heavy libraries you don't need, and use SnapStart for Python if cold starts matter.
Testing, unit-test business logic directly, test handlers with sample events, and use moto to mock AWS services, or LocalStack for integration-style tests.
Security, least-privilege execution roles, and secrets from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, not plain-text environment variables.

p17-883.q: Right, Python's datetime objects are either naive, with no time zone info, or aware, with a tzinfo attached. Mixing them causes errors, like not being able to compare naive and aware values, and naive values cause silent bugs when code assumes a time zone that just isn't there.
p17-883.k: python timezone, naive vs aware datetime, zoneinfo python, utc python datetime, datetime pitfalls python
x: Right, Python's datetime objects are either naive, with no time zone info, or aware, with a tzinfo attached. Mixing them causes errors, like not being able to compare naive and aware values, and naive values cause silent bugs when code assumes a time zone that just isn't there.
My rules. Use aware datetimes in UTC internally. datetime now with timezone utc, not utcnow, which returns a naive value and is deprecated, and not plain now, which gives local server time.
Store UTC in databases, in timestamp with time zone columns in Postgres, or as UTC with a clear naming convention in SQL Server.

Convert to the user's or site's local time only for display, or for business rules that depend on local time, using zoneinfo with IANA names, like Asia slash Kolkata, which handles daylight saving properly. Never use fixed offsets for regions that switch for daylight saving.
Use date, not datetime, for business dates without a time, like a visit date or date of birth. That avoids off-by-one-day bugs when converting between zones.
Parse and format with ISO 8601. fromisoformat handles most ISO strings since 3.11, and APIs should exchange ISO strings with offsets or a trailing Z. Pydantic parses those automatically.
Arithmetic across daylight saving changes, adding 24 hours isn't always "the same time tomorrow" in local time, so for schedules compute in local time and then convert.
Testing, use freezegun or time-machine to control the current time, and test around midnight and daylight saving changes. That's where the bugs hide.
These are the same principles I follow in .NET with DateTimeOffset and DateOnly.

p17-884.q: When a consumer calls ReceiveMessage, SQS can respond two ways.
p17-884.k: sqs long polling, receive message wait time, sqs short polling, sqs message size limit, sqs extended client
x: When a consumer calls ReceiveMessage, SQS can respond two ways.

Short polling returns immediately and only checks a subset of SQS servers, so it can return nothing even when messages exist. And an idle consumer makes constant empty calls, which costs money, because SQS bills per request.

Long polling waits up to 20 seconds for messages to arrive before responding, and checks all the servers. You set the wait time seconds on the receive call, or the receive message wait time on the queue, to 20. It cuts empty responses, cost, and pickup latency. I use it by default for every consumer, and Lambda's SQS integration already uses it.
Batching, receive up to 10 messages per call with the max number of messages setting, and delete them in batches too, which cuts the request count further.

Message size. SQS messages are limited to 256 KB, recently raised to 1 MB. For bigger payloads, it's the claim-check pattern. Store the payload in S3 and send a message with a reference to it. The SQS Extended Client Library does that automatically for Java and Python, and there are equivalents for .NET. Consumers fetch the object from S3, and a lifecycle rule cleans up old payloads.
Even under the limit, I keep messages small, ids and essential data, because smaller messages are cheaper and faster, and you don't put sensitive data into queues for no reason.

Other settings that go with it, a visibility timeout longer than your processing time, a dead-letter queue with a sensible max receive count, and monitoring the age of the oldest message to catch consumers falling behind. That metric's saved us a few times, I think.

p17-885.q: Multipart upload splits a big object into parts that get uploaded independently and in parallel, and then S3 combines them. You get faster uploads through parallelism, you only retry failed parts instead of the whole file, and you can upload objects up to 5 TB. AWS recommends it over 100 MB, and it's required above 5 GB for a single PUT. The SDKs do it automatically, the TransferUtility in .NET or the Upload helper in JavaScript.
p17-885.k: s3 multipart upload, s3 performance, s3 transfer acceleration, s3 request rate, s3 large file upload
x: Multipart upload splits a big object into parts that get uploaded independently and in parallel, and then S3 combines them. You get faster uploads through parallelism, you only retry failed parts instead of the whole file, and you can upload objects up to 5 TB. AWS recommends it over 100 MB, and it's required above 5 GB for a single PUT. The SDKs do it automatically, the TransferUtility in .NET or the Upload helper in JavaScript.

The hidden cost is incomplete multipart uploads keep their parts stored, and billed, forever, unless you clean them up. So I always add a lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads after a few days. People miss that one and then wonder about the bill.
Browser uploads, the backend can start a multipart upload and return pre-signed URLs per part, so big files go straight from the browser to S3 in parallel.

Performance tips. Request rates, S3 handles at least 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second per prefix and scales automatically, so spreading keys across prefixes allows more throughput for really heavy workloads.
Parallel downloads too, byte-range fetches pull parts of a large object in parallel.
Transfer Acceleration uses CloudFront edge locations for faster long-distance uploads, say from users on other continents, at extra cost.
Same region, keep compute and buckets in the same region to avoid latency and transfer charges, and use a VPC gateway endpoint for S3 so traffic doesn't go through NAT gateways, which saves money.
And CloudFront in front of S3 for content that's read a lot.

p17-886.q: Access to S3 is decided by several layers, and basically an action's allowed only if something allows it and nothing denies it.
p17-886.k: s3 bucket policy, s3 block public access, s3 acl, s3 permissions, bucket policy vs iam policy
x: Access to S3 is decided by several layers, and basically an action's allowed only if something allows it and nothing denies it.
IAM policies are attached to users and roles and say what that identity can do, like get-object on a bucket's objects. That's the normal way to give your own applications access.

Bucket policies are resource-based policies on the bucket itself, saying who can do what to it. You need them for cross-account access, for granting AWS services access, like CloudFront through origin access control, and for enforcing rules on everyone, like denying requests that don't use TLS, requiring encryption, or allowing access only from a specific VPC endpoint.
ACLs are the old mechanism. AWS now recommends disabling them by setting object ownership to bucket owner enforced, which is the default for new buckets.

Block Public Access is a safety net at the account and bucket level. When it's on, it overrides any policy or ACL that would make data public. I keep it on at the account level and only turn it off for buckets that genuinely have to be public, which is rare, because CloudFront with origin access control serves public content without a public bucket.
Encryption, if objects use SSE-KMS, the caller also needs permission on the KMS key. That's a really common cause of AccessDenied surprises.

Good practices, least privilege with specific actions and prefixes, deny insecure transport, enable server access logging or CloudTrail data events for sensitive buckets, and use IAM Access Analyzer to spot buckets shared outside the account.

p17-887.q: CloudFront caches responses at edge locations, and cache behaviours and policies control what's cached, for how long and under which key.
p17-887.k: cloudfront cache policy, cloudfront invalidation, cache key cloudfront, cloudfront ttl, cdn caching aws
x: CloudFront caches responses at edge locations, and cache behaviours and policies control what's cached, for how long and under which key.
Cache behaviours match path patterns, like slash assets slash star or slash api slash star, each with its own origin and policies, so static files and API calls get treated differently.

The cache policy defines the cache key, which headers, cookies and query strings make a response unique, plus minimum, default and maximum TTLs. A smaller cache key means more cache hits. Include only what actually changes the response, so for static assets don't include all the cookies.
The origin request policy defines what gets forwarded to the origin without being part of the cache key, like a header the origin needs that doesn't change the response.
TTLs, the origin's Cache-Control headers set the time, bounded by the policy's min and max.

Invalidation removes objects from edge caches before they expire, using paths like slash index dot html or slash star. The first 1,000 paths a month are free, then they cost, and they take a little while to finish.

My approach for SPAs avoids frequent invalidation. Hashed file names for JavaScript and CSS, like main dot some-hash dot js, cached for a year, because every new build produces new names. And index dot html with no-cache or a very short TTL, so users get the new version right after a deployment. Then one small invalidation of index dot html, or none at all, is enough.
For APIs, I'd say caching's usually disabled with the managed caching-disabled policy, or there's short caching only for public, non-personalised GET responses.

p17-888.q: So Amazon Cognito has two parts, and people mix them up all the time.
p17-888.k: cognito user pool vs identity pool, amazon cognito, cognito federated identities, cognito jwt, cognito hosted ui
x: So Amazon Cognito has two parts, and people mix them up all the time.

User pools are a user directory and an OpenID Connect identity provider. They handle sign-up, sign-in, password policies, MFA, account recovery, and federation with external providers like Entra ID, Google or SAML providers. After login, users get JWTs, an ID token, an access token and a refresh token. APIs validate those tokens, like with a JWT authorizer in API Gateway, or JWT bearer authentication in ASP.NET Core using the user pool's issuer and JWKS. Cognito gives you a hosted login UI, now called managed login, or you can build your own UI with the SDK.

Identity pools, or federated identities, take a token from a user pool or another identity provider and exchange it for temporary AWS credentials, through IAM roles. That lets a client app, say a mobile app, call AWS services directly, upload to S3 or read DynamoDB, with permissions scoped per user, without a backend in between. They can also give limited guest access.
The simple way I put it, user pools answer "who is this user?" and issue app tokens, identity pools answer "which AWS permissions does this user get?"
Most web apps with their own backend only need a user pool. Identity pools are useful when the front end talks straight to AWS services.

Things to think about, Cognito's customisation and some features are more limited than full identity products like Keycloak or Entra ID. And migrating users out later can be hard, because password hashes can't be exported. So for a large system the choice really deserves some thought up front.

p17-889.q: Basically in ECS, tasks start and stop with changing IP addresses, so services need a way to find each other without hard-coded addresses.
p17-889.k: ecs service connect, aws cloud map, ecs service discovery, service to service ecs, ecs internal dns
x: Basically in ECS, tasks start and stop with changing IP addresses, so services need a way to find each other without hard-coded addresses.

You've got a few choices. An internal load balancer, put an internal ALB in front of each service and call it by DNS name. Simple, gives you health checks and load balancing, but it adds cost per load balancer and an extra network hop.

Cloud Map service discovery. ECS registers each task's IP in AWS Cloud Map, which creates DNS records, like orders dot internal dot local, in a private hosted zone. Callers resolve the name and get task IPs. No load balancer, but clients have to deal with DNS caching and picking healthy instances, and there's no built-in retry or metrics.

ECS Service Connect is the newer, recommended approach. ECS injects a managed Envoy proxy sidecar into each task. Services get simple names, like http colon orders on port 8080, and the proxy does load balancing across healthy tasks, retries and outlier detection, and publishes traffic metrics, request counts, latency, errors, to CloudWatch for each service, without code changes. It's built on Cloud Map namespaces underneath.

How I'd choose, Service Connect for service-to-service calls inside ECS, an ALB for traffic coming from outside or from other platforms, and for complex cross-platform meshes a full service mesh, though that adds a lot of operational complexity.

Whatever the discovery method, the calling code still needs timeouts, retries with backoff for idempotent calls and circuit breakers, and it has to propagate correlation and trace context, so requests can be followed across services in IQVIA's newer AWS services.

p17-890.q: Sometimes you need to look inside a running container, check files, environment, DNS resolution or connectivity to a database, especially on Fargate where there's no host to SSH into. That's what ECS Exec is for.
p17-890.k: ecs exec, execute command ecs, shell into fargate container, debug ecs task, ssm ecs exec
x: Sometimes you need to look inside a running container, check files, environment, DNS resolution or connectivity to a database, especially on Fargate where there's no host to SSH into. That's what ECS Exec is for.

How it works, it uses Systems Manager Session Manager. When you enable it on the service or task, ECS adds an SSM agent to the task. Then you run the aws ecs execute-command with the cluster, task, container and a command like bin slash sh, with the interactive flag, and you get a shell or run a single command. No inbound ports, no SSH keys, no bastion host.

Requirements, enable execute command on the service, give the task role permissions for SSM messages, make sure the task can reach the SSM endpoints, through a NAT gateway or VPC interface endpoints, and install the Session Manager plugin locally. If the image has no shell, like distroless or chiseled images, you can only run binaries that exist in the image, so you need other debugging approaches. That one surprises people the first time.

Security and audit, access is controlled by IAM, so only specific roles can execute commands, ideally only in non-production, or through a break-glass process in production. Sessions can be logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3 and they're recorded in CloudTrail, which matters in regulated environments.

My rule is use it for investigation, not for fixing things by hand. Changes inside a container are lost on restart and they create drift. Once I find the problem, the fix goes through code or config and a normal deployment.
It's basically the AWS equivalent of kubectl exec in Kubernetes.

p17-891.q: There are two main ways to send custom metrics, like orders processed or job duration, to CloudWatch.
p17-891.k: cloudwatch embedded metric format, emf, cloudwatch custom metrics, putmetricdata, metrics from logs aws
x: There are two main ways to send custom metrics, like orders processed or job duration, to CloudWatch.

The PutMetricData API, where the application calls CloudWatch directly. It works, but every call is a network request with latency and cost, and you need batching and error handling, which is awkward in Lambda.

Embedded Metric Format, EMF. The application writes a structured JSON log line with a special aws section describing which fields are metrics, their units and dimensions. CloudWatch Logs extracts the metrics from those log events automatically and asynchronously. No extra API calls, no latency added to the request, and the same log line carries high-cardinality context, like request id or study id, which you can query in Logs Insights without making them metric dimensions. Honestly it's a really neat trick.

To use it, Powertools for AWS Lambda, for .NET, Python and TypeScript, has a Metrics utility that writes EMF. The aws-embedded-metrics libraries do it for other workloads. On ECS, logs go to CloudWatch through the awslogs driver or the CloudWatch agent, which handles EMF too.

Dimensions and cost, each unique combination of metric name and dimension values is a separate custom metric, billed monthly. So keep dimensions low-cardinality, service, environment, operation, never user ids or request ids. That's where the bill can blow up.

If the organisation uses OpenTelemetry and a vendor like Datadog, metrics go through the OpenTelemetry SDK and collector instead, which keeps the code vendor-neutral. EMF is the simplest choice when CloudWatch is the main monitoring tool.

p17-892.q: AWS describes four disaster recovery strategies, and basically each one trades cost against recovery time, the RTO, and data loss, the RPO.
p17-892.k: aws disaster recovery strategies, pilot light, warm standby, multi site active active, rto rpo aws
x: AWS describes four disaster recovery strategies, and basically each one trades cost against recovery time, the RTO, and data loss, the RPO.

Backup and restore. Regularly back up data, with AWS Backup, snapshots and S3 cross-region replication, and keep the infrastructure as code. In a disaster, recreate the infrastructure in another region and restore the data. Cheapest, but RTO is hours and RPO depends on how often you back up.

Pilot light. Core data's continuously replicated to the recovery region, like an Aurora global database or a cross-region read replica, while compute is off or minimal. In a disaster, you scale up compute from templates and switch traffic. RTO in tens of minutes.
Warm standby. A scaled-down but fully working copy runs in the recovery region, with data replicated. It can serve traffic right after scaling up. RTO in minutes, higher cost.

Multi-site active-active. Full capacity in two or more regions, both serving traffic, with Route 53 or Global Accelerator routing users. Near-zero RTO, but the highest cost and complexity, especially with data conflicts between regions.

How to choose, start from the business. How long can the system be down, and how much data can you lose? Clinical systems that sites use to randomise patients need short RTO and near-zero RPO for transactional data, while reporting systems can tolerate more.

What makes any strategy actually work, everything as code so environments can be rebuilt, automated and tested runbooks, regular DR drills, including failing back, monitoring replication lag, and remembering dependencies like DNS, certificates, secrets and third-party allow-lists in the recovery region. People forget the allow-lists, from what I've seen.

p17-893.q: Okay, an Auto Scaling group manages a fleet of EC2 instances. It keeps the desired number running, replaces unhealthy ones, spreads them across Availability Zones, and scales in and out.
p17-893.k: auto scaling group, launch template, ec2 auto scaling, scaling policies ec2, instance refresh
x: Okay, an Auto Scaling group manages a fleet of EC2 instances. It keeps the desired number running, replaces unhealthy ones, spreads them across Availability Zones, and scales in and out.

A launch template defines how each instance is created, the AMI, instance type, security groups, IAM instance profile, a user data script for bootstrapping, storage and tags. Templates are versioned, so you can roll out changes and roll back.

Scaling policies. Target tracking keeps a metric at a target, like average CPU at 50 percent or ALB requests per target at 1,000. That's the simplest and usually the best choice. Step scaling adds or removes instances in steps based on alarm thresholds. Scheduled scaling handles known patterns, like scaling up before business hours. And predictive scaling uses history to scale ahead of expected load.
Health checks, use ELB health checks, not just EC2 status checks, so instances that are running but whose app is broken actually get replaced. That one catches people out.
Deployments, instance refresh replaces instances gradually with a new launch template version, respecting a minimum healthy percentage, with checkpoints and automatic rollback on failure.

Other useful features, lifecycle hooks to run actions when instances launch or terminate, like draining work or copying logs, warm pools of pre-initialised instances for faster scaling, and mixed instance policies combining On-Demand and Spot across several instance types to cut cost.
For a Windows and IIS-based application moved to AWS as-is, an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB with a golden AMI is a reasonable first step, before containerising.

p17-894.q: Amazon SES is AWS's email sending service, used for transactional email like notifications, password resets and reports.
p17-894.k: amazon ses, send email aws, ses dkim spf, ses bounce handling, ses sandbox
x: Amazon SES is AWS's email sending service, used for transactional email like notifications, password resets and reports.

Setup first. Verify the sending domain, and configure DKIM, with the records SES gives you, SPF, and DMARC in DNS. Those prove emails really come from your domain, which is critical for deliverability and staying out of spam folders. A custom MAIL FROM domain aligns SPF properly.
Get out of the sandbox. New accounts can only send to verified addresses with low limits, so you request production access, explaining your use case and how you handle bounces and complaints.

Sending, from .NET I'd use the AWS SDK's SES v2 client with the application's IAM role, or the SMTP interface for existing code that already uses SMTP. Use templates for consistent content, and configuration sets to group sending and track events.

One thing people miss is bounces and complaints. Subscribe to bounce, complaint and delivery events through SNS or EventBridge, process them, and stop sending to addresses that hard bounce or complain. Account-level suppression lists help. High bounce or complaint rates can get the account paused, so this isn't optional.
Reliability, send email asynchronously through a queue, so a slow or failing email call doesn't fail the business transaction, with retries and idempotency so people don't get duplicates.

Security and compliance, keep sensitive data out of email bodies and send links to the secure application instead, and use dedicated IPs or separate configuration sets for different kinds of email if volumes justify it.
And monitoring, delivery, bounce and complaint rates on a dashboard, with alarms.

p17-895.q: AWS AppConfig, part of Systems Manager, manages application configuration and feature flags that change at runtime without redeploying code.
p17-895.k: aws appconfig, appconfig feature flags, dynamic configuration aws, appconfig deployment strategy, appconfig agent
x: AWS AppConfig, part of Systems Manager, manages application configuration and feature flags that change at runtime without redeploying code.
What it adds over keeping config in Parameter Store or files. Validation, configurations can have JSON schema or Lambda validators, so an invalid change gets rejected before it's deployed.
Controlled deployments, changes roll out gradually using deployment strategies, like 10 percent of targets every few minutes, with a bake time.

Automatic rollback, tied to CloudWatch alarms. If error rates go up during a config rollout, AppConfig rolls the change back by itself. That's really valuable, because bad config changes cause a lot of outages. I've seen that happen more than bad code, honestly.
Feature flags, a dedicated flag type with on and off flags, attributes, and multi-variant flags for targeting.

How apps read it, the AppConfig Agent, as a Lambda extension, an ECS sidecar or a local process, polls for changes and caches the config, and the app reads it from a local HTTP endpoint, which is fast and cheap. Or use the SDK's configuration data API with session tokens. Apps should cache values and refresh periodically, not call AppConfig on every request.
In .NET, a configuration provider can load AppConfig data into IConfiguration, and IOptionsMonitor picks up the changes.

Compared with Azure, it's similar to Azure App Configuration with its feature manager. Compared with dedicated tools like LaunchDarkly, AppConfig is simpler and cheaper but has less user targeting and analytics.
I'd use it for kill switches, gradual feature rollouts, and operational settings like rate limits or batch sizes that need to change quickly but safely.

p17-896.q: In a multi-account AWS setup, a workload or a person in one account often needs access to resources in another, like a deployment pipeline in a tools account deploying to production, or a service reading a shared S3 bucket.
p17-896.k: cross account access aws, assumerole, sts assume role, trust policy, external id
x: In a multi-account AWS setup, a workload or a person in one account often needs access to resources in another, like a deployment pipeline in a tools account deploying to production, or a service reading a shared S3 bucket.

The mechanism's role assumption with AWS STS. In the target account, you create an IAM role with two policies. A trust policy saying which principals can assume it, like a specific role in the tools account, and a permissions policy saying what the role can do in the target account.
In the source account, the calling identity needs permission for STS AssumeRole on that role.

The caller calls AssumeRole and gets temporary credentials, valid from 15 minutes to a few hours, and uses them to call services in the target account. The SDKs and CLI profiles can do all that automatically.

Security details I'd say matter most. Trust specific roles, not the whole account root, unless that's intentional, and add conditions, like requiring MFA for humans, or source identity and session tags for auditing.
External ID, when you let a third party assume a role, require an external ID they have to provide. That protects against the confused deputy problem.
Keep session duration short.
CloudTrail logs the AssumeRole calls and the actions taken with the session, so every action traces back to the original identity.
For people, IAM Identity Center gives single sign-on into multiple accounts with permission sets, which creates and manages these roles for you, so nobody needs long-term IAM users.
And for pipelines, combine it with OIDC federation, so there are no access keys anywhere at all.

p17-897.q: Athena's a serverless query service that runs SQL directly on files in S3. You pay per amount of data scanned, and there are no servers to manage.
p17-897.k: amazon athena, query s3 with sql, athena glue catalog, athena partitions, analyze logs s3
x: Athena's a serverless query service that runs SQL directly on files in S3. You pay per amount of data scanned, and there are no servers to manage.

How it works, a table definition in the AWS Glue Data Catalog describes where the data lives in S3, its format and its columns. You create tables with DDL statements, or use Glue crawlers to infer schemas. Then you query with standard SQL, joins, aggregations, the usual.

Common uses, analysing ALB, CloudFront, VPC Flow Logs and CloudTrail logs stored in S3. Like finding which IPs caused a spike of 500 errors, or which role made a config change. Also querying data lake exports for reporting, and ad hoc analysis of exported application data.

Making it fast and cheap. Columnar formats, convert data to Parquet or ORC, compressed. Queries read only the columns they need, which often cuts scanned data by 90 percent or more compared to CSV or JSON.

Partitioning, organise S3 paths by date or other keys, year, month, day, and filter on the partition columns, so Athena skips irrelevant files. Partition projection saves you managing partitions by hand.
Avoid loads of tiny files, combine them into bigger ones.
Select only the columns you need, never select star on big tables. That's how people get surprise bills, trust me.
Governance, workgroups with per-query scan limits and separate result locations control cost, and Lake Formation can handle fine-grained permissions.
It's really useful during incident investigations, when logs in S3 are too big for quick searches elsewhere, and it complements CloudWatch Logs Insights for recent logs.

p17-898.q: A Lambda function URL is a dedicated HTTPS endpoint for a single function, switched on with one setting. Requests go straight to the function, with no API Gateway in between.
p17-898.k: lambda function url, function url vs api gateway, lambda http endpoint, lambda url auth
x: A Lambda function URL is a dedicated HTTPS endpoint for a single function, switched on with one setting. Requests go straight to the function, with no API Gateway in between.

What function URLs give you, an HTTPS endpoint with no extra service, no added cost beyond Lambda, longer timeouts, up to the function's 15 minutes, compared to API Gateway's integration timeout, response streaming for large or progressive responses, CORS configuration, and authentication either with IAM, which means SigV4-signed requests, or none, which means public.

What API Gateway adds, custom authorizers including JWT validation against Cognito or another OpenID Connect provider, request validation, throttling and usage plans with API keys, caching in REST APIs, request and response transformations, routing lots of paths to different backends, custom domains with base path mappings, direct WAF integration, and better lifecycle features like stages.

When a function URL's enough, I'd say internal webhooks with signature verification in the function, service-to-service calls using IAM auth, simple single-function backends, or endpoints that need streaming or long processing time. CloudFront can sit in front of a function URL for a custom domain, caching and WAF, with origin access control so only CloudFront can call it.
When I'd use API Gateway, public APIs with several routes, central JWT authentication, per-client throttling, or when the API is a product with documentation and keys.
For an ASP.NET Core API hosted on Lambda, either can work. But for production APIs with multiple consumers I'd still pick API Gateway or an ALB, to get centralised auth and throttling.

p17-899.q: Amazon MQ is a managed message broker service running Apache ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ. AWS handles provisioning, patching, high availability across Availability Zones, and backups, while applications use the standard broker protocols, AMQP 0-9-1 for RabbitMQ, or MQTT, STOMP or JMS for ActiveMQ.
p17-899.k: amazon mq, rabbitmq on aws, managed rabbitmq, amazon mq vs sqs, activemq aws
x: Amazon MQ is a managed message broker service running Apache ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ. AWS handles provisioning, patching, high availability across Availability Zones, and backups, while applications use the standard broker protocols, AMQP 0-9-1 for RabbitMQ, or MQTT, STOMP or JMS for ActiveMQ.

Why it exists, a lot of existing applications are built on RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ, with exchanges, routing keys, topic patterns, priority queues and existing client libraries. Rewriting them for SQS and SNS takes effort and changes behaviour. Amazon MQ lets you move them to AWS with minimal code changes, really just a new connection string and TLS settings.

When I'd use it. Lift and shift of applications on RabbitMQ, like an on-premise system with RabbitMQ workers, retry queues and dead-letter exchanges, where keeping the same messaging model reduces migration risk. Or when you need protocol-level features SQS doesn't have, complex routing, message priorities, or standard protocols for interoperability with other systems.

When I'd prefer SQS and SNS, or EventBridge, is new cloud-native services. They're serverless, scale without capacity planning, cost nothing when idle, and plug straight into Lambda and other services. Amazon MQ runs on broker instances you size and pay for all the time, and there are throughput limits per broker.

On migration, I think a sensible path for a RabbitMQ-based system is move to Amazon MQ first, keeping everything working, and then gradually move new or simpler flows to SQS, SNS or EventBridge where it makes sense. Doing both changes at once is just asking for trouble.

p17-900.q: So I'd start by picking the target, and then the migration method.
p17-900.k: migrate sql server to aws, aws dms, rds for sql server, sql server to aurora, database migration aws
x: So I'd start by picking the target, and then the migration method.

For the target, RDS for SQL Server is managed SQL Server, with backups, patching and Multi-AZ handled by AWS. Least change for the applications. The limits are no full sysadmin access, some features restricted, and SQL Server licensing is included in the price, which is expensive.
SQL Server on EC2 gives full control and every feature, for databases that need things RDS doesn't support, but then you manage everything yourself.
Aurora PostgreSQL or Babelfish is a bigger change to save licensing cost. It needs code and schema conversion, which is honestly a project in itself.

For the method, native backup and restore is the simplest. Take a full backup on-premise, upload it to S3, and restore into RDS with the native restore procedure. Reliable, and for minimal downtime you follow it with differential and log backups, then a short cutover.

AWS DMS, the Database Migration Service, copies the data and keeps replicating changes with change data capture, so the target stays in sync until cutover. Useful for heterogeneous migrations with the Schema Conversion Tool, or to keep downtime small.
Distributed availability groups or log shipping to EC2 if you need near-zero downtime.

Planning, inventory the features in use, SQL Agent jobs, linked servers, CLR, cross-database queries, SSIS packages, since some don't behave the same on RDS. Size the instance from current metrics, test performance with production-like load, rehearse the cutover, and plan the rollback.
And for a setup with many databases, like one per study, automation and wave planning are essential. Migrate a few low-risk databases first, learn from them, then scale up.

p17-901.q: Where to run scheduled and batch work really depends on duration, resources and complexity.
p17-901.k: scheduled jobs aws, ecs scheduled task, aws batch, cron jobs aws, batch processing aws
x: Where to run scheduled and batch work really depends on duration, resources and complexity.

Lambda with EventBridge Scheduler is for short jobs, under 15 minutes, like nightly cleanups, sending reminders or calling an API. Cheap and simple, with retries and dead-letter queues on the schedule.

ECS scheduled tasks, where EventBridge Scheduler starts a Fargate or EC2 task on a cron schedule. Good for longer jobs, jobs needing more memory or CPU, or jobs that already exist as containers, like a .NET console app. No time limit, and you only pay while the task runs.

AWS Batch is for large-scale batch processing with lots of jobs, queues and priorities, job dependencies and array jobs, like processing thousands of files or heavy computations. Batch manages the compute environments, Spot instances included, and schedules jobs efficiently.
Step Functions to orchestrate multi-step jobs, with retries, branching, parallel steps and error handling, calling Lambda, ECS tasks or Batch jobs, triggered by a schedule.

Whichever you pick, some design rules apply. Jobs have to be idempotent and restartable, so a job that fails halfway is safe to rerun, with checkpoints for long ones. No overlapping runs, make sure only one instance runs at a time if that matters, using locks or Step Functions. Monitoring, alarms on failures and on jobs that didn't run at all, with a heartbeat pattern, because silent non-execution is a really common problem. And timeouts and resource limits so stuck jobs don't run forever.
It's the AWS version of what we do on-premise with Quartz jobs, and what our AlertWatchDog-style checks would look like if they ran in IQVIA's newer AWS services.

p17-902.q: Amazon OpenSearch Service is a managed service for OpenSearch, the open-source fork of Elasticsearch. People mainly use it for two things.
p17-902.k: amazon opensearch, opensearch service, elasticsearch aws, full text search aws, opensearch dashboards
x: Amazon OpenSearch Service is a managed service for OpenSearch, the open-source fork of Elasticsearch. People mainly use it for two things.

Search. Full-text search with relevance ranking, fuzzy matching, autocomplete, filtering and faceting, for products, documents or records, way better than SQL LIKE queries. Data gets indexed from the main database, often through change events or a sync process, and the database stays the source of truth.

Log and observability analytics. Ingesting application logs, metrics and traces, then searching and visualising them with OpenSearch Dashboards, which is the Kibana equivalent. It's an alternative to CloudWatch Logs or commercial tools for teams that want more powerful search over big log volumes.
It also supports vector search with k-nearest-neighbour indexes, used for semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation, and you can combine keyword and vector search in one query.

Operationally, a few things matter. Sizing, pick instance types and counts, storage, and dedicated master nodes for stability, and plan shard counts carefully, because too many small shards just wastes resources. I've seen that hurt clusters badly.
OpenSearch Serverless takes away cluster management and scales automatically, with a different cost model.
High availability with multiple Availability Zones and replicas. Security with VPC access, fine-grained access control and encryption.
Index lifecycle, roll over and delete older log indexes, or move them to the cheaper UltraWarm and cold tiers, otherwise log clusters get expensive fast.

When I wouldn't use it, if search needs are simple, database full-text search might be enough. And if logs are already handled well by CloudWatch, Splunk or Datadog, adding another log platform just adds cost and complexity.

p17-903.q: AWS Systems Manager is a set of tools for managing EC2 instances and on-premise servers at scale, through the SSM agent installed on each machine.
p17-903.k: systems manager patch manager, ssm run command, aws patching, ssm state manager, fleet management aws
x: AWS Systems Manager is a set of tools for managing EC2 instances and on-premise servers at scale, through the SSM agent installed on each machine.

The parts I'd actually use for operations. Patch Manager defines patch baselines, which patches to approve, like security updates automatically after seven days, and patch groups by tags, like web servers or database servers. Patches get applied in maintenance windows, and compliance reports show which servers are missing patches.

Maintenance Windows schedule patching and other tasks during agreed times, with controlled concurrency and error thresholds, like patching 10 percent of servers at a time and stopping if more than one fails.
Run Command runs scripts or commands across many servers at once, by tag, with the output logged, instead of logging in to each one. Like collecting diagnostics or restarting a service.
State Manager keeps servers in a defined state, like making sure an agent's installed or a config's applied, and reapplies it if it drifts.
Session Manager gives shell access without SSH keys or open ports, fully audited.
Inventory collects installed software, updates and configuration from every server.
And hybrid, the agent runs on on-premise servers too, so the same tools manage cloud and data centre machines. That really helps during a long migration.
For safe patching, my approach is lower environments first, snapshots or AMIs before patching critical servers, drain servers from load balancers during patching, and check health afterwards.
In a containerised world, patching becomes rebuilding images on updated base images, but for VM-based and Windows workloads, Systems Manager is the main tool.

p17-904.q: Right, Azure Functions for .NET historically had two hosting models.
p17-904.k: azure functions isolated worker, in process vs isolated, dotnet isolated functions, functions worker model, migrate to isolated worker
x: Right, Azure Functions for .NET historically had two hosting models.

In-process, the function code ran inside the Functions host process, sharing its .NET version and assemblies. It started fast and supported some bindings directly, but your app was tied to the host's .NET version, and dependency conflicts with the host's assemblies were really common. Microsoft's ended the in-process model with .NET 8 as its last version, and support ends in November 2026.

Isolated worker, the function app runs in its own .NET process, separate from the host, talking over gRPC. You choose the .NET version, including newer ones as soon as they're supported. No assembly conflicts. Full control over startup with a normal Program file, dependency injection and configuration, just like any .NET app. And middleware support, so cross-cutting things like logging, correlation and exception handling work like in ASP.NET Core. It's the only supported model going forward.

Migration steps. Switch the project to the isolated worker packages, the Functions Worker package and the extension packages instead of the WebJobs extensions. Add a Program file with the host builder. Update function signatures, because bindings and types differ, like HttpRequestData, or the ASP.NET Core integration for HTTP functions. Replace ILogger injection patterns. Update settings, like setting the worker runtime to dotnet-isolated. And test each trigger carefully, especially Durable Functions, which have their own isolated package. That's where people usually get stuck.

If I were moving our AlertWatchDog-style scheduled checks to Azure Functions, I'd write them on the isolated model from day one, with timer triggers and dependency injection shared with our other .NET code.

p17-905.q: The concepts map reasonably well, but not one to one, so I'd plan the mapping first.
p17-905.k: rabbitmq to service bus, migrate rabbitmq azure, service bus vs rabbitmq, exchanges to topics, messaging migration azure
x: The concepts map reasonably well, but not one to one, so I'd plan the mapping first.

The mapping. A RabbitMQ queue with a single consumer group maps to a Service Bus queue. A fanout or topic exchange with several queues bound to it maps to a Service Bus topic with subscriptions, and routing keys and binding patterns become subscription filters, SQL or correlation filters. Dead-letter exchanges map to the built-in dead-letter sub-queue that every queue and subscription has. The retry queues with TTLs, which we build by hand in RabbitMQ, can be replaced with Service Bus's delivery count and max delivery count, plus scheduled messages for delayed retries. Consumer acks map to peek-lock with Complete, Abandon or DeadLetter. Ordering per key maps to sessions.

Differences to handle. Message size limits per tier, 256 KB on Standard and up to 100 MB on Premium. Lock durations need renewing for long processing, which can catch people out. And duplicate detection's built in, based on message id.
How I'd migrate. Abstract messaging behind an interface, or use a library like MassTransit that supports both brokers, so switching transport is mostly configuration.
Run both in parallel. Bridge messages from RabbitMQ to Service Bus for a period, or move one flow at a time, starting with low-risk ones.
Make consumers idempotent, because a migration raises the chance of duplicates. And watch dead-letter counts and queue lengths on both sides during cutover.

Connectivity matters for on-premise apps. They need reliable outbound access to Azure, ideally through private endpoints over ExpressRoute or VPN, and managed identity's only available to Azure-hosted workloads.

p17-906.q: Dapr, the Distributed Application Runtime, is an open-source project that runs as a sidecar next to each service and gives you common microservice capabilities through simple HTTP or gRPC APIs. So your code doesn't depend on specific infrastructure SDKs.
p17-906.k: dapr, distributed application runtime, dapr sidecar, dapr pub sub, dapr building blocks
x: Dapr, the Distributed Application Runtime, is an open-source project that runs as a sidecar next to each service and gives you common microservice capabilities through simple HTTP or gRPC APIs. So your code doesn't depend on specific infrastructure SDKs.

The building blocks. Service invocation, call another service by its app id, with discovery, retries, mTLS and tracing handled by the sidecars. Pub-sub, publish and subscribe to events, with the broker, Service Bus, RabbitMQ, Kafka or Redis, picked through configuration components. State management, key-value state with pluggable stores like Redis or Cosmos DB, with concurrency control. Bindings, input and output connectors to external systems, queues, storage, cron schedules. Secrets and configuration, read from Key Vault or other stores through one API. Workflows and actors for stateful patterns. And resiliency policies, timeouts, retries and circuit breakers defined in configuration.

Why teams use it, services in different languages, .NET, Node, Python, get the same capabilities consistently. Switching infrastructure, like RabbitMQ in one environment and Service Bus in another, is just a configuration change. And observability is built in.
Azure Container Apps has Dapr built in, switched on per app with a setting, so it's easy to try. On Kubernetes you install it in the cluster.

The costs, though. An extra sidecar per service adds latency, resource use and another moving part to run and upgrade. The abstractions hide broker-specific features. And teams have to learn its concepts. For a handful of .NET-only services, I'd say native SDKs with something like MassTransit are probably simpler.

p17-907.q: Lots of organisations run Azure DevOps Server, which used to be TFS, on-premise, like our setup, and think about moving to the cloud service. You can basically go two ways.
p17-907.k: azure devops server migration, tfs to azure devops services, data migration tool azure devops, on premise azure devops to cloud, tfs migration
x: Lots of organisations run Azure DevOps Server, which used to be TFS, on-premise, like our setup, and think about moving to the cloud service. You can basically go two ways.

High-fidelity migration with Microsoft's data migration tool. It imports a whole collection, work item history, Git and TFVC repositories, pipelines, test plans and artifacts, into Azure DevOps Services. The server has to be on a recent supported version, identities have to be synced with Entra ID, and there's a validation step that reports issues to fix first. You do a dry run, then a production run with downtime for that collection.

Selective migration. Create new projects in the cloud and move only what you need. Git repositories with full history, recent work items with tools or scripts, and pipelines rebuilt as YAML. Simpler, and a chance to clean up, but you lose some history and links.

Things to plan for. TFVC repositories are still supported in the cloud, but it's a good moment to move to Git. Classic release pipelines work in the cloud, but YAML multi-stage pipelines are where things are going.

Build agents, and this is the one people forget. On-premise deployments still need self-hosted agents inside the network, because cloud-hosted agents can't reach internal servers. The agents connect outbound to the cloud service.

Secrets and service connections need recreating, preferably with workload identity federation for Azure. Compliance, regulated environments have to confirm data residency, retention, audit logs and validation requirements. And integrations, any tools hooked to the old server.
That's partly why our MCP server talks to on-premise Azure DevOps. With work items and pipelines still on-premise, the automation had to work there, not only in the cloud.

p17-908.q: Azure Arc extends Azure's management plane to things outside Azure, on-premise servers, servers in other clouds, Kubernetes clusters and SQL Server instances. Once connected, they show up in Azure as if they were Azure resources, with a resource id, tags and RBAC.
p17-908.k: azure arc, hybrid cloud azure, arc enabled servers, manage on premise servers azure, azure arc kubernetes
x: Azure Arc extends Azure's management plane to things outside Azure, on-premise servers, servers in other clouds, Kubernetes clusters and SQL Server instances. Once connected, they show up in Azure as if they were Azure resources, with a resource id, tags and RBAC.

What you can do with Arc-enabled servers. Azure Policy and guest configuration, to audit and enforce settings, like required security configurations, across on-premise machines. Update Manager, to assess and schedule OS patching for on-premise Windows and Linux servers from Azure. Azure Monitor, collecting logs and metrics with the Azure Monitor agent into Log Analytics, so on-premise and cloud monitoring use the same queries and alerts. And Microsoft Defender for Cloud, for security posture and threat protection on those servers.

Managed identity for on-premise servers is honestly the one I find most interesting. Apps on Arc-enabled servers can get Entra ID tokens to reach Azure services like Key Vault without storing secrets, which is a big improvement for hybrid apps.

Arc-enabled SQL Server gives inventory, best-practice assessments and licensing management for on-premise SQL Server. Arc-enabled Kubernetes gives GitOps configuration and policy for clusters running anywhere.

Why it's relevant for a mostly on-premise system, it gives cloud-style governance, patching, monitoring and identity without moving the workloads. That can be a stepping stone towards a future migration, and it helps when some services already run in the cloud while the core stays in the data centre.
You need the Connected Machine agent on each server, with outbound connectivity to Azure endpoints, maybe through a proxy or private link.

p17-909.q: Exposing RDP or SSH ports to the internet is one of the most common ways VMs get compromised, because attackers scan for them constantly. Azure Bastion gives you secure access without public IPs on the VMs.
p17-909.k: azure bastion, rdp ssh without public ip, secure vm access azure, jump box azure, just in time vm access
x: Exposing RDP or SSH ports to the internet is one of the most common ways VMs get compromised, because attackers scan for them constantly. Azure Bastion gives you secure access without public IPs on the VMs.

How it works, Bastion is a managed service deployed into a dedicated subnet, the AzureBastionSubnet, in the virtual network. Users connect through the Azure portal over HTTPS, or with their native RDP or SSH client through the Azure CLI on the Standard tier, and Bastion opens the session to the VM's private IP. The VMs need no public IP, and their network security groups can allow RDP and SSH only from the Bastion subnet.

What you get, no exposed management ports, authentication through Entra ID for portal access, so MFA and Conditional Access apply, session recording on the Premium tier for audit, and with peering, one Bastion can serve VMs across peered networks.

Some controls that go well with it. Just-in-time VM access in Defender for Cloud opens management ports only when someone asks, for a limited time and a specific source IP. Entra ID login for VMs, so people sign in with their corporate identity instead of local accounts. And run commands or automation instead of interactive logins for routine tasks.
On AWS, the equivalent's Systems Manager Session Manager, which needs no network entry point at all, since the agent connects outbound.
My rule's the same anywhere. Interactive server access should be rare, audited and time-limited, and routine work should go through automation and pipelines.

p17-910.q: Both give you queues on Azure, but they're aimed at pretty different needs.
p17-910.k: storage queue vs service bus, azure storage queues, azure queue options, simple queue azure, service bus features
x: Both give you queues on Azure, but they're aimed at pretty different needs.

Azure Storage queues are part of a storage account. Simple and cheap, they can hold a huge number of messages, up to the storage account's capacity, and you access them over HTTP. Messages go up to 64 KB. Features are basic, at-least-once delivery with a visibility timeout, a dequeue count, and that's mostly it. No ordering guarantee, no topics, no built-in dead-lettering, so you handle poison messages yourself, though Azure Functions moves messages to a poison queue after several failures.

Service Bus queues are an enterprise message broker. Bigger messages, up to 256 KB on Standard or 100 MB on Premium, FIFO ordering with sessions, built-in dead-letter queues, duplicate detection, scheduled and deferred messages, transactions across operations, topics and subscriptions with filters for publish-subscribe, and AMQP support.

How I choose. Storage queues for simple background work distribution, like resizing images or sending notifications, where order doesn't matter, volume's high and cost should be minimal, or when the app already uses a storage account anyway.

Service Bus for business messaging between services, where losing, duplicating or misordering messages actually matters, like order processing or integration events, and whenever you need publish-subscribe, dead-lettering, sessions or transactions.
Event Grid and Event Hubs are different again, event notification and high-throughput streaming rather than command queues.
For business integration flows like the ones we run on RabbitMQ with retries and dead-letter handling, I'd go with Service Bus as the natural Azure equivalent.

p17-911.q: Okay, Azure Data Factory is Azure's managed data integration service for ETL and ELT, moving and transforming data between lots of sources and destinations on a schedule or a trigger.
p17-911.k: azure data factory, adf pipelines, etl azure, data integration azure, self hosted integration runtime
x: Okay, Azure Data Factory is Azure's managed data integration service for ETL and ELT, moving and transforming data between lots of sources and destinations on a schedule or a trigger.

The main concepts. Pipelines contain activities, like copy data, run a stored procedure, call a web endpoint, run a notebook, or control flow like loops and conditions. Linked services hold the connection info for sources and destinations, ideally using managed identity and Key Vault for secrets. Datasets describe the data structure in those sources.

Integration runtimes provide the compute. The Azure integration runtime works for cloud sources, and the self-hosted one is installed on a machine inside the corporate network, which lets Data Factory reach on-premise databases, file shares and SFTP servers securely through outbound connections. I'd say that's the key piece for an on-premise shop.
Mapping data flows give visual, Spark-based transformations without writing code. Triggers run pipelines on schedules, tumbling windows or storage events.

Where it fits, loading data from operational databases into a warehouse or lake, moving files between systems, scheduled exports to partners, and data migrations. It has loads of built-in connectors and monitoring for every run.

Where I'd be careful, complex business logic in visual pipelines gets hard to test and review. For that, code in Functions or a service is better, with Data Factory just orchestrating. Version control through Git integration and deployment through ARM templates or pipelines is essential. And Microsoft's moving a lot of this into Microsoft Fabric.
Compared to our integration world, it overlaps with what an integration platform like MuleSoft does for file and data transfers, but it's aimed more at data movement than API-led integration.

p17-912.q: So Key Vault holds the most sensitive stuff, secrets, keys and certificates. Protecting the vault itself matters just as much as using it.
p17-912.k: key vault soft delete, purge protection, key vault rbac vs access policies, key vault security, key vault firewall
x: So Key Vault holds the most sensitive stuff, secrets, keys and certificates. Protecting the vault itself matters just as much as using it.
Soft delete means deleted vaults and objects are kept for a retention period, 7 to 90 days, and can be recovered. It's on for all vaults by default now and you can't turn it off.

Purge protection stops anyone, even administrators, from permanently purging deleted items or vaults until the retention period ends. That protects against malicious or accidental permanent deletion, which is especially important for encryption keys, because losing a key means losing whatever data it encrypts. Once it's on, it can't be switched off. I turn it on for production vaults, especially ones holding keys used for encryption at rest.

Access control, Azure RBAC is the recommended permission model now, instead of vault access policies. RBAC gives fine-grained roles, like Key Vault Secrets User for reading secrets, can be scoped right down to individual secrets, is managed the same way as other Azure permissions, and works with Privileged Identity Management for just-in-time admin access. Access policies were vault-wide and harder to audit.
Network, disable public network access and use private endpoints, or at least the vault firewall with allowed networks.
Separate vaults per application and environment, so access and blast radius stay limited. I've seen one shared vault for everything, and honestly it's a mess to audit.
Monitoring, diagnostic logs to Log Analytics, with alerts on unusual access patterns, failed attempts and deletions.
And rotation, set expiry dates on secrets and certificates, with Event Grid notifications before they expire, and automate rotation where you can.

p17-913.q: An Azure landing zone is basically a pre-configured, well-governed environment that workloads get deployed into. It comes from Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework, so every team doesn't have to design networking, security and governance from scratch.
p17-913.k: azure landing zone, cloud adoption framework, enterprise scale landing zone, azure governance setup, management groups subscriptions design
x: An Azure landing zone is basically a pre-configured, well-governed environment that workloads get deployed into. It comes from Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework, so every team doesn't have to design networking, security and governance from scratch.

What it usually includes. A management group and subscription structure, a hierarchy like platform, landing zones for corporate and online workloads, sandbox and decommissioned, with subscriptions per application or environment, so policies and access can be applied at the right level.
Identity, Entra ID integration, least-privilege role assignments, and Privileged Identity Management for admin access.
Networking, a hub-and-spoke or Virtual WAN topology, with a central firewall, DNS, connectivity to on-premise through ExpressRoute or VPN, and private endpoints for PaaS services.
Governance, Azure Policy assignments enforcing rules, like allowed regions, required tags, no public IPs, and diagnostic settings on every resource.
Security, Defender for Cloud enabled, central logging to Log Analytics, and Sentinel for security operations.
Management, monitoring, backup, update management and cost management with budgets.

There's a split between platform and application landing zones. A central platform team owns the shared parts, and application teams get subscriptions with guardrails, where they can deploy freely within policy.
Microsoft provides reference implementations as Bicep and Terraform modules, deployed and maintained as code.

The AWS equivalent is a multi-account setup with Organizations, Control Tower and Service Control Policies. For an organisation moving workloads into the cloud, I'd say set up the landing zone first. It avoids a sprawl of inconsistent, insecure subscriptions later.

p17-914.q: Virtual Machine Scale Sets let you create and manage a group of identical or mixed VMs that scale automatically, pretty much like Auto Scaling groups in AWS.
p17-914.k: vm scale sets, vmss, azure autoscale vms, scale set orchestration modes, azure vm autoscale
x: Virtual Machine Scale Sets let you create and manage a group of identical or mixed VMs that scale automatically, pretty much like Auto Scaling groups in AWS.
The key features. Autoscale, where rules based on metrics like CPU, memory or queue length, or on schedules, add and remove instances automatically, with minimum and maximum counts.
High availability, instances spread across availability zones and fault domains.
Load balancing, it plugs into Azure Load Balancer or Application Gateway, with health probes so unhealthy instances stop getting traffic, and automatic instance repairs to replace them.

Orchestration modes. Flexible orchestration, now the default, supports mixing VM sizes and Spot with regular VMs and treats instances as normal VMs. Uniform mode uses identical instances from one model, mainly for older large-scale workloads.
Upgrades, when the model changes, like a new image, rolling upgrade policies update instances in batches, and automatic OS image upgrades keep the OS patched.

Images, build a golden image with Azure Image Builder or Packer, stored in an Azure Compute Gallery, so new instances start ready to serve instead of installing software at boot. Installing at boot is slow and flaky, from what I've seen.

Uses, stateless web tiers that can't be containerised yet, like Windows and IIS apps, build agents, since Azure DevOps supports scale set agent pools that grow with pipeline demand, and batch or compute workloads.

For new applications I'd usually prefer PaaS, App Service, Container Apps or AKS, which handle more for you. But for lifting existing VM-based apps, scale sets give elasticity and automated recovery without a rewrite.

p17-915.q: Right, an elastic pool lets many Azure SQL databases share a set amount of resources, compute and storage, instead of each database having its own fixed size. Databases take what they need from the pool, within per-database minimum and maximum limits.
p17-915.k: azure sql elastic pool, elastic pool many databases, database per tenant azure, edtu vcore pool, saas database pool
x: Right, an elastic pool lets many Azure SQL databases share a set amount of resources, compute and storage, instead of each database having its own fixed size. Databases take what they need from the pool, within per-database minimum and maximum limits.

Why it helps. In a database-per-tenant or database-per-customer model, most databases are idle or lightly used most of the time, and their peaks happen at different times. Sizing every database for its own peak wastes money. In a pool, the combined capacity can be much smaller than the sum of the individual peaks, so costs drop a lot while each database still gets resources when it's busy.
