This is really close to a system with one database per study plus a master database. Studies have different activity levels, a few are in busy enrolment phases while others are in maintenance or closing, and that fits pooling really well.

Things to think about. Sizing, monitor combined usage and size the pool for the busiest concurrent load, with per-database caps so one busy database can't starve the others. That's the noisy neighbour problem.
Very large or consistently busy databases might be better as single databases outside the pool.
Operations across lots of databases, Elastic Jobs run T-SQL across every database in a pool for maintenance or schema changes, and deployment pipelines have to update all databases consistently.
There's a max number of databases per pool, so very large estates need several pools.
High availability and backups work per database as usual, and failover groups can include pooled databases.
On-premise, the equivalent is consolidating databases on shared instances, but I think elastic pools add per-database limits and much easier scaling.

p17-916.q: Both are excellent, honestly, but they're built for different access patterns.
p17-916.k: cosmos db vs azure sql, nosql vs sql azure, when to use cosmos db, document database vs relational, azure database choice
x: Both are excellent, honestly, but they're built for different access patterns.

Azure SQL is a relational database. Strong schema, joins, complex queries and reporting, foreign keys, multi-row ACID transactions across any tables, and mature tooling. It fits most business systems, especially with complex relationships and reporting needs, like clinical supply data where studies, sites, kits and shipments are all linked.

Cosmos DB is a globally distributed NoSQL database with document, key-value and other APIs. Single-digit millisecond reads and writes at any scale, automatic horizontal scaling through partitioning, multi-region writes, tunable consistency levels, and a change feed. Transactions are limited to items within one logical partition, and cross-partition queries cost more. You design the data model around access patterns, often denormalised, and the partition key is the most important decision you'll make.

When I'd choose Cosmos DB, very high scale with predictable access by key, like user profiles, device telemetry, session state, product catalogues or event data. Globally distributed apps that need low latency in many regions. Flexible schemas that change a lot. And event-driven architectures using the change feed.
When I'd choose Azure SQL, complex relationships and queries, ad hoc reporting, strong consistency across many entities, and teams with strong SQL skills. Most line-of-business systems land here.
Cost works differently too. Cosmos DB charges by request units, so inefficient queries or a poor partition key get expensive fast. Azure SQL charges by compute and storage.
Often the best architecture uses both, SQL for the core transactional system and Cosmos DB for specific high-scale features.

p17-917.q: Operational tasks, starting and stopping VMs, cleaning up resources, rotating something on a schedule, running maintenance scripts on servers, can be automated in Azure a few ways.
p17-917.k: azure automation, runbooks azure, powershell runbook, operations automation azure, azure update manager
x: Operational tasks, starting and stopping VMs, cleaning up resources, rotating something on a schedule, running maintenance scripts on servers, can be automated in Azure a few ways.

Azure Automation runs PowerShell or Python runbooks in the cloud, or on machines through Hybrid Runbook Workers, which run on on-premise or other servers. Good for traditional IT automation written by ops teams in PowerShell, with schedules, webhooks, shared credentials and modules. The hybrid workers make it useful for on-premise tasks, like maintenance on servers in a data centre. Its older Update Management and change tracking features have moved to Azure Update Manager and Azure Monitor.

Azure Functions is event-driven code, in .NET, PowerShell, Python or others, triggered by timers, queues, HTTP or events. Better for developer-built automation with tests, dependency injection, source control and CI/CD, and for reacting to events, like processing a resource change from Event Grid.
Logic Apps is low-code workflows connecting services, like sending approvals or tickets when something happens.
And Azure Update Manager handles patching for Azure and Arc-enabled servers on schedules.

How I choose, PowerShell-heavy, admin-owned tasks, especially on servers, go to Automation. Developer-owned, event-driven or complex logic goes to Functions. Integrations with business tools and approvals go to Logic Apps.

Whichever one, my approach is managed identity instead of stored credentials, code in source control with pipelines deploying it, logging and alerting on failures, and least-privilege permissions, because automation accounts often have broad rights and they're attractive targets.

p17-918.q: Yes, definitely. Application Insights doesn't need the application to run in Azure. It only needs outbound connectivity to Azure Monitor endpoints, directly, through a proxy, or through Azure Monitor Private Link.
p17-918.k: application insights on premise, app insights iis, application insights .net framework, azure monitor agent on prem, hybrid monitoring azure
x: Yes, definitely. Application Insights doesn't need the application to run in Azure. It only needs outbound connectivity to Azure Monitor endpoints, directly, through a proxy, or through Azure Monitor Private Link.

The options for on-premise IIS apps. SDK-based instrumentation, add the Application Insights SDK to the .NET Framework 4.8 or ASP.NET Core application, configured with a connection string. It collects requests, dependencies like SQL and HTTP calls, exceptions, performance counters and custom telemetry. Gives you the most control and custom events.

OpenTelemetry, the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry distro for ASP.NET Core, or the OpenTelemetry SDK with the Azure Monitor exporter. That keeps instrumentation vendor-neutral, so the same code could send data to Datadog or another backend later.
Agent-based, codeless instrumentation. The Application Insights Agent, a PowerShell module, can instrument IIS-hosted .NET apps on-premise without code changes, which is handy for legacy apps.
Server-level monitoring, the Azure Monitor agent, ideally on Arc-enabled servers, collects Windows event logs, IIS logs and performance counters into Log Analytics.

For regulated, on-premise systems, there's more to think about. Data leaves the data centre, so check what the telemetry contains and keep personal or clinical data out of logs and custom properties. Check data residency and retention, use sampling to control cost, and make sure the security team approves the outbound connection.

In our case, monitoring goes to Splunk and Grafana for the on-premise platform, and OpenTelemetry with Datadog for the newest services. So Application Insights would be an option rather than what we use, but it shows how cloud monitoring can cover on-premise apps.

p17-919.q: The Azure Messaging ServiceBus SDK gives you ServiceBusProcessor, which handles receiving, concurrency and lock management, so I don't write receive loops by hand.
p17-919.k: servicebusprocessor, service bus consumer dotnet, azure service bus dotnet, peek lock dotnet, service bus retry
x: The Azure Messaging ServiceBus SDK gives you ServiceBusProcessor, which handles receiving, concurrency and lock management, so I don't write receive loops by hand.

Setup, create one ServiceBusClient per application, registered as a singleton, using DefaultAzureCredential with managed identity instead of connection strings. Then create a processor for a queue or topic subscription with some options. MaxConcurrentCalls to control parallelism, PrefetchCount for throughput, AutoCompleteMessages set to false so I complete messages explicitly, and a max auto lock renewal duration so locks get renewed for long-running processing.

Handlers. ProcessMessageAsync gets each message. I deserialise and validate the body, process it idempotently, checking the message id against a processed-messages store or using upserts, then call CompleteMessageAsync. For invalid messages that'll never succeed, DeadLetterMessageAsync with a reason and description. For transient failures, let the exception propagate or abandon the message so it's retried, and after the max delivery count, Service Bus dead-letters it automatically. ProcessErrorAsync logs errors from the processor itself, like connection issues.
Hosting, run the processor inside a BackgroundService, start it in StartAsync and stop it gracefully in StopAsync, so in-flight messages finish during deployments.
Ordering, for per-entity ordering, use sessions with the session processor.
Delayed retries, schedule a copy of the message for later with an attempt count and complete the original, for backoff beyond immediate redelivery.
Observability, the SDK supports distributed tracing, so traces connect producer and consumer, and monitor active and dead-letter counts with alerts.
These are pretty much the same reliability habits as our RabbitMQ consumers, just translated to Service Bus.

p17-920.q: Kubernetes is extensible. A custom resource definition, a CRD, adds a new resource type to the Kubernetes API, like PostgresCluster or Certificate, which you create with YAML and kubectl just like a Deployment.
p17-920.k: kubernetes operator, crd, custom resource definition, operator pattern, controller reconcile loop
x: Kubernetes is extensible. A custom resource definition, a CRD, adds a new resource type to the Kubernetes API, like PostgresCluster or Certificate, which you create with YAML and kubectl just like a Deployment.

An operator is a controller that watches those custom resources and makes reality match them. It runs a reconcile loop. Read the desired state from the resource, compare it with the actual state, act to close the gap, and repeat. It basically encodes operational knowledge, what a human operator would do, into software.

Examples. Database operators, like CloudNativePG, or the operators for Redis and RabbitMQ, which create clusters and handle failover, backups and upgrades from a simple resource definition. cert-manager, which issues and renews TLS certificates from Certificate resources. Prometheus Operator, which manages monitoring config through ServiceMonitor resources. And Argo CD, whose Application resource describes what to deploy.
Why they're useful, complex stateful software becomes manageable declaratively, with GitOps, and day-two operations like scaling, backups and upgrades are automated consistently.

Cautions, an operator is powerful software running with broad permissions in your cluster, so pick mature, well-maintained ones and review their RBAC. Understand what it does, because when it misbehaves you're debugging both the application and the operator. And keep operators upgraded along with the cluster, since CRD versions change.

Writing your own operator, with Kubebuilder, Operator SDK or KubeOps for .NET, only makes sense for platform teams automating something repeated many times. For most application teams, I'd go with Helm charts or Kustomize plus existing operators.

p17-921.q: Expired certificates are one of the most common causes of outages, and manual renewal just doesn't scale. cert-manager automates issuing and renewing certificates inside Kubernetes.
p17-921.k: cert manager, kubernetes tls certificates, letsencrypt kubernetes, certificate renewal kubernetes, issuer clusterissuer
x: Expired certificates are one of the most common causes of outages, and manual renewal just doesn't scale. cert-manager automates issuing and renewing certificates inside Kubernetes.

How it works, you install cert-manager in the cluster and define an Issuer or ClusterIssuer, which says where certificates come from. Let's Encrypt using the ACME protocol, an internal certificate authority, HashiCorp Vault, a cloud private CA like AWS Private CA, or a self-signed issuer for testing.

Then you request certificates, either by creating a Certificate resource with the DNS names, or by annotating an Ingress or Gateway, and cert-manager creates the certificate for you. For ACME it proves domain ownership with HTTP-01 challenges, serving a token through the ingress, or DNS-01 challenges, creating DNS records through your DNS provider, which you need for wildcard certificates. The certificate and key end up in a Kubernetes Secret, which the ingress controller uses.

Renewal's automatic, by default well before expiry, around two thirds of the way through the certificate's lifetime, and the Secret gets updated, so the ingress picks up the new certificate without downtime.
It's also used for internal mTLS certificates between services, sometimes with a service mesh, or with trust-manager to distribute CA bundles.

What I'd still monitor, certificate expiry metrics, which cert-manager exposes for Prometheus, with alerts if a certificate gets close to expiry. Renewals can fail silently because of DNS changes, rate limits or permissions. Learned that one the hard way on a non-Kubernetes setup, actually.
On managed cloud load balancers, the cloud certificate service, like ACM on AWS, often handles certificates instead.

p17-922.q: In Kubernetes, the standard practice is containers write logs to stdout and stderr, not to files. The container runtime writes those streams to files on the node, and kubectl logs reads them. But those files get rotated and lost when pods are deleted or nodes replaced, so production needs central log collection.
p17-922.k: kubernetes logging, fluent bit, fluentd kubernetes, container logs kubernetes, log collection daemonset
x: In Kubernetes, the standard practice is containers write logs to stdout and stderr, not to files. The container runtime writes those streams to files on the node, and kubectl logs reads them. But those files get rotated and lost when pods are deleted or nodes replaced, so production needs central log collection.

The common pattern is a node-level agent running as a DaemonSet, one pod per node. It reads all the container log files on that node, enriches each line with Kubernetes metadata, namespace, pod name, container name, labels, and ships them to a backend, Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, Loki, Splunk, Datadog, CloudWatch Logs or Azure Monitor.

Fluent Bit is the most popular agent for this. Lightweight, written in C, low memory, and loads of input, filter and output plugins. Fluentd is its older, heavier, Ruby-based sibling, sometimes used as an aggregator. The OpenTelemetry Collector can collect logs this way too, and cloud providers have their own agents.

What makes it work well. Structured JSON logs from the apps, so fields like level, trace id and correlation id are searchable, instead of parsing free text. Multiline handling for stack traces, configured in the agent, or avoided by logging exceptions as single JSON events. Buffering and backpressure settings, so a slow backend doesn't lose logs or overload nodes. And filtering noisy logs at the agent to keep cost down.
Sidecar log collectors are an alternative for apps that can only write to files, at the cost of extra containers.
And logs and traces linked through trace ids make investigations so much faster. Honestly that's the biggest win.

p17-923.q: Yeah, a lot of teams run containers on ARM now, like AWS Graviton, Azure Cobalt or Ampere, because the price-performance is better, often 20 to 40 percent cheaper for the same work. Developers on Apple Silicon Macs run ARM locally too. An image built only for x86 won't run natively on ARM, so we build multi-architecture images.
p17-923.k: multi arch docker image, docker buildx, arm64 images, graviton containers, multi platform build
x: Yeah, a lot of teams run containers on ARM now, like AWS Graviton, Azure Cobalt or Ampere, because the price-performance is better, often 20 to 40 percent cheaper for the same work. Developers on Apple Silicon Macs run ARM locally too. An image built only for x86 won't run natively on ARM, so we build multi-architecture images.

How, you run docker buildx build with the platform flag set to linux amd64 and linux arm64, which builds the image for both and pushes a manifest list. When a machine pulls the image, it automatically gets the variant matching its architecture.
Building approaches. Emulation with QEMU, one builder machine builds both. Simple, but slow for the foreign architecture, especially compilation-heavy builds.
Native builders, run builds on both x86 and ARM agents and combine the results into one manifest. Much faster, and CI providers offer ARM runners now.

Cross-compilation. For .NET, the SDK can build for another architecture on the build platform, using the TARGETARCH build argument with dotnet publish and the right runtime identifier, so only the final stage uses the target platform's base image. Fast, and it's what Microsoft's Dockerfile samples recommend.

Things to check, base images have to support both architectures, which the official .NET, Node and Python images do. Native dependencies, like some npm packages or Python wheels, have to exist for ARM. And actually test on ARM, don't just build, because behaviour or performance can differ.
Rollout, I'd add ARM nodes, schedule one service there with node selectors, compare performance and cost, then move more workloads over.

p17-924.q: So both are managed Kubernetes, which means the Kubernetes API and the workloads are the same. The differences are really in integration and operations.
p17-924.k: eks vs aks, aws eks vs azure aks, managed kubernetes comparison, eks aks differences, kubernetes on aws vs azure
x: So both are managed Kubernetes, which means the Kubernetes API and the workloads are the same. The differences are really in integration and operations.
Control plane cost, AKS has a free tier for the control plane, with a paid Standard tier for an uptime SLA. EKS charges per cluster per hour, and more for versions in extended support.
Identity, AKS plugs into Entra ID for user authentication and uses workload identity for pods to reach Azure resources. EKS uses IAM, with access entries for users and Pod Identity or IRSA for pods.

Networking, AKS has Azure CNI options, including overlay mode, and kubenet is being retired. EKS uses the VPC CNI, where pods get VPC IP addresses by default, which needs IP planning, with prefix delegation or custom networking to save addresses. That IP thing can catch people out on EKS.

Node management, AKS has node pools with automatic upgrades and node auto-provisioning based on Karpenter. EKS has managed node groups, Fargate profiles for serverless pods, Karpenter, and EKS Auto Mode, which manages nodes, networking and storage components for you.
Upgrades, both do in-place control plane and node pool upgrades. AKS has auto-upgrade channels, and EKS has extended support for older versions at extra cost.
Ecosystem, AKS integrates with Azure Monitor, Azure Policy, Key Vault and Defender, EKS with CloudWatch, IAM, Secrets Manager and GuardDuty.

My view, pick the one matching the cloud where the rest of your platform lives. Keep workloads portable with standard Kubernetes resources, Helm and GitOps, and isolate the cloud-specific parts, identity and storage classes, in configuration.

p17-925.q: Kubernetes makes it really easy to waste money, because teams request resources generously and clusters scale nodes to fit requests, not actual usage.
p17-925.k: kubernetes cost optimization, reduce k8s cost, rightsizing pods, spot nodes kubernetes, kubecost
x: Kubernetes makes it really easy to waste money, because teams request resources generously and clusters scale nodes to fit requests, not actual usage.

What I look at. Rightsizing requests first. Compare requested CPU and memory with actual usage, from metrics or the Vertical Pod Autoscaler in recommendation mode, and lower requests that are way above real use. Requests drive node count, so this is usually the biggest saving.

Autoscaling, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler or KEDA scales pods with demand, even down to zero for queue workers, and a node autoscaler like Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler removes empty or underused nodes and consolidates workloads.

Spot or preemptible nodes for fault-tolerant workloads, stateless services with several replicas, batch jobs, CI runners. Often 60 to 90 percent cheaper, with pod disruption budgets and spread across instance types.
Right node types, ARM-based instances for better price-performance, and fewer, larger nodes to cut per-node overhead, balanced against blast radius.
Non-production, scale down dev and test outside working hours, and delete ephemeral preview environments automatically.

Storage and networking, delete unused persistent volumes and snapshots, use cheaper storage classes where you can, and watch cross-zone and NAT data transfer costs, which can be surprisingly big. Honestly that one surprises everyone the first time they see the bill.
Visibility, tools like Kubecost or OpenCost, or the cloud cost tools, show cost per namespace, team and service, so teams see what they spend. Labels for team and application make that possible.
Commitments, savings plans or reserved capacity for the steady baseline.
And I make cost a regular review item, not a one-time clean-up.

p17-926.q: When Kubernetes stops a pod, during a deployment, a scale-down or a node drain, a sequence kicks off, and understanding it avoids errors during releases.
p17-926.k: pod termination kubernetes, prestop hook, terminationgraceperiodseconds, graceful shutdown kubernetes, sigterm kubernetes
x: When Kubernetes stops a pod, during a deployment, a scale-down or a node drain, a sequence kicks off, and understanding it avoids errors during releases.

The pod's marked Terminating. In parallel two things start. The pod's removed from Service endpoints, so load balancers and kube-proxy stop sending new traffic. And the kubelet runs any preStop hook, then sends SIGTERM to the container's main process. If the process hasn't exited after the termination grace period, 30 seconds by default, it gets SIGKILL.

The problem is removing the pod from endpoints takes a moment to reach every node, ingress controller and cloud load balancer. If the app exits immediately on SIGTERM, some requests still arrive and fail, and you get 502s during every deployment. I've seen teams live with that for ages thinking it's normal.

The fixes. A short preStop delay, like sleeping 5 to 10 seconds, so the pod keeps serving while endpoint removal propagates. Newer Kubernetes versions have a native sleep action for preStop, which works even in images without a shell.

Handle SIGTERM in the app. Stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests and messages, close connections, flush logs and telemetry. ASP.NET Core does this with its host shutdown timeout, which should fit inside the grace period. Node and Python apps need signal handlers.
Make sure the app is PID 1 or uses an init process, so it actually gets the signal.
Set the termination grace period longer than preStop plus the drain time, especially for message consumers with long tasks.
For load balancers outside the cluster, line up the deregistration delay with these timings.
With all that in place, rolling deployments become genuinely zero-downtime.

p17-927.q: Kubernetes clusters hold two kinds of state worth protecting. The resource definitions, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets and custom resources, and the data in persistent volumes.
p17-927.k: velero, kubernetes backup, backup kubernetes resources, persistent volume backup, cluster disaster recovery kubernetes
x: Kubernetes clusters hold two kinds of state worth protecting. The resource definitions, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets and custom resources, and the data in persistent volumes.

If everything's deployed through GitOps, the resource definitions are already in Git, and you can recreate a cluster from it, which is the best foundation for recovery. But Git doesn't have persistent volume data, resources created by operators at runtime, or things someone applied by hand.

Velero is the common open-source tool for cluster backups. It backs up Kubernetes resources from the API server into object storage, like S3 or Azure Blob, and backs up persistent volumes using cloud snapshots through CSI, or file-level copies with its built-in data mover. You can back up the whole cluster or selected namespaces and labels, on schedules with retention periods.
Restores can recreate resources into the same cluster or a different one, which also makes Velero useful for moving workloads between clusters or cloud regions.

Things I'd be careful about. Databases, volume snapshots of a running database might not be consistent. Use database-native backups, or Velero hooks to freeze or flush before snapshots. For managed databases outside the cluster, RDS or Azure SQL, use their own backup features.
Secrets in backups, the backup storage has to be encrypted and access-controlled.
Testing, regularly restore into a test cluster to prove backups actually work, and measure how long it takes. A backup you've never restored is just a hope, I always say.
Cloud-native alternatives, like AWS Backup for EKS or Azure Backup for AKS, offer similar things with managed integration.

p17-928.q: Okay, Podman is a container engine that's compatible with Docker's command line and image format. Most docker commands work by just swapping docker for podman, and images built by either run on both, because they follow the OCI standards.
p17-928.k: podman vs docker, rootless containers, daemonless containers, podman, docker desktop alternative
x: Okay, Podman is a container engine that's compatible with Docker's command line and image format. Most docker commands work by just swapping docker for podman, and images built by either run on both, because they follow the OCI standards.

The key differences. Daemonless. Docker uses a long-running background daemon, dockerd, that the CLI talks to, and containers are children of that daemon. Podman has no central daemon, each container runs as a child of the command or of systemd. That removes a privileged single point of failure.

Rootless by default. Podman's designed to run containers as a normal user, using user namespaces, so a container breakout only gets that user's permissions, not root. Docker supports rootless mode too, but it's not the default.
Pods. Podman can group containers into pods, like Kubernetes, and generate Kubernetes YAML from them, or run Kubernetes YAML locally.
systemd integration. Podman generates systemd units, or uses Quadlet files, to run containers as services on Linux servers, which suits Red Hat-based environments.
Tooling. Docker has Docker Desktop, Compose and a big ecosystem. Podman has Podman Desktop and supports Compose files through podman compose or the Docker-compatible API.
Licensing. Docker Desktop needs a paid subscription for larger companies, which pushed some organisations to Podman Desktop or other alternatives for developer machines.

In practice, I'd say the choice matters very little for production on Kubernetes, which uses containerd or CRI-O anyway. It matters for developer machines, security-sensitive Linux servers, and CI builds that shouldn't need a privileged daemon.

p17-929.q: kubectl reads connection details from a kubeconfig file. Clusters with API server addresses and CA certificates, users with credentials, and contexts that combine a cluster, a user and a default namespace. With several clusters, dev, test, production, you switch contexts with kubectl config use-context, or tools like kubectx and kubens.
p17-929.k: kubeconfig, kubectl contexts, multiple clusters access, kubectl config use-context, cluster credentials security
x: kubectl reads connection details from a kubeconfig file. Clusters with API server addresses and CA certificates, users with credentials, and contexts that combine a cluster, a user and a default namespace. With several clusters, dev, test, production, you switch contexts with kubectl config use-context, or tools like kubectx and kubens.

The risk is pretty obvious, running a command against production when you meant dev. Habits I use. Make the current context visible, show it in the shell prompt, and use distinct colours or names for production.
Default to non-production. Keep production credentials separate, or require explicitly selecting them, and use a read-only role for day-to-day viewing of production.
In scripts, always pass the context flag explicitly instead of relying on whatever the current context is.

Credentials, avoid long-lived static tokens or client certificates in kubeconfig files. Use exec-based authentication plugins, like kubelogin for AKS with Entra ID, or the AWS CLI for EKS, which fetch short-lived tokens tied to your corporate identity, with MFA and conditional access. Then access can be revoked centrally, and every action's audited with your identity.
Least privilege, Kubernetes RBAC roles per team and namespace, with cluster-admin only for a few people through just-in-time elevation.
Protect the file. Kubeconfig files with embedded credentials are secrets, so never commit them or paste them in chat. I've seen people do this more than you'd think.
And prefer GitOps for changes. In production, most changes should go through Git and Argo CD or Flux, so direct kubectl write access is rarely needed at all.

p17-930.q: Builds often need credentials, like a token for a private NuGet feed, an npm registry or a private Git repo. The dangerous ways are passing them as build arguments or copying a config file into the image, because build arguments and files end up in image layers and history. Anyone who pulls the image can dig them out, even if a later step deletes the file. That one can catch people out.
p17-930.k: docker build secrets, buildkit secret mount, private nuget feed docker, npm token docker build, secrets in dockerfile
x: Builds often need credentials, like a token for a private NuGet feed, an npm registry or a private Git repo. The dangerous ways are passing them as build arguments or copying a config file into the image, because build arguments and files end up in image layers and history. Anyone who pulls the image can dig them out, even if a later step deletes the file. That one can catch people out.

The right way is BuildKit secret mounts. In the Dockerfile, a RUN step uses a secret mount, for example mounting a secret with the id nugetconfig at the path where dotnet restore expects a NuGet config, or exposing an npm token as an environment variable only for that step. The secret's only there while that RUN command runs, and it's never written to any layer.

At build time, docker build passes the secret with the secret flag, reading from a file or an environment variable on the build machine. In CI, the pipeline gets the token from its secret store, an Azure Pipelines secret variable, a GitHub secret or a cloud secret manager, and passes it to the build.
For SSH access to private Git repos, BuildKit has a similar SSH mount that forwards the SSH agent.

Other good practices. Multi-stage builds, so restore and build tools stay in the build stage and only the published output reaches the final image. Short-lived, read-only tokens for package feeds. Scan images for leaked secrets with tools like Trivy or gitleaks. And if a secret was ever baked into a published image, rotate it, because deleting the image doesn't remove copies people have already pulled.

p17-931.q: A Deployment's default strategy is RollingUpdate, which swaps old pods for new ones gradually, and basically two settings control the pace.
p17-931.k: maxsurge maxunavailable, kubernetes rolling update strategy, kubectl rollout undo, rollout status, deployment strategy kubernetes
x: A Deployment's default strategy is RollingUpdate, which swaps old pods for new ones gradually, and basically two settings control the pace.
maxSurge is how many extra pods above the desired replica count can be created during the update. With 4 replicas and a max surge of 1, Kubernetes can run 5 pods for a while.

maxUnavailable is how many pods below the desired count can be unavailable during the update. With it at zero, Kubernetes never drops capacity. It adds a new pod, waits until it's ready, then removes an old one.
Both take numbers or percentages, and the defaults are 25 percent each.

Choosing values. For user-facing services where capacity matters, a surge of 1 or 25 percent with zero unavailable keeps full capacity, at the cost of needing extra resources for a bit. For large deployments where speed matters, a higher surge speeds rollouts up. If the cluster has no spare capacity, 1 unavailable with zero surge avoids needing extra nodes, but capacity dips briefly.

What makes rolling updates safe. Readiness probes that reflect real readiness, so traffic only goes to pods that can actually serve. minReadySeconds, so a pod has to stay ready for a while before it counts as available, which catches quick crashes. And progressDeadlineSeconds, which marks the rollout as failed if it stops progressing.
Operations, kubectl rollout status watches progress, rollout history shows revisions, rollout undo goes back to the previous revision, and rollout pause and resume let you step through a rollout.
For canary or blue-green with automated analysis, I'd go with something like Argo Rollouts on top.

p17-932.q: Right, a container isn't a small virtual machine. It's a normal Linux process, or a group of processes, that the kernel isolates and limits using two main features.
p17-932.k: how containers work, linux namespaces, cgroups, container vs virtual machine, container isolation
x: Right, a container isn't a small virtual machine. It's a normal Linux process, or a group of processes, that the kernel isolates and limits using two main features.

Namespaces control what a process can see. The PID namespace gives the container its own process tree, so its main process sees itself as PID 1. The network namespace gives it its own network interfaces, IP address and ports. The mount namespace gives it its own file system view, built from the image layers. And there are namespaces for hostnames, inter-process communication and user ids, so root inside a container can map to an unprivileged user outside.

Control groups, cgroups, control what a process can use. CPU shares and quotas, memory limits, I/O and the number of processes. When a container goes over its memory limit, the kernel's OOM killer stops it. When it goes over its CPU quota, it gets throttled.
Image layers are stacked with a union file system like overlayfs, with a thin writable layer on top. That's why containers start quickly and images share common layers.

Compared to virtual machines, a VM runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor with its own kernel, so stronger isolation but more overhead and slower starts. Containers share the host kernel, so they're lighter and faster, but a kernel vulnerability can affect every container on the host. That's why sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers, and Firecracker micro-VMs used by Lambda and Fargate, add stronger isolation where it's needed.
Knowing this explains things like CPU throttling, OOM kills, and why Windows containers need a Windows host. I think it's one of those fundamentals that pays off every time you debug something.

p17-933.q: DNS issues in Kubernetes show up as intermittent connection failures, slow outbound calls, or services that can't find each other. And honestly, it's DNS more often than people expect.
p17-933.k: kubernetes dns troubleshooting, coredns, ndots kubernetes, service dns not resolving, cluster dns issues
x: DNS issues in Kubernetes show up as intermittent connection failures, slow outbound calls, or services that can't find each other. And honestly, it's DNS more often than people expect.

How cluster DNS works, CoreDNS runs as pods in kube-system, and every pod's resolv conf points to it. Services get names like orders dot shipping dot svc dot cluster dot local, and pods can use short names within the same namespace.

Troubleshooting steps. Test from inside the cluster. Start a temporary debug pod with tools like nslookup or dig, and resolve the service name, the full name, and an external name. kubectl debug can attach a debugging container to an existing pod so you test from the same network namespace.
Check the Service. Does it exist in the expected namespace, and does it have endpoints? A name might resolve but connections fail if no pods are ready.
Check CoreDNS. Are its pods running and not restarting? Look at its logs for errors and its metrics for latency and errors. Under heavy load, CoreDNS might need more replicas or resources.

The ndots setting. By default, names with fewer than five dots are tried with each search domain first, so a lookup for an external API name can generate several failed queries before the real one, adding latency and load. Using fully qualified names with a trailing dot, or lowering ndots in the pod's DNS config, fixes that.
Node-level issues, conntrack races with UDP DNS packets historically caused five-second delays, and NodeLocal DNSCache reduces that and lowers CoreDNS load.
Network policies that accidentally block traffic to CoreDNS on port 53.
And application caching, some runtimes cache DNS too long or not at all, which matters when endpoints change.

p17-934.q: Docker Hub limits the number of image pulls for anonymous and free users per time window. Busy CI pipelines and clusters pulling public base images can hit those limits, so builds fail and pods get stuck in ImagePullBackOff with "too many requests" errors, usually at the worst possible moment, like during scaling or an incident.
p17-934.k: docker hub rate limit, pull through cache, registry mirror, image pull reliability, toomanyrequests docker
x: Docker Hub limits the number of image pulls for anonymous and free users per time window. Busy CI pipelines and clusters pulling public base images can hit those limits, so builds fail and pods get stuck in ImagePullBackOff with "too many requests" errors, usually at the worst possible moment, like during scaling or an incident.

How I make pulls reliable. A pull-through cache, configure the private registry to cache public images. Amazon ECR pull-through cache rules, Azure Container Registry artifact cache, Harbor, Artifactory or Nexus fetch an image once and then serve it from the private registry, and builds and clusters only pull from there.

Mirror critical base images. Import the specific base images we depend on into our own registry on a schedule, scan them, and reference them in Dockerfiles. That also protects you if upstream images get changed or removed.
Authenticate pulls. If Docker Hub has to be used, authenticate with a paid account to get higher limits.
Pin by digest for important base images, so the exact image is used every time, and update deliberately through Renovate or Dependabot.
Avoid unnecessary pulls, image pull policy IfNotPresent with immutable tags, and caching in CI runners.
Use official images from other registries where they exist, like Microsoft's .NET images from the Microsoft container registry, which don't have Docker Hub's limits.
It also improves security and compliance, I'd say, because everything running in production comes from a registry we control and scan, which regulated environments often require anyway.

p17-935.q: When a cluster runs out of capacity, Kubernetes has to decide which pods get scheduled, and PriorityClasses tell it what matters most.
p17-935.k: priorityclass kubernetes, pod preemption, pod priority, system critical pods, scheduling priority kubernetes
x: When a cluster runs out of capacity, Kubernetes has to decide which pods get scheduled, and PriorityClasses tell it what matters most.

A PriorityClass is a cluster-level object with a name and an integer value, where higher means more important. Pods reference it by name. The built-in classes, system cluster critical and system node critical, protect components like CoreDNS and networking agents.
What it affects. Scheduling order, pending pods with higher priority get scheduled before lower ones.

Preemption, if a high-priority pod can't be scheduled because there's no room, the scheduler can evict lower-priority pods from a node to make space. Evicted pods get a graceful termination and go back to pending, to be rescheduled when capacity frees up.
Eviction under node pressure also considers priority, along with resource usage against requests.

How I'd use it, a few clear tiers, like critical for core customer-facing services, default for normal services, and low for batch jobs, CI runners or experiments, so when capacity's short, batch work yields to production traffic. Low-priority classes can set the preemption policy to Never, so those pods wait in the queue without preempting anyone.

Placeholder pods are a neat trick, honestly. Some teams run low-priority "balloon" pods to reserve headroom. Real workloads preempt them instantly, and the autoscaler adds nodes for the evicted placeholders, so scaling's faster.

Cautions, too many classes, or giving everything high priority, makes it meaningless. Preemption can cause cascading disruption, so pair it with PodDisruptionBudgets, which preemption respects on a best-effort basis. And ResourceQuotas can limit who's allowed to use the high-priority classes.

p17-936.q: Honestly, it's possible and getting more common, but it isn't always the right call.
p17-936.k: database in kubernetes, stateful workloads kubernetes, postgres on kubernetes, managed database vs kubernetes, run sql in k8s
x: Honestly, it's possible and getting more common, but it isn't always the right call.

What makes it possible is StatefulSets, which give stable identities and a persistent volume per replica, storage classes for durable disks, and operators, like CloudNativePG for Postgres, or the ones for MySQL, Redis and others. Those automate replication, failover, backups, upgrades and monitoring, which used to need a skilled DBA.

The case for it is one platform and toolset for everything, with GitOps. It's great for dev, test and ephemeral environments, where databases spin up and down with the app. You get portability across clouds and on-premise, and maybe lower cost than managed services at large scale.

The case for managed databases, RDS, Aurora, Azure SQL, Cloud SQL, is that the provider handles high availability, backups, point-in-time restore, patching, encryption and performance insights, with SLAs. Databases are the most critical and hardest-to-recover part of a system, and running them well takes deep expertise in storage, failover and tuning. Kubernetes adds layers, node failures, volume attachment delays, evictions, that need careful handling.

My default is managed database services for production business data, especially in regulated domains like clinical systems, where proven backup, restore and audit really matter. Databases in Kubernetes for dev, test and preview environments, caches like Redis where data's reproducible, and special cases where the team has strong operator experience.
And if I did run a production database in Kubernetes, I'd insist on a mature operator, dedicated nodes, PodDisruptionBudgets, tested backups and restores, and monitoring of replication and storage.

p17-937.q: A filling dead-letter queue means consumers keep failing on messages, so I treat it as an incident, because business work isn't getting done.
p17-937.k: sqs dlq filling, dead letter queue alarm, messages going to dlq, sqs maxreceivecount, dlq investigation
x: A filling dead-letter queue means consumers keep failing on messages, so I treat it as an incident, because business work isn't getting done.

I start by understanding the scale. How many messages, since when, is it all messages or just some? I check whether the main queue's still being processed, and whether the timing lines up with a deployment, a config change or a downstream outage.

Then I find the reason. I look at consumer logs and traces for the failing message ids, and sample a few messages from the DLQ to look at their bodies and attributes, without deleting them. Typical causes, a new message format from a producer that the consumer can't parse. A downstream dependency, a database or API, down or throttling. A bug in the latest consumer release. A visibility timeout shorter than processing time, so messages get received again while still being processed, and those extra receives count up until they hit the max receive count. That one can bite people. Or permissions changed, like KMS key access.
Fix the cause. Roll back the consumer or producer change, raise the visibility timeout, or wait for the dependency to recover, with backoff so we don't hammer it.

Then redrive. Once it's fixed, use SQS DLQ redrive to move messages back to the source queue, ideally gradually, and make sure processing is idempotent so redelivered messages don't create duplicates. Messages that are truly invalid get archived with a note on why.
Afterwards, alarms on DLQ depth above zero and on the age of the oldest message, contract tests between producer and consumer, and a runbook for redrive.

p17-938.q: So when an ECS deployment hangs, it usually means the new tasks never become healthy, and ECS just keeps trying to replace them.
p17-938.k: ecs deployment stuck, ecs service not stabilizing, ecs tasks keep restarting deployment, deployment circuit breaker, ecs rollout hang
x: So when an ECS deployment hangs, it usually means the new tasks never become healthy, and ECS just keeps trying to replace them.

I start with the service events, in the console or with describe-services. They often tell you exactly what's going on, tasks failing to start, failing ALB health checks, or capacity problems like no container instances with enough memory.

Then I look at the stopped tasks, their stopped reason and container exit codes. Common findings. CannotPullContainerError, from a wrong image tag, missing ECR permissions on the execution role, or no route to ECR from private subnets. Essential container exited, which means the app crashed at startup, so I read its CloudWatch logs for the real error, like a missing config value, a secret it can't read, or a database it can't reach. Or OutOfMemory, meaning the memory limit's too low.

If tasks run but the deployment doesn't finish, it's usually health checks. The target group health check path or port is wrong, the app takes longer to start than the health check grace period allows, or security groups block the load balancer from reaching the task. I've seen the grace period one quite a few times with .NET apps that warm up slowly.
Capacity, on EC2-backed clusters there might be no room for extra tasks during a rolling deployment with maximum percent at 200.

To stop the bleeding, I roll back to the previous task definition revision. Going forward, I turn on the deployment circuit breaker with automatic rollback, so ECS stops and rolls back a failing deployment by itself, and add CloudWatch alarms on deployment failures.

p17-939.q: Yeah, this is a classic serverless problem. Each Lambda execution environment opens its own database connections, and in a traffic burst Lambda scales to hundreds of concurrent environments, which blows past the database's max connections pretty fast. Then everything, including other apps on the same database, starts failing.
p17-939.k: lambda too many connections, rds connections maxed, lambda database connection exhaustion, rds proxy fix, serverless database connections
x: Yeah, this is a classic serverless problem. Each Lambda execution environment opens its own database connections, and in a traffic burst Lambda scales to hundreds of concurrent environments, which blows past the database's max connections pretty fast. Then everything, including other apps on the same database, starts failing.

Immediate actions, limit the damage by setting reserved concurrency on the function, capping how many instances run at once, so the database can recover. If the trigger's a queue, the messages just wait, which is fine. Then check other critical apps can connect again.

Root fixes. RDS Proxy, put it between Lambda and the database. It pools and shares connections, so thousands of invocations use a small number of database connections. It also handles failover faster and supports IAM authentication.

Connection handling in code. Create the connection or pool outside the handler so it's reused across invocations, with a pool size of one or two per execution environment, and don't open new connections per request.
Control concurrency, reserved concurrency on the function, and for SQS triggers, the maximum concurrency setting on the event source mapping, sized to what the database can take.
Reduce database work, caching for reads, batching writes, and moving heavy queries off the hot path.
Think about the architecture too. If traffic's steady and high, a container service with a normal connection pool might honestly fit this workload better than Lambda.
Monitoring, alarms on database connections, Lambda concurrency and throttles, so we see the trend before it turns into an outage.

p17-940.q: There are several layers that can serve old content, so I just go through them in order.
p17-940.k: users see old version kubernetes, deployment not updated, image tag latest not pulled, kubernetes caching old version, rollout no effect
x: There are several layers that can serve old content, so I just go through them in order.

The pods themselves. kubectl get pods showing the image, and describe the Deployment, to confirm new pods are running the new image. A really common cause is reusing the same tag, like latest, or a version tag pushed twice, with the pull policy IfNotPresent, so nodes keep using the cached old image. The fix is immutable tags, like the commit SHA or build number, or pinning by digest. Also check the manifest really changed. With GitOps, check that Argo CD or Flux synced the right commit, and that the image updater wrote the new tag.
Old pods still serving. Another Deployment or ReplicaSet with the same labels, so the Service picks both old and new pods. Or a canary or blue-green tool still routing to the old version.
Ingress and routing. The ingress might point to a different Service than you think, or there are two environments behind similar hostnames.
Caching. CDN or browser caching of front-end files, especially index dot html cached for a long time, so users load old JavaScript. Or an API gateway or reverse proxy caching responses.
Configuration, not code. The code's new, but a feature flag or config value still has the feature switched off.

To confirm what's running, what I do is expose a version endpoint or response header with the build number and commit, so anyone can check which version they're actually hitting. That turns a confusing investigation into a quick check, and I add it to post-deployment smoke tests as well.

p17-941.q: Restarts without application errors usually mean something outside the app is killing the container. I start with kubectl describe pod, which shows the last state, the reason, the exit code, and events.
p17-941.k: pods restarting no errors, liveness probe failing under load, kubernetes restart count, container killed no logs, probe timeout restart
x: Restarts without application errors usually mean something outside the app is killing the container. I start with kubectl describe pod, which shows the last state, the reason, the exit code, and events.

Common causes. Liveness probe failures, honestly that's the big one. Under load, the health endpoint responds slowly, goes past the probe timeout, which is one second by default, and after a few failures the kubelet kills the container. The app wasn't broken, just busy, and the restart makes things worse by removing capacity. The fix is to make liveness checks really cheap, only checking the process is responsive, never calling databases or downstream services. Bump up the timeout and failure threshold. Use readiness probes for dependency health, which take pods out of traffic without restarting them, and add a startup probe for slow starts.

OOMKilled with exit code 137, the container hit its memory limit. It might only happen under load because of bigger request buffers or caches. Fix the memory limits, look into memory usage, and in .NET check the GC settings for containers.
Node pressure evictions, the node ran low on memory or disk and the kubelet evicted pods. These show as Evicted, not restarts, but they're worth checking.
The app exiting cleanly, exit code 0 or a deliberate shutdown, like a worker that stops after an unhandled background exception, with logs written only to a file and not stdout.
To see logs from the previous container instance, I use kubectl logs with the previous flag, which often shows the last messages before the kill.
Then I line up restarts against load metrics and response times, and that usually confirms the probe theory.

p17-942.q: Both problems basically come from how Celery acknowledges tasks and how the broker redelivers them.
p17-942.k: celery duplicate tasks, celery task lost, celery acks late, celery visibility timeout, celery reliability
x: Both problems basically come from how Celery acknowledges tasks and how the broker redelivers them.

Tasks running twice. Redis broker visibility timeout, with Redis, if a task isn't acknowledged within the visibility timeout, one hour by default, it's redelivered to another worker. Long-running tasks, or ETA and countdown tasks scheduled further out than the timeout, get run again. Fix, raise the visibility timeout above the longest task duration or delay, or use RabbitMQ.
acks late with crashes. With acks late turned on, a task is acknowledged only after it finishes, so if a worker dies midway, it runs again. That's intended, but it means tasks must be idempotent.

Multiple beat schedulers. Running celery beat on more than one instance schedules periodic tasks twice. Run exactly one beat, or use a scheduler with locking. People miss this one when they scale out.
Retries after partial success. A task that did some work, then failed and retried, repeats the first part.

Tasks getting lost. Default early acknowledgement, tasks are acknowledged when received, so if the worker crashes or gets killed during a deployment, the task's gone. Fix, acks late with reject on worker lost for important tasks.
Prefetch, workers reserve several tasks, and if killed, prefetched tasks can be lost or delayed. Lower the prefetch multiplier to one for long tasks.
Results expiring, or the result backend misconfigured, so it only looks lost.

The real safety net is idempotency. Tasks take ids, check whether the work was already done, and use database constraints or upserts. Plus monitoring with Flower or metrics for queue length, failures and retries, and graceful worker shutdown during deployments.

p17-943.q: A slot swap should be smooth, so errors right after it usually come from warm-up or configuration.
p17-943.k: slot swap errors, app service swap cold start, deployment slot settings, swap warm up, sticky settings
x: A slot swap should be smooth, so errors right after it usually come from warm-up or configuration.

Cold start after the swap. If the staging slot wasn't warmed up, the first requests after the swap hit a cold app and time out. App Service does warm up the source slot by hitting the root path, but if the root path doesn't initialise the app, or the app takes longer, it isn't enough. The fix is application initialization with warm-up paths in web config, or the swap warm-up ping path and status code settings, pointing to an endpoint that initialises dependencies. And use swap with preview, which applies production settings to staging, lets you verify, then completes the swap.

Slot-specific settings. Settings marked as deployment slot settings stay with the slot, others move with the code. If a connection string or feature flag is marked wrong, the app in production starts with staging's values, or the swap restarts the app to apply changed settings and you lose the warm-up benefit. I'd say that's the one that trips most teams.

In-flight state. In-memory sessions or caches are lost, so users get logged out or see errors if the app relies on them. Use a distributed cache and shared Data Protection keys, so auth cookies work across slots and instances.
Background jobs. Both slots might run scheduled jobs or consume queues at the same time, so disable them in staging with slot settings.

Database migrations. If the new code needs a schema change that wasn't applied first, or the old code can't handle the new schema, you get errors. Use backward-compatible, expand-and-contract migrations.
Monitoring the swap with availability tests confirms the fix.

p17-944.q: MaxDeliveryCountExceeded means a message was delivered the max number of times, 10 by default, without being completed. So the consumer either kept failing, or kept losing the lock.
p17-944.k: service bus dead letter maxdeliverycountexceeded, service bus lock lost, messages dead lettered, service bus retries, lock duration
x: MaxDeliveryCountExceeded means a message was delivered the max number of times, 10 by default, without being completed. So the consumer either kept failing, or kept losing the lock.
What I do. Read the dead-lettered messages, including the dead-letter reason, description and delivery count, using Service Bus Explorer in the portal or a tool, without deleting them.

Check consumer logs for exceptions on those message ids. If there's a consistent exception, like a deserialisation failure or a validation error, it's a poison message problem. The consumer should dead-letter those straight away with a clear reason, instead of retrying ten times.

If there are no errors, I suspect lock expiry. The default lock duration is 60 seconds on queues, configurable up to 5 minutes. If processing takes longer and the lock isn't renewed, the lock's lost, completion fails with MessageLockLost, and the message comes back again, counting toward the max. Fixes, set the max auto lock renewal duration on the processor, cut processing time, or move long work to a separate step.
Prefetch, a high prefetch count with slow processing means prefetched messages' locks expire before they're even processed.
Concurrency and throttling, downstream dependencies failing under load and causing repeated failures, so add backoff instead of immediate retries.
Abandoning by mistake, code that abandons messages on every exception, including non-transient ones.
After fixing, resubmit the dead-lettered messages with a tool or a small script, idempotently, and set alerts on dead-letter counts per queue and subscription.

p17-945.q: Okay, so Key Vault has service limits, a certain number of transactions per vault every few seconds. Apps that read secrets too often, or lots of instances starting at once, can hit 429 Too Many Requests. And if secrets load at startup, the app just fails to start, which can turn a scale-out or deployment into an outage.
p17-945.k: key vault throttling, key vault 429, key vault rate limit, startup secrets failure, cache key vault secrets
x: Okay, so Key Vault has service limits, a certain number of transactions per vault every few seconds. Apps that read secrets too often, or lots of instances starting at once, can hit 429 Too Many Requests. And if secrets load at startup, the app just fails to start, which can turn a scale-out or deployment into an outage.
Immediate mitigation, stagger restarts, reduce how many instances start at the same time, or scale back for a bit, so Key Vault requests drop below the limits.

Root causes I look for. Reading secrets per request, code that calls Key Vault on every request or operation instead of caching. Fix, load secrets once at startup into configuration, or cache them in memory with a refresh interval.

Config provider reloading too often. The Key Vault configuration provider with a really short reload interval across many instances generates constant traffic. Use a longer interval, or reload only when needed.
Many apps sharing one vault. Separate vaults per application and environment spread the load and improve security too.
Retries without backoff. The SDK has retry policies with exponential backoff, so make sure they're on and custom code isn't retrying aggressively.
Key operations. If you're using Key Vault for frequent crypto, like encrypting every record, switch to envelope encryption with locally cached data keys.
Alternatives, Key Vault references in App Service or App Configuration, which cache values in the platform, reduce direct calls from code.
Monitoring, Key Vault metrics for request counts and throttled requests, with alerts, so we notice rising usage before things fail.

p17-946.q: DefaultAzureCredential tries several credential sources in order. Environment variables, workload identity, managed identity, then developer tools like Visual Studio, Azure CLI and PowerShell. Locally it usually works through the developer's own login, which often has broad permissions. In Azure it has to use the managed identity, so that's where differences show up.
p17-946.k: defaultazurecredential fails in azure, managed identity not working, credentialunavailableexception, azure identity troubleshooting, 403 managed identity
x: DefaultAzureCredential tries several credential sources in order. Environment variables, workload identity, managed identity, then developer tools like Visual Studio, Azure CLI and PowerShell. Locally it usually works through the developer's own login, which often has broad permissions. In Azure it has to use the managed identity, so that's where differences show up.
Things I check. Is a managed identity actually enabled on the resource? System-assigned or user-assigned, on the App Service, Function, Container App or VM.

If it's user-assigned, did we tell the credential which one? With a user-assigned identity you have to set the client id, through the managed identity client id option or the Azure client id setting, otherwise it can't pick it. I've seen that one waste a whole afternoon.

Does the identity have the right role on the target resource, like Key Vault Secrets User, Storage Blob Data Reader or Service Bus Data Receiver, at the right scope? Locally, the developer might have Owner on the subscription, which hides missing data-plane roles. And role assignments can take a few minutes to apply.

Is it authentication or authorisation? A credential unavailable exception or an authentication failure means no identity could be used. A 403 from the service means the identity worked but lacks permission.
Network, private endpoints, firewalls or DNS might block the target service. The error looks different but often gets confused with identity issues.
Leftover environment variables. If a client secret or similar variable is set in Azure, the environment credential is tried first and might use the wrong service principal.
Turn on Azure SDK logging to see which credential was tried and why each failed.
In production, I often just use ManagedIdentityCredential directly, which removes the ambiguity.

p17-947.q: "Works on my machine" with Docker usually means something in the environment is different, even though Docker's supposed to remove those differences.
p17-947.k: docker build fails in ci, works locally not in pipeline, docker build context ci, ci build differences, buildkit ci failure
x: "Works on my machine" with Docker usually means something in the environment is different, even though Docker's supposed to remove those differences.

What I compare. Build context. Locally, files that are gitignored or generated, a local NuGet config, an env file, built front-end assets, exist on disk and get copied into the build. In CI the checkout's clean, so they're missing. A dockerignore difference can do the same thing. I check what the Dockerfile copies and whether those files exist in a clean clone. Nine times out of ten, I'd say it's this.
Credentials. Private package feeds, NuGet, npm or pip, work locally through cached credentials, but CI needs tokens passed securely as BuildKit secrets.
Base image and cache. Locally an older cached base image gets used, CI pulls a newer one with changes in the OS or SDK. Pinning base image versions or digests makes builds reproducible.
Architecture. Building on an Apple Silicon Mac produces ARM images, and CI on x86 builds a different variant, where a native dependency might fail.
Network. CI agents might be behind a proxy or firewall, or have DNS that can't reach certain registries or package sources, or they hit Docker Hub rate limits.
Docker or BuildKit version and features. Secret mounts, heredocs or cache mounts need BuildKit turned on in CI.
Resources. CI agents might have less memory or disk, so you get out-of-memory during builds or "no space left on device", especially on self-hosted agents that never prune old images.
To reproduce it, I build locally from a fresh clone with no cache and the same base image versions, or run the CI agent image locally.

p17-948.q: Kubernetes runs containers with settings that differ from a plain docker run, so I compare the environments one by one, starting with kubectl describe pod and kubectl logs with the previous flag.
p17-948.k: container crashes in kubernetes not locally, works in docker fails in k8s, read only filesystem crash, non root container crash, kubernetes environment differences
x: Kubernetes runs containers with settings that differ from a plain docker run, so I compare the environments one by one, starting with kubectl describe pod and kubectl logs with the previous flag.

Common differences. Security context, that's usually the first suspect for me. Production pods often run as non-root with a read-only root file system and dropped capabilities. An app that writes temp files, logs or caches to its own folder, or binds to port 80, just fails. The fix is to write to mounted emptyDir volumes, like slash tmp, and listen on a high port, like 8080.

Configuration. Environment variables, ConfigMaps and Secrets differ from the local env file. A missing or misnamed variable, or a secret mounted as a file instead of an environment variable, makes the app fail at startup.
Resource limits. A low memory limit causes OOMKilled, and low CPU limits make startup so slow that probes fail.
Probes. Liveness probes kill the app before it finishes starting, and a startup probe or a longer initial delay fixes it.

Networking. Services are reached by Kubernetes DNS names, not localhost. Network policies might block traffic to databases or other services, and egress to external services might need proxies or firewall rules.
Architecture. An ARM image pulled on x86 nodes, or the other way round, fails with exec format error.
User and file permissions. Files copied into the image owned by root aren't readable by the non-root user.
Time zone and locale. The container uses UTC, which can change date-dependent behaviour.
Running the container locally with the same constraints, read-only, non-root, memory limits and the same environment, usually reproduces it pretty quickly.

p17-949.q: Drift means the real infrastructure doesn't match the code anymore. The danger is the next terraform apply quietly undoes the manual change, which might've been an emergency fix. Or the manual change might itself be a mistake, or even a security incident.
p17-949.k: terraform drift production, manual change console, terraform plan unexpected changes, clickops drift, reconcile terraform state
x: Drift means the real infrastructure doesn't match the code anymore. The danger is the next terraform apply quietly undoes the manual change, which might've been an emergency fix. Or the manual change might itself be a mistake, or even a security incident.
So basically, don't apply blindly. Run terraform plan, read exactly what differs, and identify the change. CloudTrail or the Azure activity log shows who changed what and when.

Talk to whoever made the change. Was it an emergency fix during an incident, an experiment, or a mistake? If nobody can explain it, I'd treat it as a possible security issue and pull in the security team.

Then decide the source of truth. If the change should stay, update the Terraform code to match it, through a normal pull request with review, and confirm plan shows no changes. If the change was wrong, apply the code to revert it, at a safe time and knowing the impact. If it touched resources Terraform doesn't manage, think about importing them with import blocks.
Preventing repeats. Restrict console write access in production, read-only roles for day-to-day, with break-glass access for emergencies that's logged and alerts the team.
Make the emergency path codified, a fast-track pipeline for urgent infrastructure changes, so people don't need the console at all.
Detect drift automatically, a scheduled plan in CI, or tools like AWS Config and Azure Policy, alerting when drift shows up.
And afterwards I add a "back-port manual changes into code" step to the incident checklist, so emergency fixes don't stay undocumented.

p17-950.q: Look, a secret in logs is a leaked secret. Logs are often readable by lots of people, kept for a long time, and sometimes copied to other systems. So I respond the same way as for a committed secret.
p17-950.k: secret in pipeline logs, leaked secret ci logs, masked secret exposed, credential in build log, ci log leak
x: Look, a secret in logs is a leaked secret. Logs are often readable by lots of people, kept for a long time, and sometimes copied to other systems. So I respond the same way as for a committed secret.

Immediately, rotate it. Revoke and replace the credential at its source, the database password, API key or token, and update it in the secret store. Rotation's the only real fix, because I can't be sure who saw the log.

Limit exposure. Delete or restrict access to the affected pipeline run logs if the platform allows, and check whether logs were forwarded somewhere else, like a log platform, and clean them there too.
Check for misuse. Review access logs for that credential during the exposure window, looking for anything unusual.

Then find out why masking failed. Pipeline platforms mask secret variables in logs, but masking fails when the secret's transformed, base64 or URL encoded, split across lines, or embedded in JSON. Or when a tool prints it in debug or verbose mode, or a script echoes environment variables or runs with set minus x. Or when the value was never marked secret at all, like a plain variable or something read from a file at runtime.

Preventing it again. Mark all sensitive values as secrets, avoid printing commands with credentials and use files or environment variables tools read directly, keep verbose debug logging off by default, prefer short-lived credentials through OIDC federation and managed identities so leaked values expire quickly, and add secret scanning for pipeline logs and artifacts.
And then a blameless review to share what happened, because honestly this is a common, easy mistake.

p17-951.q: This one's different from a normal vulnerability. A compromised package might have run malicious code on developer machines, build agents or production, for example stealing tokens or environment variables at install time.
p17-951.k: compromised npm package, malicious dependency, supply chain attack response, compromised package response, malicious package version
x: This one's different from a normal vulnerability. A compromised package might have run malicious code on developer machines, build agents or production, for example stealing tokens or environment variables at install time.

So the starting point is, are we affected? Which versions are compromised, and do any of our lock files, builds or images contain them? I search lock files across repos, our package feed's cache, and the SBOMs of built images. Lock files and pinned versions make this answerable quickly.

If we did pull a compromised version, assume any credentials on machines that installed it are exposed. Rotate the tokens and secrets available in those environments, CI variables, cloud credentials, npm or NuGet publishing tokens, developer tokens.
Remove the version. Pin to a known-good one, rebuild and redeploy affected services, and purge it from our internal feed cache so it can't be pulled again.

Investigate. Check build and runtime logs and network activity for the malicious behaviour described in the advisory, like outbound connections to unknown hosts, and bring in the security team for incident handling.
If we didn't pull it, block the bad versions in the feed and keep monitoring.

For the future, lock files with exact versions and integrity hashes, npm ci instead of npm install in builds, install scripts disabled where possible, an internal proxy feed with a delay or approval before new versions get used, minimal permissions and short-lived credentials on build agents, and SBOMs for every build. That way "are we affected?" gets answered in minutes, which I think is the real goal.

p17-952.q: Bundle size jumps usually come from a single change, so I just compare before and after.
p17-952.k: bundle size increased, javascript bundle doubled, webpack vite bundle regression, large dependency added, bundle analysis
x: Bundle size jumps usually come from a single change, so I just compare before and after.

Find what changed. Build the previous commit and the new one with a bundle analyser, like the rollup visualizer plugin for Vite or the webpack bundle analyser, and compare the treemaps. The new big block is usually obvious.
Typical causes. A new heavy dependency, a charting, date, PDF or editor library, imported into the main bundle.

Importing a whole library instead of a part. Pulling in an entire icon set or utility library rather than named or per-file imports, or a CommonJS package that can't be tree-shaken. That one can catch people out with icon libraries.
Duplicated dependencies. Two versions of the same library, like React, MUI or lodash, because an internal package declared it as a dependency instead of a peer dependency.
Lost code splitting. A lazy-loaded route or component that's now imported statically somewhere, which pulls it into the main chunk.
Assets inlined, large images, fonts or JSON files imported into JavaScript.
Development code in production, a debug tool or mock data included by accident.
The fix follows the cause. Lazy-load heavy features, switch to lighter libraries, fix imports, align versions with peer dependencies and deduplication, and move large data to separate fetched files.

And for prevention, a size budget check in CI with something like size-limit or bundle budgets, which comments on pull requests with the size difference and fails past a threshold. Then the reviewer sees the impact before merging, instead of users finding out through a slower app.

p17-953.q: This is usually a check-then-insert race, you know. The code checks whether a record exists, finds nothing, and inserts. Two requests arriving at the same moment both pass the check before either inserts, so both insert. It happens with double-clicks, retries from clients or gateways, and parallel message consumers.
p17-953.k: duplicate records concurrency, race condition insert, check then insert race, unique constraint fix duplicates, concurrent duplicate rows
x: This is usually a check-then-insert race, you know. The code checks whether a record exists, finds nothing, and inserts. Two requests arriving at the same moment both pass the check before either inserts, so both insert. It happens with double-clicks, retries from clients or gateways, and parallel message consumers.
To confirm it, look at the timestamps of the duplicate rows, often milliseconds apart, and at logs showing two requests or two message deliveries.

Fixes, usually combined. A unique constraint in the database, that's the real guarantee. Add a unique index on the business key, like kit number per study, or on an idempotency key. The second insert fails with a duplicate key error, which the code catches and handles, returning the existing record or a 409. Before adding it to an existing table, clean up existing duplicates carefully, with business input on which record to keep.
Upsert or atomic operations. An insert with a not-exists condition in a single statement, or a merge with proper locking hints, rather than separate select and insert round trips.
Idempotency keys for APIs. Clients send a unique key per operation, and the server stores it with the result and returns the same result for repeats.
Idempotent message handling. Record processed message ids in the same transaction as the business change.
Locking, for complex cases, an application lock, like sp_getapplock in SQL Server or a distributed lock, around the critical section, though constraints are simpler and more reliable.
UI help. Disable the submit button while a request's in progress, which reduces duplicates but doesn't eliminate them.
Then I add a concurrency test that fires parallel requests to prove the fix.

p17-954.q: Redis is single-threaded for command execution, so one slow command blocks everything else. A really large key, like a hash with millions of fields, a list with hundreds of thousands of items, or a multi-megabyte string, makes commands on it slow, and every client waits.
p17-954.k: redis big key, redis latency spike, redis hot key, redis bigkeys, large redis value
x: Redis is single-threaded for command execution, so one slow command blocks everything else. A really large key, like a hash with millions of fields, a list with hundreds of thousands of items, or a multi-megabyte string, makes commands on it slow, and every client waits.
Finding it. redis-cli with the bigkeys or memkeys option scans the keyspace and reports the largest keys per type, and MEMORY USAGE on a key shows its size.
SLOWLOG GET shows recent slow commands and their arguments, which often points straight at things like HGETALL, SMEMBERS or LRANGE on huge keys, or a DEL of a big key.
LATENCY DOCTOR and monitoring tools show the spikes and their timing.
Cloud services, ElastiCache or Azure Cache for Redis, expose metrics for CPU, latency and network that highlight it.
Hot keys are a related issue. A normal-sized key that's read extremely often, concentrating load on one shard in a cluster. The hotkeys option, with an LFU eviction policy, helps find them.
Fixing. Split big keys. Shard a large hash or set into multiple keys by a bucket, like site id modulo 100, or store items as separate keys.
Avoid full reads. Use HSCAN, SSCAN or ranged reads instead of fetching everything at once, and fetch only the fields you need.
Delete safely. UNLINK instead of DEL, which frees memory in the background. I've seen a single DEL on a huge key freeze things for a noticeable moment.
Reduce value size, compress, or store only what's needed.
For hot keys, an in-process cache in front of Redis, or replicating the key across several keys and picking one at random.
Then monitoring on key sizes and slow log entries, so it doesn't creep back.

p17-955.q: My approach is evidence from our side first, then work with the partner on theirs.
