p17-955.k: webhook not received, partner missed callbacks, webhook delivery failure, outgoing webhook debugging, callback not delivered
x: My approach is evidence from our side first, then work with the partner on theirs.
Our side. Did we send it? Check that the business event happened and a webhook was created for it, in the outbox or delivery table, with the partner's endpoint and payload.
What happened on delivery? Our delivery log should have each attempt, time, URL, response status, response time and error. If there's no such log, that's the first improvement to make.

Common findings. The partner's endpoint returned errors, 401, 404 or 500, maybe after they changed URLs, credentials or certificates. Timeouts because their endpoint's slow. TLS errors, like they renewed a certificate with an incomplete chain or dropped an older TLS version. DNS changes on their side. Our outbound IP changed and their firewall allow-list blocks the new one. Or our retry policy gave up and the delivery went to a dead-letter state nobody was watching.
Configuration. The subscription might point to an old endpoint, or got disabled after repeated failures.

Their side. Share exact timestamps, request ids and signature details, so they can search their gateway and application logs. Sometimes requests actually arrived but their signature validation failed, or their system dropped them silently.
Recovery. Once it's fixed, replay the missed events from our delivery store, in order, idempotently, with their agreement.

Improvements, a delivery dashboard per partner, alerts on consecutive failures, a self-service endpoint for partners to view and replay deliveries, documented static outbound IPs, and a reconciliation API they can call to fetch events they might've missed.

p17-956.q: When a canary shows more errors, I'd say the safest move is to pause or roll back the canary straight away, since only a small slice of traffic is affected and the stable version's still there. Then I can investigate without pressure.
p17-956.k: canary errors some users, canary release higher errors, partial rollout errors, segment specific errors, canary analysis
x: When a canary shows more errors, I'd say the safest move is to pause or roll back the canary straight away, since only a small slice of traffic is affected and the stable version's still there. Then I can investigate without pressure.

Narrow down who's affected. Break errors down by dimensions in logs and metrics, endpoint, client version, browser or app version, tenant, study, region, user role, request characteristics. A canary often shows problems that only certain data or clients trigger.
Typical causes. Data-dependent bugs, where the new code fails on edge cases in some records, like null fields, old data formats or special characters that test data didn't have.
Client compatibility. Older mobile app or front-end versions send requests the new API doesn't accept anymore, or expect fields that changed.
Session or affinity issues. Users bouncing between canary and stable mid-session, where the two versions disagree on cookies, cache formats or token handling.
Configuration differences. The canary has different settings, feature flags or secrets.
Dependency limits. The new version calls a downstream service differently, hitting rate limits or timeouts for heavy users.
Schema mismatch. The canary expects a database change, or writes data the stable version can't read.
Then I reproduce it with the specific failing inputs, using trace ids from the errors to find the exact requests, fix it, add a test with that data, and release a new canary.

Process improvements, automated canary analysis comparing error rates and latency between canary and stable per segment, sticky routing so users stay on one version, and canaries that start with internal users.

p17-957.q: If throughput flattens but CPU isn't busy, the system's waiting on something, so I look for whatever's queuing.
p17-957.k: throughput plateau load test, low cpu bottleneck, load test saturation, connection pool bottleneck, scalability limit
x: If throughput flattens but CPU isn't busy, the system's waiting on something, so I look for whatever's queuing.

Connection pools. Database connection pools at their max, with requests waiting for a connection. Metrics like pool wait time, or active connections sitting at the limit, show it. Same for HTTP client connection limits per server to a downstream service.
The database or a downstream service. The bottleneck might simply be somewhere else. I check database CPU, waits, blocking and slow queries, and downstream latency in traces.
Locks and contention. A lock in the code, a single-threaded section, or database row and table locks serialising work. Traces with long waits but little actual work point here.

Thread pool starvation in .NET, honestly I'd check this early. Blocking calls, like dot Result or synchronous I/O, keep threads busy waiting. The thread pool grows slowly, so requests queue while CPU stays low, and dotnet-counters shows the thread pool queue length growing.
Rate limits and throttling, API gateways, cloud services, or our own rate limiter capping throughput.
Network and load balancer limits, bandwidth, connection limits, or too few load generator machines. I always check the load test tool itself isn't the bottleneck.
Single partition or queue, messaging with one partition or one consumer, or a hot key in a cache or database.

The method is increase load step by step, watching latency and every resource. The first resource to saturate, or the first queue to grow, is the bottleneck. Fix it, then repeat, because the next one shows up once the first is gone.
Results go into capacity planning, known limits per instance and which component to scale.

p17-958.q: Let me start with confirming it's a real leak and where the memory actually is. Using metrics or dotnet-counters, I look at GC heap size after collections, generation 2 size, and the large object heap. If the managed heap keeps growing after full collections, it's a managed leak. If process memory grows but the GC heap doesn't, it's native memory, like unmanaged buffers, native libraries or too many threads.
p17-958.k: dotnet memory leak production, memory grows until restart, managed memory leak, gc heap growing, dotnet-dump analyze
x: Let me start with confirming it's a real leak and where the memory actually is. Using metrics or dotnet-counters, I look at GC heap size after collections, generation 2 size, and the large object heap. If the managed heap keeps growing after full collections, it's a managed leak. If process memory grows but the GC heap doesn't, it's native memory, like unmanaged buffers, native libraries or too many threads.

For a managed leak, I take memory snapshots at two points, say after 30 minutes and after 3 hours, with dotnet-gcdump, which is lightweight, or a full dump with dotnet-dump. Comparing them in Visual Studio, PerfView or dotnet-dump analyze shows which types grew in count and size. Then the GC root path for a sample object shows what's keeping it alive.
Common culprits I find this way. Event handlers on long-lived objects, static events or singleton services, that short-lived objects subscribe to and never unsubscribe from.
Unbounded caches, a static dictionary or MemoryCache without size limits or expiry, often keyed by something unbounded like a user or request id.
Captive dependencies, singletons holding scoped services, like a DbContext that keeps tracking entities forever.
Timers and background tasks capturing objects.
HttpClient or other disposable objects created again and again without disposal.
Large strings or byte arrays held on to by logging or buffering.

The fix depends on the cause, and then I verify with a soak test, running the service under steady load for hours and watching memory level off. Meanwhile, a memory alert and controlled restarts limit the impact.

p17-959.q: Ah, this is a classic SQL Server puzzle, and the usual answer is that the two are getting different execution plans.
p17-959.k: fast in ssms slow in app, arithabort, slow from application fast in management studio, parameter sniffing app, different execution plans
x: Ah, this is a classic SQL Server puzzle, and the usual answer is that the two are getting different execution plans.

Why the plans differ. SET options. SSMS sets ARITHABORT on by default, while ADO.NET connections use ARITHABORT off. Plans are cached per combination of SET options, so the application and SSMS use separate plans, even for the same query.

Parameter sniffing. The application's cached plan was compiled for unusual parameter values, like a site with very few rows, and that plan performs badly for typical values. In SSMS you might test with literal values or a fresh compile and get a good plan.

Parameter data types. The application sends nvarchar parameters for varchar columns, causing implicit conversions that prevent index seeks, while the SSMS test uses literals of the right type. That one can catch people out with ORMs.
Local variables versus parameters. Testing in SSMS with local variables gives estimates based on averages, which differs from how parameters are optimised.

How I diagnose it. Find the application's actual plan, from Query Store or the plan cache, by query hash, and compare it with the SSMS plan. To reproduce in SSMS, I match the SET options, turn ARITHABORT off, and use the same parameterised form, with sp_executesql and the same parameter types.

Fixes, correct parameter types in the application, like specifying varchar with a length in Dapper or EF Core mappings. Better indexes so one plan works for all values. OPTION RECOMPILE for queries with very different parameter distributions. Or forcing a known good plan in Query Store as a short-term fix.
Just never fix it by clearing the whole plan cache in production. That only hides the problem for a while.

p17-960.q: If it works from other environments but times out from production, it's almost always the network path or configuration, not the code.
p17-960.k: partner api timeout production only, outbound connectivity production, firewall proxy timeout, tls handshake timeout, works from test not prod
x: If it works from other environments but times out from production, it's almost always the network path or configuration, not the code.

What I do is reproduce from a production host. Run a simple request with curl or PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest from the same server or container, with verbose output. Does DNS resolve? Does the TCP connection open? Does the TLS handshake finish? Where exactly does it hang?
DNS. Production might use different DNS servers that resolve the partner's name to another address, or can't resolve it at all.

Firewall and egress rules. Production usually has stricter outbound rules. A new partner endpoint or a changed IP isn't allowed, so connections hang until timeout instead of failing fast. The network team can check the firewall logs.
Proxy. Production servers might have to go through a corporate proxy and the app isn't configured to use it, or the proxy blocks the destination or breaks things with TLS inspection.
Partner allow-listing. The partner only accepts connections from known IPs, and our production outbound IP, through NAT or the firewall, isn't on their list, or it changed.

TLS. Production servers might have older TLS settings or missing intermediate certificates in the trust store, so the handshake fails. Or the partner needs a client certificate that's only set up in test.
MTU and packet issues over VPN, which cause hangs on larger requests. That one's sneaky, honestly.

Once found, the fix is usually a firewall rule, proxy config or allow-list update. I document the required network paths per integration, and add a synthetic check from production to each partner endpoint, so we know before the business does.

p17-961.q: So when Angular apps are embedded into server-rendered pages, they share the same document with the host, and changes in the host can break them.
p17-961.k: angular sub app broken by host page, embedded angular conflicts, global css conflict, jquery conflict angular, micro frontend isolation
x: So when Angular apps are embedded into server-rendered pages, they share the same document with the host, and changes in the host can break them.
Typical causes. Global CSS. The host adds or changes styles, a CSS reset, a new theme, or generic selectors like button or table, which override the sub-app's styling.

Global JavaScript. A new or upgraded script, like a different jQuery version, a polyfill, or a library that patches built-in objects, conflicts with Angular or zone.js. Two copies of zone.js from different sub-apps also cause really strange behaviour.
DOM expectations. The sub-app expects a specific container element id or data attribute that the host changed or removed.
Configuration passed through the page. The host renders config, API base URLs, tokens or user context, into the page, and the format changed.
Base href and routing. A change in the page path breaks the sub-app's router or asset paths.
Content Security Policy changes that block inline scripts or styles the sub-app needs.
Fixing and preventing it. Define a contract between host and sub-app, the mount element, the shape of the config object and the events used for communication, documented and versioned.
Isolate styles. Prefix sub-app styles, use Angular's view encapsulation, and avoid global styles in the sub-app. For strong isolation, Angular Elements with Shadow DOM.
Avoid global dependencies, and load one shared zone.js.
End-to-end smoke tests that load each sub-app inside the real host page, running in the host's pipeline, so host changes get tested against sub-apps before release.
And this is also one of the reasons for moving to a single React shell with packaged features, I'd say.

p17-962.q: A common cause, a Lambda triggered by S3 object creation writes its output into the same bucket, or the same prefix, which triggers it again, forever. Similar loops happen with SQS, where a function sends to the queue that triggers it, or SNS and EventBridge rules that match the function's own events.
p17-962.k: lambda recursive loop, lambda infinite loop s3, lambda cost spike loop, recursive invocation detection, s3 trigger loop
x: A common cause, a Lambda triggered by S3 object creation writes its output into the same bucket, or the same prefix, which triggers it again, forever. Similar loops happen with SQS, where a function sends to the queue that triggers it, or SNS and EventBridge rules that match the function's own events.

Immediate actions, because every minute costs money. Stop the loop. Set the function's reserved concurrency to zero, which throttles all invocations immediately. Or disable the trigger, the event source mapping or S3 notification.
Check side effects. How many objects or messages got created, and clean them up carefully, so the cleanup doesn't trigger anything else.
Check costs and limits. Lambda, S3 requests, CloudWatch Logs ingestion and downstream services might all have spiked.
Then fix the design. Separate input and output, write output to a different bucket, or a different prefix with the trigger filtered to the input prefix only.
Use event filtering, so the function only gets the events it should process.
Mark processed items, with metadata or tags, and skip them.

Guardrails. Lambda's recursive loop detection stops some loops automatically after a number of recursive invocations, for supported services like SQS and SNS, but not every pattern, so honestly I don't rely on it.
Reserved concurrency limits on functions, so a runaway can't scale forever.
Budgets and cost anomaly detection alerts, plus CloudWatch alarms on invocation counts per function compared with normal levels.
And code review of trigger configuration in infrastructure as code, checking specifically for loops.

p17-963.q: The first thing I run is kubectl describe hpa, which shows current and target metrics, conditions and events, and usually tells you the reason.
p17-963.k: hpa not scaling, horizontal pod autoscaler not working, hpa unknown metrics, kubernetes autoscaling not triggering, hpa troubleshooting
x: The first thing I run is kubectl describe hpa, which shows current and target metrics, conditions and events, and usually tells you the reason.

Common causes. Metrics unavailable, the current metric shows unknown. The metrics server isn't installed or healthy, or for custom metrics, the adapter, Prometheus Adapter or KEDA, isn't working or the metric name's wrong.
Missing resource requests. CPU utilisation targets are percentages of requests, so if pods have no CPU request, the HPA can't calculate utilisation and won't scale.
Requests set too high. If a pod requests 2 CPUs but uses 0.5 under heavy load, utilisation looks like 25 percent and never crosses a 70 percent target. That one can catch people out.

Wrong metric. The service is limited by something other than CPU, I/O, a connection pool or queue depth, so CPU never rises even though users are suffering. Scaling on requests per second, latency or queue length, with custom metrics or KEDA, fits better.
Max replicas reached, the HPA's already at its max.
Pods can't be scheduled. The HPA raised the desired count, but new pods are Pending because the cluster has no capacity, and the node autoscaler is slow, misconfigured or at its limit.
Scaling behaviour. Stabilisation windows and scale-up policies limit how fast it scales, and the defaults can feel slow for sudden spikes.
Readiness. New pods take a long time to become ready, so the HPA sees little relief and the effect lags.
After the fix, I load test to confirm scaling kicks in at the right point, and alert when the HPA sits at max replicas for a sustained period.

p17-964.q: "Too many open files", error EMFILE, means the process hit its limit on file descriptors. And on Linux, sockets count as files too, so this is often a connection leak, not really a file problem.
p17-964.k: too many open files python, emfile error, file descriptor leak, ulimit nofile, socket leak python
x: "Too many open files", error EMFILE, means the process hit its limit on file descriptors. And on Linux, sockets count as files too, so this is often a connection leak, not really a file problem.

Investigation. Count open descriptors over time, list the process's fd folder under proc and count it, or use lsof on the PID, and look at what they are. Regular files, TCP sockets to a particular host, pipes. A steadily rising count means something isn't getting closed.
Check the limit with ulimit or the process's limits file. Defaults like 1,024 can be too low for busy services.
Common causes in Python. Opening files without with statements or close calls, especially in error paths.

Creating a new HTTP session or client per request, a requests Session or an httpx Client, without closing it, which leaves sockets open. I've seen this one a lot. The fix is one shared client with connection pooling, closed on shutdown.
Database connections or cursors not returned to the pool, or creating engines again and again in SQLAlchemy instead of once.
Subprocesses with pipes that aren't closed or waited on.
Too much concurrency, an async service opening thousands of simultaneous connections without a semaphore limit.

Fixes, fix the leak with context managers and shared clients, limit concurrency, and raise the descriptor limit sensibly, in the container or systemd settings, as a capacity setting, not as a leak fix.
Monitoring, export open file descriptor counts as a metric, which most Prometheus client libraries do automatically for processes, and alert when it gets close to the limit.

p17-965.q: Well, a green pipeline only means the steps didn't report errors, so I check what actually happened on the targets.
p17-965.k: deployment succeeded old code running, pipeline green but not deployed, iis old version after deploy, stale deployment, release did not update
x: Well, a green pipeline only means the steps didn't report errors, so I check what actually happened on the targets.
What I verify straight away is the version endpoint, or the assembly and file version on each server, to see which servers have the old version, all of them or only some.
Common causes. Wrong artifact, the release picked an older build, like "latest" from the wrong branch, or a cached artifact.
Deployment to the wrong target. A variable pointing to another environment, server group or deployment slot, or a server missing from the deployment group.

Files locked or not replaced on IIS. The app pool kept files locked, so the copy step skipped or failed silently on some files, especially with tasks set to continue on error. Taking the app offline with an app offline file, or stopping the app pool during deployment, fixes it.
App not restarted. Files changed, but the process still runs the old code, like a Windows service or worker that wasn't restarted, or IIS shadow copying behaviour.
Load balancer pointing to old instances, a blue-green or slot setup where traffic wasn't switched.
Caching, output caching, CDN or browser cache serving old content.
Agent issues, a self-hosted agent with an old working directory, or the deployment step running on a different machine than expected.

Fixes. Deployment steps that fail loudly instead of continuing on error. Post-deployment verification that calls each instance's version endpoint and fails the pipeline if versions don't match the build. Immutable artifacts with build numbers, and smoke tests after deployment. Then a green pipeline actually means the new code's running.

p17-966.q: When a job that ran at 2 AM on a server suddenly runs at 7:30 or 8:30, nine times out of ten it's time zones.
p17-966.k: scheduled job wrong time, container time zone utc, cron wrong hour, daylight saving job time, quartz time zone container
x: When a job that ran at 2 AM on a server suddenly runs at 7:30 or 8:30, nine times out of ten it's time zones.

Containers run in UTC by default. Windows and Linux servers on-premise usually ran in the local time zone, so a cron expression for 2 AM meant 2 AM local. In a container, the same expression means 2 AM UTC, which is a different local time, and the gap shifts with daylight saving in regions that have it.

Other places it shows up. Code using DateTime Now or local time to decide what to process, like "yesterday's records", which now uses UTC boundaries. Log timestamps that look shifted. Reports cut off at the wrong day boundary.

Fixes. Be explicit about time zones in schedules. Quartz.NET lets you set a time zone on cron triggers, Kubernetes CronJobs have a time zone field, and cloud schedulers like EventBridge Scheduler and Azure Functions let you specify time zones.
Pick the right zone per job. Business jobs tied to a local day, like a site's end-of-day processing, should use that region's time zone, and technical jobs can use UTC.
In code, use UTC for storage and logic, and convert to local time zones explicitly where business rules need it, with DateTimeOffset and TimeZoneInfo, or TimeProvider for testability.
My rule is don't fix it by setting the container's time zone to local as a blanket solution. That hides the problem and causes inconsistencies between services.
And test schedules around daylight saving transitions, where jobs can run twice or get skipped in local time.

p17-967.q: Okay, so when slowness is tied to one location, the code's usually fine and the network path is what's different, but I verify instead of assuming.
p17-967.k: slow from one office, location specific slowness, network latency office, regional performance issue, vpn proxy slow
x: Okay, so when slowness is tied to one location, the code's usually fine and the network path is what's different, but I verify instead of assuming.

Gather facts. Which office, since when, all pages or some, all users there or some, and at what times. If the timing lines up with a change, a new proxy, VPN, or network upgrade, that's a strong clue.
Compare measurements. Server-side response times for those users' requests, using logs filtered by their IP range. If server time is normal, the delay's on the network or client side.

Front-end timing. Real user monitoring, or browser dev tools from an affected user, show where the time goes. DNS lookup, TCP connect, TLS handshake, waiting for the first byte, or downloading content. Big downloads over a slow link point to bandwidth, long connection setup points to latency or proxies.
Common causes. A corporate proxy or security inspection, TLS inspection or antivirus scanning web traffic, adding delay per request.
VPN routing, where traffic from that office goes through a distant VPN gateway or data centre.
Distance and latency to the hosting region, multiplied by lots of sequential requests from a chatty front end. That multiplication is what people forget.
DNS resolving to a far-away endpoint.
Local network congestion, Wi-Fi problems, or bandwidth limits.

The fix depends on the cause. Working with the network team on routing or proxy exceptions for our domains, a CDN for static assets, fewer requests and smaller payloads, compression and caching, and for global users, hosting closer to them.
Adding a synthetic monitor from that region helps confirm the fix and catch regressions later.

p17-968.q: Yeah, this pattern points really strongly to ASP.NET Core Data Protection keys not being shared between instances.
p17-968.k: random 401 multiple instances, data protection keys load balancer, antiforgery token error scale out, cookie decryption failed, shared data protection keys
x: Yeah, this pattern points really strongly to ASP.NET Core Data Protection keys not being shared between instances.

ASP.NET Core uses Data Protection to encrypt and sign auth cookies, antiforgery tokens, TempData and a few other values. By default, each instance generates its own key ring, stored locally, in memory, in the user profile or in the container's file system. So when a user's cookie was created by instance A and the next request goes to instance B, B can't decrypt it. The user looks logged out, gets 401s, or antiforgery validation fails. It looks random because it depends on which instance the load balancer picks.
It also happens after deployments or container restarts, when keys stored inside the container are lost and every existing cookie becomes invalid.

The fix is to configure Data Protection to persist keys to a shared location and protect them. Persist keys to Redis, to a DbContext, to Azure Blob Storage, or to a file share for IIS servers, combined with protecting keys with a certificate, Azure Key Vault or AWS KMS, so keys aren't stored in plain text. And set the same application name on all instances that should share cookies.
Related things to check, sticky sessions hiding the problem until the instance count changes, in-memory session state not shared, and clock differences between servers affecting token validation.

In .NET Framework apps on IIS farms, the equivalent problem is mismatched machine key settings in web config across servers, causing ViewState and forms authentication errors, and you solve it by configuring the same machine key everywhere.

p17-969.q: Indexes speed up reads, but every index has to be maintained on every insert, every update of its columns, and every delete. So a new index can hurt write-heavy tables, and creating it can cause blocking by itself.
p17-969.k: new index slowed writes, index overhead inserts, too many indexes, index caused blocking, write performance index
x: Indexes speed up reads, but every index has to be maintained on every insert, every update of its columns, and every delete. So a new index can hurt write-heavy tables, and creating it can cause blocking by itself.

What might've happened. Creation blocking. Building an index offline takes locks that block writes on the table for the whole build, which on a big table can be many minutes. Online index creation, where the edition supports it, avoids most of that.

Write overhead. A busy table with lots of indexes now does more work per write. If the new index includes frequently updated columns, every update touches it, which increases log volume, I/O and lock duration.
Lock contention and deadlocks. More indexes means more structures locked during writes, which can increase blocking and deadlocks, especially when different queries hit indexes in different orders.
Page splits. An index on a random key, like a GUID, causes fragmentation and page splits during inserts.
Plan changes. The optimiser started using the new index for some queries and produced worse plans, like key lookups on many rows.

What I do is confirm with wait stats, blocking reports and Query Store whether write latency went up after the change. Short term, drop or disable the index if it's causing an incident, since it was a recent change. Then review. Does an important query actually need it? Can an existing index be extended with INCLUDE columns instead? Can unused or duplicate indexes be removed to compensate?
Prevention, test index changes with realistic write load, check index usage stats regularly, and create indexes online during quiet hours.

p17-970.q: A failed migration can leave the schema in an unknown state, so I go carefully instead of rerunning things blindly.
p17-970.k: ef core migration failed production, partial migration, migration rollback ef core, database migration failure, schema change failed
x: A failed migration can leave the schema in an unknown state, so I go carefully instead of rerunning things blindly.

Assess the state. Check the EF migrations history table to see whether the migration got recorded, and compare the actual schema with what the migration intended, to see which steps went through. EF Core wraps each migration in a transaction on SQL Server, so often the whole thing rolled back cleanly. But some operations can't run inside transactions, or the migration might have raw SQL with its own transaction handling, so partial application is possible.

Check the application. Is the running version compatible with the current schema? If the deployment stopped before the new code went live, the old code's probably fine. If not, roll the app back to the previous version.
Recovering. If nothing was applied, fix the cause, a timeout on a large table, a data issue violating a new constraint, or missing permissions, and rerun.
If it's partially applied, write a script to either finish the remaining steps or undo the applied ones, reviewed and tested on a restored copy of production first, then apply it.
If data got damaged, restore from backup to a point before the migration, as a last resort.
Prevention, and honestly this is where I'm strict. Generate idempotent SQL scripts from migrations, review them, and run them through the pipeline, not from application startup.
Test migrations against a production-sized copy, measuring duration and locks.
Keep migrations small and backward compatible, expand-and-contract, so the old app version works with the new schema.
And take a backup or snapshot right before production migrations.

p17-971.q: Recovery comes first. Roll back to the previous image or version, which works if each deployment is an immutable artifact. Then find what changed by comparing installed package versions between the good and bad builds, with pip freeze or the lock files.
p17-971.k: python dependency broke production, unpinned dependencies, transitive dependency update, lock file python, reproducible builds python
x: Recovery comes first. Roll back to the previous image or version, which works if each deployment is an immutable artifact. Then find what changed by comparing installed package versions between the good and bad builds, with pip freeze or the lock files.

Why didn't tests catch it? Unpinned or loosely pinned dependencies, basically. The requirements file had ranges, or only top-level packages were pinned, so the production build installed a newer version of a transitive dependency than tests ran with. Builds weren't reproducible.
Different environments. Production uses a different Python version, OS or architecture, so a compiled package behaves differently or a wheel's missing.

Behaviour tests don't cover, like serialisation formats, default timeouts, or deprecation changes in a library such as Pydantic, SQLAlchemy or requests, which only matter with real data or integrations.
Prevention. Lock files. Use uv, Poetry or pip-tools to lock every package, transitive ones included, with hashes. Build from the lock file, so CI and production install exactly the same versions.
Build once. Create the container image once in CI, test that exact image, and promote it, instead of reinstalling packages per environment.
Controlled updates. Renovate or Dependabot propose upgrades as pull requests, one or a few at a time, with changelogs, so tests run against each change and a failure points to one package.
Integration and contract tests that exercise real serialisation, database access and external calls.
Staged rollout, canary or test environments get upgrades first, with monitoring.
The same discipline applies to npm and NuGet too. Lock files, build once, promote the same artifact.

p17-972.q: Third-party scripts, analytics, chat widgets, tag managers, feedback tools, they run with full access to the page. So if they're slow, buggy or compromised, our app suffers even though we didn't change a thing.
p17-972.k: third party script broke page, external javascript risk, tag manager performance, subresource integrity, csp third party scripts
x: Third-party scripts, analytics, chat widgets, tag managers, feedback tools, they run with full access to the page. So if they're slow, buggy or compromised, our app suffers even though we didn't change a thing.
Immediate response, identify the script using the browser's network and performance panels and console errors, and turn it off, through the tag manager or a feature flag, to get the page back.
Protecting against slowness. Load scripts asynchronously with async or defer, and load the non-essential ones after the main content, so they don't block rendering.
Measure their impact with real user monitoring and Lighthouse, and set a performance budget for third parties.
Use facades. Show a lightweight placeholder, like a static chat button, and load the heavy widget only when the user interacts. Honestly that trick alone saves a lot.
Protecting against breakage and attacks. Content Security Policy, allow scripts only from approved domains, so injected or unexpected scripts can't run.
Subresource Integrity. For scripts loaded from CDNs with fixed versions, the integrity attribute makes the browser refuse a file that changed.
Self-host critical libraries instead of pulling them from external CDNs.
Govern the tag manager. Changes reviewed like code, with limited access, because anyone who can add a tag can run code in our app.
Privacy and compliance. Scripts that send user data to third parties need review, especially in healthcare and clinical contexts, where pages might show sensitive information.
Error isolation, wrap integrations so their errors don't break our code, and monitor console errors from production.
And I prefer fewer third-party scripts in general, each with a clear owner and purpose.

p17-973.q: Health checks are supposed to protect availability, but badly designed ones can actually cause outages.
p17-973.k: health check causing outage, deep health check load, health check database calls, cascading failure health checks, liveness dependency checks
x: Health checks are supposed to protect availability, but badly designed ones can actually cause outages.

What usually goes wrong. Deep checks in liveness probes. The liveness endpoint checks the database, Redis and downstream APIs. When the database is slow for a moment, every instance's liveness check fails, Kubernetes or the load balancer restarts or removes all instances at once, and a small database hiccup turns into a total outage. Then instances restarting together put even more load on the database as they reconnect and warm up. I've seen exactly this happen, and it's not fun.

Expensive checks called too often. Each check runs real queries, and with many instances, several load balancers and monitoring tools all calling it every few seconds, the checks put real load on shared dependencies.
Checks calling other services' health checks, creating chains where one slow service makes everything look unhealthy.
No timeouts in the check, so it hangs and ties up threads.
Better design. Liveness is only "is this process alive and able to respond", no external dependencies.
Readiness is, can this instance serve traffic? It can check critical local requirements, but be careful with shared dependencies, because pulling every instance out of rotation helps nobody.
A separate detailed diagnostics endpoint for humans and monitoring, protected, not used by load balancers, with results cached for a few seconds so frequent calls don't hit dependencies every time.
Timeouts on each dependency check, and graceful degradation, report degraded rather than unhealthy when a non-critical dependency fails.
In ASP.NET Core, health check tags let me map different checks to liveness and readiness endpoints, which makes this separation easy.

p17-974.q: So a retry storm is when a service starts failing or slowing down, and its callers respond by retrying, which multiplies the traffic on the service that's already struggling. If each layer in a chain retries three times, one user request can become dozens of calls at the bottom. The service never recovers, because the load just keeps rising.
p17-974.k: retry storm, retries amplify outage, exponential backoff jitter, retry budget, thundering herd retries
x: So a retry storm is when a service starts failing or slowing down, and its callers respond by retrying, which multiplies the traffic on the service that's already struggling. If each layer in a chain retries three times, one user request can become dozens of calls at the bottom. The service never recovers, because the load just keeps rising.

How it usually plays out. The database slows down, API calls time out, the API's clients retry immediately, the gateway retries too, and the front end retries as well. Load triples or worse at the worst possible time.
Prevention. Exponential backoff with jitter, wait longer between each retry, with some randomness, so retries spread out instead of arriving in synchronised waves.
Limit retries. A few attempts, only for transient errors, and only for idempotent operations.
Retry at one layer. Decide where retries happen, usually closest to the failing call, and don't stack them at every layer. People miss this one a lot.
Retry budgets, allow retries only up to a percentage of normal traffic, like 10 percent, so retries can't multiply the load.
Circuit breakers. After repeated failures, stop calling the failing service for a while and fail fast, giving it room to recover.
Respect Retry-After headers and 429 or 503 responses.
Timeouts that fit together, outer timeouts longer than inner ones, so callers don't give up and retry while the inner call's still running.
Load shedding on the server, reject excess requests quickly when overloaded, rather than queuing everything.
In .NET, Polly and the standard resilience handler in .NET 8 give you backoff with jitter, circuit breakers and timeouts, which I configure deliberately instead of leaving defaults on every client.

p17-975.q: If messages are piling up but the consumer's CPU is barely used, it's spending its time waiting, not working. So I look at what it's waiting on.
p17-975.k: consumer slow cpu idle, rabbitmq prefetch 1, sequential message processing, consumer throughput low, queue backlog low cpu
x: If messages are piling up but the consumer's CPU is barely used, it's spending its time waiting, not working. So I look at what it's waiting on.

Processing one message at a time, that's the most common one in my experience. A prefetch count of one with sequential processing means each message waits for the full round trip, receive, process, call the database, acknowledge. If each message spends 50 milliseconds mostly waiting on I/O, one consumer handles at most 20 a second. Increasing prefetch and processing several messages concurrently, with a sensible limit, often multiplies throughput.
Slow downstream calls. Each message calls an API or database that's slow, and traces show where the time goes. Fixes include batching database writes, caching reference data, and fixing slow queries.
Synchronous I/O or locks, blocking calls in async code, or a lock around shared state that serialises processing.
Too few consumers or partitions. One consumer instance, or in Kafka, fewer partitions than the consumers you want, so the extra consumers just sit idle.
Acknowledgement overhead, acknowledging each message individually with a round trip, where batched acknowledgements would help.
Network latency between consumer and broker or database, like a consumer running in a different region or data centre.
Throttling, a rate limiter, or the broker applying flow control.

After changes, I measure throughput, processing time per message and queue depth, and make sure higher concurrency doesn't break ordering guarantees or overload the database. For ordered processing, I'd say parallelise across keys, like per site or study, while keeping order within each key.

p17-976.q: Ah, this is a classic redirect loop with TLS offloading. The load balancer terminates HTTPS and forwards requests to the app over plain HTTP. The app sees HTTP, thinks the user isn't on HTTPS, and redirects to the HTTPS URL. The browser follows it, the load balancer forwards it as HTTP again, and round and round it goes until the browser gives up.
p17-976.k: too many redirects load balancer, redirect loop https, x-forwarded-proto, https redirection behind proxy, ssl offloading redirect loop
x: Ah, this is a classic redirect loop with TLS offloading. The load balancer terminates HTTPS and forwards requests to the app over plain HTTP. The app sees HTTP, thinks the user isn't on HTTPS, and redirects to the HTTPS URL. The browser follows it, the load balancer forwards it as HTTP again, and round and round it goes until the browser gives up.
The fix is making the app aware of the original scheme. Load balancers add the X-Forwarded-Proto header, set to https, along with X-Forwarded-For with the client IP.

In ASP.NET Core, use the forwarded headers middleware early in the pipeline, set to include the forwarded proto and forwarded for headers, and configure known proxies or known networks so the app only trusts these headers from the load balancer, not from clients. Then HTTPS redirection, HSTS, generated URLs and cookie security flags all work properly. On IIS with the ASP.NET Core Module, some of this is handled automatically, but extra proxies in front still need configuring.
In .NET Framework apps on IIS, URL Rewrite rules that redirect to HTTPS have to check the X-Forwarded-Proto header rather than the HTTPS server variable.

Other places to check. Redirect rules on both the load balancer and the app doing conflicting things, like the load balancer redirecting HTTP to HTTPS and the app redirecting to a different host. Authentication redirects using the wrong scheme for callback URLs, which causes login loops. And cookies marked Secure not being sent when the app thinks the request is HTTP.
I'd say the other option is re-encrypting from the load balancer to the app, HTTPS end to end, which also satisfies stricter security requirements.

p17-977.q: Okay so, a matrix build runs the same job several times with different parameter combinations, in parallel. In GitHub Actions you define a strategy matrix, and in Azure Pipelines a strategy with a matrix of named configurations. Each combination becomes its own job with its own result.
p17-977.k: matrix build, matrix strategy github actions, azure pipelines matrix, test multiple versions, parallel jobs
x: Okay so, a matrix build runs the same job several times with different parameter combinations, in parallel. In GitHub Actions you define a strategy matrix, and in Azure Pipelines a strategy with a matrix of named configurations. Each combination becomes its own job with its own result.

Typical uses are testing a library against several runtime versions, like Node 18, 20 and 22, or Python 3.10 to 3.12, building on Windows and Linux, or testing against different database versions. It's also handy for building lots of similar services or packages from one pipeline, where each matrix entry is one service.

Couple of things from practice. Be careful with fail-fast. Turning it off lets you see all the failing combinations instead of stopping at the first one. Use include and exclude to skip pointless combinations, so you don't end up with an exploding number of jobs. Cache dependencies per combination, keyed by the version, or caches will clash. And keep the matrix small for pull requests, with the full matrix running nightly or on main, because every entry costs agent minutes.

In practice, I used a matrix for our shared front-end npm packages, building and testing against two React versions while the shell migration was going on, because some sub-apps were still on the older one. It caught a breaking peer dependency issue before it reached any app. For services though, I prefer one pipeline per service triggered by path filters, rather than one big matrix that rebuilds everything.

p17-978.q: Hosted agents, Microsoft-hosted agents in Azure Pipelines or GitHub-hosted runners, are fresh virtual machines created per job and thrown away afterwards. Self-hosted agents are machines you run and maintain yourself.
p17-978.k: self hosted agent, hosted agent, self hosted runner, build agent choice, private network build agent
x: Hosted agents, Microsoft-hosted agents in Azure Pipelines or GitHub-hosted runners, are fresh virtual machines created per job and thrown away afterwards. Self-hosted agents are machines you run and maintain yourself.

Hosted agents are clean every time, so no leftover state between builds, no patching, and they scale without effort. The downsides are limited control over installed tools, no access to private networks unless you add extra setup, caches that have to be restored every time, and cost or time limits at scale.

Self-hosted agents make sense when builds need to reach private resources, like an on-prem database or an internal package feed, when you need special hardware or licensed tools, when on-disk caches make builds much faster, or when the whole server's on-premises anyway. The cost is operational. You patch them, secure them, and deal with disks filling up and state leaking between builds.

Security really matters with self-hosted agents. Never run untrusted pull requests from forks on them, because a malicious build can attack the network. Run the agent as a low-privilege account, isolate pools per environment so a test build can't deploy to production, and ideally use ephemeral agents, container-based or autoscaled VMs that get recreated after each job.

In our case, the on-prem Azure DevOps Server uses self-hosted agents, since deployments go to servers inside the network. We keep separate pools for build and for production deployment, and the production pool can only be used by approved release pipelines.

p17-979.q: Signing proves an image was built by your pipeline and hasn't been changed since. Without it, anyone with push access to a registry could swap an image, and the cluster would happily run it.
p17-979.k: image signing, cosign, sigstore, notation, verify image signature, admission policy signed images, sbom attestation
x: Signing proves an image was built by your pipeline and hasn't been changed since. Without it, anyone with push access to a registry could swap an image, and the cluster would happily run it.

The common tools are Cosign from the Sigstore project and Notation from the Notary project, which Azure Container Registry supports. The pipeline builds the image, pushes it, and signs it by its digest, not its tag, because tags can move. Signing can use a key held in a key vault, or keyless signing, where a short-lived certificate is tied to the pipeline's identity through OIDC.

Alongside the signature you can attach attestations, an SBOM listing every package in the image, and provenance saying which commit and pipeline built it. Those help a lot when a new vulnerability shows up and you need to know which images contain the affected package.

Verification happens at deploy time. In Kubernetes, an admission controller like Kyverno, Gatekeeper or the Ratify project checks every pod's image and rejects anything unsigned or signed by the wrong identity. Deployments should also reference images by digest, so what was verified is exactly what runs.

I'd roll it out gradually. Sign everything to begin with, then turn on verification in audit mode to find unsigned images, like third-party ones, and only then enforce. Base images from trusted publishers can be allowed by their own signatures. And it gives you a solid answer when security reviewers ask how you know production runs only what CI built.

p17-980.q: Conventional commits is basically a simple format for commit messages, a type, an optional scope, and a description. For example, feat for a new feature, fix for a bug fix, docs, refactor, test or chore, plus a breaking-change marker when something isn't backward compatible.
p17-980.k: conventional commits, automated changelog, release notes generation, semantic release, commit message convention
x: Conventional commits is basically a simple format for commit messages, a type, an optional scope, and a description. For example, feat for a new feature, fix for a bug fix, docs, refactor, test or chore, plus a breaking-change marker when something isn't backward compatible.

Because the messages are structured, tools can read them. semantic-release or release-please can work out the next version automatically. A fix bumps the patch, a feat bumps the minor, and a breaking change bumps the major. They also generate a changelog grouped by features and fixes, create a tag, and publish the package.

To make it reliable, you enforce the format. commitlint in a Git hook catches mistakes locally, and a pull request check validates the PR title if you squash merge, since that title becomes the commit on main. Linking each commit or PR to a work item lets the release notes include the ticket ids.
And honestly it pays off. Release notes stop being a manual job at the end of a sprint, versions are consistent, and consumers of shared packages can see breaking changes clearly.

We used this pattern for our shared front-end npm packages published to the Azure DevOps feed. The version and changelog came from the commits, so teams consuming a package knew whether an upgrade was safe. For the main application, though, release notes still need business language for the validation team, so the generated list is a starting point someone edits, not the final document.

p17-981.q: All three bring a branch's changes into main, but they give you different history.
p17-981.k: merge vs rebase, squash merge, git rebase, linear history, git merge strategies, pull request merge type
x: All three bring a branch's changes into main, but they give you different history.

A merge commit keeps every commit from the branch and adds a merge commit joining the two lines. It preserves exactly what happened, but history gets noisy with lots of small commits like "fix typo", and the graph gets hard to read.

Squash merge combines the whole branch into one commit on main. History becomes one commit per pull request, which is clean and easy to revert, since reverting a feature is just reverting one commit. You lose the individual commits, though they still exist in the pull request.

Rebase replays the branch's commits on top of main, so history stays linear without a merge commit. It keeps individual commits, which is nice if they're meaningful, but because it rewrites history you should never rebase a branch others are working on, and it means force-pushing your own branch.

For me, the default for short-lived feature branches is squash merge, with the pull request title written as a good commit message, since that also works with conventional commits and changelogs. For long-lived release branches, I use real merges so the relationship between branches stays visible. Locally I use rebase to update my feature branch from main before opening a pull request, because it gives reviewers a cleaner diff.
Whatever the team picks, it should be set in branch policies so it's consistent, not left to each person.

p17-982.q: Deployment rings release a change to progressively bigger groups of users, with a pause and a health check between each group. It's how large products avoid exposing everyone to a bad release at once.
p17-982.k: deployment rings, ring based deployment, staged rollout, progressive exposure, early adopters ring
x: Deployment rings release a change to progressively bigger groups of users, with a pause and a health check between each group. It's how large products avoid exposing everyone to a bad release at once.

A typical setup has ring zero for the internal team, ring one for a small set of friendly customers or one region, ring two for a larger share, and then everyone. Each ring has a bake time, and the pipeline only moves forward if error rates, latency and business metrics stay normal. If something goes wrong, only that ring's affected, and you stop or roll back.

Rings differ from canary releases mainly in what you divide. A canary usually splits traffic randomly by percentage, while rings divide by meaningful groups like tenants, regions or customer types. In multi-tenant systems rings fit really naturally, because you can upgrade tenants or databases in batches.

To do it well, automate the gates, so promotion depends on metrics and not on someone remembering to check. Keep ring membership in configuration, make the code work with mixed versions, and keep database changes backward compatible.

In our platform, each study has its own database, so schema and data changes naturally roll out in batches. We start with internal and test studies, then low-risk studies, then the rest, with checks after each batch. A problem caught in the first batch affects a handful of non-critical databases instead of every live study.

p17-983.q: A dark launch, you know, deploys new code to production and runs it with real traffic, but users don't see its results. Shadow traffic, or traffic mirroring, is a common way to do it. Each real request goes to the current version as normal, and a copy goes to the new version, whose response just gets thrown away.
p17-983.k: dark launch, shadow traffic, traffic mirroring, test in production safely, mirror requests
x: A dark launch, you know, deploys new code to production and runs it with real traffic, but users don't see its results. Shadow traffic, or traffic mirroring, is a common way to do it. Each real request goes to the current version as normal, and a copy goes to the new version, whose response just gets thrown away.

The point is testing with real production load and real data shapes, which test environments never fully reproduce. You can compare the new version's results with the old one's, watch its latency and errors, and find performance problems before switching anyone over.

You can do it at different levels. A service mesh or proxy like Istio or Envoy can mirror a percentage of requests. In code, you can call both implementations, return the old result, and log the differences, which is the approach libraries like Scientist take.

The big risk is side effects. A shadow request must not write to the real database, charge a card or send an email twice. So shadowing works best for read paths, or the new version writes to a separate store, or calls go out with a dry-run flag.

I'd use it when replacing a critical read path, like a new search or a new calculation engine. For example, when moving a data transfer from the old integration layer to a new .NET API, running both and comparing outputs for a while gives confidence the new one produces identical results before it becomes the real path.

p17-984.q: Inconsistent environments give you the classic problem, it works in test but fails in production. What I aim for is environments that differ only in size and configuration, not in how they're built.
p17-984.k: environment parity, dev prod parity, environment drift, consistent environments, it works on my machine
x: Inconsistent environments give you the classic problem, it works in test but fails in production. What I aim for is environments that differ only in size and configuration, not in how they're built.

The biggest tool is infrastructure as code. If every environment comes from the same Terraform or Bicep modules with different variables, they can't quietly drift apart, and drift detection in the pipeline catches manual changes.

Then building once and promoting the same artifact, so test and production run identical binaries or images. Configuration comes from the environment through settings and secret stores, never baked into the build.

Matching dependency versions matters too. Same database engine version, same runtime, same message broker version. Containers and Docker Compose help locally, so a developer runs the same Redis and broker versions as production.

Data's the hard part, honestly. Test databases are often small and clean, so performance problems and odd data only show up in production. Masked copies of production data, or generated data at realistic volume, close that gap.
And the deployment process itself should be the same everywhere. If test is deployed by hand and production by pipeline, you're not really testing the deployment.

In our on-prem setup, we keep a server configuration baseline and compare IIS settings, installed runtimes and app pool settings across environments. A runtime version mismatch on one production node once caused a failure that test never showed, which is exactly why we added that check.

p17-985.q: A pull request build runs code someone else wrote, including the build scripts themselves. If that build has access to secrets or a privileged agent, a malicious pull request can steal credentials or attack your network. It's called poisoned pipeline execution.
p17-985.k: pipeline security fork pull request, pull_request_target, untrusted code ci, poisoned pipeline execution, secrets in pr builds
x: A pull request build runs code someone else wrote, including the build scripts themselves. If that build has access to secrets or a privileged agent, a malicious pull request can steal credentials or attack your network. It's called poisoned pipeline execution.

The main defences are basically about separation. Pull request builds from forks must run without secrets and with a read-only token. In GitHub Actions, the pull request event does this by default, while pull request target runs with secrets in the base repo's context, so it must never check out and run the pull request's code. That one catches people out. In Azure Pipelines, settings control whether fork builds get secrets, and that should stay off.
Run untrusted builds on hosted, throwaway agents, not self-hosted agents inside the network. And require approval before running workflows from first-time contributors.

Protect the pipeline definitions too. Changes to workflow files or templates should need review from owners, using a code owners file, and deployment pipelines should come from protected templates a pull request can't modify.

Keep deployment credentials scoped to protected environments with approvals, so even a compromised build job on a branch can't deploy to production. Pin third-party actions to a commit hash, since a tag can be moved to malicious code.

For internal repos the threat's lower, but the same rules help against a compromised developer account. Secrets live in environments with approvals, not in the pipeline used for pull request validation.

p17-986.q: Promotion means the exact image tested in one environment is the one that goes to the next, never a rebuild. With containers, that means moving or re-tagging the same digest.
p17-986.k: image promotion, promote container image, copy image between registries, acr import, ecr replication, registry per environment
x: Promotion means the exact image tested in one environment is the one that goes to the next, never a rebuild. With containers, that means moving or re-tagging the same digest.

You'll usually see two setups. With one registry, you promote by adding tags or by updating the deployment to the tested digest. It's simple, but production pulls from a registry that test pipelines can also push to.

With a registry per environment or per trust level, say a dev registry and a production registry, you copy the image across after it passes testing. Azure Container Registry has an import command that copies by digest between registries, ECR supports cross-account replication, and tools like crane or skopeo copy images without pulling them locally. Production clusters only get pull access to the production registry, and only the release pipeline can push to it.

Important details. Always copy and deploy by digest, because a tag like the version number could get overwritten. Copy signatures and SBOMs along with the image so verification still works. Run a vulnerability scan at promotion time too, since new vulnerabilities show up after build. And keep a record of which digest went to which environment, for traceability.

For anything regulated, I'd go with the separate production registry. It gives a clear boundary, if an image is in the production registry, it passed the gates. The extra copy step takes a few seconds and adds a lot of confidence.

p17-987.q: For serverless on AWS, the app and its infrastructure usually deploy together, because a Lambda function, its API Gateway route, its queue and its permissions all belong to the same unit. SAM and CDK both produce CloudFormation, which does the actual deployment.
p17-987.k: sam pipeline, cdk pipelines, deploy lambda ci cd, serverless deployment pipeline, cloudformation deploy lambda
x: For serverless on AWS, the app and its infrastructure usually deploy together, because a Lambda function, its API Gateway route, its queue and its permissions all belong to the same unit. SAM and CDK both produce CloudFormation, which does the actual deployment.

With SAM, the pipeline runs sam build to package the functions, runs unit tests, and then sam deploy with a parameter file per environment. SAM can also set up gradual deployment for Lambda through CodeDeploy, shifting traffic to the new version over a few minutes and rolling back automatically if CloudWatch alarms fire.

With CDK, you write infrastructure in a programming language like TypeScript or C#. The pipeline runs cdk synth to produce templates, which become the artifact, and then deploys those same templates to each environment. CDK Pipelines can model the stages and approvals itself, and cdk diff shows what'll change, which is handy in a pull request.

The general practices don't change. Build once and deploy the same package to every stage. Deploy with a role assumed through OIDC, not stored keys. Separate accounts per environment. Run integration tests against the deployed stack in a test stage before promotion. And watch for changes that replace resources, like renaming a table, which CloudFormation does by deleting and recreating. That one can really bite people.
For a small team, I think SAM is quicker to learn. For larger systems with shared constructs, CDK gives better reuse and type checking.

p17-988.q: A Python pipeline should check quality quickly and produce one reproducible artifact, usually a container image or a wheel.
p17-988.k: python ci pipeline, python lint test pipeline, ruff mypy pytest ci, python build pipeline, python docker pipeline
x: A Python pipeline should check quality quickly and produce one reproducible artifact, usually a container image or a wheel.

The way I set it up, it starts with the exact Python version and installs dependencies from a lock file, using uv or pip with hashes, with the package cache saved between runs. Then linting and formatting checks with Ruff, which replaces flake8, isort and black and is really fast. Then type checking with mypy or pyright, which matters in a dynamic language. Then tests with pytest, with coverage reporting and integration tests that use Testcontainers or service containers for Postgres or Redis.
Security checks come next, pip-audit for vulnerable packages, a secret scan, and bandit for risky code patterns.

Then the build. For a service, I build a Docker image with a multi-stage Dockerfile, installing dependencies in a builder stage and copying only what's needed into a slim runtime image that runs as non-root. For a library, I build a wheel and publish it to an internal feed.
After that, tag the image with the commit and version, scan it, push it, and deploy through the same promotion flow as other services.

For our Python RAG service with FastAPI and pgvector, the integration tests run against a real Postgres container with the pgvector extension, because mocking vector search wouldn't prove the queries actually work. The whole pipeline runs in a few minutes, mostly thanks to caching and Ruff's speed.

p17-989.q: Git hooks are scripts that run at points like before a commit or before a push. Pre-commit hooks catch simple problems, formatting, lint errors, committed secrets, before code ever reaches the pull request.
p17-989.k: pre commit hooks, husky, lint-staged, pre-commit framework, git hooks, shift left checks
x: Git hooks are scripts that run at points like before a commit or before a push. Pre-commit hooks catch simple problems, formatting, lint errors, committed secrets, before code ever reaches the pull request.

In JavaScript projects, Husky installs the hooks automatically when someone runs npm install, and lint-staged runs tools only on the files being committed, so it stays fast. A typical setup runs Prettier and ESLint on staged files and commitlint on the commit message.

In Python and lots of other stacks, the pre-commit framework manages hooks from a config file, with hooks for Ruff, trailing whitespace, large files, and secret scanning with tools like gitleaks. It works for any language, so it's a good pick for repos mixing Python, YAML and Terraform.
In .NET, dotnet format can run in a hook, or with Husky.Net.

My rules are pretty simple. Keep hooks fast, a few seconds, or people will just skip them with the no-verify flag. Hooks are a convenience, not a control, because anyone can bypass them, so the pipeline must run the same checks. And don't run the full test suite in a pre-commit hook. At most, quick tests in a pre-push hook.

In our front-end repos, Husky with lint-staged catches most formatting and lint issues locally, so pull request reviews focus on design instead of style comments. Secret scanning in the hook has stopped a few accidental commits of local config files before they left a laptop.

p17-990.q: Python's unittest mock gives you Mock and MagicMock objects that record how they're called and return whatever you set up. patch temporarily replaces an object during a test, as a decorator or a context manager, and the pytest-mock plugin offers the same thing through a mocker fixture.
p17-990.k: python mock, unittest.mock, patch where it is used, MagicMock, pytest monkeypatch, mocker fixture
x: Python's unittest mock gives you Mock and MagicMock objects that record how they're called and return whatever you set up. patch temporarily replaces an object during a test, as a decorator or a context manager, and the pytest-mock plugin offers the same thing through a mocker fixture.

The rule that trips most people is, patch where it's used, not where it's defined. If my module does from services import send email, the name send email now lives in my module, so I have to patch it on my module. Patching it on services won't touch the copy my module already imported. Trust me, everyone hits this once.

Other useful points. Use autospec, or create autospec, so the mock has the real function's signature. Otherwise a typo in a method name or wrong arguments still pass silently. For async functions, AsyncMock returns awaitables. Use side effect to raise exceptions or return a sequence of values, which is how I test retry logic. Assert calls with assert called once with, but don't over-assert every internal call, or tests break on harmless refactors.
pytest's monkeypatch is simpler for environment variables and attributes, and it undoes changes automatically.

Design matters more than tooling, though. If a test needs five patches, the code probably has hidden dependencies. Passing dependencies in, like through FastAPI's Depends with dependency overrides in tests, is cleaner than patching module globals. In our FastAPI RAG service, tests override the embedding client dependency with a fake, so no test calls a real model endpoint.

p17-991.q: Marble testing describes observable streams as little text diagrams, where each character is a frame of virtual time. A letter is an emitted value, a dash is time passing, a pipe is completion and a hash is an error. RxJS's TestScheduler runs the test in virtual time, so operators like debounceTime or delay finish instantly instead of actually waiting.
p17-991.k: marble testing, rxjs testing, TestScheduler, cold hot observables test, test debounceTime
x: Marble testing describes observable streams as little text diagrams, where each character is a frame of virtual time. A letter is an emitted value, a dash is time passing, a pipe is completion and a hash is an error. RxJS's TestScheduler runs the test in virtual time, so operators like debounceTime or delay finish instantly instead of actually waiting.

Inside the test scheduler's run, you create cold observables from marble strings, apply your operator chain, and use expectObservable to compare the result with an expected marble diagram and a values map. You can also write time explicitly, like 300 milliseconds, which makes debounce tests readable.

It's most useful for custom operators and complex chains, like a type-ahead search that debounces, ignores duplicates, cancels old requests with switchMap and handles errors. Testing that with real timers is slow and flaky, with marbles it's precise and deterministic. You can also check subscription timing with expectSubscriptions, which proves an old request really got unsubscribed.
For simpler cases, like a service method that just maps an HTTP response, honestly marbles are overkill. Subscribing and checking the value, or using firstValueFrom with an async test, is clearer.

In our Angular study builder, the search-and-filter panel used a chain of debounce, distinct and switchMap. Marble tests caught a bug where an error from one search killed the stream permanently, so later searches did nothing. Adding catchError inside the switchMap fixed it, and the marble test now guards that behaviour.

p17-992.q: xUnit creates a new instance of the test class for every test method, so the constructor is your per-test setup and Dispose is the teardown. That isolation's good, but expensive setup, like starting a database container, shouldn't run for every single test.
p17-992.k: xunit fixtures, IClassFixture, ICollectionFixture, xunit parallel, test collections, shared context xunit
x: xUnit creates a new instance of the test class for every test method, so the constructor is your per-test setup and Dispose is the teardown. That isolation's good, but expensive setup, like starting a database container, shouldn't run for every single test.

Fixtures solve that. A class fixture creates one shared object for all tests in a class, passed into the constructor. A collection fixture shares one object across several classes that belong to the same named collection. For async setup, the fixture implements IAsyncLifetime, with an async initialise and an async dispose. A typical example is a WebApplicationFactory or a Testcontainers database shared by all integration test classes in one collection.

Parallelism follows collections. By default each test class is its own collection, and collections run in parallel, while tests inside one collection run one after another. So putting classes in the same collection to share a fixture also makes them run sequentially, which is usually what you want for tests sharing a database. People mix this up quite often.

Things to watch. Shared fixtures mustn't hold state that tests change, or test order starts to matter. Static state breaks parallel runs. And you can tune parallelism with a runner config file, or turn it off for a specific collection.

In our integration tests, one collection fixture starts a SQL Server container and applies the schema once. Each test then runs inside a transaction that gets rolled back, so tests stay independent and the whole suite runs in a couple of minutes.

p17-993.q: pytest doesn't run coroutines by itself, so async tests need a plugin. pytest-asyncio is the common one. You mark a test with the asyncio marker, or set asyncio mode to auto in config, and the plugin runs it in an event loop. The anyio plugin's an alternative and also supports trio.
p17-993.k: pytest asyncio, test async python, async fixtures pytest, anyio pytest, test fastapi async
x: pytest doesn't run coroutines by itself, so async tests need a plugin. pytest-asyncio is the common one. You mark a test with the asyncio marker, or set asyncio mode to auto in config, and the plugin runs it in an event loop. The anyio plugin's an alternative and also supports trio.

Fixtures can be async too. An async fixture with yield can open a database connection or an HTTP client before the test and close it afterwards. Fixture scope matters here. A session-scoped async fixture needs an event loop that lives for the whole session, and newer pytest-asyncio versions let you set the loop scope explicitly, because mismatched loop scopes cause really confusing errors about the loop being closed or attached to a different loop.
For FastAPI, I use httpx's AsyncClient with an ASGI transport pointed at the app, which calls the app in-process without a real server. Dependency overrides swap real clients for fakes.
To mock async functions, use AsyncMock, so awaiting the mock works. For timing behaviour, keep timeouts small in tests and avoid real sleeps. Inject a clock or patch the sleep function.

One thing people miss is calling an async function without awaiting it, which creates a coroutine that never runs, so the test passes without testing anything. Turning warnings into errors in pytest config catches the never-awaited warning.
In our RAG service, async tests cover the retrieval endpoint against a real Postgres container, with the embedding call replaced by a deterministic fake.

p17-994.q: Code that calls AWS services, S3, SQS or DynamoDB, is a pain to test against real AWS. It's slow, costs money and needs credentials. Two tools help here.
p17-994.k: localstack, moto, test aws locally, mock aws services, s3 sqs local testing, aws integration tests
x: Code that calls AWS services, S3, SQS or DynamoDB, is a pain to test against real AWS. It's slow, costs money and needs credentials. Two tools help here.

moto is a Python library that mocks AWS APIs in memory. With a decorator or context manager, boto3 calls go to moto instead of AWS, so you can create a bucket, put an object and test your code's behaviour in milliseconds. It's ideal for unit tests of Python code.

LocalStack runs emulated AWS services in a Docker container with real HTTP endpoints. Any SDK, including .NET and Node, can point at it by overriding the service URL. It's better for integration tests and local development, and it works with Testcontainers, so each test run gets a fresh instance.

The catch is fidelity. Emulators don't perfectly copy AWS behaviour, especially IAM permissions, limits and edge cases, and some services are paid-only in LocalStack. So code can pass locally and still fail in AWS because of a missing permission. I still run a small set of smoke tests against a real test account after deployment.
Make the endpoint configurable rather than writing special code paths for testing. In .NET, the AWS SDK's service URL setting can be overridden through configuration in the test environment.

For one of IQVIA's newer services storing files in S3 and processing them through SQS, LocalStack in Testcontainers let us test the whole upload, event and processing flow in CI, and I'd say it caught a message format bug that unit tests with mocks never would have.

p17-995.q: Azure has local emulators for several services, so integration tests can run in CI without real cloud resources.
p17-995.k: azurite, azure storage emulator, cosmos db emulator, service bus emulator, test azure locally, azure integration tests
x: Azure has local emulators for several services, so integration tests can run in CI without real cloud resources.

Azurite emulates Azure Storage, blobs, queues and tables. It runs as a Docker container or an npm package, and the SDK connects with the well-known development connection string. It's good for testing file uploads, blob triggers in Azure Functions, and queue processing.
The Cosmos DB emulator runs locally, including a Linux container version, and supports the main APIs, which is useful for testing queries and partition key design.

The Service Bus emulator, which came out more recently, runs in Docker with a config file that defines queues and topics, so you can test sessions, dead-lettering and message handling without a namespace in Azure. Event Hubs has an emulator as well.
For Azure Functions, Core Tools run functions locally against these emulators. Testcontainers has modules for Azurite, Cosmos and Service Bus, so each test run gets clean instances automatically.

The limitations are like any emulator, you know. Authentication's simplified, so managed identity and RBAC aren't tested, performance and throttling differ, and some features are missing. So I keep connection settings configurable, run most tests against emulators, and run a few smoke tests against a real test subscription after deployment, which is where permission problems actually show up.
In a team learning Azure, emulators also make onboarding easier, because a developer can run the whole system locally on day one without waiting for cloud access.

p17-996.q: So fuzz testing sends huge numbers of unexpected, random or malformed inputs to a system to find crashes and unhandled cases. Normal tests check the inputs you thought of, fuzzing finds the ones you didn't.
p17-996.k: fuzz testing, api fuzzing, schemathesis, property based api testing, openapi fuzz, restler
x: So fuzz testing sends huge numbers of unexpected, random or malformed inputs to a system to find crashes and unhandled cases. Normal tests check the inputs you thought of, fuzzing finds the ones you didn't.

For APIs, schema-based fuzzers are the practical option. Schemathesis reads your OpenAPI spec and generates requests covering each endpoint with valid and edge-case values, empty strings, huge numbers, unicode, missing optional fields, boundary dates.
